In the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Academy of Sciences, there were 20 eleves; and in that of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>, 10 eleves. The eleves are to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> with the pensionaries. See Academy. The denomination eleve, however, has been since suppressed, and that of adjoint substituted in its room; because every body did not know the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> affixed to it by the academy; and now the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENSIONARY">pensionary</a> academists have not, as formerly, each of them an eleve; but the eleves are become adjoints, or associates of the academy.

ELGIN

Pages 31-31

the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Moray in Scotland, and formerly a bishop's see, is situated on the river Lossie, about six miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> from the Spey, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 25. N. Lat. 57. 40. Mr Pennant says, it is a good town, and has many of the houses built over piazzas; but, excepting its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> cattle-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>, has little trade. It is principally remarkable for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> antiquities. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, now in ruins, has been formerly a very magnificent pile. The west door is very elegant and richly ornamented. The choir is very beautiful, and has a fine and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> gallery running round it; and at the east end are two rows of narrow windows in an excellent Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> is an octagon; the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> supported by a fine single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>, with neat carvings of coats of arms round the capital. There is still a great tower on each side of this cathedral; but that in the centre, with the spire and whole roof, are fallen in; and form most awful fragments, mixed with the battered monuments of knights and prelates. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOETHIUS">Boethius</a> says, that Duncan, who was killed by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MACBETH">Macbeth</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERNESS">Inverness</a>, lies buried here. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is also crowded with a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. The cathedral was founded by Andrew de Moray, in 1224, on a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> granted by Alexander II.; and his remains were deposited in the choir, under a tomb of blue marble, in 1244. The great tower was built principally by John Innes bishop of this see, as appears by the inscription cut on one of the great pillars: "Hic Jacet in Xto, pater et dominus, Dominus Johannes de Innes, hujus ecclesiae Episcopus,—qui hoc notabile opus incepit et per septennium edificavit." Elgin is a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> borough. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> of the town and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> 4602.

ELGINSHIRE

Pages 31-31

is the middle district of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Moray. It is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by that branch of the German ocean called the Moray Frith; on the east and south-east by Banffshire; on the south-west, by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-INVERNESS_SHIRE"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol11.html#article-INVERNESS">Inverness</a>-shire; and on the west by the counties of Inverness and Nairn. It extends about 42 miles in length, and its <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> breadth is about 20. The southern <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> is rocky and mountainous, called the district of Braemaray, which is occupied with extensive

ELI

Pages 31-32
high priest of the Israelites, and judge over them for forty years, was descended from Ithamar, a junior branch of the house of Aaron, and seems to have blended the priestly with the judicial character in the year 1156 before the commencement of the Christian era. It appears that the Jews were in a state of subjection or vassalage to the Philistines during the greater part of Eli's administration, and, what may at first appear singular, he contributed to the degeneracy of his countrymen, although his own piety and goodness were unquestionably great. He did not exert his magisterial authority in the exemplary punishment of vice, and even permitted his own sons with impunity to perpetrate the most atrocious acts of impiety and debauchery. This want of firmness, to give it no worse a name, was very reprehensible in one who filled such an important office, and peculiarly so in a man who was himself a saint. The celebrated Samson made his appearance during the administration of Eli, taking part in the management of public affairs for about 20 years, by whose astonishing deeds the independent spirit of that people was in some measure revived. The circumstances attending the death of Samson, which proved so calamitous to the nobility of the Philistines, might have induced the Jews to throw off the yoke; but they did not possess a sufficient degree of virtue and public spirit for such an exertion. Eli at this period was very far advanced in years, and, if possible, still more negligent in the discharge of his duty as a chief magistrate, allowing his two sons, Hophni and Phineas, to proceed to the most extravagant height of impiety and debauchery, whose example had a most powerful influence on the manners of the people. He was far from being unacquainted with their conduct, but he reproved them with such gentleness as was highly reprehensible, and but ill calculated to produce any change on the behaviour of his sons. The deity was so justly offended with this deportment of Eli, that a sacred seer was commissioned to upbraid him for his ingratitude and want of resolution. Young Samuel likewise was favoured with a vision of the approaching ruin of Eli's family, which he related to the otherwise venerable old man, on being solemnly adjured not to conceal a single circumstance. When Eli heard the declaration of the young prophet, being fully convinced that his conduct had been highly reprehensible, he exclaimed, "It is the Lord; let him do what seemeth him good." Soon after this the Israelites sustained a considerable loss in attempting to procure their emancipation, carrying the ark of God into their camp to animate the people, and intimidate their enemies; but the ark was captured by the Philistines, and Hophni and Phineas were slain. This intelligence having been brought to Eli, he no sooner heard that the ark of God was taken, than he fell backwards from his seat, broke his neck, and died in the 98th year of his age.

ELIAS

Pages 32-32

the prophet, memorable for having escaped the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> catastrophe of mankind; being taken up alive into heaven, in a fiery chariot, about 895 B.C. See the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>.

ELIJAH

Pages 32-33

who is sometimes denominated Elias, was one of the most distinguished of the Jewish prophets, and surnamed the Tishbite, probably from the district in which he was born. He began his prophetic office about 920 years before Christ, in the reign of wicked Ahab, by whom the Sidenian idolatry was introduced among the Israelites. The prophet was commissioned to appear before this impious <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, and threaten the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> drought as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> for his crimes. The indignation of Ahab was so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> against the prophet for this prediction, that he resolved to punish him in a signal manner; but Elijah withdrew to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELI">ELI</a> Elijah a secret <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> from his fury, at the divine command, where he was sustained in a miraculous manner. He was afterwards ordered to go to Sarepta, in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SIDON">Sidon</a>, where a miraculous interposition of heaven, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of an indigent widow, sustained him for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, whose son the prophet restored to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. When the three years of famine, occasioned by the drought, were expired, the prophet was ordered to appear before the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, and exhort him to that genuine <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a> which an interposition of the deity so very remarkable unquestionably demanded. He had an interview with Obadiah, the governor of the king's house, who was a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and had frequently screened many from the vengeance of Jezebel the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, at the hazard of his own life. Fired with undaunted fortitude, the prophet said to Obadiah, "Go, tell thy <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, behold Elijah is here." The good man's regard for the prophet was so great, that he was afraid to deliver this message, since he knew that Ahab had used every effort to discover the prophet's retreat. The king was informed of his coming; and the first interview was distinguished by invectives on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the intrepid prophet and the proud sovereign, the former giving a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> on the following terms. The priests of the Sidonian gods, and an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the people of Israel, were to meet on Mount Carmel, where the prophet Elijah intended to give an incontestable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the almighty power of the God of Israel, and the total insignificance of the Sidonian divinities. For a detailed account of this memorable experiment, we must refer our readers to the book of Kings, as an abridgement of such a beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARRATION">narration</a> would do it manifest injury. It produced the fullest conviction in the minds of the Israelites, that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JEHOVAH">Jehovah</a> alone was entitled to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a>; and the priests of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAAL">Baal</a> were instantaneously put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, as the most abominable perverters of the divine <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>. This was followed by abundance of rain, in answer to the devout prayers of the prophet; but his glorious triumph over idolatry so exasperated Jezebel, that she resolved to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> the prophet, to avoid whose rage he fled into the wilderness, till the deity again employed him in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a>, but often hazardous, duties of a prophet. He afterwards foretold that Hazael should be king of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, Jehu king over Israel; and he appointed Elisha the son of Shaphat to be his own successor. He denounced dreadful judgments against Ahab and his wicked queen Jezebel; but those which respected the king were not executed during his life, on account of the genuine repentance which he discovered. The successor of Ahab having been confined to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of an accident, the god of Ekron was consulted relative to his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a>, which induced the prophet to declare that he should assuredly die. The king being informed that it was Elijah who dared to send such a message, he dispatched a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> and 50 men to force him into the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> presence; but they were destroyed by fire from heaven, and a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> shared the same fate. A third company confessed the visible interference of heaven in the prophet's behalf, and the captain throwing himself on the mercy of Elijah, went with him to the king. In the royal presence he undoubtedly repeated the same denunciation against the idolatrous monarch, which was very soon accomplished; and not long after this the holy prophet, at the divine command, divided asunder the waves of Jordan, dropped his prophetic mantle to the astonished Elisha, took the flaming chariot commissioned for his reception, and rode in majesty to heaven.

ELIQUATION

Pages 33-33

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, an operation by which a more fusible substance is separated from one that is less so, by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> sufficiently intense to melt the former, but not the latter. Thus an alloy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> may be separated by a heat capable of melting the latter, but not the former. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIS">ELIS</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELEA">ELEA</a>.

ELIS

Pages 33-34

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the district of that name in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>, situated on the Peneus, which ran through it. It was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Phaido the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, scholar of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>, and friend of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>; who inscribes with his name the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a> on the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>. Pyrrho also was of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, at the head of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> called after him Pyrrhonists. The city of Elis owed its origin to an union of small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> after the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. It was not encompassed immediately with a wall; for it had the care of the temple at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OLYMPIA">Olympia</a>, and its territory was solemnly consecrated to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>. To invade <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> not protect it was deemed impiety; and armies, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> marching through, delivered up their weapons, which, on their quitting it, were restored. Amid warring states the city enjoyed repose, was resorted to by strangers, and flourished. The region round about it was called ecode or hollow, from the inequalities. The country was reckoned fertile, and particularly fit for the raising of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>. This, which grew nowhere else in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, equalled the produce of Judaea in fineness, but was not so <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>. Elis was a school, as it were, for Olympia, which was distant 37 miles. The athletic exercises were performed there, before the more solemn <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, in a gymnasium, by which the Peneus ran. The helanodics or prefects of the games paired the rival combatants by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a>, in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> called Plethrum or The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">Acre</a>. Within the wall grew lofty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> trees; and in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, which was called the Agystes, were separate courses made for the foot races. A smaller court was called the Quadrangle. The prefects, when chosen, resided for ten months in a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> erected for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, to be instructed in the duties of their office. They attended before sunrise to preside at the races; and again at noon, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> appointed for the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENTATHLON">pentathlon</a> or five sports. The horses were trained in the agora or market-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, which was called the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HIPPODROME">Hippodrome</a>. In the gymnasium were altars and a cenotaph of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a>. The women, besides other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> their bosoms in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>, on a fixed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> towards sunset. There also was the town-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, in which extemporary harangues were spoken and compositions recited. It was hung round with bucklers for ornaments. A way led from it to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> through the Street of Silence; and another to the market-place, which was planned with streets between porticoes of the Doric order adorned with altars and images. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, one had a circular peristyle or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLONNADE">colonnade</a>; but the image had been removed and the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> was fallen in the time of Pausanias. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> was ancient, as was also a temple of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, one of the deities principally adored at Elis. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a> had a temple in the citadel, with an image of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, made <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELI">ELI</a> (it was said) by Phidias. At the gate leading to Olympia was the monument of a person, who was buried, as an oracle had commanded, neither within nor without the city. The structures of Elis, Dr Chandler observes, seem to have been raised with materials far less elegant and durable than the produce of the Iosian and Attic quarries. The ruins are of brick, and not considerable, consisting of pieces of ordinary wall, and an octagon building with niches, which, it is supposed, was the temple, with a circular peristyle. These stand detached from each other, ranging in a vale southward from the wide <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> of the river Peneus; which, by the margin, has several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, perhaps relics of the gymnasium. The citadel was on a hill, which has on the top some remnants of a wall. ELISHA the prophet, famous for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> he performed, died about 830 B.C. See the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>.

ELISION

Pages 34-34

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> suppressing a vowel at the end of a word, for the sake of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, the next word beginning with a vowel. Elisions are pretty frequently met with in English <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, but more frequently in the Latin, French, &c. They chiefly consist in suppressions of the a, e, and i, though an elision suppresses any of the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOWELS">vowels</a>.

ELIXATION

Pages 34-34

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, the extracting the virtues of ingredients by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> stewing.

ELIXIR

Pages 34-34

in Medicine, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> tincture extracted from many efficacious ingredients. Hence the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between a tincture and an elixir seems to be this, that a tincture is drawn from one ingredient, sometimes with an addition of another to open it and to dispose it to yield to the menstruum; whereas an elixir is a tincture extracted from several ingredients at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>.

ELIZABETH

Pages 34-35
queen of England, daughter of Henry VIII. and Anne Boleyn, was born at Greenwich, September 7, 1533. According to the humour of the times, she was early instructed in the learned languages, first by Grindal, who died when she was about 17, and afterwards by the celebrated Roger Ascham. She acquired likewise considerable knowledge of the Italian, Spanish, and French languages. Dr Grindal was also her preceptor in divinity, which she is said to have studied with uncommon application and industry. That Elizabeth became a Protestant, and her sister Mary a Papist, was the effect of that cause which determines the religion of all mankind; namely, the opinion of those by whom they were educated: and this difference of opinion, in their tutors, is not at all surprising, when we recollect, that their father Harry was of both religions, or of neither. But the studies of Elizabeth were not confined merely to languages and theology: she was also instructed in the political history of the ancients; and was so well skilled in music, as to sing and play "artfully and sweetly." After the short reign of her brother Edward, our heroine being then about 20 years of age, her firebrand sister ascending to the crown, Elizabeth experienced a considerable degree of persecution, so as to be not a little apprehensive of a violent death. She was accused of nobody knows what; imprisoned; and, we are told, inhumanly treated. At last, by the intercession of King Philip of Spain, she was set at liberty; Elizabeth, which she continued to enjoy, till, on the death of her pious sister, she, on the 17th of November 1558, ascended the throne of England. Her political history as a queen, is universally known and admired; but her attention to the government of her kingdom did not totally suspend her pursuit of learning. Ascham, in his Schoolmaster, tells us, that, about the year 1563, five years after her accession, she being then at Windsor, besides her perfect readiness in Latin, Italian, French, and Spanish, she read more Greek in one day than some prebendaries of that church did read Latin in a whole week, (p. 21.)—She employed Sir John Fortescue to read to her Thucydides, Xenophon, Polybius, Euripides, Æschines, and Sophocles. (Ballard, p. 219.) That the Latin language was familiar to her, is evident from her speech to the university of Oxford, when she was near sixty; also from her spirited answer to the Popish ambassador in the year 1598. And that she was also skilled in the art of poetry, appears not only from the several scraps which have been preserved, but likewise from the testimony of a contemporary writer, Puttenham, in his Art of Engl. Poetry (a very scarce book). These are his words: "But, last in re- cital, and first in degree, is the queen, whose learn- ed, delicate, noble muse, easily surmounteth all the rest, for sense, sweetness, or subtlety, be it in ode, elegy, epigram, or any other kind of poem," &c. In this author are to be found only a specimen of 16 verses of her English poetry. "But," says Mr Walpole, "a greater instance of her genius, and that too in Latin, was her extempore reply to an insolent prohibition delivered to her from Philip II. by his ambassa- dor, in this tetrameter. Te veto ne pergas bello defendere Belgas: Quae Dracus eripuit, nunc restituantur oportet: Quos pater everit, jubeo te condere cellas: Religio pape fac restitutor ad unguel. "She instantly answered him, with as much spirit as she used to return his invasions; Ad Grecas, bone rex, fient mandata kalendas." Being earnestly pressed by a Romish priest, during his persecution, to declare her opinion concerning the real presence of Christ's body in the wafer, she answered, Christ was the word that spake it; He took the bread, and brake it: And what that word did make it, That I believe and take it.—Fuller's Holy State. She gave the characters of four knights of Nottinghamshire in the following distich: Gervase the Gentle, Stanhope the stout, Markham the lion, and Sutton the stout. Wap. Cat. Coming into a grammar-school, she characterized three classic authors in this hexameter: Persius a crab-staff; bawdy Martial; Ovid a fine wag. Full. Worth. of Warw. 126. Sir Sir Walter Raleigh having wrote on a window, Fain would I climb, yet fear I to fall; She immediately wrote under it, If thy heart fail thee, climb not at all. Worth of Devonshire, 261. Doubtless, she was a woman of singular capacity and extraordinary acquirements; and if we could forget the story of the Scottish Mary, and of her favourite Essex, together with the burning of a few Anabaptists; in short, could we forbear to contemplate her character through the medium of religion and morality, we might pronounce her the most illustrious of illustrious women. See further the articles ENGLAND, MARY, and SCOTLAND. She died in her palace at Richmond, the 24th of March 1602, aged 70, having reigned 44 years; and was interred in the chapel of Henry VII. in Westminster Abbey. Her successor James erected a magnificent monument to her memory.—She wrote, 1. The Mirror, or Glass of the Sinful Soul. This was translated out of French verse into English prose, when she was eleven years old. It was dedicated to Queen Catharine Parr. Probably it was never printed; but the dedication and preface are preserved in the Soliloquy epistolarium, in Hearne's edition of Livii Floridus Juliani, p. 161. 2. Prayers and Meditations, &c. Dedicated to her father, dated at Hatfield, 1545. Manuscript, in the royal library. 3. A Dialogue out of Xenophon, in Greek, between Hiero a King, yet some time a private person, and Simonides a Poet, as touching the life of the Prince and Private Man. First printed from a manuscript in her majesty's own handwriting, in the Gentleman's Magazine for 1743. 4. Two Orations of Isocrates, translated into Latin. 5. Latin Oration at Cambridge. Preserved in the king's library: also in Hollinshed's Chron. p. 1206.; and in Fuller's Hist. of Cambr. p. 138. 6. Latin Oration at Oxford. See Wood's Hist. and Antiq. of Oxf. lib. i. p. 289, also in Dr Jebb's Append. to his Life of Mary Queen of Scots. 7. A Comment on Plato. 8. Boethius de consolatione philosophiae, translated into English anno 1593. 9. Sallust de bello Jugurthino, translated into English anno 1592. 10. A play of Euripides, translated into Latin, (Cat. of Royal Auth.). 11. A Prayer for the use of her fleet in the great expedition in 1596. 12. Part of Horace's Art of Poetry, translated into English anno 1598. 13. Plutarch de curiositate, translated into English. 14. Letters on various occasions to different persons: several speeches to her parliament; and a number of other pieces.

ELIZABETH PETROWNA

Pages 35-35

(<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>), the last empress of Russia, distinguished herself by her signal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CLEMENCY">clemency</a>. She made a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOW">vow</a> that no person should be put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> in her reign, and she strictly observed it. The example was followed, and confirmed by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, under the august sovereign of Russia, Catherine II. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> died in 1762, in the 21st year of her reign and 52d of her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>.

ELL

Pages 35-35

(elna,) a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> which obtains, under different denominations, in most countries, whereby cloths, stuffs, linens, silks, &c. are usually measured; answering nearly to the yard of England, the canna of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, the vara of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, the palm of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, &c. Servius <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> have the ell to be the space contained between the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> when stretched forth; but Suetonius makes it only the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUBIT">cubit</a>. The ells most frequently used with us are the English and Flemish; the former containing three feet <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> inches, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> one yard and a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>; the latter only 27 inches, or three <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of a yard; so that the ell English is to the Flemish ell as five to three. In Scotland, the ell contains 37 1/10 English inches. M. Ricard, in his Treatise of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, reduces the ells thus: 100 ells of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> are equal to 98 1/2 of Brabant, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a>; to 58 1/2 of England and France; to 120 of Hamburgh, Frankfort, Leipzig, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a>; 125 of Breslaw; 110 of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERGEN">Bergen</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DRONTHEIM">Drontheim</a>; and 117 of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOCKHOLM">Stockholm</a>.

ELLIOT

Pages 35-36

the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">Right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">Honourable</a> George Augustus, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Heathfield, was the youngest son of the late Sir Gilbert Elliot, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARONET">Baronet</a>, of Stobbs (A) in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-ROXBURGHSHIRE">Roxburghshire</a>; and was born about the year 1718. He received the first <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> under a private <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a>; and at an early <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> was sent to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, where he made considerable progress in classical learning, and spoke with fluency and elegance the German and French languages. Being designed for a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> life, he was sent from thence to the celebrated Ecole Royale du Genie Militaire, conducted by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Vauban at La Fere in Picardy; where he laid the foundation of what he so conspicuously exhibited at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of Gibraltar. He completed his military course on the continent by a tour, for the purpose of seeing in practice what he had studied in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> was the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, and he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> some time as a volunteer in that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. Mr Elliot returned in the 17th year of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> to his native <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, Scotland; and was the same year, 1735, introduced by his father Sir Gilbert to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIEUTENANT">Lieutenant</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEERS">Peers</a> of the 23rd regiment of foot, then lying at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, as a youth anxious to bear arms for (A) The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and honourable family of Elliot of Stobbs, as well as the collateral branch of Elliot of Minto in the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, and of Elliot of Port-Elliot in Cornwall, are originally from Normandy. Their ancestor, Mr Aliott, came over with William the Conqueror, and held a distinguished <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. There is a traditional anecdote in the family relating to an honourable distinction in their coat, which, as it corresponds with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, bears the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. When William set foot on English <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, he slipped and fell on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. He sprung up, and exclaimed that it was a happy <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OMEN">omen</a>—he had embraced the country of which he was to become the lord. Upon this Aliott drew his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, and swore by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of a soldier, that he would maintain, at the hazard of his blood, the right of his lord to the sovereignty of the earth which he had embraced. On the event of his conquest, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> William added to the arms of Aliott, which was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATON">baton</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, on a field azure, an arm and sword as a crest, with the motto, Per saxa, per ignes, fortiter et recte... for his king and country. He was accordingly entered as a volunteer in that regiment, where he continued for a year or more. From the 23d regiment he went into the engineer corps at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOLWICH">Woolwich</a>, and made great progress in that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, until his uncle Colonel Elliot brought him in his adjutant of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> troop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> grenadiers. With these troops he went upon service to Germany, and was with them in a variety of actions. At the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Dettingen he was wounded. In this regiment he bought the rank of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>, and afterwards purchased the lieutenant-colonelcy from Colonel Brewerton, who succeeded to his uncle. On arriving at this rank, he resigned his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> as an engineer, which he had enjoyed along with his other rank, and in which service he had been actively employed very much to the advantage of his country. He received the instructions of the famous engineer Bellidor, and made himself completely <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the science of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUNNERY">gunnery</a>. Had he not so disinterestedly resigned his rank in the engineer department, he would <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, by regular progression, have been at the head of that corps. Soon after this he was appointed aide-de-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> to George II. and was distinguished for his military skill and discipline. In the year 1759, he quitted the second troop of horse grenadier guards, being selected to raise, form, and discipline, the first regiment of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> horse, called after him Elliot's. As soon as they were raised and formed, he was appointed to the command of the cavalry in the expedition on the coasts of France, with the rank of brigadier-general. After this he passed into Germany, where he was employed on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>, and greatly distinguished himself in a variety of movements; where his regiment displayed a strictness of discipline, an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> and enterprise, which gained them signal honour: and indeed they have been the pattern regiment both in regard to discipline and appointment, to the many light dragoon troops that have been since raised in our service. From Germany he was recalled for the purpose of being employed as second in command in the memorable expedition against the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAVANNAH">Havannah</a>; the circumstances of which conquest are well known. On the peace, his gallant regiment was reviewed by the king, when they presented to his majesty the standards which they had taken from the enemy. Gratified with their fine discipline and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> character, the king asked General Elliot what mark of his favour he could bestow on his regiment equal to their merit? He answered that his regiment would be proud <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> his majesty should think, that, by their services, they were entitled to the distinction of Royals. It was accordingly made a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> regiment, with this flattering <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, "The 13th, or King's Royal Regiment of Light Dragoons." At the same time the king expressed a desire to confer some honour on the general himself; but the latter declared, that the honour and satisfaction of his majesty's approbation of his services was his best reward. During the peace he was not idle. His great talents in the various branches of the military art gave him ample employment. In the year 1775, he was appointed to succeed General A'<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">Court</a> as commander-in-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the forces in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>; but did not continue long in this station, not even long enough to unpack all his trunks; for finding that interferences were made by petty authority derogatory of his own, he resisted the practice with becoming spirit; and not choosing to disturb the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the sister <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> on a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> personal to himself, he solicited to be recalled. He accordingly was so, and appointed to the command of Gibraltar in a fortunate <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> for the safety of that important fortress. The system of his life, as well as his education, peculiarly qualified him for this trust. He was perhaps the most abstemious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of the age; neither indulging himself in animal food or wine. He never slept more than four hours at a time; so that he was up later and earlier than most other men. He so insured himself to habits of hardiness, that the things which are difficult and painful to other men, were to him his daily practice, and rendered pleasant by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. It could not be easy to starve such a man into a surrender, nor possible to surprise him. The example of the commander in chief in a besieged garrison has the most persuasive efficacy in forming the manners of a soldiery. Like him his brave followers came to regulate their lives by the most strict rules of discipline, before there arose a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> for so doing; and severe <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, with short diet, became habitual to them by their own choice. The military system of discipline which he introduced, and the preparations which he made for his defence, were contrived with so much judgment, and executed with so much <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, that he was able with a handful of men to preserve his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> against an attack, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a> of which, even without the vigour, had been sufficient to exhaust any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> set of men. Collected within himself, he in no instance destroyed, by premature attacks, the labours which would cost the enemy time, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a>, and expense to complete; he deliberately observed their approaches, and seized on the proper moment, with the keenest perception, in which to make his attack with success. He never spent his ammunition in useless parade or in unimportant attacks. He never relaxed from his discipline by the appearance of security, nor hazarded the lives of his garrison by wild experiments. By a cool and temperate demeanour, he maintained his station for three years of constant investment, in which all the powers of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> were employed. All the eyes of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> were on this garrison; and his conduct has justly exalted him to the most elevated rank in the military annals of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. On his return to England, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> of the British <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> was as forward as the public <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> in giving him that distinguished mark his merit deserved. Both houses of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> voted an unanimous address of thanks to the general. The king conferred on him the honour of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">Knight</a> of the Bath, with a pension during his own and a second life of his own appointment; and on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 14, 1787, his majesty advanced him to the peerage, by the title of Lord Heathfield, Baron Gibraltar, permitting him to take, in addition to his family arms, the arms of the fortress he had so bravely defended, to perpetuate to futurity his noble conduct. His lordship died on the 9th of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1790, at his chateau at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>-la-Chapelle, of a second stroke of the palsy, after having for some weeks preceding enjoyed tolerable good <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and an unusual flow of spirits. His death happened two days before he was to have set out for <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGHORN">Leghorn</a> on his way to Gibraltar; of which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> he was once more appointed to the defense,

ELLIPOPACHYSTYLA

Pages 37-37

an old <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, derived from the Greek, and expressing a crystal of the imperfect kind with a thick <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>.

ELLIPOPACROSTYLA

Pages 36-37

an old <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, from the Greek, imperfect, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>; which expresses an imperfect crystal with a long column.

ELLIPSIS

Pages 37-37

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, a curve line returning into itself, and produced from the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECTION">section</a> of a cone by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> both its sides, but not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the base. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONIC_SECTIONS">Conic Sections</a>.

ELLIPTIC

Pages 37-37
or ELLIPTICAL, something belonging to an ellipse. ELLIPTIC Turning, a method of giving a piece of wood an elliptic figure. See Supplement.

ELLISIA

Pages 37-37

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 28th order, Luridae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ELLISIS

Pages 37-37

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNTAX">syntax</a>, wherein one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more words are not expressed; and from this deficiency it has got the name <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELLIPSIS">ellipsis</a>.

ELLYS

Pages 37-37

Dr Anthony, who was born in 1693, and educated at Clarehall, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, after rising through many inferior degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of England, was, in 1752, promoted to the see of St <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a>'s. He died at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a> in 1761, and is mentioned here only for the sake of his works, which are less known than they should be in the present <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVEL">novel</a> opinions. They are, besides occasional sermons, 1. A <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">Plea</a> for the Sacramental Test, as a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> security to the Church established, and very conducive to the welfare of the State. 2. Remarks on Hume's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">Miracles</a>. 3. Tracts on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">Liberty</a> spiritual and temporal of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> in England, addressed to J. N. Esq. at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>-la-Chapelle; the first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of which was printed in 1763, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> in 1765. In these tracts, as the editors of them truly observe, he "discovers not only fine parts, extensive knowledge, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> judgment, but a heart overflowing with benevolence and candour, and a most Christian temper; for he always thought a person, though on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> side of the question, with principles of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>, to be a worse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> than he that was on the wrong." This amiable and respectable writer affords in his own conduct a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that a man may be steadily attached to a party, without wishing to encroach upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of others. ELM. See Ulmus, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ELMACINUS

Pages 37-37

GEORGE, author of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Saracens, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> towards the middle of the 13th century. His history comes <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from Mahomet to the year of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEGIRA">Hegira</a> 512, answering to the year of our <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> 1134; in which he sets down year by year, in a very concise manner, whatever regards the Saracen empire, intermixed with some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> relating to the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>. His abilities must have been considerable; since, though he professed Christianity, he held an office of trust near the persons of the Mahometan princes. He was son to Yaser Al Amid, secretary to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> under the Elmacinos sultans of Egypt for 45 years; and in 1238, when his father died, succeeded him in his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. His history Elphinston, of the Saracens was translated from Arabic into Latin by Erpinus; and printed in these two languages in folio, at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, in 1625. Erpinus died before the publication; but Golin took care of it, and added a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a>. It was dedicated by Erpinus's widow to Dr Andrews, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>. ELOCUTION. See Oratory, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">Part</a> III.

ELOGY

Pages 37-37

a praise <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> bestowed on any person or thing, in consideration of its merit. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of elogy consists in an expressive brevity. Eulogiums should not have so much as one epithet, properly so called, nor two words <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a>: they should strictly adhere to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>; for extravagant and improbable elogies rather lessen the character of the person or thing they would extol.

ELOHI

Pages 37-37

Elo, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Elohim, in scripture, one of the names of God. But it is to be observed, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>, princes, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men, judges, and even false gods, are sometimes called by this name. The sequel of the discourse is what assists us in judging rightly concerning the true meaning of this word. It is the same as Eloha. One is the singular, the other the plural. Nevertheless Elohim is often construed in the singular <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, particularly when the true God is spoken of: but when false gods are spoken of, it is construed rather in the plural.

ELOINED

Pages 37-37

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies restrained <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hindered from doing something: thus it is said, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> those within <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> be eloined, so that they cannot sue personally, their next friend shall sue for them.

ELONGATION

Pages 37-37

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, is an imperfect luxation, occasioned by the stretching <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> lengthening of the ligaments of any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>.

ELOPEMENT

Pages 37-37

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is where a married woman departs from her husband, and cohabits with an adulterer; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the husband is not obliged to allow her any alimony out of her estate, nor is he chargeable for necessaries for her of any kind. However, the bare advertising a wife in the gazette, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other public <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, is not a legal notice to persons in general not to trust her; though a personal notice given by the husband to particular persons is said to be good. An <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> lies, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> damages may be recovered, against a person for carrying away and detaining another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s wife.

ELOQUENCE

Pages 37-37

the art of speaking well, so as to affect and persuade. See Oratory.

ELPHINSTON

Pages 37-38

WILLIAM, a Scotch prelate and statesman of considerable eminence, who flourished in the end of the 15th and commencement of the 16th century, was born at Glasgow in the year 1431. At the university of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> he received his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, and in the learning which distinguished that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> he made extraordinary proficiency. His studies being completed, he went over to France, to make himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> Elphinston of the civil and canon <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, where he afterwards became a professor, and for the space of six years acquired considerable reputation in the discharge of his duty. On his return to Scotland, he entered into holy orders, was soon appointed official of Glasgow, and afterwards of St Andrews. He was admitted a member of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>; and on a misunderstanding taking <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> between James III. of Scotland and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XI. of France, his powerful mediation at the latter <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, in conjunction with the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUNKELD">Dunkeld</a> and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUCHAN">Buchan</a>, effected an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMICABLE">amicable</a> reconciliation. As Elphinston on this occasion displayed such <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> and eloquence, the king was so grateful for his meritorious services, that he rewarded him with the see of Ross, from which he was translated to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Aberdeen about the year 1484, and also appointed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> office of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, which he managed with so much moderation and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a>, that all parties esteemed and admired him. When the civil wars broke out between James and the discontented <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, Bishop Elphinston appears to have declined all interference with public affairs of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and confined himself to the discharge of his ministerial duties. But when James IV. ascended the throne, his abilities as a statesman were again called forth, and he was chosen <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Maximilian, in order to bring about a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> between his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> master and the emperor's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>; but she had been previously promised to another. Yet the bishop's mission was not without its salutary effects, as he was the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> of terminating an enmity which had <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> existed between the Dutch and Scots. This he conducted in such a masterly manner, that James never undertook any thing of importance, without first procuring the sanction of his approbation. He was equally the zealous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of learning; and it is generally believed that the establishment of a university at Aberdeen was entirely owing to his influence with the Pope, from whom he obtained a bull for that purpose; and by his exertions was King's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> undertaken and completed. He bequeathed, at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his decease, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sums of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> for its support. He terminated his mortal <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CAREER">career</a> in 1514, about 83 years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, at which advanced period his constitutional vigour was very little impaired, and all the faculties of his mind were in full force; but the serious losses at the memorable <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Flowden had broken his heart. He wrote a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of his native <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, which is among the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> of Sir Thomas Fairfax, in the Bodleian library at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>.

ELSIMBURG

Pages 38-38

a port town of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Gothland, and territory of Schonen, seated Elsinburg on the side of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">Sound</a>, over against Elsinore. It was formerly a fortress belonging to the Danes; but all the fortifications were demolished in 1679, and there is only one tower of a castle which remains undemolished. It now belongs to Sweden. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13. 20. N. Lat. 56. 2.

ELSNORE

Pages 38-38
or ELSNIEUR, a port town of Denmark, seated on the Sound, in the isle of Zealand. E. Long. 13. 23. N. Lat. 56. 0.—It was a small village, containing a few fishermen's huts, until 1445, when it was made a staple town by Eric of Pomerania; who conferred upon the new settlers considerable immunities, and built a castle for their defence. From that period it gradually increased in size and wealth, and is now the most commercial place in Denmark next to Copenhagen. It contains about 7000 inhabitants, amongst whom are a considerable number of foreign merchants, and the consuls of the principal nations trading to the Baltic. The passage of the Sound is guarded by the fortress of Cronborg, which is situated upon the edge of a peninsular promontory, the nearest point of land from the opposite coast of Sweden. It is strongly fortified towards the shore by ditches, bastions, and regular entrenchments; and towards the sea by several batteries, mounted with 60 cannon, the largest whereof are 48 pounders. Every vessel, as it passes, lowers her top-sails, and pays a toll at Elsinore. It is generally asserted, that this fortress guards the Sound; and that all the ships must, on account of the shoal waters and currents, steer so near the batteries as to be exposed to their fire in case of refusal. This, however, is a mistaken notion. On account indeed of the numerous and opposite currents in the Sound, the safest passage lies near the fortress; but the water in any part is of sufficient depth for vessels to keep at a distance from the batteries, and the largest ships can even sail close to the coast of Sweden. The constant discharge, however, of the toll, is not so much owing to the strength of the fortress as to a compliance with the public law of Europe. Many disputes have arisen concerning the right by which the crown of Denmark imposes such a duty. The kings of Sweden, in particular, claiming an equal title to the free passage of the Strait, were for some time exempted by treaty from paying it; but in 1720, Frederic I. agreed that all Swedish vessels should for the future be subject to the usual imposts. All vessels, beside a small duty, are rated at 1½ per cent. of their cargoes, except the English, French, Dutch, and Swedish, which pay only one per cent.; and in return the crown takes the charge of constructing light-houses, and erecting signals to mark the shoals and rocks, from the Categate to the entrance into the Baltic. The tolls of the Sound, and of the two Belts, supply an annual revenue of 120,000l. or according to others 150,000l.

ELUDING

Pages 39-39

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of evading <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rendering a thing vain and of no effect; a dexterous getting clear, or escaping out of an affair, difficulty, embarrassment, or the like. We say, to elude a proposition, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of chicane is, to elude the force of the laws: This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> has not resolved the difficulty, but eluded it. Alexander, says the historian, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> the Gordian knot, either eluded the oracle or fulfilled it: Ille nequiquam lacteatus cum latentibus sodis, Nihil, inquit, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, quonodo solutum; gladioque ruptis omnibus loris, oraculi sortem vel eludere vel implement.

ELUTRIATION

Pages 39-39

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, an operation performed by washing <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> substances with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, stirring them well together, and hastily pouring off the liquid, while the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> remains suspended in it, that it may thereby be separated from the heavier part. By this operation metallic ores are separated from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and other unmetallic particles adhering to them.

ELVAS

Pages 38-39

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> town, and one of the best and most important in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, seated in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALENTEJO">Alentejo</a>, a few miles from the frontiers of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESTREMADURA">Estremadura</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. It is built on a mountain, and is strongly fortified with works of free-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. The streets of the town are handsome, and the houses neat; and there is a cistern so large, that it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> hold <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> enough to supply the whole town six months. The water is conveyed to it by a magnificent aqueduct, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELY">ELY</a> three miles in length, sustained in some places by four <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, one upon another. It was bombarded by the French and Spaniards in 1756, but without effect. It has generally a garrison of 1000 men. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> founded an academy here, in 1733, for young gentlemen. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7. 28. N. Lat. 38.

ELVELA

Pages 39-39

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the cryptogama class, and order of fungi. The fungus is turbinate, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> like an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> cone. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ELY

Pages 39-39

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> and bishop's see of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGESHIRE">Cambridgeshire</a>, situated about 12 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0. 51. N. Lat. 52. 24. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of itself, including the territory around; and has a judge who determines all causes civil and criminal within its limits. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> hath undergone various alterations since it was first established by Ethelreda, the wife of Egfride, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>, who founded a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> here, and planted it with virgins, and became the first abbess of it herself. The Danes entirely ruined this establishment; then Ethelwald, the 27th bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, rebuilt the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>, and filled it with monks; to whom King Edgar, and many succeeding monarchs, bestowed many privileges, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> grants of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>; so that this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> became in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the best of any in England. Richard, the 11th <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a>, wishing to free himself of the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, within whose <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> his monastery was situated, and not liking so powerful a superior, he made great <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> with King Henry I. to get Ely erected into a bishopric; and spared neither purse nor prayers to bring this about. He even brought the bishop of Lincoln to consent to it, by giving him and his successors the manors of Bugden, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIGGLESWADE">Biggleswade</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPALDING">Spalding</a>, which belonged to the abbey, in lieu of his jurisdiction; but he lived not to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> the sweets of his industry and ambition, he dying before his abbey was erected into a see. His successor was the first bishop of Ely: but the great privileges the bishop enjoyed were almost wholly taken away, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> much restricted, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, 27th Henry VIII. regarding the restoring to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> royalties: So, instead of being palatine of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Ely, the bishop and his temporal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> were by that act declared to be from thenceforth justices of the peace in the said <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. This diocese contains all Cambridgeshire, and the isle of Ely, excepting Iselham, which belongs to the see of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a>, and 15 other parishes, that are in the diocese of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWICH">Norwich</a>; but it has a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, viz. Emmeth. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of parishes in this diocese are 141, whereof 75 are inappropriate. It hath but one archdeacon, viz. of Ely. It is valued in the king's books at 213l. 18s. 5d. The clergy's tenth amounting to the sum of 384l. 14s. 9½d. The bishopric is computed to be worth annually 8000l. The church is dedicated to St <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ETHELRED">Ethelred</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, as it now appears, has been the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of several of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>. The west parts were rebuilt by Bishop Ridal; the choir and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANTERN">lantern</a> were begun by Bishop Norwold, and finished by Bishop <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRODSHAM">Frodsham</a>. This see hath given two saints and two cardinals to the church of Rome; and to the English <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> chancellors, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> lord treasurers, one lord privy <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>, one <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of the exchequer, one chancellor to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, two masters of the rolls, and three almoners. To this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> belong a bishop, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a>, an archdeacon, eight prebendaries, with vicars, lay-clerks, choristers, a schoolmaster, usher, and 28 king's scholars.

ELYMAIS

Pages 39-39

the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> of Elam, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>. We are told (1 Mac. vi. 1.) that Antiochus Epiphanes, having understood that there were very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> treasures lodged in a temple at Elymais, determined to go and plunder it: but the citizens getting intelligence of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, made an insurrection, forced him out of the city, and obliged him to fly. The author of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> book of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACCABEES">Maccabees</a> (ix. 2.) calls this city Persepolis, in all <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> because formerly it was the capital of Persia; for it is known from other accounts, that Persepolis and Elymais were two very different cities, the latter situated upon the Euclous, the former upon the Araxis.

ELYMUS

Pages 39-39

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the triandra class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method, ranking under the fourth order, Gromino. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ELYOT

Pages 39-39

Sir Thomas, a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of eminent learning into the 16th century, was educated at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, travelled into foreign countries, and upon his return was introduced to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>. His learning recommended him to Henry VIII. who conferred the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a> on him, and employed him in several embassies: particularly in 1532, to Rome, about the divorce of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Catharine, and afterwards to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. about 1536. He wrote, The Castle of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">Health</a>, the Governor, Banquet of Sapience, Of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">Education</a> of Children, De rebus memorabilibus Angliae, and other books; and was highly esteemed by all his learned contemporaries.

ELYSIUM

Pages 39-40

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the inferi or lower world, furnished with fields, meads, agreeable woods, groves, shades, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, &c. whither the souls of good people were supposed to go after this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, and Æneas, were supposed to have have descended into Elysium in their life <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and to have returned again; (Virg. lib. vi. ver. 638 &c.).
