Tibullus (lib. i. eleg. 3.) gives us fine descriptions of the Elysian fields. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> opposes Elysium to Tartarus; which was the place where the wicked underwent their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>. *Hic locus est, partes ubi se via finit in ambas: Dextera, qua Ditis magni sub mania tendit: Hac iter Elysium nobis: at leva malorum Exercet poenas, et <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AD">ad</a> impia Tartara mittit.* He assigns Elysium to those who died for their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, to those of pure lives, to truly inspired poets, to the inventors of arts, and to all who have done good to mankind. Some authors take the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> of Elysium to have been borrowed from the Phoenicians; as imagining the name *Elysium* formed from the Phoenician *alaz*, or *alat*, or *alaz*, "to rejoice," or "to be in joy;" the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> *a* being only changed into *e*, as we find done in many other names; as in *Anakim* for *Anakim*, &c. On which footing, Elysian fields should signify the same thing as a place of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; or *Locos lectos, et amarae vireta Fortunatorum nemorum, sedesque beatas.* Virg. Others derive the word from the Greek *λαβω*, *soleo*, "I deliver, I let loose or disengage;" because here men's souls are freed or disencumbered from the fetters of the body. Beroualdus, and Hornius (Hist. Philosoph. lib. iii. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 2.) take the place to have derived its name from Eliza, one of the first persons who came into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> after the deluge, and the author and father of the Ætolians. The Elysian fields were, according to some, in the Fortunate <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, in the Atlantic. Others place them in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Leuce; and, according to the authority of Virgil, they were situated in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. According to Lucian, they were near the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>; or in the centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we believe Plutarch. Olaus Wormius contends that it was in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> the Elysian fields were placed.

ELZEVIRS

Pages 40-40

celebrated printers at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, who greatly adorned the republic of letters with many beautiful editions of the best authors of antiquity. They fell somewhat below the Stephensens in point of learning, as well as in their editions of Greek and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> authors; but as to the choice of good books, they seem to have equalled, and in the neatness and elegance of their small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, greatly to have exceeded them. Their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, Terence, and Greek <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, have been reckoned their masterpieces; and are indeed so very fine, that they justly gained them the reputation of being the first printers in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. There were five of these Elzevirs, namely, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a>, Bonaventure, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>, Lewis, and Daniel. Lewis began to be famous at Leyden in 1595, and was remarkable for being the first who observed the distinction between the *u* consonant and *v* vowel, which had been recommended by Ramus and other writers <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before, but never regarded. Daniel died in 1680 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 1681; and though he left children who carried on the business, passes nevertheless for the last of his family who excelled in it. The Elzevirs have printed several catalogues of their editions; but the last, published by Daniel Elzevir, is considerably enlarged, and abounds with new books. It was printed at Amsterdam, 1674, in 12mo, and divided into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> volumes.

EMANATION

Pages 40-40

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of flowing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> proceeding from some source or origin. Such is the emanation of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; or that of effluvia from odorous bodies; or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> from God, &c.—The word is formed of the Latin *ex*, "out of," and *manere*, "to flow or stream." Emancipation is also used for the thing that proceeds, as well as the act of proceeding. The power given a judge is an emanation from the regal power; the reasonable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> is an emanation from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINITY">Divinity</a>.

EMANCIPATION

Pages 40-40

in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, the setting free a son from the subjection of a father; so that whatever moveables he acquires belongs in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> to him, and not his father, as before emancipation. Emancipation puts the son in a capacity of managing his own affairs, and of marrying without his father's consent, though a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">minor</a>. Emancipation differs from manumission, as the latter was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> in favour of a slave, whereas the former was that of a father in favour of his son. There were two kinds of emancipation: the one tacit, which was by the son's being promoted to some <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, by his coming of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by his marrying; in all which <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> he became his own master of course. The other, express; where the father declared before a judge, that he emancipated his son. In performing this, the father was first to sell his son imaginarily to another, whom they called *pater fiduciarius*, father in trust; of whom being bought back again by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> father, he manumitted him before the judge by a verbal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a>. Emancipation formerly obtained in France with regard to minors or pupils, who were hereby set at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to manage their own effects, without the advice or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of their parents or tutors.

EMASCULATION

Pages 40-40

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of castrating <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> depriving a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> of those parts which characterize his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEX">sex</a>. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CASTRATION">Castration</a> and Eunuch.

EMAUS

Pages 40-40

Emmaus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Emmaus, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a village, 60 stadia to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, or about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles; it afterwards became a town and a Roman colony, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NICOPOLIS">Nicopolis</a> (Jerome). Rehland has another Emmaus towards Lydda, 22 miles from Jerusalem, (Itinerary); a third, near Tiberias.

EMBALMING

Pages 40-41

is the opening a dead body, taking out the intestines, and filling the space with odoriferous and desiccative drugs and spices, to prevent it putrefying. The Egyptians excelled all other nations in the art of preserving bodies from corruption; for some that they have embalmed upwards of 2000 years ago, remain whole to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and are often brought into other countries as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> curiosities. Their manner of embalming was thus: they scooped the brain with an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> scoop out at the nostrils, and threw in medicaments to fill up the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VACUUM">vacuum</a>: they also took out the entrails, and having filled the body with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYRRH">myrrh</a>, cassia, and other spices, except frankincense, proper to dry up the humours, they pickled it in nitre, where it lay. Embalming lay soaking for 70 days. The body was then wrapped up in bandages of fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>, to make it stick like <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLUE">glue</a>; and so was delivered to the kindred of the deceased, entire in all its features, the very hairs of the eyelids being preserved. They used to keep the bodies of their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, thus embalmed, in little houses magnificently adorned, and took great <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> in beholding them, alive as it were, without any change in their size, features, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>. The Egyptians also embalmed birds, &c. The prices for embalming were different; the highest was a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a>, the next 20 minae, and so decreasing to a very small <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>: but they who had not wherewithal to answer this expense, contented themselves with infusing, by means of a syringe, through the fundament, a certain liquor extracted from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a>; and, leaving it there, wrapped up the body in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> of nitre: the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> thus preyed upon the intestines, so that when they took it out, the intestines came away with it, dried, and not in the least putrefied: the body being enclosed in nitre, grew dry, and nothing remained besides the skin glued upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>. The method of embalming used by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Egyptians, according to Maillet, is to wash the body several times with rose-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which, he elsewhere observes, is more fragrant in that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> than with us; they afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERFUME">perfume</a> it with incense, aloes, and a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of other odours, of which they are by no means sparing; and then they <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURY">bury</a> the body in a winding-sheet, made partly of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> and partly of cotton, and moistened, as is supposed, with some sweet-scented water or liquid perfume, though Maillet uses only the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> moistened; this they cover with another cloth of unmixed cotton, to which they add one of the richest suits of clothes of the deceased. The expense, he says, on these occasions, is very great, though nothing like what the genuine embalming cost in former times.

EMBANKMENT

Pages 41-41

a mound <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> wall of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, or some other material, used as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> against inundations. See Supplement.

EMBARCADERO

Pages 41-41

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a>, much used along the coasts of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. It signifies a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> which serves some other considerable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> farther within <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, for a port <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> place of shipping, i.e., of embarking and disembarking commodities. Thus Calao is the embarcadero of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIMA">Lima</a>. There are some embarcaderos 50 leagues from the city they serve in that capacity.

EMBARGO

Pages 41-41

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a> on ships <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> merchandise, by public authority; or a prohibition of state, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> on foreign ships, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, to prevent their going out of port, sometimes to prevent their coming in, and sometimes both, for a limited time. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> may lay embargoes on ships, or employ those of his subjects, in time of danger, for the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; but they must not be for the private advantage of a particular trader or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>; and therefore a warrant to stay a single ship is no legal embargo. No inference can be made from embargoes which are only in war-time; and are a prohibition by advice of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, and not at prosecution of parties. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> goods be laden on board, and after an embargo or restraint from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> or state comes forth, and then the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the ship breaks ground, or endeavours to sail, if any damage accrues, he must be responsible for the same; the reason is, because his freight is due, and must be paid, even though the goods be seized as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRABAND">contraband</a>.

EMBARRASS

Pages 41-41

(Embarrassment), a French <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a>, though now naturalized; denoting a difficulty <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> obstacle which perplexes or confounds a person, &c. EMBASSADOR. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMBASSADOR">Ambassador</a>.

EMBDEN

Pages 41-41

a port-town and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Germany, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the same name, now in possession of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>. It is situated at the mouth of the river Ens. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6. 45. N. Lat. 53. 50.

EMBER-WEEKS

Pages 41-41

are those wherein the ember <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ember-days <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a>. In the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Alfred, and those of Canute, those days are called ymbren, that is, circular days, from whence the word was probably corrupted into ember-days: by the canonists they are called quattuor anni tempora, the four <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> seasons, on which the circle of the year turns: and hence Henshaw takes the word to have been formed, viz. by corruption from temper, of tempora. The ember-days are, the Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday, after Quadragesima <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a>, after Whit-sunday, after Holy-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOD">rood</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> in September, and after St Lucia's day in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>: which four times answer well enough to the four <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of the year, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">Spring</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">Summer</a>, Autumn, and Winter. Mr Sommer thinks they were originally fasts, instituted to beg God's blessing on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. Agreeable to which, Skinner supposes the word ember taken from the ashes, embers, then strewed on the head. These ember-weeks, are now chiefly taken notice of, on account of the ordination of priests and deacons; because the canon appoints the Sundays next succeeding the ember-weeks, for the solemn times of ordination: Though the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they please, may ordain on any Sunday or holiday.

EMBERIZA

Pages 41-41

a genus of birds belonging to the order of passeres. See <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EMBLEM

Pages 41-42

a kind of painted enigma, which, representing some obvious <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, with reflections underneath, instructs us in some moral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of knowledge. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVISE">Devise</a>, Enigma, &c. Such is that very significant image of Scipio holding his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in the fire; with the words, Agere et pati fortiter Romanum est, "To do and suffer courageously is Roman." The word is pure Greek, formed of the verb ἐπιλάμβανειν, "to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> in, to insert." Suetonius relates, that Tiberius made the word be erased out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, because borrowed from another <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. The emblem is somewhat plainer and more obvious than the enigma. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALE">Gale</a> defines emblem an ingenious <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, representing one thing to the eye, and another to the understanding. The Greeks also gave the name Emblems, ἐπιλάμβανειν, to inlaid or mosaic works, and even to all kinds of ornaments of vases, moveables, garments, &c. And the Latins used emblemata in the same <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. Accordingly, Cicero reproaching Verres with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> and fine wrought works he had plundered from the Sicilians, Emblem calls the ornament fixed thereto (and which on occasion might be separated from them) emblems. Add, that Latin authors frequently compare the figures and ornaments of discourse to these emblems. Thus, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Latin poet praising an orator, says, that all his words were ranged like the pieces in mosaic: Quam lepide æstue compositæ, ut tessellæ omnes, At te pavimenti, atque emblemate vermiculato.

EMBOLISMUS

Pages 42-42

ἐμβολισμός, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a>, signifies "intercalation." The word is formed of ἐμβάλλω, "to insert." As the Greeks made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> year, which is only 354 days; in order to bring it to the solar, which is 365 days, they had every two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three years an embolism, i.e. they added a 13th lunar <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> every two or three years, which additional month they called embolimæus, ἐμβολικός, because intertied, or intercalated.

EMBOSSING

Pages 42-42
or IRRIGATING, in Architecture and Sculpture, the forming or fashioning works in relief, whether cut with a chisel or otherwise. Embossing is a kind of sculpture, wherein the figure sticks out from the plane wherein it is cut: and according as the figures are more or less prominent, they are said to be in alto, mezzo, or basso relievo; or high, mean, or low relief. See Engraving.

EMBOTHRIUM

Pages 42-42

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the tetrandria class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EMBRASURE

Pages 42-42

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, the enlargement made of the aperture of a door <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> window on the inside of the wall; its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> being to give the greater play for the opening of the door or casement, or to admit the more <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>.

EMBROCATION

Pages 42-42

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> kind of remedy, which consists in an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IRRIGATION">irrigation</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> affected, with some proper liquor, as oils, spirits, &c. by means of a woollen <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth, or a sponge, dipped in the same.

EMBROIDERY

Pages 42-42

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> silver, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> thread, wrought by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> upon the cloth, stuffs, or muslin, into various figures. In embroidering stuffs, the work is performed in a kind of loom; because the more the piece is stretched, the easier it is worked. As to muslin, they spread it upon a pattern ready designed; and sometimes, before it is stretched upon the pattern, it is starched, to make it more easy to handle. Embroidery on the loom is less tedious than the other, in which, while they work <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, all the threads of the muslin, both lengthwise and breadthwise must be continually counted; but, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, this last embroidery is much richer in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, and susceptible of greater variety. Cloths too much milled are scarce susceptible of this ornament, and in effect we seldom see them embroidered. The thinnest muslins are left for this purpose; and they are embroidered to the greatest perfection in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>; in other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, however, they embroider very prettily, and especially in France. There are several kinds of embroidery: as, 1. Embroidery on the stamp; where the figures are raised and rounded, having cotton or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a> put under them to support them. 2. Low embroidery; where the gold and silver <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> low upon the sketch, and are stitched with silk of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. 3. Guimped embroidery: this is performed either in gold or silver; they first make a sketch upon the cloth, then put on cut <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VELLUM">vellum</a>, and afterwards sew on the gold and silver with silk thread: on this kind of embroidery they often put gold and silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CORD">cord</a>, tinsel, and spangles. 4. Embroidery on both sides; that which appears on both sides of the stuff. 4. Plain embroidery; where the figures are flat and even, without cords, spangles, or other ornaments. By stat. 22 Geo. II. c. 36. no foreign embroidery, or gold and silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROCADE">brocade</a>, shall be imported, upon pain of being forfeited and burnt, and penalty of 100l. for each piece. No person shall sell, or expose to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>, any foreign embroidery, gold and silver thread, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LACE">lace</a>, fringe, brocade, or make up the same into any garment, on pain of having it forfeited and burnt, and penalty of 100l. All such embroidery, &c. may be seized and burnt; and the mercer, &c. in whose custody it was found, shall forfeit 100l.

EMBRUN

Pages 42-42
or AMBRUN, a city of Dauphiny, in France, near the confines of Piedmont. E. Long. 6. 6. N. Lat. 44. 35.

EMBRYO

Pages 42-42

in Physiology, the first <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of an animal in the womb, before the several members are distinctly formed; after which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> it is denominated fetus. See <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">Generation</a> and Fetus.

EMENAGOGUES

Pages 45-46

in Medicine, such remedies as promote the menstrual discharge. They are thus called from "in," "<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>," "duce," "I <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>," because their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> periods of flowing are once a-month.

EMERALD

Pages 42-43

a precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> belonging to the genus of siliceous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. The word is derived, according to some, from the French smaragde, and that from the Latin smaragdus, signifying the same thing; by others it is said to be derived from the Italian smaraldo, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the Arabian azmorad. According to Cronstedt the emerald is the softest of all the precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, though other naturalists <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> it the next after the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> in this respect. It is perhaps the most beautiful of all the gems, and, according to Wallerius, when heated in the fire, changes its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> to a deep blue, and becomes phosphorescent; but recovers its green colour when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>. When pulverized it has a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> appearance, and, with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORAX">borax</a>, melts to a very thin and colourless glass. It becomes electric by being rubbed, and some have the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the tourmalin, viz. of being electrified by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and in that state attracting ashes or other <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> substances; though the emeralds are less powerful than the tourmalin, and after having attracted the ashes, they retain them without any signs of repulsion. Pliny mentions twelve different kinds of these precious stones; though it appears, from the vast size of some of them, that they must have been only certain kinds of green <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAR">spar</a>, or other green stone, which at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> Emerald time went under the name of emerald among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. The true emerald is found only in very small crystals, from the size of 1/6th of an inch in diameter to that of a walnut. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOPHRASTUS">Theophrastus</a>, however, mentions one four cubits <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; likewise an obelisk composed of only four emeralds, the whole length being 40 cubits, and the breadth from four to two. Engestroom informs us, that the emeralds, in their rough or native state, consist of hexagonal columns mostly truncated at both ends; and that he had some in his possession, which in a gentle heat became colourless, but in a strong heat white and opaque, without any mark of fusion. Brunick distinguishes them into two classes. 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> green emerald, which comes from the east and from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> being that of an hexagonal truncated prism, and the basis a vein of white <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTZ">quartz</a>. 2. The dark green emerald, which is also columnar, but very dark coloured, striped longitudinally, and has little transparency. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> are generally broken off longitudinally, though Davila mentions one resembling a blunt triangular <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a>; and in the imperial cabinet at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a> there is one with a five-sided pyramid. These are the emeralds which become electrical by heat; though all of them do not; and those which do so cannot be known but by actual experiment. The finest specimen of the former kind of emeralds is to be seen in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> of the holy chapel of Loreto, containing upwards of 100 of these precious stones <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> and small. A fellow to this was made by art, and both were presents to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, designed to represent two Mount Calvaries. Emeralds are distinguished by the jewellers into two kinds the oriental and occidental. The true oriental emerald is very scarce, and at present only found in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Cambay. So great indeed is the scarcity of them, that an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> prevailed that there are no oriental emeralds. This opinion is adopted, among others, by Mr. Bruce; who informs us, that he made an excursion to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of emeralds in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and endeavours to show that there never were any emeralds but what came from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and that those said to have been found in the East Indies were imported from that continent. It is probable, indeed, that in former times any kind of crystal tinged of a green colour might be called an emerald, and hence the green cockle spar brought from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> may have obtained the name of mother of emeralds; but of late some emeralds have been brought from Cambay into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, which greatly excelled those of America. The best emeralds of the western continent come from Peru, and are called oriental by the jewellers: some are found in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, principally in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a> in Germany. Rough Emeralds.—Those of the first and coarsest sort, called plasmes, for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a>, are worth 27 shillings <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a> the marc, or 8 ounces. The demi-morillons, 8l. sterling per marc. Good morillons, which are only little pieces, but of fine colour, from 2l. to 15l. per marc. Emeralds, larger than morillons, and called of the third colour or sort, are valued at from 50l. to 60l. the marc. Emeralds, called of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> sort, which are in larger and finer pieces than the preceding, are worth from 65l. to 75l. per marc. Lastly, those of the first colour, otherwise called negres cartes, are worth from 110l. to 115l. Emeralds ready cut, or polished and not cut, being of good stone, and a fine colour, are worth— | Carats | Value | |--------|-------| | One | 0 | | Two | 1 | | Three | 2 | | Four | 3 | | Five | 4 | | Six | 5 | | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> | 6 | | Eight | 7 | | <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">Nine</a> | 8 | | Ten | 9 | To counterfeit Emeralds: Take of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> crystal, four ounces; of red <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, four ounces; verdigris, forty-eight grains; crocus martis, prepared with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, eight grains: let the whole be finely pulverized and sifted: put this into a crucible, leaving one inch empty: lute it well, and put it into a potter's <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>, and let it stand there as long as they do their pots. When cold, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the crucible; and you <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> find a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of a fine emerald colour, which, after it is cut and set in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, will surpass in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> an oriental emerald.

EMERSION

Pages 43-43

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, is when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other planet, begins to re-appear, after its having been eclipsed, or hid by the interposition of the moon, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, or other body. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> is sometimes found by observing the immersions and emersions of the first of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>'s satellites. The immersions are observed from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Jupiter's being in conjunction with the sun to his opposition; and the emersions, from the opposition to the conjunction; which two intervals are usually six months a-piece, and divide the year between them. But when Jupiter is in conjunction with the sun, and 15 days before and afterwards, there is nothing to be observed; the planet, with his satellites, being then lost in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of the sun. EMERSON is also used when a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a> before hid by the sun, as being too near him, begins to re-appear and to get out of his rays.

EMERSON

Pages 43-44

William, an eminent mathematician, was born in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1701, at Hurworth, a village about three miles south of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARLINGTON">Darlington</a>; at least it is certain that he resided here from his childhood. His father <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUDLEY">Dudley</a> Emerson was a tolerable proficient in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>; and without his books and instructions, perhaps his own genius (most eminently fitted for mathematical disquisitions) would have never been unfolded. He was instructed in the learned languages by a young clergyman, then curate of Hurworth, who was boarded at his father's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. In the earlier <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> he attempted to teach a few scholars; but whether from his concise method (for he was not happy in explaining his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>), <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the warmth of his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> temper, he made no progress in his school: he therefore soon left it off; and satisfied with a moderate competence left him by his parents, he devoted himself to a studious retirement. Towards the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the year 1781 (being sensible of his approaching <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a>), he disposed of the whole of his mathematical library to a bookseller at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>; and on May 25th 1782, he died of a lingering and painful disorder at his native village, aged near 81 years. Mr Emerson in his person was rather short, but strong and well made, with an open countenance and ruddy <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>. He was exceedingly singular in his dress. He had but one coat, which he always wore open before, except the lower <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTTON">button</a>; no waistcoat; his shirt quite the reverse of one in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, no opening before, but buttoned close at the collar behind; a kind of flaxen wig which had not a crooked <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> in it, and probably had never been tortured with a comb from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of its being made. He always walked up to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> when he had anything to publish, revising sheet by sheet himself.—Trusting no eyes but his own, was always a favourite maxim with him. He never advanced any mathematical proposition that he had not first tried in practice, constantly making all the different parts himself on a small <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, so that his house was filled with all kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> instruments together or disjointed. He would frequently stand up to his middle in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> while <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>, a diversion he was remarkably fond of. He used to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> incessantly for some time, and then for relaxation take a ramble to any public-house where he could get anybody to drink with and talk to. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANCHESTER">Manchester</a> was highly pleased with his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, and used often to come to him in the fields and accompany him home, but could never persuade him to get into a carriage. On these occasions he would sometimes exclaim, "Damn your whim-wham! I had rather walk." He was a married <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; and his wife used to spin on an old-fashioned wheel, whereof a very accurate <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> is given in his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>. He was deeply skilled in the science of music, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of sounds, and the various scales both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>, but was a very <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> performer. The following is a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of Mr Emerson's works. 1. The Doctrine of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUXIONS">Fluxions</a>. 2. The Projection of the Sphere, orthographic, stereographic, and gnomonical. 3. The Elements of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIGONOMETRY">Trigonometry</a>. 4. The Principles of Mechanics. 5. A Treatise of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">Navigation</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>. 6. A Treatise of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALGEBRA">Algebra</a>, in two books. 7. The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">Arithmetic</a> of Infinites, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENTIAL">Differential</a> Method, illustrated by Examples. 8. Mechanics; or the Doctrine of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">Motion</a>. 9. The Elements of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>, in four books. 10. A System of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>. 11. The Laws of Centripetal and Centrifugal Force. 12. The Mathematical Principles of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>. 13. Tracts, 8vo. 14. Cyclomathesis; or an easy Introduction to the several branches of the Mathematics. 15. A short comment on Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton's Principia; to which is added, A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">Defence</a> of Sir Isaac against the objections that have been made to several Parts of his Works.

EMERY

Pages 44-45

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a rich <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> ore found in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> masses of no determinate shape <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> size, extremely hard, and very heavy. It is usually of a dusky brownish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> on the surface; but when broken, is of a fine bright iron-gray, but not without some tinge of redness; and is spangled all over with shining specks, which are small flakes of a foliaceous talc, highly impregnated with iron. It is also sometimes very red, and then usually contains veins of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. It makes no effervescence with any of the acid menstruums; and is found in some of the Greek <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, and some parts of Germany. Dr <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that some kinds of emery may contain the metal called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLATINA">platina</a>, and on this subject has the following curious observations. "Alonso Barba mentions a substance called chumpi; which is a hard <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> of the emery kind, participating of iron, of a gray <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, shining a little, very hard to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, because it resists the fire much, found in Potosi, Chocaya, and other places, along with blackish and reddish ores that yield gold. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> platina is really found in large masses, either generally or only now and then, one might reasonably expect those masses to be such as are here described. "Of the same kind perhaps also is the mineral mentioned by several authors under the name of Spanish emery, smirris Hispanicus, which should seem, from the accounts given of it, to be no other than platina or its matrix. The smirris is said to be found in the gold <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, and its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> prohibited; to contain films or veins of native gold; to be in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> request among the alchemists; to have been sometimes used for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADULTERATION">adulteration</a> of gold; to stand, equally with the noble metal, espellation, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-QUARTATION">quartation</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>, and the regal cement; and to be separable from it by amalgamation with <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>, which throws out the smirris and retains the gold; properties strongly characteristic of platina, and which do not belong to any known substance besides. This debasement of gold per extractum smiridis Hispanici is mentioned by Becher in his Minera arcanaria, and several times hinted at in his Physica subterranea. Both Becher and Stahl indeed call the substance which the gold receives from the emery an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, whereas platina is undoubtedly a metal; but this does not at all invalidate our supposition, for they give the name of earth also to the substance which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> receives from calamine in being made into <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, which is now known to be metallic. "From these observations I have been led to suspect, that the European emeries likewise might possibly participate of platina. If this was certain, it would account satisfactorily for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> which some of the alchemists are said to have made of emeries and other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FERRUGINOUS">ferruginous</a> ores; and we should no longer doubt, or wonder, that by treating gold with these kinds of minerals, they obtained a permanent augmentation; but this augmentation, though it resisted <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, antimony, aquafortis, and the regal cement, was separable, as Becher owns it was, by quicksilver; and that, when it exceeded certain limits, it rendered the gold <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> and brittle. "If emery contains platina, I imagined it might be discoverable by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> the powdered mineral in melted lead, and afterwards working off the lead upon a test or cupel. The experiment was made with eight ounces of the finest powder of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> emery, and the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of lead; which were covered with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> to prevent the scorching of the lead, and urged with a strong fire for two or three hours. The lead became hard, rigid, of a dark colour, and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANULATED">granulated</a> texture, as if it had really imbibed some platinum from the emery; but in cupellation it worked almost entirely off, leaving only a head about the size of a small <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PIN">pin</a>'s head, which was probably no other than silver contained in the lead. "I repeated the experiment with some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a>, thinking to obtain a more perfect <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> of the emery by vitrifying it with the lead. Two ounces of fine emery and six ounces of minium were well mixed together, and urged with a strong fire, in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> crucible, for an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>: they melted into a uniform dark brownish glass. The glass was powdered, mixed with four ounces of fixt alkaline <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> and some powdered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a>, and put into a fresh crucible, with some common salt on the surface: The fire was pretty strongly excited: but the fusion was not so perfect as could be wished, and only about two ounces of lead were found revived. This lead had suffered nearly the same change as that in the foregoing experiment; and like it, gave no appearance of platinum on being cupelled. "It seems to follow from these experiments, that the emery employed in them contained no platinum; but as it is not to be supposed that all emeries are of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, other sorts may deserve to be submitted to the same trials. Platinum may therefore possibly be found in some European ores, though there is not the least footstep of it in other parades of the same kind of ore."

EMIGRATION

Pages 45-45

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of leaving one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in another. See Supplement.

EMIMS

Pages 45-45
ancient inhabitants of the land of Canaan beyond Jordan, who were defeated by Chedorlaomer and his allies, Gen. xiv. 5. Moses tells us, that they were beaten in Shaveh Kirjathaim, which was in the country of Sihon conquered from the Moabites, Josh. xiii. 19.—21. The Emims were a warlike people, of a gigantic stature, great and many, and tall as the Anakims.

EMINENCE

Pages 45-45

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a little hillock <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ascent above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the adjoining <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a>. Eminence is also a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> given to cardinals. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of the Pope, whereby it was appointed that the cardinals should be addressed under the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of eminence, bears <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> the 10th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1630. They then laid aside the titles of illustrissimi and reverendissimi, which they had borne before. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a> is likewise addressed under the quality of eminence. The Popes John VIII. and Gregory VII. gave the same title to the kings of France. The emperors have likewise borne it. Eminentissimus, the superlative of eminent, has of late been attributed to the cardinals.

EMIR

Pages 45-45

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> among the Turks, signifying a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. This title was first given to the caliphs; but when they assumed the title of Sultans, that of emir remained to their children; as that of Caesar among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. At length the title came to be attributed to all who were judged to descend from Mahomet by his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Fatimah, and who wear the green turban instead of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>. The Turks make an observation, that the emirs, before their fortieth year, are men of the greatest gravity, learning, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>; but after this, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they are not <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> fools, they discover some signs of levity and stupidity. This is interpreted by the Turks as a sort of divine impulse in token of their birth and sanctity. The Turks also call the vizirs, bashaws, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> governors of provinces, by this name.

EMISSARY

Pages 45-45

in a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, a person employed by another to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> the opinions of people, spread certain reports, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> as a spy over other people's actions. EMISSARY Vessels, in Anatomy, the same with those more <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called EXCRETORY.

EMISSION

Pages 45-45

in Medicine, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> used chiefly to denote the ejaculation of the semen <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> seed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of coition. See COITION and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">GENERATION</a>.

EMMANUEL

Pages 45-45
or IMMANUEL, a Hebrew word, which signifies 'God with us.' Isaiah (viii. 14.), in that celebrated prophecy, wherein he declares to Ahaz the birth of the Messiah, who was to be born of a virgin, says, This child shall be called, and really be, Emmanuel, that is, God with us. The same prophet (viii. 8.) repeats the same thing, while he is speaking of the enemy's army, which, like a torrent, was to overflow Judea. 'The stretching out of his wings shall fill the breadth of thy land, O Emmanuel.' The evangelist Matthew (i. 23.) informs us, that this prophecy was accomplished in the birth of Christ, born of the virgin Mary, in whom the two natures divine and human were united, and so in this sense, he was really Emmanuel, or 'God with us.'

EMMERICK

Pages 45-45

a rich fortified town of Germany, in the circle of Westphalia, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CLEVES">Cleves</a>. It carries on a good trade with the Dutch, and both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> and Catholics have the free <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. The streets are neat and regular, and the houses tolerably built. It was taken by the French in 1672, but not retained. Since 1815 it has been subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>. It is seated near the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>. F. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. 29. N. Lat. 52. 5.

EMMIUS

Pages 45-45

Ubbo, born at Gretha in East Friesland in 1547, was a very learned professor, and chosen rector of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of Norden in 1579. This seminary flourished exceedingly under his care; and declined as visibly after he was ejected, in 1587, for refusing to subscribe the Confession of Augsburg. The year after, he was made rector of the college of Leer; and when the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRONINGEN">Groningen</a> confederated with the United Provinces, the magistrates appointed him rector of that college: which employment he filled with the highest repute near 20 years; until the college being erected into an university, he was the first rector, and one of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> ornaments of it by his lectures, till his infirmities prevented his public appearance. His <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> was equal to his learning; so that the governor of Friesland and Groningen often consulted him, and seldom failed to follow his advice. He wrote...

EMOLLIENTS

Pages 46-46

in Medicine and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, are such remedies as sheath and soften the asperity of the humours, and relax and supple the solids at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. EMOLUMENT is properly applied to the profits arising daily from an office <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> employ. The word is formed of the Latin emolumentum, which, according to some, primarily signifies the profits redounding to the miller from his mill; of molo, molere, "to grind."—The patent, or other <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, whereby a person is preferred to an office, gives him a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to enjoy all the duties, honours, profits, and emoluments belonging thereto.—Emolument is also used, in a somewhat greater latitude, for profit or advantage in the general. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMOTION">EMOTION</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">PASSION</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind, are distinguished by a celebrated writer*. An internal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> or agitation of the mind, when it passeth away without desire, is denominated an emotion: when desire follows, the motion or agitation is denominated a passion. A fine <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>, for example, raiseth in me a pleasant feeling: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> that feeling vanish without producing any effect, it is in proper <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> an emotion; but if the feeling, by reiterated views of the object, becomes sufficiently strong to occasion desire, it loses its name of emotion, and acquires that of passion. The same holds in all the other passions. The painful feeling raised in a spectator by a slight injury done to a stranger, being accompanied with no desire of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>, is termed an emotion; but if that injury raiseth in the stranger a stronger emotion, which being accompanied with desire of revenge, is a passion. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">External</a> expressions of distress produce in the spectator a painful feeling, which being sometimes so slight as to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> away without any effect, is an emotion; but if the feeling be so strong as to prompt desire of affording relief, it is a passion, and is termed pity. Envy is emulation in excess: if the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXALTATION">exaltation</a> of a competitor be barely disagreeable, the painful feeling is an emotion; if it produce desire to depress him, it is a passion. See PASSION.

EMOYU

Pages 46-47
or HIA MEN, an island and port of China, under the jurisdiction of the province of FOKIEN. The port is properly but an anchoring-place for ships, inclosed on one side by the island from which it takes its name, and on the other by the main-land: but it is so extensive, that it can contain several thousands of vessels; and the depth of its water is so great, that the largest ships may lie close to the shore without danger. In the beginning of the present century it was much frequented by European vessels; but few visit it at present, as all the trade is carried on at Canton. The emperor keeps here a garrison of 6 or 7000 men, commanded by a Chinese general. In entering this road, a large rock must be doubled which stands at the mouth of it, and divides it almost as the Mingant di- vides the harbour of Brest. This rock is visible, and rises several feet above the surface of the water. The island of Emoyu is particularly celebrated on account of the magnificence of its principal pagod, consecrated to the deity Fo. This temple is situated in a plain, terminated on one side by the sea, and on the other by a lofty mountain. Before it the sea, flowing through different channels, forms a large sheet of water, which is bordered with turf of the most beautiful verdure. The front of this edifice is 180 feet in length, and its gate is adorned with figures in relief, which are the usual ornaments of the Chinese architecture. On entering, you find a vast portico, with an altar in the middle, on which is placed a gigantic statue of gilt brass, representing the god Fo, sitting cross-legged. Four other statues are placed at the corners of this portico, which are 18 feet high, although they represent people sitting. Each of these statues is formed from a single block of stone. They bear in their hands different symbols which mark their attributes, as formerly in Athens and Rome the trident and caduceus distinguished Neptune and Mercury. One holds a serpent in his arms, which is twisted round its body in several folds; the second has a bent bow and a quiver; the two others present, one a kind of battle-axe, and the other a guitar, or some instrument of the same kind. After crossing this portico, you enter a square outer court, paved with large gray stones, the least of which is ten feet in length and four in breadth. At the four sides of this court arise four pavilions, which terminate in domes, and have a communication with one another by means of a gallery which runs quite round it. One of these contains a bell ten feet in diameter; the wooden-work which supports this heavy mass cannot be sufficiently admired. In the other is kept a drum of an enormous size, which the bonzes use to proclaim the days of new and full moon. It must be observed, that the clappers of the Chinese bells are on the outside, and made of wood in the form of a mallet. The two other pavilions contain the ornaments of the temple, and often serve to lodge travellers, whom the bonzes are obliged to receive. In the middle of this court is a large tower, which stands by itself, and terminates also in a dome, to which you ascend by a beautiful stone stair-case that winds round it. This dome contains a temple remarkably neat; the ceiling is ornamented with mosaic work, and the walls are covered with stone figures in relief, representing animals and monsters. The pillars which support the roof of this edifice are of wood varnished; and on festivals are ornamented with small flags of different colours. The pavement of the temple is formed of little shells, and its different compartments present birds, butterflies, flowers, &c. The bonzes continually burn incense upon the altar, and keep the lamps lighted, which hang from the ceiling of the temple. At one extremity of the altar stands a brazen urn, which when struck sends forth a mournful sound; on the opposite side is a hollow machine of wood, of an oval form, used for the same purpose, which is to accompany with its sound their voices when they sing in praise of the tutelary idol of the pagod. The god Poussa is placed on the middle of this altar, on a flower of gilt brass, which serves as a base, and holds holds a young child in his arms; several idols, which are no doubt subaltern deities, are ranged around him, and show by their attitudes their respect and veneration. The bonzes have traced out on the walls of this temple several hieroglyphical characters in praise of Posse; there is also to be seen an historical or allegorical painting in fresco, which represents a burning lake, in which several men appear to be swimming, some carried by monsters, others surrounded by dragons and winged serpents. In the middle of the gulf rises a steep rock, on the top of which the god is seated, holding in his arms a child, who seems to call out to those who are in the flames of the lake; but an old man, with hanging ears and horns on his head, prevents them from climbing to the summit of the rock, and threatens to drive them back with a large club. The bonzes are at a loss what answer to give, when any questions are asked them concerning this painting. Behind the altar is a kind of library, containing books which treat of the worship of idols. On descending from this dome you cross the court, and enter a kind of gallery, the walls of which are lined with boards; it contains 24 statues of gilt brass, representing the same number of philosophers, ancient disciples of Confucius. At the end of this gallery you find a large hall, which is the refectory of the bonzes; and after having traversed a spacious apartment, you at length enter the temple of Fo, to which there is an ascent by a large stone staircase. It is ornamented with vases full of artificial flowers (a work in which the Chinese excel); and here also are found the same kind of musical instruments as those mentioned before. The statue of the god is not to be seen but through a piece of black gauze, which forms a kind of veil or curtain before the altar. The rest of the pagod consists of several large chambers, exceedingly neat, but badly disposed; the gardens and pleasure grounds are on the declivity of the mountain; and a number of delightful grottoes are cut out in the rock, which afford an agreeable shelter from the excessive heat of the sun. There are several other pagods in the isle of Emooy; among which is one called The Pagod of the Ten Thousand Stones, because it is built on the brow of a mountain where there is a like number of little rocks, under which the bonzes have formed grottoes and very pleasant covered seats. A certain rural simplicity reigns here, which captivates and delights. Strangers are received by these bonzes with great politeness, and may freely enter their temples; but they must not attempt to gratify their curiosity fully, nor to enter those apartments into which they are not introduced, especially if they are accompanied by suspicious persons; for the bonzes, who are forbid under pain of severe punishment to have any intercourse with women, and who often keep them in private, might, from fear of being discovered, revenge themselves for too importunate a curiosity.

EMPALEMENT

Pages 47-48

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> kind of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, which consisted in thrusting a stake up the fundament. The word comes from the French empaler, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the Italian impalare; or rather, they are all alike derived from the Latin palus, "a stake," and the preposition in, "in or into." We find mention of empaling in Ju- Vol. VIII. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">Part</a> I. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">Emperor</a>. veeign princes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>, Mogul, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, &c., are all emperors of China, Japan, &c. In the year 1723, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CZAR">czar</a> of Muscovy assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of emperor of all Russia, and procured himself to be recognized as such by most of the princes and states of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. In the West, the title has been a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> restrained to the emperors of Germany. The first who bore it was <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>, who had the title of emperor conferred on him by Pope Leo III. though he had all the power before. The imperial prerogatives were formerly much more extensive than they are at present. At the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, A.D. 1024, they exercised the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of conferring all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> benefices in Germany; of receiving the revenues of them during a vacancy; of succeeding to the effects of intestate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>; of confirming or annulling the elections of the popes; of assembling councils, and of appointing them to decide concerning the affairs of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; of conferring the title of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> on their vassals; of granting vacant fiefs; of receiving the revenues of the empire; of governing <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> as its proper sovereigns; of erecting free cities, and establishing <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> in them; of assembling the diets of the empire, and fixing the time of their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>; of coining <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and conferring the same privilege on the states of the empire; and of administering both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and low <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> within the territories of the different states: but in the year 1437, they were reduced to the right of conferring all dignities and titles, except the privilege of being a state of the empire; of princes primordiae, or of appointing once during their reign a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITARY">dignitary</a> in each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; of granting dispensations with respect to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of majority; of erecting cities, and conferring the privilege of coining money; of calling the meetings of the diet, and presiding in them. To which some have added, 1. That all the princes and states of Germany are obliged to do them homage, and swear fidelity to them. 2. That they, or their generals, have a right to command the forces of all the princes of the empire when united together. 3. That they receive a kind of tribute from all the princes and states of the empire, for carrying on a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> which concerns the whole empire, which is called the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>. For the rest, there is not a foot of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> or territory annexed to his title: but ever since the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> IV, the emperors have depended entirely on their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> dominions as the only source of their power, and even of their subsistence. See Diet and Electors. The kings of France were anciently also called emperors, at the time when they reigned with their sons, whom they associated to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. Thus Hugh Capet, having associated his son Robert, took the title of emperor, and Robert that of king; under which titles they are mentioned in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">Council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHEIMS">Rheims</a>, by Gerbert, &c. King Robert is also called emperor of the French by Helgaud of Fleury. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> le Gros, upon associating his son, did the same. In the First <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">Register</a> of the King's Charters, fol. 166, are found letters of Louis le Gros, dated in 1116, in favour of Raymond bishop of Maguelonne, wherein he styles himself, Ludovicus, Dei ordinate providentia, Francorum imperator augustus. The kings of England had likewise anciently the title of emperors, as appears from a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> of King Edgar: Ego Edgarus An- glorum basileus, omniumque regum insularum oceani quae Britanniam circumjacent, &c. imperator et domi- nus.

EMPETRUM

Pages 48-48

BERRY-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">BEARING</a> HEATH; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the monoeica class. In the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method this genus is ranked by Linnæus under the 54th order, Miscellanea. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EMPHASIS

Pages 48-48

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, a particular stress of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, laid on such parts <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> words of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> as the orator wants to inforce upon his audience. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECLAMATION">Declamation</a>; Oratory, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">Part</a> IV.; and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">Reading</a>.

EMPHYSEMA

Pages 48-48

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, a windy tumor, generally occasioned by a fracture of the ribs, and formed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> insinuating itself, by a small wound, between the skin and muscles, into the substance of the cellular <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> adipose membrane, spreading itself afterwards up to the neck, head, belly, and other parts, much after the manner in which butchers blow up their veal.

EMPIRE

Pages 48-49
or The empire, used absolutely and without any addition, signifies the empire of Germany; called also, in juridical acts and laws, The holy Roman empire. It had its beginning with the ninth century; Charlemagne being created first emperor by Pope Leo III, who put the crown on his head in St Peter's church on Christmas-class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day in the year 800. Authors are at a loss under what form of government to range the empire. Some of them maintain it to be a monarchical state, because all the members thereof are obliged to ask the investiture of their states of the emperor, and to take an oath of fidelity to him. Others consider it as a republic, or aristocratic state, because the emperor cannot resolve or determine anything without the concurring suffrages of the princes. It is added, that if they require investiture from, and swear fealty to him, it is only as head of the republic, and in the name of the republic, and not in his own; just as at Venice every thing is transacted in name of the doge. Others will have the empire to be a monarcho-aristocratic state, i.e., a mixture of monarchy and aristocracy; because, though the emperor in many cases seems to act sovereignly, yet his decrees and resolves have no force, in case the state refuse to confirm them. Lastly, it has been called an aristo-democratic state, because the diet, wherein the sovereignty is lodged, is composed of princes and the deputies of the cities; and is divided into three orders or bodies, called colleges, viz., the college of electors, the college of princes, and the college of cities. We say, diet of the empire, circles of the empire, siefs of the empire, princes of the empire, estates of the empire, members of the empire, capitulations of the empire. See DIET, CIRCLE, PRINCE, CAPITULATION, &c. The states or estates of the empire are of two kinds, mediate and immediate. The immediate states are those who hold immediately of the empire: Whereof, again, there are two kinds; the first, such as have seats and voices in the imperial diet; the second, such as have none. The mediate states are those who hold of the immediate. The states which now compose the empire are, The princes of the empire, the counts of the empire, the free barons of the empire, the prelates of the empire, the princesses or abbesses of the empire, the nobles of the empire, and the imperial cities.

EMPIRIC

Pages 49-49

an appellation given to those physicians who conduct themselves wholly by their own <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, without studying physic in a regular way. Some even <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a>, in a still worse <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, for a quack who prescribes at random, without being at all acquainted with the principles of the art.

EMPIS

Pages 49-49
