Reaumur has alleged, that the pulsation of this artery changes its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> in the pupa, and that the blood is propelled from the head towards the tail; he says this may be plainly observed in a pupa newly stripped. Lyonnet denies the accuracy of Reaumur's observations; and says that he found a species of caterpillar, the pupa of which is very transparent, in which the longitudinal artery was to be seen very distinctly; having examined it carefully, a few days after its change, he ascertained that the motion of the artery had not at all changed its direction, and that it still <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to move from the tail towards the head as in the caterpillar. Further observations can alone determine which of these two opinions is the most correct. One anatomist has lately asserted that the dorsal canal observable in insects, serves the purpose of respiration. Cuvier has proved, that the conglomerate glands which are to be met with in all the animals that have a heart, do not exist in insects; but instead of them, that they are furnished with very long slender vessels which float in the internal cavities of the body, without being even connected into fasciculi; from this circumstance Cuvier is disposed to believe that insects have no heart. It is by means of these fine tubes that the different fluids are secreted, which are peculiar to various kinds of insects. Some insects discharge an acrid and fetid fluid, others discharge an oil of a very pleasant smell. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEE">bee</a>, the wasp, the sphex, the crysis, have two vessels situated at the bottom of their sting, which contain a very acrid fluid, secreted from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of blood, which the animal discharges at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> through a perforation in the sting; it is this fluid which causes the pain, In the scorpion, there is a fluid of a very malignant nature, which the animal discharges at pleasure through its sting; under certain circumstances, this fluid produces fatal effects. Some of the spiders discharge a fluid, which renders their bite dangerous. The *aranea avicularia*, and the *tarantula*, in particular, are well known; even the common spiders inflict a fatal wound on the insects they entangle in their web. The silk of the common silk-worm and other caterpillars, according to Malpighi, Lyonnet, and others, is a fluid contained in two vessels, which are of a considerable size at the extremity, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAPER">taper</a> towards the mouth, and become very slender. The *carabus* and *dytiscus* contain an acid which reddens the infusion of limes. The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANT">ant</a> contains an acid well known to chemists. The acid <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> contained in the body of the *lytta vesicatoria*, is used in medicine, and forms the best epispastic we are acquainted with. **Generation of Insects.** Insects are the only animals without vertebrae in which the sexes are distinguished. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPULATION">Copulation</a> is performed in them by the introduction of the parts of generation of the male into those of the female. All insects are either male or female, except in a few of the genera of the order *Hymenoptera* (such as the bee, ant, &c.), where individuals are to be found, which are neither male nor female; and, on that account, called *neuters*. Among the bees, the neuters form the far greater part of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>, and perform the office of labourers. Among the ants, the neuters are very numerous, and constitute the only <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> members of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. It has been alleged that these neuters are nothing but females, whose parts have not been developed for want of proper nourishment. Olivier, however, after strict <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, is disposed to think them really different, though he does not adduce facts sufficient to establish his opinion. The parts which distinguish the male from the female, may be divided into two classes, viz. 1. Those which are not directly connected with generation. 2. Those which are absolutely necessary for the purposes of generation. The circumstances which have no direct communication with generation, which serve to point out the distinction between the sexes, are, 1. The difference of size observable in the male and female. 2. The brightness of the colour in each. 3. The form and number of articulations of the antennae. 4. The size and form of their wings. 5. The presence or absence of a sting. The male is always smaller than the female. The female ant is nearly six times larger than the male. The female cockroach is from 12 to 15 times the size of the male. The female termites is 200 or 300 times the size of the male. The colours of the male are commonly much more brilliant than those of the female; this is particularly the case in lepidopterous insects. In some insects, the colour of the male is totally different from that of the female. The antennae of the male are commonly of a different form, and larger than those of the female. Frequently the males are furnished with wings, while the females have none; the *lampyris*, *coccus*, and *blatta*, and several moths, afford an example of this. The female bee is furnished with a sting, while the male is destitute of one. The males of some insects are furnished with sharp prominent <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, resembling horns, situated either on the head or breast, which are either not perceptible or very faintly marked in the female. The parts essential to generation afford the best distinguishing mark. In most insects they are situated near the extremity of the rectum. By pressing the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a> near to the anus they may frequently be made to protrude. But the parts of generation are not always situated near the anus. In the spiders they are situated in the feelers. In the *libellula*, the male organ is situated in the breast, while that of the female is placed at the anus. **Organs of Generation.** In male insects, the organs which serve for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of the semen, bear some resemblance to those organs in the animals which compose the class *Mammalia*. All of them have four organs, two of which may be compared to the testicles, and the other two to the *vesicula seminalis*. They vary very much in form in different species. During the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> the male is usually employed in impregnating the female, these parts are very distinct; after that, they disappear totally. In the larger aquatic insects, (particularly in the *hydrophilus*) besides these four organs already mentioned, there are other two small vesicles, which may be compared to the prostate gland of the superior animals. The *vasa deferentia* in the *hydrophilus* are somewhat reflected; its testicles are very large, and terminate in a very slender folded filament. In the grasshopper, these four organs are likewise found, but the *vesicula seminales* are of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> nature; the testicles have a good deal the appearance of those of the *mammalia*. They are of an oval form, and are fixed to the inside of the back, their convex surface is covered with several tubes of a bright <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> colour. After these <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> tubes have been removed, the testicles are easily unfolded; like all the other secretory organs of insects, they seem to be nothing but a collection of convoluted vessels. The *vesicula seminalis*, which are attached to the testicles, are formed into clusters. In the season of copulation, they increase in bulk so much as nearly to occupy three-fourths of the abdomen; they are full of a lipoid fluid, which is the semen. The *vasa deferentia*, which in most insects are very short, in the *blatta mucronata* are of a considerable length, and form several convolutions before they arrive at the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PENIS">penis</a>. The *penis*, in insects, is either single or double. Those which have a single penis, have it placed at the posterior extremity of the abdomen; in the *libellula*, however, it is placed at the anterior part: it is membranaceous externally; internally it is composed of a substance analogous to the *corpus cavernosum* of other animals; its form is either cylindrical or conical; it is furnished with two scales, one on each side, which form a sort of wedge; this wedge being introduced into the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VAGINA">vagina</a> of the female, and the scales being separated by means of particular muscles, which are situated at their base, open the vagina, and make way for the introduction of the penis. penis. This singular construction is perhaps owing to the want of a proper erection. Insects which have a double penis (such as the spider) have this organ placed at the extremity of the feelers of the lower jaw; these feelers are large in the male. During copulation, they are introduced into two vaginas situated in the anterior part of the abdomen of the female. In these insects, the two small scales are likewise to be found, which serve to open the vagina of the female. The female is furnished with two ovaries; they are long tubular <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>, in which the eggs are arranged like a string of beads. The eggs which are situated next the opening into the oviduct, are largest, and they diminish gradually as they recede from it, till they disappear altogether. The tubular canals unite, and terminate in a common canal, which communicates with an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> cavity, analogous to the uterus. It is in this cavity that the semen of the male is deposited. Malpighi asserts that the fluid penetrates into the oviduct, by means of a canal of communication, and that the eggs are fecundated the instant they pass the mouth of this canal, as they proceed towards the external orifice of the uterus. In viviparous insects, such as the hippopotamus, scorpion, &c., the ovaries are different. Sometimes the little animals are arranged in clusters; at other times they compose a spiral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CORD">cord</a>, the length of which corresponds to the number and size of the foetus. Copulation is not performed exactly in the same way by all insects. In most of the species, the male mounts on the back of the female; but the spiders, dragon-flies, and some others, have a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of performing copulation peculiar to themselves. After copulation, they soon begin to lay their eggs. Some deposit their eggs gradually, one after another; others discharge them all at once, for example, the ephemera, the very short <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> of whose existence renders this necessary. But the far greater number of insects lay them one by one. There are some which lay a considerable number at the same time. The large blue flesh-fly (<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSCA">musca</a> carnaria) when it finds carrion in a proper state for the reception of its eggs, deposits a good number of them at once in the same place; but when it does not find a proper situation in which to deposit its eggs, it can refrain for some time, till it find a proper place and opportunity. There are some insects that do not lay their eggs till a very long time after copulation; bees, wasps, &c., are impregnated before winter, but do not lay their eggs till <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>. Eggs of Insects. The eggs of insects are of two sorts; the first membranaceous, like the eggs of the tortoise and the other reptiles; the other covered with a shell like those of the birds; their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> varies exceedingly; some are round, some elliptical, some lenticular, some cylindrical, some pyramidal, some flat, some <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, but the round and oval are the most common. The eggs of insects seldom increase in size, from the time they have been deposited by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> till they are hatched. Those of the tenthredo, however, and of some others, are observed to increase in bulk. At first there is nothing to be perceived in the eggs of insects but a watery fluid; and after some little time an obscure point is observable in the centre; which, according to Swammerdam, is not the insect itself, but only its head, which first acquires consistence and colour. And the same author alleges, that insects do not increase in bulk in the egg, but that their parts only acquire shape and consistence. Under the shell of the egg there is a thin and very delicate pellicle, in which the insect is enveloped, which may be compared to the chorion and amnion which surround the foetus in quadrupeds. The little insect remains in the egg till the fluids are dissipated, and till its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> have acquired strength to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the egg, and make its escape. The different species of insects remain enclosed in the egg for very different periods. Some continue enclosed only a few days, others remain for several months. The eggs of many insects remain without being hatched during the whole winter; and the young insects do not come forth from them till the season at which the leaves of the vegetables on which they feed begin to expand. When the insects are ready to break their prison, they commonly attempt to pierce the shell with their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, and form a circular hole, through which they put forth first one leg, and then another, till they extricate themselves entirely. Number of Insects. Insects are by far the most numerous class of animals. About eleven thousand species have been described by Gmelin in the last edition of the System of Nature. A great many more have been described by other naturalists since the publication of that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and a very considerable number are to be met with in the cabinets of the curious, which have not as yet been described by any author. In those parts of the world which we are best acquainted with, we may easily suppose that many species of insects exist which have hitherto escaped notice. The minuteness of some insects makes them easily overlooked; the agility of others renders the catching of them difficult. The retired situations which many of them haunt favour their concealment. In the unexplored parts of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, many hundred species must exist utterly unknown to naturalists. All these circumstances render it very probable that not one half of the insects which exist in the world have hitherto been described. Utility of Insects. Insects afford nourishment to a great number of the superior animals; many of the fishes, reptiles, and birds, draw the principal part of their sustenance from that source. The immense swarms of different species of crab which abound in every <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, directly or indirectly form the principal part of the food of the cod, haddock, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERRING">herring</a>, and a great variety of fishes. The snake, lizard, frog, and many other reptiles, feed both on <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> and aquatic insects. Gallinaceous fowls, and many of the small birds, &c., feed on insects. Swallows, indeed, feed entirely on-winged insects. They afford food likewise to many of the mammalia, &c., to many species of the bat, to the ant-eater, &c., and even to man himself. Many species of crab, viz. lobster, common crab, shrimp, prawn, land-crab, &c., are reckoned delicacies. The larve of some coleopterous insects and locusts form part of the food of man. Insects likewise, by consuming decayed animal and vegetable... vegetable matter, which if left to undergo the putrefactive <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>, on the surface of the ground, might taint the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> with pestilential vapours, preserve the air pure for the respiration of man and other animals. Preservation of Insects in Cabinets. In collecting insects, both male and female ought if possible to be procured; and the time of the year when they are taken ought to be noted. Specimens with injured wings or antennae must be rejected. For collecting insects in their perfect state, a sort of forceps are made use of, which have their extremities covered with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAUZE">gauze</a>. Besides these, the entomologist, in his walks, should be furnished with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PIN">pin</a>-cushion, stored with pins of various sizes, and a tin box lined with cork, of a convenient size for the pocket in which the insects when caught are to be placed; the lepidopterous insects being first carefully killed by squeezing their thorax, lest their fluttering should injure their wings. Coleopterous insects are most expeditiously killed by being immersed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> water; and those who prefer this method may carry them home without injury in common pillboxes. Most insects are killed with a few drops of spirit of turpentine; the lepidoptera and hymenoptera may easily be killed by being stuck through with a pin dipt in aquafortis. When the insects are killed they are to be transixed with pins, their wings, antennae, and feet spread out and kept displayed. In some of the lepidoptera, two specimens should be preserved; the wings in the one displayed, and in the other placed as much as possible in their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> position. Insects may likewise be collected by breeding them from their larvae; and this, when it is convenient, is by far the best method for procuring fine specimens; it is chiefly practised with the lepidopterous kinds. When the caterpillars are taken, they are to be fed on the leaves of the plant or tree on which they were found, and kept in a box with some moist <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> at the bottom; they will afterwards turn into a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHRYSALIS">chrysalis</a>, either by going into the earth, by <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> a web and enclosing themselves in it, or by changing into a pupa obtecta, according to their kinds. Having continued in this state their appointed time, the perfect insect will come forth, and must then be killed before it has injured its wings by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a>. Lepidopterous insects are likewise to be collected in their pupa state, by seeking for them under the projections of garden walls, pales, and out-houses, summerhouses, &c. or by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> for them in the winter months under the trees they feed on. When thus dug up, they are to be put into a box with moist earth, and kept till they come out. When the insects are prepared in this manner, they are to be placed in the cabinet, which may consist of boxes or drawers deep enough to hold a long pin, and lined on the bottom with cork, or with wax; the insects of each order in drawers by themselves; and the different genera close together. The generic and trivial name of each insect is to be written on a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, fixed to the bottom by the same pin which supports the insect. The drawers must be made to shut very close, so as to exclude the dust and minute insects; some cover them with glass. A little camphor in each drawer is likewise useful. Insects of the aptera order, such as spiders, scolopendre, juli, &c. are best preserved in some kind of spirits. The onisci and cancri may be preserved like beetles.

ENTREPAS

in the manege, a broken pace <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> going, that is neither walk nor trot, but has somewhat of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMBLE">amble</a>. This is a pace or gait of such horses as have no reins or back, and go upon their shoulders; or, of such as are spoiled in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>.

ENTRING LADDERS

Pages 269-269

in a ship, are of two sorts; one used by the vessel's sides, in a harbour, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in fair <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, for persons to go in and out of the ship; the other is made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, with small staves for steps; and is hung out of the gallery to enter into the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>, or to come aboard the ship, when the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> runs so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> that they durst not bring the boat to the ship's side for fear of staving it.

ENTROCHUS

Pages 269-269

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a genus of extraneous fossils, usually of about an inch in length, and made up of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of round <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>, which, when separate and loose, are called trochite: They are composed of the same kind of plated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAR">spar</a> with the fossil shells of the echini, which is usually of a bluish-gray <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and very bright where fresh broken; they are all striated from the centre to the circumference, and have a cavity in the middle. The entrochi are found of all sizes, from that of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PIN">pin</a>'s head to a finger's length, and the thickness of one's middle finger; and are plainly of marine origin, having often <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-shells adhering to them. They are sometimes known by the name of St Cuthbert's beads, and are usually found in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a>.

ENTRY

Pages 269-269

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies taking possession of lands <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> tenements, where a person has a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> so to do. ENTRY of an Heir, in Scots Law, that form of law by which an heir vests in himself a proper <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to his predecessor's estate. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">Bill</a> of Entry, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. See Bill. In making entries inwards, it is usual for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> to include all the goods they have on board the same ship in one bill, though sometimes they may happen to be upwards of 20 several kinds: and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the goods are short entered, additional or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> entries are now allowed; though formerly the goods so entered were forfeited. As to bills of entry outwards, or including goods to be exported, upon delivering them, and paying the customs, you <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> receive a small piece of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a> called a cocket, which testifies your payment thereof, and all duties for such goods. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> several sorts of goods are exported at once, of which some are free, and others pay customs; the exporter must have two cockets, and therefore must make two entries; one for the goods that pay, and the other for the goods that do not pay <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>. Entries of goods, on which a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWBACK">drawback</a> is allowed, must likewise contain the name of the ship in which the goods were imported, the importer's name, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of entry inwards. The entry being thus made, and an oath taken that the customs for those goods were paid as the law directs, you must carry it to the collector and comptroller, or their deputies; who, after examining their books, will <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> warrant, which must be given to the surveyor, searcher, or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>-waiter, for them to certify the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of goods; after which the certificate must be brought back to the collector and comptroller, or their deputies, and oath made that the said goods are really shipped, and not landed again in any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>.

ENUMERATION

Pages 269-269

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERORATION">peroration</a>: in which the orator, collecting the scattered heads of what has been delivered throughout the whole, makes a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> and artful relation <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> recapitulation thereof.

ENVELOPE

Pages 269-269

in Fortification, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, sometimes in form of a simple <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a>, and at others like a small rampart with a parapet: it is raised sometimes on the ditch, and sometimes beyond it.

ENVIRONNE

Pages 269-269

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, signifies surrounded with other things: thus, they say, a lion environné with so many bezants. See BEZANTS.

ENVOY

Pages 269-269

a person deputed to negotiate some affair with any foreign <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> state. Those sent from the courts of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, France, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, &c., to any petty princes or state, such as the princes of Germany, the republics of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>, &c., go in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of envoys, not ambassadors; and such a character only do those persons bear, who go from any of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> courts of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> to another, when the affair they go upon is not very solemn or important. There are envoys ordinary and extraordinary, as well as ambassadors; they are equally under the protection of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW_OF_NATIONS"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> of nations, and enjoy all the privileges of ambassadors; only differing from them in this, that the same ceremonies are not performed to them.

EONIANS

Pages 269-270

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the followers of Eon, a wild fanatic of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Bretagne, in the 12th century, whose brain was disordered. He concluded from the resemblance between cum, in the form for exercising malignant spirits, viz. Per cum, qui venturus est judicare vivos et mortuos, and his own name Eon, that he was the son of God, and ordained to judge the quick and dead. Eon, however, was solemnly condemned by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHEIMS">Rheims</a>, in 1148, at which Pope Eugenius III. presided, and ended his days in a miserable Eosians miserable prison. He left behind him a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of followers and adherents, whom <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> so weakly and cruelly employed could not persuade to abandon his cause, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to renounce an absurdity which, says Mosheim, one would think could never have gained <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>, but in such a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> as Bedlam.

EORIA

Pages 270-270

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, a feast celebrated by the Athenians in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Erginos, who, by way of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> for their not avenging the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his father <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ICARUS">Icarus</a>, engaged the gods to inflict the curse on their daughters, that they should <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a> men who never returned their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>. The feast was instituted by the order of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>.

EOSTRE

Pages 270-270

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, a Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> to whom they sacrificed in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of April, called the month of Easter; and thence the name Easter, which the Saxons retained after their conversion to Christianity, applying it to the festival celebrated in commemoration of our Saviour's <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a>.

EPACRIS

Pages 270-270

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandra class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EPACTS

Pages 270-270

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a>, the excess of the solar <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> above the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNODICAL">synodical</a> month, and of the solar year above the lunar year of twelve synodical months; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of several solar months above as many synodical months, and several solar years above as many dozen of synodical months. The epacts, then, are either annual or menstrual. Menstrual epacts are the excesses of the civil or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a> months above the lunar month. Suppose, e.g., it were new <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> on the first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>; since the lunar month is 29 days 12h. 44' 3", and the month of January contains 31 days, the menstrual epact is 1 day 11h. 15' 57". Annual epacts are the excesses of the solar year above the lunar. Hence, as the Julian solar year is 365 days 6h. and the Julian lunar year 354 days 8h. 48' 38", the annual epact <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be 10 days 21h. 11' 22"; that is, nearly 11 days. Consequently the epact of 2 years is 22 days; of 3 years, 33 days; or rather 3, since 30 days make an embolismic or intercalary month. Thus the epact of 4 years is 14 days, and so of the rest; and thus every 19th year, the epact becomes 30 or 0; consequently the 20th year the epact is 11 again; and so the cycle of epacts expires with the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, or lunar cycle of 19 years, and begins with the same, as in the following <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>: | <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a>. Numb. | Epacts. | Gold. Numb. | Epacts. | Gold. Numb. | Epacts. | |------------|---------|------------|---------|------------|---------| | 1 | XI | 8 | XXVIII | 14 | IV | | 2 | XII | 9 | IX | 15 | XV | | 3 | III | 10 | XX | 16 | XXVI | | 4 | XIV | 11 | I | 17 | VIII | | 5 | XXV | 12 | XII | 18 | XIX | | 6 | VI | 13 | XIII | 19 | XXX | | 7 | XVII | | | | | Again, as the new moons are the same, that is, as they <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> on the same day every 19 years, so the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the lunar and solar year is the same every 19 years. And because the said difference is always to be added to the lunar year, in order to adjust Epact, or make it equal to the solar year; hence the said difference respectively belonging to each year of the moon's cycle is called the epact of the said year, that is, the number to be added to the said year, to make it equal to the solar year; the word being formed from the Greek επάκτης, induco, intercalo. Upon this mutual respect between the cycle of the moon and the cycle of the epacts, is founded this rule for finding the Julian epact, belonging to any year of the moon's cycle. Multiply the year given of the moon's cycle into 11; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the product be less than 30, it is the epact sought; if the product be greater than 30, divide it by 30, and the remainder of the dividend is the epact. For instance, I would know the epact for the year 1712, which is the third year of the moon's cycle. Wherefore 3 is the epact for 1712; for $11 \times 3 = 33$, and 33 being divided by 30, there is left 3 of the dividend for the epact. But the difference of the Julian and Gregorian years being equal to the excess of the solar above the lunar year, or 11 days, it happens that the Gregorian epact for one year is the same with the Julian epact for the preceding year.

EPAMINONDAS

Pages 270-271

a celebrated Theban, the son of Polymnus, and one of the greatest captains of antiquity. He learned <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and music under Lyssis, a Pythagorean <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>; and was from his infancy inured to all the exercises of body and mind. He was learned, generous, well-skilled in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, brave, modest, and prudent; and had such a regard for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, that he would not tell a falsehood even in jest. He served first under the Lacedemonians; saved the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PELOPIDAS">Pelopidas</a> their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, who received in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> eight wounds; and contracted a strict friendship with that general, which lasted till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. At his persuasions, Pelopidas delivered the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Thebes from the yoke of the Spartans, who had rendered themselves masters of Cadmea, which occasioned a bloody war between the two nations. Epaminondas was made general of the Thebans; on which he gained the celebrated battle of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEUCTRA">Leuctra</a>, in which Cleombrotus, the valiant <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a>, was killed. He then ravaged the enemy's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and caused the city of Messene to be rebuilt and peopled. At length, the command of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> was given to another, because Epaminondas had kept his troops in the field four months longer than he had been ordered by the people; but, instead of retiring in disgust, he now served as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> soldier, and distinguished himself by so many brave actions, that the Thebans, ashamed of having deprived him of the command, restored him to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a>, in order to carry the war into Thessaly, where his arms were always victorious. A war breaking out between the Elians and the inhabitants of Mantinea, the Thebans took the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the former. Epaminondas then resolved to endeavour to surprise Sparta and Mantinea; but not succeeding, he gave the enemy battle, in which he received a mortal wound with a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVELIN">javelin</a>, the bearded <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> remaining in the wound. Knowing that it could not be drawn out without occasioning immediate death, he would not suffer it to be touched, but <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to give his orders; and on his being told, that the enemy were entirely defeated, "I have lived <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> enough (he cried), EPANALEPSIS. See ORATORY, No 73. EPANODOS. Ibid. No 73. EPANORTHOSIS. Ibid. No 73.

EPARER

Pages 271-271

in the manege, signifies the flinging of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> his jerking and striking with his hindlegs.

EPAULEMENT

Pages 271-271

in Fortification, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> raised to cover sidewise, is either of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, gabions, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fascines loaded with earth. The epaulements of the places of arms for the cavalry, at the entrance of the trenches, are generally of fascines mixed with earth.

EPAULETTES

Pages 271-271

are a kind of shoulder-knots chosen for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, which are to be of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the facing, with a narrow <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> tape round it, and worsted fringe; those for the officers are made of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> or silver <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LACE">lace</a>, with a rich fringe; they are badges of distinction worn on one or both shoulders. Those of the dragoon-guards, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, and dragoons, are worn on the left shoulder: the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> dragoons, and officers of grenadiers, have one on each shoulder: those of the battalion wear one on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> shoulder only, which is to be made of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMBROIDERY">embroidery</a> or lace with a gold or silver fringe. Those of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> regiment of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> are to be gold and embroidery, with gold fringe or scarlet cloth, and worn on the right shoulder.

EPENTHESIS

Pages 271-271

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, the interposition <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> insertion of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a> in the middle of a word; as altium, for altium; religio, for religio; induperator, for imperator, &c.

EPEUS

Pages 271-271

of the line of Endymion, the inventor of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTERING">battering</a>-ram, an engine of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in sieges to make a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a>. He is thought to have built the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, and to have founded the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Mota-pontum.

EPHA

Pages 271-271
or EPHAH, in Jewish antiquity, a measure for things dry, equal to 3 pecks and 3 pints. EPHEBÆUM, in antiquity, the place where the ephebi or youth exercised; or, as some say, where those who designed to exercise met, and agreed what kind of exercise they should contend in, and what should be the victor's reward.

EPHANY

Pages 278-278

a Christian festival, otherwise called the Manifestation of Christ to the Gentiles, observed on the sixth of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the appearance of our Saviour to the three <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGI">magi</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> wise men, who came to adore him and bring him presents. The feast of epiphany was not originally a distinct festival; but made a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of that of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATIVITY">nativity</a> of Christ, which being celebrated 12 days, the first and last of which were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> days of solemnity, either of these might properly be called epiphany, as that word signifies the appearance of Christ in the world. The word in the original Greek, ἐπίφανες, signifies appearance or apparition; and was applied, as some critics <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> have it, to this feast, on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a> which appeared to the magi.—St Jerome and St Chrysostom take the epiphany for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of our Saviour's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, when he was declared to men by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, Hic est filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi complacui: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." And accordingly it is still observed by the Coptic and Ethiopians in that view. Others contend, that the feast of Christmas, or the nativity of our Saviour, was held in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> churches on this day; which had the denomination epiphany or appearance, by reason of our Saviour's first appearance on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. And it must be allowed, that the word is used among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greek fathers, not for the appearance of the star to the magi, but for that of our Saviour to the world: In which <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> St Paul uses the word epiphanias in his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> epistle to Timothy, i. 10. EPHONEMA. See ORATORY, No. 96.

EPHEBI

Pages 271-271

among the Athenians, a designation given to their young men when they arrived at 18 years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they had their names entered in a public <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a>. EPHE德拉, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dicotyledon class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 5th order, Coniferæ. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EPHEMERA

Pages 271-271

the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">Day</a>-fly, a genus of insects belonging to the order of neuroptera. See ENTOMOLOGY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EPHEMERIDES

Pages 271-271

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, tables calculated by astronomers, shewing the present state of the heavens for every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> at noon; that is, the places wherein all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> are found at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. It is from these tables that the eclipses, conjunctions, and aspects of the planets are determined; horoscopes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> celestial schemes, constructed, &c. We have ephemerides of Origan, Kepler, Argoli, Heckerus, Mezzarachis, Wing, De la Hire, Parker, &c. S. Cassini has calculated ephemerides of the sidera medicae or satellites of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, which are of good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in determining the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>. In England, the Nautical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALMANACK">Almanack</a>, or Astronomical Ephemeris, published annually by anticipation, under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the commissioners of longitude, is the most considerable. In France, celestial ephemerides have been published by M. Desplaces every ten years, from 1715 to 1745; they were afterwards <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> by the Abbé Caille, with many additions; of which an account may be seen in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Academy of Sciences for 1743. The Academy of Sciences have likewise published annually, from the beginning of the present century, a kind of ephemeris under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Connaissance des Temps.

EPHESUS

Pages 271-273

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of antiquity, much celebrated on account of its temple of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>, and for being the most famous mart <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> staple town of Hither <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. Ephesus was in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of all Asia. Stephanus gives it the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Ephiphanestates, or most illustrious; and Pliny styles it the ornament of Asia. The ancient city stood about 50 miles south of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a>, near the mouth of the river Cayster, and the shore of the Icarian <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, which is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the Ægean; but as it has been so often destroyed and rebuilt, it is no easy <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> to determine the precise <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. Most of our <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> travellers are of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the ancient city stood more to the south than the present; which they argue from the ruins that still remain. Ephesus was, in ancient times, known by the names of Alope, Ortigia, Morges, Smyrna, Trachae, Samornion, and Ptole. It was called Ephesus, according to Heracles, from the Greek word ephesus, signifying permission; because <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> (says he) permitted the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMAZONS">Amazons</a> to live and build a city in that place. Others tell us, that Ephesus was the name of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMAZON">Amazon</a> that founded the city; for Pliny, Justin, and Orosius, unanimously affirm that it was built by an Amazon; while others bestow this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> upon Androcles, the son of Codrus <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, who was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the Ionians that settled in Asia. But, in matters of so early a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a>, it is impossible to come at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, and therefore not worth our while to dwell on such fruitless inquiries. What we know for certain is, that the city, which in the Roman times was the metropolis of all Asia, acknowledged Lysimachus for its founder; for that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, having caused the ancient city to be entirely demolished, rebuilt, at a vast expense, a new one, in a place more convenient, and nearer the temple. Strabo tells us, that, as the inhabitants shewed a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reluctance to quit their ancient habitations, Lysimachus caused all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAINS">drains</a> that conveyed the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> into the neighbouring fens and the Cayster to be privately stopped up; whereby the city being on the first violent rains in great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> laid under water, and many of the inhabitants drowned, they were glad to abandon the ancient and retire. This new Ephesus was greatly damaged by an earthquake in the reign of Tiberius, but by that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> repaired and adorned with several stately buildings, of which there are now but few ruins to be seen, and scarce any thing worthy of ancient Ephesus. The aqueduct, part of which is still standing, is generally believed to have been the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of the Greek emperors; the pillars which support the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> are of fine marble, and higher or lower as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the water required. This aqueduct served to convey water into the city from the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of Halites, mentioned by Pausanias. The gate, now called by the inhabitants, for what reason we know not, the Gate of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSECUTION">Persecution</a>, is remarkable for three bas-reliefs on the mould, of an exquisite <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. The port, of which so many medals have been struck, is at present but an open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, and not much frequented. The Cayster was formerly navigable, and afforded a safe place for ships to ride in, but is now almost choked up with sand. But the chief ornament of Ephesus was the temple of Diana, built at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of all the states in Asia, and for its structure, size, and furniture, accounted among the wonders of the world. This great edifice was situated at the foot of a mountain, and at the head of a marsh; which place they chose, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we believe Pliny, as the least subject to earthquakes. This site doubled the charges; for they were obliged to be at a vast expense in making drains to convey the water that came <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the hill into the morass and the Cayster. Philo Byzantius tells us, that in this work they used such a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, as almost exhausted all the quarries in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and these drains or vaults are what the present inhabitants take for a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LABYRINTH">labyrinth</a>. To secure the foundations of the conduits or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEWERS">sewers</a>, which were to bear a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of such a prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, they laid beds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a>, says Pliny, well rammed, and upon them others of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>. Two hundred and twenty years, Pliny says 400, were spent in building this wonderful temple by all Asia. It was 425 feet in length, and 200 in breadth, supported by 127 marble pillars, 70 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, of which 27 were most curiously carved, and the rest polished. These pillars were the works of so many kings, and the bas-reliefs of one were done by Scopas, the most famous sculptor of antiquity; the altar was almost wholly the work of Praxiteles. Cheiromocrates, who built the city of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, and offered to form Mount <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHOS">Athos</a> into a statue of Alexander, was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a> employed on this occasion. The temple enjoyed the privilege of an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a>, which at first extended to a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FURLONG">furlong</a>, was afterwards enlarged by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MITHRIDATES">Mithridates</a> to a bow-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>, and doubled by Mark Antony, so that it took in part of the city; but Tiberius, to put a stop to the many abuses and disorders that attend privileges of this kind, revoked them all, and declared, that no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> guilty of any wicked or dishonest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> should escape <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, though he fled to the altar itself. The priests who officiated in this temple were held in great esteem, and trusted with the care of sacred virgins, or priestesses, but not till they were made <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUNUCHS">eunuchs</a>. They were called Estiatoria and Essencia, had a particular diet, and were not allowed by their constitutions to go into any private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. They were maintained with the profits accruing from the lake Selinus, and another that fell into it, which must have been very considerable, since they erected a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> statue to one Artemidorus, who being sent to Rome, recovered them after they had been seized by the farmers of the public revenues. All the Ionians resorted yearly to Ephesus with their wives and children, where they solemnized the festival of Diana with great pomp and magnificence, making on that occasion rich offerings to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>, and valuable presents to her priests. The asiarche, mentioned by St Luke, were, according to Beza, those priests whose peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> it was to regulate the public sports that were annually performed at Ephesus in honour of Diana: they were maintained with the collections made during the sports; for all Asia flocked to see them. The great Diana of the Ephesians, as she was styled by her <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> adorers, was, according to Pliny, a small statue of ebony, made by one Canitia, though <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> believed to have been sent down from heaven by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>. This statue was first placed in a niche, which, as we are told, the Amazons caused to be made in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> of an elm. Such was the first rise of the veneration that was paid to Diana in this place. In <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the veneration for the goddess daily increasing among the inhabitants of Asia, a most stately and magnificent temple was built near the place where the elm stood, and the statue of the goddess placed in it. This was the first temple; but not quite so sumptuous as that which we have described, though reckoned, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, among the wonders of the world. The second, being that above described, was remaining in Pliny's time and in Strabo's; and is supposed to have been destroyed in the reign of Constantine, pursuant to the edict by which that emperor commanded all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> of the heathens to be thrown down and demolished: the former was burnt the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> that Alexander was born, by one Erostratus, who owned on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACK">rack</a>, that the only thing which had prompted him to destroy so excellent a work, was the desire of transmitting his name to future ages. Whereupon the common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Asia made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a>, forbidding any one to name him; but this prohibition served only to make his name more memorable, such a remarkable extravagance, or rather madness, being taken notice of by all the historians who have written of those times. Alexander offered to rebuild the temple at his own expence, provided the Ephesians would agree to put his name on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a>; but they rejected his offer in such a manner as prevented the resentment of that vain prince, telling him, that "it was not fit one god should build a temple to another." The pillars, and other materials that had been saved out of the flames, were sold, and also the jewels of the Ephesian women, who on that occasion willingly parted with them; and the sum raised from thence served for the carrying on of the work till other contributions came in, which in a short time amounted to an immense <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>. This is the temple which Strabo, Pliny, and other Roman writers speak of. It stood between the city and the port, and was built, or rather finished, as Livy tells us, in the reign of King Servius. Of this wonderful structure there is nothing at present remaining but some ruins, and a few broken pillars. The Ionians first settled at Ephesus under the conduct of Androclus, who drove out the Carians and Leleges, by whom those places were possessed at his arrival. The city, whether built by him, as Strabo affirms, or by Croesus or Ephesus, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before the Ionic <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIGRATION">migration</a>, as others maintain, became soon the metropolis of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>. It was at first governed by Androclus, and his descendants, who assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> title, and exercised the regal authority over the new colony; whence, even in Strabo's time, the posterity of Androclus were styled kings, and allowed to wear a scarlet robe, with a sceptre, and all the ensigns of the royal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. In process of time, a new form of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> was introduced, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> established; but when, or on what occasion, this change happened, we know not. This kind of government <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till the time of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>, who lived before <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a> the Great, and was one of the most cruel and inhuman tyrants we read of in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>; for having driven out the senate, and taken all the power into his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, he filled the city with blood and rapine, not sparing even those who fled to the temple of Diana for shelter. Pythagoras was succeeded by Pindarus, who bore the same sway in the city; but treated the citizens with more <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>. In his time Ephesus being besieged by Croesus king of Lydia, he advised the inhabitants to devote their city to Diana, and fasten the wall, by a rope, to the pillars of her temple. They followed his advice, and were, from reverence to the goddess, not only treated with great kindness by Croesus, but restored to their former <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. Pindarus being obliged to resign his power, retired to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>. He was, according to Ælian, grandson to Alyattes king of Lydia, and Croesus's nephew. The other tyrants of Ephesus mentioned in history, are, Athenagoras, Comes, Aristarchus, and Hegesias; of whom the last was expelled by Alexander, who coming to Ephesus, after having defeated the Persians on the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANICUS">Granicus</a>, bestowed upon Diana all the tributes which the Ephesians had paid to the Persians, and established a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEMOCRACY">democracy</a> in the city. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> between Mithridates and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, they sided with the former, and, by his directions, massacred all the Romans that resided in their city; for which barbarity they were severely fined, and reduced almost to beggary by Sulla, but afterwards treated kindly, and suffered to live according to their own laws, as is plain from several ancient <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> and medals. The Ephesians were much addicted to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, sorcery, and curious arts, as the scripture styles them: whence came the proverb "Ephesian letters," signifying all sorts of spells or charms. In the time of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> Paul, Ephesus retained a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of its ancient <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>. But it was a ruinous place; when the emperor <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a> filled Constantinople with its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, and raised his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Sophia upon its columns. Since then it has been almost quite exhausted. Towards the end of the 12th century, a Turkish <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIRATE">pirate</a>, named Tangripermess, settled there. But the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>, John Ducas, defeated him in a bloody <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, and pursued the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> Turks up the Meander. In 1306, it was among the places which suffered from the exactions of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> Roger; and two years after, it surrendered to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SULTAN">Sultan</a> Sayas, who, to prevent future insurrection, removed most of the inhabitants to Tyriacon, where they were massacred. Ephesus appears to have subsisted as an inconsiderable place for some time. But now, the Ephesians are only a few Greek peasants, living in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> wretchedness, dependence, and insensibility; the representatives of an illustrious people, and inhabiting the wreck of their greatness; some, the substructions of the glorious edifices which they raised; some, beneath the vaults of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STADIUM">stadium</a>, once the crowded <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of their diversions; and some, by the abrupt precipice, in the sepulchres which received their ashes. EPHETÆ (from ἐπομένω, "I send forth"), in antiquity, a sort of magistrates among the Athenians, instituted by King Demophoon, to take cognizance of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, manslaughter, and chance-medley. Their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> was 100, whereof 50 were Athenians, and 50 Argians: they were not admitted to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> till upwards of 50 years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRACO">Draco</a> new-modelled it, excluded the Argians out of it, and made it to consist of 51 Athenians, each above 58 years of age: Ubbo Emmius de Rep. Athen. says, he transferred to them part of the jurisdiction of the Areopagites. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AREOPAGUS">AREOPAGUS</a>.

EPHOD

Pages 273-273

in Jewish antiquity, one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the priestly <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>; being a kind of girdle, which, brought from behind the neck over the two shoulders, and hanging <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> before, was put across the stomach, then carried round the waist, and made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of as a girdle to the tunic.—There were two sorts of ephods, one of plain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> for the priests, and the other embroidered for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>.

EPHORA

Pages 278-278

in Medicine, a preternatural fluxion of the eyes, when they continually discharge a sharp serous humour, which excoriates the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a>. See MEDICINE <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EPHORI

Pages 273-273

in Grecian antiquity, magistrates established in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> the regal power. The authority of the ephori was very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>. They sometimes expelled, and even put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> the kings, and abolished <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> suspended the power of the other magistrates, calling them to account at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. There were five of them, others say <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>. They presided in the public shows and festivals. They were entrusted with the public <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>; made <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> and peace; and were so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a>, that <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> makes their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> equal to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>. They were established by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LYCURGUS">Lycurgus</a>, according to the generality of authors: though this is denied by others, who <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> their origin 130 years after the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a>. Thus Plutarch, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of Cleomenes, ascribes their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> to Theopompus <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Sparta; which is also confirmed by the authority of Aristotle.

EPHORUS

Pages 273-273

an orator and historian of Cyme in Æolia, about 352 years before Christ. He was <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> to Isocrates, by whose advice he wrote a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> which gave an account of all the actions and battles that had happened between the Greeks and barbarians for 750 years. It was greatly esteemed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; but is now lost.

EPHRAIM

Pages 273-273

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, one of the divisions of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a> by tribes: Ephraim and the half tribe of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANASSEH">Manasseh</a> are blended together by the sacred writer, and it only appears that Ephraim occupied the more southern, and the half tribe of Manasseh the more northern parts, but both seem to have extended from the Jordan to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Ephraim also denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, on the separation of the 10 tribes from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a>, called also the kingdom of Israel and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMARIA">Samaria</a>.

EPHRATA

Pages 273-274

EPHRATA, a small town of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PENNSYLVANIA">Pennsylvania</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> settlement of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> called Dunkards <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Tunkers. See Tunkers.

EPHREM SYRUS

Pages 274-274

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Christian writer, in the fourth century, deacon of Edessa, was born at Nisibis in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>. He was greatly esteemed by St <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, St Gregory Nyssen, and other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men. He wrote against the opinions of Sabellius, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIUS">Arius</a>, Apollonarius, the Manichaeans, &c., and acquired such reputation by his virtue and his works, that he was called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> and the prophet of the Syrians. He died in 378. The best editions of his works are, that of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, in 1708, in folio, and that of Rome, from 1732 to 1738, in Syria, Greek, and Latin, 6 vols folio.

EPHYDOR

Pages 274-274

in antiquity, an officer in the Athenian courts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, who was to provide the plaintiff and defendant with equal <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>-glasses. When the glass was run out, they were not permitted to speak any farther; and, therefore, we find them very careful not to lose <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> mispend one drop of their water. Whilst the laws quoted by them were reciting, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any other business happened to intervene, they gave orders that the glass should be stopped. EPIBATÆ, ἐπιβάται, among the Greeks, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARINES">marines</a>, or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> who served on board the ships of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. They were armed in the same manner as the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>-forces, only that more of them wore full or heavy armour.

EPIBATERION

Pages 274-274

a poetical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greeks. When any person of condition and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> returned home after a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> absence <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> journey into another <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, he called together his friends and fellow citizens, and made them a speech, or rehearsed them a copy of verses, wherein he returned solemn thanks to the immortal gods for his happy return; and ended with an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> by way of compliment to his fellow-citizens.—These verses made what the Greeks call ἐπιβατεῖον, epibaterium, of εἰσέρχομαι, "I go abroad." At going away they had another, called ἐποδοτεῖον.

EPIBATERIUM

Pages 274-274

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the monocotyledon class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EPIC

Pages 274-274
or HEROIC, Poem, a poem expressed in narration, formed upon a story partly real, and partly feigned; representing, in a sublime style, some signal and fortunate action, distinguished by a variety of great events, to form the morals, and affect the mind with the love of heroic virtue. We may distinguish three parts of the definition, namely, the matter, the form, and the end. The matter includes the action of the fable, under which are ranged the incidents, episodes, characters, morals, and machinery. The form comprehends the way or manner of the narration, whether by the poet himself, or by any persons introduced, whose discourses are related: to this branch likewise belong the moving of the passions, the descriptions, discourses, sentiments, thoughts, style, and versification; and besides these, the similes, tropes, figures, and, in short, all the ornaments and decorations of the poem. The end is to improve our morals and increase our virtue. See Poetry.

EPICEDIUM

Pages 274-274

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, a poem rehearsed during the funeral solemnity of persons of distinction.

EPICEDON

Pages 274-274

in the Greek and Latin <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, a poem, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> poetical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of a person.—At the obsequies of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, there were three kinds of discourses usually made; that rehearsed at his bustum or funeral pile, was called ἐνεσίς; that engraven Epicedon on his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>, epitaph; and that spoken in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of his funeral, epicedion. We have two beautiful epicedions in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, that of Euryalus and that of Pallas.

EPICHARMUS

Pages 274-274

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poet and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, born in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, was a scholar of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>. He is said to have introduced <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a> in the reign of Hiero. Horace commends Plautus for imitating him, in following the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHASE">chase</a> of the intrigue so closely as not to give the readers <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> spectators <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to trouble themselves with doubts concerning the discovery. He wrote likewise treatises concerning <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and medicine; but none of his works have been preserved.
