He died aged 90, according to Laertius, who has preserved four verses <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> on his statue.

EPICHIROTONIA

Pages 274-274

among the Athenians. It was ordained by Solon, that once every year the laws should be carefully revised and examined; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any of them were found unsuitable to the present state of affairs, they should be repealed. This was called ἐπιχειροτονία τῶν νόμων, from the manner of giving their suffrages by holding up their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. See a farther account of this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> in Pott. Archæol. Græc. lib. i. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 26. tom. i. p. 242.

EPICOENE

Pages 274-274

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOUNS">nouns</a>, which, under the same gender and termination, mark indifferently the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. Such in Latin is <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUILA">aquila</a>, vespertilio, &c. which signify equally a male <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> female eagle or bat. Grammarians distinguish between epicene and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>. A noun is said to be common of two kinds, when it may be joined either with a masculine or a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMININE">feminine</a> article; and epicene, when it is always joined to some of the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, and yet signifies both genders.

EPICRAPH

Pages 277-277

among antiquarians, denotes the inscription of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, pointing out the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when, the persons by whom, the uses, and the like, for which it was erected.

EPICTETUS

Pages 274-275

a celebrated Stoic <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HIERAPOLIS">Hierapolis</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>, in the first century, was the slave of Epaphroditus, a freedman and one of Nero's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>. Domitian banishing all philosophers from Rome, about the year 94, Epictetus retired to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NICOPOLIS">Nicopolis</a> in Epirus, where he died in a very advanced <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, the earthen <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a> he made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of sold for 3000 drachmas. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>; which was eminent in his own practice, as well as in his recommendation to others: hence he used to say, "That there is no need of adorning a man's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> with rich hangings <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> paintings, since the most graceful furniture is <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a> and modesty, which are lasting ornaments, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> never be the worse for wearing." Of all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> philosophers, he seems to have made the nearest approaches to the Christian morality, and to have had the most <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of God and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">providence</a>. He always possessed a cool and serene mind, unruffled by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>; and was used to say, that the whole of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">moral <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> was included in these words, support and abstain. One <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> Epaphroditus strove in a frolic to wrench his leg; when Epictetus said, with a smile, and free from any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMOTION">emotion</a>, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> you go on, you will certainly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> my leg: but the former redoubling his effort, and striking it with all his strength, he at last broke the bone; when all the return Epictetus made was, "Did not I tell you, Sir, that you would break my Epicurean leg?" No man was more expert at reducing the rigour of the maxims of the Stoics into practice. He conformed himself strictly, both in his discourse and behaviour, to the manners of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a> and Zeno. He waged continual <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with fancy and fortune; and it is an excellence peculiar to himself, that he admitted all the severity of the Stoics without their sourness, and reformed Stoicism as well as professed it; and besides his vindicating the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> as strenuously as Socrates or any Stoic of them all, he declared openly against self-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, the lawfulness of which was maintained by the rest of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. Arrian, his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a>, wrote a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> account of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and death, which is lost; and preserved four books of his discourses and his Enchiridion, of which there have been several editions in Greek and Latin; and, in 1758, a translation of them into English was published by the learned and ingenious Miss Carter.

EPICUREAN PHILOSOPHY

Pages 275-275

the doctrine <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> system of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> maintained by Epicurus and his followers. His philosophy consisted of three parts; canonical, physical, and ethereal. The first was about the canons or rules of judging. The censure which Tully passes upon him for his despising logic, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> hold true only with regard to the logic of the Stoics, which he could not approve of, as being too full of nicety and quirk. Epicurus was not acquainted with the analytical method of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> and argumentation, nor was he so curious in modes and formation as the Stoics. Soundness and simplicity of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, assisted with some <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> reflections, was all his art. His search after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> proceeded only by the senses; to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of which he gave so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a certainty, that he considered them as an infallible rule of truth, and termed them the *first natural <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of mankind*. In the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of this philosophy he laid <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> atoms, space, and gravity, as the first principles of all things: he did not deny the existence of God, but thought it beneath his majesty to concern himself with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> affairs: he held him a blessed immortal Being, having no affairs of his own to take care of, and above meddling with those of others. As to his ethics, he made the supreme good of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to consist in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, and consequently supreme evil in pain. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> itself, says he, teaches us this truth; and prompts us from our birth to procure whatever gives us pleasure, and avoid what gives us pain. To this end he proposes a remedy against the sharpness of pain: this was to divert the mind from it, by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> our whole <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> upon the pleasures we have formerly enjoyed. He held that the wise man must be happy as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as he is wise; the pain, not depriving him of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, cannot deprive him of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>. There is nothing that has a fairer show of honesty than the moral doctrine of Epicurus. Gassendus pretends, that the pleasure in which this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> has fixed the sovereign good, was nothing else but the highest tranquillity of mind, in conjunction with the most perfect <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> of body: but Tully, Horace, and Plutarch, as well as almost all the fathers of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, gives us a very different account of it: indeed the nature of this pleasure, in which the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> happiness is supposed to be seated, is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> problem in the morals of Epicurus. Hence there were two kinds of Epicureans, the rigid and the remiss: the first were those who understood Epicurus's notion of pleasure in the best sense, and placed all their happiness in the pure pleasures of the mind, resulting from the practice of virtue; the loose or remiss Epicureans, taking the word of that philosopher in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> sense, placed all their happiness in bodily pleasures or debauchery.

EPICURUS

Pages 275-275

the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, was born at Gargettium in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>, about 340 B.C. in the 109th Olympiad. He settled at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> in a fine garden he had bought; where he lived with his friends in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> tranquillity, and educated a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of disciples. They lived all in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. The respect which his followers paid to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> is admirable: his school was never divided, but his doctrine was followed as an oracle. His birthday was still kept in Pliny's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> he was born in was observed as a continual festival; and they placed his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> everywhere. He wrote a great many books, and valued himself upon making no quotations. He raised the atomical system to a great reputation, though he was not the inventor of it, but had only made some change in that of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEMOCRITUS">Democritus</a>. As to his doctrine concerning the supreme good <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>, it was very liable to be misrepresented, and some ill effects proceeded from thence, which discredited his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. He was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with perverting the worship of the gods, and inciting men to debauchery; but he did not forget himself on this occasion; he published his opinions to the whole world; he wrote some books of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>; recommended the veneration of the gods, sobriety, and chastity; and it is certain that he lived in an exemplary manner, and conformably to the rules of philosophical <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and frugality. Timocrates, a deserter of his sect, spoke very scandalously of him. Gassendus has given us all he could collect from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> concerning the person and doctrine of this philosopher; who died of a suppression of urine, aged 72.

EPICYCLE

Pages 275-275

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, a little circle whose centre is in the circumference of a greater circle: <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> it is a small orb or sphere, which being fixed in the deferent of a planet, is carried along with it; and yet, by its own peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, carries the planet fastened to it round its proper centre. It was by means of epicycles that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> and his followers solved the various phenomena of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, but more especially their stations and retrogradations.

EPICYCLOID

Pages 275-275

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, a curve <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> by the revolution of the periphery of a circle, along the convex <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> concave side of the periphery of another circle.

EPICYEMA

Pages 275-275

among Physicians, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>; being a false <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOLE">mole</a> happening after the birth of a regular fetus.

EPIDAURUM

Pages 275-275

**EPIDAUROUS**, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> **EPITAUROUS**, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>, on the Adriatic, built the same year, as is said, with Dyrrachium, 430 years after the destruction of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>: a considerable town formerly, but now reduced to a small village, called Ragusi Vecchio; distant six miles from the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Ragusi. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 19°. Lat. 42°. 20'.

EPIDAURUS

Pages 275-276

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Argolis, Argolis, in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>, on the Saronic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, to the south of the promontory Spirecum; called sacred, because of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> veneration paid to Æsculapius, whose temple stood at the distance of five miles from the town. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, during a pestilence, being advised to convey the god to Rome, sent a ship with a solemn embassy, for his conveyance; but while the Epidaurians were in suspense to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> with him, a huge <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a> sailed to the ship; and being taken for the god, was carried to Rome in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> solemnity. Epidaurus stood in a recess of the bay, fronting the east; and was fortified by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, being inclosed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> reaching to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and rendering it difficult of access. It had several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, and in the acropolis <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> citadel was a remarkable statue of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>. The site is now called Epitheatro. The traces are indistinct, and it has probably been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> deserted. The harbour of Epidaurus is long. Its periplos or circuit was 15 stadia or near two miles. The entrance is between mountains, and on a small rocky <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> on the left <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> are ruins of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> fortress. This, it seems, was the point on which a temple of Juno stood. It is frequented by vessels for wood or corn. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROVE">grove</a> of Æsculapius was inclosed by mountains, within which all the sacrifices as well of the Epidaurians as of strangers were consumed. One was called Titthion; and on this the god when an infant was said to have been exposed, and to have been suckled by a she-goat. He was a great physician, and his temple was always crowded with sick persons. Beyond it was the dormitory of the suppliants; and near it, a circular edifice called the Tholos, built by Polycletus, of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble, worth seeing. The grove, besides other temples, was adorned with a portico, and a fountain remarkable for its <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> and decorations. The bath of Æsculapius was one of the benefactions of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ANTONINUS_PIUS">Antoninus Pius</a>, while a Roman senator; as was also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> for the reception of pregnant women and dying persons, who before were removed out of the inclosure, to be delivered or to expire in the open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. The remains are heaps of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, pieces of brick wall, and scattered fragments of marble; besides some churches, or rather piles of rubbish miscalled, being destitute of doors, roofs, or any kind of ornament. The statue of Æsculapius was half as big as that of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Olympius at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. It was made of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, and, as the inscription proved, by Thrasymedes son of Arignotus of Paros. He was represented sitting, holding his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>, with one hand on the head of a serpent, and a dog lying by him. Two Argive heroes, Bellerophon combating with the monster Chimera, and Perseus severing the head of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEDUSA">Medusa</a>, were carved on the throne. Many tablets described the cures performed by the deity, yet he had not escaped contumely and robbery. Dionysius deprived him of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>, affirming that it was unseemly in him to appear in that manner when his father <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> was always seen with his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> smooth. Sylla amassed the precious offerings belonging to him and to Apollo and Jupiter at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELPHI">Delphi</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OLYMPIA">Olympia</a>, to pay his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> before Athens. The marks in the walls testified that a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> had been plucked <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. A few fragments of white marble exquisitely carved occur in the heap of the temple. The inclosure of the temple once abounded in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century six marbles remained, on which were written in the Doric dialect the names of men and women who had been patients of the god, with the distemper each had laboured under, and the remedies he had directed. Dr Chandler found only a couple of votive inscriptions, and two pedestals of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, one of which represented a Roman, and was erected by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the Epidaurians. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STADIUM">stadium</a> was near the temple. It was of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, as most in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> were. At the upper end are seats of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, but these were <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> along the sides only a few yards. A vaulted passage leading underneath into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a>, now choked up, was a private way by which the agonothetæ or presidents with the priests and persons of distinction entered. Two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> cisterns or reservoirs remain, made by Antoninus for the reception of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. Beyond them is a dry water-course; and in the mountain side on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> hand are the marble seats of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, overgrown with bushes. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a> by the ruins are now supposed to possess many excellent properties. To these and a good air, Dr Chandler thinks, with the recreations of the theatre and of the stadium, and to the medicinal knowledge and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> of the priests, may be attributed both the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of the sick and the reputation of Æsculapius. Epidaurus, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> Limera, to distinguish it from the Epidaurus of Argolis; called so, either from its meadows or its commodious harbours (Stephanus, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLODORUS">Apollodorus</a>): a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LACONIA">Laconia</a>, on the Ionian sea, to the south of the Sinus Argolicus, situated where now Molvasia stands, in the Morea. E. Long. 23° 30'. Lat. 35° 40'.

EPIDEMIA

Pages 276-276

in Grecian antiquity, festivals kept in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>, at the stated seasons, when those deities, who could not be present everywhere, were supposed to visit different places, in order to receive the vows of their adorers.

EPIDEMIC

Pages 276-276

among physicians, an epithet of diseases which at certain times are popular, attacking <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> near the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>.

EPIDENDRUM

Pages 276-276

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the gynandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the seventh order, Orchideæ. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.—This is the plant which produces the fruit called vanilla, and which is used in perfuming chocolate, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, and snuff.

EPIDERMIS

Pages 276-276

in Anatomy, the cuticle <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> scarf-skin. See ANATOMY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The word is formed of the Greek επί, on, over; and δέρμα, skin.

EPIDICASIA

Pages 276-276

among the Athenians. Daughters inheriting their parents estate were obliged to marry their nearest relation; which gave occasion to persons of the same family to go to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> with one another, each pretending to be more nearly allied to the heiress than the rest. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> was called ανδροκάσια: and the virgin, about whom the relations contested, ἀνδροκάσια.

EPIDIDYMIS

Pages 276-277

in Anatomy, a little round body, on the back of each testicle; called also parastata. See ANATOMY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. EPIGÆA, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the decandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 18th order, Bicornes. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> Index. EPIDOTÆ, certain deities who presided over the growth- growth of children. They were worshipped by the Lacedemonians, and chiefly invoked by those who were persecuted by the ghosts of the dead, &c.

EPIGASTRIC REGION

Pages 277-277

a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> subdivision of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EPIGLOTTIS

Pages 277-277

in Anatomy, one of the cartilages of the larynx <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> windpipe. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EPIGONI

Pages 277-277

the sons and descendants of the Grecian heroes who were killed in the first Theban <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. The war of the Epigoni is famous in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. It was undertaken ten years after the first. The sons of those who had perished in the first war, resolved to avenge the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of their fathers, and marched against Thebes, under the command of Thersander; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, according to others, of Alcmenon the son of Amphiarau, about 1307 years before Christ. The Argives were assisted by the Corinthians, the people of Messenia, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEGARA">Megara</a>. The Thebans had engaged all their neighbours in their quarrel, as in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> cause. These two hostile armies met and engaged on the banks of the Glissas. The fight was obstinate and bloody, but victory declared for the Epigoni, and some of the Thebans fled to Illyricum with Leodamas their general, while others retired into Thebes, where they were soon besieged, and forced to surrender. In this war Egeialeus was the only one who was killed, and his father Adrastus was the only one who escaped alive in the first war. This whole war, as Pausanias observes, was written in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>; and Callinus, who quotes some of the verses, ascribes them to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, which <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> has been adopted by many writers. "For my <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> (continues the geographer), I own, that next to the Iliad and Odyssey of Homer, I have never seen a finer poem." The descendants of the veteran Macedonians, who served under Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, and who had children by Asiatic women, were also called Epigoni, (Justin).

EPILEPSY

Pages 277-277

in Medicine, the same with what is otherwise called the falling-sickness, from the patient's falling suddenly on the ground. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EPILLOMPHALON

Pages 278-278

in Medicine, an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERNIA">hernia</a> umbilicalis, proceeding from the omentum falling into the region of the umbilicus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> navel. EPILOON. See OMENTUM, ANATOMY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EPILOBUM

Pages 277-277

the Willow <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">Herb</a>; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the octandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 17th order, Calycanthemus. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **EPilogue**, in Oratory, the end <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> conclusion of a discourse, ordinarily containing a recapitulation of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> matters delivered. **Epilogue**, in dramatic <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, a speech addressed to the audience, after the play is over, by one of the principal <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a> therein; usually containing some reflections on certain incidents in the play, especially those in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the person that speaks it; and having somewhat of pleasantry, intended to compose the passions raised in the course of the representation: A practice which is ridiculed by the Spectator; and compared to a merry jigg upon the organ after a good sermon, to wipe away any impressions that might have been made thereby, and send the people away <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> as they came.

EPIMEDIUM

Pages 277-277

Barren-wort; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the tetradria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 24th order, Corydalis. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EPIMENIDES

Pages 277-278

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poet and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, was born at Gnososs in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>. Contrary to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, he always wore his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>; which, according to some, was because he was ashamed of being thought a Cretan; and indeed he does not seem to have had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of his countrymen, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> cited by St Paul be, as it is generally believed to be, his; "The Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, slow bellies." Many stories are related of him, too wonderful to merit <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>; however, his reputation was so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> over all <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, that he was there esteemed a favourite of the gods. The Athenians being afflicted with the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>, and commanded by the oracle to make a solemn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUSTRATION">lustration</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, sent Nicias, the son of Niceratus, with a ship to Crete, to desire Epimenides to come to them. He accepted their invitation, Epimetheus' visitation, accompanied the messengers to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, performed the lustration of the city, and the plague ceased. Here he contracted an acquaintance with Solon, whom he privately instructed in the proper methods for the regulation of the Athenian commonwealth. Having finished his business at Athens, the citizens offered him many valuable presents and high honours, and appointed a ship to carry him back to Crete; but he returned their presents, and would accept of nothing except a little branch of the sacred olive preserved in the citadel; and desired the Athenians to enter into an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with the Gnostics. Having obtained this, he returned to Crete; where he died soon after, aged 157 years: <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> as the Cretans, consistently with their character, pretended, 299. He was a great poet, and wrote 5000 verses on "the genealogy of the gods," 6500 "on the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of the ship Argo and Jason's expedition to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLCHIS">Colchis</a>," and 4000 "concerning <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOS">Minos</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHADAMANTHUS">Rhadamanthus</a>." He wrote also in prose, "Concerning sacrifices and the commonwealth of Crete." St Jerome likewise mentions his "book of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a> and responses." The Lacedemonians procured his body, and preserved it among them by the advice of an oracle; and Plutarch tells us, that he was reckoned the seventh wise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> by those who refused to admit Periander into the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>.

EPIMETHEUS

Pages 278-278

a son of Japetus and Clymene, one of the Oceanides, who inconsiderately married Pandora, by whom he had Pyrrha, the wife of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEUCALION">Deucalion</a>. He had the curiosity to open the box which Pandora had brought with her, and from thence issued a train of evils, which from that moment have never ceased to afflict the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>. Hope was the only one which remained at the bottom of the box, not having a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to escape, and it is she alone who comforts men under misfortunes. Epimetheus was changed into a monkey by the gods, and sent into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> Pithecusa.

EPIPHANIUS

Pages 278-278

St., an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> father of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, born at Besanudcan, a village in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, about the year 332. He founded a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> near the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his birth, and presided over it. He was afterwards elected bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALAMIS">Salamis</a>; when he sided with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PAULINUS">Paulinus</a> against Meletius, and ordained in Palestine Paulinius the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of St Jerome; on which a contest arose between him and John bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>. He afterwards called a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Cyprus, in which he procured a prohibition of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a>'s writings; and made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of all his endeavours to prevail on Theophilus bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> to engage St Chrysostom to declare in favour of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a>; but not meeting with success, he went himself to Constantinople, where he would not have any conversation with St Chrysostom; and formed the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of entering the church of the apostles to publish his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONDEMNATION">condemnation</a> of Origen; but being informed of the danger to which he would be exposed, he resolved to return to Cyprus; but died at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> in the year 403. His works were printed in Greek, at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, 1544, in folio; and were afterwards translated into Latin, in which <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> they have been often reprinted. Petavius revised and corrected the Greek text by two <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>, and published it together with a new translation at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1622. This edition was reprinted at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a> in 1682.

EPIPLOCELE

Pages 278-278

in Medicine, is a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERNIA">hernia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rupture, in which the omentum subsides into the scrotum.

EPIRUS

Pages 278-279

a district of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, bounded on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ETOLIA">Etolia</a>, on the west by the Adriatic, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Thessaly and Macedon, and on the south by the Ionian <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was anciently governed by its own princes, in which state it made a very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. The country, according to Josephus, was first peopled by Dodanim the son of Javan and grandson of Japhet. The people were very warlike; but they <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in their <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> state <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> after their neighbours were civilized; whence the islanders used to threaten their offenders with transportation to Epirus. Their horses were in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> request among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, as well as the dogs produced in one of the divisions called Molossus; and hence these dogs were called by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> Molossi. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Epirus commences with the reign of Pyrrhus the son of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a> by Deidamia the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Lycomedes <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Scyros. He is said to have behaved with great bravery at the siege of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>; but it would appear that he behaved with no less barbarity. After the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> was taken, he is said to have killed old King Priam with his own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; to have thrown <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTYANAX">Astyanax</a> the son of Hector and Andromache headlong from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> tower; and sacrificed Polyxena the daughter of Priam on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of his father. He carried Andromache with him into Epirus, where he settled by the advice of the famous soothsayer Helenus, one of Priam's sons, who had served during the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> both under his father and himself. The only remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of the history of Epirus is the reign of Pyrrhus II, who made war upon the Romans. He was invited into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> by the Tarentines; and embarked about 280 B.C. After having escaped many dangers by sea, he landed in that country, and with great difficulty gained a victory over the Romans; but he was afterwards utterly defeated by them, and obliged to return into his own country. To retrieve his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, he then undertook an expedition against Macedon; where he overthrew Antigonus, and at last made himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. He then formed a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of subduing all the other Grecian states; but met with such an obstinate resistance at Lacedaemon, that he was obliged to drop the enterprise; and was soon after killed at the siege of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a> by a woman, who from the wall threw a tile upon his head. Deidamia, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>-daughter of Pyrrhus, was the last that sat on the throne of Epirus. She is said to have been murdered after a short reign; upon which the Epirots formed themselves into a republic. Under the new form of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> Epirus never made any considerable figure, but seems rather to have been dependent on the kingdom of Macedon. The Romans having conquered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> king of that country, restored the Epirots to their ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>; but they, forgetful of this favour, soon after took up arms in favour of Perseus. As a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> for this ingratitude, the Romans gave orders to Paulus Emilius, after the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of Macedon, to plunder the cities of Epirus, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> them with the ground. This was punctually executed throughout the whole country on the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> and at the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>. The booty was sold, and each foot-soldier had 200 denarii, that is, six pounds <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> shillings and two pence, and each of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> of the sum. An hundred and fifty thousand men were made slaves, and sold to the best bidder for the benefit of the republic. Nor did the vengeance of Rome stop here; all the cities of Epirus, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of 70, were dismantled, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> men of the country carried to Rome, where they were tried, and most of them condemned to perpetual imprisonment. After this terrible blow, Epirus never recovered its ancient splendour. Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of the Achaean <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a>, it was made <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Macedon; but when Macedon became a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>, Epirus was made a province of itself, called the province of Old Epirus, to distinguish it from New Epirus, another province lying to the east of it. On the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the empire, it fell to the emperors of the east, and continued under them till the taking of Constantinople by the Latins, when Michael Angelus, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> nearly related to the Greek <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, seized on Etolia and Epirus, of which he declared himself <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESPOT">despot</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> prince; and was succeeded by his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Theodorus, who took several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> from the Latins, and so far enlarged his dominions, that, disdaining the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of despot, he assumed that of emperor, and was crowned by Demetrius archbishop of Bulgaria. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>, the last prince of this family, dying without lawful issue, bequeathed Epirus and Acarnania to his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> sons, who were driven out by Amurath the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a>. Great part of Epirus was afterwards held by the noble family of the Castrists; who, though they were masters of all <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBANIA">Albania</a>, yet styled themselves princes of Epirus. Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the famous George Castriot, surnamed <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCANDERBEG">Scanderbeg</a>, Epirus fell to the Venetians, who were soon dispossessed of it by the Turks; in whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> it still continues, being now known by the name of Albania, which comprehends the Albania of the ancients, all Epirus, and that part of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a> which is subject to the Turks.

EPISCOPACY

Pages 279-285

that form of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, in which diocesan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> are established as distinct from and superior to priests <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> presbyters. We have already observed, that it is a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> since the ministers of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> have been distinguished into different orders, and that it has been much controverted whether the distinction be of divine or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>; whether it was settled in the apostolic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> or afterwards (See Bishop). This controversy commenced soon after the Re-Commencement formation; and has been agitated with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> warmth between the Episcopalians on the one side, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESBYTERIANS">Presbyterians</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDEPENDENTS">Independents</a> on the other. Among the Protestant churches abroad, those which were reformed by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a> and his associates were in general episcopal; whilst such as follow the doctrines of Calvin have for the most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> thrown off the order of bishops as one of the corruptions of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPERY">popery</a>. In England, however, the controversy has been considered as of greater importance than on the Continent; for it has there been strenuously maintained by one party, that the episcopal order is essential to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of the church; and by others, that it is a pernicious encroachment on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of men, for which there is no authority in scripture. Though the question has for some time lain almost dormant, and though we have no desire to revive it; yet as a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of this kind might perhaps be deemed defective, did it contain no account whatever of a controversy which has employed some of the ablest writers of the past and present centuries, we shall give a fair though short view of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> arguments by which the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> of each contending party have endeavoured to support their own cause, leaving our readers to judge for themselves where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> lies. See Independents and Presbyterians. The Independent maintains, that under the gospel dispensation there is nothing which bears the smallest resemblance to an exclusive priesthood; that Christ and his apostles constituted no permanent order of ministers in the church; but that any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who has a firm <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a>, a principle of sincere and unaffected piety, a capacity for leading <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> and communicating instruction, and a serious inclination to engage in the important employment of promoting the everlasting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a> of mankind; is to all intents and purposes a regular minister of the New <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, especially <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he have an invitation to the pastoral office from some particular <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>. Against this scheme, which supposes the rights of Christians all equal and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, and acknowledges no authority in the church except what may be derived from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of her members, the Protestant Episcopalian reasons in the following manner. He admits, as an undoubted truth, that our blessed <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> gave to arguments none against it... none of his immediate followers authority or jurisdiction of such a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> as could interfere with the rights of the civil <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, for all such authority was disclaimed by himself: "My <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> (said he to Pilate) is not of this world:" and to a certain person who asked him to decide a question of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> between him and his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, he replied, "Man, who made me a judge or a divider over you?" But when it is considered, that Christ came into this world to "turn men from darkness to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and from the power of Satan to the living God; that he gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify to himself a peculiar people zealous of good works; that of these works many are such as unregenerate <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> has no inclination to perform, and that the doctrines which he revealed are such as human reason could never have discovered: the advocate for episcopacy thinks it was extremely expedient, if not absolutely necessary, that, when he ascended into heaven, he should establish upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> some authority to illustrate the revelation which he had given, and to enforce obedience to the laws which he had enacted. There is nothing, continues he, more strictly required of Christians, than that they live together in unity, professing the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, joining in the same worship, and practising the same virtues. But as men have very different passions, prejudices, and pursuits, such unity would be impossible, were they not linked together in one society under the government of persons authorised to watch over the purity of the faith, to prescribe the forms of public worship, and to explain the nature, and inculcate the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of the several virtues. The society of Christians, in respect of its unity and organization, is compared to the human body: for "as we have many members in one body, and all members have not the same office; so we being many are one body in Christ, and every one members one of another," (Rom. xii. 4, 5.). It is called the church, the kingdom of heaven, and the kingdom of God; and its affairs, like those of every other kingdom, are administered by proper officers in subordination to the one Lord, who, "when he ascended up on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and led <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a> captive, gave some apostles, and some prophets, and some pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ:" (Ephes. iv. 8.—13.). That those various orders of ministers were vested with real authority in the church might be inferred from principles of reason as well as from the dictates of revelation. A society without some sort of government, government without laws, or laws without an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EXECUTIVE_POWER">executive power</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> absurdity. Where there are laws, some must govern, and others be governed; some must command, and others obey; some must direct, and others submit to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. This is the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of nature; it is likewise the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of scripture. "Obey them (says the inspired author of the epistle to the Hebrews) who have the rule over you, and submit yourselves; for they watch for your souls as they that must give account." A text which shows that the authority of the ministers of religion was distinct from that of the civil magistrate, whose duty is to watch, not for the souls, but for the lives and properties, of his subjects. Of the society thus constituted, it was not, as of a philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, left to every man's choice whether or not he would become a member. All who embrace the faith of the Redeemer of the world are required to be baptized, under the pain of forfeiting the benefits of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDEMPTION">redemption</a>: but one great purpose for which <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> was instituted, is to be the rite of initiation into the church of Christ; for by one spirit are we all baptised into one body, whether we be Jews or Gentiles, whether we be bond or free;" (1 Cor. xii. 13.). Of church baptism, whatever be the importance, it is evident, that to receive it, is not, like the practice of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, or the veneration of the Supreme Being, a duty resulting from the relations of man to his Creator and fellow-creatures; that its whole efficacy, which in scripture is said to be nothing less than the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REMISSION">remission</a> of sins, is derived from positive <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>; and therefore, that the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> rite can be of no avail, but when it is administered in the manner prescribed, and by a person authorised to administer it. That all Christians are not vested with this authority, as one of the common privileges of the faith, appears from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> which our Saviour after his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a> gave to his apostles. At that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, we are assured that the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of his followers was not less than five hundred; yet we find, that to the eleven disciples only did "he come and speak, saying, All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth; go ye, therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." Of the 500 disciples there is surely no reason to believe that there were not many well qualified to instruct either a Jew or a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENTILE">Gentile</a> in the doctrines of the gospel; and it is certain, that any one of them could have washed his convert with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> in the name of the Holy Trinity as well as St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> or St John; but such an unauthorised washing would not have been Christian baptism, nor of equal validity with it, any more than the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of a lawyer at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> is the judgment of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of justice, or of equal obligation. It is the commission of the sovereign which gives force to the judgment of the court; it is the commission of Christ which gives validity to baptism. The same reasoning is applicable to the Lord's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>, which, if it be not administered by those who have authority for such administration, cannot be deemed a sacrament of Christ's institution. These two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> are the external badges of our profession. By the one, we are incorporated into that society of which our Redeemer is the head and sovereign; in the celebration of the other, we have a right to join, whilst of that society we continue members. But if by an open and scandalous disregard of the precepts of the gospel, we should prove ourselves unworthy of its privileges, the same persons who are authorised to admit us into the church, are likewise vested with authority to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> us out of it: for to them were given "the keys of the kingdom of heaven (or the church), with assurance, that whatsoever they should bind on earth, should be bound in heaven; and whatsoever they should loose on earth, should be loosed in heaven;" (Mat.xviii.18.). As baptism is to be administered so long as there shall be persons to be enlisted under the banners of Christ, and the Lord's Supper to be celebrated so long as it shall be the duty of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> to adhere to the standard of their leader and their head; and as it is likewise to be feared that there <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> never come a time when... when all Christians shall "walk worthy of the vocation wherewith they are called;" it follows, that this power of keys, which was originally given to the apostles, must continue in the church through all ages, even unto the end of the world. But as we have seen, that it was not at first intrusted to all the disciples in common, as one of the privileges inseparable from their profession, and as no body of men can possibly transfer an authority of which they themselves were never possessed; it is certain, that even now it cannot, by the election of one class of Christians, be delegated to another, but must, by some <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of succession, be derived from the apostles, who were sent by Christ as he was sent by his Father. To argue from the origin of evil to that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> government, although not very uncommon, the Episcopalian deems extremely fallacious. Of the various nations of the world, many of the sovereigns may indeed derive their authority from the suffrages of their subjects; because in a state of nature every man has an inherent right to defend his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, and property; and what he possesses in his own person, he may for the good of society transfer to another: but no man is by nature, or can make himself, a member of the Christian church; and therefore authority to govern that society can be derived only from him by whom it was founded, and who died that he might "gather together in one all the children of God." Against such reasoning as this it hath been urged, that to make institutions, which like baptism and the Lord's supper are generally necessary to the salvation of all Christians, depend for their efficacy upon the authority or commission of a particular order, appears inconsistent with the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and goodness of God; as by such an economy an intolerable domination would be established over the souls of men, and the purpose for which the Saviour of the world died might be in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> defeated by the caprice of an ignorant and arbitrary priesthood. The objection is certainly plausible; but the Episcopalian affirms, that either it has no <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, or militates with equal force against the wisdom of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> in the government of this world.—In every thing, he observes, relating to their temporal and to their spiritual interests, mankind are all subjected to mutual dependence. The rich depend upon the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, and the poor upon the rich. An infant neglected from the birth would barely cry and cease to live; nor is it easily to be conceived, that in the more rigid climates of the earth a full-grown man could provide even the necessaries of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> animal life. Of religion, it is certain that in such a state nothing could be known; for there is not the smallest reason to imagine that any individual of the human <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>—an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a>, or a Newton, had he been left alone from his infancy, without culture and without <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>,—could ever, by the native vigour of his own mind, have discovered the existence of a God, or that such speculations as <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to that discovery would have employed any portion of his time or his thoughts. Even in civilized society it would be impossible, in the present age, for any man, without the assistance of others, to understand the very first principles of our common Christianity; for the scriptures, which alone contain those principles, are written in languages which are now nowhere vernacular. In the fidelity of translators, therefore, every illiterate <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> must confide, for the truth of those doctrines which constitute the foundation of all his hopes; and as no man ever pretended that the Christian sacraments are more necessary to salvation than the Christian faith, the Episcopalian sees no impropriety or inconsistency in making those persons receive baptism and the Lord's supper by the ministration of others, who by such ministration must of necessity receive the truths of the gospel. By such arguments as these does the Episcopalian endeavour to prove that Christ constituted some permanent order of ministers in the church, to whom in the externals of religion the great body of Christians are commanded to pay obedience; and thus far the Presbyterian agrees with him; but here their agreement ends. They <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in hand attack the Independent with the same weapons, and then proceed to attack each other. The one maintains, that originally the officers of the Christian church were all presbyters or elders of one order, and vested with equal powers; whilst the other holds, that Christ and his apostles appointed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> orders of ministers in the church; that of these orders the highest alone was empowered to ordain others; and that therefore obedience, as to those who watch for our souls, can be due only to such as are episcopally ordained. In behalf of the Presbyterian <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">plea</a> it is urged, that the titles of bishop and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESBYTER">presbyter</a>, being in the New Testament indifferently given to the same persons, cannot be the titles of distinct ecclesiastical officers; which appears still more evident from the ordination of Timothy, who, although he was the first bishop of Ephesus, received his episcopal character by the imposition of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the presbytery.—That one and the same man is, in the New Testament, styled sometimes a bishop and sometimes a presbyter, cannot be denied; but although every apostolic bishop was therefore undoubtedly a presbyter, it does not of course follow, says the Episcopalian, that every presbyter was likewise a bishop. In the Old Testament, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AARON">Aaron</a> and his sons are without any discrimination of order frequently styled priests; and in the New, both St Peter and St John call themselves presbyters, as St Paul, upon one occasion, styles himself a deacon—διάκονος (Eph. iii. 7.) yet no man ever supposed those apostles to have been such ecclesiastical officers as <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> presbyters and deacons; and it is universally known, that in the Jewish priesthood there were different orders, and that Aaron was of an order superior to his sons. This being the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the presbyters, by the laying on of whose hands Timothy was made a bishop, may have been of the same order with arguments St Peter and St John; and if so, it follows that his ordination was Episcopalian. At all events, we are certain, continues the advocate for Episcopacy, that it was not, in the modern <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the word, Presbyterian; for the gift, which in the first epistle is said to have been "given by prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the presbyter," is in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> said to have been "in him by the putting on of the hands of St Paul." And here it is worthy of observation, that the preposition used in the former case is ἐπί, which signifies concurrence rather than instrumentality; but that in the latter is ἐπί, which, as every Greek scholar knows, is prefixed to the instrumental cause by which any thing is effected: so that whatever may have been the order of the presbyters. Episcopacy who concurred, St Paul appears to have been the sole ordainer. But by the confession of all parties, St Paul was a bishop in the highest sense in which that word is ever used; and the powers of the episcopate not being parcelled out among various partners, of whom each possesses only a share, the imposition of his hands was sufficient for every purpose which could have been effected by the hands of the whole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of apostles. It appears, therefore, that from the promiscuous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the titles bishop and presbyter, and from the ordination of Timothy, nothing can with certainty be concluded on either side of this celebrated question. But if, instead of resting on mere words, which when taken alone and without regard to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTEXT">context</a>, are almost all of ambiguous signification, we attend to some important facts recorded in the New Testament, the Episcopalian thinks we shall in them discover sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> that the government of the primitive church was prelatical. During our Saviour's stay upon earth, it is undeniable that he had under him two distinct orders of ministers—the twelve, and the seventy; and after his ascension, immediately before which he had enlarged the powers of the eleven, we read of apostles, presbyters, and deacons, in the church. That the presbyters were superior to the deacons, and the apostles superior to both, is universally acknowledged; but it has been said, that in Scripture we find no intimation that the apostolic order was designed for continuance. A Quaker says the same thing of water-baptism; and the Episcopalian observes, that it would be difficult to point out by what passage of Scripture, or what mode of reasoning, those who upon this plea reject the apostolic order of Christian ministers, could overthrow the principles upon which the disciples of George Fox reject the use of that rite which our Saviour instituted for the initiation of mankind into his church. They were the eleven alone to whom Christ said, "Go ye therefore and teach all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost;" and therefore, although we frequently find presbyters and deacons administering the sacrament of baptism, we must conclude, that as a judge administers justice by authority derived from his sovereign, so those inferior officers of the church administered baptism by authority derived from the apostles. Indeed, had they pretended to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> by any other authority, it is not easily to be conceived how their baptism could have been the baptism instituted by Christ; for it was not with the external washing by whomsoever performed, but with the eleven and their successors, that he promised to be "always, even unto the end of the world." That the eleven did not consider this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a>, or the commission with which it was given, as terminating with their lives, is evident from their admitting others into their own order; for which they had competent authority, as having been sent by Christ as he was sent by his father. When St Paul, to magnify his office and procure it from the Galatians due reverence, styles himself, "an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> not of men, neither by man, but by Jesus Christ and God the Father," he must have known some who derived their apostolic mission by man; otherwise he could with no propriety have claimed particular respect, as he evidently does, from what was in his own apostleship no particular distinction. At that very early period, therefore, there must have been in the church secondary apostles, if they may be so called, upon whom, by imposition of hands, or by some other significant <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, the eleven had conferred that authority which was given to them by their Divine <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">Master</a>. Such were Matthias and Barnabas; such likewise were Timothy, Titus, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> churches in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, with many others whose names and offices are mentioned in the New Testament. That Matthias and Barnabas were of the apostolic order, has never been controverted; and that Timothy and Titus were superior to modern presbyters, is evident from the offices assigned them. Timothy was Matthias, by St Paul, empowered to preside over the presbyters Barnabas of Ephesus, to receive accusations against them, to exhort, to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, and even to rebuke them; and Titus Titus, was, by the same apostle, left in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a> for the express purpose of setting things in order, and ordaining presbyters in every <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. To exhort, to charge, and with Asia, his authority to rebuke one's equal, is certainly incongruous; and therefore the Episcopalian thinks the powers conferred on Timothy altogether inconsistent with that parity of order and of office for which his antagonists so strenuously plead. Even the commission given to Titus appears in his eyes by much too extensive for a Presbyterian minister, who, after having ordained in one city, could not have proceeded to ordain in another without the consent and assistance of his brother and fellow-labourer. With respect to the angels of the Asiatic churches, he observes, that in the Old Testament the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of angel is sometimes given to the Jewish high-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, and particularly by the prophet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MALACHI">Malachi</a>, who calls him "the messenger (συνάγω) of the Lord of Hosts;" and that the angels of the churches mentioned by St John, were Christian high-priests, or bishops presiding over more than one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a>, as it is affirmed by all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers, cannot, he thinks, be denied by any man who will take the trouble to compare Scripture with Scripture. We read (Acts xix. 10. and 20.), that "in the space of two years all they who dwelt in Asia heard from St Paul the word of the Lord Jesus, both Jews and Greeks; and that there the word of God grew mightily and prevailed:" but with what truth or propriety could this have been said, if at the time of St John's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> the Apocalypse, which was 30 years after St Paul's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, all the Christians of Proconsular Asia were comprised in seven congregations, which assembled, each with its proper pastor, to perform, in one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, the duties of public worship? In a word, the advocate for Episcopacy insists, that no man, who reads without <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> the acts of the apostles, the epistles of St Paul, and the Apocalypse of St John, can seriously believe that Timothy, Titus, Euphroditus, Sosthenes, and Silvanus, with the angels of the seven churches in Asia, were mere presbyters, or that the government of the church was, in those days, by a college of elders. When from the inspired penmen of the New Testament he proceeds to examine the succeeding writers of the Christian church, the Episcopalian finds such multiplied and concurring evidence of the apostolic institution of episcopacy, as he thinks it impossible to resist without without denying the truth of all ancient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, and even shaking the pillars of revelation itself; for "in the noble <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of martyrs," the witnesses of the episcopal government of the church are earlier, and by far more numerous, than those who testify that the gospel of St Matthew was written by that apostle, or that the book of the Apocalypse is canonical Scripture. The authority of the fathers indeed is at present very low; but should they be allowed to be as fanciful divines and as bad critics as their worst enemies are pleased to represent them, this would detract nothing from their evidence when they bear witness to the constitution of the church in their own times; for of their integrity there can be no doubt; and what the Episcopalian wants of them is only their testimony to matters of fact which fell under the cognizance of their own senses, and about which therefore they could not be deceived. It is here indeed chiefly that he triumphs over his antagonists. In the second and third centuries there was no general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, nor any Christian sovereign.
