A prelacy therefore, he urges, could not have been universally introduced, during that period, either by a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> among the clergy, or by the authority of the civil magistrate. Yet that even then there was no church under heaven, of which the government was not episcopal, has been confessed by some of the most learned writers among the Presbyterians themselves; whence he concludes that episcopacy is of divine institution. The candid Episcopalian, however, allows, that in the apostolic age there may have been some churches which at first had only bishops and deacons to perform the offices of religion; for when the number of disciples in any place was so small that they could all meet in one <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, there was no necessity for any other order of ministers: but it appears that, from the very beginning, bishops, presbyters, and deacons, were settled in all the larger cities of the Roman empire; and it was in those days an allowed maxim, that without a bishop there could be no church. The better to understand the original state and institution of episcopacy, it is necessary to observe, that the empire, which contained almost all the known part of the Christian world, was by Augustus Caesar divided into provinces, subjected each to the authority of one chief magistrate, who was <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> a praetor or proconsul, and who resided in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> or chief city of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. A province comprehended the cities of a whole region; and in the age of the apostles, each city was under the immediate government of certain magistrates within its own body, known by the name of δῆμος or senatus, ordo and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CURIA">curia</a>, "the states and court of the city." Those magistrates were subordinate to the praetor or proconsul; but among them there was one superior to the rest, called sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTATOR">dictator</a> and sometimes defensor civitatis, whose jurisdiction extended not only over the city itself, but likewise over all the adjacent territory. That territory was denominated ἐπαρχία, or the suburbs, and often reached to the distance of 10 or 12 miles round the city, and sometimes much farther, containing within it many villages and small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> under the government of the city magistrates. From some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in the New Testament, and from the concurring evidence of the earliest writers of the church, it appears to have been the purpose of the apostles to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> a bishop in every city where there was a civil magistracy: but as they could not be personally present in all places at once, it was <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> for them to enter upon the great work of converting the nations by first preaching the gospel in that city of each province which was the ordinary residence of the governor; because to it there must have been the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of people, who would carry the glad tidings with them into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> when they returned. Accordingly, having dispersed themselves over the empire, and made numbers of proselytes in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> cities, they fixed in each, where they <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> it necessary, a bishop, with a college of presbyters and deacons; and gave to those bishops, who were at first called apostles, a commission, as the other cities of the province should be converted, to fix in them bishops also. In some of the smaller cities, it is extremely probable that a bishop and a deacon were for a short time the only ecclesiastical officers, till the number of Christians increased so much as to make it impossible for them all to assemble in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> for the purposes of public worship. The bishop then ordained presbyters to officiate in those congregations where he himself could not be present, and to assist him in other parts of his pastoral office; but in all their ministrations the presbyters were subordinate to him, who was the chief pastor within the city, who composed the prayers which were offered up in public, and to whom all the other ministers of religion were accountable for their conduct. So long as the number of the faithful was confined within the walls of the city, it appears that the bishop with his presbyters and deacons lived together as in a college; that divine <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> was every Lord's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, or oftener, performed in what was afterwards called the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> or mother-church, by the bishop himself, assisted by some of his clergy; and that the congregations which met in other churches, having no fixed pastors, were supplied by such presbyters as the bishop chose to send to them from his own church. Whilst matters <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in this state, the clergy had no other revenues than what arose from the voluntary oblations of the people; which were indeed so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as not only to support them with decency, but likewise to answer other ends of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> and munificence. They were commonly divided into four equal parts; of which one was allotted to the bishop, a second to the inferior clergy, a third to the poor, and a fourth to keep the churches in repair; and it was considered as a part of the bishop's duty to take care that the offerings should be faithfully applied to these purposes. When converts increased in number, and churches were built in the suburbs, each of these churches had of course a fixed pastor similar to a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>-priest among us; but still those pastors, as well as the city-clergy, ministered in subordination to the bishop, whose authority extended as far as the civil authority of the Roman magistrate, within which district or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> it was supreme over all orders of Christians. This every man knows who is acquainted with ecclesiastical history; for the bishop alone could ordain priests and deacons, administer the rite of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a>, absolve penitents who were under church censure, and exclude from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> heretics and notorious offenders; and from his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> there lay no <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> but to a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a> of comprovincial bishops. Such synods were in each province convened by the bishop. bishop of the chief city; for the apostles having been careful to place in those cities men of the most eminent gifts and abilities, the other bishops of the provinces applied to them for advice upon every emergency, and paid a particular deference to them upon every occasion. So that though all bishops were of equal authority as bishops, yet when they met to consecrate a new bishop, or to deliberate upon the affairs of the church, they yielded a precedence to the bishop of the metropolis, who called them together, and who sat as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> or moderator of the synod. Hence the origin of metropolitans or archbishops; whose authority was so considerable, that though there is not a doubt but the election of bishops was anciently placed in the clergy and people of the vacant diocese, yet the bishop elect could not be consecrated without the consent of the archbishop of the province. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the extensive powers with which the primitive bishops were vested, they are commonly styled in the writings of those times presidents, provosts, or inspectors of the church, chief priests, princes of the clergy, and even princes of the people; but their authority was wholly spiritual. Those prelates, imitating the example of their Divine Master when on earth, neither possessed nor assumed to themselves any jurisdiction over the properties or civil rights of men. In consequence of St Paul's having reprimanded the Corinthians for going to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> before the unbelievers, they were indeed often chosen as arbiters of such civil disputes as arose between individuals under their episcopal government; but on these occasions they could not act unless the submission was voluntarily made by both the contending parties, and then their decision was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FINAL">final</a>. When the empire became Christian, this privilege was confirmed to them by law; for any civil cause depending before a court of justice could be withdrawn, and by the mutual consent of parties be submitted to the arbitration of the bishop, whose award, which in former times could be enforced only by the terror of church-censures, was then enforced by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> magistrate. In criminal causes, where the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> might be for life or death, they were prohibited both by the canons of the church and by the laws of the state from acting as judges; and therefore they never suffered such causes to come before them, except when it was necessary that the person accused, if found guilty, should be excluded from the communion of the faithful. But they had so many civil causes flowing in upon them, that they were soon obliged to devolve part of that care upon other persons, in whose knowledge, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, and integrity, they could fully confide; and as the persons employed to act in the bishop's stead were often laymen, it has been conjectured that they gave rise to the office of lay-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> in the church, and to all that train of spiritual judges and spiritual courts against which such numbers are disposed to clamour. Be this as it may, it is certain that, through the piety and munificence of the Christian emperors, the bishops enjoyed large revenues and many valuable privileges; but it does not appear that they had any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> or authority, as barons or temporal princes, till the Gothic nations, which subverted the Roman empire, had embraced the Christian faith. As Christianity incapacitated the leaders of those tribes from officiating as chief priests at the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> rites which were usually celebrated at the opening of their public assemblies, the bishops came naturally to discharge that duty on such occasions, when they must have shared in the rank by sharing in the functions of the chief. The situation in which they thus appeared at the opening of all civil <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> conventions, would enable them to join with the much effect in the deliberations which ensued; and version of their superior knowledge, their sacred character, and their influence with the people, would soon acquire the power equal to their rank. They must therefore soon have been well entitled to demand admission into that Gothic council which was formed by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> and the laychiefs at the national assemblies; and as they balanced the authority of those chiefs, we cannot doubt that the king would be disposed to give the utmost effect to their claim. Accordingly, we find the dignified clergy, who received large grants of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> to be held on the same tenures with the lands of the lay-magistrates, presiding along with those magistrates in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> assemblies of every degree in all the Gothic nations, and enjoying every advantage in point of rank and authority in their national diets. Hence the bishop of Rome, and several bishops in Germany, have, like the dukes and marquises of that empire, been for a long time sovereign princes; and hence too the bishops of England and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> have always sat, and have an equal right with the lay-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> to sit, in the upper house of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. It is however obvious, that, so far as episcopacy is of apostolical institution, those peers and princes possess not the original character in any higher degree than the bishops in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, who are barely tolerated, or than those in Scotland who do not enjoy that privilege; and that confirmation administered, or holy orders conferred, by a persecuted prelate, must be as effectual to the purposes of religion, as if given by a German <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> or an English peer. In this short view of episcopacy, it has been our endeavour to do justice to the subject, without suffering ourselves to be influenced by partiality or prejudice. As we are not ourselves episcopalians, we have advanced nothing of our own; but have selected from English writers, who have at different times undertaken to defend the divine right of episcopacy, such facts and arguments as to us appear to be of the most importance, or to have the greatest weight, without remarking upon them, or offering any answer. The reasoning employed to prove that the order of bishops was instituted by the apostles, is taken from a work prepared for the press by Dr Berkeley prebendary of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, and son of the celebrated bishop of Cloyne. For the rest of the detail we are indebted chiefly to Bingham's Origines Ecclesiasticae; a performance in great estimation with those English divines who are commonly known by the appellation of high churchmen. As editors of a work of this kind, it is not our business to be of any party, or to support, in opposition to all others, a particular church, though that church should be our own: We shall therefore treat independency and presbytery as we have treated episcopacy, by employing some able writer of each society to plead his own cause. Meanwhile, we shall conclude this article with a few reflections, which, though they come from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a> of an obscure author, deserve to be engraved deep in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of every controvertist of every communion. "On complicated questions (says a late apologist for the episcopal church in Scotland), men will always differ in opinion; but conscious each of the weakness of his own understanding, and sensible of the bias which the strongest minds are apt to receive from thinking long in the same tract, they ought to differ with charity and meekness. Since unhappily there are still so many subjects of debate among those who name the name of Christ; it is doubtless every man's duty, after divesting himself as much as possible of prejudice, to investigate those subjects with accuracy, and to adhere to that side of each disputed question which, after such <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>, appears to him to be the truth: but he transgresses the favourite precept of his divine master, when he casts injurious reflections, or denounces anathemas, upon those who, with equal sincerity, may view the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> in a different light; and by his want of charity does more harm to the religion of the Prince of Peace, than he possibly could do good, were he able to convert all mankind to his own orthodox opinions." The following is a short history of the episcopal church of Scotland, extracted from a more detailed account by a member of that church. The real tenets of the Scotch episcopalians, or members of what was at one period the established church of Scotland, he observes, appear to be imperfectly understood. About the time of the reformation from popery, the want of order and decency in the worship of the reformed church was abolished in the reign of James VI., by the establishment of episcopacy on very liberal principles. This mode of worship obtained the sanction of the most respectable part of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, and continued to flourish under the auspices of government, till it was overthrown by the sticklers for the national covenant. Its restoration was effected in the year 1662, and twenty-seven years afterwards it was again abolished by the advocates of the prince of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>. It may be proper to observe, that the Scotch episcopal church had no public liturgy during her legal establishment. It is indeed true, that the English book of common <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> was used by the first reformers, and there is reason to believe that John Knox himself was by no means inimical to set forms of prayer nor to clerical subordination; but his successor, Andrew Melvil, a man much inferior to him in point of erudition, introduced an equality among the clergy, and excited the odium of the people against the liturgy to such a degree, that an attempt to modify the prayer book for the use of the church of Scotland, was productive of the solemn <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> and covenant, and the subsequent ruin of the unfortunate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>. During the reign of William III. the episcopalians were treated with some degree of severity, because they could not transfer that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> to him which they had sworn to King James. It is said that they were prohibited from officiating on the sabbath day, except "in their own hired houses, where they received such friends as chose to come in unto them." In this manner was their worship conducted, praying either extempore, or from premeditation, till the accession of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, when the English liturgy was introduced by degrees into Scotland, under the sanction of an act of parliament, passed on the 3d of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1712, "to prevent the disturbing of those of the episcopal communion in that part of Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> called Scotland, in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of their religious worship, and in the use of the liturgy of the church of England." But as their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the house of Stuart was well known, they were, at the rebellion in 1715, laid under some restraints, yet neither severe in their nature, nor of any long continuance, since in 1720 their places of worship were as numerous as before, and frequented by numbers both of rank and respectability, many of whom held places under government. In England, Dr Sancroft, archbishop of Canterbury, with five other bishops, were deprived of their sees for refusing their allegiance to King William, which occasioned a schism in the church, as they were extremely popular. Different opinions were entertained respecting the nature and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of the Lord's Supper, and the controversy infected the episcopalians of Scotland. The introduction of prayers into public worship in behalf of departed friends, was at least a very impolitic step at such a critical period, when every thing savouring of popery was held in the utmost abhorrence. On the death of Dr Rose, the proscribed bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, the diocesan form of church government was opposed by such of the presbyters as had been raised to the episcopal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, and it was proposed to govern the whole church by a college of bishops. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADOPTION">adoption</a> of which no precedent could be found in the annals of history, was successfully opposed by many of the most enlightened bishops, and it was of consequence abandoned. The Scotch episcopalians, it is well known, were always <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with an undue attachment to the Stuart family, which was even considered as their most distinguishing tenet; yet there is some reason to believe that the public opinion of this matter was rather exaggerated. They have invariably maintained that the Almighty, and not the people, is the ruler of princes, which fairly places them beyond the imputation of a republican or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVELLING">levelling</a> spirit. The several restraints laid on Scotch episcopalians from time to time, with a view to eradicate their attachment to the Stuart family, were happily removed in the year 1792, and they enjoyed a free toleration like the rest of dissenters. It was about this time that the clergy of this church, with a very few exceptions, took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> of abjuration and allegiance. It is well known, it is added by the same writer, from whose account the above is taken, that in Scotland there are chapels quite distinct from the Scotch episcopal church, where clergymen who have been ordained either in England or Ireland, make use of the liturgy of the church of England; but as each of these is strictly and properly independent of the rest, and under the guardianship of no bishop whatever, those who attend them have, in every sense of the word, a much better claim to the appellation of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONGREGATIONALISTS">congregationalists</a> than to that of episcopalians.

EPISCOPALLIANS

Pages 285-285

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, an appellation given to those who prefer the episcopal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> to all others. See EPISCOPACT. By the test <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>, none but episcopalians, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> members of the church of England, are qualified to enjoy any office civil or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a>.

EPISCOPIUS

Pages 285-286

Simon, one of the most learned men Episcopius men of the 17th century, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> supporter of the Arminian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> in 1583. In 1612, he was chosen <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> professor at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, in the room of Gomarus, who resigned; and the functions of his office, with his private studies, were <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> burdens to him, compared with the difficulties he sustained on account of the Arminian controversy: which, though it began in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, soon flew to the pulpits, from whence it spread and inflamed the people. The states of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> having invited Episcopius to take his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DORT">Dort</a>, he went thither accompanied by some remonstrant ministers; but the synod would not allow them to sit as judges, nor to appear in any other capacity than as persons summoned before them: they submitted, were deposed from their functions, and banished the territories of the commonwealth. Episcopius and his persecuted brethren retired to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>; but the times growing more favourable, he returned to Holland in 1626, and was made minister of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-REMONSTRANTS">Remonstrants</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROTTERDAM">Rotterdam</a>: in 1634, he was chosen rector of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> founded by the sect at Amsterdam, where he spent the remainder of his days. He died in 1643 of the same disorder which had killed his wife before, a retention of urine; having lost his sight some weeks previous to his end. The learned have bestowed <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> eulogiums on Episcopius; but he did not always write with that moderation which might have been wished. His works make two volumes in folio, of which the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> consists of posthumous publications.

EPISODE

Pages 286-286

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, a separate incident, story, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, which a poet invents, and connects with his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> action, that his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> may abound with a greater diversity of events; though in a more limited <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, all the particular incidents whereof the action or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARRATION">narration</a> is compounded are called episodes. See Poetry.

EPISPASTIC

Pages 286-286

in Medicine, a topical remedy, which being applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> parts of the body, attracts the humours to that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>.

EPISTATES

Pages 286-286

in the Athenian <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the proedri. See Proedri.

EPISTEMONARCH

Pages 286-286

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greek <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, an officer of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, who had the care of everything relating to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of censor. His office answered very nearly to that of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the sacred <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> at Rome.

EPISTOLARY

Pages 286-286

something belonging to an epistle. See Epistle. **EPISTOLARY Compositions.** See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">Letter</a>; and the article <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>. **EPISTROPE.** See Oratory.

EPISTYLE

Pages 286-286

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> used by the Greeks for what we call architrave, viz. a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASSIVE">massive</a> piece of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> wood, laid immediately over the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>. **EPITAPH** (from ἐπί, upon, and τάφος sepulchre,) a monumental inscription, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of a person deceased. It has been disputed whether the ancient Jews <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> epitaphs on the monuments of the dead; but be this as it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a>, epitaphs, it is certain, of very ancient <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a>, are found among them.—The Athenians, by way of epitaph, put only the name of the dead, with the epithet ἀγαθός, signifying "good," or ἄγαθος, "here," and the word ἀγαθός, signifying their good wishes: the name of the deceased's father and his tribe were frequently added.—The Lacedæmonians allowed epitaphs to none but those who had died in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> inscribed their epitaphs to the manes, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIS">dis</a> manibus; and frequently introduced the dead by way of prosopopoeia, speaking to the living; of which we have a fine instance, worthy the Augustan <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, wherein the dead wife thus bespeaks her surviving husband: *Immatura peri; sed tu, felicior, annos Vive tuos, conjux optime, vive meos.* The epitaphs of the present <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> are generally crammed with fulsome compliments which were never merited, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in its best state could scarce lay claim to, and expressions of respect which were never paid in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the deceased. Hence the proverb with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> propriety took its rise, "He lies like an epitaph."

EPITAPH

Pages 286-286

is also applied to certain elogies, either in prose <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, composed without any intent to be engraven on tombs; as, that of Alexander, *Sufficit huius tumulus, cui non sufficeret orbis.* and that of Newton,

EPITASIS

Pages 287-287

in Medicine, the increase of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> beginning of a paroxysm, particularly in a fever.

EPITHALAMIUM

Pages 287-287

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, a nuptial song <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> in praise of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDE">bride</a> and bridegroom, praying for their prosperity, for a happy offspring, &c. Epithalamia were sung among the Jews, at the door of the bride, by her friends and companions, the evening before the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. Psalm xlv. is an epithalamium. Among the Greeks the epithalamium was sung as soon as the married couple were gone to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, and attended with shouts and stamping of the feet to drown the cries of the bride. They returned in the morning, and with the same song, a little altered, saluted them again. The evening song was called εὐθαλαμία κα-ρπάξ, the morning salute was called εὐθαλαμία ἐγκέκρισις. This was the practice amongst the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> also, but their epithalamia were often obscene.

EPITHEM

Pages 287-287

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, a kind of fomentation, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> remedy of a spirituous or aromatic kind, applied externally to the regions of the heart, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a>, &c. to strengthen and comfort the same, or to correct some intemperance thereof.

EPITHET

Pages 287-287

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, an adjective expressing some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of a substantive to which it is joined; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> such an adjective as is annexed to substantives by way of ornament and illustration, not to make up an essential <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>. Nothing, says <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, tires the reader more than too <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a redundancy of epithets, or epithets placed improperly; and yet nothing is so essential in poetry as a proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of them. The writings of the best poets are full of them.

EPITRITUS

Pages 287-287

in prosody, a foot consisting of three <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> syllables and one short. Of these, grammarians reckon four kinds: the first consisting of an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IAMBUS">iambus</a> and spondees, as salūtāntēs; the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, of a trocheus and spondees, as concitāntīs; the third of a spondee and an iambus, as communicāntīs; and the fourth, of a spondee and trocheus, as incantāntīs. See the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> Spondeus, Trocheus, &c. EPITROPE. See Oratory, No 83.

EPITROPUS

Pages 287-287

a kind of judge, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather an arbitrator, which the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, under the dominion of the Turks, elect in the several cities, to terminate the differences that arise among them, and avoid carrying them before the Turkish magistrates. See ARBITRATOR. Anciently the Greeks used the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> ἐπίτροπος, in the same <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> as the Latins did procurator, viz. for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a> or intendant. Thus the commissioners of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> in the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> are called by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> and Xenophon ἐπίτροπος. In the New <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, ἐπίτροπος denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>, rendered in the vulgate procurator. EPIZEUXIS. See Oratory, No 68.

EPOCHA

Pages 287-287

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fixed point of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> whence the succeeding years are numbered or counted. See ÆRA.

EPODE

Pages 287-287

in lyric <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, the third <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> last <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ode, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> ode being divided into strophe, antistrophe, and epode. See Ode, &c. The epode was sung by the priests, standing still before the altar, after all the turns and returns of the strophe and antistrophe, and was not confined to any precise <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> or kind of verses. The epode is now a general name for all kinds of little verses that follow one or more <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> ones, of what kind soever they be, and in this <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> a pentameter is an epode after an hexameter. And as every little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, which, being put after another, closes the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, is called epode; hence the sixth book of Horace's odes is intitled liber epodon, "book of epodes," because the verses are all alternately <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and short, and the short ones generally, though not always, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> the sense of the long one.

EPOPOEIA

Pages 287-287

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>, which makes the subject of an epic poem. The word is derived from the Greek ἐπός, carmen, "<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>," and ποιῶ, facio, "I make." In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the word, however, epopeia is the same with ἐπός, or epic poem itself. See the article POETRY.

EPSOM

Pages 287-287

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURREY">Surrey</a>, about 16 miles southwest from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> famous for its mineral waters. These were discovered in 1618; and though not in such repute as formerly, yet they are not impaired in virtue, and the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> made from them is famous all over <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, for gently cleansing and cooling the body. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, galleries, and other public apartments, are now run to decay; and there remains only one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> on the spot, which is inhabited by a countryman and his wife, who carry the waters in bottles to the adjacent places, and supply the demands of dealers in London. On the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWNS">downs</a> are annually <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-races; but the inns, shops, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOWLING">bowling</a>-greens are not near so much frequented as formerly. The market is on Friday; fair, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 25. The town is about one <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and a half in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a>, from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> at Durdans, which was burnt <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> some years since, but has been rebuilt. It was once inhabited by the late <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s father. In Hudson's Lane here was Epsom <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">Court</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Saxon seat, long since converted into a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a>. Here are so many fields, meadows, orchards, gardens, and the like, that a stranger would imagine that the town was built in a wood. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> in 1811 was 2515. Epsom <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is easily imitated by art; i.e. by only dissolving half an ounce of Epsom salt in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUART">quart</a> of pure water, made somewhat brisk <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> quick by adding a little sulphuric acid and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POTASH">potash</a>, so as to let the alkali prevail.

EPULARES

Pages 287-288

in antiquity, an epithet given to those who were admitted to the sacred epule <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> entertainments. EQUATORIAL <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">INSTRUMENT</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a> Equatorial <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EQUANGULAR

Pages 289-289

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, an epithet given to figures whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> are all equal: such are a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, an equilateral triangle, &c.

EQUERY

Pages 288-289
or Ecury, a grand stable or lodge for Equestrian horses, furnished with all the conveniences thereof; as stalls, manger, rack, &c. The word is formed from the French escuirie, which signifies the same thing. Some again derive escuirie from the Latin securia, which not only denotes a place for beasts to be put up in, but also a grange or barn. But a more probable derivation is from equitie, "a stable for horses," of equus, "horse." Some hold that the word stable, in propriety, relates only to bullocks, cows, sheep, hogs, &c., and ecuary, to horses, mules, &c. A simple ecuary is that provided for one row of horses; a double ecuary that provided for two, with a passage in the middle, or two passages; the horses being placed head to head, as in the little ecuary at Versailles. Under ecuary are sometimes also comprehended the lodgings and apartments of the ecueries, grooms, pages, &c. Ecuary (ecuyer); is also an officer who has the care and management of the horses of a king or prince. Ecueries, or Ecuerries, popularly called Querries, are particularly used among us for officers of the king's stables, under the master of the horse, seven in number, who, when his majesty goes abroad, ride in the leading coach, are in waiting one at a time monthly, and have a table with the gentlemen ushers during the time, and a salary of 300l. a-year each. They used to ride on horseback by the coach-side when the king travelled; but that being more expensive to them than necessary to the sovereign, it has been discontinued. Ecueries of the Crown Stable have that appellation, as being employed in managing and breaking the saddle-horses, and preparing them for the king's riding. These are two in number; the first having an annual salary of 256l. and the second 200l. whereof one is, or always should be, in close waiting at court; and when his majesty rides, holds the stirrup, while the master of the horse, or one of the ecueries in his absence, assists in mounting him; and when his majesty rides, they usually attend him. Ecues, in antiquity. See Equestrian Order and Ecuetes. Ecues Auratus, is used to signify a knight-bachelor, called auratus, q.d. gilt, because anciently none but knights might gild or beautify their armour or other habiliments of war with gold. In law this term is not used, but instead of it miles, and sometime chevalier. Ecuestria, among the Romans, a place in the theatre where the ecuetes or knights sat. Ecuestrian (equestris), a term chiefly used in the phrase equestrian statue, which signifies a statue representing a person mounted on horseback. The word is formed of the Latin ecues, "knight, horseman," of equus, "horse." Ecuestrian Games, among the Romans, horse-races, of which there were five kinds, the prodromus or plain horse-race, the chariot-race, the decursory-race about funeral piles, the ludi sevirales, and the ludi nocturnales. Ecuestrian Order, among the Romans, signified EQU patriarch their knights or equites; as also their troopers or horse- men in the field; the first of which orders stood in con- tradistinction to the senators; as the last did to the foot military, or infantry. Each of these distinctions was introduced into the state by Romulus.

EQUIDISTANT

Pages 289-289

an appellation given to things placed at equal distances from some fixed point <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to which they are referred.

EQUILATERAL

Pages 289-289

in general, something that hath equal sides; as an equilateral triangle.

EQUILIBRIUM

Pages 289-289

in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>, is when the two ends of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEVER">lever</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> hang so exactly even and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, that neither doth ascend or descend, but both keep in a position <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the horizon; which is occasioned by their being both <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with an equal <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>.

EQUIMULTIPLES

Pages 289-289

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">Arithmetic</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, are numbers <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> quantities multiplied by one and the same <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>. Hence, equimultiples are always in the same ratio to each other as the simple quantities before multiplication, thus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> 6 and 8 are multiplied by 4, the equimultiples 24 and 32 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be to each other as 6 to 8.

EQUINOCTIAL

Pages 289-289

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>. See Equator. The shadows of those who live under this circle are <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> to the southward of them for one half of the year, and to the northward of them during the other half; and twice in a year, viz. at the equinoxes, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> at noon casts no shadow, being in their zenith. From this circle is the declination <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> latitude of pla- ces accounted in the degrees of the meridian. EQUINOCTIAL <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">Points</a>, are the two points wherein the equator and ecliptic intersect each other: the one being in the first point of Aries, is called the vernal point or equinox; and the other in the first point of Libra, the autumnal point or equinox. EQUINOCTIAL <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAL">Dial</a>, is that whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> lies <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the equinoctial. See Dial.

EQUINOX

Pages 289-289
or AEQUINOX, in Astronomy, the time when the sun enters one of the equinoctial points. The equinoxes happen when the sun is in the equi- noctial circle; when of consequence the days are equal to the night throughout the world, which is the case twice a-year, viz. about the 20th of March and the 23d of September, the first of which is the vernal and the second the autumnal equinox. It is found by observation, that the equinoctial points, and all the other points of the ecliptic, are continually moving backwards, or in antecedentia, that is, westward. This retrograde motion of the equinoctial points, is that famous and difficult phenomenon called the precession of the equinoxes. See ASTRONOMY Index.

EQUIPAGE

Pages 289-289

in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, denotes all sorts of utensils, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, &c. necessary for commencing and prosecuting with ease and success any military <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">opera</a>- tions. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMP">Camp</a> and field equipage consists of tents, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>-furniture, saddle-horses, baggage-waggons, bat- horses, &c. To EQUIP, in naval <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> borrowed from the French marine, and frequently applied to the business of fitting a ship for <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> arming her for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>.

EQUIPOLLENCE

Pages 289-289

in Logic, is when there is an equivalence between any two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more terms or propo- sitions; i.e. when they signify one and the same thing, though they express it differently. Such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a>, &c. are said to be equipollent.

EQUIRIA

Pages 289-289

in antiquity, a festival instituted by Ro- mulus, and celebrated on the 27th of February, in ho- nour of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, at which there were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-races.

EQUISETUM

Pages 289-289
Horse-tail; a genus of plants belonging to the cryptogamia class; and in the natural method ranking under the 51st order, Coniferae. See BOTANY Index.

EQUITES

Pages 289-289

amongst the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, were persons of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, immediately succeeding the senators in point of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. The equites <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> knights were required to be possessed of 400 sesterces before they could be admitted into that order; and when the knights were so reduced as to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> short of the pre- scribed revenue, they were expunged out of the eque- strian <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a>. The equestrian revenue <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned amounted to about 10,000 crowns. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">Part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> whereby the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>- hood was conferred amongst the Romans was the giving of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>; for every eques or knight had a horse kept at the public <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>: he received also the stipend of a horseman to serve in the wars, and wore a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> which was given him by the state. The equites composed a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> body of men, and constituted the Roman cavalry; for there was always a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of them in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and nothing but a review was requisite to fit them for <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. The knights at last grew too powerful, were a ba- <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCE">lance</a> for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> and people, neglected the exercises of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and betook themselves to civil employments. The equites were liable to be punished by the censors, and to suffer <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGRADATION">degradation</a>. They were degraded by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TA">ta</a>- <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> from them the horse which was kept for each of them at the public charge; this was called equum adi- <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a>.

EQUITY

Pages 289-290

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURISPRUDENCE">jurisprudence</a>, is defined a correction <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> qualification of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, generally made in that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> wherein it failleth or is too severe. It likewise signifies the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of the words of the law to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> unexpressed, yet having the same reason; so that where one thing is enacted by statute, all other things are enacted that are of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. For example, the statute of Glanvile gives <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of waste against him that holds lands for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> or years; and by the equity thereof, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> shall have action of waste against a tenant that holds but for one year, or one half-year, which is without the words of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>, but within the meaning of it; and the words that enact the one, by equity enact the other. So that equity is of two kinds. The one abridges and takes from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of the law; the other enlarges and adds to it; and statutes may be construed according to equity, especially where they give remedy for wrong, or are for expedition of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. Equity seems to be the interposing law of reason, exercised by the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> in extraordinary matters to do equal justice; and by supplying the defects of the law, gives remedy in all cases. See <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">Chancery</a>. Equity, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, sometimes confounded with Justice, a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> among the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, represented with a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> in one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> and a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> in the other. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EQUIVALENT">Equivalent</a>, is understood of something that is equal in value, force, or effect, to another. Equivalence is of various kinds; in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a>, in terms, and in things. Equivalent Propositions. See Equipollence. Equivalent Terms, are where several words that differ in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> have yet one and the same signification; as everybody was there, and nobody was absent, nihil non, and omne. Equivalent Things, are either moral, physical, or stational. Moral, as when we say that the commanding or advising a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> is a guilt equivalent to that of the murderer. Physical, as when a man who has the strength of two men is said to be equivalent to two men. Stational, whereby a less <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> becomes of equal force with a greater, by having its distance from the centre increased. Equivocal Terms or Words, among logicians, are those which have a doubtful or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> meaning. According to Mr Locke, the doubtfulness or uncertainty of words has its cause more in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> themselves, than in any incapacity of the words to signify them; and might be avoided, would people always <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> to denote the same idea or collection of ideas: but, adds he, it is hard to find a discourse on any subject where this is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>; a practice which can only be imputed to folly or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> dishonesty; since a man, in making up his accounts, might with as much fairness use the numerical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> sometimes for one sometimes for another collection of units. Equivocal <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">Generation</a>, the production of animals without the intercourse between the sexes, by the influence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> or stars, &c. This kind of generation is now quite exploded by the learned. Equivocation, the using a term or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> that has a double signification. Equivocations are expedients to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> telling the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, and yet without telling a falsity. The fathers are great patrons of equivocations and mental reservations, holding that the use of such shifts and ambiguities is in many cases allowable. Equuleus, or Eccluseus, in antiquity, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACK">rack</a> used for extorting a confession; at first chiefly practised on slaves, but afterwards made use of against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>. The equuleus was made of wood, having holes at certain distances, with a screw by which the criminal was stretched to the third, sometimes to the fourth or fifth holes, his arms and legs being fastened on the equuleus with cords; and thus was hoisted aloft, and extended in such a manner, that all his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> were dislocated. In this state <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>-hot plates were applied to his body, and he was goaded in the sides with an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> called an ungula. Equuleus, Equiculus, and Equus <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s head, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a constellation of the northern hemisphere, whose stars in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>'s catalogue are four, in Tycho's four, in Hevelius's six, and in Mr Flamstead's ten. Equus, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> belonging to the class <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">mammalia</a>, and order of belluae. See Mammalia <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. And for the diseases of the horse, see Farriery Index.

ERA

Pages 290-291

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a>. See Æra. Erancha, a public officer among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greeks, whose business was to preside over and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the alms and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> made for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. Cornelius Nepos, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Epaminondas, describes his office thus: When any person was reduced to poverty, taken captive, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> had a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> to marry, which he could not effect for want of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, &c., the erancha called an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of friends and neighbours, and taxed each according to his means and estate, to contribute towards his relief. Eranthemum, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the diandra class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Erastistratus, a celebrated physician, grandson to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>. He discovered by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a> which Antiochus had conceived for his mother-in-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> Stratonice, and was rewarded with 100 talents for the cure by the father of Antiochus. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> enemy to bleeding and violent physic. Erasmus, Desiderius, born at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROTTERDAM">Rotterdam</a> in 1467. He lost his father and mother at 14 years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and was committed to the care of certain guardians, who would force him to be an ecclesiastic, which he refused for a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. However, he was obliged to assume the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> among the canons regular in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of Stein near Tergou; but afterwards obtained a dispensation from his vows. He was the most learned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of the age in which he lived; and contributed, by his example and his writings, to the restoration of learning in the several countries in which he occasionally resided, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, France, and England: with the last, he was most satisfied; and found the greatest encouragement from Henry VIII. Sir Thomas More, and all the learned Englishmen of those days. He published a great many books; and died at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a> in 1536. He was buried honourably, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> is still held in veneration. He had, however, many enemies; and as he did not embrace the reformation, and yet censured many things in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPERY">popery</a>, he hath been treated injuriously both by the Catholics and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>. The works of Erasmus in 10 vols folio were published at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>. in 1706, in a very handsome manner, under the care of M. le Clerc. Dr Jortin published his life in one vol. 4to, 1758.

ERASTIANS

Pages 291-291

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTION">faction</a> which arose in England during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the civil wars in 1647, thus called from their leader Thomas Erastus, whose distinguishing doctrine it was, that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> had no <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, that is, no regular power to excommunicate, exclude, censure, absolve, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a>, or the like.

ERATO

Pages 291-291

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, the name of one of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">muses</a>, who presided over <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. To this muse some have ascribed the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the lyre and lute; and she is represented with a garland of myrtles and roses, holding a lyre in one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> and a bow in the other, and at her side a Cupid with his torch. There is also a Nereid of the same name.

ERATO STRATUS

Pages 291-291

an Ephesian who burnt the famous temple of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> the same night that Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> was born. This <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>, as some writers have observed, was not prevented <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> seen by the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, who was then present at the labour of Olympias, and at the birth of the conqueror of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>. Eratostratus did this villany merely to eternize his name by so uncommon an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>.

ERATOSTHENES

Pages 291-291

a Cyrenean <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, historian, and poet; called for his learning <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>. He was keeper of the famous library at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>; and was greatly in favour with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> Euergetes, by whose order he wrote a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the Theban kings of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, which succession was entirely omitted by Manetho. He thus fixed the Egyptian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a>, and his authority is by many preferred to that of Manetho. He wrote many other things, a catalogue of which is to be seen in Fabricius, Vossius, &c., but his only piece now remaining entire is a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> and fabulous account of the stars. He starved himself in old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> through grief for the dimness of his sight, about the 10th <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 12th year of Ptolemy Epiphanes, 194 B.C.

EREBUS

Pages 291-291

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> denoting darkness. According to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESIOD">Hesiod</a>, Erebus was the son of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHAOS">Chaos</a> and the night, and the father of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. This was also the name of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the inferi among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; they had a peculiar <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPIATION">expiation</a> for those who were detained in Erebus. Erebus was properly the gloomy region, and distinguished both from Tartarus the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of torment, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELYSIUM">Elysium</a> the region of bliss; according to the account given of it by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, it forms the third <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the invisible world beyond the Styx, and comprehends several particular districts, as the limbus infans, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the receptacle for <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a>; the limbus for those who have destroyed themselves; the fields of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a>, full of dark groves and woods, inhabited by those who died for <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a>; and beyond these, an open champaign <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> for departed warriors.

ERECITION

Pages 291-291

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, the art of raising <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> elevating any thing; as the erection of a perpendicular, &c. It is also used in a figurative sense; as the erection of a bishopric, marquisate, &c. Erection is particularly used by medical writers for the state of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PENIS">penis</a> when swelled and distended by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the muscles called erectores. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. There is also an erection of the clitoris, which is performed by muscles for that purpose. EREMIT. See Hermit.

ERETRIA

Pages 291-291

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Euboea, situated on the Euripus, in the south-west of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. A very ancient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and the largest of the island, after Chalcis. After being demolished by the Persians, it was restored on an adjoining spot, according to Strabo, who mentions a school of Eretrian philosophers there. The Abantes of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> were of Euboea.

ERFURT

Pages 291-291

a town of Germany, in the circle of Upper <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Thuringia, and subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a>. It is defended by good ramparts; and has a castle on an eminence, which commands the town. Its inhabitants are almost all Lutherans, but its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> churches belong to the Catholics. There are several handsome structures, both public and private; but the houses in general are but indifferently built. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11° 14'. N. Lat. 50° 49'.

ERGASTULUM

Pages 291-291

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, was a prison, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> house of correction, where slaves by the private authority of their masters were confined and kept for their offences to hard labour. The Greeks had a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of confinement of this sort called Συγκέντρωσις.

ERGOT

Pages 291-291

in Farriery, is a stub, like a piece of soft <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a>, about the bigness of a chestnut, placed behind and below the pastern <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> hid under the tuft of the fetlock. See Farriery <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

Heath, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the octandria class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 28th order, Bicornes. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a constellation of the southern hemisphere, in form of a river.—The stars in the constellation Eridanus, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>'s catalogue, are 34; in Tycho's, 19; and in the British catalogue, 84.

ERIGENA

Pages 291-292
or Scotus, John, a famous scholastic divine, born about the beginning of the ninth century; but where, is a matter of dispute among authors. Bale and Pits say he was born at St David's in Wales; Dempster, Mackenzie, and Henry, that he was born at Ayr in Scotland; which they infer from his names Erigena and Scotus, by the latter of which he was generally distinguished by his contemporary writers. But Du Pin and Sir James Ware assert that he was by birth an Irishman; Ireland being in those days called Scotia, and by the natives Erin. They agree, however, in relating that he travelled to Athens, where he acquired a competent knowledge of the Greek and other oriental languages; and that he afterwards resided many years in the court of Charles the Bald, king of France, who, on account of his singular abilities, treated him as his intimate friend and companion. He slept frequently in the royal apartment; and was constantly admitted to the king's table. "We may judge (says a modern historian) of the freedom which he used with Charles, by the following repartee. As the king and Scotus were sitting one day at table, opposite to each other, after dinner, drinking a cheerful glass, the philosopher having said something that was not quite agreeable to the rules of French politeness, the king in a merry humour asked him, Pray what is between a Scot and a Scot? To which he answered, "Nothing but the table." See Henry's History of Great Britain, vol. i. p. 344, who quotes this story from Hoveden Annual, ad ann. 86. Quer. What language were they talking when this bon mot was uttered? During his residence with Charles, he wrote several books of scholastic divinity; which, though absurd enough, were at that time not sufficiently so to secure him from the reputation of heterodoxy; and on that account the pope commanded Charles the Bold to send him to Rome; but the king had too great a reward for his companion to trust him with his Holiness. One of the chief controversies in which Scotus was engaged, and with which the pope was much offended, was concerning the real presence and blood of Christ in the wafer. His opinion of this weighty matter is expressed in these few words: "What we receive corporally is not the body of our Lord; but that which feeds the soul, and is only perceived by faith." He was also engaged in two other controversies of equal importance, but of a somewhat less delicate nature. The first was, Whether any part of the eucharist be evacuated by stool? and the second, Whether Christ was born of the Virgin Mary operta vulva? Paschasius was of opinion, that this could not be without some injury to her perpetual virginity; and therefore believed that Christ came into the world per vulvam clausam, as he came into the place where his disciples were assembled, through the door, and not through the wall, without opening the door. Concerning the first of these delicate questions, Scotus with several others declared, that part of the eucharist was certainly evacuated by stool; for which they were honoured with the appellation of Stercorists. And as to the second question, he said, that the vulva clausa was a dangerous opinion: for it would thence follow, that he was not born, but issued; non est nasci, sed erumpi. See Mackenzie, vol. i. p. 55. Whether this John Scotus returned to England, or ended his days in France, is a matter of doubt. Some of our historians tell us, that he left France in the year 864; and that, after residing about three years in Oxford, he retired to the abbey of Malmesbury, where his scholars stabbed him with their pen knives. There is no foundation for this story. Probably he died about the year 874; but whether in France or England, is uncertain, and of little importance. Some have related, that he was invited to England by King Alfred: but in this they confounded him with John, abbot of Etheling, who was assassinated in 895; and to this mistake the various accounts concerning this author are to be attributed. Regardless of his history, he appears from his writings to have been a man of parts, and, in point of learning, superior to any of his contemporaries. He wrote, 1. De divisione naturae, lib. v. 2. De praedestinatione Dei. 3. Excerpta de differentiis & societatibus Graeci Latini verbi. 4. De corpore et sanguine Domini. 5. Ambigua S. Maximi, seu scholia ejus in difficilis locos S. Gregorii Nazianzeni, Latini vers. 6. Opera S. Dionysii quattuor in Latinam linguam conversa. All published. 7. De visione Dei, and several other works, in manuscript, preserved in different libraries.

ERIGONE
