in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ICARUS">Icarus</a>, died of grief for her father's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, was translated into heaven, and makes the sign Virgo.

ERIHYLLE

Pages 293-293

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a sister of Adras- tus <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Argus, who married Amphiarous. She was <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Talaus and Lisimache. When her husband concealed himself that he might not accompany the Argives in their expedition against Thebes, where he knew he was to perish, Eriphyle suffered herself to be bribed by Polynices with a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> necklace which had been formerly given to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERMIONE">Hermione</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> Ve- nus, and she discovered where Amphiarous was. This treachery of Eriphyle compelled him to go to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; but before he departed, he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> his son Alcmeon to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> his mother as soon as he was informed of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Amphiarous perished in the expedition; and his death was no sooner known than his last injunctions were obeyed, and Eriphyle was murdered by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of her son.

ERISICHTHON

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a Thessalian, son of Triops, who derided <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a> and cut <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> her groves. This impiety irritated the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>, who afflicted him with continual <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>. He squandered all his pos- sessions to gratify the cravings of his appetite, and at last he devoured his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> for want of food. Some say that his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> had the power of transforming herself into whatever animal she pleased, and that she made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of that artifice to maintain her father, who sold her, after which she assumed another shape, and became again his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>. ERMIN. See MUSCULA, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">MAMMALIA</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ERIVAN

Pages 292-293

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Persian <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a>. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, dirty, ill-looking <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, in which are no handsome buildings, the houses being very <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a>, and raised with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> mud; but it is full of gardens and vineyards. It is situated in a plain which is surrounded on all sides with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. Two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> near it, the Zengui to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west, and the Queer Boulac to the south-west. The fortress may pass for a town of itself; it is of an oval form, and is four miles in circumference, containing about 800 houses. It is inhabited by none but the native Persians. The Armenians have shops in it, where they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> and trade in the daytime, but at night return to their habitations in the city. The fortress is surrounded with three walls, made with bricks dried in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, which have <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BATTLEMENTS">battlements</a>, and are flanked with towers, and defended with ramparts. On the north-east there is a dreadful precipice, above 200 yards in depth, at the bottom of which the river runs. The garrison usually consisted of 2000 men; but how many there are since the revolution is hard to say. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the governor of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> is within the fortress. The city ERM [267] ERP is about a cannon's <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> distant from the fortress, and the space between is full of houses and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 44° 50' N. Lat. 40° 20'.

ERMIN

an order of knights, instituted in 1450 by Francis I. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Bretagne, and formerly subsisting in France. The collar of this order was of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, com- posed of ears of corn in salter; at the end of which hung the ermin, with this inscription, à ma vie. But the order expired when the dukedom of Bretagne was an- nexed to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of France.

EROTIA

Pages 293-293

a festival in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Eros the god of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a>. It was celebrated by the Thespians every fifth year with sports and games, when musicians and others contended. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> any quarrels <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> seditions had arisen among the people, it was then usual to offer sacrifices and prayers to the god, that he would totally remove them.

EROTIC

Pages 293-293

is applied to any thing which has a relation to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a>. In medicine we find the phrase delirium eroticum used for a kind of melancholy con- tracted through excess of love.

ERPE

Pages 293-293

a celebrated professor of the Arabic <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, was born at Gorcum in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> in 1584, and edu- cated at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>. He applied himself to the oriental languages at the persuasion of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Scaliger; and afterwards travelled into England, France, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and Germany, and everywhere obtained the esteem of the learned. On his return to Holland, he was made professor of Arabic in the university of Leyden, and died there in 1624. He published a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many excellent works, which spread his reputation through the whole learned world. It is said, that the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a> admired so greatly the letters of Erpenius wrote to him in Arabic in the name of the United Pro- vinces, that he could not cease <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> them, and show- ing them to those who spoke that language naturally.

ERPETOLOGY

Pages 293-295

INTRODUCTION. THE animals of which we propose, under the general <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> Erpetology, to give the classification and na- tural <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, belong to the class <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMPHIBIA">Amphibia</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>- der <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REPTILIA">Reptilia</a>, in the Linnaean arrangement. The ani- mals included under this class have obtained the deno- mination of amphibious, from the supposed circumstance that they are equally capable of living both on <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> and in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. But in this view, the application of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> is inaccurate, for there are few, or perhaps no animals belonging to this class which can always exist, L 12 or even perform the functions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> for any considerable length of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, in the water. Many of them, however, possess this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> to a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, and therefore, the name has been extended to all which are distinguished by the same peculiarity of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> form, and a similar structure of external organs. Some naturalists have denominated this order of animals oviparous <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a>. This denomination is undoubtedly sufficiently characteristic; for although some <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are viviparous, and in this circumstance, as well as being furnished with four feet, exhibit some resemblance with the higher order of quadrupeds, the striking <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> which is discovered by the anatomist and the physiologist, affords unequivocal and decided marks of distinction. From the structure, habits, and general economy of this order of animals, we derive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> which are sufficiently distinctive between it and the class of birds, to which the term oviparous is strictly applicable. This denomination, therefore, which is also employed by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> de la Cepede, is sufficiently characteristic of the class of animals which are included under it. The word reptile, by which this order of animals has been distinguished by Linnaeus, seems not to be liable to much objection. All the individuals of which it is composed have short legs, and these are placed at a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance from each other, and so weak, that they are unable to support the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the body. The gray lizard, for instance, which is one of the most <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> of the tribe, is obliged to support itself on its belly, as soon as its progressive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> is greatly diminished; so that it employs its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> rather for the purpose of crawling than that of walking. And indeed all the animals of the order, from the peculiar structure and disposition of their limbs, when their motions are slow, must drag the body along on the belly, other modifications of their locomotive powers depending only on the great length and relation of the instruments of motion. In this view, therefore, the Linnean name of the order is not improperly applied to almost all the individuals which it comprehends. The term herpetology, which we have given to this treatise upon the order reptilia, was formerly employed by the Swedish naturalist Klein, in a more extensive <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. Under this title he included the order serpentes, as well as that of reptilia, thus comprehending the whole class of amphibia. Here we have adopted it in a more limited acceptation, and confined its meaning to the last order, pursuing the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of M. Bonnaterre, in his arrangement of the same order of animals in the Encyclopedie Methodique. Linnaeus has adopted as a mark of distinction of this order of animals, the peculiar structure of the heart, which in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the anatomist is said to be unilocular, or furnished only with one ventricle or cavity. This doctrine has been admitted by eminent anatomists, as well as by some of the greatest physiologists, such as Boerhaave, Haller, and some others; and called in question only when some exceptions have occurred, of animals belonging to this tribe, which have exhibited somewhat of a different structure. One instance of this is quoted in the heart of an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> inland tortoise, which was examined by the French academicians of the 17th century, and in which they discovered three ventricles instead of one. But other physiologists are of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the heart of this order of animal is really furnished with two ventricles, having an immediate <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> between them; they must therefore be considered as having a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> heart. The lungs of the order of reptilia, are, in their appearance and structure, widely different from those of other animals. They are in general composed of two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> bladders, or membranaceous bags, which, in the different species, are divided into a greater or smaller <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of cæcum, or subdivisions; among which are distributed the pulmonary blood-vessels. These bear but a small proportion to the vesicular <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> through which the ramifications are carried; in this respect differing greatly from the lungs of the higher order of quadrupeds, or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">mammalia</a>, in which the proportion of the blood-vessels is so much greater than that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>-cells, that the lungs have more of a fleshy than of a membranaceous appearance. In this order of animals, therefore, in which the blood is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, the vesicular system far outbalances the vascular; but in the class mammalia, which are warm-blooded animals, the vascular system prevails over the vesicular. Of all the animals which occupy the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and which the Almighty creator has dispersed throughout his works, to fill up the void space, and to produce motion, the tribe of reptiles seems at first sight to have been least the objects of beneficence and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>. In their structure, habits, and modes of life, when compared with other orders of animals, they exhibit marks of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGRADATION">degradation</a> and neglect. The body in general presents only a rude inactive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>; their senses are extremely obtuse; their instincts are limited to the grossest sensations, and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of their enjoyments reaches only to the gratifications of appetite. On the boundaries of land and water, in those vast morasses, which are remarkable only for immense depositions of mud, few or scarcely any possess the graces or elegance of other terrestrial animals; like the latter they enjoy not the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of associating together for amusement or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>; or of indulging in sportive tricks on the land or in the air. On the contrary, they crawl on the earth, on the margin of extensive <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, surrounded with unwholesome vapours; or they live in the cavities of the rocks, or in the midst of barren deserts, undisturbed by other animals, and far retired from the habitations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. Some delight in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> themselves to the rays of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; while others retire during the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> to shady, moist, and sequestered places, proceeding from their retreats only during the night, as it were to conceal their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEFORMITY">deformity</a>, and to spare man those feelings of fear, disgust, and horror, with which their presence inspires him. But as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of every part of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> chain of beings is worthy of our attentive consideration and regard, these animals, in the eyes of the careful observer of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, are far from being wanting in exciting his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> and curiosity. He cannot fail to be highly gratified with contemplating the resources which they derive from the peculiar structure of their external form, as well as from the nature of their functions. Their manners, their habits, and the relations which they bear to beings of a higher order, on the one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and the distance to which they are removed from brute <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> on the other, are objects worthy of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> of the naturalist. This study, properly directed and applied, unveils to our eyes the beneficent <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>. design and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>, and raises our admiration to the wonderful and extensive variety of animated beings. The uses of some of the animals belonging to this class, as valuable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of food in those regions where they abound, or as furnishing the tables of the luxurious in other countries with a rich delicacy; the peculiarities of external form, and of internal structure, as well as of several of their functions, such as circulation and respiration; their great length of life; the reproductive power of some, and the long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a> which others can undergo, give additional interest and importance to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> history of these animals. In the following treatise, we propose to lay before our readers a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> but comprehensive view of the natural history of this order of animals; and for the sake of perspicuity we shall treat this subject under two general heads. We shall first consider the classification and natural history of the order reptilia; and secondly, we shall give a short sketch of their anatomy, with the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> facts connected with their physiology. These <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> form the subjects of the two following chapters. CHAP. I. OF THE CLASSIFICATION AND NATURAL HISTORY OF REPTILES. IN the Linnean arrangement, the order reptilia is divided into four genera. Other naturalists have adopted a different arrangement. De la Cepède, in his history of oviparous quadrupeds, has divided this order into two great classes. The first class includes those animals which are furnished with a tail, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> comprehends those which have no tail. The following <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> exhibits a view of the classification of this eminent naturalist. Class I. Animals furnished with a tail. Genus 1. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TORTOISES">Tortoises</a>, having the body covered with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BONY">bony</a> shield. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">Division</a> 1. The fingers very unequal, and lengthened out in the form of fins. Division 2. The fingers very short, and almost equal. Genus 2. Lizard: the body having no bony covering. Division 1. The tail flattened; five fingers on the fore feet. Division 2. The tail round; five fingers on each foot, and elevated scales on the back. Division 3. The tail round; five fingers on the fore feet; scaly bands under the belly. Division 4. The tail round; five fingers on the fore feet, without scaly bands under the belly. Division 5. The fingers furnished underneath with large scales, covering each other, like the slates on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. Division 6. Three fingers on the fore and the hind feet. Division 7. Membranes in the form of wings. Division 8. Three or four fingers on the fore feet; four or five fingers on the hind feet. Class II. Animals which have no tail. Genus 1. Frogs: the head and the body lengthened out, and the one or the other angular. Genus 2. Tree frogs: the body long, with soft viscid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUBERCLES">tubercles</a> under the toes. GENUS 3. Toads: the body thick and round. Appendix. Biped reptiles. Division 1. Two fore feet. Division 2. Two hind feet. Of this arrangement it may be observed, that, although it exhibits much minuteness and ingenuity, the distinctive characters upon which some parts of it are founded, are not always constant and fixed; for it has been found that these characters vary in the different individuals in which they have been observed. This variety, it has been conjectured, arises from the difference of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and peculiarities in their food and modes of life. M. Bonnaterre has adopted a different arrangement. He has also divided the whole order of reptiles into two classes, as will appear from the following table. Class I. Reptiles which have no tail. Genus 1. Frog. Genus 2. Tree Frog. Genus 3. Toad. Class II. Reptiles which are furnished with a tail. Genus 1. Tortoise. Genus 2. Chameleon. Genus 3. Crocodile. Genus 4. Lizard. Genus 5. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">Flying</a> dragon. Genus 6. Salamander. Genus 7. Chalcis. This arrangement is undoubtedly, in many <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, convenient and proper; yet, as there seems to be in others an unnecessary multiplication of genera, we shall still adhere to the Linnean classification, which, though more simple, will in general be found not to be much less accurate; and the objects which it comprehends not being very numerous, it is sufficiently distinct. Linnaeus divided this order into four genera. The following are the characters of the genera, of which we give a translation, for the accommodation of the English reader.

in general, something that wanders, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> is not regular; hence it is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> are called erratic stars.

ERRHINES

Pages 357-357

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, medicines which when snuffed up the nose promote a discharge of mucus from that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Errhines prepared of cephalic herbs are of singular <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in oppressive pains of the head, a hemicrania, lethargic disorders, weakness of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, stuffings of the head, and coryza, mucous defluxions of the eyes, drowsiness, vertigoes, and in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> where the malignant humours <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> by the lues venerea are lodged in the membranes of the nostrils.

ERROR

Pages 357-357

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, a mistake of our judgment, giving assent to that which is not true. Mr Locke reduces the causes of error to these four; first, want of proofs; secondly, want of ability to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> them; thirdly, want of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> to use them; and, fourthly, wrong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>. He observes upon the first of these causes of error, that the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of mankind want conveniences and opportunities of making experiments and observations themselves, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of collecting the testimony of others, being prevented by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of their condition. Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of these causes, he observes, that there are many, who, from the state of their condition, might bestow <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in collecting proofs, but yet are not able to carry a train of consequences in their heads, nor weigh exactly the preponderancy of contrary proofs and testimonies, merely from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in men's understandings, apprehensions, and reasonings. Thirdly, he remarks, that though some have opportunities and leisure enough, and want neither parts, learning, nor other helps, that they never come to the knowledge of several truths within their reach, either upon account of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> or business; or otherwise because of their laziness or aversion to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. The fourth cause of error, viz. wrong measures of probability, he imputes, 1. To the practice of taking for principles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> that are not in themselves certain and evident, but, on the contrary, doubtful and false. 2. To received hypotheses. 3. To predominant passions or inclinations. And, 4. To authority, or the giving up our assent to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> received opinions either of our friends or party, neighbours or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The causes of error in philosophy, or the reasons why all former philosophers have through so many ages erred, according to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a>, are these following: 1. Want of time suited to learning. 2. The little labour bestowed upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> philosophy. 3. Few entirely addicted to natural philosophy. 4. The end of the sciences wrong fixed. 5. A wrong way chosen. 6. The neglect of experiments. 7. Regard to antiquity and authority. 8. Admiration of the works in use. 9. The artifices of teachers and writers in the sciences. 10. Ostentatious promises of the moderns. 11. Want of proposing worthy tasks. 12. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">Superstition</a> and zeal being opposite to natural philosophy, as thinking philosophy dangerous, on account of the school <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>; from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that deep natural inquiries should subvert <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. 13. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">Schools</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a> proving unfavourable to philosophy. 14. Want of rewards. And, 15. Despair, and the supposition of impossibility. ERROR Loci. Boerhaave is said to have introduced the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a>, from the opinion that the vessels were of different sizes for the circulation of blood, serum, and lymph; and that when the larger-sized globules were forced into the lesser vessels by an error of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, they were obstructed. But this opinion does not seem well grounded.

ERUCA

Pages 357-357

in general, denotes caterpillars of all kinds. The caterpillar state is that through which insects <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> before they arrive at perfection. See LARVA, Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ERUDITION

Pages 357-357

denotes learning <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> knowledge; and chiefly that of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and antiquity, of languages and of books, which is the result of hard <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> and extensive <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>. The Scaligers were men of deep erudition: the writings of M. Lannoy, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of the Oratory, are full of erudition. Mr Locke says, it is of more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to fill the head with reflections than with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of erudition. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the mind be not <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> is better than erudition, which only produces confusion and obscurity. M. Balzac calls a heap of ill chosen erudition the luggage of antiquity.

ERUPTION of Volcanoes. ERYTHEA

Pages 358-358
or ERYTHIA, an island adjoining, according to the ancients, either to or a part of Gades; nowhere now to be found by the description given of it by ancient authors. The poets feign this to be the habitation of the fabulous Geryon, disarmed by Hercules, who drove away his cattle. ERYTHRÆ, in Ancient Geography, a port-town of Aetolia, on the Corinthian bay. Another Erythre of Bœotia, near Platæa and Mount Cithæron. A third Erythre, a town of Ionia in the Hither Asia, situated in the peninsula, at its extremity, with a cognominal port. The Erythreans laid claim to the Sibyl Herophilæ, as their countrywoman, surnamed thence Erythrea. Erythre was famous for an ancient temple of Hercules. ERYTHRÆA, a town of Crete, situated in the south-east of the island, at the promontory Erythreum. ERYTHRÆUM MARE, erroneously called Rubrum by the Romans. Thus the ocean that washes Arabia and Persia, and extends a great way farther, is denominated. Hence it is, Herodotus says, that the Euphrates and Tigris fall into the Mare Erythreum. He also calls it the South Sea, on which the Persians dwell. It takes its name, not from its colour, the error of the Romans, who translated Erythreum "Rubrum;" but from Erythrus, son of Perseus and Andromeda, whose kingdom lay on the confines of that sea; whence its name Erythreum.

ERYX

Pages 358-358

a son of Butes and Venus, who relying upon his strength, challenged all strangers to fight with him in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> of the cestus. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> accepted his challenge after many had yielded to his superior dexterity; and Eryx was killed in the combat, and buried on the mountain, where he had built a temple to Venus. Virg. Æn. 5. v. 402. A mountain of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> near Drepanum, which received its name from Eryx, who was buried there. This mountain was so steep, that the houses which were built upon it seemed every moment ready to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a>. Daedalus had enlarged the top, and inclosed it with a strong wall. He also consecrated there to Venus Erycina a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> heifer, which resembled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> so much, that it seemed to exceed the power of art.

ERZERUM

Pages 358-358
or ERZERON, a city of Turkey in Asia, and capital of Armenia, or Turcomania. It is a pretty large town, five days journey from the "xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black sea, and ten from the frontiers of Persia. It stands in a delightful plain, at the foot of a chain of mountains, which hinder the Frat, or Euphrates, from falling into the Black sea. A neighbouring hill supplies very fine springs, which not only water the fields, but the streets of the town. Erzerum is surrounded with double walls, defended by pentagonal towers; but the ditches are neither deep nor well kept up. The beglerbeg, or bashaw of the province, lives in the seraglio, which is very ill built. They reckon that there are 18,000 Turks at Erzerum, 6000 Armenians, and 10,000 Greeks. The Armenians have a bishop and two churches; and the Greeks have also a bishop, but the church is a miserable place. The last are mostly braziers, inhabiting the suburbs, who work the copper brought from the neighbouring mountain. They drive a great trade in copper utensils and furs, particularly martens skins. Five or six days journey from the town there are oaks that produce plenty of gall-nuts, which are brought hither. This place is the thoroughfare and resting place of all the merchants trading to the Indies, especially when the Arabs are watching for their prey round Aleppo and Bagdad. E. Long. 40° 50' N. Lat. 39° 46'.

ES

Pages 777-803

and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> ascension EA, turned into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Put the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> ES = x, the arch FA = v, which is to be con- sidered as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a> of x, and put a for the cosine of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> E = 23° 28'. Then, by Spherical Trigono- metry, in the right-angled spherical triangle EAS, we have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAN">tan</a>. EA = cos. E × tan. ES; therefore, to deter- mine x we have tan. v = a tan. x, and \(y = x - v\), a maxi- mum. From the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of these equations we get \[ \frac{dy}{dx} = -v, \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 1 - \frac{v}{x} = 0, \] and from the first, by § 60: \[ \frac{v}{x} = \frac{a \sec^2 x}{\sec^2 v}, \] therefore, \(x = \frac{a \sec^2 x}{\sec^2 v} = 0\), and \(\sec^2 v = a \sec^2 x\), <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> \(1 + \tan^2 v = a + a \tan^2 x\), but from the first equation: \(\tan^2 v = a \tan^2 x\), therefore, \[ 1 + a \tan^2 x = a + a \tan^2 x, \] or \(a(a - 1) \tan^2 x = a - 1\), hence \(\tan. x = \frac{1}{\sqrt{a}} = 1.04416\), the tangent of 46° 14', the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> when this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the equation is a maximum. 83. We have deduced the rule of § 79. for deter- mining when a function is a maximum, or minimum, from the consideration of curve <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>. The whole the- ory of maxima and minima may however be explained in a manner purely analytical, as follows: Let us suppose that \(y\) is any function whatever of \(x\), and that \(x\) has acquired the value that produces the maximum or minimum of the function; then, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we sup- pose \(x = h\) and \(x + h\) to be substituted successively in the function instead of \(x\), the two resulting values ought to be both less than the maximum or both greater than the minimum value. Let us denote the value of the function that results from the substitution of \( x-h \) by \( y \) and that which results from the substitution of \( x+h \) by \( y' \), then by the theorem given in § 69, \[ y = y - \frac{y}{x} h + \frac{y}{x^2} h^2 - \frac{y}{x^3} h^3 + \text{&c.} \] \[ y' = y + \frac{y}{x} h + \frac{y}{x^2} h^2 + \frac{y}{x^3} h^3 + \text{&c.} \] In each of these values, \( \frac{y}{x} \), the coefficient of \( h \), must either be equal to some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, positive or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a>, or else it must \( = 0 \). Let us suppose, if possible, that it is equal to some quantity, positive or negative; now as \( h \) may be conceived to be so small that the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> \( \frac{y}{x} h \), or any other term, shall exceed the sum of all the terms that follow it in each <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a>, (D) if we suppose \( h \) to have such a value, then, because of the term \( \frac{y}{x} h \) having the sign — in the one series, and + in the other, it follows that the one value of the function is greater, and the other less than \( y \), the maximum or minimum value: But this conclusion is inconsistent with the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of a maximum or minimum, therefore \( \frac{y}{x} \) cannot in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of a maximum or minimum be equal to any positive or negative quantity whatever. If however we assume \( \frac{y}{x} = 0 \), so that the two values are, \[ y = y + \frac{y}{x^2} h^2 - \frac{y}{x^3} h^3 + \text{&c.} \] \[ y' = y + \frac{y}{x^2} h^2 + \frac{y}{x^3} h^3 + \text{&c.} \] then as the second term \( \frac{y}{x^2} h^2 \) has the same sign in both, when that term is greater than all the terms that follow and as by giving a proper value to \( h \), \( \frac{y}{x^2} h^2 \) may be rendered greater than the sum of all the following terms in each series, it follows, that \( \frac{y}{x^3} \) being supposed to be any quantity either positive or negative, because of its sign being different in the two values, the one of them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be greater, and the other less than \( y \), the maximum or minimum value, which result is inconsistent with the nature of a maximum or minimum. If however \( \frac{y}{x^3} \) be assumed \( = 0 \), then (D) If this should not appear sufficiently obvious, let \[ A h + B h^2 + C h^3 + D h^4 + \text{&c.} \] be such a series, where \( A, B, C, D, \) &c. denote quantities either positive or negative, but which are independent of \( h \). Then, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> the series thus, \[ h(A + B h + C h^2 + D h^3 + \text{&c.}) \] it is obvious that if \( h \) be conceived to be continually diminished, and at last to become \( = 0 \), the part \[ B h + C h^2 + D h^3 + \text{&c.} \] will also become \( = 0 \), therefore before it vanishes it will be less than \( A \), or any other assignable quantity, therefore \( B h + C h^2 + D h^3 + \text{&c.} \) may become less than \( A h \). \[ y = y + \frac{y}{x^4} \cdot \frac{h^4}{2 \cdot 3 \cdot 4} + \text{etc.} \] \[ y = y + \frac{y}{x^4} \cdot \frac{h^4}{2 \cdot 3 \cdot 4} + \text{etc.} \] Here again, the coefficient of the second term having in both values the same sign, the conditions of the maximum or minimum are fulfilled, and the sign of \( \frac{y}{x^4} \) shows when the one or the other is to have <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. It must now be sufficiently evident, without proceeding any further, that a function can only admit of a maximum or a minimum when the first of its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUXIONS">fluxions</a> that does not vanish, is of an even order (or is its second or fourth fluxion, &c.), and that the sign of that fluxion is negative in the case of a maximum, but positive in the case of a minimum. 85. We shall conclude this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> by applying it to an example. Let \( y \) be such a function of \( x \) that \[ y^2 - 2mxy + x^2 - a^2 = 0, \] then by § 49, \[ (y - mx)y - (my - x)x = 0, \] and hence \( \frac{y}{x} = \frac{my - x}{y - mx} = 0, \) therefore \( my - x = 0, \) and \( y = \frac{x}{m}. \) To find the value of \( x, \) let this value of \( y \) be substituted in the original equation, it thus becomes \[ \frac{x^3}{m^2} - x^2 - a^2 = 0, \] hence we find \[ x = \frac{ma}{\sqrt{(1 - m^2)}}, \] and \( y = \frac{a}{\sqrt{(1 - m^2)}}. \] We must now examine what is the nature of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> for \( \frac{y}{x^2}. \) Taking the fluxion of the equation \[ \frac{y}{x^2} = \frac{m - yx}{y - mx}, \] and considering that \( x \) is constant, we have \[ \frac{y}{x^2} = \frac{(1 - m^2)(xy - yx)}{(y - mx)^2}, \] therefore, dividing by \( x, \) \[ \frac{y}{x^2} = \frac{1 - m^2}{(y - mx)^2} \left[ \frac{y}{x} - y \right], \] but as in the present case \( \frac{y}{x} = 0, \) and \( y = \frac{m}{x}, \) this expression becomes simply \[ \frac{y}{x^2} = \frac{-m}{x \sqrt{(1 - m^2)}}, \] which equation, by putting instead of \( x \) its value \( \frac{ma}{\sqrt{(1 - m^2)}}, \) becomes \[ \frac{y}{x} = \frac{1}{a \sqrt{(1 - m^2)}}, \] and as this result is negative, we conclude that the value which we have found for \( y \) is a maximum. Of the values of fractions, the numerators and denominators of which vanish at the same time. 86. There are some fractional functions of such a nature, that by giving a particular value to the variable quantity, both the numerator and denominator of the fraction vanish, and thus the fraction is reduced to this form \( \frac{0}{0}, \) an expression from which nothing can be concluded. We have an example of this in the fraction \( \frac{x-a}{x^2-a^2}, \) which, by supposing \( x = a \) becomes \( \frac{a-a}{a^2-a^2} = \frac{0}{0}; \) we must not however conclude that the fraction has no determinate value in this particular case, for if we consider that its numerator and denominator have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> divisor, viz. \( x-a, \) it is evident that by taking this divisor out of both, the fraction \( \frac{x-a}{x^2-a^2} = \frac{x-a}{(x-a)(x+a)}, \) becomes \( \frac{1}{x+a}, \) an expression, which in the case of \( x = a \) is equal to \( \frac{1}{2a}. \) 87. In general, if we make \( x = a \) in an expression of this form \( \frac{P(x-a)^n}{Q(x-a)^n}, \) it becomes \( \frac{0}{0}; \) however its true value is either nothing, or finite, or infinite, according as \( n > m, \) or \( m = n, \) or \( m < n; \) for by taking out the factors common to the numerator and denominator, the fraction becomes \( \frac{P(x-a)^{n-m}}{Q} \) in the first case, \( \frac{P}{Q} \) in the second, and \( \frac{P}{Q(x-a)^{n-m}} \) in the third; here we suppose that \( P \) and \( Q \) are such functions as neither become nothing, nor infinite, by the supposition of \( x = a. \) 88. Therefore, when by giving a particular value to \( x \) a function of that quantity assumes the form \( \frac{0}{0}, \) to discover the true value of the function in this particular case, we must disengage the factors which are common to the numerator and denominator. This may be done in most <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> by finding their common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> (<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALGEBRA">ALGEBRA</a>, § 49;) but the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> method of fluxions furnishes us with another method. In the expression \( P(x-a), \) where \( P \) denotes any function of \( x \) that is independent of \( x-a, \) if we suppose \( x = a, \) then the expression vanishes; the fluxion however of the expression, viz. \( (x-a), \) \( P + Px, \) is a quantity which does not vanish when \( x = a, \) but is then reduced to its last term, that is to \( Px. \) Again, the function \( P(x-a)^n \) vanishes by supposing \( x = a \), but if we take its fluxion, viz. \((x-a)^n \dot{P} + 2(x-a) \dot{P} \dot{x} + \ldots + n(x-a)^{n-1} \dot{P} \dot{x}^{n-1}\), and again the fluxion of this quantity, we get \[ (x-a)^n \ddot{P} + 4(x-a) \dot{P} \dot{x} + 1 \cdot 2 \cdot P \dot{x}^2, \] an expression which does not vanish upon the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> of \( x = a \), but is reduced to its last term, viz. \( 1 \cdot 2 \cdot P \dot{x}^2 \). By proceeding in this manner, it is easy to see that by taking the fluxion of a function of the form \( P(x-a)^n \) \( m \) times successively (\( m \) being a whole <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>) we shall finally obtain an expression, all the terms of which, except the last, vanish by supposing that \( x = a \); and that the last term will be \( 1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \ldots m \cdot P \dot{x}^m \), an expression free from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACTOR">factor</a> \((x-a)^n\), and involving only the function \( P \). 89. It is not necessary that we should know the number \( n \), nor that we should exhibit the factor \((x-a)^n\), in order to determine when the expression \( P(x-a)^n \) is freed from that factor. We have only to ascertain after each operation of taking the fluxion, whether the result vanishes or not, when we substitute \( a \) instead of \( x \); for in the last case the operation is finished, and the result is the quantity \( 1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \ldots m \cdot P \dot{x}^m \). Suppose for example the function to be \( x^3 - ax^2 + ax + a^3 \), which vanishes when \( x = a \); its first fluxion also vanishes when \( x = a \), but not its second fluxion, which is \((6x-2a)\dot{x}^2\), hence we may conclude that the function has the form \( P(x-a)^3 \), which is besides obvious, because \[ x^3 - ax^2 + ax + a^3 = (x+a)(x-a)^2. \] 90. In applying these observations to the fraction \( \frac{P(x-a)^n}{Q(x-a)^m} \), it appears, that by repeating the operation of taking the fluxions of its numerator and denominator, they will be freed at once from the factor \( x-a \), if \( m = n \). If a result, which does not vanish, be obtained first from the numerator, then we may be assured, that the factor, \((x-a)\) is found in the numerator raised to a less power than in the denominator, and in this case the fraction is infinite when \( x = a \). If on the contrary the first result that does not vanish is found from the denominator, then the numerator contains a higher power of \((x-a)\) than the denominator, and in this case, when \( x = a \), the fraction vanishes. The rule for finding the value of a function which becomes \( 0 \) by giving a particular value to \( x \), may therefore be expressed thus. Take the successive fluxions of both the numerator and denominator until a result which does not vanish be obtained from either the one or the other, or from both at the same time; in the first case the function is infinite, in the second it is equal to \( 0 \), and in the last case its value is finite. 91. We proceed to illustrate this rule by a few examples. Ex. 1. The value of the function \( \frac{x^3 - 1}{x^2 - 1} \) is required when \( x = 1 \). The fluxion of the numerator is \( 3x^2 \dot{x} \), and that of the denominator is \( 2x \dot{x} \), neither of which quantities vanish when \( x = 1 \), therefore, in this particular case, the value of the fraction is \( \frac{3x^2}{2x} = \frac{3}{2} \). Ex. 2. Suppose the fraction to be \( \frac{ax^2 - 2acx + ac^2}{bx^2 - 2bcx + bc^2} \), which vanishes when \( x = c \). By taking the fluxions of the numerator and denominator we obtain \( \frac{2ax - 2ac}{2bx - 2bc} \), a fraction, the numerator and denominator of which still vanish upon the hypothesis of \( x = c \), we therefore take the fluxions a second time, and get \( \frac{2a}{2b} = \frac{a}{b} \) for the value of the proposed fraction in the particular case of \( x = c \). Ex. 3. Suppose the fraction to be \( \frac{x^3 - ax^2 + ax + a^3}{x^2 - a^2} \), which vanishes when \( x = a \). In this example, by taking the fluxions of the numerator and denominator once, we get \[ \frac{3x^2 - 2ax + a^2}{2x} = \frac{3x^2 - 2ax + a^2}{2x}, \] an expression, of which only the numerator vanishes upon the supposition of \( x = a \); hence we may conclude the true value of the fraction in this case to be \( 0 \). The contrary happens in the fraction \[ \frac{ax - a^2}{a^2 - 2a^3x + 2ax^2 - x^4}; \] we may therefore conclude that when \( x = a \), this last fraction becomes infinite. 92. The rule § 90. can only be applied when the factors common to the numerator and denominator are integer powers of \( x-a \), for as by taking the fluxions, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a> of \((x-a)^n\) is diminished by an unit at each operation; when \( m \) is a fraction we shall at last arrive at a result containing negative powers of \( x-a \), which therefore, when \( x = a \), will become infinite. The following <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of proceeding will however apply to all cases whatever. Let \( \frac{X}{X'} \) be a fraction of which the numerator and denominator both vanish when \( x = a \); by substituting in it \( a + h \) instead of \( x \), the functions \( X \) and \( X' \) may be expanded into a series of this form, \[ A h^a + B h^b + &c. \] which are ascending, that is, having the exponents of the powers positive and increasing; because the series must become \( 0 \), upon the hypothesis that \( h = 0 \). We have therefore \[ \frac{A h^a + B h^b + &c.}{A' h'^a + B' h'^b + &c.} \] instead of the proposed fraction. Now if \(a = a'\), by dividing the numerator and denominator of this expression by the factor, \(h^2\), which is common to all the terms of each, it becomes \[ \frac{A h^{a-a'} + B h^{b-b'} + \&c.}{A' + B h^{b-b'} + \&c.} \] a quantity which, by supposing \(h = 0\), is reduced to \[ \frac{0}{A'} \] that is to \(0\). If again \(a = a'\), the expression for the fraction, after dividing the numerator and denominator by \(h^2\), is \[ \frac{A + B h^{a-a'} + \&c.}{A' + B h^{b-b'} + \&c.} \] which, by supposing \(h\) to be \(0\), becomes simply \(\frac{A}{A'}\). If, however, \(a < a'\), then the expression for the fraction is \[ \frac{A + B h^{a-a'} + \&c.}{A h^{a-a'} + B h^{b-b'} + \&c.} \] which, when \(h = 0\), becomes \(\frac{A}{0}\), an expression which may be considered as infinite. Thus it appears that in each case the true value of the fraction depends only on \(A\) and \(A'\), the first terms of the series. The following rule is applicable to every function that can appear under the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDETERMINATE">indeterminate</a> form \(\frac{0}{0}\): Find the first term of each of the ascending series which express the developments of the numerator and denominator when \(a + h\) is substituted in them instead of \(x\). Reduce the new function formed of these first terms to its most simple form, and make \(h = 0\); the results shall be the different values of the proposed function when \(x\) is made equal to \(a\). Example. Suppose the function to be \[ \frac{\sqrt{x} - \sqrt{a} + \sqrt{(x-a)}}{\sqrt{(x^2-a^2)}} \] which, when \(x = a\), becomes \(\frac{0}{0}\). By substituting \(a + h\) instead of \(x\), and developing the results into series, the numerator becomes \(h^2 + \frac{h}{2\sqrt{a}} + \&c.\) and the denominator \(\sqrt{2a} + \frac{h}{2\sqrt{a}} + \&c.\). Taking now the first term of each series, we have \[ \frac{h^2}{2\sqrt{a}} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{a}} \] an expression in which \(h\) is not found; therefore the value of the function is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2a}}\), when \(x = a\). Of the Radii of Curvature. 93. Let HCF represent a material curve, or mould. Let a thread be fastened to it at \(H\), and made to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> along the curve, so as to coincide with it in its whole <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> from \(H\) to \(F\). Let the thread be now unlooped or evoluted from the curve, then its extremity \(F\) will describe another curve line FAPP'. The curve HCF is called the Evolute of the curve FAP; and the curve FAP is called the Involute of the curve HCF. 94. From this mode of conceiving the curve to be <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a>, we may draw the following conclusions. 1st. Suppose PC to be a portion of the thread detached from the evolute, then PC will be a tangent to the evolute at C. 2dly. The line PC will be perpendicular to a tangent to the curve FAP at the point P, or will be a normal to the curve at that point. For the point P may be considered as describing at the same time an element of the curve FAP, and an element of a circle \(gPq'\), whose momentary centre is C, and which has PC for its radius. 3dly. That part of the curve between F and P, which is described with radii all of which are shorter than CP, is more incurvated than a circle described on C as a centre, with a radius equal to CP. And in like manner PP', the part of the curve on the other side of P, which is described with radii greater than PC, is less incurvated than that circle. 4thly. The circle \(gPq'\) has the same curvature as the curve APP' itself has at P: hence it is called an Equicurve circle, and its radius PC is called the Radius of Curvature at the point C. 95. We are now to investigate how the radius of curvature at any point in FAP any proposed curve may be found. Let <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">AB</a> and BP be the co-ordinates at P any point in the curve, and PC its radius of curvature; and let PC meet AB in E. Put the abscissa \(AB = x\), the ordinate \(BP = y\), the arch \(AP = z\), the angle \(AEP\) (that is, the arch which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> that angle, radius being unity) \(= v\), the radius of curvature \(PC = r\). Take \(P'\) another point in the curve, and let \(P'C\) be the radius of curvature at that point. Let \(P'C\) meet \(AB\) in \(E'\), and \(PC\) in \(D\), and on \(D\) as a centre, with a radius \(= r\), describe an arch of a circle, meeting the radii \(PC, P'C\) in \(m\) and \(n\). Then the arch \(PP'\) will be the increment of \(z\); and since the angle \(PDP'\) is the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> \(<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEA">PEA</a>, PE'A\), the arch \(m n\) will be the corresponding increment of \(v\). Suppose now the point \(P'\) to approach continually to \(P\), then the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> \(C\) and \(D\) will approach to \(C\), and the ratio of the arch \(PP'\), the increment of \(z\), to the arch \(m n\) the increment of \(v\), will approach to the ratio of \(CP\) to \(C m\), that is to the ratio of \(r\) to \(1\); therefore the ratio of \(r\) to \(1\) is the limit of the ratio of \(AP'\) to \(m n\), or \(r = \lim_{m n} \frac{PP'}{m n}\), and passing to the ratio of the fluxions, \(r = \frac{PP'}{m n}\), thus we have obtained a formula expressing the radius of curvature, by means of the fluxion of the arch of the curve, and the fluxion of the angle which a normal to the curve makes with the line of the abscissas. We proceed to deduce from this formula other expressions which may involve the fluxions of \( x \) and \( y \) only. 96. Because PE is a normal to the curve at E, the tangent of the angle PEA or \( v \) is equal to \( \frac{x}{y} \) (\$75.), put \( \frac{\dot{x}}{y} = t \), then because tan. \( v = t \), we have, by taking the fluxions (\$60.), \( \dot{v} \sec^2 v = t \), but sec. \( v = 1 + \tan^2 v \) \[ = t + \frac{\dot{x}^2}{y^2} + \frac{\dot{y}^2}{y^2} = \frac{\dot{x}^2}{y^2} (\$63.), \text{ therefore } \frac{\dot{v}}{y} = t \] and \( \dot{v} = \frac{\dot{x}^2}{y^2} \). Substituting now this value of \( \dot{v} \) in the formula \( r = \frac{\dot{x}^2}{\dot{v}^2} \), it becomes \( \frac{\dot{x}^2}{\dot{y}^2} \). If we now recollect that \( t = \frac{\dot{x}}{y} \), and that \( \dot{x}^2 + \dot{y}^2 \), it will appear that this other expression which we have found for \( r \) involves in effect the fluxions of \( x \) and \( y \) only. 97. In computing the values of \( t = \frac{\dot{x}}{y} \), and \( \frac{\dot{x}^2}{\dot{y}^2} \) we may consider any two of the three quantities \( x, y, z \), as a function of the remaining quantity; and upon that hypothesis compute their fluxions. Thus if we suppose that \( y \) and \( z \) are functions of \( x \), then, as in taking the fluxions of \( y, t, \) and \( z \), we must consider \( x \) as a given or constant quantity, from the equation \( t = \frac{\dot{x}}{y} \) we have \( \dot{t} = \frac{\dot{x} \dot{y}}{y^2} \) (\$39.), and substituting this value of \( \dot{t} \) in \( \frac{\dot{x}^2}{\dot{y}^2} \), the value last found for \( r \), it becomes \[ r = \frac{\dot{y}}{\dot{x}} = \frac{(\dot{x}^2 + \dot{y}^2)^{\frac{1}{2}}}{\dot{x} \dot{y}} \] If again, instead of considering \( y \) and \( z \) as functions of \( x \), we consider \( x \) and \( z \) as functions of \( y \), then from the equation \( t = \frac{\dot{x}}{y} \) (as \( \dot{y} \) must now be reckoned constant), we get \( \dot{t} = \frac{\dot{x}}{y} \), thus the formula \( r = \frac{\dot{x}^2}{\dot{y}^2} \) becomes \[ r = \frac{\dot{y}}{\dot{x}} = \frac{(\dot{x}^2 + \dot{y}^2)^{\frac{1}{2}}}{\dot{x} \dot{y}} \] We shall now apply these formulæ to some examples. 98. Example 1.—It is required to find the general expression for the radius of curvature of a parabola. The equation of the parabola is \( y = ax^2 \), there- fore, \( \dot{y} = 2ax \), and, making \( \dot{x} \) constant, \[ \dot{y} = -\frac{2a^2x}{4x^2}, \text{ therefore, } \dot{z} = \sqrt{(x^2 + y^2)} \] \[ = \frac{\dot{x}}{2} \sqrt{\left(\frac{4x^2 + a^2}{x}\right)}, \text{ and, putting } r \text{ for the radius of curvature,} \] \[ r = \frac{\dot{x}^3}{\dot{y}^2} = \frac{(a + 4x)^{\frac{1}{2}}}{2\sqrt{a}} \] If in this general expression, we put \( x = 0 \), we find \( \frac{a^2}{2\sqrt{a}} = \frac{a}{2} \) for the radius of curvature at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERTEX">vertex</a> of the curve. Ex. 2. Suppose the curve to be an ellipse, required as in the last example. Putting \( a \) and \( c \) to denote the two axes, the equation of the ellipse is \( a^2y^2 = c^2(x^2 - x^2) \). Hence taking the first and second fluxions, we have \( 2a^2y \dot{y} = c^2 \dot{x} (a - 2x) \), and \( 2a^2 \dot{y}^2 + 2a^2 \dot{y} \dot{y} = -2c^2 \dot{x}^2 \); whence \( y = \frac{c^2 \dot{x} (a - 2x)}{2a^2 \dot{y}} \), and \( \dot{y} = \frac{a^2 \dot{y}^2 + c^2 \dot{x}^2}{a^2 \dot{y}} \), which expressions, by substituting the values of \( y \) and \( \dot{y} \), become \[ \dot{y} = \frac{c \dot{x} (a - 2x)}{2a \sqrt{(a^2 - x^2)}} \] \[ - \dot{y} = \frac{a^2 \dot{x}^2 (a - 2x)}{4a^2 \sqrt{(a^2 - x^2)}} \sqrt{(a^2 - x^2)} + \frac{c^2 \dot{x}^2}{a \sqrt{(a^2 - x^2)}} \] \[ = \frac{c \dot{x}^2 (a - 2x)^2 + 4(ax - x^2)}{4(a^2 - x^2) \sqrt{(a^2 - x^2)}} \] \[ = \frac{c \dot{x}^2}{4(a^2 - x^2)^{\frac{1}{2}}} \] therefore, \[ \dot{z} = \sqrt{(\dot{x}^2 + \dot{y}^2)} \] \[ = \sqrt{\left(\frac{c^2 \dot{x}^2 (a - 2x)^2}{4a^2 (a^2 - x^2)} + \dot{x}^2\right)} \] \[ = \frac{\dot{x}}{2a} \sqrt{\left(\frac{c^2 \dot{x}^2 + (a^2 - c^2)(ax - x^2)}{a^2 - x^2}\right)} \] and \[ r = \frac{\dot{x}^3}{\dot{y}^2} = \frac{(a^2 + 4(ax - x^2))(a^2 - x^2)^{\frac{1}{2}}}{2a^2 c} \] which expression, when \( x = 0 \), becomes simply \( \frac{a^2}{2a} \), the radius of curvature at the vertices of the transverse axis; but when \( x = a \), it becomes \( \frac{a^2}{2a} \), the radius of curvature at the vertices of the conjugate axis. PART PART II. THE INVERSE METHOD OF FLUXIONS. 99. AS the DIRECT METHOD of fluxions treats of finding the relation between the fluxions of variable quantities, having given the relation subsisting between the quantities themselves; so the INVERSE METHOD treats of finding the relation subsisting between the variable quantities, having given the relation of their fluxions. Whatever be the relation between variable quantities, we can in every case assign the relation of their fluxions; therefore the direct method of fluxions may in this respect be considered as perfect. But it is not the same with the inverse method, for there are no direct and general rules, by which we can in every case determine, from the relation of the fluxions, that of their flowing quantities or fluents. All we can do is to compare any proposed fluxion with such fluxions as are derived from known fluents by the rules of the direct method, and if we find it to have the same form as one of these, we may conclude that the fluents of both, or at least the variable parts of these fluents, are identical. 100. In the direct method we have shewn, that by proper transformations, the finding of the fluxion of any proposed function is reducible to the finding of the fluxions of a few simple functions, and of the sums, or products, or quotients of such functions. In like manner, in the inverse method we must endeavour to transform complex fluxionary expressions into others more simple, so as to reduce them, if possible, to some fluxion, the fluent of which we already know. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">Sect</a>. I. Of the Fluents of Fluxions involving one variable quantity. 101. As when $y$ is such a function of a variable quantity $x$, that $y = Ax^m + C$, where $A$, $m$ and $C$ denote constant quantities, we find by the direct method (§ 36. and § 26.) that $y = m A x^{m-1} x$, or (putting $a$ instead of $m A$, and $n$ instead of $m-1$), $y = ax^n x$; so, on the contrary, as often as we have the fluxional equation $$\dot{y} = ax^n \dot{x},$$ we may conclude that the relation of the fluents is expressed by the equation $$y = \frac{ax^n + 1}{n+1} + C,$$ for by substituting $m A$ instead of $a$, and $m-1$ instead of $n$ in this equation, it becomes $y = A x^m + C$, the same equation as that from which the fluxional equation was derived. 102. The value of the constant quantity $C$, which is generally called by writers on fluxions, the correction of the fluent, is to be determined from the particular inquiry in which the fluxional equation $\dot{y} = ax^n \dot{x}$ occurs. If it be known that $y = 0$, when $x$ acquires some known magnitude, which may be denoted by $b$, then the general equation $y = \frac{ab^{n+1}}{n+1} + C$, becomes in that particular case $$0 = \frac{ab^{n+1}}{n+1} + C;$$ Hence, by subtracting each side of this last equation from the corresponding side of the former, we get $$y = \frac{a(x^{n+1} - b^{n+1})}{n+1}$$ an equation that is independent of the constant and arbitrary quantity $C$. 103. By giving particular values to $n$ in the fluxional equation $y = ax^n \dot{x}$, and in that of the fluents $y = \frac{a(x^{n+1} - b^{n+1})}{n+1}$, we may obtain particular fluxional equations, and corresponding equations of the fluents. There is however one case which requires to be noticed; it is when $n = -1$; then the equation of the fluxions is $y = ax^{-1} \dot{x} = \frac{ax}{x}$, and that of the fluents, according to the general formula $y = \frac{a(x^{n+1} - b^{n+1})}{n+1}$ $$= \frac{a(x^0 - b^0)}{0} = \frac{a(1-1)}{0} = 0,$$ but from this expression it is manifest, that nothing can be concluded. The value of the function $\frac{a(x^{n+1} - b^{n+1})}{n+1}$, in the particular case of $n+1 = 0$ may be found by the rule given in § 90 for determining the value of a function when it assumes the form $\frac{0}{0}$; but it may be otherwise found by proceeding thus. Put $n+1 = m$, and let $p = \log_x e$, and $q = \log_b e$; then, by the formula of § 54, $$x^n = 1 + pm + \frac{p^2 m^2}{2} + &c.$$ $$b^n = 1 + qm + \frac{q^2 m^2}{2} + &c.$$ and therefore $$x^n - b^n = (p-q)m + \frac{(p^2-q^2)m^2}{2} + &c.$$ and $$\frac{x^n - b^n}{m} = (p-q) + \frac{(p^2-q^2)m^2}{2} + &c.$$ Thus Thus we have \( \frac{x^n - b^n}{m} \) or \( \frac{x^{n+1} - b^{n+1}}{n+1} \) expressed generally by a series, all the terms of which, except the first, being multiplied by \( m \) or \( n+1 \), will vanish when \( n+1=0 \), or when \( n=-1 \); hence it appears that the general equation \( y = \frac{a(x^{n+1} - b^{n+1})}{n+1} \), becomes in the particular case of \( n=-1 \), \( y = a(p-q) \), which, substituting for \( p \) and \( q \) their values, and observing that \[ \log_e x - \log_e b = \frac{1}{\log_e e} \times \log_e \frac{x}{b}, \] becomes \[ y = a \log_e \frac{x}{b}, \] where \( \log_e \) and \( \log_e \frac{x}{b} \) are to be taken according to the same system, which may be any system of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOGARITHMS">logarithms</a> whatever. So that if we take the Napierian system in which \( \log_e 1 = 1 \), then \[ y = a \log_e \frac{x}{b} = a \log_e x - a \log_e b = a \log_e x + C, \] where \( C \) denotes a constant quantity, and where the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> \( l \), in this formula, and in others in which it may occur, is put as an abbreviation of the words Napierian logarithm, so that by \( a.l.x \) is meant \( a \) multiplied by the Napierian logarithm of \( x \), &c. This expression which we have found for the value of \( y \) in the particular case of \( y = ax^n \dot{x} \) or \( \frac{dx}{x} \), coincides with what we might have found by considering that when \( y = l.x \), it has been shewn (\$ 57.), that \( y = \frac{dx}{x} \), so that conversely, when \( y = \frac{dx}{x} \), we may conclude that \( y = a.l.x + C \), where \( C \) denotes a constant quantity, to be determined from the particular question in which the fluxional equation may occur. 104. It must now be evident that if \[ y = ax^n \dot{x} + bx^{n+1} \dot{x} + cx^{n+2} \dot{x} + \ldots + C, \] where \( m, n, p, \ldots \) are constant numbers, then \[ y = \frac{ax^{n+1}}{m+1} + \frac{bx^{n+2}}{n+1} + \frac{cx^{n+3}}{p+1} + \ldots + C; \] here \( C \) denotes a constant arbitrary quantity that may be considered as the sum of the constant quantities which ought to be added to the terms \( \frac{ax^{n+1}}{m+1}, \frac{bx^{n+2}}{n+1}, \ldots \), each being regarded as a distinct fluent. 105. In general, since that when \[ y = at + bv + cu + \ldots + C, \] where \( t, v, u, \ldots \) denote any functions of a variable quantity, and \( C \) a constant quantity, we have (\$ 35. and \$ 36.) \[ y = at + bv + cu + \ldots + C. \] So, on the contrary, if we have any fluxional equation of this last form, we may conclude that \[ y = at + bv + cu + \ldots + C. \] And since that when \( u = vt + C \), where \( u, v \) and \( t \) denote any function of a variable quantity, and \( C \) a constant quantity, we have, § 37, \( u = vt + t^2 \); so, on the contrary, if \[ u = vt + t^2, \] we may conclude that \[ u = vt + C, \] and in like manner if we have \[ u = vt - vt^2 = vt - vt^2, \] we may infer from § 39. that \[ u = vt + C. \] 106. It is often convenient to denote the fluent of a fluxional expression without actually exhibiting that fluent. For this purpose we shall employ the sign \( \int \), putting it before the fluxion whose fluent we <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> to denote. Thus, by the expression \( \int ax^n \dot{x} \), is to be understood the fluent of \( ax^n \); and as this fluent has been found to be \( \frac{ax^{n+1}}{n+1} + C \), we may express this conclusion in symbols shortly thus, \[ \int ax^n \dot{x} = \frac{ax^{n+1}}{n+1} + C. \] 107. Suppose we have \( y = (ax + b)^n \dot{x} \), we may expand \( (ax + b)^n \) into a series, and multiply the series by \( \dot{x} \), and find the fluent of each term of the result. But we may also find the fluent of this expression without employing the development of \( (ax + b)^n \), by proceeding thus. Put \( ax + b = z \), then \( x = \frac{z-b}{a} \), and \( \dot{x} = \frac{\dot{z}}{a} \). Substitute now these values of \( ax + b \) and \( \dot{x} \) in the expression for \( y \), and it becomes \( y = \frac{z^n}{a} \); hence we have (\$ 101.) \( y = \frac{z^{n+1}}{a(m+1)} + C \), and consequently, by substituting \( (ax + b) \) for \( z \), \[ y = \frac{(ax + b)^{n+1}}{a(m+1)} + C. \] 108. Suppose that \( y = (ax + b)^n \dot{x} \). By putting as before \( ax + b = z \), we have \( na^{n-1} \dot{x} = \dot{z} \), and \( x = \frac{z}{na} \); hence \( y = \frac{z^n}{na} \), and \( y = \frac{z^{n+1}}{na(m+1)} + C \), and substituting for \( z \) its value \( ax + b \), \[ y = \frac{(ax + b)^{n+1}}{na(m+1)} + C. \] Let us now consider fractional functions, and to begin with a simple case let us suppose that \[ y = \frac{(ax + b)^m}{n a(m+1)} + C. \] Put \( ax + b = z \), then \( x = \frac{z - b}{a} \), \( \dot{x} = \frac{\dot{z}}{a} \), and consequently, \[ \dot{y} = \frac{A(z-b)^m}{a^{m+1}z}. \] We have now only to find the development of \((z-b)^m\), to multiply each of its terms by \( z \) and divide it by \( z^2 \), and take the fluent of the result. Let us take for example the case of \( m = 3 \), and \( n = 2 \), then \[ \dot{y} = \frac{A(z-b)^3}{a^4z^2}. \] \[ = A \left\{ \frac{z^3}{a^4} - 3 \frac{b^2z}{a^4} + 3 \frac{b^3}{a^4} \right\} + C. \] Hence, taking the fluents of the several terms, as in § 105, we have \[ y = \frac{A}{a^4} \left\{ \frac{z^4}{2} - 3 \frac{b^2z}{a^4} + 3 \frac{b^3}{a^4} \right\} + C. \] Let us now restore the value of \( z \), and then it appears that when \[ \dot{y} = \frac{A(x+b)^3}{(ax+b)^4}, \] \[ y = \frac{A}{a^4} \left\{ \frac{(ax+b)^4}{2} - 3 \frac{b(ax+b)}{a^4} + 3 \frac{b^2(ax+b)}{a^4} \right\} + C. \] If we suppose that \[ \dot{y} = \frac{Ax^n + Bx^n + Cx^n + &c.}{(a+b)^m}, \] then, we may write the equation thus, \[ \dot{y} = \frac{Ax^n}{(a+b)^m} + \frac{Bx^n}{(a+b)^m} + \frac{Cx^n}{(a+b)^m} + &c. \] and take the fluent of each term, in the same manner as we have found the fluent of \( \frac{Ax^n}{(a+b)^m} \). Of the Fluents of rational Fractions. Every fluxion that is a rational fraction is comprehended under this general formula, \[ \frac{(Ax^n + Bx^n + Cx^n + &c.)}{Ax^n + Bx^n + Cx^n + &c.}, \] which, by putting \( U \) to denote the expression between the parentheses in the numerator, and \( V \) the denominator, may be represented by \( \frac{U}{V} \). Now in the first place, we remark that the greatest exponent of the powers of \( x \) in the numerator may be supposed to be less than that of its powers in the denominator. For if it were not so, by dividing \( U \) by \( V \), and calling \( Q \) the quotient, and \( R \) the remainder, we should have \[ \frac{U}{V} = \frac{Q}{V} + \frac{R}{V}, \] and \[ \int \frac{U}{V} = \int \frac{Q}{V} + \int \frac{R}{V}. \] Now, \( Q \) being a rational and integer function \( \int Q \dot{x} \) may be found, as in § 104, and it only remains to find \( \int \frac{R}{V} \), an expression in which the highest exponent of the powers of \( x \) in \( R \) is less by unity than in \( N \); so that the fraction \( \frac{R}{V} \) may be generally expressed thus, \[ \frac{(Ax^n + Bx^n + Cx^n + &c.)}{x^n + Ax^n + Bx^n + Cx^n + &c.}. \] The general method of finding the fluent of a fractional expression of this form consists in decomposing it into a series of other fractions, the denominators of which are more simple. These fractions may be found by proceeding as follows: By putting the denominator of the proposed fraction equal to \( 0 \), we get this equation, \[ x^n + Ax^n + Bx^n + &c. = 0. \] Suppose now that the roots of this equation are found, and that they are denoted by \[ -a, -a', -a'', -a''', &c. \] which quantities we shall suppose, in the first place, are all unequal. Then the expression which has been assumed as equal to \( 0 \), may (ALGEBRA, Sect. X.) be considered as the product of \( n \) factors \[ x + a, x + a', x + a'', x + a''', &c. \] Let the proposed fraction \( \frac{R}{V} \) be now assumed as equal to the sum of the simple fractions \[ \frac{N}{x+a}, \frac{N'}{x+a'}, \frac{N''}{x+a''}, &c. \] having for their denominators the simple factors of the denominator of the proposed fraction, and for their numerators quantities which are constant, but as yet are indetermined. That we may avoid complicated calculations, and present a determinate object to the mind, let us suppose that the fluxion of which we are to find the fluent is \[ \frac{(Ax^n + Bx^n + Cx^n)}{x^n + Ax^n + Bx^n + Cx^n}, \] and that we have by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> of the cubic equation \( x^3 + Ax^2 + Bx + C = 0 \) found \[ x^3 + Ax^2 + Bx + C = (x+a)(x+a')(x+a''). \] The fractions \[ \frac{N}{x+a}, \frac{N'}{x+a'}, \frac{N''}{x+a''} \] when reduced to a common denominator are \[ \frac{N(x+a')(x+a'')x}{(x+a)(x+a')(x+a'')}, \frac{N'(x+a)(x+a'')x}{(x+a)(x+a')(x+a'')}, \frac{N''(x+a)(x+a')x}{(x+a)(x+a')(x+a'')} \] The common denominator of these fractions is the same as that of the proposed fraction, and each of the numerators, as well as their sum, is a function of \( x \) of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> lower than the denominator, that is, in the present case, it is a function of the second degree. By taking the actual products of the factors in the numerators, and adding the results, we find the sum of the fractions equal to \[ \frac{N+N'+N''x^2}{V} + \left\{ N(a+a') + N'(a+a'') + N''(a+a') \right\} x + N'a'a'' + N'a'a'' + N''a'a'' \] where \( V \) denotes the common denominator \((x+a)(x+a')(x+a'') = x^3 + A'x^2 + B'x + C'\). Setting aside the factor \( \frac{x}{V} \) of the above expression, we are now to compare that part of it which involves the three indeterminate quantities \( N, N', N'' \), with \( A.x^3 + B.x + C \), the numerator of the proposed fraction, thus we obtain these three equations \[ N+N'+N''=A, \] \[ N(a+a') + N'(a+a'') + N''(a+a') = B, \] \[ N'a'a'' + N'a'a'' + N''a'a'' = C. \] By these equations, which are all of the first degree, we may determine the values of \( N, N', N'' \), and thus we have the proposed fraction \[ \frac{(Ax^3+Bx+C)x}{x^3+A'x^2+B'x+C'} \] equal to \[ \frac{N}{x+a} + \frac{N'}{x+a'} + \frac{N''}{x+a''} \] where \( N, N', N'' \), and \( a, a', a'' \), are constant and known quantities. Put \( x+a=x \), then \( x=x \), and the fraction \( \frac{N}{x+a} \) is transformed to \( \frac{N}{x} \), of which the fluent is \( N.l.z=N.l. \) \[ (x+a) (\S 103) \] In like manner we find \( \int \frac{N'}{x+a'} = N' l.(x+a') \), and \( \int \frac{N''}{x+a''} = N'' l.(x+a'') \), and consequently \[ \int \frac{(Ax^3+Bx+C)x}{x^3+A'x^2+B'x+C'} = N l.(x+a) + N' l.(x+a') + N'' l.(x+a'') + \text{const}. \] and, it is easy to see, that by reducing these fractions to \[ \frac{M}{x+a} + \frac{M'}{x+a'} + \frac{M''}{x+a''} + \cdots + \frac{M'''}{x+a'''}. \] where by const. is meant a constant quantity. It is easy to extend this mode of proceeding to the general formula given at the beginning of this §; and it is obvious, that as often as the denominator of a rational fraction can be decomposed into real and unequal factors, the determination of the fluent of that fraction is attended with no other difficulty than this decomposition, which requires the numerical resolution of equations. 112. We have supposed that the factors of the denominator of the proposed fraction are unequal among themselves, and it is only when this is the case that the fraction can be decomposed into others, having all this form \( \frac{N}{x+a} \). If we suppose that the denominator \( x^n + A'x^{n-1} + B'x^{n-2} + \cdots + T' \) has a factor of the form \((x+a)\), then the proposed fraction \[ \frac{(Ax^{n-1}+Bx^{n-2}+Cx^{n-3}+\cdots+T)x}{x^n+A'x^{n-1}+B'x^{n-2}+C'x^{n-3}+\cdots+T} \] must be assumed equal to \[ \frac{(P.x^{n-1}+Q.x^{n-2}+R.x^{n-3}+\cdots+Y)x}{(x+a)^n} + \frac{N}{x+a} + \frac{N'}{x+a'} + \frac{N''}{x+a''} \] where \( P, Q, R, \ldots Y, N', N'' \), &c. denote indeterminate but constant quantities, and \( x+a, x+a', x+a'' \), &c. are the remaining factors of the denominator of the proposed fraction. To determine the quantities \( P, Q, R, \ldots Y, N', N'' \), &c. we must now proceed in all respects as in last §, that is, we must reduce the fractions involving these quantities to a common denominator, which will be the same as the denominator of the proposed fraction; then we must add the numerators, and put the coefficient of each power of \( x \) in the sum equal to the coefficient of the same power in the numerator of the proposed fraction. Thus we shall have as many equations as indeterminate quantities, and by resolving these equations, the value of these quantities will be found. Having thus determined all the quantities \( P, Q, R, \ldots Y \), which enter into the fraction \[ \frac{(P.x^{n-1}+Q.x^{n-2}+\cdots+Y)x}{(x+a)^n} \] its fluent may be found as shewn in § 109. But we may also assume it equal to \[ \frac{M}{x+a} + \frac{M'}{x+a'} + \frac{M''}{x+a''} + \cdots + \frac{M'''}{x+a'''}. \] a common denominator and adding them, the numerator of their sum will have the same form as that of the fraction whose fluent we are seeking; so that the values of the indeterminate quantities $M$, $M'$, &c. will be found by putting the coefficients of the same power of $x$ in both numerators equal to each other. To find the fluent of $$\frac{M}{(x+a)^p}$$ we may assume $x+a=z$, then $z=x$, and $$\int \frac{M}{(x+a)^p} = \int \frac{M}{z^p} = \frac{M}{1-p}$$ In like manner $$\int \frac{M'}{(x+a)^{p-1}} = \frac{M'}{(2-p)(x+a)^{p-1}}$$ and so on, all the fluents being algebraic, except the last $\int \frac{M''}{x+a}$ which is $M''\ln(x+a)$, a logarithmic function. 113. In resolving the equation $$x^4 + A'x^{n-1} + B'x^{n-2} + \cdots + T = 0,$$ it may happen that some of its roots $a, a', a'', \&c.$ are imaginary quantities, and then some of the simple factors $x+a, x+a', x+a'', \&c.$ will be imaginary.
