Two magnificent catafalques fill up the side arcades of this sanctuary: on one the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V., his wife, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, and two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a>, are represented in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRONZE">bronze</a>, larger than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, kneeling; opposite are the effigies of Philip II., and of his three wives, of the same materials, and in the same devout attitude. Underneath is the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a>-place of the royal family, called the Pantheon. Twenty-five steps <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to this vault, over the door of which is an inscription denoting, that. Hic locus, sacer mortalitatis exuclii Catholicorum Regum, &c. was intended by Charles the emperor; resolved upon by Philip II., begun by Philip III., and completed by Philip IV. The mausoleum is circular, 36 feet diameter, incrusted with fine marbles in an elegant <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. The bodies of the kings and queens <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in tombs of marble, in niches, one above the other. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of these sepulchres is grand, and executed with a princely magnificence; but, as a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> traveller observes, in a style rather too gay, too light, and too delicately fitted up for the idea we are apt to form of a chapel destined for the reception of the dead. The collection of pictures dispersed about various parts of the church, sacristy, and convent, has been considered as equal, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not superior, to any gallery in Europe, except that of Dresden. Formed out of the spoils of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and the wasted cabinet of that unfortunate dilettante Charles I. of England, it contains some of the most <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> works of the greatest painters that have flourished since the revival of the art. In the sacristy is an altar called La santa Forma: this is a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABERNACLE">tabernacle</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> custodia of gems, marbles, woods, and other precious materials, inlaid in gilt bronze; in which, rather than in the excellence of the workmanship or taste of the design, consists the merit of this rock of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>. Before it hangs a curtain, on which Coello has represented Charles II. and all his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a>, coming to place this Forma. This is esteemed one of the most curious collections of portraits in the world; for all the persons are drawn with the greatest strength of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, and are said to be perfect resemblances not only of the monarch and grandees, but even of the monks, servants, and guards. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, busts, and medallions of the Escorial, are not in any great number, or very remarkable for their excellence: but the library contains a most precious collection of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>, many fine drawings, and other curiosities. Notwithstanding the coldness of the exposure, the late king, for the sake of hunting, used to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> here several months in the year; and to make the place less inconvenient to his attendants and to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, he built an entire new town adjoining to it.

ESCUTCHEON

Pages 360-360
or SCUTCHEON, in Heraldry, is derived from the French escussion, and that from the Latin scutum, and signifies the shield whereon coats of arms are represented. Most nations of the remotest antiquity were wont to have their shields distinguished by certain marks painted on them; and to have such on their shields was a token of honour, none being permitted to have them till they had performed some honourable action. The escutcheon, as used at present, is square, only rounded off at the bottom.

ESDRAS

Pages 360-361

a Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTAXERXES">Artaxerxes</a> Longimanus sent him with rich presents for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> and ornament of the temple at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, rebuilt under Zerubbabel; the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> also ordered the neighbouring governors to provide him with what conduced to the pomp of the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and to exempt the priests from paying taxes. He is supposed to be the collector of the Canon of Scripture; and that, by divine <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>, he added some things which hap- pened after the deaths of the authors. It is guessed he wrote the Chronicles, besides those books which bear his name, the two last of which are exploded even by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome.

ESNE

Pages 361-361
or ESNEH, a considerable town of Upper Egypt. It is governed by an Arabian prince and by a cahief, dependent on the bey of Girze. The Mahometans have several mosques here, and the Copts a church served by two priests. "Esne (says Abulfeda,) remarkable for its public baths and its commerce, is built on the westward of the Nile, between Assouan and Cous, but nearer to this latter. It acknowledges, adds the geographer of Nubia, the Copts for founders. Its well cultivated territory abounds in grain and palm-trees. It is surrounded by gardens filled with fruit-trees. One admires here several ancient monuments constructed by the Copts, and superb ruins." This description answers to Esne in our time, which is situated on the edge of a rich country, and shaded by groves of orange trees loaded with fruits and flowers. This town, formerly called Latopolis, revered Minerva and the fish Latus (Strabo). It contains within its boundary an antique temple. Thick walls inclose it on three sides. Six large fluted columns, crowned by a capital ornamented with the palm leaf, form the façade of it; 18 others support the roof, which is composed of large squares of marble; the building is surrounded by a frieze, and innumerable hieroglyphics cover its exterior aspects. A little to the south of the town are seen the ruins of a monastery founded by St. Helena, and near it the burying-place of the martyrs, adorned with tombs crowned by cupolas, supported by arcades. The inhabitants of Esne having revolted against the persecution of Dioclesian, that emperor destroyed this town and put them to the sword. This place, consecrated by religion, is become a celebrated pilgrimage among the Copts. They repair thither from the most distant provinces of the kingdom. In the chain of mountains which stretches to the eastward of the Nile, and nearly opposite Esne, are quarries of a soft stone, called Barum. It is made use of for kitchen utensils. It hardens in the fire, and forms excellent kettles and pans, which give no bad taste to the victuals. This stone is probably the lapis alaris, or pot-stone. "Esne (says Denon) is the ancient Latopolis. Some remains are still visible of its port or quay on the bank of the Nile, which has been often repaired: but, notwithstanding all that has been done for it, still remains in a very miserable condition. This town also contains the portico of a temple, which appears to me to be the most perfect monument of ancient architecture. It is situated near the bazar in the great square, and would make an incomparable ornament to this spot, if the inhabitants had any idea of its merit; but instead of this they have deformed it by the most miserable ruined hovels, and have devoted it to the vilest purposes. The portico is very well preserved, and possesses a great richness of sculpture: it is composed of eighteen columns with broad capitals; these columns are noble and elegant, though they now appear in the most disadvantageous light: the rubbish should be cleared to find if any part of the cella remains. "The hieroglyphics in relief, with which it is covered within and without, are executed with great care; they contain, among other subjects, a zodiac, and large figures of men with crocodiles heads: the capitals, though all different, have a very fine effect; and as an additional proof that the Egyptians borrowed nothing from other people, we may remark, that they have taken all the ornaments, of which these capitals are composed, from the productions of their own country, such as the lotus, the palm-tree, the vine, the rush, &c., &c."

ESPALIERS

Pages 361-361

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>, are rows of trees planted about a whole garden <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> plantation, or in hedges, in such a manner as to enclose <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> or separate parts of a garden; and are trained up regularly to a lattice of wood-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> hedge, for the defense of tender <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> against the injuries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. They are of admirable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>-garden, serving not only to shelter the tender plants, but screen them from the sight of persons in the walks. The trees chiefly planted for espaliers, are apples, pears, and some plums: some plant apples grafted upon paradise stocks; but as these are of short <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>, it is better to plant those grafted upon crabstock, or upon what the gardeners call Dutch stocks; which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> both cause them to bear sooner, and prevent their growing too luxuriant. The best kinds of apple for this purpose, are the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> pippen, nonpareil, renette, &c.; and the best sorts of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a>, are the jargonelle, blanquette, &c. These last, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> designed for a strong moist <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, should be grafted upon quince stocks; but if for a dry soil, upon free stocks. While the trees are young, it will be sufficient to drive a few stakes into the ground on each side of them; fastening the branches to these in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> position, as they are produced. This method will do for the three first years; after which an espalier should be made of ash-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>, whereof there must be two sorts, larger and smaller; the former to be driven upright into the ground a foot asunder, and the latter, or slender poles, to be nailed across these, at about <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> inches. Some prefer to this another sort of espalier, made of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> cut to any size; these are, indeed, more sightly, but withal vastly more expensive. When the espalier is thus framed, the branches are to be fastened to it with osier twigs; observing to train them in a horizontal position, and at equal distances. Fruit trees thus managed are preferable to any others; not only as <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> better-tasted fruit, but as taking up very little room in a garden, so as to be less hurtful to plants which grow in the quarters.

ESPLANADE

Pages 361-361

in Fortification, the sloping of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a> of the covered-way towards the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a>.

ESPLEES

Pages 361-361

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, the general products which lands yield, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the profit or commodity that is to be taken or made of a thing.

ESPOUSALS

Pages 361-362

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signify a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> Esposals mise made between a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> and a woman to marry each other; and in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> where marriages may be consummated, espousals go before. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">Marriage</a> is termed an espousal de presenti. The espousals among the Jews were either by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, or by a piece of silver given and received, or by cohabitation. Amongst the Greeks, after the parents and friends of the young couple had finished their negotiation, the couple themselves pledged their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> to each other, the man swearing that he would be constant and true, the woman that she would marry him, and make him <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of all she had. Then they ratified their agreement by a kiss and joining <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. Amongst the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> the espousals consisted in an engagement of friends on both sides, whether absent or present, in public or without witnesses. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> way was by writings drawn up by common consent, and sealed by both parties: besides this, the man sent a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> to the woman, consisting of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> and without a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>.

ESQUILIAE

Pages 362-362

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> hills of Rome, which Varro <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> have to be two, viz. Cispia and Oppius; also Mons Esquilinus, softened from Exquillius; and this again from Excaubius, the watch <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a> kept here, from a jealousy he entertained of his colleague Titus Tatius. On the east side it reached the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> walls; on the south, the Via Liviana; on the west, the wide valley between Mount Coelius and the Palatine; on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, the Mons Viminalis; on the east side was the Porta Esquilina. This hill by some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> was called Suburranus, from the street Suburra to the north of it: by the poets, Esquilinus.

ESQUIMAUX

Pages 362-362

a people of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, inhabiting all that vast tract of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> known by the name of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LABRADOR">Labrador</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-NEW_BRITAIN">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. They differ very considerably, both in aspect and manners, from the other American nations; agreeing in most respects with the inhabitants of West <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GREENLAND">Greenland</a>. See New Britain and Greenland.

ESQUIRE

Pages 362-362

was originally he who, attending a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, did carry his shield; whence he was called escuier in French, and sculifer, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> armiger, i.e. armour-bearer, in Latin. Hoteman says, that those whom the French call esquires, were a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> kind of vassals, having jus scuti, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to bear a shield, and in it the ensigns of their family, in token of their gentility or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. But this addition hath not of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> time had any relation to the office or employment of the person to whom it hath been attributed, as to carrying of arms, &c. but hath been merely a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of dignity, and next in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> to a knight. For those to whom this title is now due, see the article <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMMONALTY">COMMONALTY</a>. Officers of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s courts, and of the king's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>, counsellors at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, justices of the peace, are only esquires in reputation; and he who is a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of peace has this title only during the time he is in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>, and no longer, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he is not otherwise qualified to bear. A <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> being a superior officer, bears the title of esquire during his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; in respect of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trust he has in the commonwealth. The chiefs of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> families are esquires by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a>; and in late acts of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> for poll <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, many wealthy persons <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> reputed to be such, were ranked among the esquires of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. There is a general <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that every <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of landed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> who has 300l. a-year, is an esquire; which is a vulgar <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a>: for no money whatsoever, or landed property, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> give a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> properly this title, unless he comes within one of the above rules; and no person can ascribe this title where it is not due, unless he pleases; there being no difficulty in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> the line by the accounts given above and in the article COMMONALTY: but the meaner ranks of people, who know no better, do often basely prostitute this title; and, to the great confusion of all <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and precedence, every man who makes a decent appearance, far from thinking himself any way ridiculed by finding the superscription of his letters thus decorated, is fully gratified by such an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>. ESQUIRES of the king, are such as have that title by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>, wherein there is some formality used, as the putting about their necks a collar of SS. and bestowing on them a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of silver spurs, &c. ESRAKITES. See ESCHRATITES.

ESSAY

Pages 362-362

in literature, a peculiar kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, the character whereof is to be free, easy, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>; not tied to strict order and method, nor worked up and finished like a formal system.

ESSAYING

Pages 362-362
or ASSAYING, in Chemistry and Metallurgy, signifies the examination of a small quantity of any ore or mineral by fire, in order to discover the quantity of metal it contains. This is very necessary for those who intend to deal largely in metallurgical operations, in order to avoid unnecessary expense, by becoming previously acquainted with the nature of the ore. See Chemistry Index; and ORES, Reduction of. Essay-Hatch, is the miners term for a little trench or hole, which they dig to search for shoad or ore.

ESSEDARI

Pages 362-362

a sort of gladiators, mentioned by Seneca, Suetonius, and Tully, who on some occasions engaged one another out of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a> called cedera. The essedum was a sort of heavy chariot from which the Gauls and Britons engaged the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. See GLADIATOR.

ESSENCE

Pages 362-362

in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>, that which constitutes the particular <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of each genus <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> kind, and distinguishes it from all others: being nothing but that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> idea to which this name is affixed, so that every thing contained in it is essential to that particular kind. This Mr Locke calls the nominal essence; in contradistinction to the real essence, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of substances on which this nominal essence depends. Thus the nominal essence of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> is that complex idea the word gold stands for; let it be, for instance, a body, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, weighty, malleable, fusible, and fixed: but its real essence is the constitution of its insensible parts, on which these qualities and all its other properties depend, which is wholly unknown to us.

ESSENES

Pages 362-363
or ESSENANS, in Jewish antiquity, one one of the three ancient sects among that people. They allowed a future state, but denied a resurrection from the dead. Their way of life was very singular: they did not marry, but adopted the children of others, whom they bred up in the institutions of their sect: they despised riches, and had all things in common, and never changed their clothes till they were entirely worn out. When initiated, they were strictly bound not to communicate the mysteries of their sect to others; and if any of their members were found guilty of enormous crimes, they were expelled. Pliny tells us, that they dwelt on the west side of the lake of Asphaltites; and that they were a solitary kind of men, living without women or money, and feeding upon the fruit of the palm-tree: he adds, that they were constantly recruited by new-comers, whom the surges of ill fortune had made weary of the world: in which manner the sect was kept up for several thousands of years, without any being born among them. The reason why we find no mention made of them in the New Testament, may be their recluse and retired way of life, no less than their great simplicity and honesty, whereby they lay open to no censure or reproach.

ESSENTIAL

Pages 363-363

something necessarily belonging to a thing, from which it cannot be conceived distinct: thus the primary qualities of bodies, as <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, &c. are essential <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> inseparable from them in all their changes and alterations. ESSENTIAL OILS are such as are really contained in a plant, and are drawn from it by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a> in an alembic with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; they are thus called, in contradistinction to empyreumatic oils, which are raised by a naked fire without water.

ESSEX

Pages 363-363

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of England, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Stour, which separates it from <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGESHIRE">Cambridgeshire</a>; on the east, by the German <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; on the west, by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a>; and on the south by the river <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>. It extends 46 miles in length from east to west, and about 42 in breadth from north to south, and 200 in circuit. This county is in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and gives the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> to the family of Capel. The county of Essex is divided into nineteen <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>, and contains twenty-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> market-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, 415 parishes, 125 vicarages, and 1100 villages. It sends eight members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; namely, two for the county, and two for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLCHESTER">Colchester</a>, Harwich, and Malden. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> in the inland parts is healthy; but in the marshes near the sea it produces agues, particularly in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> called the Hundreds. However, the fertility of the unwholesome part is very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, and even the higher grounds of this county are very fruitful. About Saffron Walden, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, after <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> saffron three years, it is said, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> produce good barley for 18 years successively without any manure. Its produce, which is very plentiful, consists of corn, most excellent saffron, cattle, fowl, fish, and particularly oysters. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of this county are cloth, stuffs, and particularly baize. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, besides the Thames, are the Stour, which falls into the German sea at Harwich; the Lea, its western boundary, falls into the Thames below <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STRATFORD">Stratford</a>; the Blackwater runs through the heart of the county, and passing by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHELMSFORD">Chelmsford</a> is joined by the Chelmer, and from thence runs into the Essex German sea; the Coln runs by Halsted to Colchester, and so into the sea. The Roding which rises northwards, near Dunmow, runs into the Thames near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARKING">Barking</a>. All these rivers abound in most sorts of fish. In the year 1801, the total <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants in the county of Essex amounted to 226,437 persons. Of these 111,356 are males, and 115,081 are females. In 1811 the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> was 252,473, of whom 69,590 lived in towns, and 182,883 in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>.

ESTATE

Pages 363-363

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> that a person has in lands, tenements, or other effects; comprehending the whole in which a person hath any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the same. Estates are either real or personal; otherwise distinguished into FREEHOLDS, which descend to heirs; or CHATTELS, that go to executors or administrators. A fee-simple is the ampest estate our law admits of. See Fee. Estates are obtained several ways; as, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> from a father to a son; by conveyance or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> from one person to another; by gift or purchase; by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> or will. See DESCENT, SUCCESSION, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENURE">TENURE</a>, &c.

ESTATES

Pages 363-363

in a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is used either to denote the dominions of some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the general classes into which the people are divided. In <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, the estates are the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, lords, and commons; or rather the lords and commons, who meet the king in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, for reforming abuses, and enacting good and wholesome laws.

ESTHER

Pages 363-363

a canonical book of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>; containing the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of a Jewish virgin, dwelling with her uncle Mordecai at Shushan, in the reign of Ahasuerus, one of the kings of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of this maid raised her to the throne of Persia; whereby she had an opportunity to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> her countrymen, whose destruction was plotted by Haman, a favourite of that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. The learned are not agreed who this Ahasuerus was. Archbishop Usher supposes him to be <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a> Hystaspes, and Artystona to be Esther. Scaliger makes him the same with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a>, and his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> Hanestris to be Esther. Josephus, on the contrary, positively asserts, that the Ahasuerus of the scriptures, is the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTAXERXES">Artaxerxes</a> Longimanus of profane story; and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a>, throughout the whole book of Esther, translate Ahasuerus by Artaxerxes. Most people subscribe to this last <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>; and indeed the extraordinary kindness showed by Artaxerxes to the Jews, can scarcely be accounted for otherwise than by supposing that they had so powerful an advocate as Esther to solicit for them.

ESTHONIA

Pages 363-363

is a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the Russian empire, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVONIA">Livonia</a>. It is bounded on the east by the Baltic <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINLAND">Finland</a>, on the west by Ingria, and on the south by Lettonia. It is divided into six districts: 1. Harriien; 2. Wireland; 3. Alentakin; 4. Wich; 5. Jovven; and, 6. Odepoa. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are, Revel, Weisenberg, Borchholm, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARVA">Narva</a>, Nyslot, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HABSAL">Habsal</a>, Derpt, St Elin, Pernau, and Roderswick. In former times the inhabitants of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> carried

ESTOILEE

Pages 363-364
or CROSS ESTOILLEE, in Heraldry, a star with only four long rays in form of a cross; and, accordingly, broad in the centre, and terminating in sharp points.

ESTOPPEL

Pages 364-364

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, an impediment <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, arising from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a>; against which a man is forbidden, by law, to speak, though it be to say the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>.

ESTOVERS

Pages 364-364

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is used by Bracton, for that sustenance which a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, committed for felony, is to have out of his lands <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> goods for himself and his family during imprisonment. In stat. 6 Edw. I. it is used for an allowance in meat or clothes. In some manors, the tenants have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> of estovers; that is, necessary botes or allowances out of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a>'s wood: in which last <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, estovers comprehends <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>-bote, hay-bote, and plow-bote; so that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a man have in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> these general words, de rationabili estoverio in boscis, &c. he may thereby claim all the rest. Estovers is also used for alimony, which, if the husband refuses to pay, there is, besides the ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCOMMUNICATION">excommunication</a>, a writ at common law, de estoverii habendi, in order to recover it.

ESTRAY

Pages 364-364
or STRAY, signifies any tame beast, as sheep, oxen, swine, and horses, or swans, found within a lordship, and not owned by any man; in which case being cried, according to law, in the church, and two market towns adjoining, if it be not be claimed by the owner within a year and a day, it becomes the lord's of the soil where found. If the owner claims it within the year and day, he must pay the charges of finding, keeping, and proclaiming them; and he may seize it, without telling the marks or proving his property, which may be done at the trial if contested. If the beast stray within the year to another lordship, the first lord cannot retake it. An stray must be fed and kept, uninjured, and without labour, till it is reclaimed or the limited time expires.

ESTREAT

Pages 364-364

EXTRACTUM, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is used for the true copy <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> duplicate of some original <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, especially of amercements or penalties set <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in the rolls of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, to be levied by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a> or other officer, on every offender.

ESTREMADURA

Pages 364-364

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, near the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAGUS">Tagus</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Tajo, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEIRA">Beira</a>, on the east and south by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALENTEJO">Alentejo</a>, and on the west by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>. It is about 88 miles in length, and 45 in breadth. This province is divided into six comarcas, viz. Litria, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>, Tomar, Estremadura, and Alanquar, to the north of the Tagus; and that of Setubal, to the south of this river. These are likewise the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>. Estremadura is equal, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not preferable, to any other province in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> or Portugal. The district of Santaren produces such plenty of corn, and feeds so many flocks of sheep, that it may enter into competition with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> and the wines are all excellent; and it was here that the sweet oranges brought from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> were first planted, and of which there are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities transported to foreign parts, with the wines and other fruits. The fields are covered with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> almost all the year, from which the bees collect large quantities of fine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>. The olive-trees are numerous, from which they have excellent <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> abound with good fish, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> have quarries of several kinds.

ETCHING

Pages 364-367

a method of engraving on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, in which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> strokes, instead of being cut with a tool or graver, are eaten in with aquafortis. See Engraving. Etching is of a later <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, though not very <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>, than engraving with the tool; of which it was at first only an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>, that was practised by painters and other artists, who could much sooner form their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> to, and attain a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of, working in this way, than with the graver. But being then nevertheless considered as a counterfeit kind of engraving, and therefore inferior to the other, it was cultivated in a very confined manner; the closeness of the resemblance of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> to that performed by the tool, being made the test of its merit, and consequently the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> object of aim in those who pursued it. This servile confinement of the art of etching to the imitation of the original kind of engraving, was a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> cause of retarding its advancement towards perfection, as many of the most able masters cramped their talents with the observance of it: this may be seen in the instances of Sadelers, Swaneberg, Villamena, and particularly Le Besse; who, in his treatise on engraving, has laid <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> as a principle, that the perfection of this kind consists in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> similitude of the work with that done by the tool. This absurd prepossession has been since worn out: and the method of working with aquafortis has been so far improved, that instead of being now deemed a spurious kind of engraving, it evidently appears, in many modern works, the foundation of an excellence that could never have been produced without it: since, though the neatness and uniformity of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HATCHES">hatches</a>, which attend the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the tool, is more advantageous with respect to portraits; yet the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> and facility of the other manner gives a much greater opportunity to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> the force of genius and fancy in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>-engraving; where the effect of the whole, and not the minute exactness in finishing all the parts, constitutes the principal value. There are two methods practised of engraving in this way; the one with a hard <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a> or ground, the other with a soft. The first was formerly much used, being better accommodated to the intention of imitating the engraving with the tool; as the firmness of the body of the varnish gave more opportunity of retouching the lines, lines, or enlarging them with the oval-pointed <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">needles</a>, called by the French *echoppes*, as was practised by Le Bossé and others for that purpose. The latter has now almost wholly superseded the use of the other, by the free manner of working it admits of; which affords a power of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> incompatible with the greater inflexibility of the hard varnish, that confines the lines and hatches to such a regularity and sameness, as gives a stiffness of manner and coldness of effect to the work. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of the use of the tool and aquafortis, which are now both employed in many <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, has, however, given that perfection to engraving which it possesses at present. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> and spirit of the outline that the method of working with aquafortis affords, and the variety of shades which the different kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> produce in this way, as well as other means of expressing the peculiar appearance and character of particular subjects, furnish what was defective in the sole use of the tool; while on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the exactness and regularity of the lines, which are required for finishing many kinds of designs, are supplied by the graver; and by a judicious application of both, that complete finishing is obtained, which either of them alone must necessarily want. The manner by which this art is performed, is the covering the surface of the plate with a proper varnish or ground, as it is called, which is capable of resisting aquafortis; and then scoring or scratching away, by instruments resembling needles, the parts of this varnish or ground, in the places where the strokes or hatches of the engraving are intended to be; then, the plate being covered with aquafortis, the parts that are laid naked and exposed by removing the ground or varnish, are corroded or eaten away by it; while the rest, being secured and defended, remain untouched. There are two methods of etching, as has been already observed; the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of which from each other consists, as well in the difference of the varnish or ground, as in that of the aquafortis, adapted to each kind; but the general methods of performing them are alike in both. These varnishes or grounds are distinguished by the names of hard and soft: for in their consistence, or the resistance they give to the needles, lies their essential <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> from each other. The hard varnish, it is with good reason conjectured, was not the first in use; but soon took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the other; and was, for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, the most received in practice, on account of its admitting the work to be made more like that of the graver; the soft has, however, since, in its turn, prevailed to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> of it in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, except in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of particular subjects; but not so entirely as to take away the expedience of showing how it is performed. The manner of etching with the soft varnish is now, however, one of the most important objects of the art of engraving; and it is at present in universal use, sometimes alone, but more frequently intermixed with the work of the tool, and in some cases with great advantage, even where the whole is intended to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> for being performed by the graver. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PREPARATION">Preparation</a> of the soft varnish; according to Mr Lawrence, an eminent English engraver at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. "Take of virgin wax and asphaltum, each two ounces; of black pitch and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a> pitch, each half an ounce. Melt the wax and pitch in a new earthen-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a> glazed pot; and add to them, by degrees, the asphaltum finely powdered. Let the whole boil till such time as that, taking a drop upon a plate, it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a>, when it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, on <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> two or three times betwixt the fingers. The varnish being then enough boiled, must be taken off the fire; and letting it cool a little, must be poured into warm <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, that it may work the more easily with the hands, so as to be formed into balls; which must be rolled up, and put into a piece of taffety for use." It must be observed first, that the fire be not too violent, for fear of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> the ingredients; a slight simmering will be sufficient; secondly, that while the asphaltum is putting in, and even after it is mixed with them, the ingredients should be stirred continually with the spatula; and thirdly, that the water, into which this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> is thrown, should be nearly of the same degree of warmth with it, to prevent a kind of cracking that happens when the water is too cold. The varnish ought always to be harder in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> than in winter; and it will become so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it be suffered to boil longer, or if a greater proportion of the asphaltum or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> resin be used. The experiment above mentioned, of the drop suffered to cool, will determine the degree of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> or softness that may be suitable to the season when it is used. Preparation of the hard varnish used by Cullet, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> varnish. Take four ounces of fat <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> very clear, and made of good linseed oil, like that used by painters: <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> it in a clean pot of glazed earthen-ware, and afterwards put to it four ounces of mastick well powdered; and stir the mixture briskly till the whole be well melted; then pass the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> through a piece of fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> into a glass bottle with a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> neck, that can be stopped very securely; and keep it for the use that will be below explained. Method of applying the soft varnish to the plate, and of blackening it. The plate being well polished and burnished, as also cleansed from all greasiness by chalk or Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, fix a hand-vice on the edge of the plate where no work is intended to be, to serve as a handle for managing it when warm: then put it upon a chafing-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISH">dish</a>, in which there is a moderate fire; observing to hold it so that it may melt: then cover the whole plate equally with a thin coat of the varnish; and while the plate is warm, and the varnish upon it in a fluid state, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the varnish gently with a small <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> or dauber made of cotton tied up in taffety; which operation smooths and distributes the varnish equally over the plate. When the plate is thus uniformly and thinly covered with the varnish, it must be blackened by a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAMBEAU">flambeau</a>, or of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> which affords a copious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>; sometimes two or even four such candles are used together for the sake of dispatch, that the varnish may not grow cold: which if it does during the operation, the plate must then be heated again, that it may be in a melted state when that operation is performed: but great care must be taken not to burn it; which, when it happens, may be easily perceived by the varnish appearing burnt and losing its gloss. The following expedient is made use of for the more commodiously blackening... blackening the varnish, being particularly necessary where the plates are large: Fix a strong hook in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of the room, through which pass four pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CORD">cord</a> of equal length, at the end of which are fixed four <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> rings of about four inches in diameter, for supporting the corners of the plate. The plate being thus suspended in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, with the varnished side downwards, may be blackened with great convenience: but this is not, however, absolutely requisite, except in the case of large plates that could not, without difficulty, be held up, unless this or some other such contrivance were made use of. It is proper to be very cautious in keeping the flambeau or candle at a due distance from the plate, lest the wick touch the varnish, which would both sully and mark it. If it appear that the smoke has not penetrated the varnish, the plate must be again placed for some little time over the chafing-dish; and it will be found, that, in proportion as the plate grows hot, the varnish will melt and incorporate with the black which lay above it, in such a manner that the whole will be equally pervaded by it. Above all things, the greatest caution should be used in this operation, to keep all the time a moderate fire; and to move frequently the plate, and change the place of all the parts of it, that the varnish may be alike melted everywhere, and kept from burning. Care must also be taken, that during this time, and even till the varnish be entirely cold, no filth, sparks, or dust, fly on it; for they would then stick fast, and spoil the work. Method of applying the hard varnish. This is precisely the same as for the soft; being spread equally over the warm plate with the taffety-ball, and smoked in the same manner: only after it is smoked, it must be baked, or dried over a gentle fire of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a>, till the smoke from the varnish begins to decrease; taking care not to overheat the plate, which would both soften it and burn the varnish. The plate being thus prepared, and an exact <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> of the outlines of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> made upon thin <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, the other side of the paper must be well rubbed with chalk or Spanish whitening, or, which is better, with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> chalk scraped to a powder; and the loose chalk is cleared off with a linen rag; then the stained side of the paper is laid upon the varnish, fixing the corners to the plate with wax or wafers, to prevent its shuffling; and with a blunted <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> or pointer the drawing is slightly traced, and communicated to the varnish an exact outline of the design to be etched. A variety of pointers is necessary for the work. Those used for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> large strokes ought to be very blunt, exceeding round, and well polished at the point; the sole of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHOE">shoe</a> answers very well for polishing the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>. The finest ought to be as sharp as a needle. If any scratches or false strokes happen in the working, they are to be stopped up with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> dipped in Venetian varnish, mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a> black, by which means these places will be defended from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the aquafortis. The next operation is that of eating or corroding the plate with aquafortis; in order to which, a border of soft wax (being a composition of bees wax melted and tempered with a little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> turpentine and tal- brothers that the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> should be decided by single <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>. They both fell in an engagement conducted with the most inveterate fury on either side; and it is even said that the ashes of these two brothers, who had been so inimical one to the other, separated themselves on the burning pile, as if sensible of resentment, and hostile to reconciliation.

ETERNITY

Pages 367-367

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, who had neither <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> nor altars. They represented it under the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a woman, who held the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> in one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> in the other: her symbols were a phoenix, globe, and elephant. ETESIÆ, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Etesian winds, are such as blow at stated times of the year, from what partsoever of the compass they come. They are so called from the Greek word ἑτερος, "year," being yearly or anniversary winds, such as our seamen call monsoons and trade-winds, which in some parts of the world continue constantly blowing for certain stated seasons of the year. Thus, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> winds, which, during the dog-days, constantly blow upon the coasts of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and hinder all ships from sailing out of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> for that season, are called etesiae in Caesar's Commentaries. In other authors, the west and east winds are called etesiae, when they continue blowing for certain seasons of the year. Cellarius endeavours to prove that those winds are properly etesian which blow from that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the horizon which is between the north and west about the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the solstice. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers, they are represented as of a very mild and gentle <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; and were called by mariners somniculosi and delicati, from their sleeping or ceasing to blow in the night.

ETFU

Pages 367-367

a town of Upper <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, celebrated on account of the sublime temple of Apollinopolis, which, Denon observes, is "the most beautiful of all Egypt, and next to those of Thebes, the largest. Being built (he adds) at a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> when the arts and sciences had acquired all their splendour, the workmanship of every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> is equally beautiful, the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HIEROGLYPHICS">hieroglyphics</a> are admirably executed, the figures more varied, and the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> of a higher order than in the Theban edifices, the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of which must be referred to an earlier <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. My first care was to take a general <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of the building. "Nothing can be more simply beautiful than these outlines; nothing more picturesque than the effect produced in the elevation, by the various dimensions belonging to each member of the harmonious whole. This superb edifice is seated on a rising ground, so as to overlook not only its immediate vicinity, but the whole valley; and at the foot of this greater temple, but on a considerably lower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, is a smaller one, at present almost buried. The only part still visible is in a hollow surrounded with rubbish, where may be seen a little portico of two columns, and as many pilasters, a peristyle, and the sanctuary of the temple inclosed within a pilastered gallery. A single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>, with its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> rising from the ruins, to the height of forty feet above the portico, and the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of a wall 100 feet beyond, shew that there formerly existed a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of the temple. It is remarkable of this monument, notwithstanding the skill displayed in its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, that the gates are not exactly in the middle of the sides. It seems to have been dedicated to the evil genius, for the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of Typhon is seen in relief on the four sides of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLINTH">plinth</a>, which surmounts each of the capitals. The whole frieze, and all the paintings within, appear descriptive of Isis defending herself against the attacks of this monster."

ETHERIDGE

Pages 367-367

SIR GEORGE, a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and comic genius in the reigns of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. and James II. descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a>, and born in 1636. He travelled in his youth; and, not being able to confine himself to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, devoted himself to the gayer accomplishments. His first dramatic performance, the Comical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">Revenge</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">Love</a> in a Tub, appeared in 1664, and introduced him to the leading wits of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; in 1668, he produced a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> called She would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> she could; and, in 1676, he published his last comedy, called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">Mode</a>, or Sir Fopling Flutter; which is perhaps the most elegant comedy, and contains more of the real manners of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> than any one the English stage was ever adorned with. This piece he dedicated to the beautiful duchess of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, in whose <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> he then was; and who had so high a regard for him, that when, on the accession of James II. she came to be <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, she procured his being sent <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> first to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMBURG">Hamburg</a>, and afterwards to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RATISBON">Ratisbon</a>, where he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till after his majesty quitted the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Our author being addicted to certain gay extravagances, had greatly impaired his fortune; to repair which, he paid his addresses to a rich widow; but she, being an ambitious woman, had determined not to condescend to a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> with any man who could not bestow a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> upon her; on which account he was obliged to purchase a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a>. None of the writers have exactly fixed the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of Sir George's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, though all seem to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> it not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> after the Revolution. Some say, that on this event he followed his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> James into France, and died there; but the authors of the Biographia Britannica mention a report, that he came to an untimely death by an unlucky accident at Ratisbon; for that after having treated some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with a liberal entertainment at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> there, where he had taken his glass too freely, and being, through his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> complaisance, too forward in waiting on his guests at their departure, flushed as he was, he tumbled <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> stairs and broke his neck, and so fell a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a> to mirth and jollity. As to Sir George's literary character, he certainly was born a poet, and seems to have been possessed of a genius whose vivacity needed no cultivation: for we have no proofs of his having been a scholar. His works, however, have not escaped censure on account of that licentiousness which in general runs through them, which renders them dangerous to young unguarded minds; and the more so, for the lively and genuine wit with which it is gilded over, and which has therefore justly banished them from the purity of the present stage.

ETHICS

Pages 367-368

the doctrine of manners, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the science of of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORAL_PHILOSOPHY">moral <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. The word is formed from ἔθος, ἔθειν, "mores," "manners;" because it is the object of ethics to investigate the manners or conduct of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. See Moral Philosophy.

ETHMOIDES

Pages 368-368

in Anatomy, a bone situated in the middle of the basis of the forehead <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> os frontis, and at the top of the root of the nose, filling almost the whole cavity of the nostrils. It has its name from ἐθμός, cribrum, "sieve," and ἔθηκα, "form," because all spongy and porous. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ETHNARCHA

Pages 368-368

ETHNARCH, (formed of ἐθνος, "<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>," and ἐθνος, "command"), a governor <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ruler of a nation. There are some medals of Herod I. surnamed the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, on one side whereof is found Ἑρῴδου, and on the other Ἑρῴδου, q.d. Herod the Ethnarch. After the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Philippi, we read that Antony, passing over into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, constituted Herod and Phasaël his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> tetrarchs, and in that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> committed to them the administration of the affairs of Judea, (Jos. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANT">Ant</a>. lib. xiv. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 23.). Herod therefore had the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> before ever the Parthians entered Syria, or before Antigonus's invasion, which did not happen till six or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years after Herod was commander in Galilee, (Jos. lib. xiv. cap. 24., 25.). Consequently, Herod was then truly ethnarch, for he can be no otherwise denominated; so that it must have been in that space of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that the medals were struck, which only give him this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>: which medals are a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of what we read in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the government which that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> was intrusted with before he was raised to the royalty. Josephus gives Herod the appellation of tetrarch in lieu of that of ethnarch; but the two terms come so near each other, that it is easy to confound them together. Though Herod the Great left by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> to Archelaus all Judea, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMARIA">Samaria</a>, and Idumea, yet Josephus tells us he was then only called ethnarch.

ETHNOPHRONES

Pages 368-368

in antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of heretics in the seventh century, who made a profession of Christianity, but joined thereto all the ceremonies and follies of Paganism, as judicial astrology, sortileges, auguries, and other divinations.

ETIQUETTE

Pages 368-368

a French <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a>, primarily denoting a ticket <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> affixed to a bag or bundle of papers expressing its contents. It is also used, when applied to the Spanish and some other courts, to signify a particular account of what is to be done daily in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>, and in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> ceremonies relating to it. It likewise denotes those forms that regulate the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECORUM">decorum</a> of conduct towards persons of various ranks and stations.

ETMULLER

Pages 368-368

MICHAEL, a most eminent physician, born at Leipsic in 1646. After having travelled through the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, he became professor of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, and anatomy, at Leipsic, where he died in 1683. He was a very voluminous writer, his works making no less than 5 vols folio, as printed at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> in 1728. His son Michael Ernest Etmuller was also an ingenious physician, who published several pieces, and died in 1732.

ETOLIA

Pages 368-369

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, comprehending all that tract now called the Despotat, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Little Greece. It was parted on the east by the river Evenus, now the Fidari, from the Locrenses Ozolae; on the west, from Acarnania by the Achelous; on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, it bordered on the country of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DORIANS">Dorians</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Epirus; and, on the south, extended to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of Corinth. The Eolians were a restless and turbulent people; seldom at peace among themselves, and ever at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with their neighbours; utter strangers to all <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of friendship or principles of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>; ready to betray their friends upon the least prospect of reaping any advantage from their treachery: in short, they were looked upon by the other states of Greece no otherwise than as outlaws and public robbers. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, they were bold and enterprising in war; incurious to labour and hardships; undaunted in the greatest dangers; jealous defenders of their liberties, for which they were, on all occasions, willing to venture their lives, and sacrifice all that was most dear to them. They distinguished themselves above all the other nations of Greece, in opposing the ambitious designs of the Macedonian princes; who, after having reduced most of the other states, were forced to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> them a peace upon very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> terms. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of the Eolian republic was copied from that of the Achaeans, and with a view to form, as it were, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTER">counter</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a>; for the Eolians bore an irreconcilable hatred to the Achaeans, and had conceived no small jealousy at the growing power of that state. The Cleomenic war, and that of the allies, called the social war, were kindled by the Eolians in the heart of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>, with no other view but to humble their antagonists the Achaeans. In the latter, they held out, with the assistance only of the Eleans and Lacedemonians, for the space of three years, against the united forces of Achaia and Macedon; but were obliged at last to purchase a peace, by yielding up to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> all Acarnania. As they parted with this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> much against their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a>, they watched all opportunities of wresting it again out of the Macedonian's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; for which reason they entered into an alliance with Rome against him, and proved of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> in their war with him: but growing insolent upon account of their services, they made war upon the Romans themselves. By that warlike <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> they were overcome, and granted a peace on the following severe terms: 1. The majesty of the Roman people shall be revered in all Eotlia. 2. Eotlia shall not suffer the armies of such as are at war with Rome to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through her territories, and the enemies of Rome shall be likewise the enemies of Eotlia. 3. She shall, in the space of 100 days, put into the hands of the magistrates of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CORCYRA">Corcyra</a> all the prisoners and deserters she has, whether of the Romans or their allies, except such as have been taken twice, or during her alliance with Rome. 4. The Eolians shall pay <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in ready <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, to the Roman general in Eotlia, 200 Euboean talents, of the same value as the Athenian talents, and engage to pay 50 talents more within the six years following. 5. They shall put into the hands of the cou- such hostages as he shall choose; none of whom shall be under 12, or above 40 years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>; the praetor, the general of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, and such as have been already hostages at Rome, are excepted out of this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. 6. Etolia shall renounce all pretensions to the cities and territories which the Romans have conquered, though those cities and territories had formerly belonged to the Eolians. 7. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Oenoe, and its district, shall be subject to the Acarnanians. After the conquest of Macedon by Paulus Æmilius, they were reduced to a much worse condition; for not only those among them, who had openly declared for Perseus, but such as were only suspected to have favoured him in their hearts, were sent to Rome, in order to clear themselves before the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>. There they were detained, and never afterwards suffered to return into their native country. Five hundred and fifty of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> men of the nation were barbarously assassinated by the partizans of Rome, for no other crime but that of being suspected to wish well to Perseus. The Eolians appeared before Paulus Æmilius in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a> habits, and made loud complaints of such inhuman treatment; but could obtain no redress: nay, ten commissioners, who had been sent by the senate to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> the affairs of Greece, enacted a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a>, declaring, that those who were killed had suffered justly, since it appeared to them that they had favoured the Macedonian party.
