From this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> those only were raised to the chief honours and employments in the Eolian republic who were known to prefer the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of Rome to that of their country; and as these alone were countenanced of Rome, all the magistrates of Eolia were the creatures and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> tools of the Roman senate. In this state of servile subjection they <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till the destruction of Corinth, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of the Achaean <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a>; when Eolia, with the other free states of Greece, was reduced to a Roman province, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the province of Achaia. Nevertheless, each state and city was governed by its own laws, under the superintendency of the praetor whom Rome sent annually into Achaia. The whole nation paid a certain tribute, and the rich were forbidden to possess lands anywhere but in their own country. In this state, with little <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a>, Eolia continued under the emperors, till the reign of Constantine the Great, who, in his new partition of the provinces of the empire, divided the western parts of Greece from the rest, calling them New Epirus, and subjecting the whole country to the prefectus praetoris for Illyricum. Under the successors of Constantine, Greece was parcelled out into several principalities, especially after the taking of Constantinople by the Western princes. At that time, Theodorus Angelus, a noble Grecian, of the imperial family, seized on Eolia and Epirus. The former he left to Michael his son; who maintained it against Michael Paleologus, the first <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of the Greeks, after the expulsion of the Latins. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>, the last <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of this family, dying in 1430 without lawful issue, bequeathed Eolia to his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>'s son, named also Charles; and Acarnania to his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> sons, Mennon, Turnus, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>. But, great disputes arising about this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>, Amurath II., after the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of Thessalonica, laid hold of so favourable an opportunity, and drove them all out in 1432. The Ma- hometans were afterwards dispossessed of this country by the famous prince of Epirus, George Castriot, commonly called <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCANDERBEG">Scanderbeg</a>; who, with a small <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, opposed the whole power of the Ottoman empire, and defeated those barbarians in 22 pitched battles. That <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>, at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, left great part of Eolia to the Venetians; but, they not being able to make head against such a mighty power, the whole country was soon reduced by Mahomet II., whose successors hold it to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>.

ETON

Pages 369-370

a town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUCKS">Bucks</a>, situated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, across which there is a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> leading to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a>. Eton has been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> celebrated for its school and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, which were founded by Henry VI.; and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a>'s college in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a> admits none into the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of its fellows, who have not been brought up at Eton. It lies west from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, at the distance of about 20 miles. The scholars of Eton school have a festival which has been celebrated from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> immemorial, called the Montem, the observance of which was at first biennial, but is now <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIENNIAL">triennial</a>, on the Whit Tuesday in every third year. It commences by a number of the older boys taking <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> on the bridges, and guarding every other avenue around Windsor and Eton, as soon as the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> begins to dawn. They are generally selected on account of their fine figures and superior <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>. Their dresses are all fanciful, composed of silks, satins, &c. some of them very richly embroidered, and chiefly in the appearance of running footmen, having <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and denominated <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-bearers, who demand salt of every passenger they meet, by which they <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> a contribution, and peremptorily insist on receiving it. The contribution being given, which consists of whatever the person pleases to bestow, a printed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> is delivered, containing their motto, together with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> of the year; and this being produced to any other salt-bearer, exempts the passenger from the payment of any farther contributions during that day. The motto is, "Pro more et monte. Vivant rex et <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol0.html#article-REGINA">regina</a>." They continue levying contributions in this manner from the dawn of day till about three o'clock in the afternoon, at which time the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> closes. It commences at noon, and consists of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s and other bands of music;—several standards carried by different students;—all the boys of Eton, two and two, dressed in the uniform of officers; those belonging to the king's foundation, wear blue, the rest scarlet uniform, swords, &c.—the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> standard bearer;—the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> head boy of Eton school;—the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> boy;—his majesty, attended by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, and other <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> branches of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family on horseback, with their suite;—the queen and princesses in coaches, attended by their suite;—band of music, followed by a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> concourse of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> and gentry in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>, and on horseback. The procession begins in the great <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> at Eton, proceeding through Eton to Slough, and round to Salt-hill, where the whole of the boys <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> in review before the king and queen, and ascend the montem, where an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> is delivered, and the grand standard is displayed with much activity and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> by the standard-bear- er, who is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> selected from among the elder boys. The two extraordinary salt-bearers are chosen to wait upon their majesties, dressed in fanciful habits, and decorated in the most superb manner, carrying an embroidered bag, not only for the purpose of receiving what is denominated the royal salt, but also what may be collected by the other salt-bearers, in different <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>. The donation of the king is 50 guineas, the queen's is the same sum; that of the prince of Wales is 30, and that of the other princes and princesses is 20 guineas each. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> being over, the royal family return to Windsor. A sumptuous entertainment is provided for the boys at the tavern at Salt-hill, and the beautiful gardens are laid out for ladies and gentlemen to take refreshments, where bands of music are constantly performing. At six o'clock in the evening, the boys return in the same order of procession as in the morning (but without the royal family), and after marching round the great square, are dismissed. After this the captain pays his respects to the royal family at the queen's lodge, Windsor, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to his departure for King's college, Cambridge, to defray the expenses of which, he is presented with the produce of the montem, which in the year 1796 amounted to more than 1000 guineas. This joyful day is terminated by a brilliant <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXHIBITION">exhibition</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, and fashion; a promenade on the terrace of Windsor; bands of music performing, &c.; and the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> is rendered still more interesting and delightful by the humble, affable deportment of the royal family, who readily mingle with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, and walk on the terrace till it is almost dark. ETRURIA. See HETURIA.

ETYMOLOGY

Pages 370-370

that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> which considers and explains the origin and derivation of words, in order to arrive at their first and primary signification, whence Quintilian calls it origination.—The word is formed of the Greek, ἀρχή, verus, "true," and ἀρχεῖν, disco, "I speak;" whence ἀρχεῖν, discourse, &c., and thence Cicero calls the etymology notatio and verilogium; though Quintilian chooses rather to call it origination. A judicious inquiry into etymologies is thought by some of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; because nations, who value themselves upon their antiquity, have always looked on the antiquity of their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> as one of the best titles they could plead; and the etymologists, by seeking the true and original reason of the notions and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> fixed to each word and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, may often furnish an argument of antiquity, from the traces remaining thereof, compared with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> uses. Add, that etymologies are necessary for the thorough understanding of a language. For, to explain a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> precisely, there seems a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> for recurring to its first imposition, in order to speak justly and satisfactorily thereof. The force and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of a word is generally better conceived when a person knows its origin and etymology. It is objected, however, that the art is arbitrary, and built altogether on conjectures and appearances; and the etymologists are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with deriving their words from where they please. And indeed it is no easy <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> to go back into the ancient British and Gaulish ages, and to follow, as it were, by the track, the various imperceptible alterations a language has undergone from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> to age; and as those alterations have sometimes been merely owing to caprice, it is easy to take a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> imagination <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> conjecture for a regular <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a>: so that it is no wonder the public should be prejudiced against a science which seems to stand on so precarious a footing. It must certainly be owned, that etymologies are frequently so far fetched, that one can scarcely see any resemblance or correspondence therein. Quintilian has shown, that the ancient etymologists, notwithstanding all their learning, fell into very ridiculous derivations. The etymologies of our English words have been derived from the Saxon, Welch, Walloon, Danish, Latin, Greek, &c. In the present <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> the etymologies of terms are generally noted, where their obviousness does not render it unnecessary, or their dubiety or unimportance useless.

EUBAGES

Pages 371-371

an order of priests <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> philosophers among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Celts or Gauls; some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> have the eubages to be the same with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRUIDS">druids</a> and sacerdotes of Diodorus; and others, that they were the same with what Strabo calls EVATES.

EUBOEA

Pages 371-371

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, stretching out between <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a> and Thessaly, opposite to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>; from which it is separated by a narrow strait called Euripus. This island, never exceeding 40, nor ever falling short of two miles in breadth, is in length 150 miles, and in compass 365, according to Pliny. Now NEROPONT, from its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> town, which was anciently called Chalcis.

EUCHARIST

Pages 371-371

the sacrament of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>, properly signifies giving thanks.—The word in its original Greek, Εὐχαριστία, literally imports thanksgiving; being formed of εὖ, bene, "well," and χάρις, gratia, "thanks." This sacrament was instituted by Christ himself; and the participation of it is called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>. As to the manner of celebrating the eucharist among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, after the customary oblations were made, the deacon brought <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> and presbyters, standing round the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, to wash their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; according to that of the psalmist, "I <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> wash my hands in innocency, and so will I compass thy altar, O Lord." Then the deacon cried out aloud, "Mutually embrace and kiss each other;" which being done, the whole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> prayed for the universal peace and welfare of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, for the tranquillity and repose of the world, for the prosperity of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, for wholesome <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, and for all ranks and degrees of men. After this followed mutual salutations of the minister and people; and then the bishop <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESBYTER">presbyter</a> having sanctified the elements by a solemn benediction, he brake the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, and delivered it to the deacon, who delivered it to the communicants, and after that the cup. Their sacramental wine was usually diluted or mixed with water. During the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of administration, they sang hymns and psalms; and having concluded with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> and thanksgiving, the people saluted each other with a kiss of peace, and so the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> broke up.

EUCHITES

Pages 371-371
or EUCHITÆ, a sect of ancient heretics, who were first formed into a religious body towards the end of the fourth century, though their doctrine and discipline subsisted in Syria, Egypt, and other eastern countries, before the birth of Christ; they were thus called because they prayed without ceasing, imagining that prayer alone was sufficient to save them. Their great foundation were those words of St Paul, (Thessalonians, v.17,) Pray without ceasing. The word is formed of the Greek, προσεύχεσθαι, prayer, whence προσευχή, the same with the Latin precatores, "prayers." They were also called Enthusiasts and Messalians; a term of Hebrew origin, denoting the same as Euchites. The Euchites were a sort of mystics, who imagined, according to the oriental notion, that two souls resided in man, the one good and the other evil; and who were zealous in expelling the evil soul or demon, and hastening the return of the good spirit of God, by contemplation, prayer, and singing of hymns. They also embraced the opinions nearly resembling the Manichean doctrine, and which they derived from the tenets of the oriental philosophy. The same denomination was used in the 12th century, to denote certain fanatics who infested the Greek and eastern churches, and who were charged with believing a double Trinity, rejecting wedlock, abstaining from flesh, treating with contempt the sacraments of baptism and the Lord's supper, and the various branches of external worship, and placing the essence of religion solely in external prayer, and maintaining the efficacy of perpetual supplications to the Supreme Being for expelling an evil being or genius, which dwelt in the breast of every mortal. This sect is said to have been founded by a person called Lucoperetus, whose chief disciple was named Tychicus. By degrees it became a general and inviolable appellation for persons of eminent piety and zeal for genuine Christianity, who opposed the vicious practices and insolent tyranny of the priesthood; much in the same manner as the Latins comprehended all the adversaries of the Roman pontiff under the general terms of WALDENSES and ALBIGENSES. St Cyril of Alexandrin, in one of his letters, takes occasion to censure several monks in Egypt, who, under pretence of resigning themselves wholly to prayer, led a lazy, scandalous life. A censure likewise applicable to monasteries in general.

EUCRASY

Pages 372-372

(of εὖ, well, and κράσις, temperature), in Medicine, an agreeable well proportioned mixture of qualities, whereby a body is said to be in good order, and disposed for a good state of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>.

EUDIOMETER

Pages 372-372

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> for ascertaining the purity of the atmospherical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of pure <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXYGEN">oxygen</a> or vital air contained in it, chiefly by means of its diminution, or the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSORPTION">absorption</a> of it by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> certain substances to its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>. Several kinds of eudiometers have been invented. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EUDOSIA

Pages 372-372

(Athenia), before her conversion to Christianity, a celebrated lady, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Leonius, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>; who gave her such a learned <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, that at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, he left her only a small legacy, saying she was capable to make her own fortune: but pleading at Athens without success against her two brothers, for a share in her father's estate, she carried her cause personally by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> to Constantinople; recommended herself to Pulcheria, the sister of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Theodosius the younger; embraced Christianity, was baptized by the name of Eudosia, and soon after married to the emperor. Their union lasted a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>: but a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> at last taking <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, on account of the emperor's jealousy, excited by Chrysapius the eunuch, she retired to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, where she spent many years in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> and adorning churches and in relieving the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. Dupin says, that she did not return thence till after the emperor's death: but Cave tells us, that she was reconciled to him, returned to Constantinople, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> with him till his death; after which she again went to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, where she spent the remainder of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in pious works. She died in the year 460, according to Dupin; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 459, according to Cave: the latter observes, that on her deathbed she took a solemn oath, by which she declared herself entirely free from any stains of unchastity. She was the author of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPHRASE">paraphrase</a> on the eight first books of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> in heroic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>; and of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of poems, which are lost.

EUDOXIANS

Pages 372-372

a party <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of heretics in the fourth century, so denominated from their leader Eudoxius, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> of Antioch and Constantinople, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> defender of the Arian doctrine. The Eudoxians adhered to the errors of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUNOMIANS">Eunomians</a>, maintaining, that the Son was created out of nothing; that he had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> distinct and different from that of the Father, &c. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EVE">EVE</a>. See Vigil. Eve, the mother of all mankind; who being deluded by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a>, occasioned the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, and all its dismal consequences. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>.

EUGENE

Pages 373-373

FRANCIS, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Savoy, descended from Carignan, one of the three branches of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Savoy, and son of Eugene Maurice, general of the Swiss and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRISONS">Grisons</a>, governor of Champagne, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOISSONS">Soissons</a>, was born in 1663. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV., to whom he became afterwards so formidable an enemy, thought him so unpromising a youth, that he refused him preferment both in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> and the state, thinking him too much addicted to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> to be useful in either. Prince Eugene, in disgust, quitted France; and, retiring to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>, devoted himself to the Imperial <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> between the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> and the Turks afforded the first opportunity of exerting his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> talents; and every <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> proved a new step in his advancement to the highest offices in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. He gave the Turks a memorable defeat at Zenta; commanded the German forces in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, where he foiled Marshal Villeroy in every engagement, and at length took him prisoner. Our limits do not allow a detail of his campaigns; but Prince Eugene distinguished himself greatly; when the emperor and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> united against the exorbitant power of Louis XIV. He died at Vienna in the year 1736; and was as remarkable for his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> and liberality, as for his abilities in the field and the cabinet.

EUGENIA

Pages 373-373

the YAMBOO; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ICOSANDRIA">icosandria</a> class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 19th order, Hesperidea. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EUHOLOGIUM

Pages 371-372

Εὐχολογία, a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a>, signifying literally a discourse on <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>. The word is formed of εὐχή, prayer, and λόγος, discourse. The Euchologium is properly the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RITUAL">ritual</a>, wherein are prescribed the order and manner of every thing. thing relating to the order and administration of their ceremonies, sacraments, ordinations, &c. F. Goar has given us an edition of the Greek Euchologium in Greek and Latin, with notes, at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. EUCLID of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEGARA">Megara</a>, a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and logician, flourished about 400 B.C. The Athenians having prohibited the Megareans from entering their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> on pain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, this philosopher disguised himself in women's clothes to attend the lectures of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>. After the death of Socrates, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> and other philosophers went to Euclid at Megara, to shelter themselves from the tyrants who governed <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. Euclid admitted but one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> good: which he sometimes called God, sometimes Spirit, and sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>. Euclid of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, the celebrated mathematician, flourished in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> Lagus, about 277 B.C. He reduced all the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> principles of pure <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, which had been delivered <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THALES">Thales</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>, Eudoxus, and other mathematicians before him, into regularity and order, and added many others of his own discovering: on which account he is said to be the first who reduced <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> into the form of a science. He likewise applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of mixed mathematics, and especially to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, in which he also excelled. The most celebrated of his works is his Elements of Geometry, of which there have been a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of editions in all languages; and a fine edition of all his works was printed in 1703, by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Gregory, Savilian professor of astronomy at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>.

EULOGY

Pages 376-376

likewise means an encomium on any person, on account of some virtue <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> good <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>.

EUMARIDES

Pages 376-376

of εὐμάρις, "easy," among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, a kind of shoes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to men and women.—The eumarides were used for pomp and delicacy, being neat, and painted with various colours.

EUMENES

Pages 377-377

a celebrated orator of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> about the beginning of the fourth century. Some of his harangues and orations are extant. An historical writer in Alexander's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>.

EUMENIDES

Pages 377-377

a name given to the Furies by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. They sprang from the blood of the wound which Coelus received from his son <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>. According to others, they were daughters of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">Earth</a>, and conceived from the blood of Saturn. Some make them daughters of Acheron and Night, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Pluto and Proserpine. According to the more received opinions, they were three in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, Tisiphone, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEGARA">Megara</a>, and Alecto, to which some add Nemesis. Plutarch mentions only one called Adrasta, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">Necessity</a>. They were supposed to be the ministers of the vengeance of the gods. They were stern and inexorable; and were always employed in punishing the guilty upon earth, as well as in the infernal regions. They inflicted their vengeance upon earth by wars, pestilence, and dissensions, and by the secret stings of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>; and in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a> they punished the guilty by continual flagellation and torments. They were also called Furies and Erinnyes. Their worship was almost universal; and people dared not to mention their names or fix their eyes upon their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>. They were honoured with sacrifices and libations; and in Achaea they had a temple, which when entered by any one guilty of a crime, suddenly rendered him furious, and deprived him of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his reason. In the sacrifices the votaries used branches of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a> and of alder, hawthorn, saffron, and juniper; and the victims were generally turtle doves and sheep, with libations of wine and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>. They were usually represented with a grim and frightful aspect, with a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and bloody garment, and with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a> writhing round their heads instead of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>. They held a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> torch in one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and a whip of scorpions in the other; and were always attended by Terror, Rage, Paleness, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">Death</a>. In hell they were seated around Pluto's throne, as the ministers of his vengeance.

EUMENIDIA

Pages 377-377

festivals in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUMENIDES">Eumenides</a>, called by the Athenians εὐεστάς θεάς, "venerable goddesses." They were celebrated once every year, with sacrifices of pregnant <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EWES">ewes</a>, with offerings of cakes made by the most eminent youths, and libations of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> and wine. At <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> none but freeborn citizens were admitted, such as had led a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> the most virtuous and unsullied.

EUMOLPIDES

Pages 377-377

the priests of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a> at the celebration of her festivals at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELEUSIS">Eleusis</a>. They were descended from Eumolpus, a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Thrace, who was made <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of Ceres by Erechtheus king of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>. He became so powerful after his appointment to the priesthood, that he maintained a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against Erechtheus. This war proved fatal to both. Erechtheus and Eumolpus were both killed, and peace was re-established among their descendants, on condition that the priesthood ever remained in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Eumolpus, and the regal power in the family of Erechtheus. The priesthood remained in the family of Eumolpus for 1200 years; and this is still more remarkable, because he who was once appointed to the holy office was obliged to remain in perpetual celibacy.

EUMOLPUS

Pages 377-377

a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Thrace, son of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a> and Chione. He was thrown into the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> by his mother, who wished to conceal her shame from her father. Neptune saved his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and carried him into Ethiopia, where he was brought up by a woman, one of whose daughters he married. An <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of violence to his sister-in-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> obliged him to leave Ethiopia, and he fled to Thrace with his son Ismarus, where he married the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Tegyrius the king of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. This connection to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family rendered him ambitious; he conspired against his father-in-law, and fled, when the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> was discovered, to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>, where he was initiated in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELEUSIS">Eleusis</a>, and made hierophant <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>. He was afterwards reconciled to Tegyrius, and inherited his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. He made <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against Erechtheus king of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, who had appointed him to the office of high priest, and perished in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> about 1380 years before the Christian era. His descendants were also invested with the priesthood, which remained for about 1200 years in that family.

EUNAPIUS

Pages 377-377

a native of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDIS">Sardis</a> in Lydia, a celebrated sophist, physician, and historian, who flourished in the 4th century, under the emperors <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALENTINIAN">Valentinian</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALENS">Valens</a>, and Gratian. He wrote "The lives of the Philosophers and Sophists," in which he frequently shows himself a bitter enemy to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>: also a "<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Caesars," which he deduced from the reign of Claudius, where Herodian left off, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to that of Arcadius and Honorius. The history is lost; but we have the substance of it in Zosimus, who is supposed to have done little more than copy it.

EUNOMIANS

Pages 377-378

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, Christian heretics in the 4th century. They were a branch of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a>, and took their name from Eunomius bishop of Cyzicus, whose confession of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> here follows, extracted from Cave's Historia Literaria, vol. i. p. 223. "There is one God, uncreated and without beginning; who has nothing existing before him, for nothing can exist before what is uncreated; nor with him, for what is uncreated must be one; nor in him, for God is a simple and uncompounded being. This one simple and eternal being is God, the creator and ordainer of all things; first indeed and principally of his only-begotten Son; and then, through him, of all other things. For God begot, created, and made, the Son, only by his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> operation and power, before all things, and every other creature; not producing, however, any being like himself, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> imparting any of his own proper substance to the Son: For God is immortal, uniform, indivisible; and therefore cannot communicate any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>..." Eunomians of his own proper substance to another. He alone is unbegotten; and it is impossible that any other being should be formed of an unbegotten substance. He did not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> his own substance in begetting the Son, but his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> only: nor did he beget him in the likeness of his substance, but according to his own good <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. He then created the Holy Spirit, the first and greatest of all spirits, by his own power indeed and operation immediately, yet by the immediate power and operation of the Son. After the Holy Spirit he created all other things in heaven and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, visible and invisible, corporeal and incorporeal, immediately by himself, by the power and operation of the Son," &c.

EUNOMIUS

Pages 378-378

a famous heresiarch of the 4th century, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Eulius, but abundantly more subtile than his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, as well as more bold in propagating the opinions of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, who after him are called <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUNOMIANS">Eunomians</a>. He was ordained bishop of Cyzicus; but gave so much disturbance by the intemperance of his zeal, that he was deposed more than once. At last, tired with being tossed about, he petitioned to retreat to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his birth, Dacora in Cappadocia; where he died very old about the year 374, after experiencing a variety of sufferings. The greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his works are lost. There is, however, besides two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three small pieces, a confession of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> remaining, which Cave inserted in his Historia Literaria, from a manuscript in Archbishop Tennison's library. See the preceding article.

EUNUCH

Pages 378-378

a castrated person. See the article <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CASTRATION">Castration</a>.—The word is formed from ευνοῦς, q. d. leict curam habet, "<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> keeper of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>." In <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, France, &c., <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUNUCHS">eunuchs</a> are never made but upon occasion of some <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, which renders such an operation necessary; but in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> they make <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers of children, from one to three years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, eunuchs, every year, to supply the operas and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRES">theatres</a> of all <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> with singers. M. de la Lande, in his Voyage d'ltalie, asserts, that there are public shops at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> where this cruel operation is performed, and that over the door of these shops is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> Qui si castrano ragazzii. But Dr Burney informs us, that he was not only utterly unable to see or hear of any such shops during his residence in that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, but was constantly told, both by the natives and English settled there, that the laws against such a practice were so numerous and severe, that it was never performed but with the utmost secrecy. In the eastern parts of the world, they make eunuchs in order to be guards or attendants on their women. The seraglios of the eastern emperors are chiefly served and guarded by eunuchs; and yet, from good authority, we learn, that the rich eunuchs in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> and other countries keep seraglios for their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. Those who, out of an imprudent zeal to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> themselves from sensual pleasures, made themselves eunuchs, were, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Nice, condemned and excluded from holy orders. There are several severe prohibitions in Germany against the making of eunuchs; and in France an eunuch must not marry, not even with the consent of the woman. Though the practice of castration is detestable in every point of view; yet there appears no real foundation for the injurious <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> generally entertained of eunuchs, viz. that they are all cowards, and devoid of genius for literature or any <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. "As to genius (says the author last quoted), I never found those of the first class in music deficient in intellectual abilities for more serious studies. Indeed I have seen real genius and dispositions for literary pursuits, in more than one great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">opera</a> singer; and as for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of music, not only the best singers of the pope's chapel ever since the beginning of the last century, but the best composers, are among the soprani in that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>." With respect to the operation affecting the mind so much as to deprive it of all fortitude in times of danger, there is great reason to doubt the fact: most of the generals of eastern monarchs having been at all times of this class; and the bravest stand that ever was made against Alexander the Great was at Gaza, under the command of one of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a>'s generals, who was an eunuch. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMMIANUS_MARCELLINUS">Ammianus Marcellinus</a> gives an account of Menophilus, a eunuch, to whom <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MITHRIDATES">Mithridates</a> intrusted his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>; which proves the possibility of such unfortunate persons possessing a heroism equal to that of the most determined Stoic. It is very certain, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> never supposed eunuchs to have been men of inferior intellects, or that they possessed less vigour of mind than other men. At least the Persians were not of this opinion; for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> relates, that when they had taken possession of some Ionian cities, ἐπιτίθεσαν τοὺς ἐκ τῶν ἐκδικούμενος ἀνδρῶν, εἰς ἄλληλος ἐπιστέλλοντος. It is certain, however, Herodotus, in relating the melancholy story of Hermotimus, says, that ὁ πολεμος ὁ στρατιώτης. It is ἡ ἑγγύτητος ἡ ἀμφιλοξείδεια, ἢ ἡ τοῦ στρατιώτης ἐπιστέλλοντος, "among the barbarians, the eunuchs are more valued than other men, on account of their universal fidelity." It appears from this passage of Herodotus, that in Persia eunuchs were far from being objects of contempt; and were even frequently promoted to the highest honours. This was indeed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with Hermotimus. We find in Agathias, who was one of the Byzantine historians, that a general in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, named Norses, was a eunuch. This was in the latter ages. In Plutarch's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of Aristides, Themistocles is related to have chosen an eunuch, whose name was Arnaces, from among his prisoners, to send on a secret embassy to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a>. This surely may serve to show, that mental imbecility was not supposed by the Greeks to be the characteristic of eunuchism. The same story of the confidence placed in Arnaces, who was one of the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s eunuchs, is related also in the life of Themistocles. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> paid such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> respect to Hermias, who was a eunuch and governor of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>, which is in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSIA">Mysia</a>, that he even offered sacrifices in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of him; so Lucian informs us in his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIALOGUE">Dialogue</a> entitled Eunuchus. This regard of Aristotle for Hermias has been often celebrated, and is mentioned by Suidas, Harpocratus, and others.

EUNUCHS

Pages 378-378

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of heretics in the third century, who were mad enough to castrate, not only those of their own persuasion, but even all others they could lay hold of. They took their rise from the example of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a>, who, misunderstanding the following words of our Saviour, "and eunuchs who make themselves eunuchs for the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of heaven," castrated himself.

EUODIA

Pages 379-379

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the tetrandria class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EUONYMUS

Pages 379-379

the Spindle Tree; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 43rd order, Dumasceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EUPATORIUM

Pages 379-379
Hemp Agrimony; a genus of plants belonging to the syngenesia class; and in the natural method ranking under the 49th order, Compositae. See Botany Index. EUPATRIDÆ, in antiquity, a name given by Theseus to the nobility of Athens, as distinguished from the Geomori and Demiurgi. The Eupatridæ, by Theseus's establishment, had the right of choosing magistrates, teaching and dispensing the laws, and interpreting holy and religious mysteries. The whole city, in all other matters, was reduced to an equality. The Geomori were husbandmen, and inferior to the Eupatridæ in point of fortune; the Demiurgi were artificers, and fell short of the Eupatridæ in number.

EUPHONY

Pages 379-379

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, an easiness, smoothness, and elegance of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a>. The word is formed of bene, "well;" and vox, "<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>." Quintilian calls euphonia, "vocalitas;" Scaliger, "facilis pronunciatio." Euphonia is properly a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> whereby we suppress a too harsh <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> convert it into a smoother, contrary to the ordinary rules. There are examples enough in all languages. EUPHYMISM. See Oratory.

EUPHORBIA

Pages 379-379

SPURGE; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dodecaandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 38th order, Tricoccæ. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EUPHORBIUM

Pages 379-379

in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>, a gummi-resinous substance, which exudes from a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> oriental tree, (Euphorbia officinarum). See Materia Medica <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EUPHORBUS

Pages 379-379

a famous Trojan, son of Panthous. He was the first who wounded <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATROCLUS">Patroclus</a>, whom Hector killed. He perished by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of Menelaus, who hung his shield in the temple of Juno at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>, the founder of the doctrine of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEMPSYCHOSIS">metempsychosis</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> transmigration of souls, affirmed that he had been once Euphorbus, and that his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> recollected many exploits which had been done while it animated that Trojan's body. As a further <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of his assertion, he showed at first sight the shield of Euphorbus in the temple of Juno. EUPHORION of Chalcis, a poet and historian, born in the 126th Olympiad. Suetonius says that Tiberius composed verses in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of Euphorion, Rianius and Parthenius; with whom he was charmed to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that he ordered their writings and their pictures to be kept in all the public <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a>, among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and celebrated authors.

EUPHRASIA

Pages 379-379

Eye-Bright; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the didynamia class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 40th order, Personatae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EUPHRATES

Pages 379-380

a river universally allowed to take its rise in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a>; but in what particular spot, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in what <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> it afterwards shapes its course, there is the greatest disagreement. Strabo says, that the Euphrates rises in Mount Abus, which he joins with, or accounts a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of, Mount Taurus; that its beginning is on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of Mount Taurus; and that running, first westward through Armenia, then striking off to the south, it forces its way through the mountain; and thus it rises in the south of Armenia, Mount Taurus being the boundary on that side; and runs through its south part, quite to Cappadocia, contemnial with Armenia <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>; or quite to this last, or to its south limit; to reach which, it must <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> its west course a little north; because Taurus, from which it rose, lies lower, or more to the south, and almost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> with Melitene: and that then it turns to the south, in order Euphrates to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> through Taurus, and escape to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, and then take a new bend to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLONIA">Babylonia</a>. To this account of Strabo, Pliny runs quite <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTER">counter</a>; adverting eye-witnesses, who carry the Euphrates from north to south in a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> line, till it meets Mount Taurus; placing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> to the east, as Strabo does; whence, he says, it runs in a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> course westward, before it <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDS">bends</a> south; and that it rises not from Mount Taurus, but far to the north of it; and he makes it run straight west from its rise, then turn south spontaneously, without any interposing obstacle, in a manner quite different from Strabo, Mela, and others, who make Taurus the cause of this turn. The Euphrates naturally divides into two channels, one through <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>, and the other through <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SELEUCIA">Seleucia</a>, besides the several <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> cuts made between it and the Tigris about Babylon: and these cuts or trenches are what the Psalmist calls the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> of Babylon, on the willows of which the captives hung their harps. It is probable, that the Euphrates naturally poured into the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> at one particular mouth, before these cuts were made. A thing appearing so evident to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, that Pliny has set <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the distance between the mouths of the Euphrates and the Tigris; and he says, some made it 25, and others 7, miles; but that the Euphrates being for a long <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> back intercepted in its course by cuts, made for watering the fields, only the branch called the Pastigris fell into the sea, the rest of it into the Tigris, and both together into the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a>. Overflowing the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> through which it runs, at stated times of the year, like the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>, it renders it fertile.

EUPOLIS

Pages 380-380

an Athenian comic poet, flourished about the 85th Olympiad. He took the freedom of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> in lashing the vices of the people. He lost his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> fight between the Athenians and Lacedemonians; and his fate was so much lamented, that after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> it was enacted that no poet should serve in the wars. Some say <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALCIBIADES">Alcibiades</a> put him to death for his satirical freedom.

EURIPIDES

Pages 380-380

one of the Greek poets who excelled in tragedy, was born about 486 B.C. in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALAMIS">Salamis</a>, whither his father and mother had retired a little before <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a> entered <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>. He learned <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> under Prodicus, morality under <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> under <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANAXAGORAS">Anaxagoras</a>; but at 18 years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> abandoned philosophy, in order to apply himself to dramatic <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. He used to shut himself up in a cave to compose his tragedies, which were extremely applauded by the Greeks. The Athenian <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, commanded by Nicias, being defeated in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> purchased their lives and liberties by reciting the verses of Euripides; such esteem and veneration had the Sicilians for the pieces wrote by this excellent poet. Socrates, the wisest of the philosophers, set such a value upon them, that they were the only tragedies he went to see acted; and yet his performances seldom gained the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>. Euripides frequently intersperses through them moral sentences, and severe reflections on the fair <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEX">sex</a>; whence he was called the Woman-hater. He was, nevertheless, married: but the scandalous lives of his two wives drew upon him the railly of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOPHANES">Aristophanes</a>, and other comic poets; which occasioned his retiring to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Archelaus, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Macedon, where he was well received. That <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> was fond of learned men, and drew them to him by his liberality. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> we may believe Solinus, he made Euripides his minister of state, and gave him other extraordinary proofs of his esteem. He had, however, passed but a few years there, when an unhappy accident put an end to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He was walking in a wood, and, according to his usual manner, in deep meditation; when, unfortunately happening upon Archelaus's hounds, he was by them torn in pieces. It is not certain whe-

EURIPUS

Pages 380-381

a canal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> strait which divides the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Euboea, now <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGROPONT">Negropont</a>, from the continent of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. In one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> it is so narrow, that a galley can scarcely <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through it. The agitations of the Euripus were much spoken of by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. Some say that the canal has a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> and reflux six times in 24 hours; others, that it ebbs and flows <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> times a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; but Livy does not allow this flux and reflux to be so regular. Father Babin, a Jesuit of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> learning, who made many observations on the spot during his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> abode in the island of Negropont, tells us, that the Euripus is regular in its ebbing and flowing the first eight days of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>: the same regularity he observed from the 14th to the 26th day inclusive, and in the three last days: but in the other days of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, it is not so regular; for it sometimes ebbs and flows 11, 12, 13, and 14 times in the space of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> day. In this place, as the story <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> goes, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> drowned himself out of chagrin, for not being able to account for so unusual a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. Euripus has since become a general name for all straits, where the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is in great motion and agitation. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> circuses had their euripi, which were no other than pits or ditches on each side of the course, into which it was very dangerous falling with their horses and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a> as they ran races. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> euripus was more particularly applied by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to three <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> or ditches which encompassed the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CIRCUS">circus</a> on three sides, and which were filled occasionally to represent naumachiae or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> battles. The same people called their smaller fountains or canals in their gardens euripuses; and their largest, as cascades, &c. miles.

EUROCLYDON

Pages 381-381

(of Εὖρος, east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, and κλύδων, wave), is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of wind, of which we have an account only in Acts xxvii. 14, and concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of which critics have been much divided. Bochart, Grotius, Bentley, and others, substitute another <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>, supported by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIAN">Alexandrian</a> MS. and the Vulgate, viz. Εὐροκλυδών <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Euro-aquilo; but Mr Bryant defends the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> reading, and considers the Euroclydon, i.e. Εὖρος κλύδων, as an east wind that causes a deep <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> or vast inundation. He maintains, in opposition to Dr Bentley's reasoning, who supposes that the mariners in the ship, the voyage of which is recited in this passage, were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, that they were Greeks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, and that the ship was an Alexandrian ship employed in the traffic of carrying corn to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; and therefore, that the mariners had a name in their own <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> for the particular typhonic or stormy wind here mentioned. He also shows from the passage itself, that the tempestuous wind called Euroclydon, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> (κατὰ τὸ ἀνέμο) upon the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>; and therefore, as this is a relative <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, referring to the situation of the person who speaks of it, who was at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WINDWARD">windward</a> or south of it, the wind blew up- on shore, and must have come from the south or south-east; which, he adds, is fully warranted by the point where the ship was, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> it ran in afterwards, which was towards the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and north-west.

EUROPA

Pages 381-381

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Agenor <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Phoenicia and Telephassa. She was so beautiful that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> became enamoured of her; and the better to seduce her, he assumed the shape of a bull and mingled with the herds of Agenor, while Europa, with her <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> attendants, were gathering <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> in the meadows. Europa caressed the beautiful animal; and at last had the courage to sit upon his back. The god took advantage of her situation; and with precipitate steps retired towards the shore, crossed the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> with Europa on his back, and arrived safe in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>. Here he assumed his original shape, and declared his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NYMPH">nymph</a> consented, though she had once made vows of perpetual celibacy; and she became mother of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOS">Minos</a>, Sarpedon, and Rhadamantus. After this distinguished <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMOUR">amour</a> with Jupiter, she married Asterius, king of Crete. This monarch seeing himself without children by Europa, adopted the fruit of her amours with Jupiter, and always esteemed Minos, Sarpedon, and Rhadamantus, as his own children. Some suppose, that Europa lived about 1552 years before the Christian era.

EUROPE

Pages 381-385

one of the four <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of the world. This is considerably the smallest of the four <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> divisions of the terraqueous globe. Its length, from east to west, according to the most authentic accounts, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> about 3300 miles British <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, and its breadth 2350. The continental <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it is bounded on the south by the Mediterranean <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, on the west by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>, comprehending the most distant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Europe, viz. that of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICELAND">Iceland</a>, for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GREENLAND">Greenland</a> is now considered as constituting a part of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. Many geographers of eminence have given the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AZORES">Azores</a> to Europe, from their greater <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROXIMITY">proximity</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a> than to any other continental <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and have considered the Madeiras as a constituent part of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> for a similar reason. Europe is bounded on the north by the Arctic ocean and the new <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>; while its eastern limits appear to be more uncertain in the estimation of geographers. It appears evident, however, that a very <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> limit might be ascertained by the river Oufa, the Kama, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOLGA">Volga</a>, which would make its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> extremely natural to the town of Sarepta; it requiring only an imaginary line of very small <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> from that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to the river <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">Don</a>. The superficies of Europe, including the Azores, Iceland, &c. is about 3,432,000 miles. The western and southern parts of Europe anciently consisted of the people called Celts; the Fins occupied the north-east; and the Laplanders, a people equally <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> with the Samoeds of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, possessed its remotest parts toward the north, who rendered their own <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> less uncouth and barbarous by assimilating it to that of the Fins. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a> from Asia seem to have driven those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> inhabitants towards the east and north, whose descendants occupy the greater part of Europe. From the Slavonic tribes, who also came from Asia, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POLES">Poles</a>, Russians, &c. were descended. These were accompanied by the Heruli, who made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of what is now denominated the Lettic speech, to be met with in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURLAND">Courland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVONIA">Livonia</a>, Lithuania, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMOGITIA">Samogitia</a>. Samogitia, and nearly allied to the Slavonic language, according to the account of Tooke in his view of Russia. At an early <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> the colony of Iberi and northern Mauritani came over into <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; and at a later period both the Hungarians and Turks emigrated from Asia. Notwithstanding the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> character of d'Anville as a geographer, we believe that his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> respecting the geographical knowledge of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> is greatly exaggerated. It appears evident that nothing more of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCANDINAVIA">Scandinavia</a> was known to the ancients than the southern part as far as the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> of Weter and Wenner. It is no doubt true that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, by means of their shipping, even in the imperfect state of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> at that period, traversed the southern shores of the Baltic, as far as to the river Rubo, ascertaining the names of various tribes along that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a>; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the maps of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> are admitted as decisive proofs in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, it is certain that they were wholly unacquainted with the interior of Germany; and consequently the tribes of which he makes mention, may rather be considered as having dwelt along the northern shores of the Baltic, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the southern parts on the left of the Danube. They were no doubt acquainted with the Carpathian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; but their knowledge of Europe towards the north-east was undoubtedly circumscribed by the 50th or 52nd <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of north latitude. In many barbarous languages, the same word was often used indiscriminately either for a mountain or a forest, the want of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to which has frequently been the prolific source of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a>, and placed mountains of the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> where the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> had planted trees. It has been supposed that the Riphean mountains were the Uralian chain, of which the ancients knew nothing, instead of a forest of prodigious extent from east to west. It is also well known that the Venedici Montes of Ptolemy have no existence upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and therefore must once have been a very extensive forest with which the moderns are unacquainted, and perhaps no traces of it are now anywhere to be met with. Christianity is the predominant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> all over Europe, except in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>; and even there it has been computed, that about one-half of the inhabitants are members of the Greek <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The Christian religion has always been accompanied in its progress with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFUSION">diffusion</a> of knowledge, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of industry, and the civilization of manners, whereas the barbarous tribes in the northern parts of Europe advanced by very slow degrees, and the Scandinavians <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in a state of pagan <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> till the eleventh century.
