Some tribes of Slavonia to the south of the Baltic, were not converted to Christianity till the thirteenth century, and of course were for many ages in a state little superior to brutality; and the people of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAPLAND">Lapland</a> were not converted to the Christian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> till about a century ago, by means of missionaries sent from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>. The people of Europe, as to matters of religion, are divided into catholics and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">protestants</a>, the former being chiefly confined to the southern parts of it, where the imagination requires the gratifications arising from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> pomp and parade; and the latter in the northern parts of it, the simplicity of which is much better calculated to please the predominant <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of the judgment. The Christian religion being thus diffused all over Europe, that division of the globe has hence become a kind of republic in respect of literature, every scientific <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> and discovery being transmitted from one portion of it to another with the utmost dispatch. For this reason Europe has been sometimes compared to ancient <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, and it is to be hoped that Russia <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> never prove another Macedon. The greater part of this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the globe lies within the northern temperate zone, a distinction which is now nearly annihilated by the interesting discoveries of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">Climate</a> is found to depend very frequently on causes which are purely local, since the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, in a southern latitude, exhibit mountains of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a> which are not known even in Lapland, while the torrid zone is plentifully supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> and habitations, and for any thing which can be determined to the contrary, it may contain mountains which are covered with snow. As it is happily delivered from those intense heats which are peculiar to Asia and Africa, the inhabitants are in general blessed with greater bodily vigour and intellectual strength. One of the most striking features of Europe in a general point of view is its inland seas, which give it a decided superiority over the other more extensive divisions of the earth, and contribute powerfully to the extension of its industry, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, and civilization. If such blessings had been enjoyed by Africa, it is more than probable that the consequences of her industry would have been diffused far and wide. Of these inland seas, the Mediterranean holds the most distinguished place, as the centre of civilization both to the ancient and modern inhabitants of Europe. It is about 2000 miles in length to its farthest extremity in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, but the maps of antiquity make it 300 more. The gulfs of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> and the Archipelago open on its northern side, formerly denominated the Adriatic and Egean seas, from the last of which there is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the sea of Marmora, or the Propontis, by means of the Hellespont; and the strait of Constantinople leads into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> sea, to the north of which is the sea of Azof, (Palus Maeotis), or utmost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> boundary of Europe in that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. This vast expanse of water is beautifully ornamented with numerous <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> and an opulent sea coast, exhibiting delightful specimens of almost every thing in nature which is sublime and beautiful. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-TIDES">Tides</a> cannot be perceived except in straits of very small dimensions, although naturalists have observed, that a current sets along the shores of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> from west to east, while its direction is from east to west towards the coast of Africa. In the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Venice the current runs along <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a> in a north-west direction, and returns by the opposite shore of Italy. There is abundance of fish to be met with in the Mediterranean, some of which are but rarely to be found in more northern latitudes. This sea in particular abounds with coral, now certainly known to be the production of marine insects. This imaginary plant is tri-coloured, composed of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, vermillion and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and does not exceed eleven inches in height. It is hard in the sea, and in this respect undergoes not the smallest change by exposure to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>; and the nets made use of for procuring it, measure from 60 to 125 feet. From the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of its rocks or perilous navigation, the Black sea is said to have derived its name. As the sea of Azof almost always exhibits a muddy appearance, it was for that reason denominated Palus by the ancients, and it is united to the Euxine or Black sea by the strait of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAFFA">Caffa</a>. The next inland sea of Europe is the Baltic, to which the Germans have given the name of the Eastern sea, which accounts for the people denominated Easterlings in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of England, who undoubtedly came from the shores of the Baltic. It opens from the German sea by a gulf trending north-east, known by the name of the Skager <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACK">Rack</a>, from whence it passes southward in the Cattgat, to the south-east of which we meet with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of Elsinore, where vessels become in some degree tributary to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Denmark. It is afterwards divided into two branches of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> extent, called the gulfs of Bothnia and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINLAND">Finland</a>, both of which are covered with ice for nearly five months in the year. The greatest depth of the Baltic is said not to exceed 50 fathoms; and according to the opinion of naturalists its extent suffers a diminution of four feet every century. It has been affirmed that its waters do not contain above one-thirtieth of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, while other sea-waters frequently contain one-tenth, which has been ascribed to the vast <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of ice; and when the north <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> blows, these waters, it is also said, may be employed for the purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> economy. There are no tides in the Baltic, and but very few fish. The White sea, in the northern parts of Russia, is the last inland sea of Europe, which was well known to the English in particular, before the commerce of Archangel was transferred to Petersburgh. It went by the name of Quen sea in the reign of Alfred the Great; and the writers of Iceland called it the sea of Ganwick, on the shores of which stood their Biarmia. There are a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of islands in the White sea, but the accounts which geographers have hitherto given us, are neither circumstantial nor satisfactory. The German sea deserves to be mentioned among the other maritime divisions of Europe, which has received the appellation because it waters the western shores of ancient Germany, from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a> to the farthest boundary of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUTLAND">Jutland</a>. It may properly be regarded as constituting a part of the Atlantic ocean, ending at the straits of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a>, from whence the British channel extends to the west. Another extensive inlet of the Atlantic is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISCAY">Biscay</a>; for the British channel is rather to be considered as the wide frith of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>. St George's channel lies on the south between Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, and the Irish sea leading to the North channel, is situated in the centre. What the ancients called the Deucaliedon sea lies to the north of Scotland, which was likewise denominated the Sarmatian, as extending throughout the Baltic. The Arctic ocean lies to the north of Europe, the dismal receptacle of countless miles of ice, piled up in mountains, the hoary majesty of which, while it captivates the eye, can scarcely fail to strike terror into the heart of the mariner. Yet from those dreary regions, which at first appear only as a prodigious waste in the works of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>, the benevolent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">Parent</a> of the universe diffuses innumerable millions of herrings for the use of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. This is worthy of the divine being whose goodness is whispered to us in every breeze, which glows in the starry firmament of heaven, and is diffused through the whole creation. The Goodwin sands in the vicinity of the Kentish coast, are as dangerous to the mariner as uninviting to the fisher; but excellent fish are to be found on many banks on the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, among which may be ranked the cod, the soal, and the plaice. What are called the Silverpits of the mariners, lying between the Dogger and Well <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, supply the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> market with cod, which discovers a predilection for the deep waters in the vicinity of the banks. The Hornriff, a narrow strip extending to Jutland, is situated towards the north east of the Dogger bank. The Juttsriff extends from the mouth of the Baltic to the German sea, in the form of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a>. The Mar bank takes its rise opposite to Berwick, which is little more than 15 miles in length. To the eastward of this lies the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a> Forties, extending from Buchanness to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>, and from between 40 and 100 miles from the shore; and a bank reaches across the German sea towards Juttsriff, from the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUCHAN">Buchan</a>. It was thought necessary, in this concise account of Europe, to mention some of the most considerable banks or comparative shoals, which have often been regarded as the summits of lofty mountains beneath the surface of the deep; and which, as the haunts of fishes of different <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, have arrested the attention of national industry. A <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> of Europe will be given in our account of the countries through which they respectively flow. The greater part of the Wolga is considered as belonging to Europe; the next highly celebrated river is the Danube, after which we may <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> the Nieper, the Rhine, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>. The Alps are the loftiest mountains; next the Pyrenees; and that vast ridge by which <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a> is divided from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>. The Carpathian mountains, the chain called Eminch, and the Apennines, are of inferior magnitude. The European states and kingdoms may properly be divided into three classes. 1. Despotic monarchies, of which Russia and Turkey may serve as specimens. 2. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">Absolute</a> monarchies, such as Spain and Denmark. And 3. Those of a limited nature, as the Germanic empire, and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Great Britain. Since the peace in 1815, constitutions formed on the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of that of England have been adopted by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WURTEMBERG">Wurtemberg</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BADEN">Baden</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESSE">Hesse</a> Darmstadt, and some other of the smaller states. Spain and Portugal have established governments on a more democratic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>. The two old commercial aristocracies of Venice and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a> have been suppressed. It is customary with some geographers to divide the constituent parts of Europe into first, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, and third orders, according to their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> importance; the first order including the united kingdoms of Great Britain and Ireland, France, Russia, the Austrian dominions, Prussia, Spain, Turkey. In the second order stand the United Provinces, Denmark, Sweden, Portugal, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> states of Germany and Italy constitute the third, a detailed account of which our readers will find in this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> under their proper names. For a detailed account of the recent changes in this quarter of the globe, see the article EUROPE in the Supplement.

EURYALE

Pages 385-385

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, one of the Gorgons, daughters of Phorcys, and sister of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEDUSA">Medusa</a>; she was subject neither to old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> nor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>.

EURYANDRA

Pages 385-386

Euryandra, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the polyandria class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Eurydice, in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the wife of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a>, who <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> from Aristaeus that endeavoured to ravish her, was slain by a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a>. Her husband went <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the shades, and by the force of his music persuaded Pluto and Proserpine to give him leave to carry back his wife; which they granted, provided he did not look on her till he came to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>; but breaking the condition, was forced to leave her behind him. See Orpheus. Eurymedon, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a noble river running through the middle of Pamphylia; famous for a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> fight on the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, in which the Athenians under Cimon the son of Miltiades, defeated the Persians. The sea fight happened first in the sea of Pamphylia, towards Cyprus; the land engagement, the following night on the Eurymedon. Cimon, after defeating the Persian fleet, armed his men with the armour of the captives, and set sail for the enemy, who lay on the banks of the Eurymedon, in the ships taken from the Persians; who on seeing their own ships and their own people in appearance, were off their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, and thus became an easy conquest. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EURYSTHEUS">Eurystheus</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a> and Mycenae, son of Sthenelus and Nicippe the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELOPS">Pelops</a>. Juno hastened his birth by two months, that he might come into the world before <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> the son of Alcmena, as the younger of the two was doomed by order of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> to be subservient to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> of the other. (See Alcmena). This <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> was cruelly exercised by Eurystheus, who was jealous of the fame of Hercules; and who, to destroy so powerful a relation, imposed upon him the most dangerous and uncommon enterprises, well known by the name of the twelve labours of Hercules. The success of Hercules in achieving those perilous labours alarmed Eurystheus in a greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, and he furnished himself with a brazen vessel, where he might secure himself a safe retreat in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of danger. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Hercules, Eurystheus renewed his cruelties against his children, and made <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CEYX">Ceyx</a> king of Trachinia, because he had given them support, and treated them with hospitality. He was killed in the prosecution of this war by Hyllus the son of Hercules. His head was sent to Alcmena the mother of Hercules; who, mindful of the cruelties which her son had suffered, insulted it, and tore out the eyes with the most invertebrate fury. Eurystheus was succeeded on the throne of Argos by Atreus his nephew. The death of Eurystheus happened about 30 years before the Trojan war. Eurythmy, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">Painting</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SCULPTURE">Sculpture</a>, is a certain majesty, elegance, and easiness, appearing in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> members <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> parts of a body, painting, or sculpture, and resulting from the fine proportion of it. Eusden, Laurence, an Irish clergyman, rector of Conesby in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>, and poet laureat after the death of Mr Rowe. His first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> was the eminent <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALIFAX">Halifax</a>; whose poem, on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOYNE">Boyne</a>, he translated into Latin, and dedicated to his lordship. He was esteemed by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>, who rewarded an epithalamium he wrote on his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of poet laureat. He was the author of many poetical pieces, though but little known before his pre-ferment: he died in 1730. Eusebius, a denomination given to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of Eusebians <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a>, on account of the favour and countenance which Eusebius, bishop of Cesarea, showed and procured for them at their first rise. See Arians and Eusebius. Eusebius, surnamed Pamphilus, a celebrated bishop of Cesarea in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, and one of the most learned men of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, was born in Palestine about the latter end of the reign of Gallienus. He was the intimate friend of Pamphilus the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">Martyr</a>; and, after his death, took his name in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. He was ordained bishop of Cesarea in 313. He had a considerable share in the contest relating to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIUS">Arius</a>; whose cause he, as well as several other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of Palestine, defended, being persuaded that Arius had been unjustly persecuted by Alexander bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>. He assisted at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Nice in 325; when he made a speech to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Constantine on his coming to the council, and was placed next him on his right <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. He was present at the council of Antioch, in which <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUSTATHIUS">Eustathius</a> bishop of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> was deposed; but though he was chosen by the bishop and people of Antioch to succeed him, he absolutely refused it. In 335, he assisted at the council of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a> held against Athanasius; and at the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of bishops at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, at the time of the dedication of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> there. By these bishops he was sent to the emperor Constantine to defend what they had done against Athanasius; when he pronounced the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> made on that emperor during the public rejoicings in the beginning of the 30th year of his reign, which was the last of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Eusebius survived the emperor but a short time, for he died in 338. He wrote, 1. An <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> History, of which Valetius has given a good edition in Greek and Latin; 2. The life of Constantine; 3. A treatise against <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HIEROCLES">Hierocles</a>; 4. Chronicon; 5. Preparations Evangelicae; 6. De demonstratione Evangelicae, of which there are but 10 books extant out of 20; and several other works, some of which are lost. Eustachius, Bartholomew, physician and anatomist at Rome, flourished about the year 1550. His anatomical plates were discovered there in 1712, and published in 1714. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EUSTATHIANS">Eustathians</a>, a name given to the Catholics of Antioch in the 4th century, on occasion of their refusal to acknowledge any other bishop beside St Eustathius, deposed by the Arians. The denomination was given them during the episcopate of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PAULINUS">Paulinus</a>, whom the Arians substituted to St Eustathius, about the year 330, when they began to hold their assemblies apart. About the year 350, Leontius of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>, called the eunuch, who was an Arian, and was put in the see of Antioch, desired the Eustathians to perform their <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in his church; which they accepting, the church of Antioch served indifferently both the Arians and Catholics. This, we are told, gave occasion to two institutions, which have subsisted in the church ever since. The first was psalmody in two choirs; though M. Baillet thinks, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they instituted an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> psalmody between two choirs, it was between two Catholic choirs, and not by way of response to an Arian choir. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> was the doxology, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">Glory</a> be to the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Ghost. See Doxology. This conduct, which seemed to imply a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> with the Arians, gave <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> offence to abundance

EUSTATHIUS

Pages 386-387

bishop of Thessalonica, in the 12th century, under the reigns of the emperors Emmanuel, Alexander, and Andronicus Comnenus. He was a very eminent grammarian; and wrote commentaries upon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, and Dionysius the geographer. The best edition of his Commentaries on Homer is that of Rome, printed in Greek, in 1542, in four volumes folio. His Commentaries on the Periegesis of Dionysius were printed by Mr Hudson at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, in 1697, 8vo. Eustathius appears to have been alive in the year 1194.

EUSTATIA

Pages 387-387

St Eustatia, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Eustatius, one of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CARIBBEE_ISLANDS">Caribbee <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, belonging to the Dutch, and situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 62° 36'. N. Lat. 17° 29'. It is little else than a huge mountain, which formerly has, in all <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, been a volcano. Its situation is so strong, that it has but one landing <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; and that is fortified in such a manner as to be almost impregnable. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">Tobacco</a> is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> product of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>; and it is cultivated to the very top of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a> which terminates in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> plain surrounded with woods, but having a hollow in the middle, which serves as a large den for wild beasts. No fewer than 3000 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> people and 15,000 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> subsist on this spot, where they rear hogs, kids, rabbits, and all kinds of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>, in such abundance, that they can supply their neighbours, after having served themselves. The first Dutch colony sent to this island consisted of about 1600 people. They were dispossessed by the English from Jamaica in 1665. Soon after, the Dutch and French becoming confederates, the English were expelled in their turn. The French continuing to hold a garrison in the island till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREDA">Breda</a>, when it was restored to the Dutch. Soon after the revolution, the French drove out the Dutch, and were in their turn driven out by the English under Sir Timothy Thornhill, with the loss of no more than eight men killed and wounded, though the fort they took mounted 16 guns, and was in every other respect very strong. Sir Timothy found it necessary for the protection of the Dutch, to leave a small English garrison in the fort; but he granted the French no terms of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a>, except for their lives and baggage. By the peace of Ryswick, the entire <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of this island was restored to the Dutch. This island was reduced by the British in the year 1781. Though not 20 miles in circumference, it abounded at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, by reason of the vast conflux of trade from every other island in these seas. Being a free port, it was open to all the subjects of the belligerent powers; and thus a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> was established among them, through which they were enabled to carry on a commercial correspondence, which greatly mitigated the inconveniences of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. The greatest benefit, however, was reaped by the Dutch; who, by transacting all trading business for other nations, were thus intrusted with numberless commissions, and likewise enjoyed vast profits from the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of the merchandises to which they were entitled. At the time the attack was made upon them, they were so little under the apprehensions of such an event, that their warehouses were not sufficient to contain the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of commercial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> imported for sale, and the beach and streets were covered with hogsheads of tobacco and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>. In this situation, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> Rodney having received orders to commence hostilities against the Dutch, suddenly appeared before the island with such an armament of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> forces, as in its defenceless situation was not only useless but ridiculous. The governor could scarcely <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> the officer who summoned him to surrender; but being convinced how matters stood, the only possible step was taken, namely, to surrender the whole island and every thing in it, at <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>. Along with the island there fell into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the captors a ship of 60 guns, with 250 sail of merchantmen, while the value of property on the island was estimated at no less than four millions <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. This capture became afterwards a subject of discussion in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, where the conduct of the British commanders was severely scrutinized by Mr Burke. The admiral and general made their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> in person; but the minority at that time were far from being satisfied; and it was supposed that on the change of ministry a rigid inquiry would have been set on foot, had not the splendour of Admiral Rodney's victory over de Grasse put an end to all thoughts of that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. The island of St Eustatius is naturally of such difficult access, as already observed, that it is almost impossible for an enemy to effect a landing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> proper care is taken by those who are in possession of it. This very circumstance proved the ruin of the new possessors. The British, secure in their inaccessible situation, conducted themselves in such a manner as induced the Marquis de Bouillé to make an attempt to regain it. Having sailed from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARTINICO">Martinico</a> at the head of 2000 men, he arrived on the 26th of November 1781, off one of the landing places

EUTROPIUS

Pages 387-388

Flavius, a Latin author, in the 4th century, was secretary to Constantine the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, and afterwards bore arms under the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Julian, and followed that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> in his expedition against the Persians. He wrote an Abridgement of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMAN_HISTORY">Roman <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, from the foundation of Rome to the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALENS">Valens</a>; the best edition of which is that of Miss Eustachi-Le Fevre, afterwards Madame Dacier, published at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the Dauphin, in 4to, in the year 1683.

EUTYCHIANS

Pages 388-389
ancient heretics, who denied the duplicity of natures in Christ; thus denominated from Eutyches, the archimandrite, or abbot of a monastery at Constantinople, who began to propagate his opinion A.D. 448. He did not, however, seem quite steady and consistent in his sentiments: for he appeared to allow of two natures, even before the union; which was apparently a consequence he drew from the principles of the Platonic philosophy, which supposes a pre-existence of souls: accordingly, he believed that the soul of Jesus Christ had been united to the divinity before the incarnation; but then he allowed no distinction of natures in Jesus Christ since his incarnation. This heresy was first condemned in a synod held at Constantinople by Flavian, in 448, approved by the council of Ephesus, called conventus latronum, in 449, and re-examined, and culminated in the general council of Chalcedon in 451. The legates of Pope Leo, who assisted at it, maintained that it was not enough to define, that there were two natures in Jesus Christ; but insisted strenuously, that, to remove all equivocations, they must add these terms, without being changed, or confounded, or divided. The heresy of the Eutychians, which made a very great progress throughout the east, at length became divided into several branches. Nicephorus makes mention of no fewer than twelve: some called Schematiki, or Apparentes, as only attributing to Jesus Christ a phantom or appearance of flesh, and no real flesh; others, Theodosians, from Theodosius bishop of Alexandria; others, Jacobites, from one James (Jacobus), of Syria; which branch established itself principally in Armenia, where it still subsists. Others were called Acephali, q.d. without head; and Severians, from a monk called Severus, who seized on the see of Antioch in 513. These last were subdivided into five factions, viz. Agnoeter, who attributed some ignorance to Jesus Christ; the followers of Paul; Monans, that is, the black Angelites, thus called from the place where they were assembled; and lastly, Adrites and Comonites. EUTYCHIANS was also the name of another sect, half Arian half Eunomian; which arose at Constantinople in the fourth century. It being then a matter of mighty controversy among the Eunomians at Constantinople, whether or not the Son of God knew the last day and hour of the world, particularly with regard to that passage in the gospel of St Matthew, chap. xxiv. ver. 36, or rather that in St Mark, xiii. 32, where it is expressed, that the Son did not know it, but the Father only; Eutychius made no scruple to maintain, even in writing, that the Son did not know it; which sentiment displeasing the leaders of the Eunomian party, he separated from them, and made a journey to Eunomius, who was then in exile. That heretic acquiesced fully in Eutychius' doctrine, and admitted him to his communion. Eunomius dying soon after, the chief of the Eunomians at Constantinople refused to admit Eutychius; who, upon this, formed a particular sect of such as adhered to him, called Eutychians. This same Eutychius, with one Theophronius, as was said in Sozomen's time, were the occasions of all the changes made by the Eunomians in the administration of baptism; which consisted, according to Nicephorus, in only using one immersion, and not doing it in the name of the Trinity, but in memory of the death of Jesus Christ. Nicephorus calls the chief of that sect, not Eutychius, but Euphychius, and his followers Eunomianpsychians.

EUTYCHIUS

Pages 389-389
patriarch of Alexandria, lived about the ninth age; and wrote annals in the Arabic language, printed at Oxford in 1618, with a Latin version by Mr Pococke. Selden had printed something of his before. EUXINE or "xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">BLACK SEA, forms part of the boundary betwixt Europe and Asia. It receives the Nieper, the Danube, and other large rivers; and extends from 28 to 41 degrees of E. Long. and from 41 to 47 of N. Lat. The ancients imagined this sea to have been originally only a lake or standing pool which broke first into the Propontis, and then into the Egean, washing away by degrees the earth which first kept it within bounds, and formed the two channels of the Bosphorus Thracus and Hellespont, now the Dardanelles.—It was anciently called the Axenus, supposed to be from Ashkenaz, the son of Gomer, who is said to have settled near it. This original being forgot in length of time, the Greeks explained it by inhospitable, which the word Axenos literally signifies; and therefore, when they came to consider the inhabitants of these coasts as more civilized and hospitable, they changed the name into Euxinus. See Black Sea, Supplement.

EVACUANTS

Pages 370-370

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, are properly such medicines as diminish the animal <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>, by throwing out some morbid <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> redundant humour; or such as thin, attenuate, and promote the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> and circulation thereof.

EVACUATION

Pages 370-370

in Medicine, the art of diminishing, emptying, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> attenuating, the humours of the body.

EVAGRIUS SCHOLASTICUS

Pages 370-370

a famous historian, born at Epiphania, about the year 536. He practised the profession of an advocate, from which he was called Scholasticus, which name was then given to the pleaders at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>. He was also tribune and keeper of the prefect's dispatches. He wrote an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, which begins where <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a> and Theodore ended theirs; and other works, for which he was rewarded by the emperors Tiberius and Mauricius. M. de Valois published at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> a good edition of Evagrius's ecclesiastical history, in folio; and it was republished at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a> in 1620, in folio, by William <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">Reading</a>, with additional notes of various authors.

EVANDER

Pages 370-370

a famous Arcadian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, called the son of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, on account of his eloquence, brought a colony of his people into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, about 60 years before the taking of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>; when Fauns, who then reigned over the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABORIGINES">Aborigines</a>, gave him a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, in which he settled with his friends. He is said to have taught the Latins the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of letters, and the art of husbandry. He kindly received <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> when he returned from the conquest of Geryon, and he was the first who raised him altars. He gave Æneas assistance against the Rutuli, and distinguished himself by his hospitality. It is said that he first brought the Greek <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a> into Italy, and introduced there the worship of the Greek deities. He was honoured as a god after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, and his subjects raised him an altar on Mount Aventine.

EVANGELISTS

Pages 370-371

the inspired authors of the gospels. The word is derived from the Greek εὐαγγέλιον, formed of εὖ, bene, "well," and αγγέλος, "angel <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> messenger." The denomination evangelists was likewise given in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> to such as preached the gospel up and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, without being attached to any particular church, being either commissioned by the apostles to instruct the nations, or of their own <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ACCORD">accord</a> abandoning every worldly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a>, and consecrating themselves EUC <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EUCARIST">EUCARIST</a> to the sacred office of preaching the gospel. In which <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> some interpreters think it is that St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>, who was one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> deacons, is called the evangelist, in the 21st <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of the Acts of the Apostles, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> 8. Again, St Paul <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> to Timothy, ep. ii. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. iv. ver. 5, bids him do the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of an evangelist. The same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a>, Eph. iv. 11, ranks the evangelists after the apostles and prophets.

EVANID

Pages 371-371

a name given by some authors to such colours as are of no <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>, as those in the rainbow, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> before and after sunset, &c. Evandid colours are also called fantastical and emphatical colours.

EVANTES

Pages 371-371

in antiquity, the priestesses of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, thus called, because in celebrating the orgia they ran about as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> distracted, crying, Evan, evan, oh! evan. See BACCHANALIA.

EVAPORATION

Pages 371-371

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, signifies the conversion of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> into vapour, so that it becomes specifically <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">CHEMISTRY</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEOROLOGY">METEOROLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EVASION

Pages 371-371

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is used for any subtle endeavour to set aside <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to escape the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of the law, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> not be endured. Thus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a person says to another that he will not strike him, but will give him a pot of ale to strike him first, and accordingly he strikes, the returning of it is punishable; for no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> shall evade the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the law by such a pretence to cover his malice.

EVATES

Pages 371-371

a branch <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRUIDS">druids</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Celtic philosophers. Strabo divides the British and Gaulish philosophers into three sects; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARDS">bards</a>, evates, and druids. He adds, that the bards were the poets and musicians; the evates, the priests and naturalists; and the druids were moralists as well as naturalists: But Marcellus and Hornius reduce them all to two sects, viz. the BARDS and DRUIDS.

EVCVATION

Pages 379-379

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> always observed by them at the undertaking a siege, wherein they solemnly called upon the gods and goddesses of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to forsake it and come over to them. Without the performance of this ceremony, they either thought that the place could not be taken, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that it would be a sacrilege to take the gods prisoners. They always took it for granted that their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> was heard, and that the gods had deserted the place and come over to them, provided they were able to make themselves masters of it.

EVELYN

Pages 372-373

John, a most learned and ingenious writer and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, was born at Wotton in Surry, the seat of his father, in 1620. After making the tour of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, he returned to England about the year 1651, and lived very retired at his rural retreat, Say's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">Court</a>, near <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPTFORD">Deptford</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>; where his disgust at the violence and confusion of the times operated so far upon his studious disposition, that he actually proposed to Mr Boyle the establishing a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> for persons of the same turn of mind, where they might associate together without care <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> interruption. It was owing to Mr Evelyn's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> became possessed of the famous Arundelian marbles; which he persuaded the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Henry Howard to bestow on that university. He was very assiduous in transmitting to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> whatever fell within the compass of his inquiries; and used humbly to style himself a pioneer in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. When the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of books he published is considered, the many he left behind him unfinished and unpublished, and the variety of subjects on which he employed his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, his industry and application are astonishing. "His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> (says the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> Mr Walpole) was a course of inquiry, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, curiosity, instruction, and benevolence. The works of the Creator, and the mimic labours of the creature, were all objects of his pursuit. He unfolded the perfections of the one, and assisted the imperfections of the other. He adored from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>; was a courtier that flattered only by informing his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, and by pointing out what was worthy for him to countenance; and was really the neighbour of the Gospel, for there was no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> that might not have been the better for him. He was one of the first promoters of the Royal Society, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of the ingenious and indigent, and peculiarly serviceable to the lettered world; for, besides his writings and discoveries, he obtained the Arundelian marbles for the university of Oxford, and the Arundelian library for the Royal Society: nor is it the least <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his praise, that he who proposed to Mr Boyle the erection of a philosophic college for retired and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECULATIVE">speculative</a> persons, had the honesty to write in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> life against Sir George Mackenzie's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on Solitude. He knew that retirement in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> was industry and benefit to mankind; but in those of others, laziness and instability." There are five small <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> of this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>'s journey from Rome to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, drawn and etched by him; and among his published works are, 1. A Character of England; 2. The State of France; 3. An Essay on the the first book of Lucretius De rerum natura; 4. The French gardener; 5. A <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PANEGYRIC">Panegyric</a> on <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II.'s coronation; 6. Fumifugium, or the inconvenience of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> dissipated; 7. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> and Art of Engraving on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">Copper</a>; 8. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>; 9. Silva, or a discourse of forest trees; and several others. This amiable gentleman died, full of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, in 1706. His son John Evelyn, born in 1654, distinguished himself by his elegant translations and poems: He was one of the commissioners of the revenue in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>; but died early in life, in 1668.

EVERGETES

Pages 373-373

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> signifying benefactor, given to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> of Macedon, and to Antigonus Doson, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. It was also <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> given to the kings of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> and Pontus, and we often see among the former an Alexander Evergetes, and among the latter a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MITHRIDATES">Mithridates</a> Evergetes. Some of the Roman emperors also claimed that epithet of Benevolent and Humane.

EVERGREEN

Pages 373-373

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of perennials, which continue their verdure, leaves, &c. all the year: such are hollies, phillyreas, laurustinuses, bays, pines, firs, cedars of Lebanon, &c. EVERLASTING <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEA">pea</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LATHYRUS">LATHYRUS</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. EVES-DROPPERS. See EAVES-Droppers. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EVESHAM">Evesham</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Evesholm, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Evesham, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTERSHIRE">Worcestershire</a>, seated on a gentle ascent from the river Avon, over which there is a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>. It is 95 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, 14 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>, and has a harbour for barges. It is an old borough, reckoned the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>; and sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. It had formerly an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> with a mitred <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a>; which abbey when standing was one of the largest and most stately of any in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. It was governed by a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a>, till <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> James I. at the request of his son <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Henry, gave it a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> for a mayor, 7 aldermen, 12 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> burgesses, a recorder, and chamberlain, who are all of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, with 24 other burgesses called assistants. Four of the aldermen, and the mayor for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> being, are justices of the peace; and of oyer and terminer, and of gaol delivery, for all offences in the corporation, except <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>; and the corporation has power to try and execute felons within the borough. Here are two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>-churches; but the bells of both have been removed to a beautiful old tower which was one of the gates of the abbey. The town is noted for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> victory obtained near it by Prince Edward, afterwards King Edward I., over Simon <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MONTFORT">Montfort</a>, the great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a>, who was killed in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. There is an open prospect from hence of the spacious valley called the vale of Evesham or vale of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a>, which so abounds with the best of corn, as well as pasture for sheep, that it is reckoned the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANARY">granary</a> of all these parts. The vale runs all along the banks of the Avon, from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEWKESBURY">Tewkesbury</a> to Pershore, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STRATFORD">Stratford</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICKSHIRE">Warwickshire</a>, and the river is so far navigable. It has a weekly market and four <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>. The market-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, built by Sir Edward Hobby, has its upper apartments used by the corporation for a sessions-house, and formerly for the assizes of the county. There are considerable garden grounds around the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, the produce of which supplies the adjacent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>.

EVICTIO

Pages 373-373

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of lands <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> tenements by law.

EVIDENCE

Pages 373-373

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> by testimony of men upon oath, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by writings or records. It is called evidence, because thereby the point in issue in a cause to be tried is to be made evident to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURY">jury</a>; for probatones debent esse evidentes et perspicue. The system of evidence, as now established in our courts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law, is very full, comprehensive, and refined; far different from, and superior to, any thing known in the middle ages;—as far superior in that as in all other improvements and refinements in science, arts, and manners. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of evidence during the ages of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> was extremely imperfect, and the people were incapable of making any rational improvement. Thus it was the imperfection of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> reason that caused the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> and introduction of the ORDEAL, as an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> to the Supreme Being. As men are unable to comprehend the manner in which the Deity carries on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the universe, by equal, fixed, and general laws, they are apt to imagine, that in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> which their passions or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> render important in their own eyes, the Supreme Ruler of all ought visibly to display his power in vindicating innocence, and punishing vice.

EVIL

Pages 373-376

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, &c. is either moral <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>. Moral evil is the disagreement between the actions of a moral <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGENT">agent</a>, and the rule of those actions, whatever it is. Natural evil is, whatever destroys or disturbs the perfection of natural beings; such as <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol2.html#article-BLINDNESS">blindness</a>, diseases, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a>'s Evil, or Scrophula. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Evil-Merodach, the son and successor of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-NEBUCHADNEZZAR">Nebuchadnezzar</a>. Evil-Merodach, king of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>, succeeded to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> in the year of the world 3443; but governed the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> during the indisposition of his father, who, after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years, having recovered his understanding, once more ascended the throne; and, as some believe, imprisoned his son Evil-Merodach. In this confinement it is supposed that Evil-Merodach made an acquaintance and friendship with Jehoiachim king of Judah, who had been carried to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar. However that was, it is certain, that soon after his succession to the throne, he delivered the king of Judah out of prison, after a confinement of 37 years, heaped many favours on him, and placed him above all the other kings who were at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Babylon, (2 Kings xxv. 27, Jer. lii. 31). Evil-Merodach reigned but one year, according to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a> of Archbishop Usher; but Dr Prideaux <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> have him to have reigned two years; and was succeeded by Neriglissar his sister's husband, who having been at the head of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> that put him to death, reigned in his stead. Others will have it, that this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> was immediately succeeded by his son <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELSHAZZAR">Belshazzar</a>. Euler, Leonard, professor of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, member of the imperial academy of Petersburgh, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> academy of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>, and fellow of the royal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, as also correspondent member of the royal academy of sciences at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, April 15, 1707, of reputable parents. The years of his infancy were passed in a rural retreat at the village of Richen, of which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> his father was minister.—Being sent to the university of Basil, he attended regularly the different professors. As his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> was prodigious, he performed his academical tasks with uncommon rapidity; and all the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he gained by this was consecrated to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, which soon became his favourite <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. The early progress he made in this science, only added new ardour to his application; and thus he obtained a distinguished place in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> and esteem of Professor John Bernouilli, who was at that time one of the first mathematicians in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. In 1723, M. Euler took his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts; and delivered on that occasion a Latin discourse, in which he drew a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> between the philosophy of Newton and the Cartesian system, which was received with the greatest applause. He afterwards, at his father's desire, applied himself to the study of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> and the oriental languages. Though these studies were foreign to his predominant propensity, his success was considerable even in this line; however, with his father's consent, he returned to geometry as his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> object. He <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to avail himself of the counsels and instructions of M. Bernouilli; he contracted an intimate friendship with his two sons Nicholas and Daniel; and it was in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of these connexions that he became afterwards the principal ornament of the academy of Petersburgh. The project of erecting this academy, which had been formed by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, was executed by Catherine I.; and the two young Bernouillis being invited to Petersburgh in 1725, promised Euler, who was desirous of following them, that they would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> their utmost endeavours to procure for him an advantageous settlement in that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, by their advice, he applied himself with ardour to the study of physiology, to which he made a happy application of his mathematical knowledge; and he attended the medical lectures of the most eminent professors of Basil. This study, however, did not wholly engross his time: it did not even relax the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> of his vast and comprehensive mind in the cultivation of other branches of natural science. For while he was keenly engaged in physiological researches, he composed A Dissertation on the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> and Propagation of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">Sound</a>, and an answer to a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>-question concerning the masting of ships; to which the academy of sciences adjudged the accessit, or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, in the year 1727. From this latter discourse, and other circumstances, it appears that Euler had early embarked in the curious and important study of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, which he afterwards enriched with so many valuable discoveries. M. Euler's merit would have given him an easy admission to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> preferment, either in the magistracy or university of his native city, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> both civil and academical honours had not been there distributed by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a>. The lot being against him in a certain promotion, he left his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, set out for Petersburgh, and was made <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> professor with his countrymen Messrs Hermann and Daniel Bernouilli in the university of that city. At his first setting out in his new <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CAREER">career</a>, he enriched the academical collection with many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a>, which excited a noble emulation between him and the Bernouillis; and this emulation always continued, without either degenerating into a selfish jealousy, or producing the least <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> in their friendship. It was at this time that he carried to new degrees of perfection the integral <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CALCULUS">calculus</a>, invented the calculation of sinuses, reduced analytical operations to a greater simplicity, and was thus enabled to throw new <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> on all the parts of mathematical science. In 1730, he was promoted to the professorship of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY">natural philosophy</a>; and in 1733 he succeeded his friend D. Bernouilli in the mathematical <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>. In 1735, a problem was proposed by the academy which required expedition, and for the solution of which several eminent mathematicians had demanded the space of some months. The problem was solved by Euler in three days, to the great astonishment of the academy: but the violent and laborious efforts it cost him threw him into a fever, which endangered his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and deprived him of the use of his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> eye. The academy of sciences at Paris, which in 1738 had adjudged the prize to his memoir concerning the Nature and Properties of Fire, proposed for the year 1740 the important subject of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-TIDES">tides</a>; a problem whose solution required the most arduous calculations, and comprehended the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of the solar system. Euler's discourse on this question was adjudged a masterpiece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> and geometry; and it was more honourable for him to share the academical prize with such illustrious competitors as Colin Maclaurin and Daniel Bernouilli, than to have carried it away from rivals of less magnitude. Rarely, if ever, did such a brilliant competition adorn the annals of the academy; and no subject, perhaps, proposed by that learned body was ever treated with such accuracy of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> and force of genius, as that which here displayed the philosophical powers of these three extraordinary men. In the year 1741, M. Euler was invited to Berlin to augment the lustre of the academy, that was there rising rising into fame. He enriched the last volume of the miscellanies (melanges), of Berlin with five memoirs, which make an eminent, perhaps the principal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in that collection. These were followed with an astonishing rapidity by a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of important researches, which are scattered through the memoirs of the Prussian academy; of which a volume has been regularly published every year since its establishment in 1744. The labours of Euler will appear more especially astonishing, when it is considered, that while he was enriching the academy of Berlin with a prodigious number of memoirs, on the deepest parts of mathematical science, containing always some new <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of view, often sublime truths, and sometimes discoveries of great importance; he did not discontinue his philosophical contributions to the academy of Petersburgh, which granted him a pension in 1742, and whose memoirs display the marvellous fecundity of Euler's genius. It was with much difficulty that this great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> obtained, in 1766, permission from the king of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> to return to Petersburgh, where he desired to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the rest of his days. Soon after his return, which was graciously rewarded by the munificence of Catherine II, he was seized with a violent disorder, which terminated in the total loss of his sight. A cataract, formed in his left eye, which had been essentially damaged by a too ardent application to study, deprived him entirely of the use of that organ. It was in this distressing situation that he dictated to his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>, a taylor's apprentice, who was absolutely devoid of mathematical knowledge, his elements of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALGEBRA">algebra</a>; which by their intrinsical merit, in point of perspicuity and method, and the unhappy circumstances in which they were composed, have equally excited applause and astonishment. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, though purely elementary, discovers the palpable characteristics of an inventive genius; and it is here alone that we meet with a complete theory of the analysis of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIOPHANTUS">Diophantus</a>. About this time M. Euler was honoured by the Academy of Sciences at Paris with the place of one of the foreign members of that learned body; and, after this, the academical prize was adjudged to three of his memoirs, Concerning the Inequalities in the Motions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">Planets</a>. The two prize questions proposed by the same academy for 1770 and 1772 were designed to obtain from the labours of astronomers a more perfect theory of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>. M. Euler, assisted by his eldest son, was a competitor for these prizes, and obtained them both. In this last memoir, he reserved for further consideration several inequalities of the moon's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, which he could not determine in his first theory, on account of the complicated calculations in which the method he then employed had engaged him. He had the courage afterward to review his whole theory, with the assistance of his son and Messrs Kraft and Lexell, and to pursue his researches until he had constructed the new tables, which appeared, together with the great work, in 1772. Instead of confining himself as before, to the fruitless integration of three <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENTIAL">differential</a> equations of the second degree, which are furnished by mathematical principles, he reduced them to the three ordinates, which determine the place of the moon; he divided into classes all the inequalities of that planet, as far as they depend either on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELONGATION">elongation</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and moon, or upon the eccentricity, or the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARALLAX">parallax</a>, or the inclination of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> orbit. All these means of investigation, employed with such art and dexterity as could only be expected from analytical genius of the first order, were attended with the greatest success; and it is impossible to observe, without admiration, such immense calculations on the one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and on the other the ingenious methods employed by this great man to abridge them, and to facilitate their application to the real motion of the moon. But this admiration will become astonishment, when we consider at what <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> and in what circumstances all this was effectuated by M. Euler. It was when he was totally <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a>, and consequently obliged to arrange all his computations by the sole powers of his memory and his genius. It was when he was embarrassed in his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> circumstances by a dreadful fire, that had consumed great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his substance, and forced him to quit a ruined <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, of which every corner was known to him by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, which, in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, supplied the place of sight. It was in these circumstances that Euler composed a work, which, alone, was sufficient to render his name immortal. The heroic <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> and tranquillity of mind which he displayed here, need no <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>: and he derived them not only from the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of science, but from the power of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. His philosophy was too genuine and sublime to stop its analysis at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> causes; it led him to that divine philosophy of religion which ennobles <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> nature, and can alone form a habit of true <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGNANIMITY">magnanimity</a> and patience in suffering. Some time after this, the famous Wenzell, by couching the cataract, restored M.
