Euler's sight; but the satisfaction and joy that this successful operation produced, were of short <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. Some instances of negligence on the part of his surgeons, and his own impatience to use an organ, whose cure was not completely finished, deprived him of his sight a second time; and this relapse was accompanied with tormenting pain. He, however, with the assistance of his sons, and of Messrs Kraft and Lexell, continued his labours; neither the loss of his sight, nor the infirmities of an advanced <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> could damp the ardour of his genius. He had engaged to furnish the academy of Petersburgh with as many memoirs as would be sufficient to complete its acts for 20 years after his death. In the space of seven years he transmitted to the academy by Mr Golswin, above 70 memoirs, and above 200 more, which were revised and completed by the author of this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>. Such of the memoirs as were of ancient <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> were separated from the rest, and form a collection that was published in the year 1783, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Analytical Works. Euler's knowledge was more universal than could be well expected in one who had pursued with such unremitting ardour mathematics and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> as his favourite studies. He had made a very considerable progress in medical, botanical, and chemical science. What was still more extraordinary, he was an excellent scholar, and possessed what is generally called erudition in a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> degree. He had read, with attention and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, the most eminent writers of ancient Rome; the civil and literary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of all ages and nations were familiar to him; and foreigners, who were only acquainted with his works, were astonished to find. find in the conversation of a man, whose <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> life seemed solely occupied in mathematical and physical researches and discoveries, such an extensive acquaintance with the most interesting branches of literature. In this respect, no doubt, he was much indebted to a very uncommon memory, which seemed to retain every idea that was conveyed to it, either from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> or from meditation. He could repeat the Æneid of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, from the beginning to the end, without hesitation, and indicate the first and last line of every page of the edition he used. Several attacks of a vertigo, in the beginning of September 1783, which did not prevent his calculating the motions of the aerostatical globes, were, nevertheless, the forerunners of his mild and happy passage from this <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> to a better. While he was amusing himself at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a> with one of his grandchildren, he was struck with an apoplexy, which terminated his illustrious career at the age of 76. His <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> was uncommonly strong and vigorous; his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> was good; and the evening of his long life was calm and serene, sweetened by the fame that follows genius, the public esteem and respect that are never withheld from exemplary virtue, and several domestic comforts which he was capable of feeling and therefore deserved to enjoy.

EVOCATI

Pages 378-379
soldiers among the Romans, who having served their full time in the army, went afterwards volunteers at the request of some favourite general; on which account they were called by the honourable names of Emeriti and Beneficiarii.

EVOLUTION

Pages 379-379

in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> made by a body of troops, when they are obliged to change their form and disposition, in order to preserve a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> occupy another, to attack an enemy with more advantage, or to be in a condition of defending themselves the better. It consists in doublings, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTER">counter</a>-marches, conversions, &c. A battalion doubles the ranks, when attacked in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> or rear, to prevent its being flanked or surrounded; for then a battalion fights with a larger front. The files are doubled, either to accommodate themselves to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of a narrow ground, or to resist an enemy that attacks them in flank. But <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the ground <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> allow it, conversion is much preferable; because, after conversion, the battalion is in its first form, and opposes the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FILE">file</a>-leaders, which are generally the best men, to the enemy; and likewise, because doubling the files in a new or not well-disciplined regiment, they may happen to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into disorder. See Doubling. [Merged from <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECTION">SECTION</a> OF THE SANS-CULOTTES, p.107] Copy of the extract of the deliberations of the General <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">Assembly</a> of the sitting of the fifth of the first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECADE">decade</a> of the 3rd <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of the 2nd year of the French Republic one and indivisible. It appears, that after the report made to the fraternal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of the section of the sans-culottes concerning the good civism and acts of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> which the Shepherd Daubenton has always testified, the General Assembly unanimously decrees to give him a certificate of civism, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> followed by several members of the said assembly give him the fraternal hug, with all the acclamations due to a true <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of humanity, which has been testified by several renewals of the hug. (Signed) R. G. Darde, President. Besides his publications, Daubenton was of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to science as a lecturer. From 1775 he gave lectures on <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of medicine. In 1783 he lectured on rural economy. He was appointed professor of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERALOGY">mineralogy</a> by the convention at the garden of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, and he gave lectures during the ephemeral existence of the Normal school. He was likewise one of the editors of the Journal des Scavans, and contributed to both the Encyclopedias. As a lecturer he was extremely popular, and what is uncommon, he retained his popularity to the last. Notwithstanding the feebleness of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, he arrived at a very advanced <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> without much <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> or loss of his faculties. This may be, in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, ascribed to the gentleness of his temper, and his remarkable resignation. He was temperate and moderate even in his studies. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">Part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was spent in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> romances with his wife. In the year 1799 he was appointed one of the members of the conservative <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, and he resolved to attend the meeting of it. This obliged him to alter his regimen. The season was severe. At the first meeting that he attended he fell from his seat in an apoplectic fit. The most speedy assistance was procured, and by its means he was restored to his senses. With the utmost calmness he pointed out with his fingers the progress of the paralysis in different parts of his body, and died, on the first of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1800, without a struggle.

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 29th order, Campanaceae. EVREMONT

Pages 380-380
CHARLES DE ST DENIS, a polite scholar and soldier, was born at St Denis le Guast in Lower Normandy in 1613. He was intended for the profession of the law, and entered on the study; but he soon quitted it, and was made an ensign before he was 16. A military life did not hinder him from cultivating polite literature; and he signalized himself by his politeness and wit as much as by his bravery. The king made him a mairechal de camp, and gave him a pension of 3000 livres per annum. He served under the duke of Candale in the war of Guience; and in Flanders, till the suspension of arms was agreed on between France and Spain: he afterwards accompanied Cardinal Mazarine when he went to conclude the peace with Don Lewis de Haro, the king of Spain's first minister. He wrote, as he had promised, a long letter to the marquis de Crequi, of this negotiation; in which he showed, that the cardinal had sacrificed the honour of France to his own private interest, and rallied him in a very satirical manner. This letter falling into the hands of the cardinal's creatures some time after his death, was represented as a state crime, and he was obliged to fly to Holland. He had too many friends in England (whither he had taken a tour the year before with the count de Soissons, sent to compliment Charles II. upon his restoration) to make any long stay in Holland; and therefore passed over into England, where he was received with great respect, and Euripides admitted into intimate friendship with several persons of distinction. The king gave him a pension of 3000 a-year. He had a great desire to return to his native country; and, after the peace of Nimeguen, wrote a letter in verse to the king of France to ask leave, but in vain. Upon the death of King Charles, he lost his pension. He did not rely much on King James, though that prince had shown himself extremely kind to him. The Revolution was advantageous to him. King William, who had known him in Holland, gave him substantial marks of his favour. He died of a strangury in 1703, aged 92; and was interred in Westminster abbey, where a monument is erected to his memory. His behaviour was engaging, his humour cheerful, and he had a strong disposition to satire: he professed the Roman religion, in which he was born; but at the bottom was certainly a freethinker. He always spoke of his disgrace with the resolution of a gentleman: and whatever strong desire he had to return to his country, he never solicited the favour with meanness; therefore, when this leave was signified to him unexpectedly in the decline of his life, he replied, that the infirmities of age did not permit him to leave a country where he lived agreeably. There have been many editions of his works: but the best is that of Amsterdam in 1726, in 5 vols. 12mo, to which is prefixed his life by Doctor Des Maizeaux; who has also given an accurate English translation of them in 3 vols. 8vo.

EWERY

Pages 389-389

in the British custome, an office in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>, to which belongs the care of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, of laying the cloth, and serving up <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> in silver ewers after dinner.

EX

Pages 389-389

a river that rises in a barren tract of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, called Exmore, in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a>; and after being joined by several little streams, runs by Tiverton, where there is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over the river. About <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> miles below Tiverton, it is joined by a pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> stream called the Colombon; and about two miles lower, by another stream formed by the junction of the Horton and Credy. With these additions, it washes the walls of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>. At <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOPSHAM">Topsham</a>, above four miles below Exeter, it receives another considerable addition to its stream; two miles farther, it is joined by the Ken; and falls into the ocean at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXMOUTH">Exmouth</a>, after a course of about 40 miles. Ships of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> burden go up to Topsham, from whence vessels of 150 tons are conveyed to the quay at Exeter, by means of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> canal. The Ex is navigable for vessels of considerable burden to Topsham. The passage, however, at the mouth of the river, is but narrow, having rocks on the east side and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> sands on the west; nor is the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> more than six <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet deep at low water, but the tide rises 14 or 15 feet, so that it is deep enough at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> water. When ships are within the bar they may ride afloat at a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> called Starcross, about a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and a half from the river's mouth; but those that go to Topsham <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGROUND">aground</a> on the ooze at low water.

EX OFFICIO

Pages 389-389

among lawyers, signifies the power a person has, by virtue of his office, to do certain acts without being applied to. Thus a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of peace may, ex officio, at his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>, take surety of the peace, without complaint made by any person whatsoever. There was formerly an oath ex officio, whereby a supposed offender was compelled in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> to confess, accuse, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> clear himself of a crime; but this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> is repealed. Ex <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">Post</a> Facto, in Law, something done after another; thus an estate granted may be good by <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> ex post facto, that was not so at first, as in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>. EXACERBATION. See Paroxysm.

EX-POST-FACTO

Pages 425-425

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, denotes something done after another thing that was committed before. An estate granted may be made good by <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> ex-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a>-facto, that was not so at first by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>, &c.

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a wrong done by an officer, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a person in pretended authority, in taking a reward or fee that is not allowed by all. A person guilty of exaction may be fined and imprisoned. It is often confounded with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTORTION">Extortion</a>.

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the te-trandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 20th order, Rotaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. EXAGGERATION

Pages 389-389

in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">Painting</a>, a method by which the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>, in representing things, changes them too much, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> makes them too strong, either in respect of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> or colouring. It differs from caricaturing, in that the latter perverts or gives a turn to the features of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>, &c. which they had not, whereas exaggeration only heightens or improves what they had.

EXALTATION

Pages 389-390
or ELEVATION, is chiefly used in a figurative sense, for the raising or advancing a person to some ecclesiastical dignity; and particularly to the papacy. EXALTATION of the Cross is a feast of the Romish church, held on the 14th of September; in memory, as is generally supposed, of this, that the emperor Heraclius brought back the true cross of Jesus Christ on his shoulders, to the place on Mount Calvary from which it had been carried away 14 years before by Cosroes king of Persia, at his taking of Jerusalem, under the reign of the emperor Phocas. The cross was delivered up by a treaty of peace made with Siroe, Cosroes's son. The institution of this treaty is commonly said to have been signalized by a miracle; in that Heraclius could not stir out of Jerusalem with the cross while he had the imperial vestments on enriched with gold and precious stones, but bore it with ease in a common dress. But long before the reign of Heraclius there had been a feast of the same denomination observed both in the Greek and Latin churches, on occasion of what our Saviour said in St John xiii. 32. And I, if I be exalted, or lifted up, will draw all men unto me. And again, in chap. viii. ver. 28. When you have exalted, or lifted up the Son of Man, then shall ye know that I am he. The feast of the dedication of the temple built by Constantine was held, says Nicodemus, on the 14th of September. Exaltation, September, the day on which the temple had been consecrated in the year 235; and this feast was also called the exaltation of the cross, because it was a ceremony therein, for the bishop of Jerusalem to ascend a high place, built by Constantine for that purpose, in manner of a pulpit, called by the Greeks the sacred mysteries of God, or the holiness of God, and there hoist up the cross for all the people to see it. Exaltation, in Physics, denotes the act, or operation, of elevating, purifying, sublating, or perfecting any natural body, its principles and parts; also the quality or disposition which bodies acquire by such operation. The term exaltation has been peculiarly affected by the chemists and alchemists; who imagining it to have some extraordinary emphasis, are employing it on every occasion. Exaltation, in Astrology, is a dignity which a planet acquires in certain signs or parts of the zodiac; which dignity is supposed to give it an extraordinary virtue, efficacy, and influence. The opposite sign, or part of the zodiac, is called the dejection of the planet. Thus the 13th degree of Cancer is the exaltation of Jupiter, according to Allumazor, because it was the ascendant of that planet at the time of the creation; that of the sun is in the 19th degree of Aries, and its dejection in Libra; that of the moon is in Taurus, &c. Ptolemy gives the reason of this in his first book De Quadrup. Examination, an exact and careful search or inquiry, in order to discover the truth or falsehood of a thing. Self-Examination, is a point much insisted on by divines, and particularly the ancient fathers, by way of preparation to repentance. St Ignatius reduces it to five points; viz. 1. A returning thanks to God for his benefits. 2. A begging of grace and light, to know and distinguish our sins. 3. A running over all our notions, occupations, thoughts, and words, in order to learn what has been offensive to God. 4. A begging of pardon, and conceiving a sincere sorrow for having displeased him. And, 5. Making a firm resolution not to offend him any more; and taking the necessary precautions to preserve ourselves from it. Examiners, in chancery, two officers of that court, who examine, upon oath, witnesses produced in causes depending there, by either the complainant or defendant, where the witnesses live in London or near it. Sometimes parties themselves, by particular order, are examined. In the country, above 20 miles from London, on the parties joining in commission, witnesses are examined by commissioners, being usually counsellors or attorneys not concerned in the cause. Example, in a general sense, denotes a copy or pattern. Example, in a moral sense, is either taken for a type, instance, or precedent, for our admonition, that we may be cautioned against the faults or crimes which others have committed, by the bad consequences which have ensued from them; or example is taken for a pattern for our imitation, or a model for us to copy after. That examples have a peculiar power above the naked precept, to dispose us to the practice of virtue and holiness, may appear by considering, 1. That they most clearly express to us the nature of our duties in their subjects and sensible effects. General precepts form abstract ideas of virtue; but in examples, virtues are most visible in all their circumstances. 2. Precepts instruct us in what things are our duty; but examples assure us that they are possible. When we see men like ourselves, who are united to frail flesh, and in the same condition with us, to command their passions, to overcome the most glorious and glittering temptations, we are encouraged in our spiritual warfare. 3. Examples, by secret and lively incentive, urge us to imitation. We are touched in another manner by the visible practice of good men, which reproaches our defects, and obliges us to the same zeal which laws, though wise and good, will not effect. The example of our Saviour is most proper to form us to holiness; it being absolutely perfect, and accommodated to our present state. There is no example of a mere man that is to be followed without limitation: But the example of Christ is absolutely perfect; his conversation was a living law: "He was holy, harmless, undefiled, and separate from sinners." Example, in Rhetoric, denotes an imperfect kind of induction or argumentation; whereby it is proved, that a thing which happened on some other occasion will happen again on the present one, from the similitude of the cases. As, "The war of the Thebans, against their neighbours the Phocians, was ruinous; consequently, that of the Athenians against their neighbours, will likewise be fatal." Exanthema, among Physicians, denotes any kind of efflorescence or eruption, as the measles, purple spots in the plague, or malignant fevers, &c. Exarch, in antiquity, an appellation given, by the emperors of the east, to certain officers sent into Italy, in quality of vicars, or rather prefects, to defend that part of Italy which was yet under their obedience, particularly the city of Ravenna, against the Lombards, who had made themselves masters of the greatest part of the rest. The residence of the exarch was at Ravenna; which city, with that of Rome, was all that was left the emperors. The first exarch was the patrician Boetius, famous for his treatise, De Consolatione Philosophiae; appointed in 368 by the younger Justin. The exarchs subsisted about 185 years, and ended in Eutychius: under whose exarchate the city of Ravenna was taken by the Lombard king Astulphus, or Astolphus. The emperor Frederic created Heraclius, archbishop of Lyons, a descendant of the illustrious house of Montboissier, exarch of the whole kingdom of Burgundy; a dignity till that time unknown anywhere but in Italy, particularly in the city of Ravenna. Homier, Philo, and other ancient authors, give likewise the name exarchus to the choragus or master of the singers in the ancient choruses, or him who sung first: the word ἐξαρχομαι or ἐξαρχεῖμαι, signifying equally to begin, and to commend. Exarch of a Diocese was, anciently, the same with primate. This dignity was inferior to the patriarchal, yet greater than the metropolitan.

EXARCH ALSO

Pages 390-391

h also denotes an officer, still subsisting in the Greek <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; being a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> legate à latere of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a>, whose office it is to visit the provinces allotted him, in order to inform himself of the lives and manners of the clergy; take cognizance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> causes; the manner of celebrating divine <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>; the administration of the sacraments, particularly confession; the observance of the canons; monastic <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>; affairs of marriages, divorces, &c., but above all, to take an account of the several revenues which the patriarch receives from several churches; and, particularly, as to what regards the collecting the same. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXARCH">exarch</a>, after having greatly enriched himself in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a>, frequently rises to the patriarchate itself. Exarch is also used, in the eastern church antiquity, for a general or superior over several monasteries; the same that we otherwise call archimandrite; being exempted, by the patriarch of Constantinople, from the jurisdiction of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>; as are now the generals of the Roman monastic orders.

EXAUCTORATIO

Pages 391-391

in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, differed from the missio, which was a full discharge, and took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> after they had served in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> 25 years; whereas the exauctoratio was only a partial discharge: they lost their pay indeed, but still kept under their colours <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> vexilla, though not under the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUILA">aquila</a> (or eagle), which was the standard of the legion; whence, instead of Legionarii, they were called Subsignarii, and were retained till they had either served their full <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> or had lands assigned them. The exauctoratio took place after they had served 17 years.

EXCALCEATION

Pages 391-391

among the Hebrews, was a particular <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, whereby a widow, whom her husband's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> refused to marry, had a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to summon him to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>; and, upon his refusal, might excalceate him, that is, pull off one of his shoes, and spit in his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>; both of them actions of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> ignominy.

EXCELLENCY

Pages 391-391

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> anciently given to kings and emperors, but now to ambassadors, generals, and other persons who are not qualified for that of highness, and yet are to be elevated above the other inferior dignities.

EXCENTRIC

Pages 391-391

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to circles and spheres which have not the same centre, and consequently are not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a>; in opposition to concentric, where they are parallel, having one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> centre.

EXCENTRICITY

Pages 391-391

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, is the distance of the centre of the orbit of a planet from the centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; that is, the distance between the centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELLIPSIS">ellipsis</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a> thereof.

EXCEPTION

Pages 391-391

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, denotes a stop <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> stay to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>; and is either dilatory or peremptory, in proceedings at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law; but in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a> it is what the plaintiff alleges against the sufficiency of an answer, &c. An exception is no more than the denial of what is taken to be good by the other party, either in point of law or pleading. The counsel in a cause are to take all their exceptions to the record at one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and before the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> has delivered any <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of it.

EXCESS

Pages 391-391

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">Arithmetic</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, is the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between any two unequal numbers <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> quantities, or that which is left after the lesser is taken from or out of the greater.

EXCHANGE

Pages 401-405

e signifies also a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in most consider- able trading cities, wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, negotiants, agents, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANKERS">bankers</a>, brokers, interpreters, and other persons concerned in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, meet on certain days, and at certain times thereof, to confer and treat together of matters relating to exchanges, remittances, payments, adventures, assurances, freightments, and other merchan- tile negotiations, both by <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and several cities of France, these places are called bourses; at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> and Lyons, places de change; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANSE">Hanse</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, colleges of merchants. These assemblies are held with so much exactness, and merchants and negotiants are so indis- pensably required to attend at them, that a person's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a>- sence alone makes him to be suspected of a failure <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bankruptcy. The most considerable exchanges in Eu- rope, are that of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>; and that of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, called the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Exchange. Even in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, there were places for the merchants to meet, in most of the consi- derable cities of the empire. That said by some to have been built at Rome in the year of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> 259, 493 years before our Saviour, under the consulate of Appius Claudius and Publius Servilius, was called col- legium mercatorum; whereof it is pretended there are still some remains, called by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Romans loggia, the lodge; and now usually the place of St George. This notion of a Roman exchange is supposed to be founded. Exchange founded on the authority of Livy, whose words are as follows: *Certamen consulibus incidet uter dedicaret Mercurii eodem. Senatus à se rem <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AD">ad</a> populum rejicit: utri corum dedicatio jussu populi <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATA">data</a> esset, cum praesae annona, mercatorum collegium instituere jussit.* Liv.lib. ii. But it must be here remarked, that *collegium* never signified a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> for a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> in the purer ages of the Latin tongue; so that *collegium mercatorum instituere* must not be rendered to build an exchange for the merchants, but to incorporate the merchants into a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. As <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a> was the god of traffic, this *aedes Mercurii* seems to have been chiefly designed for the devotions of this company or corporation. **Exchange, Bills of.** The following information concerning the origin of bills of exchange is extracted from Beckmann's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Inventions. "I shall not here repeat (says he) what has been collected by many learned men respecting the important history of this noble <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, but only lay before my readers an ordinance of the year 1394, concerning the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ACCEPTANCE">acceptance</a> of bills of exchange, and also two bills of the year 1404, as they may serve to illustrate farther what has been before said on the subject by others. These documents are, indeed, more modern than those found by Raphael de Turre in the writings of the jurist Baldus, which are dated <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> the 9th 1328; but they are attended with such circumstances as sufficiently prove that the method of transacting business by bills of exchange was fully established so early as the fourteenth century; and that the present form and terms were even then used. For this important information I am indebted to Mr Von Martens, who found it in a book which, as far as I know, has never been noticed in any literary journal, though it is much more deserving of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> than many others better known. It is a history, written in Spanish, of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> trade and other branches of commerce at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARCELONA">Barcelona</a>, taken entirely from the archives of that city, and accompanied with documents from the same source, which abound with <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> highly interesting." Among these is an ordinance issued by the city of Barcelona in the year 1394, that bills of exchange should be accepted within twenty-four hours after they were presented; and that the acceptance should be written on the back of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a>. "In the year 1404, the magistrates of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUGES">Bruges</a>, in Flanders, requested the magistrates of Barcelona to inform them what was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> practice, in regard to bills of exchange, when the person who presented a bill raised <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> on it in an unusual manner, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of its not being paid, and by these means increased the expenses so much that the drawer would not consent to sustain the loss. The bill which gave occasion to this question is inserted in the memorial. It is written in the short form still used; which certainly seems to imply <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity. It speaks of usance; and it appears that first and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> bills were at that time drawn, and that when bills were not accepted, it was customary to protest them." "As this article is of great importance I shall here transcribe it, from vol. ii. p. 293: 'Cum de mensibus Aprilis et Maii ultimo elapsis Antonius Quarti, merca- tor Lucanus residentis in villa Brugensi, a Joanne Colom, mercatore civitatis Barchinonae, etiam residente in pre- dieta villa Brugensi, duo millia scutorum Philippi, quo- libet scuto pro xxii grossis computato, solvendi per Fran- cicum de Prato mercatorem Florentiae, more solito, in Barchinona, mediatiim Petro Gilberto et Petro Olivo, et mediatiim Petro Scorp, et supradicto Petro Gilberto, mercatoribus Cardone: prout de dictis cambiis appa- ret quatuor litteras papireis, quarum tenores sub- sequuntur.' 'Superscriptio autem primae litterae fuit talis: Franc- do Prato et comp. à Barcelona. Tenor vero ejusdem ad intra fuit talis: Al nome di Dio, Amen, à di xxviii. Aprile 1404. Pagate per questa prima di camb. à usanza à Pietro Gilberto, è Pietro Olivo scuti mille à sold. x. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">Bar</a>- celonesi per scuto, i quali scuti mille sono per cambio che con Giovanni Colomba à grossi xxii. di g. scuto: et pag. à nostro conto, et Christo ci guardi. Subtus vero erat scriptum: Antonio Quarti Sal de Bruggias.' 'Superscriptio vero secundae litterae fuit talis: Fran- cisco de Prato et comp. à Barcelona. Et ab intra sic habebatur: Al nome de Dio, Amen, à di xviii. di Magio 1404. Pagate per questa prima di comp. à usanza à Pietro Gilberto et à P. de Scorpo scuti mille de Feipigo à sold. x. Barcelonesi per scuto: i quali scuti mille sono per camb. che con Gio. Colomba à grossi xxii. di g. scuto: et pag. à nostro conto: et Christo vi guardi. Subtus vero erat sic scriptum: <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANT">Ant</a>. Quadri Sul de Bruggias.'" Bills of exchange are justly considered as of the greatest importance to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of commerce; but several queries have been proposed respecting them, which do not as yet appear to have received a satisfactory solution. It still seems to be a disputed point, whether the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> ought to consider them as nothing more than a deposit belonging to the drawer, and successively confided to the remitters; or as <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> capable of being transferred, and entirely vested in the holder at all times, who should be alone responsible for neglecting it, when its value is vitiated. Professor Busch of Hamburgh thought that bills of exchange should always be viewed as the exclusive property of the person holding them, which, in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> published --- (a) "Memorias historicas sobre la marina comercio y artes de la antigua ciudad de Barcelona, por D. Antonio de Capmany y de Montpalau. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a> 1799, 2 vol. 4to. As a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of what I have said above, I shall mention the following important article, which may be found in this work. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM_HOUSE"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> tariff, written in Latin, of the year 1221, in which occur a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of remarkable names and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of merchandise not explained. Another of the like kind in the year 1252. Letters of power to appoint consuls in distant countries, such as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, &c. dated in the years 1266, 1268, and 1321. An ordinance of the year 1458, respecting insurances, which required that underwriting should be done in the presence of a notary, and declared policies & scriptures privadas to be null and void. A privilegium of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Andronicus II. to the merchants of Barcelona, written in Greek and Spanish, in 1290. Account of the old Spanish trade with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, and saffron; and of the oldest guilds or incorporated <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> of tradesmen at Barcelona," &c. Officers of the receipt may take one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENNY">penny</a> in the Exchequer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a>, as their fee, for sums issued out; and they are obliged, without delay, to receive the money brought thither; and the money received is to be put into chests under three different locks and keys, kept by three several officers. All sheriffs, bailiffs, &c., are to account in the exchequer; and in the lower <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, termed the receipt, the debtors of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, and persons in debt to them, the king's tenants, and the officers and ministers of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, are privileged to sue one another, or any stranger, and to be sued in the like actions as are brought in the court of king's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">bench</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMMON_PLEAS">common pleas</a>. The judicial part of the exchequer, is a court both of law and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a>. The court of law is held in the office of pleas, according to the course of common law, before the barons: in this court, the plaintiff ought to be a debtor or accountant to the king; and the leading <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is either a writ of subpoena, or quo minus, which last goes into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, where no process out of courts of law ought to run, except a capias utiagatum. The court of equity is held in the exchequer chamber, before the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, and barons; but generally, before the barons only: the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> baron being the chief judge to hear and determine all causes. The proceedings of this part of the exchequer are by English bill and answer, according to the practice of the court of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>; with this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, that the plaintiff here must set forth, that he is a debtor to the king, whether he be so or not. It is in this court of equity that the clergy exhibit bills for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITHES">tithes</a>, &c. Here too the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTORNEY_GENERAL">attorney-general</a> exhibits bills for any matters concerning the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; and a bill may be exhibited against the king's attorney by any person aggrieved in any cause prosecuted against him on behalf of the king, to be relieved therein; in which case the plaintiff is to attend on the attorney-general, with a copy of the bill, and procure him to give an answer thereto; in the making of which he may call in any person interested in the cause, or any officer, or others, to instruct him, that the king be not prejudiced thereby; and his answer is to be put in without oath. But, besides the business relating to debtors, farmers, receivers, accountants, &c., all penal punishments, intrusion, and forfeitures upon popular actions, are matters --- (a) In Vol. III. p. 613, under the article BILL, the old duty on stamps is mentioned, and the new entirely omitted. The following are the duties on such stamps for the year 1820. The duty on promissory notes for the payment of money to the bearer on demand, for a sum not exceeding £1. 1s. is 5d. For a sum exceeding £1. 1s. and not £2. 2s.; 10d. For a sum exceeding £2. 2s. and not £5. 5s.; 1s. 3d. For a sum exceeding £5. 5s. and not £10.; 1s. 9d. Which notes may be reissued after payment as often as shall be thought fit. Bill of exchange, draft, or promissory or other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, payable to the bearer on demand or otherwise, not exceeding 2 months after <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a>, or 60 days after sight, for 40s. and not exceeding £1. 5s.; 1s. Bill of exchange, draft, order, or promissory note for the payment of money, where the sum shall exceed £5. 5s. and not £10.; 1s. 6d. Exceeding £10. and not £30.; 2s. Above £30. and not £50.; 2s. 6d. Above £50. and not £100.; 3s. 6d. Above £100. and not £200.; 4s. 6d. Above £200. and not £300.; 5s. Above £300. and not £500.; 6s. Above £500. and not £1000.; 8s. 6d. Foreign bills of exchange drawn in sets, where the sum shall not exceed £100.; for each bill in each set, 1s. 6d. Exceeding £100. and not £200.; 3s. Exceeding £200. and not £500.; 4s. Exceeding £500. and not £1000.; 5s. Exchequer, ters likewise cognizable by this court; where there also sits a puisne-baron, who administers the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> sheriffs, bailiffs, auditors, receivers, collectors, comptrollers, surveyors, and searchers of all the customs, &c. The exchequer in Scotland has the same privileges and jurisdiction as that of England; and all matters competent to the one are likewise competent to the other. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Book of the Exchequer, is a book under the keeping of the two chamberlains of the exchequer; said to have been composed in 1175 by Gervais of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TILBURY">Tilbury</a>, nephew of King Henry II., and divided into several chapters. Herein is contained a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the court of England, as it then stood, its officers, their ranks, privileges, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a>, perquisites, power, and jurisdiction; and the revenues of the crown, both in money, grain, and cattle. Here we find, that for one <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a>, as much <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> might be bought as would serve 100 men a whole <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; that the price of a fat bullock was only 12 shillings, and a sheep four, &c. Chancellor of the Exchequer. See Chancellor. Exchequer Bills. By statute 5 Ann. c. 13, the lord treasurers may cause exchequer bills to be made of any sums not exceeding £500,000 for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; and the duties upon houses were made chargeable with 4l. 10s. per cent. per annum to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> for circulating them. The bank not paying the bills, actions to be brought against the Company, and the money and damages recovered; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any exchequer bills be lost, upon affidavit of it before a baron of the exchequer, and certificate from such baron, and security to pay the same if found, duplicates are to be made out: also when bills are defaced, new ones shall be delivered. The king, or his officers in the exchequer, by former statutes, might borrow money upon the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of bills, payable on demand, with interest after the rate of 3d per diem for every 100l. bill. And by 8 and 9 W. III. c. 20, an interest of 5d. a day was allowed for every 100l. But 12 W. III. c. 1, lowered the interest on these bills to 4d. a-day per cent. And by 12 Ann. c. 11, it is sunk to 2d. a-day. Forging exchequer bills, or the endorsements thereof, is felony. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCISE">Excise</a>, (from the Belgic accisiæ, tributum, "tribute,") an inland duty or imposition, paid sometimes upon the consumption of the commodity, or frequently upon the wholesale, which is the last stage before the consumption. This is doubtless, impartially speaking, the most economical way of taxing the subject; the charges of levying, collecting, and managing the excise duties, being considerably less in proportion than in other branches of the revenue. It also renders the commodity cheaper to the consumer, than charging it with customs to the same amount would do; for the reason <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> now given, because generally paid in a much later stage of it. But, at the same time, the rigour and arbitrary proceedings of excise laws seem hardly compatible with the temper of a free <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. For the frauds that might be committed in this branch of the revenue, unless a strict watch is kept, make it necessary, wherever it is established, to give the officers a power of entering and searching the houses of such as <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> in exciseable commodities, at any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of the day, and, in many <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, of the night, likewise. And the proceedings, in case of transgressions, are so summary and sudden, that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> may be convicted in two days' time in the penalty of many thousand pounds, by two commissioners or justices of the peace; to the total <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURY">jury</a>, and disregard of the common law. For which reason, though Lord Clarendon tells us, that to his knowledge the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEDFORD">Bedford</a> (who was made lord treasurer by King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. to oblige his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>) intended to have set up the excise in England, yet it never made a part of that unfortunate <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>'s revenue; being first introduced, on the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of the Dutch prototype, by the parliament itself after its rupture with the crown. Yet such was the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of its general unpopularity, that when in 1642 "aspersions were <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> by malignant persons upon the house of commons, that they intended to introduce excises, the house for its vindication therein did declare, that these rumours were false and scandalous, and that their authors should be apprehended and brought to condign <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>." Its original establishment was in 1643, and its progress was gradual; being at first laid upon those persons and commodities where it was supposed the hardship would be least perceivable, viz. the makers and venders of beer, ale, cider, and perry; and the royalists at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> soon followed the example of their brethren at Westminster, by imposing a similar duty: both sides protesting that it should be <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> no longer than to the end of the war, and then be utterly abolished. But the parliament at Westminster soon after imposed it on <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, wine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, and such a multitude of other commodities, that it might be fairly denominated general: in pursuance of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> laid <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by Mr Pymme (who seems to have been the father of the excise), in his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to Sir John Hotham, signifying, "that they had proceeded in the excise to many particulars, and intended to go on farther; but that it would be necessary to use the people to it by little and little." And afterwards, when the nation had been accustomed to it for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of years, the succeeding champions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> boldly and openly declared "the impost of excise to be the most easy and indifferent levy that could be laid upon the people;" and accordingly continued it during the whole usurpation. Upon King Charles's return, it having then been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> established, and its produce well known, some part of it was given to the crown, in 12 Car. II. by way of purchase for the feudal tenures and other oppressive parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> revenue. But, from its first original to the present time, its very name has been odious to the people. It has, nevertheless, been imposed on abundance of other commodities in the reigns of King William III. and every succeeding prince, to support the enormous expenses occasioned by our wars on the continent. Thus brandies and other spirits are now excised at the distillery; printed silks and linens, at the printer's; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STARCH">starch</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> powder, at the maker's; <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver wire, at the wiredrawer's; all plate whatsoever, first in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the vender, who pays yearly for a license to sell it, and afterwards in the hands of the occupier, who also pays an annual duty for having it in his custody; and coaches and other wheel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>, for which the occupier is excised; though not with the same circumstances of arbitrary strictness with regard to plate and coaches as in the other instances. To these we may add coffee and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a>, chocolate and cocoa paste, for which the ty is paid by the retailer; all <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> wines, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called sweets; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> and pasteboard, first when made, and again, if stained or printed; malt, as before mentioned; vinegars; and the manufacture of glass; for all which the duty is paid by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANUFACTURER">manufacturer</a>; hops, for which the person that gathers them is answerable; candles and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>, which are paid for at the makers; malt liquors brewed for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>, which are excised at the brewery; cider and perry at the vendor's; <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> and skins, at the tanner's; and, lately, tobacco, at the manufacturer's: A <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a>, which no friend to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> would wish to see farther increased. The excise was formerly farmed out: but is now managed for the king by commissioners in both kingdoms, who receive the whole product of the excise, and pay it into the exchequer. These commissioners are <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> in number in England, and five in Scotland. The former have a salary of £1000 a-year, the latter £600. They are obliged by oath to take no fee or reward but from the king himself; and from them there lies an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> to five other commissioners called commissioners of appeals.

EXCISION

Pages 405-405

in a scripture <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, means the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off of a person from his people, by way of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> for some sin by him committed. The Jews, Selden informs us, reckon 36 crimes, to which they pretend this punishment is due. The Rabbins reckon three kinds of excision; one, which destroys only the body; another, which destroys the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> only; and a third, which destroys both body and soul. The first kind of excision they pretend is an untimely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is an utter extinction of the soul; and the third, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> of the two former: thus, making the soul mortal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> immortal, says Selden, according to the degrees of misbehaviour and wickedness of the people. EXCLAMATION. See ORATORY, No 85.

EXCLUSION

Pages 405-405
or Bill of Exclusion, a bill proposed about the close of the reign of King Charles II. for excluding the duke of York, the king's brother, from the throne, on account of his being a Papist.

EXCLUSIVE

Pages 405-405

is sometimes used adjectively, thus: A patent carries with it an exclusive privilege. Sometimes adverbially: as, He sent him all the numbers from No 145 to No 247 exclusive; that is, all between these two numbers, which themselves were excepted.

EXCOECARIA

Pages 405-405

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dicotyledon class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 38th order, Tricoceraceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EXCOMMUNICATION

Pages 405-407

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> penalty <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> censure, whereby such persons as are guilty of any notorious crime or offence, are separated from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and deprived of all spiritual advantages. Excommunication is founded on a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> which all <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> have, of excluding out of their body such as violate the laws thereof; and it was originally instituted for preserving the purity of the church; but ambitious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a> converted it by degrees into an engine for promoting their own power, and inflicted it on the most frivolous occasions. The power of excommunication, as well as other acts of ecclesiastical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, was lodged in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the clergy, who distinguished it into the greater and lesser. The lesser excommunication, simply called aphorismos, "separation or suspension," consisted in excluding men from the participation of the eucharist, and the prayers of the faithful. But they were not expelled the church; for they had the privilege of being present at the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> of the Scriptures, the sermons, and the prayers of the catechumens and penitents. This excommunication was inflicted for lesser crimes; such as neglecting to attend the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the church, misbehaviour in it, and the like. The greater excommunication, called panteles aphorismos, "total separation and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANATHEMA">anathema</a>," consisted in an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> and entire <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> from the church and the participation of all its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a>. When any person was thus excommunicated, notice of it was given by circular letters to the most eminent churches over all the world, that they might all confirm this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of discipline, by refusing to admit the delinquent to their communion. The consequences of this latter excommunication were very terrible. The excommunicated person was avoided in civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> and outward conversation. No one was to receive him into his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, nor eat at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> with him; and when dead, he was denied the solemn rites of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a>. The Romish pontifical takes notice of three kinds of excommunication. 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">minor</a>, incurred by those who have any correspondence with an excommunicated person. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>, which falls upon those who disobey the commands of the holy see, or refuse to submit to certain <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of discipline; in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which they are excluded from the church militant and triumphant, and delivered over to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>. 3. Anathema, which is properly that pronounced by the pope against heretical princes and countries. In former ages, these papal fulminations were most terrible things; but at present, they are formidable to none but a few petty states of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. Excommunication, in the Greek church, cuts off the offender from all communion with the 318 fathers of the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Nice, and with the saints; consigns him over to the devil and the traitor Judas; and condemns his body to remain after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> as hard as a flint or piece of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, unless he humbles himself and makes atonement for his sins by a sincere <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a>. The form abounds with dreadful imprecations; and the Greeks assert, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a person dies excommunicated, the devil enter into the lifeless corpse; and therefore, in order to prevent it, the relations of the deceased cut his body in pieces, and boil them in wine. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> annually to excommunicate the pope and the church of Rome; on which occasion, together with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of idle <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, he drives a nail into the ground with a hammer, as a mark of malediction. The form of excommunication in the church of England anciently ran thus: "By the authority of God the Father Almighty, the Son and Holy Ghost, and of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> the blessed mother of God, we excommunicate, anathematize, and sequester from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> of the holy mother church," &c. The causes of excommunication in England are, contempt of the bishop's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>, neglect of public worship and the sacraments, incontinency, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADULTERY">adultery</a>, simony, &c. It is described to be twofold. The less is an ecclesiastical cen- Excommunicate, excluding the party from the participation of the sacraments; the greater proceeds farther, and excludes him not only from these, but from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>. But if the judge of any spiritual court excommunicates a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> for a cause of which he hath not the legal cognizance, the party may have an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> against him at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and he is also liable to be indicted at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>. Heavy as the penalty of excommunication is, considered in a serious <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, there are, notwithstanding, many obstinate or profligate men, who would despise the brutum fulmen of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> ecclesiastical censures, especially when pronounced by a petty surrogate in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, for railing or contumelious words, for non-payment of fees or costs, or other trivial cause. The common law, therefore, compassionately steps in to their aid, and kindly lends a supporting <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> to an otherwise tottering authority. Imitating herein the policy of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Britons, among whom, according to Caesar, whoever were interdicted by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRUIDS">druids</a> from their sacrifices, "In numero impiorum ac sceleratorum habentur: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> his omnes decedunt, aditum eorum sermone nemque defuigunt, ne quid ex contagione incommodi accipiant: neque eis petentibus jus redditur, neque honos ullos communicatur." And so with us, by the common law, an excommunicated person is disabled to do any act that is required to be done by one that is probus et legalis homo. He cannot serve upon juries; cannot be a witness in any court; and, which is the worst of all, cannot bring an action, either real or personal, to recover lands or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> due to him. Nor is this the whole: for if, within 40 days after the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> has been published in the church, the offender does not submit and abide by the sentence of the spiritual court, the bishop may certify such contempt to the king in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>. Upon which there issues out a writ to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, called from the bishop's certificate a significavit; or from its effect, a writ de excommunicato capitendo; and the sheriff shall thereupon take the offender and imprison him in the county jail, till he is reconciled to the church, and such reconciliation certified by the bishop; upon which another writ de excommunicato deliberando, issues out of chancery to deliver and release him. Excommunication was also practised among the Jews, who used to expel from their synagogue such as had committed any grievous crime. See the Gospel according to St John, ix. 22. xii. 42. xvi. 2. And <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>. Antiq. Jud. lib. ix. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 22. and lib. xvi. cap. 2. Godwyn, in his Moses and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AARON">Aaron</a>, distinguishes three degrees, or kinds, of excommunication among the Jews. The first he finds intimated in John ix. 22. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> in 1 Cor. v. 5. And the third in 1 Cor. xvi. 22. See Niddul. The rule of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENEDICTINES">Benedictines</a> gives the name of excommunication to the being excluded from the oratory, and the common table of the house; in our inns of court called discomuning. This was the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of such monks as came too late. Excommunication, or a being secluded from a participation in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, was also in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> under paganism. Such as were thus excommunicated were forbidden to assist or attend at the sacrifices, or enter within the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>; and were afterwards delivered over to the demons and furies of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a>, with certain imprecations; which was called among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> diris devovere. See Excruciation. The Druids among the ancient Britons and Gauls likewise, made use of excommunication against rebels; and interdicted the communion of their mysteries to such as refused to acquiesce in their decisions. See Druids. Excoriation, in Medicine and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, the galling or rubbing off the cuticle, especially of the parts between the thighs and about the anus. In adults, it is occasioned by riding, much walking, or other vehement <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, and may be cured by vulnerary applications. In children there is often an excoriation, not only of the parts near the pudenda, chiefly of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROIN">groin</a> and scrotum, but likewise in the wrinkles of the neck, under the arms, and in other places; proceeding from the acrimony of urine and sweat; and occasioning itching pains, crying, watching, restlessness, &c. To remedy this, the parts affected may be often washed with warm <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and sprinkled with drying powders, as chalk, hartshorn, but especially tutty, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPIS">lapis</a> calaminaris, and ceruss, which may be tied loosely in a rag, and the powder shook out on the parts. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCREMENT">Excrement</a>, whatever is discharged out of the body of animals after digestion; or the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the aliment, mixed with the bile, saliva, and other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>. Urine and the feces are the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> excrements that are discharged out of the bladder or belly. Other excrements are the various humours that are secreted from the blood through the different strainers in the body, and which serve for several uses; such as the saliva, sweat, bile, the pancreatic juice, lymph, the semen, nails, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, the horns and hoofs of animals. Alchemists, who have sought everywhere for their great <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, as they called it, have particularly operated much on the excrements of men and other animals; but philosophical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a> has acquired no knowledge from all these alchemical labours, from the obscurity with which their authors have described them. The philosophic chemists have not much examined animal excrements. Of these <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMBERG">Homberg</a> is the only one who has particularly analyzed and examined <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> ordure; and this was done to satisfy an alchemical project of one of his friends, who pretended that from this <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> could be obtained, without smell, and capable of fixing <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> into silver. The oil was found by Homberg, but mercury was not fixed by it. The labours of this able chemist were not, however, useless, like those of the alchemists; because he has clearly related the experiments he made on this matter, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> of the Academy of Sciences. These experiments are curious, and teach several essential things concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of excrements. The result of these experiments is as follows: Fresh human feces, being distilled to dryness in a water bath, furnish a clear, watery, insipid liquor, of a disagreeable smell, but which contains no volatile alkali; which is a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that this matter, although nearly in a putrefactive state, is not however putrefied; for all substances really putrid furnish with this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> a manifest volatile alkali. The dry residuum of the foregoing experiment, being distilled in a retort with a graduated fire, furnishes a volatile alkaline spirit and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. EXE Human feces, diluted and lixiviated in water, furnish by filtration and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a> of the water an oily salt of a nitrous nature, which deflages like nitre upon ardent coals, and which inflames in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> vessels when heated to a certain degree. The same matter yielded to Homberg, who treated it by a complete <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>, excited by a digestion during 40 days in a gentle water-bath heat, and who afterwards distilled it, an oil without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and without bad smell, and such as he endeavoured to find; but which did not, as we said before, fix mercury into silver.

EXCRESCE

Pages 407-407

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, denotes every preternatural tumour which arises upon the skin, either in the form of a wart <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> tubercle. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> they are born with a person, as they frequently are, they are called naevi materni, or marks from the mother; but if the tumour is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, so as to depend from the skin, like a fleshy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, it is then called a sarcoma. See Surgery.

EXCRETION

Pages 407-407
or Secretion, in Medicine, a separation of some fluid, mixed with the blood, by means of the glands. Excretions, by which we mean those that evacuate superfluous and heterogeneous humours, purify the mass of blood; the humours which are generated in the blood are excreted by the glands, and are replaced by a sufficient quantity of aliment.

EXCRETORY

Pages 407-407

in Anatomy, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to certain little ducts <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> vessels, destined for the reception of a fluid, secreted in certain glandules, and other viscera, for the excretion of it in the appropriated places.

EXCUBIAE

Pages 407-407

in antiquity, the watches and guards kept in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> by the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. They are contradistinguished from the vigiliae which were kept in the night.
