The excubiae were placed either at the gates and intrenchments <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>; for the latter there was allowed a whole manipulus to attend before the praetorium, and four soldiers to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENT">tent</a> of every tribune. The excubiae at the gates of the camp, and at the entrenchments, were properly called stationes. One <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of foot and one troop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> were assigned to each of the four gates every day. To <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a>, or abandon their corps of guards, was an unpardonable crime. The triarii, as the most <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> order of soldiers, were excused from the ordinary watches; yet being placed opposite to the equites, they were obliged to have an eye over them.

EXCUSATI

Pages 407-407

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> used to denote slaves, who <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> to any church for sanctuary, were excused and pardoned by their masters; but these were obliged to take an oath to the purpose before they could have them again; and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they broke the oath, they were punished and fined as persons guilty of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERJURY">perjury</a>.

EXEAT

Pages 407-407

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, a Latin <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> used for a permission which a bishop grants a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> to go out of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> to go out of his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>.

EXECRATION

Pages 407-407

in antiquity, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, consisting of direful curses and marks of infamy: such was that used against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Macedon by the Athenians. A general <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the people being called, they made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a>, that all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> and images of that king, and of all his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, should be demolished, and their very name razed; that all the festivals, sacred <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a>, priests, and whatever else had been instituted in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of him, should be profaned; that the very places where there had been any monument <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> inscription to his honour, should be detestable; that nothing should be set up, or dedicated in them, which could be done in clean places; and, lastly, that the priests, as often as they prayed for the Athenian people, allies, armies, and fleets, should as many times detest and execrate Philip, his children, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> forces, and the whole <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> and name of the Macedonians. At the taking and demolishing of cities, it was usual among the Jews, Greeks, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, to pronounce curses upon, and load with direful execrations, the rebuilders of them.

EXECUTION

Pages 409-409

in the French music, is used to denote the manner of singing, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of the performance of a song. "As to the manner of singing, called in France execution, no <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> may, with any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, dispute it with the French. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the French, by their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> with the Italians, have gained a bolder <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, the Italians have made their advantage of the French, in learning of them a more polite, moving, and exquisite execution." — St Evremond. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EXECUTIVE_POWER">EXECUTIVE POWER</a>. The supreme executive power of these kingdoms is vested by our laws in a single person, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> being. See the article King. The executive power, in this state, hath a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, i.e., to refuse assent to any acts offered; otherwise the two other branches of legislative power would, or might, become despotic.

EXECUTOR

Pages 409-409

in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies either the person entitled to succeed to the moveable estate of one deceased, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> who by law or special appointment is intrusted with the administration of it.

EXECUTORY

Pages 409-409

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is where an estate in fee, that is, made by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fine, is to be executed afterwards by entry, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIVERY">livery</a>, or writ. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LEASES">Leases</a> for years, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANNUITIES">annuities</a>, conditions, &c., are termed inheritances executory.

EXECUTRY

Pages 409-409

in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is the moveable estate falling to the executor. Under executry, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> moveables, is comprehended every thing that moves itself, or can be moved; such as corns, cattle, furniture, ready <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, &c.

EXEDRAE

Pages 409-409

in antiquity, denoted halls with many seats, where the philosophers, rhetoricians, and men of learning, met for discourse and disputation. The word occurs in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers as a general name for such buildings as were distinct from the main body of the churches, and yet within the limits of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> taken in its largest <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. Among the exedrae the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAPTISTERY">Baptistery</a>.

EXEGESIS

Pages 409-409

a discourse by way of explanation <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> comment upon any subject. In the Scotch <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, there is an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> among the students in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, called an exegesis, in which a question is stated by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESPONDENT">respondent</a>, who is then opposed by two or three other students in their turns; during which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the professor moderates, and solves the difficulties which the respondent cannot overcome.

EXEGETES

Pages 409-409

(formed of ἐξηγέομαι, "I explain,") among the Athenians, persons learned in the laws, whom the judges used to consult in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> causes.

EXEGETICA

Pages 409-409

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALGEBRA">Algebra</a>, the art of finding, either in numbers <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, the roots of the equation of a problem, according as the problem is either numerical or geometrical.

EXEMPLAR

Pages 409-409

a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> original, to be imitated or copied. See Model.

EXEMPLAR ALSO

Pages 409-409

R also denotes the idea, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> image, conceived or formed in the mind of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>, whereby he conducts his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. Such is the idea of Caesar, which a painter has in his mind when he goes to make a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of Caesar. EXEMPLIFICATION of Letters Patent, denotes an exemplar, or copy of letters patent, made from the enrolment thereof, and sealed with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> of England. Such exemplifications are as effectual to be showed or pleaded, as the letters patent themselves.

EXEMPTION

Pages 409-409

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a privilege to be free from some <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of appearance: thus, barons and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> of the realm are, on account of their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, exempted from being sworn upon inquests; and knights, clergymen, and others, from appearing at the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>'s turn. Persons of 70 years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, apothecaries, &c., are also by law exempted from serving on juries; and justices of the peace, attorneys, &c., from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> offices.

EXERCISE

Pages 409-412

among physicians, such an agitation of the body as produces salutary effects in the animal economy. Exercise may be said to be either <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a>. The active is walking, hunting, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>, playing at bowls, and the like; as also speaking and other labour of the body and mind. The passive is riding in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COACH">coach</a>, on horseback, or in any other manner. Exercise may be <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to a beginning of weariness, and ought to be used before dinner in a pure <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>; for which reason, journeys, and going into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, contribute greatly to preserve and re-establish <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. Exercise increases the circulation of the blood, attenuates and divides the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>, and promotes a regular perspiration, as well as a due secretion of all the humours; for it accelerates the animal spirits, and facilitates their distribution into all the fibres of the body, strengthens the parts, creates an appetite, and helps digestion. Whence it arises, that those who accustom themselves to exercise are generally very robust, and seldom subject to diseases. Boerhaave recommends bodily exercise in diseases of a weak and lax <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIBRE">fibre</a>. By riding on horseback, says his commentator, the pendulous viscera of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a> are shaken every moment, and gently rubbed as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were one against another, while in the meantime the pure air acts on the lungs with greater force. But it is to be observed that a weak <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> should not ride with a full stomach, but either before dinner, or after the digestion is nearly finished; for when the stomach is distended, weak people do not bear these concussions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> without difficulty; but when the prime vises are nearly empty, the remaining feces are discharged by this concussion. Sailing in a ship is also an exercise of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to weak people. If the vessel moves with an even <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, by increasing perspiration it usually excites a wonderful alacrity, creates an appetite, and promotes digestion. These exercises are more especially serviceable to weak people; but, in order to strengthen the body by muscular motion, running and bodily exercises are to be used. In these we should begin with the most gentle, such as walking, and increase it by degrees till we come to running. Those exercises of the body are more especially serviceable which give delight to the mind at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENNIS">tennis</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FENCING">fencing</a>, &c.; for which reason, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> of antiquity appointed rewards for those who excelled in these gymnastic exercises. Exercise, exercises, that by this means the bodies of their youth might be hardened for warlike toils. As nothing is more conducive to health than moderate exercise, so violent exercise dissipates the spirits, weakens the body, destroys the elasticity of the fibres, and exhausts the fluid parts of the blood. No wonder, then, that acute and mortal fevers often arise from too violent exercise of the body; for the motion of the venous blood towards the heart being quickened by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> of the muscles, and the veins being thus depleted, the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a> more easily propel their contained humours through the smallest extremities into the now less resisting veins; and therefore the velocity of the circulation <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be increased through all the vessels. But this cannot be performed without applying the humours oftener, or in a greater <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, to the secretory organs in the same time, whence the more fluid parts of the blood will be dissipated, and what remains will be inspissated; and by the greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the vessels upon their contained fluids, and of the reacting fluids upon the vessels, the blood acquires an inflammatory density. Add to this, that by the violent attrition of the solids and fluids, together with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> thence arising, all the humours will incline to a greater acrimony, and the salts and oils of the blood will become more acrid and volatile. Hence, says Boerhaave, those fevers which arise from too much exercise or motion, are cured by rest of body and mind, with such ailments and medicines as moisten, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DILUTE">dilute</a>, and soften or allay acrimony. The exercise of a soldier in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, considered as conducive to health, Dr Pringle distinguishes into three heads; the first relating to his duty, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> to his living more commodiously, and the third to his diversions. The first, consisting chiefly in the exercise of his arms, will be no less the means of preserving health than of making him expert in his duty: and frequent returns of this, early, and before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> grows hot, will be made more advantageous than repeating it seldom, and staying out <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> at a time; for a camp affording little convenience for refreshment, all unnecessary fatigue is to be avoided. As to the second article, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> boughs for shading the tents, making trenches round them for carrying off the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, airing the straw, cleaning their clothes and accoutrements, and assisting in the business of the mess, ought to be no disagreeable exercise to the men for some <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. Lastly, As to diversions, the men must be encouraged to them either by the example of their officers, or by small premiums to those who shall excel in any kind of sports as shall be judged most conducive to health: but herein great caution is necessary, not to allow them to fatigue themselves too much, especially in hot <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> or sickly times; but, above all, that their clothes be kept dry, wet clothes being the most frequent causes of camp diseases. Exercise, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> affairs, is the ranging a body of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> in form of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, and making them perform the several motions and military evolutions with different management of their arms, in order to make them expert therein. See also Words of Command. Exercise, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, is the preparatory practice of managing the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> and small arms, in order to make the ship's crew perfectly skilled therein, so as to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> its execution successfully in the time of battle. The exercise of the great guns was formerly very complicated, and abounding with superfluities, in our navy, as well as all others. The following method was, it is said, successfully introduced by an officer of distinguished abilities. 1st, Silence. 2nd, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">Cast</a> loose your guns. 3rd, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">Level</a> your guns. 4th, Take out your tompions. 5th, Run out your guns. 6th, Prime. 7th, Point your guns. 8th, Fire. 9th, Sponge your guns. 10th, Load with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARTRIDGE">cartridge</a>. 11th, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHOT">Shot</a> your guns. 12th, Put in your tompions. 13th, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">House</a> your guns. 14th, Secure your guns. Upon <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> to arms (every body having immediately repaired to their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>) the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDSHIPMAN">midshipman</a> commanding a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of guns, is to see that they are not without every necessary article, as (at every <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a>) a sponge, powder <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a>, with its priming wires, and a sufficient quantity of powder, crow, handspike, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, quoins, train tackle, &c. sending without delay for a supply of anything that may be wanting; and for the greater certainty of not overlooking any deficiency, he is to give strict orders to each <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> under him, to make the like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> at his respective gun, and to take care that every requisite is in a serviceable condition, which he is to report accordingly. And (besides the other advantages of this regulation) for the still more certain and speedy account being taken upon these occasions, the midshipman is to give each man his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> at quarters (as expressed in the form of the monthly report), who is to search for his particular implements, and, not finding them, is immediately to acquaint his captain, that, upon his report to the midshipman, they may be replaced. The man who takes care of the powder is to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> himself on the opposite side of the deck from that where we engage, except when fighting both sides at once, when he is to be amid ships. He is not to suffer any other man to take a cartridge from him but he who is appointed to serve the gun with that article, either in time of a real engagement or at exercise. Lanthorns are not to be brought to quarters in the night, until the midshipman gives his orders for so doing to the person he charges with that article. Everything being in its place, and not the least lumber in the way of the guns, the exercise begins with, 1. "Silence." At this word every one is to observe a silent <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the officers. 2. "Cast loose your guns." The muzzle lashing is to be taken off from the guns, and (being coiled up in a small compass) is to be made fast to the eye-bolt above the port. The lashing tackles at the same time to be cast loose, and middle of the breeching seized to the thimble of the pomillion. The sponge to be taken <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and, with the crow, handspike, &c. laid upon the deck by the gun. N. B. When prepared for engaging gaging an enemy, the seizing within the clinch of the breeching is to be cut, that the gun may come sufficiently within board for loading, and that the force of the recoil may be more spent before it acts upon the breeching. 3. "Level your guns." The breech of your metal is to be raised so as to admit the foot of the bed's being placed upon the axletree of the carriage, with the quoin upon the bed, both their ends being even one with the other. N.B. When levelled for firing, the bed is to be lashed to the bolt which supports the inner end of it, that it may not be thrown out of its place by the violence of the gun's motion when hot with frequent discharges. 4. "Take out your tompons." The tompon is to be taken out of the gun's mouth, and left hanging by its laniard. 5. "Run out your guns." With the tackles hooked to the upper bolts of the carriage, the gun is to be bowed out as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> as possible, without the assistance of crows or handspeaks; taking care at the same time to keep the breeching clear of the trucks, by hauling it through the rings; it is then to be bent so as to run clear when the gun is fired. When the gun is out, the tacklefalls are to be laid alongside the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a> in neat fakes, that, when the gun by recoiling overhauls them, they may not be subject to get foul, as they would if in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> coil. 6. "Prime." If the cartridge is to be pierced with the priming wire, and the vent filled with powder, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAN">pan</a> also is to be filled; and the flat space having a score through it at the end of the pan, is to be covered, and this part of the priming is to be bruised with the round part of the horn. The apron is to be laid over, and the horn hung up out of danger from the flash of the priming. 7. "Point your guns." At this command the gun is, in the first place, to be elevated to the height of the object, by means of the side sights; and then the person pointing is to direct his fire by the upper sight, having a crow on one side and a handspeak on the other, to heave the gun by his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> till he catches the object. N.B. The men who heave the gun for pointing are to stand between the ship's side and their crows or handspeaks, to escape the injury they might otherwise receive from their being struck against them, or splintered by a shot; and the man who attends the captain with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATCH">match</a> is to bring it at the word, "Point your guns," and kneeling upon one knee opposite the train-truck of the carriage, and at such a distance as to be able to touch the priming, is to turn his head from the gun, and keep blowing gently upon the lighted match to keep it clear from ashes. And as the missing of an enemy in action, by neglect or want of coolness, is most inexcusable, it is particularly recommended to have the people thoroughly instructed in pointing well, and taught to know the ill consequences of not taking proper means to <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HIT">hit</a> their mark; wherefore they should be made to elevate their guns to the utmost nicety, and then to point with the same exactness. Having caught the object through the upper sight, at the word, 8. "Fire." The match is instantly to be put to the bruised part of the priming; and when the gun is discharged, the vent is to be closed, in order to smother any spark of fire that may remain in the chamber of the gun; and the man who sponges is immediately to place himself by the muzzle of the gun in readiness; when, at the next word, 9. "Sponge your guns." The sponge is to be rammed down to the bottom of the chamber, and then twisted round, to extinguish effectually any remains of fire; and, when drawn out, to be struck against the outside of the muzzle, to shake off any sparks or scraps of the cartridge that may have come out with it; and next, its end is to be shifted ready for loading; and while this is doing, the man appointed to provide a cartridge is to go to the box, and by the time the sponge is out of the gun, he is to have it ready; and at the word, 10. "Load with cartridge." The cartridge (with the bottom-end first, seam downwards, and wad after it) is to be put into the gun, and thrust a little way within the mouth, when the rammer is to be entered; the cartridge is then to be forcibly rammed down; and the captain at the same time is to keep his priming-wire in the vent, and feeling the cartridge, is to give the word home, when the rammer is to be drawn, and not before. While this is doing, the man appointed to provide a shot is to provide one (or two, according to the order at that time) ready at the muzzle, with a wad likewise; and when the rammer is drawn, at the word, 11. "Shot your guns." The shot and wad upon it are to be put into the gun, and thrust a little way down, when the rammer is to be entered as before. The shot and wad are to be rammed down to the cartridge, and there have a couple of forcible strokes; when the rammer is to be drawn, and laid out of the way of the guns and tackles, if the exercise or action is continued; but if it is over, the sponge is to be secured in the place it is at all times kept in. 12. "Put in your tompons." The tompons to be put into the muzzle of the cannon. 13. "House your guns." The seizing is to be put on again upon the clinched end of the breeching, leaving it no slackner than to admit of the guns being housed with ease. The quoin is to be taken from under the breech of the gun, and the bed, still resting upon the bolt within the carriage, thrust under, till the foot of it falls off the axletree, leaving it to rest upon the end which projects out from the foot. The metal is to be let down upon this. The gun is to be placed exactly <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>; and the muzzle is to be close to the wood, in its proper place for passing the muzzle-lashings. 14. "Secure your guns." The muzzle-lashings must first be made secure, and then with one tackle (having all its parts equally taught with the breeching) the gun is to be lashed. The other tackle is to be bowed taught, and by itself made fast, that it may be ready to cast off for lashing a second breeching. N.B. Care must be taken to hook the first tackle to the upper bolt of the carriage, that it may not otherwise obstruct the reeving of the second breeching, and to give the greater length to the end part of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a>. No pains must be spared in bowing the lashing very taught, that the gun may have the least play that is possible, as their being loose may be productive of very dangerous Exercise, dangerous consequences. The quoins, crow, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>- Exercises, spike are to be put under the gun, the powder-horn hung up in its place, &c. Being engaged at any time when there is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> swell, a rough <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, or in squally weather, &c., as the ship may be liable to be suddenly much heeled, the port-tackle fall is to be kept clear, and (whenever the working of the gun will admit of it) the man <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with that office is to keep it in his hand; at the same time the muzzle-lashing is to be kept fast to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> of the port, and being hauled taught, is to be fasten- ed to the eye-bolt over the port-hole, so as to be out of the gun's way in firing, in order to haul it in at any time of danger. This precaution is not to be omitted, when enga- ging to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WINDWARD">windward</a>, any more than when to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEE">lee</a>- <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">ward</a>, those situations being very subject to alter at too short a warning. A train tackle is always to be made use of with the lee guns; and the man stationed to attend it is to be very careful in preventing the guns running out at an improper time. Exercise, may also be applied with propriety to the forming our fleets into orders of sailing, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of battle, &c., an art which the French have termed exer- cices, or tactiques. In this <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> exercise may be de- fined, the execution of the movements which the dif- ferent orders and disposition of fleets occasionally re- quire, and which the several ships are directed to per- form by means of signals. See <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TACTICS">Tactics</a>. Exercises, are also understood of what young gentlemen learn in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a> and riding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, such as fencing, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a>, riding the great horse, &c. How useful, how agreeable soever, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> may be to the mind, it is very far from being equally salutary to the body. Every one observes, that the Creator has formed an intimate connexion between the body and the mind; a perpetual action and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REACTION">reaction</a>, by which the body instantly feels the disorders of the mind, and the mind those of the body. The delicate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> of our frail <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> lose their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> and become ener- vated, and the vessels are closed by obstructions, when we totally desist from exercise, and the consequences necessarily affect the brain; a more studious and se- dentary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> is therefore equally prejudicial to the body and the mind. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> likewise become stiff; we <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> an awkward constrained manner; a certain disgustful air attends all our actions, and we are very near being as disagreeable to ourselves as to others. An inclination to study is highly commendable; but it ought not, however, to inspire us with an aversion to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> of man is to live among his fellows: and whatever may be the condition of our birth, or our situation in life, there are a thousand oc- casions where a man must naturally desire to render himself agreeable; to be active and adroit; to dance with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>; to command the fiery steed; to defend himself against a brutal enemy; to preserve his life by dexterity, as by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAPING">leaping</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a>, &c. Many ra- tional causes have therefore given rise to the practice of particular exercises; and the most sagacious and be- nevolent legislators have instituted, in their academies and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, proper methods of enabling youth, who devote themselves to study, to become expert also in laudable exercises.

EXERCITOR

Pages 412-412

in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, he who employs a Exercitor ship in trade, whether he be owner, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> only freights her from the owner. EXERGIA. See Oratory, No. 90.

EXERGUM

Pages 412-412

among antiquarians, a little space around <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> without the figures of a medal, left for the inscription, cipher, device, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a>, &c.

EXETER

Pages 412-414

the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, situated on the river Ex, ten miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of the British chan- nel. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 40'. N. Lat. 50° 44'. Anciently the name of this city was Iex, and Isa Dumniorum. The present name is a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> of Excester, that is, a city upon the Ex. It is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, populous, and wealthy, with gates, walls, and suburbs: the circumference of the whole is about three miles. It is the see of a bishop, transferred hither from Crediton, by Edward the Confessor; and is one of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> cities in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, for its buildings, wealth, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of its inhabitants. It had six gates, besides many turrets, several of which are now pulled <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. It had formerly so many <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, that it was called Monk- town, till <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Athelstan changed its name to Exeter, about the year 940; at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he also fortified the city (which had before been only enclosed with a ditch and a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>) with circular walls, em- <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BATTLEMENTS">battlements</a>, towers, and turrets of squared <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, en- circling the whole, except the western side, with a deep <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOAT">moat</a>. Besides chapels and five large meeting- houses, there are now 15 churches within the walls, and four without. St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, is a magnificent pile; though little now remains of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> fabric of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, except that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> which is called Our Lady's Chapel. It has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> of 12 bells, reckoned the largest ring of the largest bells in England; as is also its organ, whose largest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> are 15 inches in di- ameter. In 1763 the cathedral was repaired, beauti- fied, and new paved; when, in removing the old pave- ment, was found the leaden <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a> of Bishop Bitton, who died in 1307; the top of which, being decayed, afforded an opportunity of viewing the skeleton lying in its proper form; near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of the finger was found a sapphire ring set in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>; the stone con- siderably large, but of no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> value, on account of several flaws in it. Near this stood a small neat chalice and paten of silver gilt, but the damp had de- stroyed the greatest part of the gilding. In the centre of the paten was engraved a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, with the two fore- fingers extended in the attitude of benediction. The top of the crozier was also found, but totally decayed. A most beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> painted glass window has been lately erected at the western end of the cathedral, the eastern end having before a remarkable fine antique one. In the other windows there is much fine ancient paint- ed glass. The altar is remarkable for its beautiful de- sign and execution. On the left hand side of it there yet exists the seat where Edward the Confessor and his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> sat and installed Leofoicus, his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, the first bishop of Exeter; and in the fourth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> aisle is the monument of the same Leofoicus, who died 1073, which at the time of his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERMENT">interment</a> was a part of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a>, but by the enlarging of the church by his successors, became nearly the middle of the build- ing. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> western end of the church is most magnificently adorned with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of the pa- triarchs, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> was built in 1439. The beautiful throne for the bishop was constructed about 1466, and is said to be the grandest of the kind in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. The great north tower was completed in 1485, which contains a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a>, that weighs 12,500 pounds; and exceeds the great Tom of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a> by 2,500 pounds. This city has had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> charters granted, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> confirmed by most of our kings; but it was made a mayor town in the reign of King John, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of itself by King Henry VIII. It is governed by a mayor, 24 aldermen, four bailiffs, a recorder, chamberlain, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, town-clerk, &c. They have a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>-bearer, and four stewards, four sergeants at mace wearing gowns, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>-bearers in liveries with silver badges. It had anciently a mint; and in the reigns of King William III. and Queen <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, many pieces of silver <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> were coined here, which have the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> E under the bust. Here are 12 or 13 incorporate city companies. All pleas and civil causes are tried by the mayor, recorder, aldermen, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>; but criminal causes, and those relating to the peace, are determined by eight aldermen, who are justices of the peace. Here are four principal streets, all entering in the middle of the city, which is therefore called Carfax, from the old Norman word Quatre voix, i.e. the four ways. Near it is a conduit, lately removed from the centre to the side of the principal street, which was first erected by William <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a>, mayor of the city, in the reign of Edward IV., and there are others well supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> brought in pipes from the neighbourhood. There is an old castle in the north-east part of the city, called Rougemont, from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> it stands on; from thence there is a pleasant prospect from the walls. It is supposed to have been built by the West Saxon kings, and that they resided here, as did afterwards the earls and dukes of Cornwall. This castle was remarkably strong both by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and art. The gate which originally led into it, was walled up by order of William the Conqueror, in token of his having reduced it to his obedience after a very obstinate resistance; and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> by it an inferior gate was made in the wall in which state they both remain. The outward stone facing is kept in tolerable repair; but the inside being but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, is gradually crumbled down. Here yet remains the ancient chapel, built in 1260, and kept in good repair, where prayers are read, and a sermon preached in sessions weeks. The city itself is healthy, and pleasantly situated on the sides of a hill, having other hills to its N.W. and S. by which it is sheltered from the force of storms. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> which sustained the ditch that in a great part surrounded the castle, is planted and gravelled, and accommodated with seats, it being the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> for walking for the inhabitants; and the ditch between it and the castle being filled up, is now thickly planted with elms, which form a delightful <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROVE">grove</a>. The old <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> is now entirely demolished, and an elegant sessions house erected, where the assizes, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>-sessions, and county courts are held. In the city and suburbs are <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-PRISONS">prisons</a> both for debtors and malefactors; a workhouse, alms-houses, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>; an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> for the sick and lame <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> of the city and county, upon the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of the infirmaries of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> and Westminster; and two free <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>-schools. It has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> on Wednesdays and Fridays; and four <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> in the year. Great trade is carried on here in serges, perpetuanas, long ells, and other woollen goods, in which it is computed that at least 600,000l. a year is traded for; yet no markets were erected here for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, yarn, and kerseys, till the 30th of Henry VIII. Before that time the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> drove a considerable trade to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> and France: they were incorporated in the reign of Queen <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> I. by the name of "The Governor, Consuls, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of Merchant adventurers, trading to France." Here is also a weekly <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERGE">serge</a> market, the greatest in England, next to the Brigg market at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEEDS">Leeds</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>. It is said that some weeks as many serges have been sold here as amount to 80,000l. or 100,000l.; for besides the vast quantities of their woollen goods shipped for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, Spain, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, the Dutch give large commissions for buying up serges, perpetuanas, &c. for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> and Germany. It is particularly remarked of this city, that it is almost as full of gentry as of tradesmen; and that more of its mayors, and bailiffs have descended from, or given rise to good families, than in any other city of its bigness in the kingdom: for the great trade and flourishing state of this city tempted gentlemen to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> their sons in it, contrary to the practice of many of the inland as well as northern counties, where, according to the vain and ruinous notion of the Normans, trade was despised by the gentry as fit for only <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a> and the vulgar. This city was under the jurisdiction of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, whose coins have been frequently dug up in and about it. After they left England, the Saxons drove the Britons out of it into Cornwall, and encompassed it with a ditch, besides bulwarks. The Danes attacked and spoiled it in 875; and afterwards in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> of the general massacre of the Danes by the English, Sweyn one of their kings, came hither with a great force, put the men to the sword, ravished the women, massacred the children, burnt the city, and defaced the walls. A long time after this, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> as it was reviving, William the Conqueror besieged and took it; and it was again besieged in the reigns of King Stephen and Edward IV. In the reign of Henry VII. it was again besieged by Perkin Warbeck, and battered furiously; but the citizens forced him to raise the siege; which so pleased the king that he came hither, and presented a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a> of maintenance to the city, and gave the very sword from his side to be borne always before the mayor. In the reign of Edward VI. in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1544, it was smartly cannonaded by the rebels of Cornwall and Devon, who almost starved it by breaking down its bridges, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off its water, and stopping up all <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a>; but it held out till the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> John Russel came with a force and raised the siege on the 6th of August, which was then appointed as an anniversary <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of thanksgiving by the city, and is still observed as such. King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I.'s queen, to whom this city gave shelter in the civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, was here delivered of Henrietta, afterwards duchess of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>; whose <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> is in its guildhall, as are also General Monk's and George I.'s, &c. In the south-east quarter of the city was a house called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEDFORD">Bedford</a> house, wherein the above queen was delivered of the princess. This having lately been taken down, an elegant <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CIRCUS">circus</a> is built on the spot, with a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> adjoining it; and for the convenience of the inhabitants, a passage has been made through the town wall to Southern Hay, on which green stands the county hospital, already spoken of, besides a considerable number of new buildings. Exeter are remains of several ancient structures, which are daily giving way to modern erections; among the rest, an old <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, said to have been a palace of King Athelstan. The guildhall is a spacious and convenient building, whose <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> or portico projects a great way into the street, and was first erected in 1330, to which its present front was rebuilt in 1593, and repaired in 1720. An arm of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> formerly flowed nearly up to the city's wall, till 1316, when Hugh Courtenay <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Devon, in revenge for an affront, ruined the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, by constructing weirs and dams in the river; but to remedy it, in 1539, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> passed for making a navigable canal, for the better conveyance of goods in barges to and from the city to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOPSHAM">Topsham</a>. This was carried into execution in 1581, but not completed till 1675; nor was it after all found sufficient, till the present haven was constructed in 1697, when it was rendered capable of bringing ships of 150 tons quite to the quay, constructed near the walls of the city. In short, Exeter, by a constant adherence to its motto, Semper fidelis, has been applauded by all historians for its inviolable fidelity to its sovereigns, whether they held their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> or parliamentary <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>. The city sends two members to parliament; and gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of earl to the Cecils. The number of houses in Exeter, according to the return ordered by act of parliament in 1811, was 2971, and the number of inhabitants amounted to 18,866. The see of Exeter was once one of the most wealthy in the kingdom; but its revenues were most shamefully wasted by Bishop Voysey, who alienated its lands. What little he left was so much encumbered, that the see has never been able to recover its former <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>; and so small are its present revenues, that it has been found necessary for the bishop to hold some other preferment for the better support of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> contains the entire counties of Devonshire and Cornwall, wherein are 604 parishes, whereof 239 are impropriate. It hath four archdeacon, viz. of Cornwall, Exeter, Barnstaple, and Totness. The diocese was formerly valued in the king's books at £1561, 14s. 6d.; but, since Bishop Voysey's time, it is lowered to £500l. and is computed to be worth annually £2700l. The clergy's tenth is £200l. 15s. 2½d. To the cathedral belong a bishop, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a>, four archdeacons, a chancellor, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, a chantor, 24 prebendaries, and other inferior officers and servants.

EXFOLIATION

Pages 414-414

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> used by surgeons for the scaling of a bone, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the separation of the dead <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a bone from the living part.

EXHALATION

Pages 414-414

a general <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> for all effluvia <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> steams raised from the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> in form of vapour.

EXHAUSTIONS

Pages 414-414

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">Mathematics</a>. Method of exhaustions, is a way of proving the equality of two magnitudes, by a reductio <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AD">ad</a> absurdum; showing, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> one be supposed either greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> less than the other, there <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> arise a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a>. The method of exhaustions was of frequent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> mathematicians; as Euclid, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHIMEDES">Archimedes</a>, &c. It is founded on what Euclid says in his tenth book; viz. that those quantities whose <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> is less than any assignable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, are equal; for if they were unequal, be the difference never so small, yet it may be so multiplied, as to become greater than either of them; if not so, then it is really nothing. This he assumes in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of Prob. I. book x. which imports, that if, from the greater of two quantities, you take more than its half, and from the remainder more than its half, and so continually, there will, at length, remain a quantity less than either of those proposed. On this foundation it is demonstrated, that if a regular polygon of infinite sides be <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> in, or circumscribed about a circle; the space, which is the difference between the circle and the polygon, will, by degrees, be quite exhausted, and the circle become equal to the polygon.

EXHEREDATION

Pages 414-414

in the civil <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, with us ordinarily called disinheriting, is the father's excluding his sons from inheriting his estate. There are 14 causes of exheredation, expressed in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a>'s Novellae; without some one of which causes, he decrees the exheredation null, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TESTAMENT">testament</a> inefficacious, as the civilians call it. Indeed, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Roman law, the father might pronounce exheredation without any cause; but the rigour of this law was restrained and moderated by Justinian.

EXHIBIT

Pages 414-414

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is where a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, being produced in a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>, to be proved by witnesses, the examiner, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a> appointed for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of any such, certifies on the back of the deed or writing, that the same was shewn to the witness at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his examination, and by him sworn to.

EXHIBITION

Pages 414-414

in our old writers, is used for an allowance of meat and drink, such as was customary among the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> appropriators of churches, who usually made it to the depending <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a>. The benefactions settled for the maintaining of scholars in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> not depending on the foundation, are also called exhibitions.

EXHORTATION

Pages 414-414

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, differs only from suasion, in that the latter principally endeavours to convince the understandings, and the former to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> on the affections.

EXHUMATION

Pages 414-414

(of ex, "out of," and humus, "ground"); the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> up a body interred in holy ground, by the authority of the judge. In France, the exhumation of a dead body is ordered, upon <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that he was killed in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUEL">duel</a>. By the French laws, a parson has a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to demand the exhumation of the body of one of his parishioners, when interred out of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> without his consent.

EXIGENCE

Pages 414-414
or EXIGENCY, that which a thing requires, or which is expedient or suitable thereto.

EXIGENT

Pages 414-414

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a writ which lies where the defendant in a personal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> cannot be found, nor any effects of his within the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, by which he might be attached <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> distrained.

EXIGENTERS

Pages 414-415

four officers in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMMON_PLEAS"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> pleas, who make all exigents and proclamations, in all actions where <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of outlawry lies. Writs of supersedeas, as well as the prothonotaries, upon exigents, are likewise drawn up in their office. EXILE. See BANISHMENT. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, the word *exilium* properly signified an interdiction <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> and fire; the necessary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which was, that the interdicted person must betake himself into some other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, since there was no living without fire and water.—Thus Cicero, *<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AD">ad</a> Herenn.* observes, that the form of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> did not express *exilium*, but only *<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUA">aqua</a> et ignis interdictio*. The same author remarks, that exile was not properly a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, but a voluntarily <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> or avoiding the punishment decreed: *Exilium non esse supplicium, sed perfigium, partusque supplicii*. He adds, that there was no crime among the Romans, as among other nations, punished with exile; but exile was a resource to which people flew voluntarily, in order to avoid chains, ignominy, starving, &c. The Athenians frequently sent their generals and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men into exile, out of envy of their merits, or distrust of their too great authority. See OSTRACISM.

EXISTENCE

Pages 415-415

that whereby any thing has an actual essence, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> is said to be. See the article <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHYSICS">METAPHYSICS</a>.

EXITERIA

Pages 415-415

in antiquity, oblations <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> prayers to any of the gods for a prosperous expedition or journey. There were also feasts under this denomination, which were celebrated by the Greeks with sacrifices and prayers, when their generals undertook expeditions against an enemy.

EXOCETUS

Pages 415-415

the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">FLYING</a>-FISH, a genus of fishes belonging to the order of abdominales. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">ICHTHYOLOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EXODIARY

Pages 415-415

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Roman tragedy, was the person who, after the drama <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> play was ended, sung the EXODIUM.

EXODIUM

Pages 415-415

in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a>, signifies the end <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> conclusion of a feast. Particularly, it is used for the eighth <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the feast of tabernacles, which, it is said, had a special view to the commemoration of the exodus or departure out of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>.

EXODUS

Pages 415-415

a canonical book of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>; being the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> five books of Moses. It is so called from the Greek ἐξόδος, the "going out" or departure of the children of Israel from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of which is delivered in this book, together with the many <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> wrought on that occasion.

EXOMPHALUS

Pages 415-415

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, called also omphalocèle and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERNIA">hernia</a> umbilicalis, is a preternatural tumor of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>, at the navel, from a rupture <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> distension of the parts which invest that cavity.

EXORCISM

Pages 415-415

the expelling of devils from persons possessed, by means of conjurations and prayers. The Jews made <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> pretences to this power. Josephus tells several wonderful tales of the great success of several exorcists. One Eleazer, a Jew, cured many demoniacs, he says, by means of a root set in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a>. This root, with the ring, was held under the patient's nose, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> was forthwith evacuated. The most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of conjurors of this class were impostors, each pretending to a secret nostrum <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARM">charm</a> which was an overmatch for the devil. Our Saviour communicated to his disciples a real power over demons, or perhaps over the diseases said to be occasioned by demons. See DEMONIAC. Exorcism makes a considerable part of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Rome, the rituals of which forbid the exorcising any person without the bishop's leave. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> is performed at the lower end of the church, towards the door. The exorcist first signs the possessed person with the sign of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, makes him kneel, and sprinkles him with holy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. Then follow the litanies, psalms, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>; after which the exorcist asks the devil his name, and adjures him by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> not to afflict the person any more: then, laying his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> on the demoniac's head, he repeats the form of exorcism, which is this: "I exorcise thee, unclean spirit, in the name of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ: tremble, O Satan! thou enemy of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, thou foe of mankind, who hast brought <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> into the world; who hast deprived men of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and hast rebelled against <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>: thou seducer of mankind, thou root of evil, thou source of avarice, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCORD">discord</a>, and envy." The Romanists likewise exorcise houses and other places, supposed to be haunted by unclean spirits; and the ceremony is much the same with that for persons possessed.

EXORCISTS

Pages 415-415

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, an order of men, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> church, whose employment it was to exorcise <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> out devils. See the preceding article.

EXORDIUM

Pages 415-415

in Oratory, is the preamble <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> beginning, serving to prepare the audience for the rest of the discourse. Exordiums are of two kinds; either <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> and formal, or vehement and abrupt. The last are more suitable on occasions of extraordinary joy, indignation, or the like. See ORATORY, No. 26.

EXOSTOSIS

Pages 415-416

in Anatomy, an acute eminence <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> excrescence, pushing preternaturally above the bone. EXOTERIC and ESOTERIC, are terms denoting <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> and internal, and applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> doctrine of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> philosophers: the one was public or exoteric; the other secret, or esoteric. The first was that which they openly professed and taught to the world; the latter was confined to a small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of chosen disciples. This method was derived originally from the Egyptians; who, according to the united testimony of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, Diodorus Siculus, Strabo, Plutarch, &c. had a twofold <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, one secret and sacred, another public and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>. The same practice also obtained among the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGI">Magi</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRUIDS">Druids</a> of the Gauls, and the Brachmans of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. The Egyptian priests, with whom it originated, sustained the character of judges and magistrates, and probably introduced this distinction with a view to the public welfare, and to serve the purpose of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEGISLATION">legislation</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. Clement of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> informs us, that they communicated their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> principally to those who were concerned in the administration of the state; and Plutarch confirms the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a>. However, others have supposed that they invented the fables of their gods and heroes, and the other external ceremonies of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> and conceal <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and moral truths; but whatever was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> of their practice, it was certainly applied to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> purposes.

EXOTIC

Pages 416-416

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> properly signifying foreign <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> extraneous, i.e. brought from a remote or strange <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. In which <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> we sometimes say exotic or barbarous terms or words, &c. The word is derived from the Greek ἐξωτικός, extra, "without, on the outside." Exotic, is chiefly applied to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> which are natives of foreign countries, particularly those brought from the East or West Indies, and which do not naturally grow in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The generality of exotics, or exotic plants, do not thrive in England without some peculiar care or culture: they require the warmth of their own climates; whence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of hot beds, glass frames, green houses, &c. See <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EXPANSION

Pages 416-416

among metaphysicians, denotes the idea which we have of lasting distance, all whose parts exist together. Expansion, in Physics, the enlargement <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> increase of bulk in bodies, chiefly by means of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. This is one of the most general effects of that sublime principle, being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to all bodies whatever, whether <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> or fluid. In some few <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, indeed, bodies seem to expand as they grow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of freezing: but this is found to be owing to a new arrangement of the particles, or to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRYSTALLIZATION">crystallization</a>; and is not at all a regular and gradual expansion like that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, or any other solid or fluid substance by means of heat. In certain metals also, an expansion takes <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> when they <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> from a fluid to a solid state: but this too is not to be accounted any proper effect of cold, but of the arrangement of the parts of a metal in a peculiar manner; and is therefore to be ascribed to a kind of crystallization. The expansion of bodies by heat is very various, and in solids does not seem to be guided by any certain rule. In the 48th volume of the Phil. Trans. Mr Smeaton has given a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of the expansions of many different substances. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EXPECTANCY

Pages 416-416

estates in, are of two sorts; one created by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of the parties, called a remainder; the other, by act of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, called <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVERSION">reversion</a>.

EXPECTATION

Pages 416-416

in the doctrine of chances, is applied to any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINGENT">contingent</a> event, and is capable of being reduced to the rules of computation. Thus a sum of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> in expectation when a particular event happens, has a determinate value before that event happens; so that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a person is to receive any sum, e.g., 10l. when an event takes <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> which has an equal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> of happening and failing, the value of the expectation is half that sum <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 5l.; and in all <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> the expectation of obtaining any sum is estimated by multiplying the value of the sum expected by the fraction which represents the probability of obtaining it. The expectation of a person who has three chances in five of obtaining 100l. is equal to \(\frac{3}{5} \times 100\) or 60l. and the probability of obtaining 100l. in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> is equal to \(\frac{60}{100} = \frac{3}{5}\). EXPECTATION of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a>, signifies, in the doctrine of life <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANNUITIES">annuities</a>, that share or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the years of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> life, which a person of any given <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> may expect to enjoy on an equality of chance. According to Mr Simpson, by the expectation of life we are not to understand that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> which a person may have an equal chance of surviving, which is a different and more simple consideration; but the number of years at which the purchase of an annuity ought to be valued, granted on it without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCOUNT">discount</a> of money. There <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be a greater or less <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in this number of years, in proportion to the various degrees of mortality to which the different stages of human life are exposed. Thus, it is more than an equal chance that an infant <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> come into the world, will not reach the age of 10 years; yet the expectation of life, or share of existence due to it, is almost 20 years upon an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a>. The reason of this vast difference is the excess of the probability of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> in the first tender years of existence above that which respects the more advanced stages. If the numbers of those who die at every assignable period were always found to be on an equality, the two quantities already mentioned would be the same; but when these numbers constantly become less and less, the expectation must of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> become the greater of the two.

EXPECTORANTS

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, medicines which promote EXPECTORATION. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EXPECTORATION

Pages 416-416

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of evacuating <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bringing up phlegm or other matters out of the trachea, lungs, &c. by coughing, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAWKING">hawking</a>, spitting, &c.

EXPEDITION

Pages 416-416

the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> to some distant <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, with a view of hostilities.
