Such were the expeditions of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a> against <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTAXERXES">Artaxerxes</a>, and of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a> and Alexander into the Indies. Expeditions for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of the Holy <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">Land</a> were called croisades.

EXPERIENCE

Pages 416-417

a kind of knowledge acquired by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> without any teacher. It consists in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of things we have seen <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> read, which the judgment has reflected on, to form for itself a rule or method. Authors make three kinds of experience: The first is the simple uses of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> senses, whereby we perceive the phenomena of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> things without any <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> thereto, or making any application thereof. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is, when we premeditate and designedly make trials of various things, or observe those done by others, attending closely to all effects and circumstances. The third is that preceded by a foreknowledge, or at least an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> of the event, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIMENTAL_PHILOSOPHY">EXPERIMENTAL <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">PHILOSOPHY</a> Is that which has its foundation in experience, wherein nothing is assumed as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> but what is founded upon ocular demonstration, or which cannot be denied without violating the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> and perceptions of all mankind. In former times philosophers, when reasoning about natural things, instead of following this method, assumed such principles as they imagined sufficient for explaining the phenomena, without considering whether these principles were <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> or not. Hence for a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of ages no progress was made in science; but systems were heaped upon systems, having neither consistency with one another nor with themselves. No proper explanations indeed were given of anything; for all these systems, when narrowly examined, were found to consist merely in changes of words, which were often very absurd and barbarous. The first who deviated from this method of philosophizing, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we may call it by that name, was Friar <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a>, who lived in the 13th century, and who spent 2000l. (an immense sum in those days) in making experiments. The Admirable Crichton, who flourished about the year 1580, not only disputed against the philosophy of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, which had for so long been in vogue, but wrote a book against it. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">Contemporary</a> with this celebrated personage was Francis Bacon <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of England, who is looked upon to be the founder of the present <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of philosophizing by experiments. But though others might lay the foundation, Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton is justly allowed to have brought this kind of philosophy to perfection; and to him we are certainly indebted for the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it. Unfortunately, however, neither Lord Bacon nor Sir Isaac Newton had an opportunity of knowing many important facts relating to the principles of fire and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">electricity</a>, which have since been brought to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. Hence all their philosophy was merely <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a>, or derived from the visible operations of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> bodies, or of the grosser <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>, upon one another. In such <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, therefore, where the more subtile and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> fluids were concerned, they fell into mistakes, or were obliged to deny the existence of the principles altogether, and to make use of terms which were equally unintelligible and incapable of conveying any information with those of their predecessors. A remarkable instance of the errors into which they were thus betrayed, we have in the doctrine of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROJECTILES">projectiles</a>, where the most enormous deviations from truth were sanctified by the greatest names of the last century, merely by reasoning from the resistance of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> to bodies moving slowly and visibly, to its resistance to the same bodies when moved with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> degrees of velocity. In other cases they were reduced to make use of words to express immechanical powers, as <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a>, repulsion, rarefaction, &c., which have since tended in no small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> to embarrass and confound science by the disputes that have taken <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> concerning them. The foundations of the present system of experimental philosophy are as follows: I. All the material substances of which the universe is composed are called natural bodies. What we perceive uniform and invariable in these substances we call their properties. Some of these are general and common to all <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a>; others are proper to particular substances, for instance fluidity; while some appear to be compounded of general and particular properties, and thus belong to a still smaller number; as the properties of air, which are derived from the general <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of extension combined with those of fluidity, elasticity, &c. II. In taking a particular review of the properties of bodies we naturally begin with that of extension. This manifests itself by the three dimensions of length, breadth, and thickness. Hence proceeds the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISIBILITY">divisibility</a> of matter; which the present system supposes to reach even to infinity: but though this proposition be supported by mathematical demonstrations, it is impossible we can either have any distinct idea of it, or of the opposite doctrine, which teaches that matter is composed of excessively minute particles called atoms, which cannot be divided into smaller ones. The subtlety indeed to which solid bodies may be reduced by mechanical means is very surprising; and in some cases is so great, that we might be tempted to suppose that a farther <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> is impossible. Thus, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> a speculum, the inequalities of its surface are so effectually worn off, that the whole becomes in a certain degree invisible, showing not itself by the light which falls upon it, but the image of other bodies; but the smallest scratch which disturbs the equality of the surface is at once distinctly visible. III. From the arrangement of these ultimate particles of matter, whatever we suppose them to be, arise the various figures of bodies: and hence <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> is a property of all bodies no less universal than extension, unless we choose to speak of the ultimate particles of matter, which, as they are supposed to be destitute of parts, must consequently be equally destitute of figure; and the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> follow whether we adopt this supposition or the other. The figures of bodies are so extremely various and dissimilar, that it is impossible to find any two perfectly alike. It is indeed the next thing to impossible to find two in which the dissimilarity may not be perceived by the naked eye; but if any such should be found, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a> will quickly discover the imbecility of our senses in this respect. Solidity is another property essential to all matter. By this we <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> that property which one <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of matter has of excluding any other from the space which itself occupies.

EXPERIMENTAL PHILOSOPHY

Pages 417-420

occupies at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Hence arises what we call resistance, which is always an indication of solidity; and no less so in those bodies which we call fluid than in those which are the most <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>. This may at first seem to be a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a>; but <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> yield only when they can get away from the pressure; in all other <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> they resist as violently as the most solid bodies. Thus <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> confined in a tube <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> as effectually resist the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of a piston thrust <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> upon it as though it were the most solid substance. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">Air</a> indeed will yield for a certain time; but this, as appears from several experiments, is entirely owing to a more subtile fluid, viz. that of elementary fire, being pressed out from among its particles. As <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as this fluid can be forced out, either from among the particles of air, water, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any other more <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> fluid substance, the latter will be found compressible, as a heap of wet sand would be by squeezing the water out from it; but when we come to the most subtile of all elements, such as we suppose that of fire to be, there cannot be any possibility of compressing it, even though we had a vessel so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> as to prevent it from escaping through its sides; because its parts are already as near each other as they can be. IV. The distance of the parts of bodies from each other is what we call their porosity, and was formerly supposed to be owing to a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VACUUM">vacuum</a> interspersed between them; but now it is generally allowed that the pores of solid bodies as well as of fluids are filled with an extremely subtile <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> which pervades all <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. The porosity of bodies with regard to one another may be thus explained. Wood or a sponge is porous with regard to water; but water itself is porous with regard to air, which it absorbs in considerable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>. But air and water are porous with regard to the element of fire, which produces very considerable changes upon them, according to the quantity of it they contain, or the manner it acts in their pores. The element itself, however, is not porous with regard to any other substance. Its pores, therefore, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it has any, must be <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> vacuities, destitute of any matter whatever. Vacuities of this kind indeed are supposed to be absolutely necessary to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>: for though we may say, matter being divisible almost <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AD">ad</a> infinitum, that a body or substance more solid may move in another substance that is more subtile, and that will give way to its motion, we must nevertheless have recourse to a last <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a>, and admit of an ultimate vacuum, which will give room sufficient to the least corpuscle, that its <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> A may take the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of its part B without the least resistance: besides, it is not to be imagined, that nature, in fact, admits of that infinite <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISIBILITY">divisibility</a> which our imagination can conceive, and that every thing which is possible in idea, is at all times practicable. All that exists is possible, but all that is possible does not however exist. By density, is understood the proportion between the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> and solidity of a body; one body therefore is more dense than another, when, under the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of extension, it contains more solid matter: and this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> arises from condensation and compression. Elasticity is nothing more than that effort by which certain bodies, when compressed, endeavour to restore themselves to their former state; and this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> supposes them compressible. As all these <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> properties of bodies are of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> utility in explaining the principles of physics, and in applying them to all the arts, experimental <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> proves their reality by a thousand examples. V. We discover still other properties in bodies; such as mobility, which we must not here confound with motion. This mobility arises from certain dispositions which are not in an equal degree in all bodies: from whence it comes that some are more easily moved than others: and this proceeds from the resistance to motion which is perceived in all bodies: having regard merely to their masses; and this resistance is called vis inertiae, or inert force. A body is said to be in motion when it is actually moving from one place to another: or, whenever a body changes its situation with regard to the objects that surround it, either nearly or remotely, it is said to be in motion. There are three <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> matters to be considered in a moving body; its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, its velocity, and the quantity of its motion: and here physics explains the force or moving power; it likewise distinguishes between simple and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> motion. Simple motion is that which arises from only one force, or which tends to one point only. It describes the laws, and explains the resistance, of mediums; the resistance of friction; the difficulties of a perpetual motion; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> of direction occasioned by the opposition of a fluid matter; reflected or reverberated motion; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> of motion by the shock of bodies, &c. Compound motion is that of a body impelled to move by several causes or powers which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> according to their different directions. Physics here likewise investigates the laws of motion; and is particularly applied to the explaining, under this head, what are called the central forces, which produce a motion that is either circular or in a curve line, and which incessantly urge the moving body either to approach or recede from the centre. To distinguish these from each other, the former is called the centripetal force, and the latter the centrifugal force. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYNAMICS">DYNAMICS</a>. VI. By gravity, or ponderosity, is to be understood that force which occasions bodies to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> from a higher to a lower place, when nothing opposes their course, or when the obstacles are not sufficient to stop them: <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECULATIVE">Speculative</a> philosophy investigates its cause, and perhaps in vain. Experimental philosophy contents itself with describing the phenomena, and teaching the laws of gravity, which are thoroughly established by a thousand reiterated experiments. In order properly to understand this subject, we must take care not to confound the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> gravity with that of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. By the former, we understand that force which urges bodies to descend through a certain space in a given time. By the latter, is meant the quantity of a heavy body that is contained under the same bulk. The phenomena are explained by the experiments themselves, and by inferences deduced from them. VII. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HYDROSTATICS">Hydrostatics</a> is a science of which the object is the gravity and equilibrium of fluids in particular. Though the gravity of these bodies is the same with that of others, and is subject to the same laws, yet their state of fluidity gives rise to particular phenomena, which it is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> to know. But as hydrostatics cannot be successfully treated without the assistance of calculation, it has been ranked among the mathematical sciences. VIII. We say the same with regard to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>; which is the art of employing, by the aid of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a>, the motion of bodies, in conformity to its properties and laws, as well with regard to solids as fluids, either more commodiously or more advantageously. IX. After it has made the most accurate experiments, and the most judicious observations, on all these different subjects, and the properties of bodies in particular, Experimental Philosophy passes to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of the air, the water, fire, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, colours, &c. The air is a fluid with which we are surrounded from the instant of our birth, and without which we cannot exist. It is by the properties and the influences of the air, that nature gives increase and perfection to all that it produces for our wants and conveniences: it is the spirit of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>: <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, speech itself, are nothing more than percussions of the air: this globe that we inhabit is completely surrounded by air; and this kind of coverture, which is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, has such remarkable functions, that it evidently appears to concur to the mechanism of nature. Experimental physics, therefore, considers the air, 1. Of itself, independent of its bulk, and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of its whole body: it examines its essential properties; as its gravity, density, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, &c. The air-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PUMP">pump</a> is here of indispensable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; and by this machine physics examines in what manner space, or a vacuum, is made. It likewise shows the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of air to the preservation of animal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; the effect it has on sound, fire, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>, in vacuo; and a hundred other experiments of various degrees of curiosity. 2. It considers the air as the terrestrial atmosphere, sometimes as a fluid at rest, and sometimes as in motion. And by these means it accounts for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAROMETER">barometer</a>, and why it sinks in proportion as the height of the atmosphere diminishes; as also for the figure, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, and weight of the atmosphere: it shows the method of determining the height of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, the nature of sound in general, of its propagation, and of sonorous bodies. The late discoveries have added greatly to experimental philosophy, of which an account is given under the article <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, &c. X. It is here also, that experimental philosophy considers the nature of the wind; which is nothing more than agitated air, a portion of the atmosphere that moves like a current, with a certain velocity and determinate direction. This fluid, with regard to its direction, takes different names according to the different <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the horizon from whence it comes, as east, west, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and south. Winds are likewise distinguished into three sorts; one of which is called general or constant, as the trade winds which continually blow between the tropics: another is the periodical, which always begin and end within a certain time of the year, or a certain <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, as the monsoons, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> breezes and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> breezes, which arise constantly in the morning and evening; and lastly, such as are variable, as well with regard to their direction as their velocity and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. M. Mariotte computes the velocity of the most impetuous wind to be at the rate of 32 feet in a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, and Mr <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DERHAM">Derham</a> makes it 66 feet in the same time. The first, doubtless, meant the wind of the greatest velocity that had then come to his knowledge. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of aerostatic machines has tended more to show the real velocity of the wind than any other invention as yet made public; but all of them move slower than the aerial current; so that the real velocity of the wind remains yet undetermined. XI. The force of the wind, like that of other bodies, depends on its velocity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>: that is, the quantity of air which is in motion; so the same wind has more or less force on any obstacle that opposes it, in proportion as that obstacle presents a greater or a less surface: for which reason it is that they spread the sails of a vessel more or less, and place the wings of a windmill in different directions. The machine by which the winds are measured, are called anemometers. They show the direction, the velocity, and the duration of winds. It is by the agitations of the winds that the air is purified; that the seeds of trees and herbs are conveyed through the forests and fields; that ships are driven from one pole to the other; that our <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a> turn upon their axles, &c.; and art, by imitating nature, sometimes procures us <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> winds, by which we refresh our bodies, invigorate our fires, purify our corn, &c. XII. Water is an universal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGENT">agent</a>, which nature employs in all her productions. It may be considered as in three states: 1. As a liquid; 2. As a vapour; 3. As <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a>. These three different states do not in any manner change its essence, but make it proper to answer different ends. The natural state of water would be that of a solid body, as fat, wax, and all those other bodies which are only fluid when heated to a certain degree; for water would be constantly ice, if the particles of fire, by which it is penetrated in the temperate climates, did not render it fluid, by producing a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> motion among its parts; and, in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> is continually strong enough to maintain the congelation, the assistance of art is necessary to make it fluid in the same manner as we do <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, &c. Water, when not in ice, is a fluid that is insipid, transparent, without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> and without smell, and that easily adheres to the surface of some bodies, that penetrates many, and extinguishes fire. Experimental philosophy investigates the origin of fountains; the cause of the saltness of the sea; the means of purifying water; what is its weight, and what are its effects when heated, &c. It likewise examines this fluid in the state of vapour; and finds that a drop of water, when in vapour, occupies a space vastly greater than it did before. It explains the condensation and its effects; fire engines; and the force of vapour that gives motion to immense machines in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> and elsewhere, &c. And lastly, It considers water in the state of ice. Ice consequently is more cold than water; and its coldness increases if it continues to lose that matter, already too rare, or too little <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, to render it fluid. Experimental physics endeavours to investigate the causes of the congelation of water, and why ice is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> than water; from whence it derives that expansive force by which it breaks the containing vessel; the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> there is between the congelation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and that of standing waters; why ice becomes more cold by the mixture of salts; and many other similar phenomena. XIII. The nature of fire is yet very much unknown to the most learned philosophers. As objects when at a great distance are not perceptible to our senses, so when we examine them too nearly, we discern them but confusedly. It is still disputed whether fire be a homogeneous, unalterable matter, designed, by its presence, or by its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, action, to produce <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, inflammation, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a>, in bodies; or if its essence consists in motion only, or in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a> of those particles which we call inflammable, and which enter as principles, in greater or less quantities, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of mixed bodies. The most learned inquirers into nature incline to the former <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>; and to have recourse to a matter which they regard as the principle of fire. They suppose that there is in nature a fluid adapted to this purpose, created such from the beginning, and that nothing more is necessary than to put it in action. The numberless experiments which are daily made in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">electricity</a> seem to favour this opinion, and to prove that this matter, this fluid, this elementary fire, is diffused through all nature, and in all bodies, even ice itself. We cannot say to what important knowledge this great discovery of electricity may lead if we continue our inquiries concerning it. It appears, however, that we may believe, without any inconvenience or absurdity, that fire and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, considered in their first principle, are one and the same substance differently modified. XIV. Be this matter however as it may, experimental philosophy is employed in making the most ingenious and most useful researches concerning the nature of fire, its propagation, and the means by which its power may be excited or augmented; concerning the phosphorus and its inflammation; fire excited by the reflection of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>'s rays from a mirror; and on the effects of fire in general; concerning <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a> and its effects; the fusion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>; gunpowder and its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPLOSION">explosion</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> and the aliments of fire; and an infinity of like objects which it explains, or concerning which it makes new discoveries, by the aid of experiments. XV. By the word light, we understand that agent by which nature affects the eye with that lively and almost constantly pleasing <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>, which we call seeing, and by which we discern the size, figure, colour, and situation of objects, when at a convenient distance. All philosophers agree, that the light which is diffused in any place, is a real body. But what this body is, and by what means it enters that place where it is perceived, is a question about which philosophers are divided. XVI. Experimental philosophy is applied in discovering or proving, by an infinity of experiments, what is the nature of light, in what manner it is propagated, what its velocity and progressive motion. It also investigates and explains the principle of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">optics</a> properly so called, and shows the directions which light observes in its motions. From thence it proceeds to the examen of the principles of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CATOPTRICS">catoptrics</a>, and describes the laws and effects of reflected light. It next treats of the principles of dioptries, and explains the laws of refracted light; and lastly, it teaches, from the principles of natural and artificial vision, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of optical instruments, as lunes, concave <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MIRRORS">mirrors</a>, prisms, telescopes, &c. &c. and the uses to which they are applied. XVII. By resolving or separating the rays of light, philosophy has obtained true and clear discoveries of the nature of colours. We are naturally led to imagine that colours, and their different degrees, make a part of the bodies that present them to our sight; that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> is inherent in snow, green in leaves and grass, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> in a stuff dyed of that colour. But this is far from being true. If an object, which presents any colour to our sight, be not illuminated, it presents no colour whatsoever. In the night all is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>. Colours therefore depend on light; for without that we could form no idea of them; but they depend also on bodies; for of several objects presented to the same light, some appear white, others red, blue, &c. But all these matters being separate from our own bodies, we should never acquire any idea of them, if the light, transmitted or reflected by these objects, did not make them sensible to us, by striking upon the organs of our sight, and if these impressions did not revive in us those <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> which we have been used to express by certain terms. For these reasons philosophy considers colours from three points of view, 1. As in the light; 2. In bodies, as being coloured; and, 3. From the relation they have to our visual faculties, which they particularly affect, and by which we are enabled to distinguish them. It is unnecessary in this place to say more, either on colour in particular, or experimental philosophy in general. The different subjects of this collective article are particularly treated under their proper names, in the order of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>: the reader will therefore turn, as he has occasion, to Acoustics, Catoptrics, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHROMATICS">Chromatics</a>, Dioptries, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HYDRODYNAMICS">Hydrodynamics</a>, Mechanics, Optics, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PNEUMATICS">Pneumatics</a>, Electricity, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGNETISM">Magnetism</a>, &c. &c. &c. Also, Aerostation, Atmosphere, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">Burning</a> Glass, Chemistry, &c. &c. ---

EXPERIMENTUM CRUCIS

Pages 420-424

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, leading, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> decisive experiment; thus termed, either on account of its being like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> placed in the meeting of several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, guiding men to the true knowledge of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of that thing they are inquiring after; or, on account of its being a kind of torture, whereby the nature of the thing is as it were extorted by force. **EXPHORESIS.** See Oratory, No 85. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPIATION">EXPIATION</a>,** a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>, by which satisfaction or atonement is made for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of some crime, the guilt done away, and the obligation to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> cancelled. Expiations among the Heathens, were of several kinds; as sacrifices and religious washings. They were used for effacing a crime, averting any calamity, and on numberless other occasions, as purifying <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, and sacred places, and armies before and after <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. And they were performed for whole cities as well as particular persons. The method of expiation among the Jews was chiefly by sacrifice, whether for sins of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>, or to purify themselves from certain pollutions. Feast of Expiation, among the Jews, called by our translators the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of atonement, was held on the tenth day of Tisri, or the seventh <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of the Jewish year, answering to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of our September and October. It was instituted by God himself, Levit. xxiii. 27, &c. On that day the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYPE">type</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, entered into the most holy <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and confessed his sins; and, after several ceremonies, made an atonement for all the people, to wash them from their sins. Lev. chap. xvi. See Scape-Goat. Expiation, in a figurative <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is applied by divines to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> procured to the sins of the penitent by the merit of Christ's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. See the article CHRISTIANITY. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">Expiration</a>, in Medicine. See Expiration. Expiration, is also used figuratively, for the end of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> granted, agreed on, or adjudged. Explicit, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, something clear, distinct, formal, and unfolded. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPLOSION">Explosion</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, a sudden and violent expansion of an aerial or other <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> fluid, by which it instantly throws off any obstacle that happens to be in the way, sometimes with incredible force, and in such a manner as to produce the most astonishing effects upon the neighbouring objects. Explosion differs from expansion, in that the latter is a gradual and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> power, acting uniformly for some time, whereas the former is always sudden, and only of momentary <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. The expansions of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> substances do not terminate in violent explosions, on account of their slowness, and the small space through which the metal, or other expanding substance, moves; though their strength may be equally <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> with that of the most <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> aerial <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>. Thus we find, that though wedges of wood, when wetted, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> cleave solid blocks of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, they never throw them to any distance, as is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, it is seldom that the expansion of any elastic fluid bursts a solid substance without throwing the fragments of it to a considerable distance, the effects of which are often very terrible. The reasons of this may be comprised in the two following particulars: 1. The immense velocity with which the aerial fluids expand, when affected by a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>; and, 2. Their celerity in acquiring heat and being affected by it, which is much superior to that of solid substances. Thus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, heated as much as <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> when brought to a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> heat, is expanded to four times its bulk; but the metal itself will not be expanded the 500th part of the space. In the case of gunpowder, which is a violent and well known explosive substance, the velocity with which the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> moves is calculated by Mr Robins, in his Treatise upon <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUNNERY">Gunnery</a>, to be no less than 7000 feet in a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, or little less than 79 miles per minute. Hence the impulse of the fluid is inconceivably great, and the obstacles on which it strikes are hurried off with vast velocity, though much less than that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned; for a cannon bullet, with the greatest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of powder that can be conveniently given, does not move at a greater rate than 2400 feet per second, or little more than 27 miles per minute. The velocity of the bullet again is promoted by the sudden propagation of the heat through the whole body of air, as soon as it is extricated from the materials of which the gunpowder is made; so that it is enabled to strike all at once, and thus greatly to augment the momentum of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>. It is evident that this contributes very much to the force of the explosion, by what happens when powder is wetted or mixed with any substance, which prevents it from taking fire all at once. In this case the force of the explosion, even when the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of powder is made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of, cannot be compared to that of dry powder. Upon these principles we may conclude that the force of an explosion depends, 1. On the quantity of elastic fluid to be expanded; 2. On the velocity it acquires by a certain degree of heat; and, 3. On the celerity with which the degree of heat affects the whole of the expansive fluid. These three take place in the greatest perfection where the electric fluid is concerned: as in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, earthquakes, and volcanoes. This fluid, as is shewn in many parts of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, differs not from elementary fire or the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; it pervades the whole system of nature; its expansion is nothing else than its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> from a centre towards a circumference, for it does not seem capable of any proper expansion by a separation of its parts like any other fluid. Hence, when it begins to expand in this manner, the motion is propagated through it with a velocity far exceeding that of any other fluid whatever. Thus, even when the quantity is excessively small, as when an electric spark is sent through a glass full of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> or of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, the expansion is so violent as to dissipate the glass into innumerable fragments, with great danger to the bystanders, as is observed under the article <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">ELECTRICITY</a>. In violent lightning, where the electric fluid collects itself into balls, the strength of the explosion is proportionable to the quantity. Every one has heard of the prodigious effects of lightning when it happens to strike buildings, trees, or even the most solid rocks; and in some cases, where the quantity of electricity is still greater than in any flash of lightning, we hear of still more tremendous consequences ensuing. Dr Priestley gives an instance of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fire ball (undoubtedly a quantity of electric <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>) rolling on the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, which after rising up to the topmast of a ship of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, burst with such violence that the explosion resembled the discharge of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a> of cannon fired at once. Great damage was done by it; but there is not the least doubt that most of its force was spent on the air, or carried <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the sea by the mast and iron work of the ship. Indeed, considering that in all cases a great part of the force of electric explosions is dissipated in this manner, it may justly be doubted whether they can be measured by any method applicable to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENSURATION">mensuration</a> of other forces. Even in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> electricity the force is prodigiously great; insomuch that Dr Van Marum calculated that of the great <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a> belonging to the machine in Teyler's <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a> to be upwards of 900 pounds. In those cases where the electrical matter acts like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> fire, the force of the explosions, though exceedingly great, is capable of mensuration by comparing the distances to which the bodies are thrown with their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. This is most evident in volcanoes, where the projections of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> rocks and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAVA">lava</a> manifest the greatness of the power, at the same time that they afford a method of measuring it. These explosions, as is shown under the article Volcano, are owing to extrication of aerial vapours, and their rarefaction by intense heat. In all of them the air is originally in a state of decomposition, viz. its invisible and solid part is joined with some terrestrial substances. Thus, when fixed air, for instance, is exposed to any pure <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> which attracts it, as calcined <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGNESIA">magnesia</a>, a decomposition instantly takes place. All these vapours are composed of elementary fire and some invisible substance capable of assuming a solid form. The decomposition just mentioned is therefore easily explained; the solid part of the air joins itself to the magnesia, while the elementary fire or latent heat is dissipated, and passes through the sides of the vessel. Were it now in our power suddenly to restore the latent heat to the whole of the fixed air, so that it would at once assume its former expansion, a violent explosion would follow. This seems to be precisely the case with the volcanic explosions. An immense quantity of the fixed part of different aerial fluids is united to the various substances found below the surface of the earth. By means of the electric fire which kindles the volcanoes, the aerial fluids are suddenly restored to their elastic state; and not only so, but their natural elasticity is greatly augmented, so that the explosions take place with great violence. The case is the same with gunpowder; only that the condensed air in this case is at first of the deplogisticated kind, but is quickly phlogisticated by reason of the combustible matters mixed with the nitre, while the heat produced by the inflammation augments the elasticity of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> air to four times what it usually is, so that the whole force of the explosion is calculated at 1000 times the pressure of the common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>. Thus the explosions of gunpowder and of volcanoes are essentially the same. The reason of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> quickness of those of gunpowder is, that it takes fire so readily by the intimate mixture and combustibility of all the materials. In volcanoes the explosions likewise follow one another very quickly, and are by no means inferior in strength to those of gunpowder: but here the quantity of vapour makes up for the comparative slowness with which it is affected by the heat. Thus, though we could not by any means contrive to fire cannon in quick succession by means of calcareous earth as we can do with gunpowder, yet in the huge <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a> of a volcano the elastic matter is supplied in such quantities, that the explosions are in a manner unremitting; and even in ordinary experiments the confinement of aerial vapours has often occasioned violent explosions in chemical vessels. In one case too the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a> of fixed air adds excessively to the force of an explosion, viz. in that of pulvis fulminans. This is compounded of sulphur, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> of tartar. The latter we know contains much fixed air: and it is probable that the violence of the explosion is occasioned by this air; for the greater quantity of it that the alkaline salt contains, the greater force does it explode with. Fulminating <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> emits a quantity of phlogisticated air, to which its explosive power is supposed to be owing, as is explained under the article <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>; but that of fulminating silver is so extraordinary, that scarce any force of aerial vapour that can be extricated is likely to produce it, and it seems probable that electricity itself is concerned. Next in strength to the aerial vapours are those of aqueous and other liquids. The most remarkable effects of these are observed in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM">steam</a> engines; but there is one particular case from which it has been inferred that aqueous steam is vastly stronger than the flame of gunpowder. This is when water is thrown upon melted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>; for here the explosion is so strong as almost to exceed imagination; and the most terrible accidents have been known to happen from such a slight cause as per one of the workmen spitting in the furnace where copper was melting. Here, however, it is most probable that a decomposition of the water takes place. That owing to this element can be decomposed, or resolved into elastic vapours, has been completely established by the most satisfactory experiments, and is now, we believe, universally admitted by chemical philosophers. See Water, Chemistry <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The position is indeed denied by the phlogistians; but their arguments appear not to be conclusive; nor is it a fact which militates in the least against their principles. On the supposition that the water is decomposed in the present case, however, the phenomenon in question is easily solved. The water being thrown in substance upon the melted copper, is decomposed by the violent heat; and one part of it adheres to the metal, thus converting it into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALX">calx</a>, or oxide, while the other is converted into inflammable air, or hydrogen <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAS">gas</a>, which expanding suddenly, throws the melted metal all about with the greatest violence by means of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REACTION">reaction</a>. To understand the manner in which this is accomplished, we must consider some of the principles of Gunnery laid down by Mr Robins, and related under that article. One of these is, that though the air, in cases of ordinary velocity, makes no great resistance, it is far otherwise where the velocity of the moving body becomes very great. In all cases of explosion also there is in the first instance a resisting <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VACUUM">vacuum</a> made by the exploding fluid; and consequently the weight of the atmosphere is to be overcome, which amounts to about 14 pounds on every <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> inch of surface. Supposing the surface of the exploding fluid, then, on that of melted copper, to contain an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of 4 square inches, it meets with a resistance of 60 pounds from the atmosphere, and consequently communicates an equal pressure to the fluid metal. Even this must of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> throw it about, unless the same pressure was exactly diffused over every part of the surface. But much more must this effect be increased by the immense velocity with which the fluid moves, and by which the resistance of the atmosphere is augmented in a prodigious degree, as is explained under the article Gunnery. The elastic fluid generated is then confined not only by the fluid metal and sides of the furnace, but by the air itself, which cannot get out of the way; so that the whole resembles a cannon closed at the mouth, and filled with inflamed gunpowder. Hence not only the melted metal, but the furnace itself and the adjacent walls of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, are hurried off as they would be by the firing of a great quantity of gunpowder in a small space, and which is well known to produce analogous effects. In explaining the phenomenon in question, Dr <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> supposes that the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> heat of the metal applied to the aqueous steam produces the explosion; and in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of this alleges, that copper imbibes a greater quantity of heat during fusion than any other metal. Aqueous steam, however, seems to be too slow for producing such sudden and violent effects. Explosions, it is true, will be occasioned by it, but then it must be confined for a very considerable time; whereas the effects of water thrown upon melted copper are instantaneous. It may now be asked, Why such explosions do not take place with any other metal, iron for instance, when water is thrown upon its surface in fusion? In answer to this we must observe, That though water is decomposed by being applied to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>-hot iron in the form of steam, yet there is a possibility, that when the same element is applied in substance to the fluid metal, no decomposition may ensue. Something like this indeed happens with copper itself; for, notwithstanding the violent effects which take place on the contact of water in substance with the melted metal, no explosion happens though aqueous steam be blown upon its surface. On the contrary, the upper part of the metal is thus cooled, and forms itself into cakes, which are afterwards taken off, and new ones formed in the same manner; neither does aqueous steam affect red-hot copper in the manner that it does iron in the same state. A decisive proof that the explosion is not occasioned by the mere heat of the aqueous steam may be deduced from the example of melted glass, which produces no explosion though we pour water upon it in that state; and yet the heat of melted glass is undoubtedly equal at least to that of melted copper. It must be observed, however, that in all cases where a very hot body is thrown upon a small quantity of water in substance, an explosion will follow; but here the water is confined and suddenly rarefied into steam, which cannot get away without throwing off the body which confines it. Examples of this kind frequently occur where masons or other <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a> are employed in fastening cramps of iron into <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, where, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there happens to be a little water in the hole into which the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> is poured, the latter will fly out in such a manner as sometimes to burn them severely. Terrible accidents of this kind have sometimes happened in founderies, when large quantities of melted metal have been poured into wet <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a>. In these cases, the sudden expansion of the aqueous steam has thrown out the metal with violence; and if any decomposition has taken place at the same time, so as to convert the aqueous into an aerial vapour, the explosion must be still greater. To this last kind of explosion we must refer that which takes place on pouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> water into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> or burning oil or tallow. Here the case is much the same whether we pour the oil on the water, or the water on the oil. In the former case, the water which lies at the bottom is rarefied into steam, and explodes; in the latter, it sinks down through the oil by its superior specific gravity, and explodes as it passes along. In either case, however, the quantity of aqueous fluid must be but small in proportion to that of the oil: a very great quantity would put out the flame, or destroy the heat, in whatever way we applied it. Another kind of explosion is that which takes place in solid substances, where we can scarcely suppose either aqueous or aerial vapours to be concerned. The most remarkable of these are the volcanic bombs mentioned by Sir William <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a> in the great eruption of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VESUVIUS">Vesuvius</a> in 1779. They were large pieces of lava which burst in pieces like bombs as they fell to the ground; but he does not inform us whether their bursting was attended with any great violence or not. Indeed, amidst such scenes of horror, and the continual tremendous explosions of the volcano, smaller phenomena of this kind would probably be overlooked. Other examples are the Glass Tears, of which an account is given under that article; the bursting of electrical globes, when put in motion; of other glass vessels spontaneously, and seemingly without any cause; and lastly, the bursting of large <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> metal vessels in the act of cooling. These are all so similar to one another, that it is probable they depend on one general cause. All of them agree in this respect, that the extreme parts of them are considerably cooled, while the internal remain very hot. Thus, in the volcanic bombs, the current of air, formed by their swift passage through it in falling, necessarily carries off a great quantity of heat from the parts which are in contact with it, while the rest are scarce at all cooled. The glass tears are artificially cooled on the outside by dropping them upon water; and in consequence of this, their explosion is probably more violent in proportion to their bulk than that of the volcanic bombs. Glass vessels only burst spontaneously when they have not been well annealed; and we know that this bad <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNEALING">annealing</a> consists only in applying cold too suddenly to the outside. Something like this probably takes place when cast-iron vessels explode; and we are certain it does so with electrical globes, for these last are not apt to burst if they have been well annealed. In all cases, therefore, there is a remarkable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> of the outward surface by the cold, while the internal parts remain as much expanded as ever. In this case there must be a continual effort of that subtle fluid called elementary fire, from the internal to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> part, as the contraction gradually proceeds the contrary way. Thus, when a volcanic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOMB">bomb</a>, for instance, is cooled on the outside, its parts are consolidated so that the internal fluid has not such an easy passage through it as is necessary. In consequence of this it makes a greater effort, which is still farther augmented by the cooling and contraction of the internal parts squeezing the fluid out from among themselves, and forcing it to recoil upon that in the centre, as well as to exert itself against the external part; from which united operation the effect already mentioned at last takes place. This explanation, however, does not hold with respect to electrical globes, glass tears, or ill annealed glass: but in order to accommodate it to all these, we have only to remember, that fire, and the electric fluid acting from a centre to a circumference, are not in the least different; so that from whatever cause the electric matter is disposed to act in this manner, the same effect will follow, i.e., an explosion will take place if the substance does not afford an equally ready passage through all its parts, and that whether any sensible heat is felt in it or not. The only other kind of explosion we have to take notice of is that produced by inflammable and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPHLOGISTICATED">dephlogisticated</a> hydrogenated air, or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXYGEN">oxygen</a> and hydrogen gases, when mixed and oxygen together and set on fire. This differs from any of those hitherto considered, because in reality there is an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a>... Explosion. Inte condensation rather than an expansion throughout the whole of the operation; and the result is the formation of water; and could the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-AIRS">airs</a> be made to take fire throughout their whole substance absolutely at the same instant, there would be no explosion, but only a sudden production of heat. From this cause also is derived a very singular phenomenon, taken notice of by Dr Priestley in his experiments on that subject, recorded in the Phil. Trans. Having enclosed several quantities of inflammable and deplogisticated air in a copper vessel, firing them afterwards by the electric sparks, he found that the force of the explosion was directed more towards one part of the vessel than another; least on that part where the electrical discharge was made, and most upon that which was farthest from it. This inequality was very considerable; insomuch that he could not repeat his experiments any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of times without injuring the vessel in that part which was farthest from the discharge. The reason he gives for this is, that the mixture was not fired at the same instant, but first at the place where the discharge was made. This first explosion would have acted equally upon all parts of the vessel, had it not been for the intervention of the air. By the first momentary explosion, however, the air in the farthest part of the vessel was condensed, so that the next explosion was made stronger, while the copper in the fore part of the vessel had the whole of this strong explosion to resist, the hinder part being but little concerned, as the air in it was condensed and reduced almost to a vacuum. Though the phenomena of explosions are sometimes very destructive, they are likewise of considerable use in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, by removing obstacles which could scarcely be got the better of by any <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> power whatever. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of these are the blowing up of rocks, the separating of stones in quarries, and other purposes of that kind. The destruction occasioned by them in times of war, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> formed upon the principle of explosion for the destruction of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, are well known; and if we cannot call these useful, we must allow them at least to be necessary evils. For the production of explosions, gunpowder is the only substance that has yet been found to answer; nevertheless, as its use is attended with considerable expense, several attempts have been made to find out a cheap substitute for it. One of the most remarkable of these was by mixing small quantities of water, enclosed in little bladders or some easily destructible vehicles, along with a charge of powder. By this contrivance it was hoped that the water being converted into vapour when the powder was inflamed, would augment the force of the explosion: but instead of this, it was found greatly to diminish it. The reason was evident, viz. that the conversion of the water into steam required so much of the latent heat of the inflamed gunpowder, that enough was not left to give the necessary expansion to the aerial fluid produced. A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen gases has also been tried; but the explosion here has always been found too weak. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, indeed, very terrible effects are produced by such a mixture, but in these the quantity is immense; so that the comparative weakness of the mixture cannot be discovered. Electricity therefore seems to be the only resource we have except by adding ingredients to gunpowder which may increase the strength of it. There can be no doubt indeed that the electric fluid is possessed of sufficient strength to perform every thing we could desire; and electricians have supposed, perhaps justly enough, that a cannon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with water might, by means of electricity, become more dangerous than one charged with gunpowder: but this fluid is so exceedingly capricious, so imperceptible and unmanageable, that the use of it cannot as yet be thought practicable, nor in all <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> ever will be so. The effects of explosions, when violent, are felt at a considerable distance, by reason of the concussions they give to the atmosphere; for, as has been already hinted, all of them act upon the atmospherical fluid with and alter the very same force they exert upon terrestrial substances subjected to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>. Sir William Hamilton relates, that at the explosions of Vesuvius in 1767, the doors and windows of the houses at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> flew open if unbolted, and one door was burst open though it had been locked. A great quantity of gunpowder being put into the ditch of a fortified <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and set on fire, destroyed part of the wall, and broke down one of the gates. The blowing up of powder magazines or powder <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a> will destroy buildings and kill people, though certainly without the reach of the flame, and untouched by any part of the shattered <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a> or mill. But the most curious effect is, that they electrify the air, and even glass windows, at a considerable distance. This is always observable in firing the guns of the Tower at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; and some years ago, after an explosion of some powder mills in the neighbourhood of that city, a great number of people were alarmed by a rattling and breaking of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">china</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a>; which by the vulgar was taken for a supernatural phenomenon, but undoubtedly was owing to some commotion in the electrical fluid from the violent concussion of the atmosphere. In this respect, however, the effects of electrical explosions themselves are most remarkable, though not in the uncommon way just mentioned; but it is certain that the influence of a flash of lightning is diffused for a great way round the place where the explosion happens, producing many very perceptible changes both on the animal and vegetable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>.

EXPOENT

Pages 424-424

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALGEBRA">Algebra</a>, the same with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a>. See ALGEBRA. EXPOENT is also used in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>, in the same <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> as index <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> logarithm. EXPOENTIAL <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CALCULUS">Calculus</a>, the method of differencing, or finding the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUXIONS">fluxions</a> of exponential quantities, and of summing up those differences, or finding their fluents. EXPOENTIAL Curve, is that whose <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> is defined or expressed by an exponential equation; as the curve denoted by $a^x = y$, or by $x^a = y$. EXPOENTIAL Equation, is one in which is contained an exponential <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>; as the equation $a^x = b$, or $x^a = b$, &c. EXPOENTIAL Quantity, is that whose power is a variable quantity; as the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> $a^x$, or $x^a$. Exponential quantities are of several degrees and orders, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of exponents or powers, one over another.

EXPORTATION

Pages 424-424

the shipping and carrying out of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> wares and commodities for other countries. See the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">COMMERCE</a>, TRADE, and SHIPPING.

EXPOSING

Pages 424-425

EXPOSING, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of setting a thing to public view. In the Romish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, the sacrament is said to be exposed when it is shown in public uncovered on festival days, and during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of plenary indulgences. EXPOSING is also used with a farther latitude; thus we say, It is prohibited to expose false and clipped <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. Such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> stands very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and has a delicious prospect; but it is exposed to all the four winds. Such a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> being on the frontiers, and not fortified, is exposed to the insults of every party of forces. EXPOSING of Children, a barbarous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> practised by most of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> excepting the Thebans, who had an express <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> to the contrary, whereby it was made <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> to expose children; ordaining at the same time, that such as were not in a condition to educate them should bring them to the magistrates, in order to be brought up at the public expence. Among the other Greeks, when a child was born, it was laid on the ground; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the father designed to educate his child, he immediately took it up; but if he forbore to do this, the child was carried away and exposed. The Lacedemonians indeed had a different custom; for with them all new-born children were brought before certain triers, who were some of the gravest men in their own tribes, by whom the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a> were carefully viewed; and if they were found lusty and well favoured, they gave orders for their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, and allotted a certain proportion of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> for their maintenance; but if weakly <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> deformed, they ordered them to be <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> into a deep cavern in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, near the mountain Taygetus, as thinking it neither for the good of the children themselves nor for the public <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, that defective children should be brought up. Many persons exposed their children only because they were not in a condition to educate them, having no intention that they should perish. It was the unhappy fate of daughters especially to be thus treated, as requiring more charges to educate and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> them in the world than sons. The parents frequently tied jewels and rings to the children they exposed, or any other thing whereby they might afterwards discover them, if <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> took care for their safety. Another <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> in adorning these infants was either to encourage such as found them to nourish and educate them, if alive, or to give them <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a> if dead. The places where it was usual to expose children were such as people frequented most. This was done in order that they might be found, and taken up by compassionate persons who were in circumstances to be at the expense of their education. With this intention, the Egyptians and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> chose the banks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, and the Greeks the high-ways.

EXPOSITION

Pages 425-425

in a literary <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, the explaining an author, passage, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like, and setting their meaning in an obvious and clear <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>.

EXPOSITOR

Pages 425-425
or EXPOSITORY, a title which some writers have given to a lesser kind of dictionaries or vocabularies, serving to expound or explain the meaning of the obscure or difficult words of a language. It is also used in the same sense with commentary and paraphrase.

EXPOSTULATION

Pages 425-425

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, a warm <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> to a person who has done another some injury, representing the wrong in the strongest terms, and demanding redress.

EXPOSURE

Pages 425-425

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>, the situation of a garden wall, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like, with respect to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the compass, as south or east. See Gardening.

EXPRESSED OILS

Pages 425-425

such oils as are obtained from bodies only by pressing. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EXPRESSION

Pages 425-425

in Medicine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, &c. the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of expressing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> extracting the juices or oils of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, or other matters, by squeezing, wringing, or pressing them in a press. After having let the herbs infuse a due <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, their juice must be drawn by expression in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth or by a press.

EXPULSION

Pages 425-425

in Medicine, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> whereby any thing is forcibly driven out of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in which it is: thus we say, the expulsion of the fetus in delivery.

EXSICCATION

Pages 425-425

(formed of ex and sicca, "dry.") in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, &c. the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of drying up <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> evaporating the moisture of a thing.

EXSPIRATION

Pages 425-425

in Physic, that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of respiration by which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is expelled <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> driven out of the lungs. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a> and Respiration.

EXSUDATION

Pages 425-425
or Exudation, the act of sweating out. In which manner, gums, balsams, &c. are usually produced from trees.

EXTANT

Pages 425-425

something that still subsists, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> is in being. It is but <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Livy, of the writings of Cicero, Caesar, &c. that are extant, the rest are lost.
