We have nothing extant of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>, though he wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a>.

EXTASY

Pages 425-425

in Medicine, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of catalepsy, when a person perfectly remembers, after the paroxysm is over, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> he conceived during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it lasted.

EXTENSION

Pages 425-425

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> and essential properties of body; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that by which it possesses or takes up some <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of universal space, which is called the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of that body. See <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>.

EXTENT

Pages 425-426

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is used in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. Sometimes it signifies a writ <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> command to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> for the valuing of lands or tenements; and sometimes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of the sheriff, or other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a>, upon this writ. Old and New Extent, in Scots Law. See LAW <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EXTENUATION

Pages 426-426

is also a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, opposite to the hyperbole. The Greeks call it ἀλήσεις.

EXTERMINATION

Pages 426-426

in general, the extirpating <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> destroying something. EXTERMINATION or EXTERMINATING, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALGEBRA">Algebra</a>, is used for taking away. Thus algebraists speak of exterminating surds, fractions, and unknown quantities out of equations. See MacLaur. Algebr. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">Part</a> I. Chap. 12. where we have some general theorems for the exterminating unknown quantities in given equations.

EXTERNAL

Pages 426-426

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> of relation applied to the surface <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> outside of a body, or that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> which appears or presents itself to the eye, touch, &c., in contradistinction to internal. EXTERNAL is also used to signify any thing that is without side a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, or that is not within himself, particularly in his mind; in which <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> we say, external objects, &c.

EXTINCTION

Pages 426-426

in general, denotes the putting out <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> destroying something, as a fire or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>. See Extinguishing of Fire.

EXTINGUISHMENT

Pages 426-426

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is a consolidation <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> union, as where one has due to him a yearly rent out of lands, and afterwards purchases the lands out of which the rent arises; in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, both the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> and the rent being united in one possessor, the rent is said to be extinguished. EXTRIPATION (formed of ex and strips, "root,") the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of pulling up or destroying a thing to the very roots. Among the prayers of the Romish jubilee, there is one for the extirpation of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>. EXTRIPATION is also used, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> entirely; as a wen, &c. or the eating it away, as a wart, &c. by corrosive medicines.

EXTISPES

Pages 426-426

in antiquity, the person who drew presages from viewing the entrails of animals offered in sacrifice.

EXTORTION

Pages 426-426

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is an illegal manner of wresting any thing from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, either by force, menace, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> authority. It is also the exaction of unlawful usury, winning by unlawful games, and taking more than is due under pretence of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, as excessive tolls in millers, &c. At the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law, extortion is punishable by fine and imprisonment; and the statute of 3 Eliz. 1. c. 30. has enacted, that officers of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> guilty of extortion for the expedition of business, &c. shall render to the party treble value. There are likewise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> other statutes for punishing extortions of sheriffs, bailiffs, gaolers, clerks of the assize and of the peace, attorneys, solicitors, &c.

EXTRACT

Pages 426-426

in matters of literature, is something copied <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> collected from a book or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>.

EXTRACTION

Pages 426-426

in genealogy, implies the stock <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> family from which a person is descended. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">DESCENT</a>. EXTRACTION of Roots, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALGEBRA">Algebra</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">Arithmetic</a>, the method of finding the roots of given numbers or quantities. See ALGEBRA and ARITHMETIC.

EXTRACTOR

Pages 426-426

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDWIFERY">Midwifery</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> forceps for extracting children by the head.

EXTRAJUDICIAL

Pages 426-426

something done out of the proper <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the ordinary course of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>. As when judgment is given in a cause, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, not depending in that court where such judgment is given, or wherein the judge has no jurisdiction.

EXTRAORDINARIUS

Pages 426-426

amongst the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, was a body of men consisting of the third <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the foreign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and a fifth of the foot, which was separated from the rest of the forces borrowed from the confederate states with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> policy and caution, to prevent any <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> that they might possibly entertain against the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> forces. A more choice body of men were drawn from among the extraordinarii, under the name of oblecti. See ABLLECTI.

EXTRAORDINARY

Pages 426-426

something out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> course. EXTRAORDINARY Couriers are those sent express on some urgent occasion. EXTRAORDINARY <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMBASSADOR">Ambassador</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> envoy, is such a one as is sent to treat or negotiate some special and important affair, as a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a>, confederacy, &c. or even on occasion of some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, as condolence, congratulation, &c. A gazette, journal, or other newspaper extraordinary is that published after some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> and notable event, containing the detail or particulars thereof, which are not found in the ordinary papers.

EXTRAVAGANTES

Pages 426-426

those decretal epistles which were published from the Clementines. They were so called, because at first they were not digested <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ranged with the other papal constitutions, but seemed to be, as it were, detached from the canon <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>. They <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to be called by the same name when they were afterwards inserted in the body of the canon law. The first extravagantes are those of John XXII. successor of Clement V. The last collection was brought <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the year 1483, and was called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> extravagantes, notwithstanding that they were likewise incorporated with the rest of the canon law.

EXTRAVASATION

Pages 426-426

in contusions, fissures, depressions, fractures, and other accidents of the cranium, is when one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more of the blood-vessels, that are distributed

EXTREME

Pages 426-427

is applied to the last and outermost <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of any thing; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that which finishes and terminates it on that side.

EXTREMES

Pages 427-427

in Logic, denote the two <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> terms of the conclusion of a syllogism; viz. the predicate and subject. They are called extremes, from their relation to another <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a>, which is a medium <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> between them. The predicate, as being likewise had in the first proposition, is called the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a> extremum, greater extreme; and the subject, as being put in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> proposition, is called the minor extremum, lesser extreme. Thus, in the syllogism, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a> is an animal; <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> is a man, therefore Peter is an animal;" the word animal is the greater extreme, Peter the less extreme, and man the medium. See SYLLOGISM. EXTREME and mean proportion, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, is when a line is so divided, that the whole line is to the greater segment, as that segment is to the other: Or, as it is expressed by Euclid, when the line is so divided that the rectangle under the whole line, and the lesser segment, is equal to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> of the greater segment. EXTREME Unction. See UNCTION. EXTREMITIES of figures, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">Painting</a>, is used for the head, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and feet. These should be drawn with more nicety and exactness, or more terminated than other parts; and thus help to render the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> more expressive.

EXTRINSIC

Pages 427-427

among metaphysicians, is taken in various senses. Sometimes it signifies a thing's not belonging to the essence of another; in which <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> the efficient cause and end of a thing are said to be extrinsic. Sometimes it signifies a thing's not being contained within the capacity of another; in which sense, those causes are called extrinsic which introduce something into a subject from without, as when a fire introduces <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. Sometimes it signifies a thing added <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> applied to another; in which sense accidents and adherents are said to be extrinsic to the subjects to which they adhere. Sometimes the vision is said to be extrinsic from some form which does not exist in that thing, but is adjacent to it, or by some means or other without it.

EXTUBERANCES

Pages 427-427

in Medicine, are swellings <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> risings up in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> or other parts of the body.

EXUBERANCE

Pages 427-427

(compounded of ex and uber, "plentiful"), in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, a redundancy. See REDUNDANCE and PLEONASM. EXUDATION. See EXUSURATION. EXVERRÆ, in antiquity, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a> used in cleansing houses, out of which a dead person had been carried.

EXULCERATION

Pages 427-427

in Medicine, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of causing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> producing ulcers. Thus, arsenic exulcerates the intestines; corrosive humours exulcerate the skin. EXULCERATION is sometimes also used for an ulcer itself; but more generally for those beginning erosions which wear away the substance, and form ulcers.

EXUVIAE

Pages 427-427

among naturalists, denote the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> off parts <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> coverings of animals, as the skins of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a>, caterpillars and other insects. EXUVIAE is also used for shells and other marine bodies, frequently found in the bowels of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; supposed to have been deposited there at the deluge; as being the real spoils of once living creatures. See DELUGE, <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">CONCHOLOGY</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOLOGY">GEOLOGY</a>.

EYE

Pages 427-427

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, 22 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IPSWICH">Ipswich</a> and 91 from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It may be called an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, because it is surrounded by a brook near the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>. It was incorporated by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> John; has two bailiffs, 10 <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> burgesses, 24 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, a recorder, and town clerk. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a>-built <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, with narrow streets. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> manufacture is bone-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LACE">lace</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a>. Here is, however, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> handsome <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; and near it are the ruinous walls of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> castle and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>. The market is on Saturday, the fair on Whit-Monday. It has only sent members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> since the reign of Edward IV. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> 1893 in 1811. EYE-Bright. See EUPHRASIA, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EYMOUTH

Pages 427-428

a town of Scotland in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Berwick, formerly fortified to curb the garrison of Berwick, EZE wick, from which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> it is distant six miles. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 50'. N. Lat. 55° 50'. It gave <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of baron in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Scotland to Churchill, afterwards the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a>; but he having no <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> issue, it became extinct. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> 962 in 1811.

EYRAC

Pages 428-428
or IRAC, ARABIA, a province of Turkey in Asia, 345 miles in length, and 190 in breadth; of which Bagdad is the capital. EYRAC Agermi, the principal province of Persia, anciently called Parthia.

EYRIE

Pages 428-428

in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FALCONRY">Falconry</a>, a brood <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> nest, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where hawks build and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HATCH">hatch</a> their young.

EZEKIEL

Pages 428-428

a canonical book of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, referring chiefly to the degenerate manners and corruptions of the Jews of those times. It abounds with fine sentences and rich comparisons, and discovers a good <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of learning in profane matters. Ezekiel was carried captive to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a> with Jehoiachin, and began his prophecies in the fifth year of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>. He was cotemporary with Jeremiah, who prophesied at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in Judea. He foretold many events, particularly the destruction of the temple, the fatal catastrophe of those who revolted from Babylon to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and the happy return of the Jews to their own <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>. EZION-GABER. See ASIONGABER.

EZRA

Pages 428-428

a canonical book of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>; comprehending the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the Jews from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a>'s edict for their return, to the 20th year of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTAXERXES">Artaxerxes</a> Longimannus. It specifies the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Jews who returned, and Cyrus's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> for the rebuilding the temple, together with the laying its foundation, the obstruction it met with, and the finishing thereof in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a>. The illustrious author of this book was also the restorer and publisher of the canon of the Old Testament. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">BIBLE</a>. The books of Ezra, called in the English version the First and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">Second</a> Book of Esdras, though held by some, particularly the Greeks, for canonical, are thrown by the English <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> into the number of apocryphal books, being only extant in Greek. F. F, THE fourth consonant; and sixth <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>. The letter F is borrowed from the digamma <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> gamma of the Æolians, as is evident from the inscription on the pedestal of the Colossus at Delos; and was undoubtedly formed from the old <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> vau: and though this letter is not found in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Greek alphabet, yet it was in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> one, from whence the Latins received it and transmitted it to us. It is formed by a strong <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of the breath, and joining at the same time the upper <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> and under lip. It has but one sort of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, which has a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> with v and ph; the latter being written for it by us in all Greek words, as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, &c. though the Italians write it filosofia. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> for some time used an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a> F, J, instead of V consonant, which had no peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in their alphabet. Thus, in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> we meet with TERMINA JIT, DIJI, &c. Lipsius and others say, that it was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Claudius who introduced the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the inverted digamma, or J: but it did not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> subsist after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; for Quintilian observes, that it was not used in his time. F, or FA, in Music, is the fourth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> in rising in this order of the gamut, ut, re, mi, fa. It likewise denotes one of the Greek keys in music, destined for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASS">bass</a>. F, in physical <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a>, stands for Fiat, or "Let it be done." Thus f. s. a. signifies fiat secundum artem. F, was also a numeral letter signifying 40; according to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, Sexta quaterdenos gerit qua distat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> alpha. And when a dash was added at top, thus, F, it signified forty thousand. F, in the civil <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>. Two f's joined together thus, ff, signify the Pandects. See PANDECTS. F, in the civil law, a stigma or brand put upon felons with a hot <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, on their being admitted to the benefit of clergy; by stat. 4 Hen. VII. c. 13. FABA. See VICIA, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FABAGO

Pages 428-428

a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of bean-caper. See ZYGOPHYLLUM, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. FABER. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ZEUS">ZEUS</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">ICHTHYOLOGY</a> Index.

FABIAN

Pages 428-428

ROBERT, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALDERMAN">alderman</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> in the year 1494, was a person of learning for the times he lived in, a good poet, and author of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHRONICLE">Chronicle</a> of England and France, entitled The Concordance of Stories, in two volumes folio, beginning with Brute, and ending with the 20th of Henry VII. 1504. It contains several curious particulars relative to the city of London, not elsewhere to be found. Stow calls it "a painful labour, to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the city, and of the whole realm:" We are told that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Wolsey caused as many copies of this book as he could procure to be burned, because the author had made too clear a discovery of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> revenues of the clergy. Fabian died in 1512.

FABII

Pages 428-429

a noble and powerful family at Rome, who derived their name from faba, a bean, because some of their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> cultivated this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>. They were once so numerous that they took upon themselves to wage a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against the Veientes. They came to a general engagement near the Cremera, in which all the family, consisting of 306 men, were totally slain, in the year of Rome 277. There only remained one whose tender <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> had detained him at Rome, and from him arose the noble Fabii in the following ages.

FABIIUS

Pages 429-429

styled Pictor, a Roman general and historian. He first introduced <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> at Rome; and having caused the walls of the temple of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">Health</a> to be painted, some authors have erroneously reckoned him a painter. He died about 216 B.C.

FABIIUS MAXIMUS RULLIANUS

Pages 429-429

was the first of the Fabii who obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of Maximus, for lessening the power of the populace at elections. He was <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>: and his victory over the Samnites in that capacity nearly cost him his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, because he engaged the enemy without the command of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTATOR">dictator</a>. He was five times <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>, twice dictator, and once censor. He triumphed over <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> different nations in the neighbourhood of Rome, and rendered himself illustrious by his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIOTISM">patriotism</a>.

FABIIUS RUSTICUS

Pages 429-429

an historian in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of Claudius and Nero. He was intimate with Seneca; and the encomiums which Tacitus passed upon his style, make us regret the loss of his compositions. Q. FABIIUS MAXIMUS, a celebrated Roman, who from a dull and inactive childhood was raised to the highest offices of the state. In his first consulship he obtained a victory over Liguria; and the fatal <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Thrasymenus occasioned his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> to the dictatorship. In this important office he began to oppose <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a>, not by fighting him in the open field, like his predecessors, but he continually harassed his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> by countermarches and ambuscades, from which he received the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of Cunctator <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Delayer. Hannibal sent him word, "That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he was as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> as he would be thought, he ought to come into the plain and give him battle." But Fabius coldly replied, "That if he was as great a captain as he would be thought, he would do well to force him to fight." Such operations for the commander of the Roman armies gave offence to some; and Fabius was even accused of cowardice. He, however, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> firm in his first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>; and patiently bore to see his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> raised to share the dictatorial <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> with himself by means of his enemies at home. When he had laid <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> his office of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTATOR">dictator</a>, his successors for a while followed his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>; but the rashness of Varro, and his contempt for the operations of Fabius, occasioned the fatal battle of Cannae. Tarentum was obliged to surrender to his arms after the battle of Cannae; and on that occasion the Carthaginian army observed that Fabius was the Hannibal of Rome. When he had made an agreement with Hannibal for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a> of the captives, which was totally disapproved by the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, he sold all his estates to pay the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, rather than forfeit his word to the enemy. The bold proposal of young Scipio to go and carry the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, was rejected by Fabius as chimerical and dangerous. He did not, however, live to see the success of the Roman armies under Scipio, and the conquest of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> which he treated with contempt and heard with indignation. He died in the 100th year of his age, after he had been five times <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>, and twice honoured with a triumph. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> were so sensible of his great merit and services, that the expences of his funeral were defrayed from the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>. His son bore the same name, and shewed himself worthy of his noble father's virtues. During his consulship he received a visit from his father on horseback in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>. The Fabius son ordered his father to dismount; and the old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> cheerfully obeyed, embracing his son, and saying, "I wished to know whether you knew what it is to be consul?" He died before his father, and Cunctator, with the moderation of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, delivered a funeral <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> over the dead body of his son.

FABLE

Pages 429-429

is also used for the plot of an epic <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> dramatic poem; and is, according to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, and, as it were, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> of the poem. See <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">POETRY</a>.

FABRI

Pages 429-429

HONORIUS, a laborious Jesuit, born in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Bellay, distinguished himself by his skill in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, and by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of books; the most curious of which treat of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">optics</a>, the lodestone, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, the ebbing and flowing of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, &c. He died at Rome in 1688.

FABRIANO

Pages 429-429
Gentile da, painter of history, was born at Verona in 1332, and became a disciple of Giovanni da Fiesole. In that early age of painting he rendered himself very famous, and was employed to adorn a great number of churches and palaces at Florence, Urbino, Siena, Perusia, and Rome, but particularly in the Vatican; and one picture of his, representing the Virgin and Child, attended by Joseph, which is preserved in the church of S. Maria Maggiore, was highly commended by Michael Angelo. By order of the doge and senate of Venice, he painted a picture in the great council chamber, which was considered as so extraordinary a performance, that his employers granted him a pension for life, and conferred on him the highest honour of their state, which was, the privilege

FABRIC

Pages 429-430

in general, denotes the structure <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of any thing; but particularly of buildings, as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, &c. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">ARCHITECTURE</a>. FABRIC Lands, those formerly given towards rebuilding and repairing of cathedrals and other churches; for anciently almost every body gave more or less, by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a>, to the fabric of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> church where he dwelt.

FABRICIUS

Pages 430-430

Baron, one of the finest gentlemen of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and known to the public by his letters relating to the transactions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> XII. of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> during his residence in the Ottoman empire, was descended from a good family in Germany. He was taken early into the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLSTEIN">Holstein</a>; and was sent in a public character to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Sweden whilst he was at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDER">Bender</a>; where he soon acquired the good graces of that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. He accompanied him in his exercises; gave him a turn for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>; and it was out of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> Charles snatched Boileau's satires, when he tore out those that represented Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> as a madman. Fabricius was also in favour with Stanislaus, and with our King George I. whom he accompanied in his last journey to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a>, and was with him when he died. A translation of his letters was published in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> 1761.

FABROT

Pages 430-430
CHARLES HANNIBAL, one of the most celebrated civilians of his time, was born at Aix in 1681; and acquired an extraordinary skill in the civil and canon law, and in the belles lettres. He published the Basilicae, or Constitutions of the Emperors of the East, in Greek and Latin, with learned notes, in seven vols. folio; and editions of Cedrenus, Nicetas, Anastasius Bibliothecarius, Constantine Manasses, and Cujas, with learned and curious notes.

FABULOUS

Pages 430-430

something consisting of, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> connected with, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>. FABULOUS <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">Age</a>, among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> historians. See AGE.

FACE

Pages 430-433

is particularly used for the visage of an animal, and especially of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; and comprehends, in the latter, all that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the head which is not covered with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>. The Latins call it facies, vultus, os, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> face is called the image of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, as being the seat of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> organs of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, emotions, &c. of the soul are chiefly set to view. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">Pride</a> and disdain are shown in the eyebrows, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a>, majesty in the forehead, head, &c. It is the face shows the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERAMENT">temperament</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, &c. The face, considered as the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a> of the passions, habits, &c. of the person, makes the subject of physiognomy. See Physiognomy. Face, among painters and artists, is used to denote a certain <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIMENSION">dimension</a> of the human body, adopted for determining the proportion which the several parts should bear to one another. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">Drawing</a>. Face, in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, a word of command, intimating to turn about; thus, face to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, is to turn upon the left heel a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>-round to the right; and, face to the left, is to turn upon the right heel a quarter-round to the left. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACIES_HIPPOCRATICA">Facies Hippocratica</a>, in Medicine, is when the nostrils are sharp, the eyes hollow, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> low, the tips of the ears contracted and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, the forehead dry and wrinkled, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> or livid.—The Hippocratic face is chiefly observed towards the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of phthisis pulmonalis, and other consumptions, and is held a sure prognostic of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> it appear within three days after the attack of an acute disease, it is deemed to indicate death. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTION">Faction</a>, a cabal or party formed in a state, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. Faction, in antiquity, a name given to the different companies of combatants in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CIRCUS">circus</a>. They were four, viz. the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, the green, and the blue; to which Domitian added another of purple <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. They were so denominated from the colour of the liveries they wore; and were dedicated, according to M. Aur. Cassiodorus, to the four seasons of the year; the green being consecrated to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, the blue to winter, the red to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, and the white to autumn. It appears from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>, that each faction had its procurators and physician; and from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, that party rage ran so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> among them, that in a dissension between two factions, in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a>, almost 40,000 men lost their lives in the quarrel. Factitious, any thing made by art, in opposition to what is the production of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. Thus, factitious <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a> is opposed to native cinnamon. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACTOR">Factor</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, is an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> employed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> residing at other places, to buy or sell goods, or negotiate bills, or transact any kind of business on their account; and entitled to a certain allowance for his trouble. A succargo differs from a factor in this: The business of the former is limited to the care of a particular cargo; he goes along with it, and generally returns when his business is completed: the latter has a fixed residence abroad, and executes business for different merchants. But their duties, and the circumstances for which they are accountable, are the same. The duty of a factor is to procure the best intelligence of the state of trade at his place of residence; of the course of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>; of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of goods at market, their present price, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> that it may rise or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a>; to pay exact obedience to the orders of his employers; to consult their advantage in matters referred to his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>; to execute their business with all the dispatch that circumstances admit; to be early in his intelligence, distinct in his accounts, and punctual in his correspondence. A factor's power is either <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> or limited. Though intrusted with ample discretionary powers, he is not warranted to take unreasonable or unusual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, or do anything contrary to his employer's <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>; but it is incumbent on the employer, if he challenge his proceedings, to prove that he could have done better, and was guilty of wilful mismanagement. When a factor's power is limited, he must adhere strictly to his orders. If he exceeds his power, though with a view to his employer's interest, he is liable for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. For example, if he gives <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> when not empowered, or longer credit if not empowered, for the sake of a better price, and the buyer proves insolvent, he is liable for the debt. A factor has no power to give credit unless authorized: But if the goods consigned be generally sold on credit at the place of consignment, the factor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be vindicated for selling at the usual credit, unless expressly restricted. Although <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> will never justify the factor for departing from orders, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> sometimes will. If he be limited not to sell goods under a certain price, and the goods be perishable, and not in a situation for being kept, he may sell them, to prevent their destruction, even under the price limited. A factor is never warranted to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> on trust, except with persons in good credit at the time. If the employer challenges the debtors, it is incumbent on him to prove that their bad circumstances were known at the time of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>; and the factor will be vindicated, if he trusted them at the same time for goods of his own. If the factor sells his employer's goods on trust, and, after the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of payment is elapsed, receive payment from the purchaser for a debt of his own, he becomes liable in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a> for the debt. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of bankruptcy, the factor ought immediately to lay attachments, and advise his employers; and he cannot withdraw his attachments, nor <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> debts, without orders. If a factor sells goods belonging to different merchants to the same person, and the buyer proves insolvent, they shall bear the loss in equal proportions; and if the buyer has paid part before his insolvency, without specifying for which, the payment ought to be distributed in equal proportions; but, if the days of payment be fixed, and part of the debts only due, the payment ought to be applied, in the first place, to such debts as were due. If he makes a wrong entry at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM_HOUSE"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and the goods be seized in consequence thereof, he must bear the loss, unless the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> be occasioned by a mistake in the invoice, or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of advice. The owner bears the loss of goods seized when attempted to be smuggled by his orders; but the factor complying with an unlawful order is liable in such penalties as the laws exact. If a factor saves the duty of goods due to a foreign <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, he shall have the benefit; for, if detected, he bears the loss. If a factor sells goods bought by his employer's orders for his own advantage, the employer may recover the benefit, and the factor shall be amerced for the same. If a factor receives bad <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> in payment, he bears the loss; but if the value of the money be lessened by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, the employer bears the loss. A factor is not liable for goods spoiled, robbed, or destroyed by fire. If a factor receives counterfeit jewels from his employer, and sells them, the employer is liable to indemnify him for any penalties he may incur. If a factor be ordered to make <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSURANCE">insurance</a>, and neglect it, and the subject be lost, he is liable to make it good, providing he had effects in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. If a factor buys goods for his employer, his bargain shall be binding on the employer. In case of a factor's insolvency, the owner may reclaim his goods; and if they be sold on trust, the owner (and not the factor's creditors) shall recover payment of the debts. **Factor**, in multiplication, a name given to the multiplier and multiplicand, because they constitute the product. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">Arithmetic</a>. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACTORAGE">Factorage</a>**, called also <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>, is the allowance given to factors by the merchant who employs them. A factor's commission in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, on most kinds of goods, is 2½ per cent.; on <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and some other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, 2 per cent.; in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, 2½ per cent.; in France, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMBURG">Hamburg</a>, and Dantzig, 2 per cent.; in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, 3 per cent.; in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, 5 per cent. on sales, and 5 per cent. on returns; in the West Indies, 8 per cent. for commission and storage. In some places, it is customary for the factors to ensure the debts for an additional allowance, generally 1½ per cent. In that case, they are accountable for the debt when the usual <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> of credit is expired. Factorage on goods is sometimes <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> at a certain rate per cask, or other package, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, especially when the factor is only employed to receive or deliver them. **<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-FACTORY">Factory</a>** is a place where a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of factors reside, to negotiate for their masters or employers. See Factor. The most considerable factories belonging to the British are those established in the East Indies, Portugal, Turkey, &c. There are also English factories established at Hamburg, Petersburgh, Dantzig, and in Holland; all endowed with certain privileges. **Factum**, in Arithmetic, the product of two quantities multiplied by each other. **Faculae**, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, certain bright and shining parts, which the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> astronomers have, by means of telescopes, observed upon or about the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; they are but seldom seen.—The word is pure Latin; being a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> of *fax*, "torch;" and supposed to be here applied from their appearing and disappearing by turns. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">Faculty</a>**, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a privilege granted to a person, by favour and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a>, of doing what, by law, he ought not to do. For granting these privileges, there is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> under the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, called the court of the faculties. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> officer of this court is styled <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the faculties, and has a power of granting dispensations in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>: as to marry without the banns being first published, to eat <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> on days prohibited, to ordain a deacon under age, for a son to succeed his father in his benefice, a clerk to hold two or more livings, &c. **Faculty**, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, a term applied to the different members of an university, divided according to the arts and sciences taught there: thus in most <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> there are four faculties, viz. 1. Of arts, which include <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. 2. Of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>. 3. Of physic. And, 4. Of civil law. **Faculty of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">Advocates</a>.** See Advocates. **Faculty** is also used to denote the powers of the human mind, viz. understanding, will, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, and imagination. See <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>. **Fæces**, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, or sediment, that settles at the bottom after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a>, and the like.—The fæces of wine are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LEES">Lees</a>. **Fæces**, in Medicine, the excrements voided by stool. See Excrements. **Fæculent**, in general, is applied to things abounding with fæces or dregs: thus the blood and other humours of the human body are said to be fæculent, when without that purity which is necessary to health. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAENZA">Faenza</a>**, a city and bishop's see of Italy, situated in the pope's territories, about 30 miles east of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>. E. Long. 12° 38'. N. Lat. 44° 30'. **Faenza**, a city of Romagna in Italy with a bishop's see. It is an ancient place, and has undergone various revolutions. The river Amona washes its walls, and passes between the city and the suburbs, which are joined by a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> defended by two good towers. The city is remarkable for its earthen <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, which is the best in all Italy. **Faernus, Gabriel**, a native of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREMONA">Cremona</a> in Italy, was an excellent Latin poet and critic of the 16th century. He was so skilled in all parts of polite literature, that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> de Medicis, afterwards Pope Pius IV, was particularly fond of him. He was the author of some Latin elegies; of 100 Latin fables, selected from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, written in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IAMBIC">iambic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>; and of several pieces of criticism, as *Censura emendationum Livianarum*, *De Metris Comicis*, &c. He was remarkably happy in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECIPHERING">deciphering</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>, and restoring ancient authors to their purity: he took such pains with Terence in particular, that Bentley has adopted all his notes in the edition he gave of that writer. He died at Rome in 1561; and Thuanos, who wrote his eulogy, says that the learned world was greatly obliged to him; yet had been still more so, if, instead of suppressing the then unknown fables of Phaedrus, for fear of lessening the value of his own Latin fables, written in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of Æsop, he had been content with imitating them. M. Perrault, however, who translated Faernus's fables into French, has defended him from this imputation, by affirming that the first MS. of Phaedrus's fables, found in the dust of an old library, was not discovered till about 30 years after Faernus's death. **Fagara, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">Iron</a> Wood**; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the tetrandria class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 43rd order, Dumosa. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. **Fage, Raimond de la**, an excellent designer and engraver, highly esteemed by Carlo Maratti, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOULOUSE">Toulouse</a> in 1648. He applied himself to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGNING">designing</a>, through inclination, in spite of his parents; and had no master nor any assistance; but his superior talents supplied the want of them, and he became one of the best designers in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; his performances on li- centious subjects are the most esteemed. It is reported of this <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>, that he never made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of money, but contracted debts; and when the accounts were brought him, he made some <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> upon the back of the bills, and bid the owners sell the drawings to connoisseurs for the amount, by which they were generally <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> gainers. Several of those drawings are yet in the cabinets of the curious. He led a loose, depraved <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; and his repeated debaucheries put an end to it at the age of 42.

FAGGOT

Pages 433-433

in times of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a> here, was a badge worn on the sleeve of the upper garment of such persons as had recanted <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> abjured what was then termed <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>; being put on after the person had carried a faggot, by way of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a>, to some appointed <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of solemnity. The leaving off the wear of this badge was sometimes interpreted a sign of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOSTASY">apostasy</a>.

FAGGOTS

Pages 433-433

among <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> men, persons hired by officers, whose companies are not full, to muster and hide the deficiencies of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>; by which means they cheat the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of so much <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>.

FAGIUS

Pages 433-433

PAUL, alias BUCHLIN, a learned Protestant minister, born at Rheinzaehem in Germany in 1504. He was a schoolmaster at Isna; but afterwards became a zealous preacher, and wrote many books. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> in Germany menacing danger to all who did not profess the Romish doctrines, he and Bucer came over to England in 1549, at the invitation of Archbishop Cranmer, to perfect a new translation of the Scriptures. Fagius took the Old <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, and Bucer the New, for their respective parts; but the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> was at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> frustrated by the sudden deaths of both. Fagus died in 1550, and Bucer did not live above a year after. Their bodies were dug up and burned in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>.

FAGONIA

Pages 433-433

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the deciduous class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 14th order, Gruinales. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FAGUS

Pages 433-433

the Beech Tree; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the monocotyledonous class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 50th order, Amentaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The chestnut tree, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> belonging to this genus, sometimes grows to an immense size. The largest in the known world are those which grow upon Mount Etna in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>. At Tortworth in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a>, is a chestnut tree 52 feet round. It is proved to have stood there ever since the year 1150, and was then so remarkable, that it was called the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> chestnut of Tortworth. It fixes the boundary of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANOR">manor</a>, and is probably near 1000 years old. As an ornamental, the chestnut, though unequal to the oak, the beech, and the elms, has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of greatness belonging to it which recommends it strongly to the gardener's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. Its uses have been highly extolled; and it may deserve a considerable share of the praise which has been given it. As a substitute for the oak, it is preferable to the elm. For door-jams, window-frames, and some other purposes of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> carpenter, it is nearly equal to oak itself; but it is very apt to be shakey, and there is a deceitful brittleness in it which renders it unsafe to be used as beams, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in any other situation where an uncertain load is required to be borne. It is universally allowed to be excellent for liquor casks; as not being liable to shrink nor to change the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the liquor it contains; it is also strongly recommended as an underwood for hop-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>, stakes, &c. Its fruit too is valuable, not only for swine and deer, but as a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> food: <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">Bread</a> is said to have been made of it. Upon the whole, the chestnut, whether in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of ornament or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, is undoubtedly an object of the planter's notice.

FAINT ACTION

Pages 433-433

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a feigned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> such as, although the words of the writ are true; yet for certain causes, the plaintiff has no <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to recover thereby.

FAINT PLEADER

Pages 433-433

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a covinous, false, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> compulsory manner of pleading, to the deceit of a third person. FAINTING. See LIPOTHYMA, MEDICINE <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FAINTS

Pages 433-433

in the distillery, the weak spirituous liquor that runs from the still in rectifying the low wines after the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>-spirit is taken off. FAINTS are also the lastrunings of all distilled spirits. The clearing the worm of these is so essential a point in order to the obtaining a pure spirit by the subsequent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>, that all others are fruitless without it.

FAIR

Pages 433-435

a greater kind of market, granted to a town, by privilege, for the more speedy and commodious providing of such things as the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> stands in need of. The word fair, is formed from the French foire, which signifies the same thing; and foire is by some derived from the Latin forum, "market;" by others from the Latin feria, because anciently <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> were always held in the places where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAKES">wakes</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> feasts of the dedications of churches, called feriae, were held. See Feriae. It is incident to a fair, that persons should be free from being arrested in it for any other debt or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> than what was contracted in the same; or, at least, promised to be paid there. These fairs are generally kept once or twice a-year; and, by statute, they shall not be held longer than they ought by the lords thereof, on pain of their being seized into the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, &c. Also <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> is to be made, how <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> they are to continue; and no person shall sell any goods after the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the fair is ended, on forfeiture of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the value, one-fourth to the prosecutor and the rest to the king. There is a toll usually paid in fairs on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of things, and for stallage, picage, &c. Fairs abroad are either free, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with toll and impost. The privileges of free fairs consist chiefly, first, in that all traders, &c., whether natives or foreigners, are allowed to enter the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, and are under the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> protection, exempt from duties, impositions, tolls, &c. Secondly, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, in going or returning, cannot be molested or arrested, or their goods stopped. They are established by letters-patent from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. Fairs, particularly free fairs, make a very considerable article in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, especially that of the Mediterranean, and inland parts of Germany, &c. The most celebrated fairs in Europe are those, 1. Of Frankfort, held twice a-year, in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> and autumn: the first commencing the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> before Palm-Sunday, and the other on the Sunday before the eighth of September. Each lasts 14 days, or two weeks: the first of which is called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ACCEPTANCE">acceptance</a>, tance, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> the week of payment. They are famous for the sale of all kinds of commodities; but particularly for the immense <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of curious books nowhere else to be found, and whence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOOKSELLERS">booksellers</a> throughout all Europe used to furnish themselves. Before each fair, there is a catalogue of all the books to be sold thereat, printed and dispersed, to call together purchasers: though the learned complain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> unfair practices therein; as fictitious titles, names of books purely imaginary, &c. beside <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> faults in the names of the authors, and the titles of the real books. 2. The fairs of Leipsic, which are held thrice a year; one beginning on the first of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>; another three weeks after Easter; and a third after Michaelmas. They hold 12 days a-piece; and are at least as considerable as those of Francfort. 3. The fairs of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVI">Novi</a>, a little <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> in the Milanese, under the dominion of the republic of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>. There are four in the year, commencing on the second of February, the second of May, the first of August, and second of September. Though the commodities bought and sold here be very considerable; yet, what chiefly contributes to render them so famous, is the vast concourse of the most considerable merchants and negotiants of the neighbouring kingdoms, for the transacting of affairs and settling accounts. 4. The fairs of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGA">Riga</a>, whereof there are two in the year; one in May and the other in September. They are much frequented by the English, Dutch, and French ships, as also from all parts of the Baltic. The best time for the sale of goods at Riga is during the fairs. Since the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of the famous city of Petersburgh, these fairs have suffered some diminution. 5. Fairs of Archangel, during which all the trade foreigners have with that city is managed. It holds a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, or six weeks at most, commencing from the middle of August. The Muscovite merchants attend here from all parts of that vast empire; and the English, Dutch, French, Swedish, Danish, and other ships in the port of that city, on this occasion, ordinarily amount to 300. But this is no free fair as the rest are: The duties of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> and importation are very strictly paid, and on a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> footing. 6. The fair of St Germain, one of the suburbs of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, commencing on the third of February, and holding till Easter; though it is only free for the first 15 days. 7. The fairs of Lyons, which Mons. du Chesne, in his Antiquity of Cities, would insinuate, from a passage in Strabo, were established by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; though it is certain, the fairs, as they now stand, are of a much later <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a>. There are three in the year, each lasting 20 days, and free for ever. They begin on Easter Monday, the 26th of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, and the first of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>. 8. Fair of Guibray, a suburb of the city of Falaise in the Lower Normandy. It is said to have been established by our William the Conqueror, in consideration of his being born at Falaise. It commences on the 16th of August; and holds 15 days free by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>, and longer by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>. 9. Fair of Beaucaire, held partly in a city of that name, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>, and partly in the open <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, under tents, &c. It commences on the 22d of July, and only holds for three days; yet it is the greatest and most celebrated of all the fairs in that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Europe, both for the concourse of strangers from all parts of the world, and for the traffic of all kinds of goods: the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> returned in these three days amounting sometimes to above six millions of livres. The fairs of Porto Bello, Vera Cruz, and the Havana, are the most considerable of all those in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. The two first last as long as the flota and galleons continue in those ports; and the last is opened as soon as the flota or galleons arrive there upon their return for <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; this being the place where the two fleets join. See Flota and Galleons. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> British fairs are, 1. Sturbridge fair, near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, by far the greatest in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, and perhaps in the world. 2. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a> has two fairs, very near as great as that of Sturbridge. 3. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>. 4. West <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>. 5. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>. 6. Wheylhill; and 7. Bursford fair; both for sheep. 8. Pancras fair, in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a>, for saddle-horses. 9. Bartholomew fair, at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, for lean and Welsh <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle. 10. St <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">Faith</a>'s, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, for Scotch runts. 11. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-YARMOUTH">Yarmouth</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> fair for herrings; the only fishing fair in Great Britain. 12. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IPSWICH">Ipswich</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a> fair. 13. Woodborough-hill, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a>, for west country <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, as kerseys, draggets, &c. 14. Two cheese fairs at Chipping <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NORTON">Norton</a>: with innumerable other fairs, besides weekly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>, for all sorts of goods as well our own as of foreign growth. Fair, in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, is used for the disposition of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, when it is favourable to a ship's course, in opposition to that which is contrary or foul. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> fair is more comprehensive than <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and includes about 16 or 18 <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the compass; whereas large is confined to the beam or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, that is, to a wind which crosses the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEEL">keel</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, or obliquely from the stern, but never to one right a-stern. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAIR_ISLE">Fair <a c</a>lass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a>, a small <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> lying between Orkney and Shetland, 10 or 12 leagues E. N. E. from the former; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>, eight, or 10 leagues S. W. from the latter. It is three miles long, and scarcely half a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, very craggy, with three high rocks which are visible both from Orkney and Shetland. It contains a small quantity of arable <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, which is very fruitful and well manured; excellent pasturage for sheep; and affords great plenty of sea and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> fowl, and all kinds of fish upon the coasts. There is in effect no port, though they have two that are nominally so; one at the south end, which is full of rocks, where only small boats can <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a>; the other at the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east end, larger and safer in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, so that it serves commodiously enough for their fishery.
