The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEDINA_SIDONIA">Medina Sidonia</a>, when commander of the famous Spanish armada in 1588, was wrecked on the east <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of this island. The ship broke to pieces, but the duke and 200 made their escape. They lived here so long, that both they and the inhabitants were almost famished. At length the duke and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> remains of his people were carried over to the main land of Shetland, and thence to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUNKIRK">Dunkirk</a>, by one Andrew Humphry, for which <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> Andrew was rewarded with 3000 merks. This island produced to its former proprietor between 50 and 60l. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. It was sold at Edinburgh in 1766, for about 850l. to James Stewart of Burgh, Esq. Fair-curve, is a winding line, used in delineating ships, whose shape is varied, according to the part of the ship which it is intended to describe. Fair-way, in sea language, the path or channel of a narrow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, river, or haven, in which ships usually advance advance in their passage up and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>; so that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any vessels are anchored therein, they are said to lie in the fair-way.

FAIRFAX

Pages 435-435

Sir Thomas, general of the parliamentary forces against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I., in 1644. See (<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of) <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, No. 127. et seq. He resigned in 1650; after which he lived privately, till he was invited by General Monk to assist him against Lambert's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. He cheerfully embraced the occasion; and, on the third of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1659, appeared at the head of a body of gentlemen of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>; when, upon the reputation of his name, a body of 12,000 men forsook Lambert and joined him. He was at the head of the committee appointed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of commons to attend <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Charles II. at The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a>, to desire him speedily to return to England; and having readily assisted in his restoration, returned again to his seat in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; where he lived in a private manner till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened in 1671, in the 60th year of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>.—He wrote, says Mr Walpole, Memorials of Thomas <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Fairfax, printed in 1699; and was not only an historian, but a poet. In Mr Thoresby's <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a> were preserved in manuscript the following pieces: The Psalms of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a>, the Canticles, the Songs of Moses, and other parts of Scripture, versified, a poem on Solitude; Notes of Sermons, by his lordship, by his lady <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Horace Lord Vere, and by their daughter <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> the wife of George <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUCKINGHAM">Buckingham</a>; and a Treatise on the Shortness of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a>. But of all Lord Fairfax's works, says Mr Walpole, the most remarkable were the verses he wrote on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> on which Charles II. rode to his coronation, and which had been bred and presented to the king by his lordship. How must that merry monarch, unapt to keep his countenance on more serious occasions, have smiled at this awkward homage from the old victorious <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> of republicanism and the covenant! He gave a collection of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> to the Bodleian library.

FAIRFORD

Pages 435-435

a town in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a>, with a market on Thursdays. It is remarkable for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, which has curious painted glass windows. They are said to have been taken in a ship by John Tame, Esq., towards the end of the 17th century, who built the church for their sake. They are preserved entire, and the figures are extremely well drawn and coloured. They represent the most remarkable histories in the Old and New <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>. They are frequently visited by travellers, and many go on purpose to view them, as one of the greatest curiosities in England. The painter was Albert Durer. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> 1442 in 1811. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>, i. 46. N. Lat. 51. 42.

FAIRY

Pages 435-437

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> traditions and romances, signifies a sort of deity, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> imaginary genius, conversant on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and distinguished by a variety of fantastic actions either good or bad. They were most usually imagined to be women of an order superior to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, yet subject to wants, passions, accidents, and even <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; sprightly and benevolent while young and handsome; morose, peevish, and malignant, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> ugly, or in the decline of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>; fond of appearing in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, whence they are often called the white ladies. Concerning these imaginary beings, no less a person than Jervaise of Tilleberry, marshal of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARLES">Arles</a>, who lived in the beginning of the 13th century, writes thus in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Otho IV.: "It has been asserted by persons of unexceptionable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>, that fairies used to choose themselves gallants from among men, and rewarded their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> with an affluence of worldly goods; but if they married, or boasted of a fairy's favours, they as severely smarted for such indiscretion." The like tales still go current in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>; and throughout the whole <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, there is not a village without some ancient seat or cavern which had the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of being a fairy's residence, or at least some <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> where a fairy used to bathe. This idea of fairies has a near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> with that of the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, concerning the nymphs of the woods, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>; and an ancient scholiast on <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOCRITUS">Theocritus</a> says, "The nymphs are demons which appear on the mountains in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of women;" and what is more surprising, the Arabs and other orientals have their gin and peri, of whom they entertain the like notions. But fairies have been likewise described as of either <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, and generally as of minute stature, though capable of assuming various forms and dimensions. The most charming representation imaginable of these children of romantic fancy, is in the Midsummer Night's Dream of Shakespeare; in referring to which, we no doubt have been anticipated by the recollection of almost every reader. Spenser's Faery Queene is an epic poem, under the persons and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of fairies. This sort of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> raises a pleasing kind of horror in the mind of the reader, and amuses his imagination with the strangeness and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a> of the persons who are represented in it; but, as a vehicle of instruction, the judicious object to it, as not having <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> enough to make any moral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> of fairies still subsists in many parts of our own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The "Swart fairy of the mine" (of German <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>), has scarce yet quitted our subterraneous works; (vid. next article. Puck, or Robin Goodfellow, still haunts many of our villages. And in many parts of Scotland, new-born children are watched till the christening is over, lest they should be stolen or changed by some of these fantastical existences. Fairy of the Mine: an imaginary being, an inhabitant of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a>. The Germans believed in two <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; one fierce and malevolent; the other a gentle <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, appearing like little old men dressed like the miners, and not much above two feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. These wander about the drifts and chambers of the works; seem perpetually employed, employed, yet do nothing; some seem to cut the ore, or fling what is cut into vessels, or turn the windlass: but never do any harm to the miners, unless provoked; as the sensible Agricola, in this point credulous, relates in his book de Animantibus Subterraneis. Fairy Circle or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">Ring</a>, a phenomenon pretty frequent in the fields, &c., supposed by the vulgar to be traced by the fairies in their dances. There are two kinds of it; one of about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> yards in diameter, containing a round bare path, a foot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, with green grass in the middle of it. The other is of different largeness, encompassed with a circumference of grass. Messrs. Jessop and Walker, in the Philosophical Transactions, ascribe them to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>; which is thought to be confirmed by their being most frequently produced after storms of that kind, as well as by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> and brittleness of the grass roots when first observed. Lightning, like all other fires, moves round, and burns more in the extremity than in the middle; the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> circle arises from the first, the grass burnt up growing very plentifully afterwards. Others maintain that these circles are made by ants, which are frequently found in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers therein.—Mr. Cavallo, in his treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">electricity</a>, does not think that lightning is at all concerned in the formation of them: "They are not (says he) always of a circular figure; and, as I am informed, they seem to be rather beds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUSHROOMS">mushrooms</a> than the effects of lightning. We have frequently observed beds of mushrooms arranged in a circular form like what are called fairy rings; but it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be difficult to account for the mushroom seed being disposed in this manner. It is probable that the seed is dispersed over the whole field, and remains dormant till it is acted on by some stimulus to excite its vegetating powers. Perhaps this stimulus is atmospheric electricity, which acting on particular spots only, produces on them an abundant crop of mushrooms, while none appear in other places. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">Faith</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a>, that assent which we give to a proposition advanced by another, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of which we do not immediately perceive from our own reason or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>; or it is a judgment or assent of the mind, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> whereof is not any intrinsic <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a>, but the authority or testimony of some other who reveals or relates it. Hence, as there are two kinds of authorities and testimonies, the one of God, and the other of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, faith becomes distinguished into divine and human. Divine Faith, is that founded on the authority of God; or it is that assent we give to what is revealed by God. The objects of this faith, therefore, are matters of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a>. See Revelation and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">Religion</a>. Human Faith, is that whereby we believe what is told us by men. The object hereof is <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of human testimony and evidence. See <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>. Faith, in practical theology, makes the first of the theological virtues or graces. Faith in God, in this <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, denotes such a conviction of his being, perfections, character, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, as produces <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, trust, worship, obedience, and resignation. Faith in Christ, as it has been defined by some, is a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> assent to the gospel as true; according to others, it signifies such a persuasion that he is the Messiah, and such a desire and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of the blessings which he has promised in his gospel to his sincere disciples, as engage the mind to fix its dependence upon him, and subject itself to him in all the ways of holy obedience. See Theology. Faith, likewise, in respect to futurity, is a moral principle, implying such a conviction of the reality and importance of a future state, as is sufficient to regulate the temper and conduct. Earth, or Fidelity (Fides), was deified by the ancient Romans, and had a temple in the Capitol consecrated to her by Attilius Catalinus. Her priests wore white veils; unbloody sacrifices were offered to her, and the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> were taken in her name. Horace clothes her in white, places her in the retinue of Fortune, and makes her the sister of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">Justice</a>, Od. 24, 35. l. i. Public Faith is represented in a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of medals; sometimes with a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASKET">basket</a> of fruit in one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and some ears of corn in the other; and sometimes holding a turtle-dove. But the most usual symbol is two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> joined together. The <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> are generally, Fides Augusti, Fides Exercitus, or Fides Militum, &c. Faithful, an appellation assumed by the Mahometans. See Mahometans. Faithorn, William, an ingenious English <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>, a native of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, was the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Peak the painter, and worked with him three or four years. At the breaking out of the civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, Peak espoused the cause of his sovereign: and Faithorn, who accompanied his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, was taken prisoner by the rebels at Baringhouse, from whence he was sent to London, and confined in Aldersgate. In this uncomfortable situation he exercised his graver; and a small head of the first Villars <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUCKINGHAM">Buckingham</a>, in the style of Melan, is reckoned among his performances at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The solicitations of his friends in his favour at last prevailed; and he was released from prison, with permission to retire to the continent. In France he found encouragement and protection from the Abbé de Marolles; and it was at this time that he formed an acquaintance with Nanteuil, from whose instructions he derived very considerable advantages. About the year 1650 he returned to England, and soon after married the sister of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Ground. By her he had two sons; Henry, who was a bookseller, and William an engraver in mezzotinto. Faithorn opened a shop near Temple-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">Bar</a>, where he sold not only his own engravings, but those of other English artists, and imported a considerable number of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, France, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. About the year 1680, he retired from his shop, and resided in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">Printing</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">House</a> Yard; but he still <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to work for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOOKSELLERS">booksellers</a>, especially <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYSTON">Royston</a>, Martin, and Peak the younger, his former master's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>. He painted portraits from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in crayons; which art he learned of Nanteuil during his abode in France. He also painted in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINIATURE">miniature</a>; and his performances in both these styles were much esteemed. His spirits were broken by the indiscretion and dissipation of his son William; and a lingering consumption put an end to his life in 1691. He wrote a book Upon <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">Drawing</a>, Graving, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ETCHING">Etching</a>, for which he was celebrated by his friend Thomas Flatman the poet. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAKIRS">Fakirs</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> monks or friars. They outdo the severity and mortification of the ancient Anchores or Solitaries. Some of them make a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOW">vow</a> of continuing all their lifetime in one posture, and keep it effectually. Others never <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>; but continue in a standing posture all their lives, supported only by a stick, or rope under their arm pits. Some mangle their bodies with scourges and knives. They look upon themselves to have conquered every <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, and triumphed over the world; and accordingly scruple not, as if in a state of innocence, to appear entirely naked in public. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people of East <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a> are thoroughly persuaded of the virtue and innocence of the fakirs; notwithstanding which, they are accused of committing the most enormous crimes in private. They have also another kind of fakirs, who do not practise such severities: these flock together in companies, and go from village to village; prophesying, and telling fortunes. They are wicked villains, and it is dangerous for a man to meet them in a lone <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>: nevertheless the Indian idolaters have them in the utmost veneration. They make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of drums, trumpets, and other musical instruments, to rouse their souls, and work themselves up to an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> ecstasy, the better to publish their pretended prophecies. Some of the votaries of these sages most devoutly kiss their privy parts; and they receive this monstrous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> of respect with a kind of ecstatic <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. The most sober and discreet Indians consult them in this preposterous attitude; and their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> votaries <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> with them a considerable time with the most indecent freedom. The fire they burn is made of cows dung, dried in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. When they are disposed to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, they repose themselves on cows dung, and sometimes on ordure itself. They are so indulgent towards every living creature, that they suffer themselves to be overrun with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VERMIN">vermin</a>, or stung by insects, without the least reluctance or complaint. It is more than probable, those Indian friars have some secret art to lull their senses asleep, in order to render themselves in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> insensible of the excessive torments they voluntarily undergo. Ovington assures us, that "as he was one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> in an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of fakirs, he observed, that they drank opiates infused in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; the intoxicating virtue thereof was enough to turn their brain." The garment of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> fakirs consists of three or four yards of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>-coloured <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, which they tie round them, and a tiger's skin, which hangs over their shoulders. Their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> is woven in tresses, and forms a kind of turban. The superior of the fakirs is distinguished from the rest by having a greater number of pieces in his garment, and by a chain of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, two yards <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, tied to his leg. When he designs to rest in any place, a garment is spread upon the ground; on which he sits and gives audience, whilst his disciples publish his virtues. Some persons of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> in India have become fakirs: among others, five great lords belonging to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Schah Gehan, Mogul of the Indies. It is said, there are about two millions of fakirs in the East Indies.

FALASHA

Pages 437-438

a people of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>, of Jewish origin, described by Mr Bruce, who was at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> pains to acquaint himself with their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> by cultivating the friendship of the most learned persons among them he could meet with. According to the accounts received from them, the Falasha are the descendants of those Jews who came from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a> into Ethiopia, as attendants of Menilek the son of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of Sheba <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Saba by <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>. They agree in the relation given by the Abyssinians of that princess, but deny that the posterity of those who came with Menilek ever embraced the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, as the Abyssinians say they did. They say, that at the decline of the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, when the ports of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> fell into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of other nations, and no intercourse took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> betwixt them and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, the Jewish inhabitants quitted the sea coasts and retired into the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEMBEA">Dembea</a>. While they remained in the cities on the Red sea, they exercised the trades of brick and tile making, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-POTTERY">pottery</a>, thatching houses, &c. and after leaving these coasts, they chose the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Dembea on account of the plenty of materials it afforded for exercising the trades they professed. Here they carried the art of pottery to a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of perfection, multiplied exceedingly, and became very numerous and powerful about the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that the Abyssinians were converted to Christianity. As this event was accounted by them an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOSTASY">apostasy</a> from the true religion, they now separated themselves from the Abyssinians, and declared one <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PHINEAS">Phineas</a>, of the line of Solomon, their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>. Thus, they say, they have still a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Judah for their sovereign, though their assertion is treated with contempt, and a nickname bestowed on the Falashan family by the other Abyssinians. About the year 960 the queen of this people, after extirpating the Abyssinian princes on the rock Damo, assumed the sovereignty of the whole empire, which they retained for some time; but their power being by degrees reduced, they were obliged to take up their residence among the rugged <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Samen; one of which they chose for their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, and which has ever since been called the Jew's Rock. About the year 1600, they were almost entirely ruined by an overthrow from the Abyssinians, in which both their king and queen were slain; since which time they have been in subjection to the emperors of that country, but are still governed by their own princes. When Mr Bruce was in Abyssinia they were supposed to amount to about 100,000 effective men. Gideon and Judith were the names of the king and queen at that time; and these, according to our author, seem to be preferred to others for the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of this people is very different from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, Samaritan, or any other which the Jews ever spoke in their own country. On being interrogated concerning it by Mr Bruce, they said, that it was probably one of those spoken by the nations on the Red sea, among whom they had settled at their first coming. They arrived in Abyssinia, speaking Hebrew, and with the advantage of having books in that language; but had now forgot it, which indeed is not to be wondered at, as they had lost their Hebrew books, and were entirely ignorant of the art of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. At the time of their leaving Jerusalem, they were in possession both of the Hebrew and Samaritan copies of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>; but when their fleet was destroyed in the time of Rehoboam, and no farther <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with Jerusalem took place, they were obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> translations of the Scriptures, or those copies which were in possession of the shepherds, who, they say, were all Jews before the time of Solomon. On being asked, however, where the shepherds got their copy, and being told, that notwithstanding the invasion of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> by <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-NEBUCHADNEZZAR">Nebuchadnezzar</a>, there was still a communication with Jerusalem by means of the Ishmaelite Arabs through <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, they frankly acknowledged that they could not tell: neither had they any memorials of the history either of their own or any other country; all that they believed in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> being derived from <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>, their histories, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any existed, having been destroyed by the famous Moorish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> Gragné. They say that the first book of Scripture they received was that of Enoch; and they place that of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOB">Job</a> immediately after it, supposing that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> to have lived soon after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>. They have no copy of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> in the Falasha language, what they make use of being in that of Geez. This is sold to them by the Abyssinian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, who are the only scribes in that country. No <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> takes place about corruptions of the text; nor do the Falasha know anything of the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALMUD">Talmud</a>, Targum, or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CABALA">Cabala</a>. See Abyssinia.

FALCADE

Pages 438-438

in the manege, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> when he throws himself upon his haunches two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three times, as in very quick curves; which is done in forming a stop and half stop. See Stop.

FALCATED

Pages 438-438

something in the form of a sickle: thus the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> is said to be falcated when she appears horned.

FALCO

Pages 438-438

the eagle and hawk, a genus of birds belonging to the order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCIPITRES">accipitres</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FALCON

Pages 438-438
or Faucon, a bird of prey of the hawk kind, superior to all others for courage, docility, gentleness, and nobleness of nature*. Several authors take the name falcon to have been occasioned by its crooked talons or pounces, which resemble a falx or sickle. Giraldos derives it à falcando, because it flies in a curve. The falcon, or falcon gentle, is both for the fist and for the lure. In the choice, take one that has wide nostrils, high and large eyelids, a large black eye; a round head, somewhat full on the top; barb feathers on the clap of the beaks, which should be short, thick, and of an azure colour; the breast large, round and fleshy; and the thighs, legs, and feet, large and strong, with the soars of the foot soft and bluish: the pounces should be black, with wings long and crossing the train, which should be short and very pliable. The name falcon is restrained to the female: for the male is much smaller, weaker, and less courageous than the female; and therefore is denominated tassel, or tirolet. The falcon is excellent at the river, brook, and even field; and flies chiefly at the larger game, as wild goose, kite, crow, heron, crane, pye, shoveler, &c. For further particulars, see Falconry and Hawking. The custom of carrying a falcon extended to many countries, and was esteemed a distinction of a man of rank. The Welsh had a saying, That you may know a gentleman by his hawk, horse, and greyhound. In fact, a person of rank seldom went without one on his hand. Harold, afterwards king of England, is painted going on a most important embassy, with a hawk on his hand and a dog under his arm. Henry VI. is represented at his nuptials, attended by a nobleman and his falcon. Even the ladies were not without them in earlier times; for in an ancient sculpture in the church of Milton Abbas, in Dorsetshire, appears the consort of King Athelstan with a falcon on her royal fist tearing a bird.

FALCONER

Pages 438-438

William, an ingenious Scots sailor, who, about the year 1762, came up to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> with a pretty pathetic poem, called the Shipwreck, founded on a disaster of his own <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. The publication of this piece recommended him to the late <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>; and he would in all <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> have been suitably preferred, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> shipwreck, as may be supposed, had not proved fatal to him, and to many gentlemen of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and fortune with whom he sailed. In 1770, he went out a volunteer in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AURORA">Aurora</a> frigate, sent to carry Messrs Vansittart, Scratton, and Ford, the supervisors appointed to regulate our East <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a> settlements; which vessel, after it had touched at the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope, was never more heard of. Before his departure, he published a very useful Marine <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, in one volume 4to.

FALCONRY

Pages 438-440

a kind of sport <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> amusement, respecting the antiquity of which different opinions have been entertained by the learned. It is denied by Blondus, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAURENTIUS">Laurentius</a> Valla, and others, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greeks knew anything about falconry; but the learned Professor Beckmann, on the most unequivocal authority, maintains that they did. He admits that they might be ignorant of the art of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAWKING">hawking</a>, or of chasing chasing <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAME">game</a> with birds trained for that purpose; but he contends that they employed some <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the most rapacious of the winged tribe in hunting and fowling. In the days of Ctesias, the Indians hunted hares and foxes by means of rapacious birds; and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> says expressly, "In Thrace, the men go out to catch birds with hawks. They <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> the reeds and bushes which grow in marshy places, in order to raise the small birds, which the hawks pursue and drive to the ground, where the fowlers kill them with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>." Respecting Thrace, which is situated above Amphipolis, a wonderful circumstance is related, which to many may appear almost incredible. We are informed that boys went into the fields, and pursued birds by the assistance of hawks. When they found a convenient <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for their purpose, they called their hawks by their particular names, which came immediately on hearing their voices, and pursued the birds into the bushes, where the boys killed them with sticks, and thus made them their prey. When the hawks themselves laid hold of any birds, they threw them to the fowlers, and received, for their fidelity, a share of the game. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> we add the spaniel, now employed to find out the game, the hood placed upon the head of the hawk, and the thong for holding it, we may clearly perceive in these ancient accounts the practice of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times. Falconers still give a portion of the game to the hawk, as was the usual practice of the boys in Thrace. According to the testimony of Philo, Pliny, Ælian, and others, the birds were sometimes driven into nets by the hawks employed in these sports. From <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a> and Thrace, therefore, it seems manifest, that the Greeks obtained their first information as to the method of fowling with birds of prey; but they themselves do not appear to have adopted the practice at a very early <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, however, it must have been extremely well understood, since it is mentioned by Martial and Apuleius as a thing everywhere known. After being once known, it was never totally forgotten; but it shared the fate of other inventions in this respect, that it was originally admired, and afterwards much neglected, by which means it received no material improvements for a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; yet it was at length brought to the utmost perfection. We find mention made of this sport in the Roman laws, and in many authors of the fourth and subsequent century. In the time of Constantine the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, Julius Firmicus Maternus assures us, according to the superstitious notions of that period, that such as are born under certain signs, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> become great sportsmen, and keep hounds and falcons. Sidonius, who flourished about the end of the fifth century, praises Herdicus, the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of his wife, because he was the first in his territories who practised hunting and fowling with dogs and hawks. Falconry appears to have been carried to the greatest perfection, and to have been much esteemed at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> courts of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, so early as the 12th century, for which reason some have ascribed the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Frederic I., whereas he appears to have been only the first who introduced the practice into Italy, according to the testimony of Rodericus and Collenuccio; and Frederic II. wrote a book entitled, De arte venandi cum avibus, to which the practice has been much indebted. Falconry has had a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of admirers among the fair <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, perhaps in a superior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> to any other sport or amusement whatever of a similar <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; but their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> was destroyed by the invention of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>, which was accompanied both with alarm and danger. We conclude our remarks on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of falconry with an observation of Demetrius, who flourished in the 13th century, and who expressly wrote at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> on this subject. He desires sportsmen to say their prayers (τελεσθείης εὐχαριστίας) before they go out to the field, which appears wholly incompatible with the practice of modern times, and seems as impious as to crave assistance of God when preparing for a piratical expedition. Falconry, the art of training all manner of hawks, but more especially the larger ones called falcons, to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of hawking. See Hawking. When a falcon is taken, she must be seeled in such a manner, that, as the seeling slackens, she may see what provision lies before her; but care ought to be taken, not to see her too hard. A falcon or hawk newly taken should have all new furniture, as new jesses of good <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, malled leashes with buttons at the end, and new bewets. There should also be provided a small round stick, to stroke the hawk; because, the oftener this is done, the sooner and better will she be manned. She must also have two good bells, that she may be found when she scattereth. Her hood should be well fashioned, raised, and embossed against her eyes, deep and yet strait enough beneath, that it may fasten about her head without hurting her; and her beak and talons must be a little coped, but not so near as to make them bleed. If it be a soar-falcon, which had already passed the seas, she will indeed be harder to reclaim, but will prove the best of falcons. Her food must be good and warm, and given her twice or thrice a-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> till she be full gorged: the best for this purpose is pigeons, larks, or other live birds; because she must be broken off by degrees from her accustomed feeding. When she is fed, you must hoop and lure, as you do when you call a hawk, that she may know when you intend to give her meat. On this occasion she must be unhooded gently; and after giving her two or three bits, her hood must be put on again, when she is to get two or three bits more. Care must be taken that she be <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> seeled; and after three or four days, her diet may be lessened: the falconer setting her every night to perch by him, that he may awaken her often in the night. In this manner he must proceed, till he find her to grow tame and gentle; and when she begins to feed eagerly, he may give her a sheep's heart. He may now begin to unhood her in the daytime; but it must be far from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, first giving her a bit or two, then hooding her gently, and giving her as much more. When she is sharp set, he may now unhood her, and give her some meat <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> against his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> and eyes, which will make her less afraid of the countenance of others. She must be borne continually on the fist, till she is properly manned, causing her to feed in company, giving her in the morning, about sunrise, the wing of a pullet; and in the evening the foot of a hare or coney, cut off above the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a>, flayed and laid in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which being squeezed, is to be given her with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PINION">pinion</a> of a hen's wing. For two or three days give her washed meat, and then plumage in more or less <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> as she is thought to be more or less foul within. After this, being hooded again, she Falcoary, is to get nothing till she has gleamed and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a>, when a little hot meat may be given her in company; and, towards evening, she may be allowed to plume a hen's wing in company also. Cleanse the feathers of her casting, if foul and slimy; if she be clean within, give her gentle castings; and when she is reclaimed, manned, and made eager and sharp set, he may venture to feed her on the lure. However, three things are to be considered before the lure be showed her: 1. That she be bold and familiar in company, and not afraid of dogs and horses. 2. Sharp set and hungry, having regard to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of morning and evening, when you would lure her. 3. Clean within, and the lure well garnished with meat on both sides; and when you intend to give her the length of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEASH">leash</a>, you must abscond yourself. She must also be unhooded, and have a bit or two given her on the lure as she sits on your fist; afterwards take the lure from her, and hide it that she may not see it; and when she is unseened, cast the lure so near her, that she may catch it within the length of her leash, and as soon as she has seized it, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> your <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> as falcons do, feeding her upon the lure, on the ground, with the heart and warm thigh of a pullet. Having so lured your falcon, give her but little meat in the evening; and let this luring be so timely, that you may give her plumage, and a juck of a joint next morning on your fist. When she has cast and gleamed, give her a little reaching of warm meat. About noon, tie a creance to her leash; and going into the field, there give her a bit or two upon her lure: then unwind the creance, and draw it after you a good way; and let him who has the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> hold his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> on the tassel of her hood, ready to unhood her as soon as you begin to lure; to which if she come well, stoop roundly upon it, and hastily <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> it, let her cast two or three bits thereon. Then, unseizing and taking her off the lure, hood her and give her to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> again; and, going farther off, lure and feed her as before. In this manner is the falconer to proceed, luring her every day farther and farther off, till she is accustomed to come freely and eagerly to the lure; after which she may be lured in company, taking care that nothing affright her. When she is used to the lure on foot, she is to be lured on horseback; which may be effected the sooner, by causing horsemen to be about her when she is lured on foot. When she has grown familiar to this way, let somebody on foot hold the hawk, and be on horseback must call and cast the lure about his head, the holder taking off the hood by the tassel; and if she seize eagerly on the lure without fear of man or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, then take off the creance, and lure her at a greater distance. And if you would have her <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a> dogs as well as the lure, call dogs when you give her her living or plumage. See HAWKING.

FALERII

Pages 440-440

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Etruria, on the west <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> side of the Tiber; Falisci, the people of the town and territory. The territory was famous for its rich pastures; hence the gramen Faliscum in authors. Eutropius and Frontinus call the town Falisci; which, according to the last, was surmanned Colonia Junonia. The Falisci are called Equi by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>; because they afforded supplemental laws to the tables, (Servius). Here they made an excellent sausage, called Venter Faliscus (Martial). When the Falisci were besieged by Camillus, a schoolmaster went out of the gates of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> with his pupils, and proposed to betray them into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Roman enemy, that by such a possession he might easily oblige the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to surrender. Camillus heard the proposal with indignation, and ordered the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to be stripped naked, and whipped back to the town by those whom his perfidy wished to betray. This instance of generosity operated upon the people so powerfully that they surrendered to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>.

FALERNUS

Pages 440-440

Mons Massicus so called, (Martial); Falernus <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-AGER">ager</a>, a district at the foot of Mount Massicus in Campania; famous for its generous wines, (Horace, Pliny). Now-called Monte Massico. FALISCI. See FALERII.

FALKIA

Pages 440-440

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the hexandra class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FALKIRK

Pages 440-440

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STIRLINGSHIRE">Stirlingshire</a> in Scotland, situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 48'. N. Lat. 56° 20'. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ill-built <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and is supported by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle from the Highlands. A great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> is also got here by the carriage of goods landed at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARRON">Carron</a> wharf to Glasgow. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of the town and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>, in 1811, was 9929. This town is remarkable for a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought in its neighbourhood between Edward I. of England, and the Scots commanded by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> of Scotland, Cummin of Badenoch, and Sir William Wallace. The latter had been invested with the supreme command; but perceiving that this gave umbrage to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, he resigned his power into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the noblemen above mentioned, reserving to himself only the command of a small body who refused to follow another leader. The Scots generals placed their pikemen along the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, and lined the intervals between the three bodies of which their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> was composed, with archers; and dreading the great superiority of the English cavalry, endeavoured to secure their front by pallisadoes tied together with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>. The battle was fought on the 22d of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1298. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of England divided his army likewise into three bodies; and by the superiority of his archers, defeated the Scots with great slaughter. Wallace alone preserved entire the troops he commanded; and retiring behind the Carron, marched leisurely along the banks of that river, which protected him from the enemy. In this battle fell John de Graham, a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> much celebrated for his valour, and styled the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of the gallant Wallace. His epitaph is still to be seen on a plain <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a> of Falkirk. On the 18th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1746, a battle was fought here between the king's forces commanded by General Hawley, and the Highlanders headed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Stuart. The former was seized with a panic, and fled; but <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Husk with two regiments, who kept their ground, prevented the Highlanders from pursuing their victory. Extensive ruins are perceived in the neighbourhood of this town, supposed by some antiquarians to have been the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Pictish <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>; but others believe them to be the remains of some Roman stations.

FALKLAND

Pages 440-442

a small town of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIFESHIRE">Fifeshire</a> in Scotland, made a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> burgh by James II. in 1458. Here stood one of the seats of the Macduffs earls of Fife. the attainder of Munro Stewart, the 17th <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a>, it became forfeited to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> in 1324. James V., who grew very fond of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, enlarged and improved it. The remains evince its former magnificence and elegance, and the fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of the princely <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a>. The gateway is placed between two fine round towers; on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> joins the chapel, whose <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> is of wood, handsomely gilt and painted, but in a most ruinous condition. Beneath are several apartments. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> next to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> was beautifully adorned with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, heads in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASS">bass</a> relief, and elegant columns not reducible to any order, but of fine proportion, with capitals approaching the Ionic scroll. Beneath some of these pillars was <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> I. R. M. G. 1537, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Jacobus Rex, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a> de Guise.—This place was also a favourite residence of James VI. on account of the fine <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARK">park</a> and plenty of deer. The east side was accidentally burnt in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II., and the park ruined during Cromwell's usurpation, when the fine oaks were cut <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in order to build the fort at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PERTH">Perth</a>.—This place gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of viscount to the English family of Carey; Sir Henry Carey being so created by James VI. 1620. His son was the celebrated Lucius, who sacrificed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in a fit of loyal despair at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWBURY">Newbury</a>, and from whom the present family is lineally descended. Falkland, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>. See Carey. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">Fall</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> of a heavy body towards the centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. It is also the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of length used in Scotland, containing six ells. Fall of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a>, in sacred <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, that terrible event by which sin and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> were introduced into the world. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTEDILUVIANS">Antediluvians</a>, and Original Sin. The account which Moses gives of this transaction is extremely <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> and concise. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a>, he informs us, being more subtle than any beast of the field, asked the woman, whether it was true that God had not granted her and her husband leave to eat of every tree in the garden? She answered, That God had allowed them to eat of all, except only the fruit of the tree in the midst of the garden; which he commanded they should not taste, nor so much as touch, lest they should die. The serpent replied, That they should not die; for God knew the virtue of the tree; and that so soon as they ate of it, their eyes would be opened, and they would become like gods, knowing good and evil. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EVE">Eve</a>, seeing the fruit tempting to the view, took of the fruit and ate; and gave also to her husband of it, and he did eat. Immediately the eyes of both were opened; when perceiving they were naked, they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves aprons. Adam and Eve, hearing the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of God walking in the garden in the cool of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, hid themselves among the trees; but, on God's calling for Adam, he excused himself for not appearing, because he was naked. God demanded of him, who it was that told him he was naked; and whether he had disobeyed his command in eating the forbidden fruit? Adam confessed that the woman had offered him the fruit, and he had tasted it. She being examined likewise, acknowledged what she had done; but said, the serpent had seduced and deceived her. God then proceeded to judgment; he first cursed the serpent above all beasts, and condemned him to go on his belly, and eat the dust; adding, that he would put enmity between him and the woman, and their offspring; that the seed of the woman should bruise the serpent's head, who should bruise the other's heel. The woman was subjected to the pains of childbirth, as well as the dominion of her husband; and as to the man, God cursed the ground for his sake, declaring that it should bring forth thorns and thistles, and he should earn his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> by the sweat of his brow, till he returned to the dust, from whence he was taken. At last, having clothed them both with skins, he turned them out of the garden, lest they should take of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever; then, to prevent any attempt to return to their former habitation, he placed cherubims at the east of the garden, and a flaming <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> which turned every way, to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> the passage to the tree of life. This concise account being, at first view, encumbered with some difficulties, several learned and pious men have been inclined to believe the whole ought to be taken in an allegorical <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, and not according to the strictness of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>: they allege, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, and particularly the eastern nations, had two different ways of delivering their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, one popular, and the other mysterious; that the Scripture uses both occasionally; sometimes accommodating itself to the capacities of the people, and at other times to the real but more veiled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>; and that, to obviate the many difficulties which occur in the literal history of this sad catastrophe, the safest way is to understand it as a parabolical story, under which the real circumstances are disguised and concealed, as a mystery not fit to be more explicitly declared. Though it cannot be denied that some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> philosophers affected such an allegorical way of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, to conceal their notions from the vulgar, and keep their learning within the bounds of their own school; yet it is apparent Moses had no such <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>; and as he pretends only to relate matters of fact, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> as they happened, without art or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a>, it cannot be supposed but that this history of the fall is to be taken in a literal sense, as well as the rest of his writings. It is generally agreed, that the serpent which tempted Eve was the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>, who envying the privileges of man in innocence, tempted him, and was the cause of his forfeiting all those advantages which he had received from God at his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>; and that to this end he assumed the form of a serpent. These interpretations are supported by many <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of Scripture, where the devil is called the serpent, and the old serpent, (See John viii. 44, 2 Cor. xi. 3, and Rev. xii. 9.) Some believe that the serpent had then the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of speech, and conversed familiarly with the woman, without her conceiving any distrust in him; and that God, to punish the malice with which he had abused Eve, deprived him of the use of speech. Others maintain, that a real serpent having eaten of the forbidden fruit, Eve from thence concluded, that she too might eat of it without danger; that in effect she did eat of it, and incurred the displeasure of God by her disobedience. This, say these last authors, is the plain <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of fact which Moses would relate under the allegorical representation of the serpent conversing with Eve. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of such as believe this was not a real serpent, but only the devil under that name, is no less liable liable to exception than any of the rest. For though the devil is frequently styled in Scripture the serpent and the old serpent, yet why he should be called the most subtile beast of the field, we cannot conceive; ne- ither <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> inflicted on the serpent suffer us to doubt, but that a serpent's body at least was em- ployed in the transaction. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the forbidden fruit is another circum- stance in this relation that has occasioned no less va- riety of conjectures. The Rabbins believe it was the vine; others that it was wheat; and others, from the circumstance of Adam and Eve's covering themselves with fig leaves immediately after their transgression, tell us, that this fruit must have been the fig; some think it was the cherry; and the generality of the Latin will have it to be the apple. Those who admire allegorical interpretations, will have the forbidden fruit to have been no other than the sensual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>, for which the punishment in- flicted on the woman was the pain of child-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a>. But this opinion has not the least foundation in the words of Moses, especially <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we consider that Adam knew not his wife till after their expulsion out of Pa- radise. Many have been the suppositions and conjectures upon this subject in general; and some have so far in- dulged their fancy in the circumstances of the fall, that they have perverted the whole <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARRATION">narration</a> of Moses into a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> full of the most shameful extravagances.

FALLACY

Pages 442-442

a deception, fraud, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> false appear- ance. The Epicureans deny that there is any such thing as a fallacy of the senses: for according to them, all our sensations and perceptions, both of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> and phantasy, are true; whence they make sense the primary criteri- on of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. The Cartesians, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, maintain, that we should suspect as false, or at most as dubious, every thing that presents itself to us by means only of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> senses, because they frequently deceive us. They add, that our senses, as being fallacious, were never given us by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> for the discovery of truth, or the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> of the principles of things; but only for pointing out to us what things are convenient or hurtful to our bodies. The <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PERIPATETICS">Peripatetics</a> keep a middle course. They say, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a sensible object be taken in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> or ge- neral view, the sense cannot be deceived about it; but that if the object be taken under its specific view, the sense may be mistaken about it, from the want of the dispositions necessary to a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>, as a disor- der in the organ, or any thing uncommon in the me- dium: thus, in some disorders of the eye, all objects appear <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>; a stick in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> appears broken or crooked, &c. FALLING sickness, or EPILEPSY. See Medi- cine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. FALLING-STARS. See <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">STAR</a>.

FALLOPIAN TUBES

Pages 442-442

in Anatomy, two ducts aris- ing from the womb, one on each side of the fundus, and thence extended to the ovaries, having a consider- able share in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a>. They are called tubes, from their form, which bears some resemblance to a trum- pet; and their denomination Fallopiana, they take from Gabriel Fallopius, mentioned in the next article. Fallopian See ANATOMY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FALLOPIUS

Pages 442-442

GABRIEL, a most celebrated physi- cian and anatomist, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODENA">Modena</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the year 1523, and descended of a noble family. He made several discoveries in anatomy, one of which was that of the tubes, called from him the Fallopian tubes. He travelled through the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and obtained the character of being one of the ablest phy- sicians of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He was made professor of anatomy at <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISA">Pisa</a> in the year 1548, and at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a> in the year 1551: here he died in 1562, aged 39. His writings, which are numerous, were first printed separately, and afterwards collected under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of "<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">Opera</a> genui- na omnia, tam practica quam theoretica, in tres to- mos distributa." They were printed at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> in 1585 and in 1626, at Frankfort in 1629, cum operum ap- pendice; and in 1666, in folio.

FALLOW

Pages 442-442

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> like that of brick half burnt; such is that of a fallow deer. FALLOW Field, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Fallow ground; <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> laid up, or that has been untillled for a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. FALLOWING of LAND, a particular method of improving land. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">AGRICULTURE</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FALMOUTH

Pages 442-442

a port town of Cornwall in Eng- <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 30' N. Lat. 50° 15' on a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> on the English channel. It is the richest and most trading town in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, and larger than any three of its boroughs that send members to parlia- ment. It is so commodious a harbour, that ships of the greatest burden come up to its quay. It is guarded by the castle of St Mawes and Pendennis, on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> rock at the entrance: and there is such shelter in the many creeks belonging to it, that the whole <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> may ride safe here in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, it being next to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLYMOUTH">Plymouth</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILFORD">Milford</a>-Haven, the best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> for shipping in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. It is well built; and its trade is consid- erably increased since the establishment of the packet- boats here for <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, and the West Indies, which not only bring vast quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> in specie and in bars, on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; but the Falmouth merchants trade with the Portuguese in ships of their own, and they have a great share also in the gainful pilchard trade. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM_HOUSE"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> for most of the Cornish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, as well as the head collec- tor, is settled here, where the duties, including those of the other ports, are very considerable. The num- ber of houses in 1664 amounted to 200; in 1801, they amounted to 468; in 1811, 478, and at this last <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants was 3933.

FALSE

Pages 442-444

in general, something contrary to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> not what it ought to be: thus we say a false ac- tion, false weights, false claim, &c. False <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">Action</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> brought against one whereby he is <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> into prison, and dies pending the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> gives no remedy in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, because the truth or falsehood of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> cannot appear before it is tried; and if the plaintiff is barred, or non-suited at com- mon law, regularly all the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> is amerce- ment. False Imprisonment, is a trespass committed against a person, by arresting and imprisoning him without <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> cause, contrary to law; or where a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is un- lawfully detained without legal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>: and it is al- so used for a writ which is brought for this trespass. If a person be any way unlawfully detained, it is false imprisonment; and considerable damages are recoverable in those actions. False News, spreading of, in order to make <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCORD">discord</a> between the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, or concerning any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> man of the realm, is punishable by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law with fine and imprisonment; which is confirmed by statutes Westm. I. 3 Edw. I. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 34. 2 Rich. II. stat. 1. cap. 5, and 12 Rich. II. cap. 11. False Oath. See <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERJURY">Perjury</a>. False Prophecy. See Prophecy. False <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">Quarter</a>, in Farriery. See <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">Quarters</a>, Farriery <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. False <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">Bay</a>, a bay lying to the eastward of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope; frequented by vessels during the prevalence of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-westerly winds, which begin to exert their influence in May, and render it dangerous to remain in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> bay. It is terminated to the eastward by False Cape, and to the westward by the Cape of Good Hope. It is 18 miles wide at its entrance, and the two capes bear due east and west from each other. Falsi crimen, in the civil law, is fraudulent subornation or concealment, with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to darken or hide the truth, and make things appear otherwise than they are. The crimen falsi is committed, 1. By words, as when a witness swears falsely. 2. By <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, as when a man antedates a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>, or the like. 3. By <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a>, as when he sells by false <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-WEIGHTS_AND_MEASURES">weights and <a class</a>="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>. Falsify, in Law, is used for proving any thing to be false. Hence we find, Falsifying a record, for showing it to be erroneous. Thus lawyers teach, that a person purchasing <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> of another, who is afterwards outlawed of felony, &c., may falsify the record, not only as to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> wherein the felony is supposed to have been committed, but also as to the point of the offence.
