But where a man is found guilty by verdict, a purchaser cannot falsify as to the offence; though he may for the time, where the party is found guilty generally in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a>, because the time is not material upon <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a>. Falstaff. See Fastolf. Falx, in Anatomy, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the dura mater, descending between the two hemispheres of the brain, and separating the fore part from the hinder. It is called falx, i.e. "sickle;" because of its curvature, occasioned by the convexity of the brain. It divides the brain as low as the corpus callosum. Fama clamosa, in the judicial procedure of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Scotland, a ground of action before a presbytery against one of its members, independent of any regular complaint by a particular accuser. See Presbytery. Any person who is of a good character, may give to the presbytery a complaint against one of their members; but the presbytery is not to proceed to the citation of the person accused, until the accuser under his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> gives in the complaint, with some account of its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, and undertakes to make out the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBEL">libel</a>, under the pain of being considered as a slanderer. When such an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> is brought before them, they are obliged candidly to examine the affair. But, besides this, the presbytery considers itself obliged to proceed against any of its members, if a fama clamosa of the scandal is so great that they cannot be vindicated unless they begin the process. This they can do without any particular accuser, after they have inquired into the rise, occasion, and authors, of this report. It is a maxim of the kirk of Scotland, that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> must suffer if the scandalous or immoral actions of a minister are not corrected. And wherever a minister is reputed guilty of any immorality (although before the most popular preacher in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>), none almost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> attend upon his ministry. Therefore the presbytery, for the sake of religion, is obliged to proceed against a minister in case of a fama clamosa. This, however, is generally done with great tenderness. After they have considered the report raised against him, then they order him to be cited, draw out a full copy of what is reported, with a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of the witnesses names to be led for proving this allegation. He is now to be formally summoned to appear before them; and he has warning given him, at least 10 days before the time of his appearance, to give in his answers to what is termed the libel; and the names of the witnesses ought also to be sent him. If at the time appointed the minister appear, the libel is to be read to him, and his answers are also to be read. If the libel be found relevant, then the presbytery is to endeavour to bring him to a confession. If the matter confessed be of a scandalous <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, such as uncleanness, the presbytery generally depose him from his office, and appoint him in due time to appear before the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> where the scandal was given, and to make public confession of his crime and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a>. If a minister absent himself by leaving the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and be contumacious, without making any relevant excuse, a new citation is given him, and intimation is made at his own church when the congregation is met, that he is to be holden as confessed, since he refused to appear before them; and accordingly he is deposed from his office. Fame, a heathen <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>, celebrated chiefly by the poets. She is feigned to have been the last of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TITANS">Titans</a> produced by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, to have her <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and to have a vast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of eyes, ears, and tongues. She is mentioned by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESIOD">Hesiod</a>, and particularly described by Ovid and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>. Famescanina. See Bulimia, Medicine Index. Famia, or Afamia, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> name of one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Apameas. See Apamea. Familiars of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">Inquisition</a>, persons who assist in apprehending such as are accused, and carrying them to prison. They are assistants to the inquisitor, and called familiars, because they belong to his family. In some provinces of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> they are called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-bearers, and in others the scholars of St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a>; and they wore a cross before them on the outside garment. They are properly bailiffs of the inquisition; and the vile office is esteemed so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a>, that noblemen in the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a> have been ambitious of belonging to it. Nor is this surprising, when it is considered that Innocent III. granted very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> indulgences and privileges to these familiars; and that the same plenary <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> is granted by the pope to every single <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of this office, as was granted by the Lateran <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> to those who succoured the Holy Land. When several persons are to be taken up at the same time, these familiars are commanded Family manded to order matters, that they may know nothing of one another's being apprehended; and it is related, that a father and his three sons, and three daughters, who lived together in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, were carried prisoners to the inquisition without knowing anything of one another's being there till <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years afterwards, when they that were alive were released by an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>.

FAMILY

Pages 444-444

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> used to express any order of animals, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other natural productions, which exhibit certain affinities, or the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>.

FAMINE

Pages 444-444

dearth, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> scarcity of food. For preservatives against <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a> in times of famine, see the article HUNGER.

FAN

Pages 444-444

a machine used to raise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, and cool the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> by agitating it. That the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the fan was known to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> is very evident from what Terence says, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> hoc flabellum, et ventulum huic sic facito; and from Ovid, Art. Amand. I. 161. Profuit et tenues ventos movisse flabello. The fans of the ancients were made of different materials; but the most elegant were composed of peacocks feathers, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> perhaps painted so as to represent a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEACOCK">peacock</a>'s feather. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> which now prevails among the ladies of wearing fans, was borrowed from the east, where the hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> renders the use of fans and umbrellas almost indispensable. In the east they chiefly use <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fans made of feathers, to keep off the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and the flies. In <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> they have a large sort of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> fans, suspended in the middle of their apartments, and particularly over the tables: these, by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> at first given them, and which they retain a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> on account of their perpendicular suspension, help to cool the air and drive off flies. In the Greek <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, a fan is put into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the deacons in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of their ordination, in allusion to a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the deacon's office in that church, which is to keep the flies off the priests during the celebration of the sacrament. What is called a fan amongst us and throughout the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> parts of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, is a thin skin, or piece of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, taffety, or other <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> stuff, cut semicircularly, and mounted on several little sticks of wood, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, tortoiseshell, or the like. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the paper be single, the sticks of the mounting are pasted on the least ornamented side: if <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>, the sticks are placed between them. Before they proceed to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the sticks, which they call mounting the fan, the paper is to be plaited in such a manner, as that the plates may be alternately inward and outward. It is in the middle of each plait, which is usually about half an inch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, that the sticks are to be pasted; and these again are to be all joined and rivetted together at the other end; they are very thin, and scarcely exceed one-third of an inch in breadth; and where they are pasted to the paper, are still narrower, continuing thus to the extremity of the paper. The two outer ones are bigger and stronger than the others. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of sticks rarely exceeds 22. The sticks are usually provided by the cabinet-makers or toy-men; the fan-painters plait the papers, paint, and mount them. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> is either in colours or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, applied on a silvered ground, both prepared by the goldbeaters. Sometimes they paint on a gold ground, but it is rarely; true gold being too dear, and false too paltry. To apply the silver leaves on the paper, they use a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, which they pretend is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> secret, but which appears to be no other than <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a> arabic, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CANDY">candy</a>, and a little <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, melted in common <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and mixed with a little brandy. This composition is laid on with a sponge; then laying the silver leaves thereon, and pressing them gently <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> stuffed with cotton, they catch hold, and adhere together. When, instead of silver, gold ground is laid, the same method is observed. The ground being well dried, a number of the papers are well beaten together on a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCK">block</a>, and by this means the silver or gold get a lustre as if they had been burnished. FAN is also an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> to winnow corn. The machine used for this purpose by the ancients seems to have been of a form similar to ours. The fan, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> calls mystica cannum Iaechi, was used at initiations into the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of the ancients: For as the persons who were initiated into any of the mysteries, were to be particularly good, this instrument, which separates the wheat from the chaff, was the fittest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMBLEM">emblem</a> that could be of setting apart the good and virtuous from the vicious and useless part of mankind. It is figuratively applied in a similar manner in Luke iii. 17.

FANATICS

Pages 444-444

wild, enthusiastic, visionary persons, who pretend to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> called those fanatici who passed their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> (fana), and being often seized with a kind of enthusiasm, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> inspired by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, showed wild and antic gestures. Prudentius represents them as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> and slashing their arms with knives. Shaking the head was also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> among the fanatici; for Lampridius informs us, that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Helioabalus was arrived at that pitch of madness, as to shake his head with the gashed fanatics. Hence the word was applied among us to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANABAPTISTS">Anabaptists</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUAKERS">Quakers</a>, &c. at their first rise, and is now an epithet given to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> prophets, Muggletonians, &c.

FANIONS

Pages 444-444

in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, small flags carried along with the baggage.

FANNERS

Pages 444-444

a machine for winnowing corn, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> for separating the chaff from the grain. See, for its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">MECHANICS</a>.

FANSHAW

Pages 444-445

SIR RICHARD, famous for his embassies and writings, was the tenth and youngest son of Sir Henry Fanshaw of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">Ware</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARK">Park</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a>, where it is supposed he was born about the year 1657. He distinguished himself so early by his abilities, that in 1635 he was taken into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> employments by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. and sent resident to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; whence being recalled in the beginning of the troubles troubles in 1641, he adhered to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, and was employed in several important matters of state. During his vacant hours he wrote several poems, and made several translations. At the Restoration it was expected he would have been made one of the secretaries of state; however, he was made <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the requests; a station in those times of considerable profit. Afterwards, on account of his skill in the Latin <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, he was made secretary for that tongue. In 1661, he was sent envoy to the king of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>. In 1662, he was again sent to that court with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a>, and negotiated the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> of his master King Charles II. with the infanta Donna Catherine. Upon his return he was made one of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>. In 1664, he was sent ambassador to both the courts of Spain and Portugal; at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the foundation of peace betwixt those crowns and England was laid by him. His conduct during his former employments in those courts gained him such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> esteem there, that his reception was magnificent, exceeding all that were before, which those kings declared was not to be a precedent to succeeding ambassadors. He died at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a> in 1666, on the very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> he had fixed for setting out on his return to England. Besides some original poems, and other translations, he published a translation of Bathista Guarini's Pastor Fido, and another of the Lusiad of Camoens. Among his posthumous publications are, "Letters during his embassies in Spain and Portugal; with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> prefixed.

FANTASIA

Pages 445-445

in the Italian music, signifies fancy; and is used for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, wherein the composer ties himself to no particular <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, but ranges according as his fancy leads, amidst various movements, different <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-AIRS">airs</a>, &c. This is otherwise called the capricious style: before sonatas were used, there were many of this kind, some of which remain even now.

FANUM

Pages 445-445

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, a temple <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> consecrated to some deity. The deified men and women among the heathens had likewise their fana; even the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> Cicero erected one to his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Tullia. FANUM Vacuna, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a village of the Sabines, situated between Cures and Mandela; where stood the temple of Vacuna, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of the idle or unemployed, in an old decayed state; and hence the epithet putre, used by Horace. Now called Vocone, in the Ecclesiastic State.

FARANDMAN

Pages 445-445

a traveller, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> merchant stranger, to whom, by the laws of Scotland, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> ought to be done with all expedition, that his business or journey be not hindered.

FARCE

Pages 445-445

was originally a droll, petty show, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> entertainment, exhibited by charlatans, and their buffoons, in the open street, to gather the crowd together. —The word is French, and signifies literally, "force-meat or stuffing." It was applied on this occasion, no doubt, on account of the variety of jests, gibes, tricks, &c., wherewith the entertainment was interlarded. Some authors derive farce from the Latin faciei; others from the Celtic farce, "mockery;" others from the Latin forceire, "to stuff." At present it is removed from the street to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>: and instead of being performed by merry-andrews to amuse the rabble, is acted by comedians, and become the entertainment of a polite audience. Poets have reformed the wildness of the primitive farces, and brought them to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and manner of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the two on our stage is, that comedy keeps to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, and therefore is confined to certain laws prescribed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> critics; whereas farce disallows of all laws, or rather sets them aside on occasion. Its end is purely to make merry; and it sticks at nothing which may contribute thereto, however wild and extravagant. Hence the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a> is usually low, the persons of inferior <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> trivial or ridiculous, and nature and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> everywhere heightened and exaggerated to afford the more palpable <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a>.

FARCIN

Pages 445-445
or Farcy, a disease in horses, and sometimes in oxen, &c. somewhat of the nature of a scabies or mange. See Farriery Index.

FARDING-DEAL

Pages 445-445

the fourth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">acre</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>. See ACRE.

FAREWELL-CAPE

Pages 445-445

the most southerly promontory of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GREENLAND">Greenland</a>, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 50°, and N. Lat. 60°.

FARINA

Pages 445-445

a Latin <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> signifying <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the flour of corn. See CORN. Farina fecundans, among Botanists, the supposed impregnating meal or dust on the apices or anthere of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. See Pollen. The manner of gathering the farina of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> for microscopical observations is this: Gather the flowers in the midst of a dry, sunshiny <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEW">dew</a> is perfectly off, then gently shake off the farina, or lightly <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a> it off with a soft <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>, upon a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>; then take a single talc or isinglass between the nippers, and, breathing on it, apply it instantly to the farina, and the moisture of the breath <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> make the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> powder stick to it. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> too <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> be found adhering to the talc, blow a little of it off; and, if there is too little, breathe upon it again, and take up more. When this is done, put the talc into the hole of a slider, and, applying it to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>, see whether the little grains are laid as you desire; and if they are, cover them up with another talc, and fix the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a>; but be careful that the talcs do not press upon the farina in such a manner as to alter its form.

FARLEU

Pages 445-445
money paid by the tenants in the west of England, in lieu of a heriot. In some manors of Devonshire, farleu is often distinguished to be the best goods, as heriot is the best beast, payable at the death of a tenant.

FARM

Pages 445-449

FARIN, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Ferm, (Firma), in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies a little <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> messuage or district, containing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, with other conveniences; hired, or taken by lease, either in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, or parole, under a certain yearly rent. See Lease. This in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> parts is differently termed: in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, it is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TACK">tack</a>; in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a>, fermebolt; in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, a wike, &c. In the corrupted Latin, firma signified a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> inclosed or shut in: whence, in some provinces, Menage Farm. observes, they call closure, or closure, what in others they call a farm. Add, that we find locare <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AD">ad</a> firmam, to signify to let to farm; probably on account of the sure hold the tenant here has in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of tenants at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a>. Spelman and Skinner, however, choose to derive the word farm from the Saxon fearme, or feorme, that is, victus, "provision;" by reason the country people and tenants anciently paid their rents in victuals and other necessaries, which were afterwards converted into the payment of a sum of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. Whence a farm was originally a place that furnished its landlord with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. And among the Normans they still distinguish between farms that pay in kind, i.e. provisions, and those which pay in money; calling the former simply ferme, and the latter blanche ferme, "<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> farm." Spelman shows, that the word firma, anciently signified not only what we now call a farm, but also a feast or entertainment, which the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> gave the proprietor or landlord, for a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of days, and at a certain rate, for the lands he held of him. Thus fearme in the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Canute is rendered by Mr Lambard, victus: and thus we read of reddere firmum unius noctis, and reddebat unum diem de firma; which denote provision for a night and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, the rents about the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Conquest being all paid in provisions; which <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> is said to have been first altered under King Henry I. We also say to farm duties, imposts, &c. Culture of a Farm. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a>. Farm, as connected with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">gardening</a>, and susceptible of embellishment. See Gardening. In speculation, it might have been expected that the first essays of improvement should have been on a farm, to make it both advantageous and delightful; but the fact was otherwise; a small plot was appropriated to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, the rest was reserved for profit only. And this may, perhaps, have been a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> cause of the vicious <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> which <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> prevailed in gardens. It was imagined that a spot set apart from the rest should not be like them: the conceit introduced deviations from <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, which were afterwards carried to such an excess, that hardly any objects truly rural were left within the enclosure, and the view of those without was generally excluded. The first step, therefore, towards a reformation, was by opening the garden to the country, and that immediately led to assimilating them; but still the idea of a spot appropriated to pleasure only prevailed, and one of the latest improvements has been to blend the useful with the agreeable; even the ornamental farm was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> in time to the more rural; and we have at last returned to simplicity by force of refinement. 1. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of pastoral <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> seem now to be the standard of that simplicity; and a place conformable to them is deemed a farm in its utmost purity. An allusion to them evidently enters into the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of the Leasowes (A), where they appear so lovely as to endear the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of their author; and justify the reputation of Mr Shenstone, who inhabited, made, and celebrated the place: it is a perfect <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of his mind, simple, elegant, and amiable; and will always suggest a doubt, whether the spot inspired his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, or whether, in the scenes which he formed, he only realized the pastoral images which abound in his songs. The whole is in the same taste, yet full of variety; and, except in two or three trifles, every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> is rural and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>. It is literally a grazing farm lying round the house; and a walk, as unaffected and as unadorned as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> field-path, is conducted through the several enclosures. But for a detail of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> and scenery, as illustrative of the present subject, the reader is referred to the particular <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the Leasowes published by the late Mr Dodsley. We shall only take notice of one or two circumstances independent on the general delineation. The art with which the divisions between the fields are diversified is one of them. Even the hedges are distinguished from each other: a common quickest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> is in one place the separation: in another, it is a lofty hedge-row, thick from the top to the bottom; in a third, it is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> range of trees, with all their stems clear, and the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> appearing in the intervals between their boughs, and the bushes beneath them; in others, these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of trees are broken, a few groups only being left at different distances; and sometimes a wood, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROVE">grove</a>, a coppice, or a thicket, is the apparent boundary, and by them both the shape and the style of the enclosures are varied. The <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>, which abound in the place, are another striking peculiarity: they are well known and justly admired; and the elegance of the poetry, and the aptness of the quotations, atone for their length and their number. But, in general, inscriptions please no more than once: the utmost they can pretend to, except when their allusions are emblematical, is to point out the beauties, or describe the effects, of the spots they belong to; but those beauties and those effects must be very faint, which stand in need of the assistance. Inscriptions, however, to commemorate a departed friend, are evidently exempt from the censure; the monuments would be unintelligible without them; and an urn, in a lonely grove, or in the midst of a field, is a favourite embellishment at the Leasowes: they are indeed among the principal ornaments of the place; for the buildings are mostly <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> seats, or little root-houses; a ruin of a priory is the largest, and that has no peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> to recommend it: but a multiplicity of objects are unnecessary in the farm; the country it commands is full of them; and every natural advantage of the place within itself has been discovered, applied, contrasted, and carried to the utmost perfection, in the purest taste, and with inexhaustible fancy. Among the ideas of pastoral poetry which are here introduced, its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a> is not omitted: but the allusions are both to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> fables; sometimes to the fairies; and sometimes to the naiads and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">muses</a>. The objects also are borrowed partly from the scenes which this country exhibited some centuries ago, and partly from those of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>: the priory, (A) In <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHROPSHIRE">Shropshire</a>, between <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRMINGHAM">Birmingham</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STOURBRIDGE">Stourbridge</a>. Farm. priory, and a Gothic seat, still more particularly characterized by an inscription in obsolete <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, belong to the one; the urns, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>'s obelisk, and a rustic temple of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAN">Pan</a>, to the other. All these allusions and objects are indeed equally rural; but the images in an English and classical eclogue are not the same; each <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> is a distinct imitative character. Either is proper; either will raise the farm it is applied to above the ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>; and within the compass of the same place both may be introduced; but they should be separate; when they are mixed, they counteract one another; and no representation is produced of the times and the countries they refer to. A certain district should therefore be allotted to each, that all the fields which belong to the respective <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> may <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> together, and the corresponding ideas be preserved for a continuance. 2. In such an assortment, the more open and polished scenes will generally be given to the Arcadian shepherd; and those in a lower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of cultivation, will be thought more conformable to the manners of the ancient British yeomanry. We do not conceive that the country in their time was entirely cleared, or distinctly divided; the fields were surrounded by woods, not by hedges; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a considerable tract of improved land lay together, it still was not separated into a number of inclosures. The subjects, therefore, proper to receive this character, are those in which cultivation seems to have encroached on the wild, not to have subdued it; as the bottom of a valley in corn, while the sides are still overgrown with wood; and the outline of that wood indented by the tillage creeping more or less up the hill. But a glade of grass, this circumstance, does not peculiarly belong to the species; that may occur in a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARK">park</a> or pastoral farm; in this, the pastures should rather border on a waste or common; if <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, they may be broken by straggling bushes, thickets, or coppices; and the scattered trees should be beset with brambles and briars. All these are circumstances which improve the beauty of the place; yet appear to be only remains of the wild, not intended for embellishment. Such interruptions must, however, be less frequent in the arable parts of the farm; but there the opening may be divided into several lands, distinguished, as in common fields, only by different sorts of grain. These will sufficiently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the sameness of the space; and the tillage does not furnish a more pleasing <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>, than such a space so broken, if the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> be moderate, and the boundary beautiful. As much wood is essential to the character, a spot may easily be found, where turrets rising above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COVERT">covert</a>, or some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> seen within it, may have the resemblance of a castle or an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>. The partial concealment is almost necessary to both; for to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ACCORD">accord</a> with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, the buildings must seem to be entire; the ruins of them belong to later days: the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> is, however, advantageous to them as objects; none can be imagined more picturesque, than a tower bosomed in trees, or a cluster appearing between the stems and the branches. But the superstitions of the times furnish other objects which are more within compass: hermitages were then real; solitary chapels were common; many of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> of the country being deemed holy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a>, were distinguished by little Gothic domes built over them; and every <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMLET">hamlet</a> had its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, even this, when perfect, set on a little rustic pillar, and that raised upon a base of circular steps, may in some scenes be considerable: if a situation can be found for a Maypole, whence it would not obtrude itself on every view, that also might not be improper; and an ancient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, however unwelcome it may be when it breaks into the design of a park or a garden, in such a farm as this would be a fortunate accident; nor would the old yew in the church-yard be indifferent; it would be a memorial of the times when it was useful. Many other objects, significant of the manners of our <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, might perhaps, upon recollection, occur; but these are amply sufficient for a place of considerable extent; and cottages must abound in every age and every country; they may therefore be introduced in different forms and positions. Large pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> are also particularly proper; and all the varieties of rills are consistent with every species of farm. From the concurrence of so many agreeable circumstances in this, be the force or the effect of the character what it may, a number of pleasing scenes may be exhibited, either in a walk or riding, to be contrasted to those which in another part of the place may be formed on Arcadian ideas; or even to be substituted in their stead, if they are omitted. 3. A part may also be free from either of these imitative characters, and laid out in a common simple farm. Some of the greatest beauties of nature are to be found in the fields, and attend an ordinary state of cultivation: wood and water may there be exhibited in several forms and dispositions; we may enlarge or divide the inclosures; and give them such shapes and boundaries as we please; every one may be an agreeable spot; together, they may compose beautiful views; the arable, the pasture, and the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAD">mead</a>, may succeed one another; and now and then a little wild may be intermixed without impropriety; every beauty, in short, which is not unusual in an inclosed country, whether it arises from neglect or improvement, is here in its place. The buildings, also, which are frequent in such a country, are often beautiful objects; the church and the mansion are considerable: the farm-yard itself, if an advantageous situation be chosen for it; if the ricks, and the barns, and the out-houses, are ranged with any design to form them into groups, and if they are properly blended with trees; may be made a picturesque <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>. Many of them may be detached from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROUP">group</a>, and dispersed about the grounds: the dove-cot, or the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAIRY">dairy</a>, may be separated from the rest; they may be elegant in their forms, and placed wherever they will have the best effect. A common barn, accompanied by a clump, is sometimes pleasing at a distance; a Dutch barn is so when near; and a hay-stack is generally an agreeable circumstance in any position. Each of these may be single; and besides these, all kinds of cottages are proper. Among so many buildings, some may be converted to other purposes than their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> denotes; and, whatever be their exterior, may within be made agreeable retreats, for refreshment, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a>, or shelter. With such opportunities of improvements, even to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECORATION">decoration</a> within itself, and with advantages of prospect into the country about it, a simple farm may undoubtedly be delightful. It will be particularly acceptable ceptable to the owner, if it be <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to his park or his garden: the objects which constantly remind him of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, impose a kind of constraint; and he feels himself relieved, by retiring sometimes from the splendor of a seat into the simplicity of a farm: it is more than a variety of scene; it is a temporary change of situation in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, which has all the charms of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a>, ease, and tranquillity, to recommend it. A place, therefore, can hardly be deemed perfect, which is not provided with such a retreat. But if it be the whole of the place, it seems inadequate to the mansion; a visitor is disappointed; the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> is dissatisfied; he is not sufficiently distinguished from his tenants; he misses the appendages incidental to his seat and his fortune; and is hurt at the similarity of his grounds with the country about them. A pastoral or an ancient farm is a little above the common level; but even these, if brought close up to the door, set the house in a field, where it always appears to be neglected and naked. Some degree of polish and ornament is expected in its immediate environs; and a garden, though it be but a small one, should be interposed between the mansion and any species of farm. 4. A <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of the propriety of such improvements about a seat, joined to a taste for the more simple delights of the country, probably suggested the idea of an ornamental farm, as the means of bringing every rural circumstance within the verge of a garden. This idea has been partially executed very often; but nowhere, perhaps, so completely, and to such an extent, as at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOBURN">Woburn</a> farm, near (Weybridge in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURREY">Surrey</a>). The place contains 150 acres: of which near 35 are adorned to the highest degree; of the rest, about two-thirds are in pasture, and the remainder is in tillage. The decorations are, however, communicated to every part: for they are disposed along the sides of a walk, which, with its appendages, forms a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> belt round the grazing-grounds; and is continued, though on a more contracted <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, through the arable. This walk is properly garden; all within it is farm; the whole lies on the two sides of a hill, and on a flat at the foot of it: the flat is divided into corn fields; the pastures occupy the hill; they are surrounded by the walk, and crossed by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> carried along the brow, which is also richly dressed, and which divides them into two lawns, each completely encompassed with garden. These are in themselves delightful; the ground in both lies beautifully: they are diversified with clumps and single trees; and the buildings in the walk seem to belong to them. On the top of the hill is a large octagon structure; and, not far from it, the ruin of a chapel. To one of the lawns the ruin appears, on the brow of a gentle ascent, backed and grouped with wood; from the other is seen the octagon, upon the edge of a steep <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, and by the side of a pretty grove, which hangs <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the declivity. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAWN">lawn</a> is further embellished by a neat Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>; the former by the house, and the lodge at the entrance; and in both, other objects of less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, little seats, alcoves, and bridges, continually occur. The buildings are not, however, the only ornaments of the walk; it is shut out from the country, for a considerable length of the way, by a thick and lofty hedge-row, which is enriched with woodbine, jessamine, and every odoriferous plant whose tendrils will entwine with the thicket. A path, generally of sand or gravel, is conducted in a waving line, sometimes close under the hedge; sometimes at a little distance from it; and the turf on either <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> is diversified with little groups of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, of firs, or the smallest trees, and often with beds of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>: these are rather too profusely strewed, and hurt the eye by their littlenesses; but then they replenish the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> with their perfumes, and every <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALE">gale</a> is full of fragrancy. In some parts, however, the decoration is more chaste; and the walk is carried between larger clumps of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EVERGREENS">evergreens</a>, thickets of deciduous shrubs, or still more considerably open plantations. In one place it is entirely simple, without any appendages, any gravel, or any sunk fence to separate it from the lawn; and is distinguished only by the richness of its verdure, and the nicety of its preservation. In the arable part it is also of green sward, following the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the hedges about the several inclosures: these hedges are sometimes thickened with flowering shrubs; and in every corner or vacant space, is a rosary, a close or an open clump, or a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> of flowers: but if the parterre has been rifeled for the embellishment of the fields, the country has on the other hand been searched for <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> new in a garden; and the shrubs and the flowers which used to be deemed peculiar to the one, have been liberally transferred to the other; while their number seems multiplied by their arrangement in so many and such different dispositions. A more moderate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of them would, however, have been better; and the variety more pleasing, had it been less licentious. But the excess is only in the borders of the walk; the scenes through which it leads are truly elegant, everywhere rich, and always agreeable. A peculiar cheerfulness overspreads both the lawns, arising from the number and splendor of the objects with which they abound, the lightness of the buildings, the inequalities of the ground, and the varieties of the plantations. The clumps and the groves, though separately small, are often massed by the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a>, and gathered into considerable groups, which are beautiful in their forms, their tints, and their positions. The brow of the hill commands two lovely prospects: the one gay and extensive, over a fertile plain, watered by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, and broken by St <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>'s Hill and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a> Castle; a large mead, of the most luxuriant verdure, lies <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> below the eye, spreading to the banks of the river; and beyond it the country is full of farms, villas, and villages, and every mark of opulence and cultivation. The other view is more wooded: the steeple of a church, or the turrets of a seat, sometimes rise above the trees; and the bold <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of Walton <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> is there a conspicuous object, equally singular and noble. The inclosures on the flat are more retired and quiet; each is confined within itself; and altogether they form an agreeable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> to the open exposure above them. With the beauties which enliven a garden are everywhere intermixed many properties of a farm: both the lawns are pastured; and the lowings of the herds, the bleating of the sheep, and the tinklings of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a>-wether, resound through all the plantations: even the clucking of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a> is not omitted; for a menagerie of a very simple design is placed near the Gothic building; A small serpentine river is provided for the water-fowl; while the others stray among the flowering shrubs on the banks, or straggle about the neighbouring lawn: and the corn fields are the subjects of every rural employment which arable land from seed-time to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> can furnish. But though so many of the circumstances occur, the simplicity of a farm is wanting; that idea is lost in such a profusion of ornament; a rusticity of character cannot be preserved amidst all the elegant decorations which may be lavished on a garden.

FARMER

Pages 450-450

in mining, is the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the field, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> one that farms the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> and cope of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>.

FARN ISLANDS

Pages 450-450

two groups of little <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> and rocks, 17 in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, lying opposite to Bamborough castle in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>. At low <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of several others are visible besides the 17 <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned. The nearest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> to the shore is called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">House</a>-island, and lies exactly one <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and 68 chains from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. The most distant is about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> eight miles. Their produce is kelp, feathers, and a few seals, which the tenant watches and shoots for the sake of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> and skins. Some of them yield a little grass that may serve to feed a cow or two; which the people transport over in their little boats. The largest or House-island is about one mile in compass, and has a fort and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTHOUSE">lighthouse</a>. It contains about six or seven acres of rich pasture; and the shore abounds with good coals which are dug at the ebb of tide. St Cuthbert is said to have passed the two last years of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> on this island. A priory of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENEDICTINES">Benedictines</a> was afterwards established here, for six or eight monks, subordinate to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> tower, the remains of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and some other buildings, are still to be seen on this island; and a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a>, which is pretended to be that of St Cuthbert. At the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> end of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> is a deep chasm, from the top to the bottom of the rock, communicating with the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; through which, in tempestuous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, the water is forced with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> violence and noise, and forms a fine jet d'eau of 60 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. It is called by the inhabitants of the opposite coast, the Churn. One of the islands in the most distant <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROUP">group</a> is called the Pinnacles, from some vast columnar rocks at the south end, even at their sides, flat at the tops, and entirely covered with guillemots and shags. The fowlers <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> from one to the other of these columns by means of a board, which they <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> from top to top, forming a narrow <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over such a dreadful <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAP">gap</a> that the very sight of it strikes one with horror.

FARNABIE

Pages 450-451

THOMAS, son of a carpenter at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, born in 1575, staid a short while at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; where being enticed to abandon his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and was there educated in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> belonging to the Jesuits. Being weary of their severe <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, he went with Sir John Hawkins and Sir Francis Drake in their last voyage in 1595. He was afterwards a soldier in the Low Countries; but being redu- Farnabie returned to England, where wandering about for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> under the name of Thomas Baines, the anagram of his name, he settled at Mattock in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a>, and taught a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>-school with good reputation. He removed to London, and opened a school with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> accommodations for young gentlemen. While he taught this school, he was made <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, and incorporated into the university of Oxford. Thence he removed, in 1636, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a>-oaks in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>; and taught the sons of several noblemen and gentlemen, who boarded with him, with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> success, and grew rich. His works gained him reputation. Upon the breaking out of the civil commotions in 1641, he was <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> into prison. It was debated in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of commons, whether he should be sent to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>; but this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> being rejected, he was removed to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELY">Ely</a>-house in Holborn, and there he died in 1647. Mr Farnabie was a very eminent grammarian; and many writers have spoken with great approbation of his labours. Mr Bayle in particular says, "His notes upon most of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Latin poets have been of very great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to young beginners; being short, learned, and designed chiefly to clear up the text."

FARNHAM

Pages 451-451
or Fernham; a town of Surry, and capital of the hamlet of its own name, 41 miles from London on the Winchester road. It is a large populous place, situated on the river Wey, and supposed to have its name from the fern which abounded here. It was given by the West Saxon king Ethelbald to the see of Winchester; the bishops of which have generally resided in the castle here, in the summer time, ever since the reign of King Stephen, whose brother, its then bishop, first built it. It was a magnificent structure, with deep moats, strong walls and towers at proper distances, and a fine park; but it is much decayed. The town, which contains 437 houses, and 2508 inhabitants, is governed by 12 masters or burgesses, of whom two are bailiffs, (chosen annually). They have the profit of the fairs and markets, and the assize of bread and beer; and hold a court every three weeks, which has power of trying and determining all actions under 40s. From Michaelmas to Christmas here is a good market for oats; and one of the greatest wheat markets in England, especially between All-Saints day and mid-summer. The toll-dish here was once reckoned worth 200l. a year; but it is much diminished, since the people about Chichester and Southampton began to send their meal to London by sea. But this loss is amply made up by the vast growth of hops, of which there are 300 or 400 acres of plantations about this town, and they are said to excel the Kentish hop-yards both in quantity and quality. This town sent members to parliament in the reign of Edward II. but never since. The magistrates have their privileges from the bishop of Winchester, to whom they pay an acknowledgement of 12d. a-year. The market is on Thursday; and there are three fairs annually, and a great market for Welsh hose.

FARNOVIANS

Pages 451-451

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of Socinians, so called from Stanislaus Farnovius, who separated from the other Unitarians in the year 1568, and was followed by several persons eminent for their learning. This sect did not last <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>; for having lost their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, who died in 1615, it was scattered abroad and reduced to nothing. Farnovius was engaged by Gonesius to prefer the Arian system to that of Farquhar, the Socinians, and consequently asserted, that Christ had been produced out of nothing by the Supreme Being before the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> of this terrestrial globe. His sentiments concerning the Holy Ghost are not certainly known; however, it appears that he warned his disciples against paying the tribute of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> worship to the Divine Spirit.

FARQUHAR

Pages 451-452

GEORGE, an ingenious poet and dramatic writer, the son of a clergyman in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDONDERRY">Londonderry</a> in 1678. He was sent to Trinity <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>; but his volatile disposition not relishing a college <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, he betook himself to the stage; where, having dangerously wounded a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a> in a tragic <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>, by forgetting to change his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> for a foil, it shocked him so much that he left the Dublin <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> and went to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. Here he procured a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Ormonde; which he held several years, and gave many proofs both of courage and conduct. In 1698, he wrote his first <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> called <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">Love</a> and a Bottle; which for its sprightly <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a> and busy scenes, was well received. In the beginning of the year 1700, which was the jubilee year at Rome, he brought out his Constant Couple, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a Trip to the Jubilee; and suited Mr Wilks's talents so well in the character of Sir Harry Wildair, that the player gained almost as much reputation as the poet. This tempted him to continue it in another comedy called Sir Harry Wildair, or The sequel of the Trip to the Jubilee; in which Mrs Oldfield acquired <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> applause. In 1702, he published his Miscellanies, which contain a variety of humorous sallies of fancy. In 1703, appeared the Inconstant, or the Way to Win him; in 1704, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARCE">farce</a> called the Stage-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COACH">coach</a>; in 1705, the Twin Rivals; and in 1706, the Recruiting Officer, founded on his own observations while on a recruiting party at Shrewsbury. His last comedy was the Beaux Stratagem, of which he did not live to enjoy the full success. Mr Farquhar married in 1703. Before that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> his manner of life had been rather dissipated. The lady, therefore, who afterwards became his wife, having fallen violently in love with him, but judging that a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of his humour would not easily be drawn into the trammels of matrimony, contrived to have it given out that she was possessed of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fortune; and finding means afterwards to let Mr Farquhar know her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to him, interest and vanity got the better of his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, and the lady and he were united in the hymeneal bands. But how great was his disappointment when he found all his prospects overclouded so early in life (for he was then no more than 24), by a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> from which he had nothing to expect but an annual increase of family, and an enlargement of expense in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of it far beyond what his income would support. Yet, to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> be it told, though he found himself thus deceived in a most essential particular, he never was known once to upbraid his wife with it; but generously forgave an imposition which love for him alone had urged her to, and even behaved to her with all the tenderness and delicacy of the most indulgent husband. Mrs Farquhar, however, did not very <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> enjoy the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> she had purchased by this stratagem; for the circumstances that attended this union were in some respects perhaps the FAR For, finding himself considerably involved in debt in consequence of their increasing family, he was induced to make application to a certain noble courtier, who had frequently professed the greatest friendship for him, and given him the strongest assurances of his intended services. This pretended <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> repeated his former <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a>; but expressing much concern that he had nothing at present immediately in his power, advised him to convert his commission into <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to answer his present occasions, and assured him that in a short time he would procure another for him. Farquhar, who could not bear the thoughts of his wife and family being in distress, followed this advice, and sold his commission; but, to his great mortification and disappointment, found, on a renewal of his application to this inhuman nobleman, that he had either entirely forgotten, or had never intended to perform, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> he had made him. This distracting frustration of all his hopes fixed itself so strongly on our author's mind, that it soon brought on him a sure, though not a very sudden, declension of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, which at length carried him off the stage of life in 1707, before he arrived at 30 years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>.—His comedies have so much humour, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> are so <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>, that his plays still continue to be represented to full houses.

FARRIER

Pages 452-452

one whose employment is to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHOE">shoe</a> horses, and cure them when diseased <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> lame.
