FEE

Pages 633-634

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies a complete feudal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>. Hence, where the bare fiefment of any feudal subject is meant to be conveyed to A, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> property to B, that meaning is expressed thus; "to A in fiefment, and to B in fee." See LAW, No lxix. cclxv. Fees are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> divided into absolute, otherwise called fees-simple; and limited, one <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of which we usually call fee-tail. I. Tenant in fee-simple (<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> as he is frequently styled, tenant-in-fee), is he that hath lands, tenements, or hereditaments, to hold to him and his heirs for ever; generally, absolutely and simply; without mentioning what heirs, but referring that to his own <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, or to the disposition of the law. The true meaning of the word fee (feodum) is the same with that of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEUD">feud</a> or sef-fief*, and in its original <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it is taken in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to allodium; which latter the writers on this subject define to be every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s own <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, which he possesseth merely in his own <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, without owing any rent or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to any superior. This is property in its highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>; and the owner thereof hath absolutum et directum dominium, and therefore is said to be seized thereof absolutely in dominico suo, in his own demesne. But feodum or fee, is that which is held of some superior, on condition of rendering him service; in which superior the ultimate property of the land resides. And therefore Sir Henry Spelman defines a feud or fee to be, The right which the vassal or tenant hath in lands to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the same and take the profits thereof to him and his heirs, rendering to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> his due services; the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> allodial property of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> always remaining in the lord. This allodial property no subject in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> has; it being a received and now undeniable principle in the law, that all the lands are holden mediately or immediately of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>. The king therefore only hath absolutum et directum dominium; but all subjects lands are in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of feodum or fee, whether derived to them by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> from their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, or purchased for a valuable consideration; for they cannot come to any man by either of those ways, unless accompanied with those feudal clogs which were laid upon the first feudatory when it was originally granted. A subject therefore hath only the usufruct, and not the absolute property, of the soil; or, as Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COKE">Coke</a> expresses it, he hath dominium utile, but not dominium directum. And hence it is, that, in the most solemn acts of law, we express the strongest and highest estate that any subject can have, by these words, "he is seized thereof in his demesne, as of fee." It is a man's demesne, dominium, or property, since it belongs to him and his heirs for ever: yet this dominium, property, or demesne, is strictly not absolute or allodial, but qualified or feudal: it is of his demesne, as of fee; that is, it is not purely and simply his own, since it is held of a superior lord, in whom the ultimate property resides. This is the primary sense and acceptation of the word fee. But (as Sir Martin Wright very justly observes) the doctrine, "that all lands are holden," having been for so many ages a fixed and undeniable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-AXIOM">axiom</a>, the English lawyers do very rarely (of late years especially) use the word fee in this its primary original sense, in contradistinction to allodium or absolute property, with which they have no concern; but generally use it to express the continuance or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of estate. A fee therefore, in general, signifies an estate of inheritance; being the highest and most extensive <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> that a man can have in a feud: and when the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> is used simply, without any other adjunct, or has the adjunct of simple annexed to it (as, a fee, or a fee-simple), it is used in contradistinction to a fee-conditional at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law, or a fee-tail by the statute; importing an absolute inheritance, clear of any condition, limitation, or restrictions to particular heirs, but descendible to the heirs-general, whether <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>, lineal, or collateral. And in no other sense than this is the king said to be seized in fee, he being the feudatory of no man. Taking therefore fee in this its secondary sense, as a state of inheritance, it is applicable to, and may be had in, any kind of hereditaments either corporeal or incorporeal. But there is this distinction between the two species of hereditaments; that of a corporeal inheritance a man shall be said to be seized in his demesne, as of fee; of an incorporeal one he shall only be said to be seized as of fee, and not in his demesne. For as incorporeal hereditaments are in their nature collateral to, and issue out of, lands and houses, their owner hath no property, dominium, or demesne, in the thing itself, but hath only something derived out of it; resembling the servitudes, or services, of the civil law. The dominium, or property, is frequently in one man, while the appendage or service is in another. Thus Gaius may be seized as of fee, of a way going over the land, of which Titius is seized in his demesne as of fee. The fee-simple or inheritance of lands and tenements is generally vested and resides in some person or other; though <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> inferior estates may be carved out of it. As <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> one grants a lease for 21 years, or for one or two lives, the fee-simple remains vested in him and his heirs; and after the determination of those years or lives, the land reverts to the grantor or his heirs, who shall hold it again in fee-simple. Yet sometimes the fee may be in abeyance, that is (as the word signifies) in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> in law; there being no person in esse, in whom it can vest and abide, though... though the law considers it as always potentially existing, and ready to vest whenever a proper owner appears. Thus, in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> to John for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and afterwards to the heirs of Richard, the inheritance is plainly neither granted to John nor Richard, nor can it vest in the heirs of Richard till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, nam nemo est haeres viventis: it remains therefore in waiting, or abeyance, during the life of Richard. This is likewise always the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of a parson of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, who hath only an estate therein for the term of his life; and the inheritance remains in abeyance. And not only the fee, but the freehold also, may be in abeyance; as, when a parson dies, the freehold of his glebe is in abeyance until a successor be named, and then it vests in the successor. The word heirs is necessary in the grant or donation, in order to make a fee or inheritance. For if land be given to a man for ever, or to him and his assigns for ever, this vests in him but an estate for life. This very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> nicety about the insertion of the word heirs in all feoffments and grants, in order to vest a fee, is plainly a relick of the feudal strictness: by which it was required, that the form of the donation should be punctually pursued: or that, as Craig expresses it in the words of Baldus, donationes sint stricti juris, ne quis plus donandis praesumatur quam in donatione expresserit. And therefore, as the personal abilities of the donee were originally supposed to be the only inducements to the gift, the donee's estate in the land extended only to his own person, and subsisted no longer than his life; unless the donor, by an express provision in the grant, gave it a longer continuance, and extended it also to his heirs. But this rule is now softened by many exceptions. For, 1. It does not extend to devises by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a>; in which, as they were introduced at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when the feudal rigour was apace wearing out, a more liberal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> is allowed: and therefore by a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVISE">devise</a> to a man for ever, or to one and his assigns for ever, or to one in fee-simple, the devisee hath an estate of inheritance; for the intention of the devisor is sufficiently plain from the words of perpetuity annexed, though he hath omitted the legal words of inheritance. But if the devise be to a man and his assigns, without annexing words of perpetuity, there the devisee shall take only an estate for life; for it does not appear that the devisor intended any more. 2. Neither does this rule extend to fines or recoveries, considered as a species of conveyance; for thereby an estate in fee passes by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> and operation of law without the word heirs; as it does also for particular reasons, by certain other methods of conveyance, which have relation to a former grant or estate, wherein the word heirs was expressed. 3. In creations of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> by writ, the peer so created hath an inheritance in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, without expressing the word heirs; for they are implied in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>, unless it be otherwise specially provided: but in creations by patent, which are stricti juris, the word heirs must be inserted, otherwise there is no inheritance. 4. In grants of lands to sole corporations and their successors, the word successors supplies the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of heirs; for as heirs take from the ancestor, so doth the successor from the predecessor. Nay, in a grant to a bishop, or other sole spiritual corporation, in frankalmogin, the word frankalmogin supplies the place of successors (as the word successors supplies the place of heirs) ex vi <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERMINI">termini</a>; and in all these <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> a fee-simple vests in such sole corporation. But, in a grant of lands to a corporation aggregate, the word successors is not necessary, though usually inserted: for, albeit such simple grant be strictly only an estate for life, yet as that corporation never dies, such estate for life is perpetual, or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to a fee-simple, and therefore the law allows it to be one. Lastly, In the case of the king, a fee-simple will vest in him, without the words heirs or successors in the grant; partly from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a>, and partly from a reason similar to the last, because the king, in judgment of law, never dies. But the general rule is, that the word heirs is necessary to create an estate of inheritance. II. We are next to consider limited fees, or such estates of inheritance as are clogged and confined with conditions or qualifications of any sort. And these we may divide into two sorts: 1. Qualified or base fees; and, 2. Fees conditional, so called at the common law; and afterwards fees-tail, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the statute de donis. 1. A base or qualified fee, is such a one as has a qualification subjoined thereto, and which must be determined whenever the qualification annexed to it is at an end. As, in the case of a grant to A and his heirs, tenants in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> of Dale; in this instance, whenever the heirs of A cease to be tenants of that manor, the grant is entirely defeated. So, when Henry VI. granted to John Talbot, lord of the manor of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KINGSTON">Kingston</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LISLE">Lisle</a> in Berks, that he and his heirs, lords of the said manor, should be <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> of the realm, by the title of Barons of Lisle; here John Talbot had a base or qualified fee in that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>; and the instant he or his heirs quitted the seigniory of this manor, the dignity was at an end. This estate is a fee, because by possibility it may endure for ever in a man and his heirs; yet as that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> depends upon the concurrence of collateral circumstances, which qualify and debase the purity of the donation, it is therefore a qualified or base fee. 2. As to fees-conditional, or fee-tail, see the article TAIL.

FEE ALSO

Pages 634-635

e also denotes a settled perquisite of public officers, payable by those who employ them. The fees due to the officers of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM_HOUSE"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> are expressly mentioned in a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCHEDULE">schedule</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, which is hung up in public view in the said office, and in all other places where the said fees are to be paid or received. And <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any officer shall offend, by acting contrary to the regulations therein contained, he shall forfeit his office and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and be for ever after incapable of any office in the custom-house. The other public offices have likewise their settled fees, for the several branches of business transacted in them. Fee-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">Farm</a>, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a> without homage, fealty, or other <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, except that mentioned in the feoffment; ment; which is usually the full rent, or at least a fourth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of this tenure is, that if the rent be behind, and unpaid for two years, then the seoffer and his heirs may have an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of the lands.

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a name used by some for the horns of INSECTS.

FEELING

Pages 635-635

one of the five <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> senses, by which we obtain the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>, hard, soft, rough, hot, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, wet, dry, and other tangible qualities. See ANATOMY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. FEET. See FOOT. Feet-Bearer, the name of an officer in the courts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Anglo-Saxon and Welsh kings. He was a young <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> whose duty it was to sit on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, with his back towards the fire, and hold the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s feet in his bosom all the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he sat at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, to keep them warm and comfortable; a piece of state and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> unknown in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times.

FEICALES

Pages 632-633
or FOECIALES, an order of priests or officers, consisting of 20 persons, among the ancient Romans, appointed to proclaim war, negotiate peace, &c. Festus derives the word from ferio, "I strike;" as ferire facius signifies "to conclude a treaty;" and ac- cordingly, instead of feciales, he would have it written feriales. Others derive it from facius, which was an- ciently written fedus; or from fides, "faith." Others from facio, feci, "I make," &c. because they made war and peace. Vossius chooses to derive it from fatu, of the verb fari, "to speak:" in which sense the feciales should be the same with oratores; which sentiment is also confirmed by the authority of Varro, who says they were called indifferently feciales and oratores. The feciales were a sort of heralds, who, when the Romans had any dispute with their neighbours, were sent first to demand the thing intended to be usurped, or require satisfaction for the injury alleged to be done. If an answer was not returned by them that was satis- factory to the people and the senate, they were despatch- ed again to declare war, and the like in treating for peace; the feciales being the only persons appointed to negotiate between the senate, &c. and the enemy. Plutarch in the life of Numa, and Halicarnassus (lib. ii.), observes, that they were first instituted by that prince. The latter adds, that they were first cho- sen out of the best families in Rome; that their office, which was reputed a sort of sacerdotium, or priesthood, only ended with their life; that their persons were sac- red and inviolable, as those of other priests; that they were even charged to see the republic did not declare war unjustly; that they were to receive the complaints and remonstrances of nations who pretended to have been any way injured by the Romans; that if those complaints were found just, they were to seize the criminals, and deliver them up to those they had offended; that they were invested with the rights and privileges of ambassadors; that they concluded treaties of peace and alliance, and took care they were executed; and, lastly, abolished them, if they were found not to be equitable. Livy, lib. i. cap. 24. ascribes their institution to Ancus Martius, in the year of Rome 114.—Varro assures us, that in his time most of these functions of the faciales were set aside; though Plutarch observes, that they had still some authority in his time. The faciales were crowned with verbenae, "vervain," when they went to declare war. Their head was covered with a veil, over which the crown was applied. In this equipage they proceeded to the frontiers of the new enemy's country, and threw a bloody dart or javelin into the ground within the same. In Livy and other ancient authors we have the formula used in such declarations.

FEINT

Pages 635-635

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FENCING">fencing</a>, a show of making a thrust at one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, in order to deceive the enemy, that you may really strike him in another. A simple feint is a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WRIST">wrist</a>, without stirring the foot.

FELAPTON

Pages 635-635

in Logic, one of the six first modes of the third <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of syllogisms; whereof the first proposition is an universal <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> an universal affirmative, and the third a particular negative.

FELIBIEN

Pages 635-635

ANDRE, was born at Chartres in 1619, and went secretary under the Marquis de Fontenay Mareuil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Rome in 1647. On his return, M. Colbert procured him the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of historiographer to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, superintendant of his buildings, and of the arts and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> in France. He became afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> comptroller general of the bridges and dykes in that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; and died in 1695. He wrote several pieces relating to the fine arts: the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which is his "Dialogues on the Lives and Works of the most eminent Painters."

FELICITAS

Pages 635-635

(Felicity, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">Happiness</a>); was deified by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Pagans. Lucullus built a temple to her. She had another erected by Lepidus. The Greeks paid divine worship to Macaria, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, the same with Felicitas. This deity is often pictured upon medals, and generally with a cornucopie in one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and a caduceus in the other. The <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> are, Felicitas Temporum, Felicitas Augusti, Felicitas Publica, &c.

FELIS

Pages 635-635

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> belonging to the order of ferae, and class <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">mammalia</a>. See MAMMALIA <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. FELLING of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">Timber</a>.—Many circumstances are well known and constantly observed in the felling of timber for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, which, though to a hasty observer they might appear trifling, yet prove, on <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, to be of the utmost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. One thing observed by M. de Buffon, which very greatly increases the solidity and strength of timber, is, that the trees intended to be felled for <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> should first be stripped of their bark, and suffered to stand and die upon the spot before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a>. The sappy <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> blea of the oak becomes by this means as hard and firm as the heart; and the real strength and density of the wood has been proved, by many experiments, to be greatly increased by it: nor is this a practice of any detriment to the proprietor, since the remaining stumps of these trees send up their young shoots as vigorously as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they had been cut <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> condition. When any tree is to be cut down for timber, the first thing to be taken care of is a skilful disbranching of such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> as may endanger it in its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a>: many trees are utterly spoiled for want of a previous care of this kind. In arms of timber that are very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, it is always necessary to chop or sink in them <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLE">bole</a>, and then meeting it with downright strokes, it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be severed from the tree without splitting. In felling the tree, take care always to cut it as close to the ground as possible, unless it is intended to be grubbed up: and the doing this is of advantage both to the timber and to the wood: for timber is never so much valued, if it be known to grow out of old stocks.

FELONY

Pages 635-636

in the general acceptation of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, comprises every <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of crime, which occasions at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law the forfeiture of lands <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> goods. This most frequently happens in those crimes for which a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> either is or was to be inflicted: for those felonies that are called clergyable, or to which the benefit of clergy extends, were anciently punished with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> in all lay or unlearned offenders; though now, by the statute law, that punishment is for the first offence universally remitted. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">Treason</a> itself, says Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COKE">Coke</a>, was anciently comprised under the name of felony; and in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of this we may observe, that the statute of treasons, 25 Edw. III. c. 2. speaking of some dubious crimes, directs a reference to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; that it may be there adjudged, "whether they be treason or other felony." All treasons, therefore, strictly speaking, are felonies; though all felonies are not treason. And to this also we may add, that all offences, now capital, are in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> or other felony; but this is likewise the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with some other offences, which are not punished with death; as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUICIDE">suicide</a>, where the party is already dead; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMICIDE">homicide</a> by chance-medley, or in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SELF_DEFENCE">self-<a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>; and petit-larceny, or pilfering; all which are (strictly speaking) felonies, as they subject the committers of them to forfeitures. So that, upon the whole, the only adequate <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> of felony seems to be that which is before laid <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>; viz. an offence which occasions a total forfeiture of either lands or goods, or both, at the common law; and to which capital or other punishment may be superadded, according to the degree of guilt. To explain this <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> a little farther: The word felony, or felonia, is of undoubted feudal original, being frequently to be met with in the books of feuds, &c. but the derivation of it has much puzzled the juridical lexicographers, Pratensis, Calvinus, and the rest: some deriving it from the Greek, φελος, "an impostor or deceiver;" others from the Latin, fullo, feliti, to countenance. Felony, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of forfeiture to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, being thus <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> terms in the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol9.html#article-FEUDAL_LAW">feudal law</a>, we may easily trace the reason why, upon the introduction of that law into England, those crimes which induced such forfeiture or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESCHEAT">escheat</a> of lands (and, by a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFECTION">defection</a> from the original <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, such as induced the forfeiture of goods also) were denominated felonies. Thus it was that suicide, robbery, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RAPE">rape</a>, were felonies; that is, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of such crimes was forfeiture; till by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> we began to signify by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> of felony, the actual crime committed, and not the penal consequence. And upon this system only can we account for the cause, why treason in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times was held to be a species of felony; viz. because it induced a forfeiture. Hence it follows, that equal punishment does by no means enter into the true idea and definition of felony. Felony may be without inflicting capital punishment, as in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> instanced of self-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, excusable homicide, and petit-larceny; and it is possible that capital punishments may be inflicted, and yet the offence be no felony; as in case of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a> by the common law, which, though capital, never worked any forfeiture of lands or goods, an inseparable incident to felony. And of the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> was the punishment of standing <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MUTE">mute</a>, without pleading to an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a>; which at the common law was capital, but without any forfeiture, therefore such standing mute was no felony. In short, the true criterion of felony is forfeiture: for, as Sir Edward Coke justly observes, in all felonies which are punishable with death, the offender loses all his lands in fee-simple, and also his goods and chattels; in such as are not punishable, his goods and chattels only. The idea of felony is indeed so generally connected with that of capital punishment, that we find it hard to separate them; and to this usage the interpretations of the law do now conform. And therefore, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a statute makes any new offence felony, the law implies that it shall be punished with death, viz. by hanging, as well as with forfeiture: unless the offender prays the benefit of clergy; which all felons are entitled once to have, unless the same is expressly taken away by statute. Felonies by statute are very numerous; and as this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> not admit of a proper enumeration, we must refer to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of the quarto edition of the Statutes, where they are set forth in alphabetical order.

FELTING

Pages 636-637

the method of working up <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> into a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of cloth, independent of either <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEAVING">weaving</a>. Felting in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> is not much practised, excepting in the manufacturing of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>; and as the generality even of those who are employed in making them, are unacquainted with the principles on which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>, a few observations on the method of felting, may, to such, be both useful and agreeable. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> wool, the hair of a rabbit, hare, beaver, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> hair, be examined with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a> of the greatest magnifying power, the surface of each hair appears perfectly smooth, or if any inequalities are observed, they do not appear so much to arise from an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> surface, as from some peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> and transparency of the substances examined; for if their image be viewed by a solar microscope, it terminates in even <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, without the smallest vestige of any roughness. Yet nothing is more evident than that the surfaces of hairs are not perfectly smooth, but either composed of lamellae covering each other from the root to the point, resembling the scales of fishes; or, what some have deemed more probable, of zones placed over each other, similar to the structure of horns; and to this texture hair, wool, &c. owe their disposition for what is denominated felting. Let a person take hold of a hair by the root with one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and draw it between two fingers of the other, from the root towards the point, he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> scarcely perceive any friction, or hear any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>; but should he hold the hair by the point, and draw it between his fingers from the point towards the root, he will feel a sensible opposition or resistance which could not be felt before. A sort of tremulous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> is likewise produced, which can be distinguished by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>. From this simple experiment it is obvious that the texture of the surface of a hair is not the same from the point to the root, as it is from the root to the point. If a hair is taken hold of by the fore-finger and thumb, and rubbed in a longitudinal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, a progressive motion is the result, which is invariably towards the root. This is wholly independent of the texture or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the skin of the fingers; for if the hair be turned, and the point of it placed where the root formerly was, the movement becomes contrary, or, in other words, it is still directed towards the root. It is found a very difficult task to unite a knot made in the middle of a hair, on account of its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> thinness; but if the hair is placed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> of the hand, the knot being in a line with the little finger, and if the hair is grasped by closing the hand, and the fist struck several times against the knee, the knot is thereby opened, because the asperities of one end of the hair are in a contrary direction to those of the other, by which means each end of it recedes a little. By the introduction of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PIN">pin</a> into the eye thus formed at the knot, it is easily untied. Although these observations have a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> reference to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> hair; yet they are equally applicable to wool, furs, and almost every species of animal hair. The surface of all these consists of hard lamellae, placed upon each other like tiles, in the direction from the root to the point. By attending to these remarks, it is easy to see why the contact of woollen stuffs is rough to the skin. The asperities on the surface of the fibres of wool produce a disagreeable <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>, by fixing themselves in the skin, which can only be endured by being accustomed to feel it frequently. The injury done to wounds by the application of wool, is not the result of any chemical <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, but is entirely occasioned by the asperities of its surface. A hatter separates the hairs from each other, by striking the wool with the string of his bow, causing them to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> up in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> in every possible direction, forming a layer of a particular thickness, which is covered by the workmen with a cloth, pressing it with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and moving the hairs backwards and forwards in different directions. In this manner the hairs are brought against each other, and their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of contact considerably multiplied, and the agitation gives each hair a progressive motion towards the root, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which the hairs become twisted together. As the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> becomes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a>, the pressure ought to be increased, in order to keep up the progressive motion and twisting of the hairs, which is then performed with greater difficulty. The hair designed for the manufacturing of hats is always cut off with a sharp <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, and not pulled out by the roots, because the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BULB">bulb</a> of the hair which would come out with it in the latter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, would render the end which was fixed in the skin very obtuse, and nearly destroy its disposition to unite with the adjacent hairs. But in addition to the tendency of hairs to move progressively towards the root, they should not be straight like <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">needles</a>, for in this case they could not produce any compactness in the stuff. The fibres of wool having naturally a crooked form, that substance is well adapted to the operation of felting. The hair of beavers, rabbits, hares, &c. being straight, it cannot be employed in felting by itself, till it has been subjected to a previous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>, viz. rubbing and combing on the skin, the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a> being dipped in a solution of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> in nitric acid. This substance, by acting only on one side of the hair, gives them the disposition to felting which is <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to wool. When it is not intended that the hairs shall enter into the body of the mass, but serve only as an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> coating, which is sometimes given to the outer surface of hats, the operation with the nitric acid need not be performed. They must be uniformly spread upon the surface to which the coating is to be applied, and being covered with a cloth, it is pressed with the hands, and agitated for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. They receive a particular direction afterwards by means of a brush, and are enabled to keep it by having a hot <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> passed over them. Woollen cloth is thickened by fulling, on the same principles that wool and hair become capable of felting. FEL-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAR">Spar</a>, FEL-Spar, or Fel-Spar, a mineral substance. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERALOGY">MINERALOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FELTRIA

Pages 637-637

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town on the borders of Rhaetia towards <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. Now Feltrii, in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, on the Piava. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12° 16'. N. Lat. 46° 0'.

FELUCCA

Pages 637-637

in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> affairs, a little vessel rowed with six oars, frequent in the Mediterranean; which has this peculiarity, that its helm may be applied either in the head <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> stern, as occasion requires.

FEMALE

Pages 637-637

(FEMINA), a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> peculiar to animals, signifying that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEX">sex</a> which conceives and generates its young within itself. See SEX and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">GENERATION</a>. Female is also applied, figuratively, to things without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, from the resemblance they bear to the females of animals. Thus we say a FEMALE Screw. See Screw. FEMALE Flower. See Femenius Flos. FEMALE Plant. See Femenia Planta.

FEMININE

Pages 637-637

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, one of the genders of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOUNS">nouns</a>. See GENDER.

FEMME COVERT

Pages 637-637

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a married woman. See COVERTURE. Femme Sole, an unmarried woman, whose debts, contracted before <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, become those of her husband after it. A femme sole merchant, is where a woman, in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, uses a trade alone, without her husband; on which account she shall be <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> without him.

FEN

Pages 638-638

a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> overflowed with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> abounding with bogs. See Bog and Draining, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Fens are either made up of a congeries of bogs; or consist of a multitude of pools or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, with dry spots of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> intermixed, like so many little <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. Several statutes have been made for the draining of fens, chiefly in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGESHIRE">Cambridgeshire</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEDFORDSHIRE">Bedfordshire</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>; and by a late <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>, 11 Geo. II. commissioners shall be appointed for the effectually draining and preserving of the fens in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELY">Ely</a>, who are authorized to make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAINS">drains</a>, dams, and proper works thereon; and they may <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> the landholders therein with a yearly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">acre</a>-tax, and in default of payment, sell the defender's lands. The wet grounds called fens, in Lincolnshire and elsewhere in England, bring many advantages to the inhabitants of those counties. Fowl and fish are very plentiful in them. The pike and eels are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and easily caught, but they are usually coarse. The duck, mallard, and teal, are in such plenty as is scarce to be conceived. They are taken by decoys in prodigious flocks at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. They send these fowl from Lincolnshire to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, twice a-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, on horseback, from Michaelmas to Lady-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; and one decoy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> furnish 20 dozen, or more, twice a-week, for the whole season in this manner. The decoy-men <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> with the people, who bring them to London at a certain rate, and they are obliged to take off their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> the whole <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> that is catched. Two teal are usually reckoned equal to one duck; and six ducks and twelve teal are accounted a dozen of wild fowl; and the usual market price is about 9s. for such a dozen. About midsummer, during the moulting season, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> number also are destroyed by the people in the neighbourhood. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> birds at this season are neither able to swim nor fly well; and the people going in with boats among the reeds where they <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a>, knock them <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>. A little before Michaelmas, vast flights of these birds arrive at the decoys from other places; they soon grow fat in them, and continue there a prey to the masters or owners, as long as the decoys are unfrozen; but, when they are iced over, they fly away again, and go to the neighbouring seas for food. The fens also abound in a sort of herbage that is very nourishing to cattle. Sheep and horses always grow fat upon it. The fens are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, and the owners of cattle mark them that they may be known. It is remarkable, that, though all is open, the cattle used to one particular spot of ground seldom leave it, but the owner may always find them in or near the same place. The fens have many large and deep drains. In these the pike and eel grow to a vast size; and they are full of geese which feed on the grass; but these eat <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and muddy, and may even be smelt as soon as a person comes into the room where they are roasting. But the people have another very great advantage from these birds besides the eating of them, namely, their feathers and quills; and the produce of these is so great, that the customhouse books in the town of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOSTON">Boston</a> show, that there are frequently sent away in one year 300 bags of feathers, each containing a hundred and a half <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. Each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of feathers brings in the owner twopence; and it may be thought strange by people unacquainted with these things, but it is a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, that the owners pull them five or six times a year for the feathers, and three times for the quills. Each pulling comes to about a pound, and many people have 1000 geese at a time, or more. They are kept at no charge, except in deep snowy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, when they are obliged to feed them with corn. Oats also grow very well in many of the fen countries, and in good seasons bring great increase and advantage to the owners. There is also another vegetable of great profit to them. This is the *rapum silvestre*; the seed of which they call *cole-seed*; and they make an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> from it of great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in trade. They grind the seed between two large <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, the one standing perpendicularly on the other. The stones are made of a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> marble, and are brought from Germany. They sometimes turn them by sails, and sometimes by the drains which carry off the water from the fen lands. The fens lying low, and being of a vast <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, are very subject to be overflowed by waters from the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> countries; and though great care and expense is used to keep them dry, they are often like a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; and the sheep are obliged to be carried off in boats, and the people to live in their upper rooms, and to be supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> also with boats.

FENCE

Pages 638-640

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a> and Husbandry, a hedge, wall, ditch, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other enclosure, made round gardens, fields, woods, &c. In hot climates, where they have not occasion for walls to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a> their fruit, their gardens <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> open, where they can have a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> fence, and prospects; or else they bound their gardens with groves, in which are fountains, walks, &c. which are much more pleasing to the sight than a dead wall: but, in colder countries, we are obliged to have walls to shelter and ripen our fruit, although they take away much from the pleasant prospect of the garden. Brick walls are accounted the best and warmest for fruit: and these walls, being built pannelwise, with pillars at equal distances, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, in that the walls may be built thinner than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> without these panels, for then it would be necessary to build them thicker everywhere; and, besides, these panels make the walls look the handsomer. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">Stone</a> walls, however, on account of their durability, are to be preferred to those of brick, especially those of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> hewn <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. Those that are made of rough stones, though though they are very dry and warm, yet, by reason of their unevenness, are inconvenient to nail up trees to, except pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> be laid in them here and there for that purpose. But, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> gardens, it is better to have the prospect open to the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> garden; which should be surrounded with a fosse, that from the garden the adjacent <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> may be viewed. But this must depend on the situation of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>: for, if the prospect from the garden is not good, it had better be shut out from the sight than be open. As also, when a garden lies near a populous town, and the adjoining grounds are open to the inhabitants; if the garden is open, there will be no walking there in good <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, without being exposed to the view of all passers-by, which is very disagreeable. Where the fosses are made round a garden which is situated in a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARK">park</a>, they are extremely proper; because hereby the prospect of the park will be obtained in the garden, which renders those gardens much more agreeable than those that are confined.—In the making these fosses there have been many inventions; but, upon the whole, none seem preferable to those which have an upright wall next the garden, which, (where the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> will admit of a deep trench) should be five or six feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; and, from the foot of this wall, the ground on the outside should rise with a gradual easy slope, to the distance of 18 or 20 feet; and where it can be allowed, if it slopes much farther it will be easier, and less perceptible as a ditch, to the eye, when viewed at a distance; but, if the ground is naturally wet, so as not to admit a deep fosse, then, in order to make a fence against cattle, if the wall be four feet high, and slight posts of three feet high are placed <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> behind the wall, with a small chain carried on from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> to post, no cattle or deer will ever attempt to jump against it; therefore it will be a secure fence against them; and if these are painted green, they will not be discerned at a distance, and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the chain will secure persons walking in the garden from tumbling over. In places where there are no good prospects to be obtained from a garden, it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to make the enclosure of park paling; which, if well performed, will last many years, and has a much better appearance than a wall; and this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> may be hid from the sight within, by plantations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EVERGREENS">evergreens</a>; or there may be a quick hedge planted within the pale, which may be trained up, so as to be an excellent fence by the time the pales begin to decay. Fences round parks are generally of paling; which, if well made of winter-fallen oak, will last many years. But a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> thing to be observed, in making these pales, is not to make them too heavy: for, when they are so, their own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> will cause them to decay; therefore the pales should be cleft thin; and the rails should be cut triangular, to prevent the wet lodging upon them; and the posts should be good, and not placed too far asunder. If these things are observed, one of these pales will last, with a little care, upwards of 40 years very well. The common way of making these fences is, to have every other pale <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> or ten inches above the intermediate ones; so that the fence may be six feet and a half high, which is enough for fallow deer; but where there are <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> deer, the fence should be one foot higher, otherwise they will <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a> over. Some enclose their parks with brick walls; and in countries, where stone is cheap, the walls are built with this material; some with, and others without, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a> garden, if rightly contrived, will contain walling enough to afford a supply of such <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> as require the assistance of walls, for any family; and this garden, being situated on one side, and quite out of sight of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, may be surrounded with walls which will screen the kitchen garden from the sight of persons in the pleasure garden; and, being locked up, the fruit will be much better preserved than it can be in the public garden; and the having too great a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of walling is often the occasion that so many ill managed trees are frequently to be seen in large gardens. The height of garden walls should be 12 feet, which is a moderate proportion; and, if the soil be good, it may in time be well furnished with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> wood in every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, especially that part planted with pears, notwithstanding of the branches being trained horizontally from the bottom of the walls. With regard to the different kinds of fences, see <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Fence-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">Month</a>, the month wherein deer begin to fawn, during which it is unlawful to hunt in the forest. It commences 15 days before Midsummer, and ends 15 days after it. This month, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> foresters, is called defense-month. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FENCING">Fencing</a>, the art of making a proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, as well for attacking an enemy as for defending one's self. This art is acquired by practising with foils, called in Latin rudes; whence fencing is also denominated gladiatura rudaria.—It is one of the exercises learnt in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a> (see <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">Exercise</a> and Academy); and is an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ACCOMPLISHMENT">accomplishment</a> both agreeable and useful:—agreeable, as it affords gentlemen a noble and distinguished amusement:—useful, as it forms their body; and furnishes them with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, whether it be of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> or their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, when the one or the other is attacked by those turbulent and dangerous persons whose correction is of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> in general. Pyrrard assures us, that the art of fencing is so highly esteemed in the East Indies, that none but princes and noblemen are allowed to teach it. They wear a badge or cognizance on their <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> arms, called in their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> eurru; which is put on with great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, like the badges of our orders of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a>, by the kings themselves. Fencing is divided into two parts, simple and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a>. Simple is that performed directly and nimbly, on the same line; and is either offensive or defensive.—The principal object of the first, is whatever may be attempted, in pushing or making passes from this or that point, to the most uncovered part of the enemy. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> consists in parrying and repelling the thrusts aimed by the enemy. The compound includes all the possible arts and inventions to deceive the enemy, and make him leave that part we have a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> on bare and unguarded, upon Fencing finding we cannot come at it by force, nor by the agility of the simple play. The principal means hereof are, on the offensive side, feints, appeals, clashings, and entanglings of swords, half thrusts, &c., and, on the defensive, to push in parrying. Of all which a detail would be here useless, as they are only to be understood and acquired from personal instructions conjoined with practice.

FENELON

Pages 640-640

FRANCIS DESALIGNAC DE LA MOTTE, was of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and illustrious family, and born at the castle of Fenelon in Perigord in 1651. In 1689, he was appointed <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to the dukes of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a> and Anjou; and in 1655 was consecrated archbishop of Cambrai. After this preferment, a storm arose against him, that obliged him to leave the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> for ever, occasioned by his performance entitled, An Explication of the Maxims of the Saints concerning the Interior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a>; in which he was supposed to favour the extravagant notions of Madame Guyon, and the principles of Quietism. A controversy on this occasion was for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> carried on between him and M. Bossuet, bishop of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEAUX">Meaux</a>; which terminated in an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> to the pope; when his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a> condemned the archbishop's book, by a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> dated <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 12, 1699. Some friends indeed pretend, that there was more of court policy than <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> zeal in this affair; but be this as it may, the archbishop submitted patiently to this determination; and, retiring to his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Cambrai, acquitted himself punctually in all the duties of his station, and led a most exemplary life. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> that gained him the greatest reputation, and which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> render his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> immortal, is his Adventures of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TELEMACHUS">Telemachus</a>; the style of which is <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>, the fictions well contrived, the moral sublime, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> maxims tending all to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of mankind. Hence it is thought, as the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> of this work was stopped at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, that the prelate's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a> was in politics instead of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; and though his disgrace was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to this work, he had, while he was tutor to the young princes, taught them the same principles asserted and exemplified in Telemachus. Fenelon died in 1715; and a collection of all his religious works was afterwards printed at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROTTERDAM">Rotterdam</a>, under the care of the marquis de Fenelon his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>-nephew, when <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> to the States-General. FENNEL. See ANETHUM, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FENTON

Pages 640-640

Elijah, descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHELTON">Shelton</a> near <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>, but in what year is uncertain. He was the youngest of 12 children, and was intended for the ministry; but embracing principles contrary to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, while at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, he became disqualified for entering into holy orders. After he quitted the university, he was secretary to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORRERY">Orrery</a>; but seems to have spent the most of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> amongst his friends and relations, and used to pay an annual visit to his elder <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> who enjoyed an estate of 1000l. a-year. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> tenderness and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, enjoyed the fairest reputation, and was much esteemed by Mr Pope; who, when he died in 1730, paid him the tribute of a very elegant epitaph. He published a volume of poems in the year 1717; and in 1723 was acted his tragedy of Mariamne, built upon her story collected from Josephus in the third volume of the Spectator. FENUGREEK. See TRIGONELLA, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FEOD

Pages 640-640
or FEUN, is defined to be a right which a vassal hath in lands or some immoveable thing of his lord's, to use the same, and take the profits thereof hereditarily, rendering unto the lord such feudal duties and services as belong to military tenure, &c., and the property of the soil always remaining to the lord.

FEODAL

Pages 640-647

of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> belonging to a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEUD">FEUD</a> or FEE. FEODAL System, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of FEIFS or FEUDS. About 12 centuries ago, this system was so universally received in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, that Sir Henry Spelman calls it the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW_OF_NATIONS"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> of nations in our western world. Hence it deserves our <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> in a particular manner: a knowledge of the different feuds being indispensably requisite for a proper understanding either of the civil <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of our own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, or of the laws by which its landed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> is regulated. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> policy of the Celtic or northern nations, known by the names of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>, Vandals, Franks, Huns, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOMBARDS">Lombards</a>, furnished the original constitution or system of feuds. These people pouring out in vast multitudes from the same officina gentium or "storehouse of nations," overran all the European countries on the declension of the Roman empire. They brought the feudal system along with them from the countries out of which they emigrated; and, supposing it to be the most proper method of securing their new conquests, they introduced it into their more southerly colonies. According to this system, the victorious general allotted considerable tracts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> to his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> officers; while they, in like manner, divided their possessions among the inferior officers, and even those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> who were thought to be the most deserving. Allotments of this kind were named feoda, fiefs, fees, or feuds, from a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of words, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of these barbarians, signifying a reward or stipend bestowed on certain conditions (A). The condition upon which these rewards were given was, that the possessors should faithfully serve the person from whom they were received, both at home and abroad, in the military way. To this they engaged themselves by a juramentum fidelitatis, or oath of fealty; in the event of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of which, either by not performing the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> Feudal service, or... service agreed upon, by deserting their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, &c., the lands were to return to their original possessor. Thus the possessors of feudal allotments became interested in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of them; and not only the receivers but those who gave them; were equally and mutually bound to defend their possessions, none of them being able to pretend any <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> but that of conquest. For this purpose government and subordination were absolutely necessary; it being impossible to conduct any system of defence where every thing was tumultuous and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>. Every person, therefore, who was a feudatory, i.e. who had received lands, was bound to do everything in his power to defend the lord of his fee; while, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the latter was no less subordinate to his immediate superior; and so on to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> himself. In like manner a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> bond of defence existed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from the prince to the lowest feudists. Such were the foundations on which the feudal system was properly established; and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> was, a military subjection throughout the whole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>. The prince could always collect an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of feudatories ready to defend not only the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> in general, but the particular possessions of each person; and the propriety of this constitution was soon apparent in the strength which these newly erected kingdoms acquired, and the valour with which their conquests were defended. Besides these feudal grants, however, which were held only on the terms of military service above mentioned, there were others called allodial, which were given upon more enlarged principles. To these every free <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> had a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>; and could not only claim his territory as well as the rest, but dispose of it at his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> (a); and this freedom was denominated allodiality. These allodials, however, were not exempted from military service. A <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of their freedom consisted in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to go to the wars; for this, in the barbarous times we speak of, was the only way to acquire any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of renown. Only the slaves were destined to follow the arts of peace; while every free person was not only at liberty to defend his country, but under an obligation to do it in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of any urgent <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>. Thus there was a feudal and a national <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>. The feudal vassals constituted the army, properly so called; while the national militia was composed of the allodial proprietors. This allodiality, however, was not confined to landed property, but included likewise moveable estates or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>; so that proprietors of the latter kind were obliged also in times of danger to bear arms and appear in the field. Between the feudal and allodial proprietors, however, there was this farther <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, that the latter had no concern with any private quarrels which might take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> among the allodial lords themselves; so that they were never obliged to appear in the field unless when called forth by the sovereign against the enemies of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>. This circumstance we might suppose to be an advantage, but it ultimately operated otherwise; becoming the means of changing the allodial right into a feudal <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a>. For some time the holders of fiefs had an eminent advantage over the allodial proprietors. This was owing to the imperfection of government in those days; so that the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> had it in their power to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> their own quarrels, while the weak were equally exposed to the insults of both parties. The lord and his vassals therefore were always formidable; but the allodial proprietors, however, were not exempted from military service. (a) The author of A View of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> in Europe, has traced the remote sources of the feudal laws in an elegant and spirited manner (book i. chap. ii. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. i.). Tacitus informs us, that the individuals of each of the German nations cultivated by turns a tract of land proportionable to their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the whole; after which each individual received such an allotment of the cultivated tract as his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> seemed to require. These nations had not altered their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> principles at the time they overran the Roman empire; and hence the provinces of it were then divided after the same manner. The most considerable allotment was bestowed on the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, as being the most dignified person in the community, and this allotment was styled his domain; while the shares of citizens and warriors, which were likewise in proportion to the merit or dignity of each, constituted what was called allodiality. But as it often happened that all the land was not exhausted by these partitions, what remained was considered as the property of the community, and in the barbaric codes was called the lands of the fisc. In such German nations as had thus obtained a settlement, it was necessary that there should be a more <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> connexion betwixt the sovereign and the chiefs, as well as between the chiefs and the people, than in others. This was effected by means of the lands of the fisc; for of these the sovereign took possession, dealing them out to the chiefs under the burden of appearing in arms whenever he should please to call; while the chiefs in like manner dealt out lands to those called their retainers, who were also obliged to supply them with military assistance in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of necessity. Hence a political system was founded, which had a prodigious effect on society in all those countries where it prevailed. The intention and tendency of this system was to render the nation independent both at home and abroad; for, while the people were all armed in their common defence, individuals were also properly guarded against the attacks of despotism.
