He was so happy as to cure her; which was the first cause of that esteem which Henry II., who was then but dauphin, and was in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a> with that lady, conceived for him. This <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> offered him, even then, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of first physician to him; but Fernel, who infinitely preferred his studies to the hurry of a court, would not accept the employment. When Henry came to the throne, he renewed his entreaties: but Fernel represented that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> which was offered him was due, for several reasons, and as an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, to the late king's physician; and that, as for himself, he wanted some time to make experiments concerning several discoveries he had made relating to physic. The king admitted this: but as soon as Francis I.'s physician died, Fernel was obliged to go and fill his place at Henry II.'s court. And here just the contrary of what he dreaded came to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>; for he enjoyed more rest and more leisure at court than he had done at Paris; and he might have considered the court as an agreeable retirement, had it not been for the journey which the new civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> obliged the king to take. He died in 1558, leaving behind him a great many works, besides what have been mentioned; as, De additis rerum causis, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> books on <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATHOLOGY">Pathology</a>, a book on Remedies, &c. They have been printed several times, with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> prefixed, written by William Plantius his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a>.

FERONIA

Pages 651-651

the Pagan <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of woods and orchards. This deity took her name from the town Feronia, situated at the foot of Mount Soracte in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, where was a wood and temple consecrated to her. That town and wood are mentioned by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, in the catalogue of Turnus's forces. Strabo relates, that those who sacrificed to this goddess, walked barefoot upon <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> coals, without being hurt. She was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> deity of freed men, who receive their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> at her temple.

FERRARA

Pages 651-652

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the territory of the pope, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of the same name. It is seated in an agreeable and fertile plain; watered by the river Po, which is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> on one side; and on the other is encompassed by a strong wall and deep <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> ditches full of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, as well as by a good citadel, finished by Pope Paul. In the middle of the city is a magnificent castle, which was formerly the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the dukes, and is now not the least ornament of Ferrara. It is quite surrounded with water; and the arsenal, which is near it, deserves the observation of travellers. Over against the palace is the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a>'s garden; with a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARK">park</a>, called Belvidere. Ferrara. Retwidere on account of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. Behind the garden there is a palace, built with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble, called the palace of diamonds, because all the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> are cut <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> fashion. Ferrara had formerly a considerable trade; but it is now much deserted. It is said to contain 24,000 inhabitants. The fortifications are now neglected, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> university is dwindled into a wretched <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of the Jesuits. However, in 1755, it was advanced to an archbishopric by Pope Clement XII. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> about it is so marshy, that a shower <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> two of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> renders the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> almost impassable. It is 24 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>; 38 north-west of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAVENNA">Ravenna</a>, 70 north-west of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, and 190 north of Rome. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURAT">Murat</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> was defeated here in 1815 by the Austrians. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12° 14'. N. Lat. 44° 36'. Ferrara, the duchy of; a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> in the pope's territory, bounded on the north by the Austrian territories, on the west by the duchies of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIRANDOLA">Mirandola</a>, on the south by the Bolognese and by Romagna, of which it was formerly a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, and on the east by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. It is 50 miles in length, and 43 in breadth along the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a>; but grows narrower and narrower towards the Mantuan. This country is almost surrounded by the branches of the Po, which often overflow the country, and form the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> morass of Comacchio, which has a bad effect on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. It is thin of people, and indifferently cultivated, though fit for corn, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>. The Po and the lake of Comacchio yield a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fish. Ferrara is the capital town; besides which there are Arano, Comacchio, Magnavacca, Belriguardo, Cento, Buendeno, and Fichera. This duchy was formerly possessed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol9.html#article-ESTE">Este</a>. But the pope took possession of it in 1598. The part of it beyond the Po was annexed to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LOMBARDY">Lombardy</a> in 1815.

FERRARIA

Pages 652-652

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the gynandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the sixth order, Ensatae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FERRARS

Pages 652-652

George, a lawyer, poet, historian, and accomplished <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, was descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a>, and born about the year 1510, in a village near St Albans. He was educated at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and thence removed to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>'s Inn; where applying with uncommon diligence to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, he was soon distinguished for his eloquence at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>. Cromwell, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> minister of Henry VIII, introduced him to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, who employed him as his menial <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>, and in 1535, gave him a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> of Flamstead, in his native <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>. This is supposed to have been a profitable estate; nevertheless, Mr Ferrars being a gay courtier, and probably an expensive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years after was taken to execution by a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>'s officer for a debt of 200 merks, and lodged in the compter. Being at this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> member for <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLYMOUTH">Plymouth</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of commons immediately interfered, and he soon obtained his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. He <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in favour with the king to the end of his reign, and in that of Edward VI, he attended the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> protector Somerset as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in his expedition to Scotland in 1548. In the same reign, the young king being then at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a>, Mr Ferrars was proclaimed lord of misrule, that is, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of sports and pastimes; which office he discharged during 12 days, in Christmas holidays, to the entire satisfaction of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>. This is all we know of Mr Ferrars; except that he died in 1579, at Flamstead in Hertfordshire, and was buried in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. He is not less celebrated for his valour in the field, than for his other accomplishments as a gentleman and a scholar. He wrote, 1. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>; published in Grafton's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHRONICLE">chronicle</a>, 1569, fol. 2. Six tragedies, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> dramatic poems; published in a book called the Mirror for Magistrates, first printed in 1559, afterwards in 1587, and again in 1610. FERRET. See Mustela; <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FERRETS

Pages 652-652

among glassmakers, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> with which the workmen try the melted metal, to see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it be fit to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>.—It is also used for those irons which make the rings at the mouth of the bottles.

FERRETTO

Pages 652-652

in glass-making, a substance which serves to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> glass. This is made by a simple calcination of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, but it serves for several colours: there are two ways of making it. The first is this. Take thin plates of copper, and lay them on a layer of powdered brimstone, in the bottom of a crucible; over these lay more brimstone, and over that another layer of the plates, and so on alternately till the pot is full. Cover the pot, lute it well, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> it in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>, and make a strong fire about it for two hours. When it is taken out and cooled, the copper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be found so calcined, that it may be crumbled to pieces between the fingers like a friable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. It will be of a reddish, and, in some parts, of a blackish colour. This must be powdered and sifted fine for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. Another way of making ferretto is as follows. Make a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of stratifications of plates of copper and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> vitriol alternately in a crucible; which place on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> of the glass furnace near the eye; and let it stand there three days; then take it out, and make a new stratification with more fresh vitriol; calcine again as before. Repeat this operation six times, and a most valuable ferretto will be obtained.

FERRO

Pages 652-654

(W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 19°, N. Lat. 28°), the most westerly of the Canary <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, near the African <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, where the first meridian was lately fixed in most maps; but now, the geographers of almost every <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> make their respective capitals the first meridian, as we do <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It is a dry and barren spot, affording no <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> except what is supplied in a very surprising manner by a tree which grows in these islands, called the Fountain-Tree. Ferro, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FARO">Faro</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Feroe Islands; a cluster of little islands lying in the Northern ocean, between 61° 15' and 62° 21' N. Lat. and between 5° and 8° W. Long. They belong to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>. There are 17 which are habitable; each of which is a lofty mountain arising out of the waves, divided from the others by deep and rapid currents. Some of them are deeply indented with secure harbours; <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> seeming to have favoured mankind with the safest retreats in the most boisterous seas. All are very steep, and most of them faced with most tremendous precipices. The surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> consists of a shallow <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of remarkable fertility; for barley, the only corn sown here, yields above 20 for one; and the grass affords abundant pasture for sheep. The exports are, salted mutton and tallow, goose quills, feathers, and eider <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>; and, by the industry of the inhabitants, knit woollen waistcoats, caps, and stockings. No trees beyond the size of juniper or stunted willows <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> grow here, nor are any wild <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> to be met with except rats and mice, originally escaped from the shipping. Vast quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> fowl frequent the rocks; and the taking of them furnishes a very perilous employment to the natives, as described under the article <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">Bird</a>-Catching. The sea which surrounds these islands is extremely turbulent. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> vary greatly on the western and eastern sides. On the first, where is received the uninterrupted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a> of the ocean from the remote <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GREENLAND">Greenland</a>, the tide rises <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> fathoms; on the eastern side it rises only three. Dreadful whirlwinds, called by the Danes ves, agitate the sea to a strange <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>; catch up a vast <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of water, so as to leave a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> temporary chasm in the spot on which it falls, and carries away with it, to an amazing distance, any fishes which may happen to be within the reach of its fury. Thus great shoals of herrings have been found on the highest mountains of Feroe. It is equally restless on <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>; tearing up trees, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and animals, and carrying them to very distant places. Among the numerous whirlpools of these seas, that of Suderoe, near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the same name, is the most noted. It is occasioned by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRATER">crater</a> 61 fathoms in depth in the centre, and from 50 to 55 on the sides. The water forms four fierce circumjurgations. The point they begin at is on the side of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> basin, where commences a range of rocks running spirally and terminating at the verge of the crater. This range is extremely rugged, and covered with water from the depth of 12 to 8 fathoms only. It forms four equidistant wreaths with a channel from 35 to 20 fathoms in depth between each. On the outside beyond that depth, the sea suddenly sinks to 80 and 90. On the south border of the basin is a lofty rock, called Simboe Munk, noted for the multitude of birds which frequent it. On one side, the water is only 3 or 4 fathoms deep; on the other 15. The danger at most times, especially in storms, is very great. Ships are irresistibly drawn in; the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDDER">rudder</a> loses its power; and the waves <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>; so that an escape is almost miraculous; yet at the reflux, and in very still <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, the inhabitants will venture in boats for the sake of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>. Innumerable flocks of aquatic birds are continually to be seen perched on the extremities of the rocks, which make their nests in the clefts above the precipices; and vast numbers of them may be killed by the discharge of a single musket, and the rest will not stir, so little are they accustomed to be disturbed. One of the islands contains but a single habitation, which can be visited by the curate only in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. In the southern parts of these islands coal-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> were discovered about the beginning of the eighteenth century, and trials of the coals were only made in 1777, when it was judged that working them would be of sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARRY">quarry</a> was determined by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSARY">commissary</a> to be about 12,000 feet long, 4000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> on a medium, and five feet deep; but so great did the difficulty of working it appear, that the idea was abandoned. The coals were analyzed by the celebrated professor Kratzenstein of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>, who found that they were superior to those of England, as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> longer, and giving a more intense <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, but not so easily kindled. A <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of them has been made in Scotland, and they are allowed to be of a superior <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. It is a favourable circumstance to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> of the produce of those islands, that their harbours are never frozen, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> of consequence could meet with no interruption during the winter. The measles and smallpox never attack the inhabitants but when they are brought there by strangers, when the ravages they make are almost as terrible as those of the pestilence; but for 70 years back they have not been subjected to this dreadful visitation. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is temperate, and neither too hot in summer, nor extremely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> in winter. There are frequent mists on these islands, but they do not seem to be injurious to the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> of the inhabitants. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> often blows with such violence, that the people on horseback are obliged to dismount at its approach, which is announced by a whistling across the rocks; and persons on foot must throw themselves flat on their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>, to avoid the dreadful consequences of the irresistible hurricane. So sudden is its approach at some times, that a burning <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> might be carried in the open air but a few seconds before it. There is seldom any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> on these islands; but when the phenomenon does happen, its awful and incessant roar among the rocks is truly alarming. Potatoes, the cultivation of which is rapidly advancing, thrive well, and the same is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with radishes and turnips. Corn is not much cultivated, which would require excessive labour in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> so mountainous, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> fishery requires all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> that can be spared. Trees cannot be made to grow upon them, and of consequence there is no wood. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants amounted to 5209 in 1812, and they are in general well made, with fair complexions, and their whiteness is very seldom impaired by the influence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. They are not deficient in understanding; and although phlegmatic, yet they are benevolent and hospitable, and are seldom known to quarrel. They are fond of brandy, and yet it is said that they are very rarely seen in a state of intoxication. They are frugal and upright, yet extremely credulous, and much addicted to superstitious practices. There are no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> among them, as parents educate their own children, and their knowledge of consequence is very circumscribed. They abound in skilful players at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHESS">chess</a>, but are wholly unacquainted with instruments of music, and dance to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>. See Faroe, Supplement. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FERROL">Ferrol</a>, a sea port town in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALICIA">Galicia</a>, seated on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>. It has a good harbour, and is frequented by the Spanish fleet in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. W. Long. 8° 46'. N. Lat. 43° 26'. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FERRUGINOUS">Ferruginous</a>, any thing partaking of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, or which contains particles of that metal. Ferrugo, Rust, or oxide of iron. See Iron, Outside of, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Ferrum, Iron. See Iron, Chemistry Index. Ferry, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a>, or by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a>, to have a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> for passage, on a frith or river, for carrying passengers, horses, &c. over the same for a reasonable toll. Fertility, that quality which denominates a thing fruitful or prolific. Nothing can produce fertility in either <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, but what promotes Fertility promotes perhaps health; nothing but good blood, spirits, and perfect animal functions, that is, high health, can beget perfect fecundity; and therefore, all means and medicines, all nostrums and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIFICS">specifics</a>, to procure fertility, different from those which procure good blood and spirits, are arrant quackery. Dr Cheyne says, that water-drinking males are very rarely infertile; and that, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any thing in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> can prevent infertility, and bring fine children, it is a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a> and seed diet persevered in by both parents. To increase the fertility of vegetables, says <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a>, we must not only increase the vigour of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> and of the plant, but also preserve what would otherwise be lost: whence he infers that there is much saved by setting, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of sowing. It is reported, continues he, that if nitre be mixed with water to the thickness of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, and after a vine is cut, the bud be anointed therewith, it will sprout within eight days. If the experiment be true, the cause may be in the opening of the bud, and contiguous parts, by the spirit of the nitre; for nitre is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of vegetables. How far this may be true, is not perhaps sufficiently shown, notwithstanding the experiments of Sir Kenelm Digby and M. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMBERG">Homberg</a>. Consult Mr Evelyn's Sylva, the Philosophical Transactions, the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a>, and Dr Stahl's Philosophical Principles of Chemistry; but a proper set of accurate experiments seems still wanting in this view.

FERULA

Pages 654-654

Fennel-giant, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandria class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 45th order, Umbellatae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The drug assafectida is obtained from a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of ferula.

FESCENNIA

Pages 654-654
or FESCENNIUM, in Ancient Geography, a town of Etruria, above Falerni; where the Fescennine verses were first invented. Now Galese, in the Ecclesiastical State, near the Tiber.

FESCENNINE VERSES

Pages 654-654

in antiquity, were a kind of satirical verses, full of wanton and obscene expressions, sung <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rehearsed by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, with many indecent gestures and dances, at the solemnization of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; (Hor. lib. v. ep. i. 145.) The word is borrowed, according to Macrobius, from facinum, "a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARM">charm</a>;" the people taking such songs to be proper to drive away witches, or prevent their effect; but its more probable origin is from Fescennium, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Campania, where such verses were first used.

FESSE WAYS

Pages 654-654
or IN FESSE, denotes anything borne after the manner of a fesse; that is, in a rank across the middle of the shield. [Merged from PARTY PER FESSE, p.654] implies a parting across the middle of the shield, from side to side, through the fesse point.

FESTI DIES

Pages 654-654

in Roman antiquity, certain days in the year devoted to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the gods. Numa, when he distributed the year into 12 months, divided the same into the dies festi, dies profecti, and dies intercisi. The festi were again divided into days of sacrifices, banquets, games, and feriae. See FERIE. The profecti were those days allowed to men for the administration of their affairs, whether of a public <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> private <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>: these are divided into fasti, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMITIA">comitia</a>, &c. See FASTI, COMITIALES, &c. The intercisi were days <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> both to gods and men, some parts of which were allotted to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the one, and some to that of the other.

FESTINO

Pages 654-654

in Logic, the third mood of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the syllogism, the first proposition whereof is an universal <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a>, the second a particular affirmative, and the third a particular negative; as in the following example: FES No bad <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> can be happy. TI Some rich men are bad men. NO Ergo, Some rich men are not happy.

FESTIVAL

Pages 654-654

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of feasting. See FEAST.—The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> is particularly applied to anniversary days of civil <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> joy.

FESTOON

Pages 654-654

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SCULPTURE">Sculpture</a>, &c., an ornament in form of a garland of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and leaves, intermixed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> twisted together. It is in the form of a string or collar, somewhat bigger in the middle, where it falls <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>; being extended by the two ends, the extremities of which hang down perpendicularly. Festoons are now chiefly used in friezes, and other vacant places which want to be filled up and adorned; being done in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> clusters of flowers, which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> placed on the doors of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> and houses on festival occasions.

FESTUCA

Pages 654-654

FESCUE GRASS, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the triandria class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 34th order, Graminae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FESTUS POMPEIUS

Pages 654-654

a celebrated grammarian of antiquity, who abridged a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of Verrius Flaccus, De Significatione Verborum; but took such liberties in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CASTRATION">castration</a> and criticising, as, Gerard Vossius observes, are not favourable to the reputation of his author. A complete edition of his Fragments was published by M. Dacier in 1681, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the Dauphin. Scaliger says, that Festus is an author of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> use to those who would attain the Latin tongue with accuracy.

FETLOCK

Pages 654-654

in the manege, a tuft of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> growing behind the pastern <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> of many horses; for those of a low size have scarce any such tuft.

FETTI

Pages 654-655

Domenico, an eminent painter in the style of Julio Romano, was born at Rome in 1589, and educated under Ludovico Civoli of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>. He painted but little for churches, but excelled in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>; his pictures are much sought after, and are scarce.—He abandoned himself to disorderly courses; and put an end to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> by excesses, in the 35th year of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. FETUS. See FOETUS.

FEU-DUTY

Pages 655-655

in Scots <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is the annual rent <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> duty which a vassal, by the tenor of his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, becomes bound to pay his superior. FEU-Holding, in Scots Law, is that particular <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a> by which a vassal is taken bound to pay an annual rent or feu-duty to his superior. FEVER. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> deified the diseases, as well as the passions and affections of men. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> places them in the entrance into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a>, Æn. vi. 273. Among these Fever had a temple on Mount Palatine, and two other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Rome; and there is still extant an inscription to this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>. FEBRI DIVÆ. FEBRI. SANCTÆ. FEBRI. MAGNÆ. CAMILLA. AMATA. PRO. FILIO. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">MALE</a>. AFFECTO.

FEUD

Pages 655-655

in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> customs is used for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> quarrel <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> enmity, not to be satisfied but with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the enemy; and thence usually called deadly feud.—Feud, called also feida, and faida, in the original German, signifies guerran, i.e. bellum, "<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>." Lambert writes it feeth, and saith it signifies capitatis inimicitia, or "implacable hatred." In Scotland, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of England, feud is particularly used for a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of kindred, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> the death of any of their blood, against the killer and all his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, or any other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> enemy.

FEUDAL

Pages 655-655
or Feodal, of or belonging to a feud or fee. See Feodal.

FEUDATORY

Pages 655-655
or Feodatory, a tenant who formerly held his estate by feodal service. See Feodal Tenure.

FEVER

Pages 655-655

in Farriery. See Farriery <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. FEVERFEW. See Matricaria, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index.

FEVERSHAM

Pages 655-655

a town of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KENT">Kent</a> in England, situated on a branch of the river <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, which is navigable for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOY">hoy</a>. It was a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> demesne A.D. 811, and called in Kenulf's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a>'s little Town, though it is now a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> one. It was inhabited by the Britons <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before the invasion of Caesar. In 903, King Athelstan held a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> here. King Stephen erected a stately <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, 1147, whose abots sat in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; and he was buried in it, together with Maud his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, and Eustace his son; but of this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, two <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> gate-houses are all that now remain. The town was first incorporated by the name of the barons of Feversham; afterwards by Henry VIII. with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the mayor and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMMONALTY">commonalty</a>; and lastly, by that of the mayor and jurats and commonalty. It contained 3655 inhabitants in 1811, and consists chiefly of two long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> streets, with a market-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in the centre, built 1574. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> was rebuilt in 1754, at the expense of 2300l. but was originally built in Edward II's reign. There Feversham is a free <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> school in this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, built and endowed by Queen <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> in 1582; also two <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>. It is a member of the cinque-port of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a>, and has a manufactory of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> are supplied from hence with abundance of apples and cherries, and the best oysters for stewing. These last were at one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> carried away in such quantities by the Dutch, that many men and boats were employed in the winter to dredge for them; and it is said they carried home as many as amounted to above 2000l. a-year. The fishermen admit none to take up their freedom but married men.

FEVILDEA

Pages 655-655

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dioica class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 54th order, Cucurbitaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FEVRE

Pages 655-655

Claud le, an eminent French painter, was born at Fontainbleau in 1633, and studied in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> there, and then at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> under Le Sueur and Le Brun; the latter of whom advised him to adhere to portraits, for which he had a particular <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a>, and in his style equalled the best masters of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. He died in England in 1675, aged 42.

FEZ

Pages 655-657

the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of the same name in Barbary, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. It is described as a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, surrounded with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> walls, within which there are hills and valleys, only the middle being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> and flat. The river which runs through the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, is divided into two streams, from which <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> are cut into every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the town: so that the mosques, colleges, palaces, and the houses of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men, are amply supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. They have generally <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> marble basins in the middle of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of their houses, which are supplied with water by marble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> that <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through the walls. They constantly run over, and the stream returns back into the street, and so into the river. The houses are built with brick <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; and are adorned on the outside with fine mosaic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, or tiles like those of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. The wood work and ceilings are carved, painted and gilt. The roofs are flat; for they <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> on the tops of the houses in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. Most of the houses are two stories high, and some three. There are piazzas and galleries running all round the court on the inside, so that you may go under cover, from one apartment to another. The pillars are of brick, covered with glazed tiles, or of marble, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> between. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> work is carved and painted with gay colours; and most of the rooms have marble cisterns of water. Some of the great men build towers over their houses several stories high, and spare no expense to render them beautiful; from hence they have a fine prospect all over the city. There are in this city 700 mosques, great and small, 50 of which are magnificent, and supported with marble pillars and other ornaments. The floors are covered with mats, as well as the walls to the height of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. Every mosque has a tower or minaret, like those in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, with a gallery on the top, from whence they call the people to prayers. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> mosque is near a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and a half in circumference. The middle <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> is 150 yards in length, and 80 in breadth, with a tower proportionally high. Round this to the east, west, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, there are great colonnades 30 or 40 yards <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>. There are 900 lamps lighted every night; and in the middle of the mosque are large branches, which are capable of holding 500 lamps each. Along the walls are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> pulpits, from which the doctors of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> teach the people. The business of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> is only to read prayers, and distribute alms to the people; to support which, there are large revenues. Besides the mosques, there are two colleges built in the Moorish manner, and adorned with marble and paintings. In one of them there are 100 rooms, besides a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>. In this there is a great marble vase full of water, adorned with marble pillars of various colours, and finely polished. The capitals are gilt, and the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> shines with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, azure, and purple. The walls are adorned with Arabic verses in gold <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. The other colleges are not near so beautiful, or rather are all gone to ruin since the neglect of learning. There are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a> in the city, where formerly all strangers were maintained three days gratis. But the estates belonging to them have been confiscated for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. There are above 100 public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>, many of which are stately buildings. People of the same trade or business live in streets by themselves. Though the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> about Fez is pleasant and fertile, and in many places abounding with corn and cattle, yet a great part of it lies waste and uncultivated, not so much for want of inhabitants as from the oppression of the governors; which makes the people choose to live at some distance from the high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, where they cultivate <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> as much <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> as is necessary for their own subsistence. Round the city there are fine marble tombs, monuments, and gardens full of all manner of fruit trees. Such are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> accounts of this city. The following are given by M. Chenier, in his Recherches Historiques sur les Maures. Fez was built in the end of the eighth century by Edris, a descendant of Mahomet and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALI">Ali</a>; whose father, in order to avoid the proscriptions of the caliph Abdulla, retired to the extremity of Africa, and was proclaimed sovereign by the Moors. Sidy Edris, having succeeded to the throne of his father, built the city of Fez in the year 793. He caused a mosque to be erected, in which his body was interred, and the city ever afterwards became an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> for the Moors, and a place of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. In the first moments of fervour, which a new worship inspires, another mosque was built, called carabin, which is perhaps one of the largest and most beautiful edifices in Africa. Several others were successively built, besides colleges and hospitals; and the city was held in such veneration, that when the pilgrimage to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a> was interrupted in the fourth century of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEGIRA">Hegira</a>, the western Mahometans substituted that of Fez in its stead, while the eastern people went to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>. When the Arabs had overspread <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, Africa, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, they brought to Fez the little knowledge they had acquired in the sciences and arts; and that capital conjoined, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a> where <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> was taught, together with medicine and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>. This last gradually degenerated; <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> brought astrology into repute, and this quickly engendered the arts of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINATION">divination</a>. Fez soon became the common <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of all Africa. The Mahometans went thither for the purposes of devotion; the affluence of strangers introduced a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; libertinism quickly followed; and as its progress is most rapid in warm countries, Fez, which had been the nurse of sciences and arts, became a harbour for every kind of vice. The public baths, which <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, cleanliness, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, had rendered necessary, and which were everywhere respected as sacred places, became scenes of debauchery; where men introduced themselves in the habits of women: youths in the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a>, with a distaff in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, walked the streets at sunset in order to entice strangers to their inns, which were less a place of repose than a convenience for prostitution. The usurpers who disputed the kingdom of Fez after the 16th century overlooked these abuses, and contented themselves with subjecting the masters of the inns to furnish a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COOKS">cooks</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. It is to this laxity of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> that Fez owed its first splendour. As the inhabitants are beautiful, the Africans flocked thither in crowds; the laws were overturned, morals despised, and vice itself turned into an engine of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> resource. The same spirit, the same inclinations, the same depravity, still exist in the hearts of all the Moors. But libertinism is not now encouraged; it wears there, as in other places, the mask of hypocrisy; and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARES">dares</a> not venture to show itself in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. The Mahometans of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>, those of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a> and Cordova, migrated to Fez during the different revolutions that agitated <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; they carried with them new customs and new arts, and perhaps some slight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of civilization. The Spanish Moors carried from Cordova to Fez the art of staining goat and sheep skins with a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, which were then called Cordova <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, and now <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a> leather, from that city where the art is less perfect. They manufacture gauzes at Fez, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> stuffs, and girdles elegantly embroidered with gold and silk, which show how far their ingenuity might be carried <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> industry were more encouraged. There is still some taste for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> preserved at Fez, and the Arabic <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> is spoken there in greater purity. FEZ purity than in any other part of the empire. The rich Moors send their children to the schools at Fez, where they are better instructed than they could be elsewhere. Leo Africanus, in the 16th century, gave a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of this city, from which most of those that have been afterwards made are copied; but its situation, its schools, and the industry and great urbanity of its inhabitants, are the only circumstances that give it any preference to the other cities of the empire. There are some pretty convenient inns here, consisting of two or three stories. The houses have no elegance externally: the streets are ill paved, and so strait that two persons riding abreast can hardly pass. The shops are like stalls; and have no more room in them than is sufficient to serve for the owner, who is always seated with his wares around him, which he shows to the passengers. But though the Moors of Fez are more civilized than the rest, they are vain, superstitious, and intolerant; and an order must be obtained from the emperor before a Christian or a Jew can be allowed to enter the city. The situation of Fez is exceeding singular. It lies in the bottom of a valley surrounded by little hills in the shape of a funnel; the declivities are divided into gardens planted with tall trees, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, and all sorts of fruit trees; a river meanders along the declivity, and turns a number of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>, which disperse the water abundantly to all the gardens, and almost to every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> to the city, which stands in the centre, is long; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> lies through these gardens, which it traverses in a serpentine <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. The gardens, seen from the city, form a most delightful <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>. Formerly each garden had a house in which the inhabitants spent the summer. These houses were destroyed in the times of the civil wars, and in the revolutions to which Fez has been subject, and few individuals have restored them. Ali Bey estimates the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of Fez at 100,000; and Mr Jackson at 380,000. But the latter estimate, though founded on public documents, is most probably an exaggeration. On the height above Fez, in a plain susceptible of rich cultivation, stands New Fez, finely situated, and enjoying excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, containing some old palaces, in which the children of the emperor live, and where he sometimes resides himself. New Fez is inhabited by some Moorish families, but by a greater number of Jews. Fez is seated on the river Cebu. W. Long. 4° 25'. N. Lat. 33° 58'.

FEZZAN

Pages 657-658

a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, about 300 miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south, and 200 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> from east to west. It is bounded on the east by the Harutsch and line of the deserts; by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Tibboes on the south and south-east; by that of the Nomadic Touricks on the south-west; and the country which forms the western boundary is inhabited by Arabs. It contains 101 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and villages, of which Mourzouk is the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of this kingdom is neither temperate nor agreeable at any season whatever; for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> is almost intolerable, even to the inhabitants, especially when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> blows from the south; and the prevalence of the north wind during winter makes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> so intense, as not only to chill the natives, but those also who visit it from northern regions. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">Rain</a> falls but seldom in this country, and in very small quantities. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">Thunder</a> is also a rare phenomenon: Mr Horneman assures us that there was not a single storm from November 1798 to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1799; and that on the last <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1799 there were some faint flashes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, unaccompanied by any claps of thunder. Winds, however, blow very frequently, both from the north and south, whirling up the dust and sand in such a manner as to give the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> a yellowish appearance. There is neither river nor rivulet of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> in the whole country, according to Mr Horneman, who informs us that the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is a deep sand, beneath which is found calcareous rock <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and sometimes a stratum of an argillaceous substance. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">Date</a> trees may be considered as the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> production of Fezzan, in the western parts of which some senna grows, of a superior <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> to that which is imported from the country of the Tibboes. Culinary <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, and almost every vegetable peculiar to the garden, are met with in abundance. Wheat and barley seem well adapted to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the soil, as well as to the climate; yet corn is not raised in sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> for home consumpt, which is brought from those parts of Africa bordering on the northern parts of the kingdom. This is most probably owing to the native indolence of the people, the despotism of their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and the difficulties inseparable from their peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of tillage. They bestow little <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> on the rearing of cattle, which are only found in the most fertile parts of the country, and even in these their numbers are but small. They are made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of to draw <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a>, and are never killed but in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> animal is the goat; and although sheep are reared in the southern parts of the country, the most abundant supply is furnished by the Arabs on the borders. They make coarse cloths of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, which constitute the apparel of the inhabitants in general. Their horses are not numerous, as they make most use of asses, either for carriage, draught, or burden. Camels bear a most extravagant price, being only made use of by the higher ranks, or by opulent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>; and the common food of all these animals is the fruit of the date tree. Although the trade of Fezzan consists entirely of foreign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, it is nevertheless considerable. Mourzouk is the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> market and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of general <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> for different <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CARAVANS">caravans</a> from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>, Bengasi, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIPOLI">Tripoli</a>, and other places, between the months of October and February. The caravans which come to Mourzouk from the west or south, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> in ostrich feathers, tiger skins, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> dust, and also in slaves of both sexes as articles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">Tobacco</a> and snuff, with other articles manufactured in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, are brought to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> by the merchants from Bengasi; and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, fire-arms, sabres, knives, and woollen cloth, are conveyed to it from Tripoli. Fezzan is governed by a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a>, a descendant of the family of the Shereefs; and according to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> of the country, his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> came from the western parts of Africa, invaded and made a conquest of it about 500 years ago. He reigns over his dominions with absolute It is difficult to ascertain anything like an accurate statement of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of Fezzan; but Mr Horne- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> conjectures that they may amount to about 75,000, all of them professing the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of Maho- met. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> of the people varies consider- ably; those in the northern parts <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> in this respect a striking resemblance to the Arabians, while those in the southern districts are very much like the Tibboes and Tuaricks. Those who are strictly indigenous are of ordinary stature, and their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> far from being muscular; of a deep <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, short <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, with their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> formed like the people of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and their nose not so flat as that of the negro. Their walk, mien, and gesture, indicate a total want of energy, either of body or mind. The women of this country are in general fond of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>, and the wanton manners and public freedoms in which they are permitted to indulge, are frequently astonishing, even to Mahometans from other countries; and the men are very much addicted to the vice of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRUNKENNESS">drunkenness</a>, using the juice of the date-tree, or a drink that is called bussa, which is of an intoxicating nature. Different <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the venereal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> prevail in this country, but that which is brought from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUDAN">Soudan</a> is reckoned the most inveterate. The common lues ve- nerea is called franzi, for the cure of which they make use of salts and colocynth as powerful cathartics, healing the sores with natron water or dissolved soda. They are sometimes afflicted with hemorrhoids, the cure of which is no doubt rendered more difficult by the too liberal use of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>; and a fever and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGUE">ague</a> which are very pernicious to foreigners. They are entirely unacquainted with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHLEBOTOMY">phlebotomy</a>, yet they sometimes draw blood by means of cupping; and some are as much acquainted with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a> as to be able to cure a simple fracture. Their houses are miserable structures, composed of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> or bricks mixed with clay, and dried in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the labourer are all the tools which are employed in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. When the walls are finished, they are covered over with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a> made of calca- reous earth, which is also done with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. Their houses are extremely low, and there is no other entrance for the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> but by the door. They are uncommonly abstemious in respect of diet. Indeed they can never abstain from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTCHER">butcher</a> meat when it is placed before them; but this is not an article of food with the gene- rality, and their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> for a rich man is, "that he eats <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and meat every day." FEWEL. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">FUEL</a>.

FIASCONE

Pages 658-658

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the territories of the pope, remarkable for its good wine. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13. 12. N. Lat. 42. 20.

FIBRARLE

Pages 658-658

an old <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to minerals of a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> structure.

FIBRE

Pages 658-660

in Anatomy, a perfectly simple body, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> at least as simple as any thing in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> structure; being fine and slender like a thread, and serving to form other parts. Hence some fibres are hard, as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BONY">bony</a> ones; and others soft, as those destined for the formation of all the other parts. The fibres are divided also, according to their position and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, into such as are straight, oblique, transverse, annular, and spiral; as they are arranged in these directions in different parts of the body. Fibre is also used to denote the slender filaments which compose other bodies, whether animal, vegetable, or mineral; but more especially the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CAPILLARY">capillary</a> roots of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. Fibrose, or <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">Fibrous</a>, something consisting of fibres, as the roots of plants. See Root. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FIBULA">Fibula</a>, in Anatomy, the outer and smaller of the of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of the leg. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Fibula, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> for the closing of gaping wounds.—Celsus speaks of the fibula as to be used when the wound was so patent as not easily to admit of being sewed. (Op. lib. vii. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 25. epud <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FIN">fin</a>.). Fibula, in Antiquity, was a sort of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTTON">button</a>, buckle, or clasp, made use by the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> for keeping <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> or tying up some <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of their clothes. They are of various forms, and often adorned with precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. Men and women wore them in their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> and at their shoes. Players and musicians, by way of preserving the voices of children put under their care to learn their arts, used to keep close the prepuce with a fibula, lest they should have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> with women. Fichte, John Theophilus, a late eminent German metaphysician. See Supplement. Ficinus, Marsilius, a celebrated Italian, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> in 1433, and educated at the expense of Lawrence de Medicis. He attained a perfect knowledge of the Greek and Latin tongues, and became a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, a great physician, and a great divine. He was in the highest favour with Laurence and Cosmo de Medicis, who made him a canon of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Florence. He applied himself intensely to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>; and while others were striving who should be the deepest read in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, who was then the philosopher in fashion, he devoted himself wholly to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>. He was indeed the first who restored the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATONIC">Platonic</a> philosophy in the west; for the better effecting of which, he translated into Latin the whole works of Plato. There goes a story, that his friend Marcus Musurus disliking the translation, he did it all over again. He next translated <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLOTINUS">Plotinus</a>; and afterwards the works, or part of them at least, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLUS">Proclus</a>, Jamblicus, Porphyrius, and other celebrated Platonists.—In his younger years, Ficinus lived like a philosopher; and too much so, as is said, to the neglect of piety. However, Savonarola coming to Florence, Ficinus went with everybody else to hear his sermons; and while he attended them for the sake of the preacher's eloquence, he imbibed a strong <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and devoted himself henceforward more especially to the duties of it. He died at Correggio in 1499; and as Boronius assures us upon the testimony of what he calls credible authors, appeared immediately after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> to his friend Michael Mercatus: to whom, it seems, he had promised to appear, in order to confirm what he had taught concerning the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>. His writings, sacred and profane, which are very numerous, were collected and printed at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, in 1516, at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a> in 1561 and 1576, and at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> 1641, in two vols folio. Twelve books of his Epistles, among which are many treatises, were printed separately in folio at Venice 1495, and at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUREMBERG">Nuremberg</a>, 1497, in 4to. Ficoïdes, the specific name given to several plants as the mesembryanthemum, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSA">musa</a>, and opuntia. See Mesembryanthemum, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. Fiction. See <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">Fable</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>. Ficus, the Fig-tree; a genus of plants, belonging to the polygamy class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 53d order, Scabridae. See Botany Index. The ficus religiosa, or Banian tree, is a native of several parts of the East Indies. It has a woody stem, branching to a great height and vast <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, with heart-shaped entire leaves ending in acute <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>. Of this tree the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a> contain a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> equally beautiful and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a>: There soon they chose The fig-tree: not that tree for fruit renown'd; But such as, at this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> to Indians known In Malabar or Decan, spreads her arms, Branching so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, that in the ground: The bended twigs take root, and daughters grow. About the mother tree, a pillar'd <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">High</a> overarch'd, and echoing walks between; There oft' the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> herdsman, shunning <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, Shelters in cool; and tends his pasturing herds At loop-holes cut through thickest shade. Par. Lost, Book. ix. l. 1100. The Banian tree, or Indian fig, is perhaps the most beautiful of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a>'s productions in that genial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, where she sports with the greatest profusion and variety. Some of these trees are of amazing size and great extent, as they are continually increasing, and, contrary to most other things in animal and vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, they seem to be exempted from decay.
