He seldom refuses the red worm in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, the caddis in June, or the grasshopper in June, April, and September. This fish does not only delight in worms, but also in sweet paste; of which there is great variety; the best is made of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, and ought to be thrown into the water some hours before you begin to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a>; neither will small pellets thrown into the water two or three days before be worse for this purpose, especially if chickens guts, garbage, or blood mixed with bran and cow dung, be also thrown in. But more particularly, as to a paste very proper for this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, you may make it in the manner following: Take a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of flour, and mingle it with veal, cut small, making it up with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> of honey; then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> all together in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a> till they are so tough as to hang upon the hook without washing off. In order to effect which the better, mingle whitish <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> with it; and if you keep it all the year round, add some virgin wax and clarified honey. Again, If you fish with gentles, anoint them with honey, and put them on your hook, with a deep scarlet dipped in the like, which is a good way to deceive the fish. Honey and crumbs of wheat <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, mixed together, make also a very good paste. In taking a carp either in pond or river, if the angler intends to add profit to his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, he must take a peck of ale-grains, and a good quantity of any blood to mix with the grains, baiting the ground with it where he intends to angle. This food will wonderfully attract the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>-fish, as carp, tench, roach, dace, and bream. Let him angle in a morning, plumbing his ground, and angling for carp with a strong line; the bait must be either paste or a knotted red worm; and by this means he will have sport enough. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">Description</a> of proper Baits for the several sorts of Fish referred to in the annexed <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">Table</a>. Elies. 1. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">Stone</a> fly, found under hollow stones at the sides of rivers, is of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> streaks on the back and belly, has large wings, and is in season from April to July. 2. Green drake, found among stones by river sides, has a yellow body striped with green, is long and slender, with wings like a butterfly, his tail turns on his back, and from May to midsummer is very good. 3. Oak-fly, found in the body of an oak or ash, with its head downwards, is of a brown colour, and excellent from May to September. 4. Palmer fly or worm, found on leaves of plants, is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called a caterpillar, and when it comes to a fly is excellent for trout. 5. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANT">Ant</a> fly, found in ant hills from June to September. 6. The May fly is to be found playing at the river side, especially against <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>. 7. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> fly is to be found upon every hawthorn after the buds are come off. Pastes. 1. Take the blood of sheep's hearts, and mix it with honey and flour worked to a proper consistence. 2. Take old cheese grated, a little <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a> sufficient to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> it, and colour it with saffron; in winter use rusty <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">bacon</a> instead of butter. 3. Crumbs of bread chewed or worked with honey or sugar, moistened with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a> ivy water. 4. Bread chewed, and worked in the hand till stiff. Worms. 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> bob, found in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> ground after ploughing; it is <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, with a red head, and bigger than a gentle; another is found in heathy ground, with a blue head. Keep them in an earthen vessel well covered, and a sufficient quantity of the mould they harbour in. They are excellent from April to November. 2. Gentles to be had from putrid <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>; let them lie in wheat bran a few days before used. 3. Flay worms, found in the roots of flags; they are of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> yellow colour, are longer and thinner than a gentle, and must be scoured like them. 4. Cow-turd bob, or clap bait, found under a cow turd from May to Michaelmas; it is like a gentle, but larger. Keep it in its native earth like the earth bob. 5. Caddis worm, or cod bait, found under loose stones in shallow rivers; they are yellow, bigger than a gentle, with a black or blue head, and are in season from April to July. Keep them in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLANNEL">flannel</a> bags. 6. Lob worm, found in gardens; it is very large, and has a red head; a streak down the back, and a flat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> tail. 7. Marsh-worms, found in marshy ground; keep them in moss ten days before you use them; their colour is a bluish red, and are a good bait from March to Michaelmas. 8. Brandling red worms, or blood worms, found in rotten dunghills and tanners bark; they are small red worms, very good for all small fish, have sometimes a yellow tail, and are called tug-tail. FISH Fish and Insects. 1. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-MINNOW">Minnow</a>. 2. Gudgeon. 3. Roach. 4. Dace. 5. Smelt. 6. Yellow frog. 7. Snail slit. 8. Grasshopper. Fishing Fly, a bait used in angling for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> kinds of fish. See Fishing. The fly is either natural or artificial. I. Natural flies are innumerable. The more usual for this purpose are mentioned in the preceding page. There are two ways to fish with natural flies; either on the surface of the water, or a little underneath it. In angling for chevin, roach, or dace, move not your natural fly swiftly when you see the fish make at it; but rather let it glide freely towards him with the stream; but if it be in a still and slow water, draw the fly slowly sidewise by him, which will make him eagerly pursue. II. The artificial fly is seldom used but in blustering weather, when the waters are so troubled by the winds, that the natural fly cannot be seen, nor rest upon them. Of this artificial fly there are reckoned no less than 12 sorts, of which the following are the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a>. 1. For March, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUN">dun</a> fly; made of dun wool, and the feathers of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PARTRIDGE">partridge</a>'s wing; or the body made of black wool, and the feathers of a black drake. 2. For April, the stone fly; the body made of black wool, dyed yellow under the wings and tail. 3. For the beginning of May, the ruddy fly; made of red wool, and bound about with black silk, with the feathers of a black <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPON">capon</a> hanging dangling on his sides next his tail. 4. For June, the greenish fly; the body made of black wool, with a yellow <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> on either side, the wings taken off the wings of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUZZARD">buzzard</a>, bound with black broken <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>. 5. The moorish fly, the body made of duskish wool, and the wings of the blackish mail of a drake. 6. The tawney fly, good till the middle of June; the body made of tawney wool, the wings made contrary one against the other of the whitish mail of a white drake. 7. For July, the wap fly; the body made of black wool, cast about with yellow silk, and the wings of drakes feathers. 8. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> fly; good in the middle of July; the body made with greenish wool, cast about with the feathers of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEACOCK">peacock</a>'s tail, and the wings made of those of the buzzard. 9. For August, the drake fly; the body made with black wool cast about with black silk; his wings of the mail of a black drake, with a black head. The best rules for artificial fly fishing are: 1. To fish in a river somewhat disturbed with rain; or in a cloudy day, when the waters are moved by a gentle breeze: the south <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> is best; and if the wind blow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, yet not so but that you may conveniently <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> your tackle, the fish will rise in plain deeps; but if the wind be small, the best angling is in swift streams. 2. Keep as far from the water side as may be; fish down the stream with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> at your back, and touch not the water with your line. 3. Ever angle in clear rivers, with a small fly and slender wings; but in muddy places, use a larger. 4. When, after rain, the water becomes brownish, use an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> fly; in a clear day, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>-coloured fly; a dark fly for dark waters, &c. 5. Let the line be twice as long as the rod, unless the river be encumbered with wood. 6. For every sort of fly, have several of the same differing in colour, to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> with the different complexions of several waters and weathers. 7. Have a nimble eye, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> hand, to strike presently with the rising of the fish; or else he will be apt to spue out the hook. 8. Let the fly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> first into the water, and not the line, which will scare the fish. 9. In slow rivers, or still places, cast the fly across the river, and let it sink a little in the water, and draw it gently back with the current. Salmon flies should be made with their wings standing one behind the other, whether two or four. This fish delights in the gaudiest colours that can be; chiefly in the wings, which must be long, as well as the tail.

FISHING BY

Pages 707-709

g by means of birds, a method peculiar to the Chinese, who train certain birds for the purpose in the same manner as falcons are taught to pursue <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAME">game</a>. For this purpose they have trained a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of pelican, resembling the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> corvus, which they call the Leu-tse, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>. Sir George Staunton, who, when the embassy was proceeding on the southern branch of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> canal, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> these birds employed, tells us, that on a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> lake, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the east side of the canal, are thousands of small boats and rafts, built entirely for this species of fishery. On each <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> or raft are ten or a dozen birds, which, at a signal from the owner, plunge into the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; and it is astonishing to see the enormous size of fish with which they return, grasped within their bills. They appeared to be so well trained, that it did not require either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CORD">cord</a> about their throats to prevent them from swallowing any portion of their prey, except what their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> was pleased to return to them for encouragement and food. The boat used by these fishermen is of a remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> make, and is often carried to the lake, together with the fishing birds, by the men who are there to be supported by it. The same author saw the fishermen busy on the great lake Wee-chuang-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEE">lee</a>; and he gives the following account of a very singular method practised by them for catching the fish of the lake without the aid of birds, of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a>, or of hooks. To the one side of a boat a flat board, painted <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, is fixed, at an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of about 45 degrees, the edge inclining towards the water. On moonlight nights the boat is so placed that the painted board is turned to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, from whence the rays of light striking on the whitened surface, give to it the appearance of moving water; on which the fish being tempted to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a> on their element, the boatmen raising with a string the board, turn the fish into the boat. Water-fowl are much sought after by the Chinese, and are taken upon the same lake by the following ingenious device. Empty jars or gourds are suffered to float about upon the water, that such objects may become familiar to the birds. The fisherman then wades into the lake with one of these empty vessels upon his head, and walks gently towards a bird; and lifting up his arm, draws it <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> below the surface of the water without any disturbance or giving alarm to the rest, several of whom he treats in the same manner, until he fills the bag he had brought to hold his prey. The contrivance itself is not so singular, as it is that the same exactly should have occurred in the new continent, as Ulloa asserts, to the natives of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARTHAGENA">Carthagena</a>, upon the lake Cienega de Tesias. Fishing Floats, are little appendages to the line, serving An Epitome of the whole art of Fishing, wherein is shown, (at one view), the harbours, seasons, and depths, for catching all sorts of fish usually angled for; also the various baits for each, so digested as to contain the essence of all the treatises ever written on the subject, exempt from the superfluities, which tend more to perplex than instruct. | Names | Where found | Season | <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">Time</a> to ang. | Depth from ground | Proper Baits | Fish and Insects | <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">Worms</a>. Sunrise to 9 | Touch ground | Dito | 1 to 7 | 1 | 3 | 2 | Fishing Hook, a small <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> made of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> wire, of a proper form to catch and retain fish. The fishing hook in general ought to be <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> in the shank, somewhat thick in the circumference, the point even and straight; let the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> be in the shank. For setting the hook on, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> strong but small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, laying the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> on the inside of your hook; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it be on the outside, the silk <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> fret and cut it asunder. There are several sizes of these fishing hooks, some big, some little; and of these, some have peculiar names; as, 1. Single hooks. 2. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">Double</a> hooks; which have two bendings, one contrary to the other. 3. Snappers, or gorgers, which are the hooks to whip the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> fly upon, or bait with the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> fly. 4. Springers, or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> hooks; a kind of double hooks, with a spring, which flies open upon being struck into any fish, and so keeps its mouth open. Fishing-Line, is either made of hair twisted; or silk; or the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> grass. The best colours are the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SORREL">sorrel</a>, white, and gray; the two last for clear waters, the first for muddy ones. Nor is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> watery green despisable; this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> is given artificially, by steeping the hair in a liquor made of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOOT">soot</a>, and the juice of walnut leaves, boiled together. Fishing Rod, a long slender rod or wand, to which the line is fastened, for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLING">angling</a>.—Of these there are several sorts; as, 1. A troller, or trolling rod, which has a ring at the end of the rod, for the line to go through when it runs off a reel. 2. A whipper, or whipping rod; a top rod, that is weak in the middle, and top heavy, but all slender and fine. 3. A dropper; which is a strong rod and very light. 4. A snapper, or snap rod; which is a strong pole, peculiarly used for the pike. 5. A bottom rod; being the same as the dropper, but somewhat more pliable. 6. A snagging or procking stick; a forked stick, having a short strong line, with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a>, baited with a lob worm; this is only for eels in their holes. Fishing Frog, or Angler. See Lophius. <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">Right</a> of Fishing, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of fish. It has been held, that where the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> hath the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> on both sides of the river, it is good <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> that he hath a right of fishing; and it puts the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> upon him who claims liberam piscariam: but where a river ebbs and flows, and is an arm of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, there it is common to all, and he who claims a privilege to himself must prove it; for if the trespass is brought for fishing there, the defendant may justify, that the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where is brachium maris, in quo unusquisque subditus domini regis habet et habere debet liberam piscariam. In the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a> the soil belongs to the owners of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> on each side; and the soil of the river <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a> is in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, but the fishing is common to all. He who is owner of the soil of a private river, hath separatis piscaria; and he that hath liberam piscariam, hath a property in the fish, and may bring a possessory <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> for them; but communis piscaria is like the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of all other commons. One that has a close pond in which there are fish, may call them pisces-suo, in an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a>, &c. but he cannot call them <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BONA">bona</a> et catalla, if they be not in trunks. There needs no privilege to make a fish pond, as there doth in the case of a warren. See Franchise.

FISSURES

Pages 709-709

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOLOGY">Geology</a>, certain interruptions, that in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> manner divide the several <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> of which the body of our globe is composed. See Geology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Fissure of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">Bones</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, is when they are divided either transversely or longitudinally, not quite through, but cracked after the manner of glass, by any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> force. See Surgery.

FISTULA

Pages 709-709

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> music, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> kind, resembling our <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> flageolet. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> wind instruments of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, were the tibia and the fistula. But how they were constituted, wherein they differed, or how they were played upon, does not appear. All we know is, that the fistula was at first made of reeds, and afterwards of other matters. Some had holes, some none; some again were single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>; others a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of several; witness the syringa of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAN">Pan</a>. Fistula, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, a deep, narrow, and callous ulcer, generally arising from abscesses. It differs from sinus, in its being callous, the latter not. See Surgery <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Fistula, in Farriery. See Farriery Index. Fistularia, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">Tobacco</a>-Pipe Fish; a genus of fishes, belonging to the order of abdominales. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> Index. FIT. See Paroxysm. Dr Cheyne is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that fits of all kinds, whether epileptic, hysterick, or apoplectic, may be cured solely by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a> diet, of about two quarts of cows milk a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, without any other medicine. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FITCHES">Fitches</a>, in Husbandry, a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, more generally known by the name of chick-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEA">pea</a>. See Cicer, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> Index. Fitches are cultivated either for feeding cattle, or improving the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>. They make a wholesome and nourishing food, whether given in the straw or thrashed out. When sown only to improve the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, they are ploughed in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> as they begin to blossom, by which means a tough stiff clay soil is much enriched. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol7.html#article-FITCHET">Fitchet</a>, a name used in some places for the weasel, called also the jowmart. See Mustela, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> Index. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FITCHY">Fitchy</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, (from the French fishe, i.e. fixed); a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> when the lower branch ends in a sharp point: and the reason of it Mackenzie supposes to be, that the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> were wont to carry crosses with them wherever they went; and when they stopped on their journey at any <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, they fixed those portable crosses in the ground for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>'s sake. FITZ; makes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of some of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> sons of the kings of England, as Fitz-roy; which is purely French, and signifies the "<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s son."

FITZ-STEPHEN

Pages 709-710

William, a learned monk of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, of Norman <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>, but born of respectable parents in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. He lived in the 12th century; and being attached to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of Archbishop Becket, was present at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>. In the year 1174, he wrote in Latin, *The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of St. Thomas, archbishop and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a>*; in which, as Becket Fitzmillner was a native of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>, he introduces a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the city of London, with a miscellaneous detail of the manners and usages of the citizens: this is deservedly considered as a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> curiosity, being the earliest professed account of London extant. Fitz-Stephen died in 1191.

FITZHERBERT

Pages 709-709

Sir Anthony, a very learned lawyer in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry VIII. was descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family, and born at Norbury in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a>. He was made one of the judges of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMMON_PLEAS"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> pleas in 1523; and distinguished himself by many valuable works, as well as by such an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> discharge of the duties of his office, as made him esteemed an oracle of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>. His writings are, The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> Abridgement; The Office and Authority of Justices of Peace; the Office of Sheriffs, Bailiffs of Liberties, Escheators, Constables, Coroners, &c.; Of the Diversity of Courts; The New Natura Brevis; Of the Surveying of Lands, and The Book of Husbandry. He died in 1538.

FIXATION

Pages 710-710

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, the rendering any volatile substance fixed, so as not to fly off upon being exposed to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>: hence,

FIXED BODIES

Pages 710-710

are those which bear a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> without evaporating, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> losing any of their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. Some of the most fixed bodies are diamonds, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, &c. **Fixed or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEXIBLE">Flexible</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">Air</a>**, an invisible and permanently <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> fluid, superior in gravity to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> atmospheric air and most other aerial <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>, exceedingly destructive to animal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; produced in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities, naturally from combustible bodies, and artificially by many chemical processes. From its acid properties it has obtained the name of aerial acid, cretaceous acid, and carbonic acid; from its noxious qualities, it has been called mephitic air, or mephitic <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAS">gas</a>; and, from the circumstance of being produced in vast quantities during the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMBUSTION">combustion</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a>, it first obtained from Van Helmont the name of gas sylvestre. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> fixed air has been given from its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of readily losing its elasticity, and fixing itself in many bodies, particularly those of the calcareous kind; and though some objected to the propriety of the term, the fluid in question is so well known by the name of fixed air, that we choose still to retain it. See **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">CHEMISTRY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">INDEX</a>**. For an account of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> for impregnating <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> with fixed air or carbonic acid, see **<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">MATERIA MEDICA</a> INDEX**. **Fixed Stars**, are such as constantly retain the same position and distance with respect to each other; by which they are distinguished from erratic or wandering stars, which are continually shifting their situation and distance. The fixed stars are properly called stars; the rest have the peculiar denomination of planet and comet. See **<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">ASTRONOMY</a> INDEX**.

FIXITY

Pages 710-710
or FIXEDNESS**, in Chemistry, is in a peculiar manner used for the affixture opposite to volatility; i.e. the property whereby bodies bear the action of the fire, without being dissipated in fumes.

FIXLMILLNER

Pages 710-710

PLACIDUS**, an eminent astronomer, was born at Achleiten near Linz, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, on the 28th of May, 1720. He received the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of Kremsmunster, of which his uncle Alexander was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a>. Here he studied during six years, and delighted so much in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> straight and curve-line figures, that his mother called him the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALMANACK">almanack</a>-maker. He went afterward to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALZBURG">Salzburg</a>, where he studied a regular course of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and particularly turned his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> under a professor Stuard, whose method of teaching that science was truly extraordinary, as he never made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of any figures, and yet conveyed such a clear idea of every proposition as made it perfectly easy. He was admitted as a novice into Kremsmunster in 1737, and the next year he took the solemn <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOW">vow</a> in presence of his uncle. After being two years in this monastery, during which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he devoted every leisure <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of mathematics and philosophy, he went to Fixmillner Salzburg to finish his studies in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURISPRUDENCE">jurisprudence</a>, acquiring at that time a competent knowledge of oriental and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> languages, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and antiquities. In the year 1745, he obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of D.D., after which he received <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>'s orders in his own monastery, and was created professor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, which office he held for 40 years, discharging the duties belonging to it till within a few days of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. He was also chosen <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of the higher <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, and regent of the young <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, which he retained during <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He wrote a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a> on the *Jus Canonicum*, notwithstanding his extensive epistolary correspondence, and the management of the whole business of the monastery; but this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was never published. He was, by the intrigues of his friends, induced to publish his *Reipublicae sacrae origines divinae, seu Ecclesiae Christi exterior junctura, imperium, et hierarchia, exprimigenia ejus institutione crudel et demonstrata*. His commendable diligence procured him universal esteem, but it was his knowledge of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> which rendered him illustrious. His uncle Alexander fitted up an apartment for containing the instruments necessary for the dissemination of mathematical knowledge, and he also erected an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a>, which was begun in 1748, and completed in 1758, under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANSELM">Anselm</a> Dering of Emdorf, a celebrated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a>. While the observatory was <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, Fixmillner led a life of retirement and severe study, his favourite subject during these ten years being astronomy. When it was finished, one Dobler, a celebrated mathematician, was appointed first astronomer; but the successors of Fixmillner's uncle having discovered his extensive mathematical knowledge, made him an offer of the astronomical department, and the sole direction of the observatory. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> he accepted in the year 1762, still retaining his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> as professor of ecclesiastical law. He was not yet <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the learning which practical astronomy requires, to remedy which defect he attentively perused Lalande's *Exposition du Calcul Astronomique*, soon after which he obtained the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> astronomical work of the same <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and in 1766 he published his *Meridianus specula Astronomico-Cremifonensis*, by which he acquired considerable reputation. Ten years after this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> he gave the world his *Decennium Astronomicum*, containing many curious and important particulars respecting the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> and practice of astronomy. His *Acta Astronomica Cremifonensis*, which did not appear till after his decease, still farther increased his astronomical reputation; and he was a large contributor to many periodical publications in different countries. He made and collected a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of observations of the planet <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, which were at that period both scarce and difficult, the importance of which was publicly acknowledged by Lalande, as they greatly assisted him in constructing his tables of that planet. Fixmillner was one of the first astronomers who calculated the orbit of the new planet Uranus (Georgium Sidus), and his tables respecting it may be seen in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a> almanack for 1789. He also proved the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of what was formerly conjectured, that the 34th <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a> of Taurus, which Flamsteed observed in 1690, was the new planet. It may be said of most philosophers, that they observe a great

FLACCUS

Pages 710-711
CAIUS VALERIUS, an ancient Latin poet, of whom we have very imperfect accounts remaining. He wrote a poem on the Argonautic expedition; of which, however, he did not live to finish the eighth book, dying at about 30 years of age. John Baptista Pius, an Italian poet, completed the eighth book of the Argonautics; and added two more from the fourth of Apolloiunus; which supplement was first added to Aldus's edition in 1523.

FLAG

Pages 711-711

in the marine, a certain banner <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> standard, by which an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> is distinguished at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> from the inferior ships of his squadron; also the colours by which one <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> is distinguished from another. See Plate CCXVIII. In the British <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, flags are either <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, or blue; and are displayed from the top of the main-mast, fore-mast, or mizen-mast, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of the admiral. When a flag is displayed from the flag-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a> on the main-mast, the officer distinguished thereby is known to be an admiral; when from the foremast, a vice-admiral; and when from the mizen-mast, a rear-admiral. The first flag in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> standard, which is only to be hoisted when the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> are on board the vessel: the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is that of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> of hope, which characterizes the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> admiral, or lords commissioners of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a>: and the third is the union flag, in which the crosses of St George and St Andrew are blended. This last is appropriated to the admiral of the fleet, who is the first <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> officer under the lord high admiral. The next flag after the union is that of the white squadron at the main-mast head; and the last, which characterizes an admiral, is the blue, at the same mast head. For a vice-admiral, the first flag is the red, the second the white, the third the blue, at the flag staff on the fore-mast. The same order proceeds with regard to the rear-admirals, whose flags are hoisted on the top of the mizen-mast: the lowest flag in our navy is accordingly the blue on the mizen-mast. To Lower or Strike the FLAG, in the marine, is to pull it <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> upon the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a>, or to take it in, out of the respect, or submission, due from all ships or fleets inferior to those any way justly their superiors. To lower or strike the flag in an engagement is a sign of yielding. The way of leading a ship in triumph, is to tie the flags to the shrouds, or the gallery, in the hind <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ship, and let them hang down towards the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and to tow the vessels by the stern. Livy relates, that this was the way the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> used those of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>. To Heave out the FLAG, is to put out or put abroad the flag. To Hang out the White FLAG, is to ask <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>; or it shows when a vessel is arrived on a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, that it has no hostile intention, but comes to trade or the like. The red flag is a sign of defiance and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. FLAG is also used for a sedge, a kind of rush. Corn-FLAG. See GLADIOLUS, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Sweet-scented FLAG. See ACORUS, BOTANY Index. FLAG-Officers, those who command the several squadrons of a fleet; such are the admirals, vice-admirals, and rear-admirals. The flag officers in our pay, are the admiral, vice-admiral, and rear-admiral, of the white, red, and blue. See ADMIRAL, FLAG, and FLEET. FLAG-Ship, a ship commanded by a general or flag-officer, who has a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to carry a flag, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to the secondary vessels under the command thereof. FLAG-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">Stone</a>, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAND_STONE">sand-stone</a> of a slaty structure, on account of which it is much employed for the purpose of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PAVING">paving</a> foot-paths or the floors of apartments in which wood is unsuitable.

FLAGELLANTES

Pages 711-712

a set of wild fanatics who chastised and disciplined themselves with whips in public. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of the Flagellantes had its rise in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> in the year 1260; its author was one Rainier a hermit; and it was propagated from hence through almost all the countries of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. It was in all <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> no more than the effect of an indiscreet zeal. A <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of persons of all ages and sexes made processions, walking two by two with their shoulders bare, which they whipped till the blood ran <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, in order to obtain mercy from God, and appease his indignation against the wickedness of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. They were then called the devout; and having established a superior, he was called the general of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. Though the primitive Flagellantes were exemplary in point of morals, Flagellants, morals, yet they were joined by a turbulent rabble who were infected with the most ridiculous and impious opinions; so that the emperors and pontiffs thought proper to put an end to this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> frenzy, by declaring all devout whipping contrary to the divine <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and prejudicial to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>'s eternal rest. This sect revived in Germany towards the middle of the next century, and rambling through many provinces, occasioned great disturbances. They held among other things, that flagellation was of equal virtue with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> and the other sacraments; that the forgiveness of all sins was to be obtained by it from God without the merits of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ; that the old law of Christ was soon to be abolished, and that a new law enjoining the baptism of blood to be administered by whipping was to be substituted in its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; upon which Clement VII. by an injudicious as well as unrighteous policy, thundered out anathemas against the Flagellantes, who were burnt by the inquisitors in several places; but they were not easily extirpated. They appeared again in Thuringia and Lower <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a> in the 15th century, and rejected not only the sacraments, but every branch of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> worship, and placed their only hopes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> and flagellation, to which they added other strange doctrines concerning evil spirits. Their leader <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONRAD">Conrad</a> Schmidt and many others were committed to the flames by German inquisitors in and after the year 1414.

FLAGEOLET

Pages 712-712
or **FLAEOLET**, a little flute, used chiefly by shepherds and country people. It is made of box or other hard wood, and sometimes of ivory; and has six holes besides that at the bottom, the mouth-piece, and that behind the neck.

FLAGS

Pages 711-711

in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, are small banners of distinction stuck in the baggage waggons to distinguish the baggage of one brigade from another; and of one battalion from another; that they may be marshalled by the waggon-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> general according to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of their brigades, to avoid the confusion that might otherwise arise.

FLAIL

Pages 712-712

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> for thrashing corn. It consists of the following parts. 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> piece held in the thrasher's hand. 2. The swiple, or that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> which strikes out the corn. 3. The caplins, or strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> leathers, made fast to the tops of the hand-staff and swiple. 4. The middle band, being the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> thong or fish skin that ties the caplins together.

FLAIR

Pages 712-712

in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. The seamen say that the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> doth flair over, when a ship is housed in near the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, so that the work hangs over a little too much, and this is let out broader aloft than the due proportion <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> allow.

FLAKE

Pages 712-712

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>, a name given by the florists to a sort of carnations which are of two colours only, and have very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> stripes, all of them going quite through the leaves. **<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">White</a> Flake**, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">Painting</a>, is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> corroded by means of the pressing of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a ceruse prepared by the acid of grapes. It is brought from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and far surpasses, both with regard to the purity of its whiteness and the certainty of its standing, all the ceruse or white lead made with us in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>. It is used in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a> painting for all purposes where a very clean white is required. The white flake should be procured in lumps as it is brought over and levigated by those who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> it; because that which the colourmen sell in a prepared state is levigated and mixed up with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STARCH">starch</a>, and often with white lead, and worse sophistications.

FLAMBEAU

Pages 712-712
or **FLAMBOY**, a luminary made of several thick wicks, covered over with wax, serving to burn at nights in the streets; as also at funeral processions, illuminations, &c. Flambeaux differ from links, torches, and tapers. They are made square, sometimes of white wax and sometimes of yellow. They usually consist of four wicks or branches near an inch thick, and about three feet long, made of a sort of coarse hempen yarn half twisted. They are made with the ladle much as torches or tapers are; viz. by first pouring the melted wax on the top of the several suspended wicks, and letting it run down to the bottom. This they repeat twice. After each wick has thus got its proper cover of wax, then lay them to dry; then roll them on a table, and so join four of them together by means of a red hot iron. When joined, they pour on more wax till the flambeau is brought to the size required, which is usually from a pound and a half to three pounds. The last thing is to finish their form or outside, which they do with a kind of polishing instrument of wood by running it along all the angles formed by the union of the branches. The flambeaux of the ancients were different from ours. They were made of woods dried in furnaces or otherwise. They used divers kinds of wood for this purpose; the wood most usually was pine. Pliny says, that in his time they frequently also burnt oak, elm, and hazel. In the seventh book of the Æneid, mention is made of a flambeau of pine; and Servius on that passage remarks, that they also made them of the cornel-tree. **FLAMBOROUGH head**, in Geography, a cape or promontory on the eastern coast of Yorkshire, five miles east of Burlington, and 215 from London.—E. Long. 20°. N. Lat. 54. 15.—This was the Flambourg of the Saxons; so called, as some think, from the lights made on it to direct the landing of Ina, who in 547 joined his countrymen in these parts with a large reinforcement from Germany, and founded the kingdom of Northumberland. In the time of Edward the Confessor, Flamborough was one of the manors of Harold, earl of the West Saxons, afterwards king of England. On his death, the Conqueror gave it to Hugh Lupus; who, in perpetual alms, bestowed it on the monastery of Whitby.—The town is on the north side, and consists of about 150 small houses, entirely inhabited by fishermen; few of whom, as is said, die in their beds, but meet their fate in the element they are so conversant in. The cliffs of the Head are of a tremendous height and amazing grandeur. Beneath are several vast caverns; some closed at the end, others pervious, formed with a natural arch. In some places the rocks are insulated, and of a pyramidal figure, soaring up to a vast height. The bases of most are solid, but in some pierced through and arched. The colour of all these rocks is white, from the dung of the innumerable flocks of migratory birds, which quite cover the face of them, filling every little projection, every hole that will give them leave to rest.

FLAME

Pages 712-713

is a general name for every kind of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUMINOUS">luminous</a> vapour, provided the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> it emits hath any considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of intensity. The name flame, how- ever, is most generally applied to such as are of a conical <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, like those arising from our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> fires; without this they are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called luminous vapours, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> simple lights. According to Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton, flame is only <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>-hot <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, or the vapour of any substance raised from it by fire, and heated to such a degree as to emit light copiously. This <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> seems to be the most accurate and expressive of any. It is certain, that bodies are capable of emitting flame only in proportion to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of vapour that rises from them. Thus wood, coals, &c., which emit a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantity of vapour, flame violently; while <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, tin, &c., which emit but a small fume, can scarce be perceived to flame at all. This rule, however, is by no means to be depended upon in all <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. Some vapours seem to be in their own <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> uninflammable, and capable of extinguishing flame; as those of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, the mineral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>, sal-ammoniac, arsenic, &c.; while others take fire on the slightest approach of a flaming substance; such as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-ETHER">ether</a>, spirit of wine, &c. These last-mentioned substances also exhibit a remarkable phenomenon; namely, that they cannot be made to flame without the approach of some substance actually in flames beforehand. Thus, spirit of wine poured on a red-hot <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, though instantly dissipated in vapour, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> not flame; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> touch its surface, the whole is set in a flame at once. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> is otherwise with oils, especially those of the grosser kind; for the vapours will readily be changed into flame by the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> increase of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, without the approach of any flaming substance. There is, however, no kind of vapour, perhaps, that is incapable of being converted into flame, provided it is exposed to a sufficient degree of heat. Thus the vapour of water made to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through burning coals produces an exceedingly strong and bright flame.—It is remarkable, that this kind of vapour seems to be more powerful than almost any other in absorbing heat, and detaining it in a latent state. When any quantity of aqueous vapour is condensed, more heat will be separated from it than would have been sufficient to heat an equal bulk of iron red hot.—It is most probably to this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> which all vapours have of absorbing heat, and detaining it in a latent state, that we are to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> the phenomena of flame, and also the exceeding great elasticity of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM">steam</a>. It is certain, that vapours, of water at least, have a much greater power of absorbing and retaining heat, than the water from which they are raised. In open vessels, water cannot be heated more than to 212 degrees of Fahrenheit's thermometer; but in Papin's digester, where the vapour is forcibly confined, it has been heated to 400 of the same degrees; and, no doubt, might have been heated a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> more, had the vessels been strong enough to bear the expansive force of the steam. On opening the vessels, however, the excess of heat was found to have resided entirely in the vapour; for the water in the vessel very soon sunk <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to 212, while the steam issued forth with great violence. From these experiments it appears, that the steam of water, after it has absorbed as much heat in the latent state as it can contain, continues to absorb or detain among its particles, an unlimited quantity of sensible heat; and if the steam could be confined till this quantity became great enough to be visible by emission of light, there cannot be the least doubt that the vapour would then be converted into flame. In what manner the heat is detained among the particles of steam, is perhaps impossible to be explained; but to this heat we must undoubtedly ascribe the violent expansive force of steam of every kind. It seems probable, that when smoke is converted into flame, the latent heat with which the vapour had combined, or rather that which made an essential <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it, breaks forth, and adds to the quantity of sensible heat which is already present. This seems probable, from the sudden <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPLOSION">explosion</a> with which all flames <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> out. If a vessel full of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> is set over the fire, a smoke or vapour begins to arise from it; which grows gradually thicker and thicker; and at last begins to shine in some places very near the surface of the oil, like an electric light, or sulphur <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> kindled. At this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the oil is very hot, as well as the steam which issues from it. But this last is continually giving off its sensible heat into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>; so that at the distance of an inch or two from the surface of the oil, the heat of the steam will not exceed 400 degrees of Fahrenheit, or perhaps may not be so much; but if a burning candle is held in the steam for a moment, the whole is immediately converted into flame, with something like an explosion; after which the oil burns quietly until it is all consumed. The flame, as soon as it appears, is not only much hotter than the steam from whence it was produced, but even than the oil which lies below it. Whence, then, has this sudden and great increase of heat arisen? It could not be the sensible heat of the vapour, for that was greatly inferior; nor could it be communicated from the oil, for that could communicate no more than it had to itself. The candle, indeed, would communicate a quantity of heat to the vapour which touched its flame; but it is impossible that this quantity should extend permanently over a surface perhaps 100 times larger than the flame of the candle, in such a manner as to make every part of that surface equally hot with the flame of the candle itself; for this would be to suppose it to communicate 100 times more heat than really was in it. The heat therefore must have originally resided in the vapour itself; and as, in the freezing of water, its latent heat is extricated and becomes sensible, and the water thereupon loses its fluidity; so, in the ascension of vapour, the latent heat breaks forth with a bright flash, and the vapour is then totally decomposed, and converted into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOOT">soot</a>, ashes, or water, according to the different nature of the substances which produce it, or according to the intensity of the heat.—Several other hypotheses have been invented to solve the phenomena of burning and flaming-bodies; for an account of which, see <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IGNITION">IGNITION</a> and HEAT, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Flames are of different colours, according to the substances from which they are produced. Thus, the flame of sulphur and spirit of wine is blue; the flame of nitre and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZINC">zinc</a>, of a bright <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>; that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, of a greenish blue, &c.—These varieties afford an opportunity of making a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of agreeable representations in fireworks, which could not be done if the flame produced from every different substance was of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. See PYROTECHNICS.

FLAMEN

Pages 713-714

in Roman antiquity, the name of an order order of priests, instituted by <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Numa: authors not being agreed on this head. They were originally only three, viz. the Flamen Dialis, Flamen Martialis, and Flamen Quirinalis. The Flamen Dialis was sacred to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, and a person of the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> and authority in the state. He discharged several <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> duties which properly belonged to the kings, and was honoured with many eminent privileges beyond all other officers, but was obliged to observe several superstitious restraints. The Flamen Martialis was sacred to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, and was ordained to inspect the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of that god. The Flamen Quirinalis was sacred to, and superintended the rites of, Quirinus Romulus. The Flamines last mentioned, though of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> authority, were much inferior to the Flamen Dialis. All three were chosen by the people, and consecrated by the Pontifex Maximus. In latter times several priests of the same order and name were added to them, but inferior in power. The whole <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> at last amounted to 15; the three first of whom were senators, and called Flamines maiores; the other 12 taken from among the people, being denominated Flamines minores.—Some authors tell us the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> had a Flamen for every deity they worshipped. The greater Flamines wore the robe edged with purple, like the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> magistrates; had an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, and a seat in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>. They wore a little band of thread about their heads, whence their name is said to be derived, quasi Filamines.—The wife of the Flamen Dialis was called Flaminia, and wore a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>-coloured <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, on which was painted a thunderbolt, and above her head-dress she had green oak boughs, to indicate that she belonged to Jupiter the thunderer, to whom the oak was sacred. The Flamines wore each of them a hat or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a> called Flammum or Aper.

FLAMINIUS

Pages 714-714
or FLAMININUS, T. Q. a celebrated Roman, raised to the consulship in the year of Rome 554, though under the age of 30. He was trained in the art of war against Hannibal; and he showed himself capable in every respect to discharge with honour the great office with which he was intrusted. He was sent at the head of the Roman troops against Philip king of Macedon, and in his expedition he met with uncommon success. The Greeks gradually declared themselves his firmest supporters; and he totally defeated Philip on the confines of Epirus, and made all Locris, Phocis, and Thessaly, tributary to the Roman power. He granted peace to the conquered monarch, and proclaimed all Greece free and independent at the Isthmian games. This celebrated action procured the name of Patrons of Greece to the Romans, and insensibly paved their way to universal dominion. Flaminius behaved among them with the greatest policy; by his ready compliance to their national customs and prejudices, he gained uncommon popularity, and received the name of father and deliverer of Greece. He was afterwards sent ambassador to King Prusias, who had given refuge to Hannibal; and there his prudence and artifice hastened out of the world a man who had long been the terror of the Romans. Flaminius was found dead in his bed, after a life spent in the greatest glory, in which he had imitated with success the virtues of his model Scipio. Flaminius, or FLAMINIO, Mark Antony, one of the best Latin poets in the 16th century, of Imola in Italy, son and grandson of very learned men. The Flaminio pope had chosen him secretary to the council in 1545; but he refused that employment, because, favouring the new opinions, he would not employ his pen in an assembly where he knew these opinions were to be condemned.—He paraphrased 38 of the psalms in Latin verse, and also wrote notes on the Psalms; and some letters and poems which are esteemed. He died at Rome in 1550.

FLAMSTEED

Pages 714-715

John, an eminent English astronomer, and the first who obtained the appointment of astronomer-<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DERBY">Derby</a> in the year 1646. He was educated at the free school of Derby, where he was head scholar at 14 years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, at which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, naturally tender and delicate, was much tried by a severe illness. When some of his companions went to the university, the state of his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> prevented him from accompanying them. He afterwards met with a book De Sphera, written by John Sacrobosco, which was perfectly suited to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> turn of his genius, and therefore he perused it with uncommon satisfaction, translating as much of it into English as he thought could be necessary for him; and from the Astronomia Carolinae of Strut he learned the method of calculating eclipses, and ascertaining the places of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>. Mr Hatton, a mathematician, sent him Kepler's Tabulae Rudolphinae, and Riccioli's Almagestum Novum, together with some other astronomical works to which he was as yet a stranger. In 1669 he calculated an eclipse of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, which had been omitted in the Ephemerides for the following year, together with five appulses of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> to fixed stars, and sent them to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Brouncker, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the Royal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, who submitted them to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of that learned body, by which they were greatly applauded, and he received a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of thanks from Mr Oldenburg the secretary. He likewise received a letter of thanks from Mr Collins, one of the members. In 1670 he was invited to come up to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> by his father, that he might become personally acquainted with his learned correspondents, of which he gladly accepted, and had an interview with Mr Oldenburg and Mr Collins, by the latter of whom he was introduced to Sir Jonas Moore, who became the warm friend and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of Mr Flamsteed. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this journey he became acquainted with many astronomical instruments, and was presented by Sir Jonas Moore with Townley's micrometer, who also assisted him in procuring glasses at a moderate rate for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of telescopes. On his way home again he returned by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, where he paid a visit to the celebrated Dr <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARROW">Barrow</a>. In the year 1672, he made <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> extracts from the letters of Gascoigne and Crabtree, by which his knowledge of dioptries was very much improved; and during the same year he made a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of celestial observations when the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> would permit, which were afterwards published in the Philosophical Transactions. In 1673 he composed a treatise on the true and apparent diameters of the planets, when at their greatest and least distance from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, which even the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Newton did not scruple to borrow, and made some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it in his Principia in 1685. He published an Ephemeris in 1674, in which he exposed the folly and absurdity of astrology, and the same year he drew up a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> for the use of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, with an astronomical account of their ebbing and flowing, which Sir Jonas Moore assured him would be well received by his majesty. Sir Jonas received from Mr Flamsteed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of barometers, with directions how to use them, which he presented to the king and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, to whose notice he embraced every opportunity of introducing Mr Flamsteed. Having taken the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of M.A. at Cambridge, he formed the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> of entering into holy orders, when Sir Jonas wrote to him to come to London, where he had an appointment for him very different from that of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. But as he found that nothing could make him abandon the resolution he had formed, he obtained a situation for him which was perfectly consistent with the character of a clergyman. This was the new office of astronomer to the king, with a salary of £100 per annum. He received ordination at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELY">Ely</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> by Bishop Gunning, in Easter 1675; and on the 10th of August in the same year the foundation <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> of the royal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a> was laid, which received the designation of Flamsteed house, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the first astronomer royal. Till this edifice was erected, he made his observations in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s house at Greenwich, and in 1681 his Doctrine of the Sphere was published by Sir Jonas Moore in his System of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">Mathematics</a>. Notwithstanding his extraordinary merit, he never rose higher in the church than to the living of Burslow in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURREY">Surrey</a>, although he was deservedly esteemed by the greatest men in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. He corresponded with the great Newton, Dr Halley, Mr W. Molyneux, Dr Wallis, and many others; and M. Cassini and he imparted their discoveries to each other with the utmost confidence and cordiality. But none of his works contributed so much to render his fame immortal as his "Historia Coelestis Britannica," in three vols. folio. Mr Flamsteed was suddenly carried off by a strangury on the 31st of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1719; and notwithstanding the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> delicacy of his constitution and incessant labours, he reached the 73rd year of his age.

FLANDERS

Pages 715-715

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, bounded by the German <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and the United Provinces on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, by the province of Brabant on the east, by Hainault and Artois on the south, and by another <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Artois and the German sea on the west; being about 60 miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 50 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. Flanders is a perfectly champaign <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, with not a rising ground <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hill in it, and watered with many fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>. Its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> commodities are fine <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LACE">lace</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>. In this country some important arts were invented and improved. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEAVING">Weaving</a> in general was greatly improved, and that of figures of all sorts in linen was invented; also the art of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a> cloths and stuffs, and of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> colours; the curing of herrings, &c. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of this country are not now in the flourishing state they were formerly; yet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, cotton, and woollen stuffs, &c. are still manufactured here in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities. This province had counts of its own from the ninth century to the year 1369, when it went by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> to the dukes of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>; and afterwards from them, by marriage also, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>. France, in 1667, seized the southern part; and the States General obtained the northern. It was overrun by the French in 1794, but was united to the new <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of the Netherlands in 1814. For a more particular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Flanders, see the article NETHERLANDS.

FLANEL

Pages 715-716
or FLANNEL, a kind of slight, loose, woollen stuff, composed of a woof and warp, and wove on a loom with two treddles, after the manner of baize. Dr Black assigns as a reason why flanel and other substances of the kind keep the body warm, that they compose a rare and spongy mass, the fibres of which touch each other so lightly, that the heat moves slowly through the interstices, which being filled only with air, and that in a stagnant state, give little assistance in conducting the heat.
