Pages 728-728

the covering of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> shorn off the bodies of sheep. See WOOL. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">Golden</a> FLEECE. See ARGONAUTS, and GOLDEN Fleece

FLEET

Pages 728-728

is also a noted prison in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, where persons are committed for contempt of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> and his laws, particularly of his courts of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> for debt, where any person <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> not or is unable to pay his creditors. There are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> rules and a warden belonging to the Fleet prison; which had its name from the float or fleet of the river or ditch, on the side whereof it stands.

FLEETWOOD

Pages 728-728

WILLIAM, a very learned English bishop in the beginning of the 18th century, of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a>. He distinguished himself during <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> William's reign, by his Inscriptionum Antiquorum Syllago, by several sermons he preached on public occasions, and by his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">Miracles</a>. He was designed by King William to a canonry of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> did not <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the seals before the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> gave it him, and he was installed in 1702. In 1723, he took a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> to retire; and in 1707, published, without his name, his Chronicon Pretiosum. In 1708, he was nominated by the queen to the see of St Asaph. The change of the queen's ministry gave him much regret. In 1715, he published a pamphlet entitled, "The 13th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> vindicated from the abusive senses put upon it." In 1714, he was translated to the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELY">Ely</a>; and died in 1723, aged 67. He published several other sermons and tracts, and was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> learning and exemplary piety.

FLEMINGIANS

Pages 728-728
or FLANDRIANS, in ecclesiastical history, a sect of rigid Anabaptists, who acquired this name in the 16th century, because most of them were natives of Flanders, by way of distinction from the WATERLANDIANS. In consequence of some dissensions among the Flemingians relating to the treatment of excommunicated persons, they were divided into two sects, distinguished by the appellations of Flandrians and Frieslanders, who differed from each other in their manners and discipline. Many of these in process of time came over to the moderate community of the Waterlandians, and those who remained separate are still known by the name of the old Flemingians or Flandrians; but they are comparatively few in number. These maintain the opinion of Menno with respect to the incarnation of Christ; alleging, that his body

FLESH

Pages 728-731

in Anatomy, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> substance, consisting of the various softer solids of the animal body, and so denominated in contradistinction to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>. See ANATOMY, p. 35. Flesh is also used, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a>, in speaking of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of the incarnation and eucharist. "The word was made flesh," Verbum caro factum est. The Romanists hold, that the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> in the sacrament of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a> is turned into the real flesh of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ. See Transubstantiation. Flesh is sometimes also used by botanists for the soft pulpy substance of any fruit, enclosed between the outer rind <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> skin and the seeds or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; or for that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a root, fruit, &c. fit to be eaten. Flesh-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">Colour</a>. See Carnation. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FLETA">Fleta</a>, the name given to an unknown writer who lived about the end of the reign of Edward II. and beginning of Edward III. and who being a prisoner in the Fleet, wrote there an excellent treatise on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> of England. Fletcher. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUMONT_AND_FLETCHER">Beaumont and Fletcher</a>. Fletcher, Andrew, of Salton, a celebrated Scots' patriot and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> writer, was descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family who trace their origin to one of the followers of William the Conqueror. He was the son of Sir Robert Fletcher of Salton and Innerpeffer, and born in the year 1650. The tuition of our author was committed by his father, on his deathbed, to Mr (afterwards Bishop) Burnet, then his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> minister; by whose care he received a pious, learned, and polite <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. Endowed with uncommon genius, and possessed of virtues and abilities peculiarly suited to the times in which he lived, Mr Fletcher quickly shone forth the ornament of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and the champion of its freedom. Having in the course of his classical studies and historical <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> been impressed with an enthusiastic admiration both of ancient and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> republics, he had early contracted an ardent <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, and an aversion to arbitrary rule. Hence his spirit the more readily took alarm at certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. Being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of the shire for <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOTHIAN">Lothian</a> to that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> where the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a> was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a>, he openly opposed the designs of that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a> of accession. He had a share with <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Viscount Stair in framing the test <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>, by which the duke of York complained that he lost Scotland. On these accounts he became peculiarly obnoxious to the duke; and was at last obliged to flee to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, to avoid the fatal consequences of prosecutions which on various pretence were commenced against him. Being cited before the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> and justiciary courts, and not appearing, he was declared traitor, and his estate confiscated. In Holland, he and Mr Baillie of Jerviswood were the only persons whom the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Argyle consulted concerning the designs which were then in agitation. In 1681 they came over to England, in order to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> matters with their party in that country; and were the only two who were intrusted so far as to be admitted to the secrets of Lord Russell's council of six. Mr Fletcher managed his part of the negotiation with so much <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, that administration could find no <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRETEXT">pretext</a> for seizing him; nor could they fix upon him those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> on account of which Mr Baillie was condemned; to whose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> let it be remembered, that although offered a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> on condition of his accusing his friend, he persisted in rejecting the proposal with indignation. Mr Fletcher having joined the duke of Monmouth upon his landing, received a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> command under him; but the duke was deprived of his services on the following occasion, as related by Sir John Dalrymple. Being sent upon an expedition, and not <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, he had seized for his own riding the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> of a country <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> [the mayor of Lynne] which stood ready equipped for its <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. The master, hearing this, ran in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> to Fletcher, gave him opprobrious <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, shook his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANE">cane</a>, and attempted to strike. Fletcher, though rigid in the duties of morality, having been accustomed to foreign <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> both by <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, in which he had acquired <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of the honour of a soldier and a gentleman, and of the affront of a cane, pulled out his pistol, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> him dead on the spot. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> was unpopular in countries where such refinements were not understood. A clamour was raised against it among the people of the country: in a body they waited upon the duke with their complaints; and he was forced to desire the only soldier, and almost the only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of parts, in his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, to abandon him. With Fletcher all Monmouth's chance of success in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> left him." But, in a manuscript memoir belonging to the family, we have the following notice concerning Mr Fletcher's connection with Monmouth, in which his separation from that prince is very differently accounted for: "To Lord Marischal Mr Fletcher explained the motives which first induced him to join, and afterwards abandon, the duke of Monmouth. The former he ascribed to the duke's manifesto in Scotland relating to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and in England to liberty. For the latter he accounted by the disgust produced in his own mind and that of his associates, when the duke declared himself <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, and broke <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> with all who embarked with him on his principles. He complained heavily of the account <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> given of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the mayor of Lynne: and mentioned to Lord Marischal, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the contrary, that he did not leave the duke till he came to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAUNTON">Taunton</a>, where he was proclaimed king, several weeks after the death of the mayor of Lynne." Seeing all the efforts of himself and his friends in favour of liberty frustrated at Taunton, he endeavoured to secure his own personal freedom by taking his passage in the first ship bound to a foreign country. It was his misfortune to land in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; where he was immediately arrested, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> into prison, and guarded by three three different bands of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, till a vessel should be prepared to carry him a victim in chains to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. But on the morning before the ship could sail, whilst he looked pensive through the bars that secured the window of his room, he was hailed by a venerable personage who made signs to speak with him. The prison doors he found open; and whilst his friendly conductor waved to him to follow him, he passed through three different guards of soldiers all fast asleep. Without being permitted to offer his thanks to his deliverer, he found himself obliged to prosecute with all speed the journey, in which he was directed by a person concerning whom he could never collect any information; and in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> he proceeded in safety through Spain. He felt a peculiar <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> in relating to his friends instances of the care of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> which he had experienced during his exile; and entertained them often with narratives of this kind, which he always mingled with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> reflections. Of these, another may be here mentioned. Happening in the evening to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the skirt of a wood at a few miles distance from a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> where he intended to lodge, he came to a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> met. After he had entered upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, he was accosted by a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> of a respectable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, who warned him to turn back, and take the road to the left; for that in the other there was danger which he could not escape <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to proceed. His friendly monitor suddenly retired into the wood, out of which she had issued no less unexpectedly. Having arrived at the city, the inhabitants were soon after alarmed by an account of the robbery and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of several travellers who that evening had fallen into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of a banditti upon the very way in which he had intended to travel. From these and other instances of preservation from dangers, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> of his mind, habituated from his infancy to an intercourse with heaven, led him to conclude that he was in a peculiar manner the care of Providence, and that in critical <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> his understanding received its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> from a supernatural impulse. During his exile, he maintained a frequent and extensive correspondence with the friends of liberty at home; and he partly employed himself in making a curious collection of books, which compose the best private library in Scotland. But his genius also prompted him to engage in more <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> employments. He repaired to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, and served several campaigns as a volunteer under the duke of Lorraine with great reputation. At length, understanding that the great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> then projected in Holland, and upon the issue of which he considered the liberties of Britain to be suspended, had attained a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of maturity, he hastened thither; where his counsels and address were of eminent service. He came over with King William; and in zeal, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>, penetration, and political skill, proved inferior to none of the leaders in the Revolution. Such, however, was his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGNANIMITY">magnanimity</a>, that from a survey of King William's papers, it appears that while others laboured to turn this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> event to the emolument of themselves and the aggrandisement of their family, Mr Fletcher asked nothing. His estate had been forfeited, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> abandoned to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>; his fortune was greatly shattered, and his family reduced to circumstances of distress. Nothing was given him in recompense of all his sufferings. On the contrary, he, together with the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a>, was distinguished by marks of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> and ministerial dislike. Still, whatever private resentment he might entertain, it appeared that his ruling principle was the good of his country; and that to this grand object of his heart he was willing to sacrifice all personal considerations. For when, in 1692, the abdicated king meditated an invasion, Mr Fletcher addressed a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> (preserved in Sir John Dalrymple's collection) to the duke of Hamilton, in which every argument is employed with skill and energy to engage his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> to forget his injuries, and in the present crisis to employ the extensive influence and authority he then possessed in the cause of freedom and of his country. This letter produced its full effect; and the duke returned to his duty, from which he had in part begun to deviate. To follow our author through all the mazes of his political <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> subsequent to the Revolution, is beyond our purpose, and would exceed our limits. One or two circumstances more shall therefore suffice. Being elected a member for the parliament 1683, he showed an uniform zeal for the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of his country. The thought of England's domineering over Scotland was what his generous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> could not endure. The indignities and oppression which Scotland lay under galled him to the heart; so that in his learned and elaborate discourses, he exposed them with undaunted courage and pathetical eloquence. In that great event, the Union, he performed essential service. He got the act of security passed, which declared that the two crowns should not pass to the same head till Scotland was secured in her liberties civil and religious. Therefore Lord Godolphin was forced into the Union, to avoid a civil war after the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEMISE">demise</a>. Although Mr Fletcher disapproved of some of the articles, and indeed of the whole frame of the Union; yet, as the act of security was his own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, he had all the merit of that important transaction. We must not omit mentioning, that in the ardour of his political <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CAREER">career</a> Mr Fletcher forgot not the interests of the place that gave him birth. He esteemed the education of youth one of the noblest objects of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. On this subject he wrote a treatise, still extant, most characteristic of himself; and he established at Salton a foundation for the same purpose, of great utility while it lasted. This great man died at London 1716, aged 66. His remains were conveyed to Scotland, and deposited in the family vault at Salton. That Mr Fletcher received neither honours nor emoluments from King William, may perhaps be in part attributed to himself; a circumstance, however, which must add greatly to the lustre of his character. His uncomplying virtue, and the sternness of his principles, were ill calculated to conciliate courtly favour. He was so zealous an assertor of the liberties of the people, that he was too jealous of the growing power of all princes; in whom he thought ambition so <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>, that he was not for trusting the best of kings with the power which ill ones might make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of against their subjects; he was of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that all princes were made by, and for the benefit of, the people; and that they should have no power but that of doing good. This, which made him oppose King Charles, and invade King James, led him also to oppose the giving so much power to King William, whom he would never serve after his establishment. So we are told by the author of Short Political <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">Characters</a>, a MS. in the library of the late T. Rawlinson, Esq.—Mr Lockhart, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a>, p. 72, expresses a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> that his aversion to the English and to the Union was so great, that, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> to them, he was inclined to side with the abdicated family: "But (adds he) as that was a subject not fit to be entered upon with him, this is only a conjecture from some innuendos I have heard him make; but so far is certain, he liked, commended, and conversed with high-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> Tories, more than any other set of men; acknowledging them to be the best countrymen, and of most honour, integrity, and ingenuity." It seems difficult to reconcile this with Mr Fletcher's avowed principles and the general tenor of his conduct. May we suppose, that chagrin, if not at the neglect or the ill treatment which he had himself received from government since the Revolution, yet at the public measures relating to his native country, might have occasioned him to relent in his sentiments with regard to the exiled family?—In the family memoirs already quoted, we are informed, That, "Lord Marischal held Mr Fletcher's character in high admiration;" and that, "when governor of Neufchatel, where Rousseau resided about the year 1766, he prevailed with this very extraordinary genius to write the life of a man whose character and actions he wished to have transmitted to posterity with advantage. For this purpose his lordship applied to an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> relation of Mr Fletcher's for materials; which by him were transmitted to Lord Marischal: but the design failed through Rousseau's desultory and capricious disposition." This anecdote must appear incompatible with the known loyalty and attachments of the Earl Marischal, unless we suppose him to have been privy to some such sentiments of Mr Fletcher as those alluded to by Mr Lockhart; for how could we suppose him anxious to promote a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, in which the task would be to celebrate principles diametrically opposite to his own, and to applaud actions subversive of that royal family in whose cause he had ventured his life, and forfeited his fortune, and foregone his country!—But however these circumstances may be reconciled, as the integrity, disinterestedness, and public spirit of Mr Fletcher, have been universally acknowledged, there is reason to believe, that all his sentiments and actions were founded in honour, and that he never once pursued a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> further than he judged it to be for the interest of his country. Mr Fletcher was master of the English, Latin, Greek, French, and Italian languages; and well versed in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the civil law, and all kinds of learning. In his travels, he had not only acquired considerable knowledge in the art of war, but also became versant in the respective interests of the several princes and states of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. In private life, he was affable to his friends, and free from all manner of vice. He had a penetrating, clear, and lively <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a>; but is said to have been too much wedded to opinions, and impatient of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a>.—He possessed an uncommon elevation of mind, accompanied with a warmth of temper, which would suffer him to brook from no <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> among men, nor in any place, an indignity. Of this he exhibited a singular proof in the Scots parliament. The earl of Stair, secretary of state and minister for Scotland, having in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of debate used an improper <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> against Mr Fletcher, he seized him by his robe, and insisted upon public and immediate satisfaction. His lordship was obliged instantly to beg his pardon in presence of parliament. Mr Fletcher was by far the finest speaker in the parliament of Scotland; the earl of Stair alone rivalled him. The latter was famed for a splendid, the former for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> and nervous, eloquence. He formed his style on the models of antiquity; and the small volume of his works, Sir John Dalrymple observes, though imperfectly collected, is one of the very few classical compositions in the English language.

FLETWOOD

Pages 731-731

WILLIAM, an eminent English lawyer and recorder of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>. He was very zealous in suppressing masshouses, and committing popish priests; but once rushing in upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> at the Portuguese <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, he was committed to the Fleet for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of privilege, but soon released. Mr Wood says, "He was a learned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and a good antiquary, but of a marvellous merry and pleasant conceit." He was a good popular speaker, and wrote well upon subjects of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> works are, 1. Annalium tom regum Edwardi V. Richardi III. et Henrici VII. quam Henrici VIII. 2. A <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> of the Reports of Edmund Plowden. 3. The Office of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">Justice</a> of Peace. He died about the year 1593.

FLEURI

Pages 731-731
CLAUDE, an able French critic and historian, was born at Paris in 1640. He applied himself to the law, was made advocate for the parliament of Paris, and attended the bar nine years; he then entered into orders, and was made preceptor to the princes of Conti. In 1689, the king made him sub-preceptor to the dukes of Burgundy, Anjou, and Berry; and in 1706, when the education of these young princes was completed, the king gave him the priory of Argenteville belonging to the Benedictines in the diocese of Paris. In 1716, he was chosen counsellor to Louis XV. and died in 1723. He was the author of a great number of esteemed French works; the principal of which are, 1. An ecclesiastical history, in 20 volumes, the last of which ends with the year 1414. 2. The manners of the Israelites and Christians. 3. Institutions of ecclesiastical law. 4. An historical catechism. 5. On the choice and method of study. 6. The duties of masters and servants, &c.

FLEVILLEA

Pages 731-731

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dioecia class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FLEXIBLE

Pages 731-731

in Physics, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to bodies capable of being bent <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> diverted from their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>.

FLEXOR

Pages 731-731

in Anatomy, a name applied to several muscles, which are so called from their office, which is to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> the parts to which they belong; in opposition to the extensors, which open <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> stretch them. See Anatomy, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> of the Muscles.

FLIGHT

Pages 731-732

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the manner, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>, &c. thereof. Almost every kind of bird has its particular flight; the eagle's flight is the highest; the flight of the sparrow-hawk and vulture is noble, and fit for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> enterprise. FLIGHT. In melting the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> ore in the works at Mendip, there is a substance which flies away in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> which is called the flight. The workmen find it sweetish upon their lips, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> their faces happen to be in the way of the smoke, which they avoid as much as possible. This, falling on the grass, kills cattle that feed thereon; and being gathered and carried home, kills rats and mice in their houses; that which falls on the sand, they gather and melt upon a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a> hearth into <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> and sheet lead.

FLINT

Pages 732-732

a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of simple <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, chiefly composed of siliceous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERALOGY">MINERALOGY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Breaking of FLINTS. The art of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather breaking flint stones into uniform figures, is by some supposed to be one of the arts now lost. That it was known formerly, appears from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDEWELL">Bridewell</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWICH">Norwich</a>, from the gate of the Augustinian friars at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, that of St John's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">Abbey</a> at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLCHESTER">Colchester</a>, and the gate near Whitehall, Westminster. But that the art is not lost, and that the French know it, appears from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a> on the top of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; which, instead of being leaded, is paved with flint cut or broken into regular figures. GLASS FLINTS. For the method of manufacturing, see MINERALOGY Index.

FLINTS

Pages 732-732

the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLINTSHIRE">Flintshire</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. It is commodiously seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEE">Dee</a>; and is but a small <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, though it sends one member to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. It was formerly noted for its castle, where Richard II. took shelter on his arrival from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>; but having quitted it, he was taken prisoner by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a>. The castle now is in a ruinous condition. This castle stands <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on a rock, which in various parts forms several feet of its foundation. It covers about three <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">acre</a>. The assizes are still held in the town. It is 195 miles north-west of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> 1433 in 1811.

FLINTSHIRE

Pages 732-732

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east and east by an arm of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, which is properly the mouth of the river <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEE">Dee</a>; on the north-west by the Irish sea; and on the south-south-west and west by Denbighshire. It is the least of all the counties in Wales, being but 33 miles in length and 9 in breadth. It is divided into five <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>; in which are two market <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and 28 parishes; and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> in 1811 was 46,578. The greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of this county lies in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of St Asaph, and the rest belongs to that of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>. It sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, one for the county and one for Flint; and pays one part of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> tax. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, but healthful. It is full of hills, intermixed with a few valleys, which are very fruitful, producing some wheat and plenty of rye. The cows, though small, yield a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a> in proportion to their size, and are excellent beef. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> are well stored with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, coal, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MILLSTONES">millstones</a>. This county also produces good <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, cheese, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>. See FLINTSHIRE, Supplement.

FLOAT

Pages 732-732

a certain <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> bound together with rafters athwart, and put into a river to be conveyed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the stream; and even sometimes to carry burdens down a river with the stream. FLOAT-Boards, those boards fixed to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> of under-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>, serving to receive the impulse of the stream, whereby the wheel is carried round. See the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> WHEEL and MILL. It is no advantage to have too <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of float-boards; because, when they are struck by the water in the best manner that it can be brought to come against them, the sum of all the impulses <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be but equal to the impulse made against one float-board at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, by all the water coming out of the penstock through the opening, so as to take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> on the float-board. The best rule in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> is to have <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> so many, that each of them may come out of the water as soon as possible, after it has received and acted with its full impulse. As to the length of the float-board, it may be regulated according to the breadth of the mill. See MILL. FLOATS for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">Fishing</a>. See FISHING Floats.

FLOATAGES

Pages 732-736

all things floating on the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; a word much used in the commissions of water bailiffs. FLOATING BODIES are those which swim on the surface of a fluid, the most interesting of which are ships and vessels employed in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. It is known to every seaman, of what vast moment it is to ascertain the stability of such vessels, and the positions they assume when they float freely on the surface of the water. To be able to accomplish this, it is necessary to understand the principles on which that stability and these positions depend. This has been done with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> ingenuity by Mr Atwood, of whose reasoning the following is a summary account, taken from the Philosophical Transactions for 1796. A floating body is pressed downwards by its own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> in a vertical line passing through its centre of gravity; and it is supported by the upward pressure of a fluid, which acts in a vertical line that passes through the centre of gravity of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> which is under the water; water; and without a coincidence between these two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, in such a manner as that both centres of gravity may be in the same vertical line, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> turn on an axis, till it gains a position in which the equilibrium of floating will be permanent. From this it is obviously necessary to find what proportion the part immersed bears to the whole, to do which the specific gravity of the floating body must be known, after which it must be found by geometrical methods, in which positions the solid can be placed on the surface of the fluid, so that both centres of gravity may be in the same vertical line, when any given part of the solid is immersed under the surface. These things being determined, something is still wanting, for positions may be assumed in which the circumstances now mentioned concur, and yet the solid will assume some other position wherein it will permanently float. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the specific gravity of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a> be to that of the fluid on which it floats as 3 to 4, and its axis to the diameter of the base as 2 to 1: if it be placed on the fluid with its axis vertical, it will sink to a depth equal to a diameter and a half of the base; and while its axis is preserved in a vertical position by outward force, the centres of gravity of the whole solid and immersed part will remain in the same vertical line; but when the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> force is removed, it will deviate from its upright position, and will permanently float with its axis <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a>. If we suppose the axis to be half the diameter of the base, and placed vertically, the solid will sink to the depth of three-eighths of its diameter, and in that position it will float permanently. If the axis be made to incline to the vertical line, the solid will change its position till it permanently settles with its axis perpendicular to the horizon. Whether a solid floats permanently, or oversets when placed on the surface of a fluid, provided the centre of gravity of the solid and that of the immersed part be in the same vertical line, it is said to be in a position of equilibrium, of which there are three kinds; the equilibrium of stability, in which the solid permanently floats in a given position; the equilibrium of instability, in which the solid spontaneously oversets, if not supported by external force; and the equilibrium of indifference, or the insensible equilibrium, in which the solid rests on the fluid indifferent to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, without tendency to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> itself when inclined, or to incline farther. If a solid body floats permanently on the surface of a fluid, and external force be applied to turn it from its position, the resistance opposed to this inclination is termed the stability of floating. Some ships at sea yield to a given impulse of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, and suffer a greater inclination from the perpendicular than others. As this resistance to heeling, duly regulated, has been considered of importance in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of vessels, many eminent mathematicians have laid <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> rules for ascertaining the stability of ships from their known dimensions and weight, without recurring to actual experiment. Bouguer, Euler, Chapman, and others, have laid down theorems for this purpose, founded on the supposition that the inclinations of ships from their quiescent positions are evanescent, or very small in a practical point of view. But ships at sea have been found to heel 15°, 20°, or 30°, and therefore it may be doubted how far such rules are applicable in practice. If <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STATICS">statics</a> can be applied to naval <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, it seems necessary that the rules should be extended to those <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> in which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> of inclination are of any magnitude, likely to occur in the practice of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>. A solid body placed on the surface of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> fluid, at such a depth as corresponds to the relative gravities, cannot alter its position by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of its own weight and the pressure of the fluid, except by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> on some horizontal axis passing through the centre of gravity; but, as many axes may be drawn through this point of the floating body, in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the horizon, and the motion of the solid regards only one axis, this must be determined by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the body and the particular <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>. When this axis of motion is ascertained, and the specific gravity of the solid found, the positions of permanent floating will be determined, by finding the several positions of equilibrium through which the solid may be conceived to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, while it turns round the axis of motion; and by determining in which of these positions the equilibrium is permanent, and in which of them it is momentary. The whole of Mr Atwood's valuable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> relates to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of naval architecture, in so far as it is dependent on the laws of pure <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>. If the proportions and dimensions adopted in the construction of individual vessels are obtained by exact geometrical measurement, and observations are made on the performance of these vessels at sea; a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of experiments of this nature, judiciously varied, are the proper grounds on which theory may be effectually applied, in reducing to system those hitherto unperceived causes, which contribute to give the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of excellence to vessels of every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>. Naval architecture being reckoned among the practical branches of science, every voyage may be viewed in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of an experiment, from which useful truths are to be deduced. But inferences of this nature cannot well be obtained, except by acquiring a thorough knowledge of all the proportions and dimensions of each part of the ship, and by making a sufficient number of observations on the qualities of the vessel, in all the varieties of situation to which a ship is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> subject in the practice of navigation. The following is an ingenious <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> of the same subject by Mr English, which we give in his own words. "However operose and difficult (says he) the calculations necessary to determine the stability of nautical vessels may, in some cases, be, yet they all depend, says this author, upon the four following simple and obvious theorems, accompanied with other well known stereometrical and statistical principles. "Theorem 1. Every floating body displaces a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the fluid in which it floats, equal to its own weight; and consequently the specific gravity of the fluid will be to that of the floating body, as the magnitude of the whole is to that of the part immersed. "Theorem 2. Every floating body is impelled downward by its own essential power, acting in the direction of a vertical line passing through the centre of gravity of the whole; and is impelled upward by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REACTION">reaction</a> of the fluid which supports it, acting in the direction of a vertical line passing through the centre of gravity of the part immersed; therefore, unless these two lines are coincident, the floating body thus impelled must revolve round an axis, either in motion or at rest, until the equilibrium is restored. "Theorem 3. If by any power whatever a vessel be deflected..." Floating bodies deflected from an upright position, the perpendicular distance between two vertical lines passing through the centres of gravity of the whole, and of the part immersed respectively, will be as the stability of the vessel, and which will be positive, nothing, or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a>, according as the metacentre is above, coincident with, or below, the centre of gravity of the vessel. "Theorem 4. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> centre of gravity of any system of bodies being given in position, if any one of these bodies be moved from one part of the system to another, the corresponding motion of the common centre of gravity, estimated in any given direction, will be to that of the aforesaid body, estimated in the same direction, as the weight of the body moved is to that of the whole system. "From whence it is evident, that in order to ascertain the stability of any vessel, the position of the centres of gravity of the whole, and of that part immersed, must be determined; with which, and the dimensions of the vessel, the line of floatation, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of deflection, the stability or power either to right itself or overturn, may be found. "In ships of war and merchandise, the calculations necessary for the purpose become unavoidably very operose and troublesome; but they may be much facilitated by the experimental method pointed out in the New Transactions of the Swedish Academy of Sciences, first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the year 1787, page 48. "In river and canal boats, the regularity and simplicity of the form of the vessel itself, together with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> disposition and homogenous <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the burden, render that method for them unnecessary, and make the requisite calculations become very easy. Vessels of this kind are generally of the same transverse <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECTION">section</a> throughout their whole length, except a small part in prow and stern, formed by segments of circles or other simple curves; therefore a length may easily be assigned such, that any of the transverse sections being multiplied thereby, the product will be equal to the whole solidity of the vessel. The form of the section ABCD is for the most part either rectangular, as in fig. 1. Plate CCXVIII. trapezoidal as in fig. 2. or mixtilinear as in fig. 3. in all which MM represents the line of floatation when upright, and EF that when inclined at any angle MXE; also G represents the centre of gravity of the whole vessel, and R that of the part immersed. "If the vessel be loaded quite up to the line <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">AB</a>, and the specific gravity of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> and burden be the same, then the point G is simply the centre of gravity of the section ABCD; but if not, the centres of gravity of the boat and burden must be found separately, and reduced to one by the common method, namely, by dividing the sum of the momenta by the sum of weights, or areas, which in this case are as the weights. The point R is always the centre of gravity of the section MMCD, which, consisting of different figures, must also be found by dividing the sum of the momenta by the sum of the weights as common. These two <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> being found, the next thing necessary is to determine the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of the two equal triangles MXE, MXF, their centres of gravity o, o, and the perpendicular projected distance n n of these points on the water line EF. This being done, through R and parallel to EF draw RT = a fourth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> to the whole area MMCD, either triangle MXE or MXF, and the distance n n; through T, and at right angles to RT or EF, draw TS meeting the vertical axis of the vessel in S the metacentre; also through the points G, B, and parallel to ST, draw NGW and BV; moreover through S, and parallel to EF, draw WSV, meeting the two former in V and W; then SW is as the stability of the vessel, which will be positive, nothing, or negative, according as the point S is above, coincident with, or below, the point G. If now we suppose W to represent the weight of the whole vessel and burden (which will be equal to the section MMCD multiplied by the length of the vessel), and P to represent the required weight applied at the gunwale B to sustain the vessel at the given angle of inclination; we shall always have this proportion: as VS : SW :: W : P; which proportion is general, whether SW be positive or negative; it must only in the latter case be supposed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> upward to prevent an overturn. "In the rectangular vessel, of given weight and dimensions, the whole <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is so evident, that any farther explanation would be unnecessary. In the trapezoidal vessel, after having found the points G and R, let <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AD">AD</a>, BC be produced until they meet in K. Then, since the two sections MMCD, EFDC are equal; the two triangles MMK, EFK are also equal; and therefore the rectangle EK X KF = KM X KM = KM²; and since the angle of inclination is supposed to be known, the angles at E and F are given. Consequently, if a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> proportional be found between the sines of the angle at E and F, we shall have the following proportions: "As the mean proportional thus found: sine ∠ F :: KM : KF, and in the said mean proportional: sine ∠ F :: KM : KE; therefore ME, MF become known; from whence the area of either triangle MXE or MXF, the distance n n, and all the other requisites, may be found. "In the mixtilinear section, let AB = 9 feet = 108 inches, the whole depth = 6 feet = 72 inches, and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ALTITUDE">altitude</a> of MM the line of floatation 4 feet or 48 inches; also let the two curvilinear parts be circular quadrants of two feet, or 24 inches radius each. Then the area of the two quadrants = 904.7808 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> inches, and the distance of their centres of gravity from the bottom = 13.8177 inches very nearly, also the area of the included rectangle abce = 1440 square inches, and the altitude of its centre of gravity 12 inches; in like manner, the area of the rectangle AB cd will be found = 518.4 square inches, and the altitude of its centre of gravity 48 inches: therefore we shall have \[ \begin{align*} \text{Momentum of the two quad.} & = 904.7808 \times 13.8177 = 12501.9866016 \\ \text{Moment of the rectan. abce} & = 1440 \times 12 = 17280 \\ \text{Moment of the rectan. AB cd} & = 518.4 \times 48 = 24832 \\ \end{align*} \] Now the sum of the momenta, divided by the sum of the areas, will give \( \frac{27861.39866016}{75287808} = 37.006 \) inches, the altitude of G, the centre of gravity of the section. section ABCD above the bottom. In like manner, the altitude of R, the centre of gravity of the section MMCD, will be found to be equal \[ \frac{1239379866616}{49367858} = 24'934 \text{ inches}; \text{and consequently their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, or the value of GR} = 12'572 \text{ inches}, \text{will be found.} \] Suppose the vessel to heel \(15^\circ\), and we shall have the following proportion; namely, As radius : tangent of \(15^\circ\) :: MX = 54 inches = ME or MF; and consequently the area of either triangle MXE or MXF = 390'663 square inches. Therefore, by theorem 4th, as 4936'7858 : 390'663 :: 72 = n = \( \frac{1}{2} \) AB : 5'6975 inches = RT; and again, as radius : sine of \(15^\circ\) :: 12'572 = GR : 3'1245 inches = RN; consequently RT - RN = 5'6975 - 3'1245 = 2'573 inches = SW, the stability required. Moreover, as the sine of \(15^\circ\) : radius :: 5'6975 = RT : 22'013 = RS, to which if we add 24'934, the altitude of the point R, we shall have 46'947 for the height of the metacentre, which taken from 72, the whole altitude, there remains 25'033; from which, and the half width = 54 inches, the distance BS is found = 59'529 inches very nearly, and the angle SBV = 80° - 06' - 42''; from whence SV = 38'645 inches. Again: Let us suppose the mean length of the vessel to be 40 feet, or 480 inches, and we shall have the weight of the whole vessel equal to the area of the section MMCD = 4936'7858 multiplied by 480 = 236995'4784 cubic inches of water, which weighs exactly 8'758 pounds avoirdupoise, allowing the cubic foot to weigh 62'5 pounds. And finally, as SV : SW (i.e.) as 38'645 : 2'573 :: 85708 : 3760 + , the weight on the gunwale which will sustain the vessel at the given inclination. Therefore a vessel of the above dimensions, and weighing 38 tons 5 cwt. 28lbs. will require a weight of one ton 13 cwt. 64lbs. to make her incline \(15^\circ\). In this example the deflecting power has been supposed to act perpendicularly on the gunwale at B; but if the vessel is navigated by sails, the centre velique must be found; with which and the angle of deflection, the projected distance thereof on the line SV may be obtained; and then the power calculated as above, necessary to be applied at the projected point, will be that part of the wind's force which causes the vessel to heel. And conversely, if the weight and dimensions of the vessel, the area and altitude of the sails, the direction and velocity of the wind be given, the angle of deflection may be found. Floating <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">Bridge</a>. See Bridge. Flock Paper. See Paper. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">Flood</a>, a deluge or inundation of waters. See Deluge. Flood is also used in speaking of the tide. When the water is at lowest, it is called ebb; when rising, young flood; when at highest, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> flood; when beginning to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, ebb water. Flood-mark, the mark which the sea makes on the shore at flowing water and the highest tide, it is also called high-water mark. Flook of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>. See Anchor. Flooding, among miners, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> used to express a peculiarity in the load of a mine. The load or quantity of ore is frequently intercepted in its course by the crossing of a vein of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, or some different metallic substance; in which case the load is moved to one side, and this transient part of the load is called a flooding. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FLOOR">Floor</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, the underside of a room, or that part we walk on. Floors are of several sorts; some of earth, some of brick, others of stone, others of boards, &c. For brick and stone Floors, see Pavement. For boarded Floors, it is observable that the carpenters never floor their rooms with boards till the carcass is set up, and also enclosed with walls, lest the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> should injure the flooring. Yet they generally rough-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> their boards for the flooring before they begin any thing else about the building, that they may set them by to dry and season, which is done in the most careful manner. The best wood for flooring is the fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> well seasoned, which when well laid, will keep its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> for a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> while; whereas the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> sort becomes <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> by often washing, and looks very bad. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> of the boards are commonly made plain, so as to touch each other only; but, when the stuff is not quite dry, and the boards shrink, the water runs through them whenever the floor is washed, and injures the ceiling underneath. For this reason they are made with feather edges, so as to cover each other about half an inch, and sometimes they are made with grooves and tenons; and sometimes the joints are made with dove tails; in which case the lower edge is nailed down, and the next drove into it, so that the nails are concealed. The manner of measuring floors is by squares of 10 feet on each side, so that taking the length and breadth, and multiplying them together and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off two decimals, the content of a floor in square will be given. Thus 18 by 16 gives 288 or 2 squares and 88 decimal parts. Earthen Floors, are commonly made of loam, and sometimes, especially to make malt on, of lime and brook sand, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a> dust or anvil dust from the forge. Ox blood and fine clay, tempered together, Sir Hugh Plat says, make the finest floor in the world. The manner of making earthen floors for plain <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> habitations is as follows: Take two-thirds of lime and one of coal ashes well sifted, with a small quantity of loam clay; mix the whole together, and temper it well with water, making it up into a heap: let it <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> or ten days, and then temper it over again. After this heap it up for three or four days, and repeat the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERING">tempering</a> very high, till it becomes smooth, yielding, tough, and gluey. The ground being then levelled, lay the floor therewith about 2½ or 3 inches thick, making it smooth with a trowel: the hotter the season is the better; and when it is thoroughly dried, it will make the best floor for houses, especially malt houses. If any one would have their floors look better, let them take lime made of rag <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, well tempered with whites of eggs, covering the floor about half an inch thick with it, before the under-flooring is too dry. If this be well done, and thoroughly dried, it will look when rubbed with a little <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> as transparent as metal or glass. In elegant houses, floors of this nature are made of stucco, or of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> beaten and sifted, and mixed with other ingredients. FLOOR of a Ship, strictly taken, is only so much of her bottom as she rests on when <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGROUND">aground</a>. Such ships as have long, and withal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> floors, lie on the ground with most security, and are not apt to heel, or tilt on one side; whereas others, which are narrow in the floor, or in the sea phrase, cranked by the ground, cannot be grounded without danger of being overturned.

FLOOR TIMBERS

Pages 736-736

in a ship, are those parts of a ship's timbers which are placed immediately across the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEEL">keel</a>, and upon which the bottom of the ship is framed; to these the upper parts of the timbers are united, being only a continuation of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> timbers upwards.

FLORA

Pages 736-736

the reputed <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, was, according to Lactantius, only a lady of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, who having gained <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sums of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> by prostituting herself, made the Roman people her heir, on condition that certain games called Floralia might be annually celebrated on her birth-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> afterwards, however, such a foundation appearing unworthy the majesty of the Roman people, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, to ennoble the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, converted Flora into a goddess, whom they supposed to preside over flowers; and so made it a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> to render her propitious, that it might be well with their gardens, vineyards, &c. But Vossius (de Idol. lib. i. c. 12.) can by no means allow the goddess Flora to have been the courtezan above mentioned: he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> rather have her a Sabine deity, and thinks her worship might have commenced under <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>. His reason is, that Varro, in his fourth book of the Latin tongue, ranks Flora among the deities to whom Tatius <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Sabines offered up vows before he joined <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. Add, that from another passage in Varro it appears, that there were priests of Flora, with sacrifices, &c. as early as the times of Romulus and Numa. The goddess Flora was, according to the poets, the wife of Zephyrus. Her image in the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASTOR">Castor</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLLUX">Pollux</a> was dressed in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, and she held in her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> the flowers of pease and beans: but the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> poets and painters have been more lavish in setting off her charms, considering that no parts of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> offered such innocent and exquisite entertainment to the sight and smell, as the beautiful variety which adorns, and the odour which embalms, the floral <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>.

FLORALES LUDI

Pages 736-736
or FLORAL GAMES, in antiquity, were games held in honour of Flora, the goddess of flowers.—They were celebrated with shameful debaucheries. The most licentious discourses were not enough, but the courtezans were called together by the sound of a trumpet, made their appearance naked, and entertained the people with indecent shows and postures: the comedians appeared after the same manner on the stage. Val. Maximus relates, that Cato being once present in the theatre on this occasion, the people were ashamed to ask for such immodest representations in his presence; till Cato, apprised of the reservedness and respect with which he inspired them, withdrew, that the people might not be disappointed of their accustomed diversion. There were several other sorts of shows exhibited on this occasion; and, if we may believe Suetonius in Galba, c. 6. and Vopiscus in Carinus, these princes presented elephants dancing on ropes on these occasions. The ludi florales, according to Pliny, lib. xviii. c. 29. Florence were instituted by order of an oracle of the Sibyls, on the 28th of April; not in the year of Rome 1326, as we commonly read it in the ancient editions of that author; nor in 1344, as F. Hardouin has corrected it, but, as Vossius reads it, in 513: though they were not regularly held every year till after 580. They were chiefly held in the night time, in the Patrician street: some will have it there was a circus for the purpose on the hill called Hortulorum.

FLORALIA

Pages 736-736

in antiquity, a general name for the feasts, games, and other ceremonies, held in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> FLORA. See FLORA and FLORALES LUDI.

FLORENCE

Pages 736-738

the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, and one of the finest cities in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. It is surrounded on all sides but one with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> hills, which rise insensibly, and at last join with the lofty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> called the Apennines. Towards <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISA">Pisa</a>, there is a vast plain of 40 miles in length; which is so filled with villages and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> houses, that they seem to be a continuation of the suburbs of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. Independent of the churches and palaces of Florence, most of which are very magnificent, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> of the houses in general is in a good <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; and the streets are remarkably clean, and paved with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> chiseled so as to prevent the horses from sliding. The city is divided into two unequal parts by the river Arno, over which there are no less than four bridges in sight of each other. That called the Ponte dell Trinità, which is uncommonly elegant, is built entirely of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble, and ornamented with four beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> representing the Seasons. The quays, the buildings on each side, and the bridges, render that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Florence through which the river runs by far the finest. Every corner of this beautiful city is full of wonders in the arts of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, statuary, and architecture. The streets, squares, and fronts of the palaces, are adorned with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of statues; some of them by the best <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> masters, Michael Angelo, Bandinelli, Donatello, Giovanni di <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>, Benvenuto Cellini, and others. Some of the Florentine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> formerly were men of vast wealth, and lived in a most magnificent manner. One of them, about the middle of the fifteenth century, built that noble fabric, which, from the name of its founder, is still called the Palazzo Pitti. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> was ruined by the prodigious expense of this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, which was immediately purchased by the Medici family, and has <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> ever since to be the residence of the sovereigns. The gardens belonging to this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> are on the declivity of an eminence. On the summit there is a kind of fort, called <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELVEDERE">Belvedere</a>. From this, and from some of the higher walks, you have a complete view of the city of Florence, and the beauteous vale of Arno, in the middle of which it stands. This palace has been enlarged since it was purchased from the ruined family of Pitti. The furniture is rich and curious, particularly some tables of Florentine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, which are much admired. The most precious ornaments, however, are the paintings. The walls of what is called the Imperial Chamber, are painted in fresco, by various painters; the subjects are allegorical, and in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Lorenzo of Medicis, distinguished Florence, distinguished by the name of the Magnificent. The famous gallery attracts every stranger. One of the most interesting parts of it, in the eyes of many, is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of Roman emperors, from Julius Caesar to Galienus, with a considerable number of their empresses arranged opposite to them. This series is almost complete; but wherever the bust of an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> is wanting, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is filled up by that of some other distinguished Roman. The celebrated Venus of Medici, which has been removed to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, is thought to be the standard of taste in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and proportion, and stood formerly in a room called the Tribunali. The inscription on its base mentions its being made by Cleomenes an Athenian, the son of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLODORUS">Apollodorus</a>. It is of white marble, and surrounded by other masterpieces of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, some of which are said to be the works of Praxiteles and other Greek masters. In the same room are many valuable curiosities, besides a collection of admirable pictures by the best masters. There are various other rooms, whose contents are indicated by the names they bear; as, the Cabinet of Arts, of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, of Medals, of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORCELAIN">Porcelain</a>, of Antiquities; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SALOON">Saloon</a> of the Hermaphrodite, so called from a statue which divides the admiration of the amateurs with that in the Borghese villa at Rome, though the excellence of the execution is disgraced by the vulgarity of the subject; and the Gallery of Portraits, which contains the portraits of the most eminent painters (all excelled by themselves) who have flourished in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> during the three last centuries. Our limits <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> not admit of a detail of the hundredth part of the curiosities and buildings of Florence. We must not, however, omit mentioning the chapel of St Lorenzo, as being perhaps the finest and most expensive habitation that ever was reared for the dead; it is incrusted with precious stones, and adorned by the workmanship of the best modern sculptors. Mr Addison remarked, that this chapel advanced so very slowly, that it is not impossible that the family of Medicis may be extinct before their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a> place is finished. This has actually taken place: the Medici family is extinct, and the chapel remains still unfinished. Florence is a place of some strength, and contains an archbishop's see and an university. The number of inhabitants is calculated at 80,000. They boast of the improvements they have made in the Italian tongue, by means of their Academia della Crusca; and several other <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a> are now established at Florence. Though the Florentines affect great state, yet their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> and gentry drive a retail trade in wine, which they sell from their cellar windows, and sometimes they even hang out a broken flask, as a sign where it may be bought. They <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a>, besides wine and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver stuffs.
