The Jews are not held in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of odium, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> subjected to the same humiliating distinctions here, as in most other cities of Europe; and it is said that some of the richest merchants are of that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. As to the manners and amusements of the inhabitants, Dr Moore informs us, that besides the conversations, which they have here as in other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of Italy, a number of the nobility meet every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> called the Casino. This <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> is pretty much on the same footing with the clubs in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. The members are elected by ballot. They meet at no particular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, but go at any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that is convenient. They play at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILLIARDS">billiards</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CARDS">cards</a>, and other games, or continue conversing the whole evening, as they think proper. They are served with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a>, coffee, lemonade, ices, or what other refreshments they choose; and each person pays for what he calls for. There is one material <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between this and the English clubs, that women as well as men are members. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of both sexes behave with more frankness and familiarity to strangers as well as to each other, than is customary in public assemblies in other parts of Italy. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">opera</a> is a place where the people of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> pay and receive visits, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> as freely as at the Casino above mentioned. This occasions a continual passing and repassing to and from the boxes, except in those where there is a party of cards formed; it is then looked on as a piece of ill manners to disturb the players. From this it may be guessed, that here, as in some other towns in Italy, little <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> is paid to the music by the company in the boxes, except at a new opera, or during some favourite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. But the dancers command a general attention: as soon as they begin, conversation ceases; even the card-players lay <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> their cards, and fix their eyes on the ballette. Yet the excellence of Italian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a> seems to consist in feats of strength, and a kind of jerking agility, more than in graceful movement. There is a continual contest among the performers, who shall <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> highest. You see here none of the sprightly alluring gaiety of the French comic dancers, or of the graceful attitudes and smooth flowing motions of the performers in the serious opera at Paris. It is surprising that a people of such taste and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> as the Italians, should prefer a parcel of athletic jumpers to elegant dancers. On the evenings on which there is no opera, it is usual for the genteel company to drive to a public walk immediately without the city, where they remain till it begins to grow duskish. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12. 24. N. Lat. 43. 34. Florence, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> piece of English gold <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-COIN">coin</a>. Every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of standard gold was to be coined into 50 Florences, to be current at six shillings each; all which made in tail 15 pounds; or into a proportionate number of half Florences, or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> pieces, by indenture of the mint: 18 Edw. III. Florentia, in Ancient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Etruria, on the Arno; of great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> in Sylla's wars. Now called Firenze or Fiorenza by the Italians; Florence in English. E. Long. 11. Lat. 43. 30. Florentine marble. See Citadinesca. Florescentia (from floresco, "to flourish or bloom"); the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of flowering, which Linnæus and the sexualists compare to the act of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> in animals; as the ripening of the fruit in their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> resembles the birth. See Flower. Florid style, is that too much enriched with figures and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FLORIDA">Florida</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, bounded on the south by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, on the north by <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALABAMA">Alabama</a>, on the east by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and on the west by Alabama. It was first discovered, in 1497, by Sebastian Cabot, a Venetian, then in the English <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>; whence a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was claimed by the kings of England; and this province, as well as Georgia, was included in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> granted by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. to Carolina. Florida. In 1512, however, Florida was more fully discovered by Ponce de Leon, an able Spanish navigator, but who undertook his voyage from the most absurd motives that can be well imagined.—The Indians of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CARIBBEE_ISLANDS">Caribbee <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> had among them a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>, that somewhere on the continent there was a fountain whose waters had the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of restoring youth to all old men who tasted them. Ponce de Leon, who set out with this extravagant view as well as others, re-discovered Florida; but returned to the place from whence he came, visibly more advanced in years than when he set out. For some time this country was neglected by the Spaniards, and some Frenchmen settled in it: But by orders of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> II. of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, a force was fitted out; the French intrenchments were forced, and most of the people killed. The prisoners were hanged on trees; with this inscription, "Not as Frenchmen, but as Heretics." This cruelty was soon after revenged by Dominie de Gourgues, a skilful and intrepid seaman of Gascony, an enemy to the Spaniards, and passionately fond of hazardous expeditions and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>. He sold his estate; built some ships; and with a select band of adventurers like himself embarked for Florida. He drove the Spaniards from all their posts with incredible valour and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>; defeated them in every encounter; and by way of retaliation, hung the prisoners on trees, with this inscription, "Not as Spaniards, but as Assassins." This expedition was attended with no other consequences; Gourgues blew up the forts he had taken, and returned home, where no notice was taken of him. It was conquered in 1539 by the Spaniards under Ferdinand de Soto, not without a great deal of bloodshed; as the natives were very warlike and made a vigorous resistance. The settlement, however, was not fully established till the year 1565; when the town of St Augustine, the capital of the colony while it remained in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Spaniards, was founded. In 1586, this place was taken and pillaged by Sir Francis Drake. It met with the same fate in 1665, being taken and plundered by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Davis and a body of bucaniers. In 1702, an attempt was made upon it by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> More, governor of Carolina. He set out with 300 English and 700 Indians; and having reached St Augustine, he besieged it for three months; at the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of which, the Spaniards having sent some ships to the relief of the place, he was obliged to retire. In 1740 another attempt was made by General Oglethorpe; but he being outwitted by the Spanish governor, was forced to raise the siege with loss; and Florida continued in the hands of the Spaniards till the year 1763, when it was ceded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> to Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>.—During the American <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, which terminated in 1783, it was again reduced by his Catholic majesty, and it remained subject to Spain till 1818, when General Jackson alleging that support had been given by the Spaniards to some hostile <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> tribes, seized Pensacola and St Marks, the only fortified posts in the country except St Augustine. The province was since ceded by treaty to the United States, and the treaty after much delay has at length been ratified (1821.) Florida is about 400 miles in length, from north to south, and occupies an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of about 50,000 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. The country is in general flat, and without hills. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is good, but overrun with pines and brushwood. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is considered better than that of the neighbouring state of Georgia. The whole white inhabitants and slaves probably do not exceed 12,000 or 15,000. See Florida, Supplement.

FLORILEGIUM

Pages 738-738

Florilege, a name the Latins have given to what the Greeks call anthologiae, anthology; viz. a collection of choice pieces, containing the finest and brightest things in their kind. Florilege, is also particularly used for a kind of breviary, in the Eastern <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, compiled by Arcadius, for the conveniency of the Greek priests and monks, who cannot carry with them, in their travels and pilgrimages, all the volumes wherein their office is dispersed. The florilegium contains the general rubrics, psalter, canticles, the horologium, and the office of the feriae, &c.

FLORIN

Pages 738-738

is sometimes used for a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, and sometimes for a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> of account. Florin, as a coin, is of different values, according to the different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> and different countries where it is struck. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> florins are most of them of a very coarse alloy, some of them not exceeding thirteen <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fourteen carats, and none of them seventeen and a half. See Money <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">Table</a>. Florin, as a money of account, is used by the Italian, Dutch, and German <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANKERS">bankers</a>, but admits of divisions in different places. Ibid.

FLORINIANS

Pages 738-738
or Floriani, a sect of heretics, of the second century, denominated from its author Florinus, or Florianus, a priest of the Roman church, deposed along with Blastus for his errors. Florianus had been a disciple of St Polycarp, along with Irenaeus. He made God the author of evil; or rather asserted, that the things forbidden by God are not evil, but of his own appointing. In which he followed the errors of Valentinius, and joined himself with the Carpocratiens. They had also other names given them. Philastrius says, they were the same with the Carpophorians. He adds that they were also called soldiers, milites, quia de militariibus fuerant. St Irenaeus calls them Gnostics; St Epiphanius Philionites; and Theodoret, Barbarites, on account of the impurities of their lives. Others call them Zaccheans; others Coddians, &c. though for what particular reasons, it is not easy to say, nor perhaps would be worth while to inquire.

FLORIS

Pages 738-738

Francis, an eminent historical painter, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a> in 1520. He followed the profession of a statuary till he was twenty years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>; when preferring <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, he entered the school of Lambert Lombard, whose manner he imitated very perfectly. He afterwards went to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and completed his studies from the most eminent masters. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> progress he made in historical painting, at his return procured him much employment; and his countrymen complimented him with the flattering appellation of the Flemish Raphael. He got much <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and might have rendered his acquaintance more worthy of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the great, had he not debased himself by frequent <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRUNKENNESS">drunkenness</a>. He died in 1570, aged 50.

FLORIST

Pages 738-739

a person curious <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> skilled in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>; their kinds, names, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, culture, &c. It is also applied to an author who writes what is called the flora of any particular <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, that is, a catalogue of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> and trees which are found spontaneously growing there.

FLORUS

Pages 739-739

LUCIUS ANNÆUS**, a Latin historian, of the same family with Seneca and Lucan. He flourished in the reigns of Trajan and Adrian; and wrote an abridgement of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMAN_HISTORY">Roman <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, of which there have been many editions. It is composed in a florid and poetical style; and is rather a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> on many of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> actions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, than a faithful and correct recital of their history. He also wrote <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, and entered the lists against the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Adrian, who satirically reproached him with frequenting taverns and places of dissipation.

FLORY

Pages 739-739

FLOWERY, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Fleury**, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> that has <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> at the end circumflex and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>; different from the potence, in as much as the latter stretches out more like that which is called patee.

FLOTA

Pages 739-739
or Flotta, fleet**: a name the Spaniards give particularly to the ships which they send annually from Cadiz to the port of Vera Cruz, to fetch thence the merchandises gathered in Mexico for Spain. It consists of the captains, admiral, and patch, or pinace, which go on the king's account; and about 16 ships, from 400 to 1000 tons, belonging to particular persons. They set out from Cadiz about the month of August, and are 18 or 20 months before they return. Those sent to fetch the commodities prepared in Peru are called galleons. The name flotilla is given to a number of ships which get before the rest in their return, and give information of the departure and cargo of the flota and galleons.

FLOTSON

Pages 739-739
or Flotsom**, goods that by shipwreck are lost, and floating upon the sea; which, with jetson and lagan, are generally given to the lord admiral: but this is the case only where the owners of such goods are not known. And here it is to be observed that jetson signifies any thing that is cast out of a ship when in danger, and afterwards is beat on the shore by the water, notwithstanding which the ship perishes. Lagan is where heavy goods are thrown overboard, before the wreck of the ship, and sink to the bottom of the sea.

FLOUNDER

Pages 739-739

FLUKE, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> BUT.** See Pleuronectes, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Flounders may be fished for all <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, either in a swift stream, or in the still deep <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; but best in the stream, in the months of April, May, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>: the most proper baits are all sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>, wasps, and gentles.

FLOUR

Pages 739-739

the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> of wheat-corn, finely ground and sifted. See Meal. The grain itself is not only subject to be eaten by insects in that state; but, when ground into flour, it gives birth to another <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of destroyers, who eat it unmercifully, and increase so fast in it, that it is not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before they wholly destroy the substance. The finest flour is most liable to breed these, especially when <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STALE">stale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ill prepared. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it be examined in a good <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be observed to be in continual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, and on a nicer inspection there will be found in it a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of little animals of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the flour, and very nimble. If a little of this flour is laid on the plate of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>, the insects are very distinctly seen in great numbers, very brisk and lively, continually crawling over one another's backs, and playing a thousand antic tricks together; whether in diversion or in search of food, is not easy to be determined. These animals are of an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> and slender form; their heads are furnished with a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> or hollow tube, by means of which they take in their food, and their body is composed of several rings. They do vast mischief among magazines of flour laid up for armies and other public uses. When they have once taken possession of a parcel of this valuable commodity, it is impossible to drive them out; and they increase so fast, that the only method of preventing the total loss of the parcel is to make it up into <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> as soon as can be done. The way to prevent their breeding in the flour is to preserve it from damp: nothing gets more injury by being put up damp than flour; and yet nothing is more frequently put up so. It should be always carefully and thoroughly dried before it is put up, and the barrels also dried into which it is to be put; then, if they are placed in a room tolerably warm and dry, they will keep it well. Too dry a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> never does flour any hurt, though one too moist almost always spoils it. Flour, when carefully analyzed, is found to be composed of three very different substances. The first and most abundant is pure <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STARCH">starch</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> fecule, insoluble in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, but soluble in hot <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of mucous substances; which, when dissolved, form water glues. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is the gluten, most of whose properties have been described under the article Bread. The third is of a mild nature, perfectly soluble in cold water, of the nature of saccharine extractive mucous matters. It is susceptible of the spirituous <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a>, and is found but in small <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> in the flour of wheat. See Bread, Gluten, Starch, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">Sugar</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FLOWER

Pages 739-741

Flos**, among botanists and gardeners, the most beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of trees and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, containing the organs <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> parts of fructification. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">Flowers</a>, designed for medical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, should be plucked when they are moderately blown, and on a clear <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> before noon; for conserves, roses must be taken in the bud. Flowers, in antiquity. We find flowers in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> request at the entertainments of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, being provided by the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the feast, and brought in before the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> course; or, as some are of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, at the beginning of the entertainment. They not only adorned their heads, necks, and breasts, with flowers, but often bestrewed the beds whereon they lay, and all parts of the room with them. But the head was chiefly regarded. See Garland. Flowers were likewise used in the bedecking of tombs. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURIAL">Burial</a>. Eternal Flower. See Xeranthemum, Everlasting Flower. See Grapalium, Flower-Piece. See Poinciana, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">Sun</a>-Flower. See Helianthus, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SULTAN">Sultan</a>-Flower. See Cyanus, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRUMPET">Trumpet</a>-Flower. See Bignonia, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">Wind</a>-Flower. See <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ANEMONE">Anemone</a>, Flower-de-lis, or Flower-de-luce, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> representing the lily called the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of flowers, and the true hieroglyphic of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> majesty; but of late it is become more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, being borne in some coats one, in others three, in others five, and in some some or spread all over the escutcheon in great numbers. The arms of France are, three flowers-de-lis or, in a field azure. Flower-de-Luce. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRIS">Iris</a>. Botany Index. Flowers, in Heraldry. They are much used in coats of arms; and in general signify hope, or denote <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> frailty and momentary prosperity. Flowers, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>. By this name are generally understood bodies reduced into very fine parts, either spontaneously, or by some operation of art; but the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> is chiefly applied to volatile <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> substances, reduced into very fine parts, or into a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> by sublimation.—Some flowers are nothing else than the bodies themselves, which are sublimed entire, without suffering any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> or decomposition; and other flowers are some of the constituent parts of the body subjected to sublimation. Colours of Flowers. See the article <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">Colour</a> (of Plants.) Colours extracted from Flowers. See Colour-Making. Preserving of Flowers. The method of preserving flowers in their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> through the whole year has been much sought after by many people. Some have attempted it by gathering them when dry and not too much opened, and burying them in dry sand; but this, though it preserves their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> well, takes off from the liveliness of their colour. Muntingius prefers the following method to all others. Gather roses, or other flowers, when they are not yet thoroughly open, in the middle of a dry day; fill the vessel up to the top with them; and when full sprinkle them over with some good French wine, with a little <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> in it; then set them by in a cellar, tying <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the mouth of the pot. After this they may be taken out at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; and, on setting them in the sun, or within reach of the fire, they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> open as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> growing natural- ly; and not only the colour, but the smell also will be preserved. The flowers of plants are by much the most difficult parts of them to preserve in any tolerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of perfection; of which we have instances in all the collections of dried plants, or herbaria. In these the leaves, stalks, roots, and seeds of the plants, appear very well preserved; the strong texture of these parts making them always retain their natural form, and the colours in many <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> naturally remaining. But where these fade, the plant is little the worse for use as to the knowing the species by it. But it is very much otherwise in regard to flowers; these are naturally by much the most beautiful parts of the plants to which they belong; but they are so much injured in the common way of drying, that they not only lose, but change their colours one into another, by which means they give a handle to many errors; and they usually also wither up, so as to lose their very form and natural shape. The primrose and cowslip kinds are very eminent instances of the change of colours in the flowers of dried specimens; for those of this class of plants easily dry in their natural shape; but they lose their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, and, instead of it, acquire a fine green colour, much superior to that of the leaves in their most perfect state. The flowers of all the violet kind lose their beautiful blue, and become of a dead <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>; so that in dried specimens there is no <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the blue-flowered violet and the white-flowered kinds. Sir Robert Southwell has communicated to the world a method of drying plants, by which this defect is proposed to be in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> remedied, and all flowers preserved in their natural shape, and many in their natural colours.—For this purpose two plates of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> are to be prepared of the size of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> half-sheet of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, or larger, for particular occasions; these plates must be made so thick as not to be apt to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a>; and there must be a hole made near every corner for receiving a screw to fasten them <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> together. When these plates are prepared, lay in readiness several sheets of paper, and then gather the plants with their flowers when they are quite perfect. Let this be always done in the middle of a dry day; and then lay the plant and its flower on one of the sheets of paper doubled in half, spreading out all the leaves and petals as nicely as possible. If the stalk is thick, it must be pared or cut in half, so that it may <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> flat; and if it is woody, it may be peeled, and only the bark left. When the plant is thus expanded, lay round about it some loose leaves and petals of the flower, which may serve to complete any part that is deficient. When all is thus prepared, lay several sheets of paper over the plant, and as many under it; then put the whole between the iron plates, laying the papers smoothly on one, and laying the other evenly over them; screw them close, and put them into an oven after the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> is drawn, and let them lie there two hours. After that, make a mixture of equal parts of aquafortis and common brandy; shake these well together, and when the flowers are taken out of the pressure of the plates, rub them lightly over with a camel's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> dipped in this liquor; then lay them upon fresh <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> paper, and covering them with some other sheets, press them between this and other papers with a handkerchief till Flowers, the wet of these liquors is dried wholly away. When flowering, the plant is thus far prepared, take the bulk of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a>- meg of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a> dragon; put this into a pint of fair <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, and let it stand 24 hours; it will in this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> be wholly dissolved; then dip a fine hair pencil in this liquor, and with it daub over the back sides of the leaves, and lay them carefully down on half a sheet of white paper fairly expanded, and press them down with some more papers over these. When the gum- water is fixed, let the presser and papers be removed, and the whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is finished. The leaves retain their verdure in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, and the flowers usually keep their natural colours. Some care, however, must be taken, that the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the oven be not too great. When the flowers are thick and bulky, some art may be used to pare off their backs, and dispose the petals in a due order; and after this, if any of them are wanting, their places may be supplied with some of the supernumerary ones dried on purpose; and if any of them are only faded, it will be prudent to take them away, and lay down others in their stead; the leaves may be also disposed and mended in the same manner. Another method of preserving both flowers and fruit found throughout the whole year is also given by the same author. Take <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>, one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a>; Armenian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLE">bole</a>, two pounds; clean common sand, three pounds; mix all well together. Then gather fruit of any kind that is not fully ripe, with the stalk to each; put these in, one by one, into a wide-mouthed glass, laying them in good order. Tie over the top with an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>- cloth, and carry them into a dry cellar, and set the whole upon a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> of the prepared <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of four inches thick in a box. Fill up the remainder of the box with the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>; and let it be four inches thick, all over the top of the glass, and all round its sides. Flowers are to be preserved in the same sort of glasses, and in the same manner; and they may be taken up after a whole year as plump and fair as when they were buried. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">Artificial</a> Flowers of the Chinese. See TONG-

FLOWERS

Pages 741-743

Flowers, in the animal economy, denote women's monthly purgations <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> menses.—Nicod derives the word in this <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, from fluere, q. d. flows. Others <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> have the name occasioned hence, that women do not conceive till they have had their flowers; so that these are a sort of forerunners of their fruit. Flowers, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, are figures or ornaments of discourse, by the Latins called florescui. FLOWERING of Bulbous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">Plants</a>. These plants will grow and flower in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> alone, without any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and make a very elegant appearance. We daily see this practised in single roots; but there is a method of doing it with several roots in the same vessel. Take a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> small garden pot; stop the hole at the bot- tom with a cork, and lute in the cork with putty that no water can get through; then fit a board to the top of the pot, and bore six or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> holes in it at equal distances, to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the bulbs in; and as many smaller ones nearer them, to receive sticks, which will serve to tie up the flowers. Then fill up the pot with water to the board; and place tulips, jonquils, narcissuses, and the like plants in the root upon the holes, so that the bottom of the roots may touch the water: thus will they all flower early in the season, and be much more beautiful than any pot of gathered flowers, and will last many weeks in their full perfection. After the season of flowering is over, the roots will gradually shrink through the holes of the board, and get loose in- to the water: but, instead of being spoiled there, they will soon increase in size; so that they cannot return through the holes, and will produce several offsets. It is <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to try from this the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of keeping the roots under water during the whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of their blowing; and in this way they have been found to succeed very well, and flower even stronger and more beautifully than when in the ground. They may thus, also, with proper care, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> in the room, be kept flowering from before Christmas till <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> or April. It is not easy, in this last manner, to manage the keeping the boards under water, for which reason it is better to procure some sheet-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> of about four pounds to the foot, and cut this to the size of the mouth of the pot. In this there should be bored holes for the bulbs, and other holes for the sticks: and, in order to keep the sticks quite firm, it is pro- per to have another plate of lead shaped to the bottom of the pot, with holes in it, answering to those of the upper plate made for the sticks. The sticks will by this means be always kept perfectly steady; and the roots, being kept under water by the upper plate of lead, will flower in the most vigorous and beautiful manner imaginable. Some have thought of adding to the virtues of the water by putting in nitre in small quantities, and others have added earth and sand at the bottom; but it has always been found to succeed better without any addition. It may be more agreeable to some to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> glass jars in this last method with the leads, instead of earthen pots. The bulbs succeed full as well in these; and there is this advantage, that the progress of the roots is seen all the while, and they are managed better as to the supply of water. By repeated experiments in this way on dried bulbs, and on those taken fresh out of the ground, the former have been found to succeed the best. For those taken fresh out of the ground being full of moisture, will not so soon, upon changing their element, be nourished fully by a new one; and the fibres which they had struck in the ground, always rot when put into the wa- ter, and new ones must be formed in their places; so that it requires more time for them to come to flower- ing. The bulbs themselves will not rot in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>- ner; but they will never be so strong as those which were put into the water dry, which gradually fill themselves with moisture from it, and regularly plump up. The best method of managing the whole <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is this: Place the bulbs at first only on the surface of the water; for thus they will strike out their fibres most strongly. When they have stood thus six weeks, pour in the water so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as to cover them entirely, and keep them thus till they have done flowering. Sometimes the roots will become mouldy in several parts while they stand above the water, and the clean- ing them of it is to no purpose; for it will eat and spread the farther, and frequently eat through two or three of their coats. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> they must be imme- diately covered with water; when the mould will be stopped, Flowering stopped, and the roots become <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, and flower as well as those which never had any such distemper. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the roots are suffered to remain in water all the year, they will not decay; but will flower again at their proper season, and that as vigorously as those which have been taken out and dried. The old fibres of those roots never rot till they are ready to push forth new ones. It is found by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, that the hyacinth, and many other plants, grow to a greater degree of perfection when thus in water than when in the ground. There is a peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of hyacinth called Keyser's <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JEWEL">jewel</a>; this never, or very rarely, produces seed-vessels in the common way of flowering in the ground; but it will often produce some pods when blown in water. Mr Miller has intimated, in the Philosophical Transactions, that bulbs set in glasses grow weaker, and should be renewed every other year: but it is found, that, when managed in this manner, and kept under water, at the time of taking them up, they are as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and some of them larger, than when planted; and if these be dried at a proper season, they will flower, year after year, as well as fresh ones. Ranunculus and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ANEMONE">anemone</a> roots have been found to shoot up their stalks very well in this way; but the flowers are usually blasted, which seems to arise from want of free <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. Pinks will flower very well in this manner; auriculas also may, with care, be brought to flower, but not strongly. Roses, jessamines, and honeysuckles, may also be made to flower this way, and will thrive and send out suckers; the best pieces to plant, are suckers cut off about three inches under ground, without any fibres. The succulent plants may also be raised this way; for instance, the opuntia or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> fig. If a fragment of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> of this plant be cut, and laid by to dry for a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> till it is an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> skin, as soon as it is put in this manner into water, it begins to plump up, and soon sends out <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> roots, and produces new leaves as quickly as it would do in the ground. This is the more singular in these sort of plants, because in their natural state in the ground, they cannot bear much water. This method of growing in water is not peculiar to the bulbous-rooted ones, but others may even be raised from seed by it. A bean or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEA">pea</a>, set in this manner, will grow up to its proper standard, and will flower and produce pods which will <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a> their seed. The smaller seeds may be also raised in this manner, by the help of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> to support them. No vegetable transplanted out of the earth into water will thrive kindly; but any plant, whether raised from the root or seed in water, may be transplanted to the earth, and will succeed very well. It may be possible, therefore, from this method of raising plants in water, to come at a better way than is usually practised of raising some roots in the earth which are subject to rot there; such as anemones, ranunculuses, and hyacinths. A <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BULB">bulb</a> dropped by chance upon the ground, will strike out both stronger and more numerous fibres than those which are planted in the usual way in the ground. On this principle, it may be proper to take out the earth of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> where the bulbs are to stand at the time of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> them, to such a depth as they are to be placed under it when set for flowering. The bulbs are then to be set in their flowering places, on the surface of this low ground; and to stand there till they have <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> out their fibres and their head: then the earth is to be added over them by degrees, till they are covered as high above the head as they are in the usual manner of planting them; thus they would be preserved from the danger of rotting; and their fibres would be much stronger, and consequently they would draw more nourishment, and flower better than in the common way. The common method of planting these roots renders them liable to be destroyed by either <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> of a wet or a dry season. In the first case, they immediately rot by the abundance of moisture they receive; and, in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, they become dry as a stick and mouldy, so that they are infallibly rotted by the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> that falls afterwards. The directions necessary to the success of the bulbs planted in water are these. When the leaden false bottoms are fixed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> tight within two or three inches of the bottom of the vessel (which is only designed to hold the sticks steady which are to support the leaves and stalks), then lay on the lead upon which the bulbs are to rest, placing the notched <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> opposite to that in the false bottom, as near as the sticks, when placed, will suffer it; then place the bulbs one in each hole, and fill up with water to the upper lead. The bottom of the bulb will then touch the water; and as the water diminishes in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, keep it supplied with more up to the same height for a month or six weeks; in which time the bulbs will have shot strong fibres. Then fill up the water about half an inch above the surface of the lead; and by degrees, as the fibres strengthen, and the plume shoots from the head, keep the water higher and higher, till at length the whole bulb is covered. The water is to be kept at this standard till the season for drying them returns. At the time of planting the bulbs, they must be carefully cleaned from any foulness at the bottom by scraping them with the point of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> till the sound part of the bulb appears; clear them likewise from any loose skins, and even take off their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> skin till they appear <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>; otherwise this brown skin will tinge the water, and the growth will not succeed so well. The notches in the side of each lead are intended to give easy passage to the water, that, if there should be any foulness or sediment in it, on shaking it a little it may all run through, and fresh water be put in its place. But this shifting the water need not be done more than once or twice in a winter, as there may be occasion from the foulness; and when this is done, the sides of the vessel should be cleaned with a painter's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>, and rinsed out again, and the bulbs themselves washed, by pouring water on them at a little distance. At any time when the outer skins of the bulbs dry, they are to be peeled off, that they may not occasion foulness in the water; and if any dust or foul <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> be at any time observed <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a> on the surface, the method is to fill up the pot or vessel to the rim, and let it run over: this will carry off that <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> foulness, and the water may afterwards be poured away to the proper standard. Bulbs of equal bigness should be planted together in the same pot, that they may all have the same benefit of the water. Narcissuses and hyacinths do well together; as also tulips and jonquils, and crocuses and snowdrops.

FLUDD

Pages 743-743

ROBERT, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and physician of some celebrity in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, was the son of Sir Thomas Fludd, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>; and was born at Milgate in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, in the year 1574. He received his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at St John's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and afterwards spent six years in travelling through <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. He acquired a strong <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the Rosicrucian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, which chiefly consisted of mysticism and jargon, and such as were admitted among them had certain secrets analogous to those of free masonry. On his return home, he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of M.D. settled in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and was chosen a fellow of the college of physicians. His piety was of an enthusiastic <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and the seeming depth of his knowledge procured him much admiration, and gave him a temporary fame. It is said that he employed a kind of unintelligible cant when speaking to his patients, which sometimes contributed to their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a>, as it operated on their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. He is chiefly known as a sectary in philosophy, and not as a physician. He blended the incomprehensible reveries of the Cabalists and Paracelsians, forming a new physical system replete with mystery and absurdity. He believed in two universal principles, the northern <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> condensing, and the southern or rarefying power. Innumerable geniuses he conceived to preside over these, and committed the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of diseases to legions of spirits collected from the four winds of heaven. In his estimation, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> subsisted between the macrocosm and the microcosm, or the world of nature and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. All his fancies and whims it is impossible to enumerate, yet they attracted the notice of the philosophers of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, being supported by mysterious gravity and the shadow of erudition. Even Kepler himself thought his extravagant jargon worthy of refutation, and Gassendi for this purpose wrote his Eramus Philosophiae Fluddiana. One of Fludd's performances, entitled Nexus utriusque Cosmi, is illustrated by some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> of a very singular and extraordinary nature.

INTERPOLATION. Few disquisitions in modern mathematics have greater practical utility than those concerning the extension and interpolation of the terms of numerical progressions. But the modes of solution generally proposed, however ingenious and refined, are often too complex for ordinary purposes. We therefore avail ourselves of this opportunity to point out a procedure of extreme simplicity and most ready application. It will embrace any system of numbers, but seems peculiarly fitted for the computation of logarithms. Napier first published, in 1614, his canon Mirificus Logarithmorum, comprised in a very thin and small quarto volume, exhibiting, as far as seven places, the logarithms only of the sines and tangents to every minute of the quadrant; those of the ordinary numbers being left to be deduced from the nearest sines or tangents. In the summer following, Briggs, then Professor of Geometry in Gresham College at London, who was enchanted by that noble discovery, paid a visit to its illustrious author at Merchiston, in the vicinity of Edinburgh. During an agreeable stay of a month, it was concerted between them, to change the natural system of logarithms into another of a more artificial form, but adapted to our denary scale of notation, the labour of the calculation, however, being devolved upon Briggs, as younger and enjoying robust health. Next season, Briggs performed a second journey to Edinburgh, and showed to Napier a table which he had computed of the new logarithms for the first chilid or thousand of the series of natural numbers. But the great inventor was now fast declining in years, and expired on the 3rd of April 1618. Briggs employing most skilfully all the abbreviations which ingenuity could devise, prosecuted his most arduous task with such vigour and active perseverance, as to compute, in the space of seven years, to fourteen places of figures, not only the logarithms of... the sines and tangents of every degree and centesimal minute of the quadrant, but also the logarithms of thirty chilids of numbers. These tables were printed, in 1624, in a folio volume, entitled *Arithmetica Logarithmica*. In his anxiety, however, to bring out this stupendous work, Briggs contented himself with calculating the logarithms from unit to 20,000, and from 90,000 to 100,000, leaving the computation of the seventy intervening chilids to be afterwards supplied. The very ingenious author annexed a full explanation of his mode of framing the tables, grounded chiefly on the consideration of differences, and he thus traced the first steps of that important theory. But he likewise gave instructions for the reader filling up of the intermediate logarithms, abridging the toil of calculation no doubt, yet detailing a procedure sufficiently irksome and complicated. "To encourage some skilful persons to perform this task, he offered to furnish them with paper he had by him, ready prepared, and divided into columns proper for that purpose, as likewise to inform them at what part to begin, that they might not interfere one with another; and promised, when the whole was finished, to endeavour to procure a new edition of the work so completed." This slender boon seems not to have tempted the mathematicians in England. In Holland, however, Adrian Vlacq, chancing to meet two years afterwards with a copy of the work, and prompted only by his patriotic zeal, had the resolution to revise and compute the whole canon, reducing it to ten places of figures, which he printed in folio at Gouda, as early as 1628. The same able calculator, only five years afterwards, published, likewise in folio, at Gouda, a very extensive system of logarithmic sines and tangents, to every ten seconds of the quadrant, having restored the sexagesimal subdivision, which Briggs had partly changed into a centesimal one. These two volumes may be deemed a precious *thesaurus* of logarithms, from which succeeding compilers have drawn very liberally. They form the basis of the *Tables* published by Vega at Leipsic in 1794, which are esteemed the best and completest now extant. But though the *Tables* of Vlacq, carried only to ten places of figures, are sufficiently accurate for every ordinary purpose, and even for the most delicate calculations in astronomy, yet many persons have often regretted that the original system of Briggs was never completed. The celebrated Legendre has employed that table, imperfect as it is, in some of his most refined numerical investigations. It is well known that Mr Baron Masseres devoted a considerable portion of his time, and of his fortune, to the republication of the works of the early writers on logarithms. In the course of this extensive undertaking, he entertained some thoughts of giving a new edition of the *Arithmetica Logarithmica*, and expressed an earnest wish that the vacant chilids were filled up. To promote the liberal designs of the Baron, the Author of this Article was induced to bestow some reflection on the subject, and a very simple mode occurred to him, which would have reduced the labour of computing those logarithms to little more than the trouble of mere transcription. But the project of completing the canon was deferred for a time, and afterwards gradually forgotten. The method of interpolation then proposed seems, however, to deserve notice on account of its great simplicity, and its ready application, not only to the immediate object, but to other questions of a similar nature. We shall, therefore, now state the principle, and illustrate its application by a few examples. The square root of the quantity $a^2 + 1$ is evidently expressed by the continued fraction $\frac{a+1}{2a}$. If two terms only of the fractional part be taken, the expression will become $\sqrt{a^2 + 1} = \frac{4a^2 + 3a}{4a^2 + 1}$, and consequently $\sqrt{\left(\frac{a^2 + 1}{a^2}\right)}$ or $\sqrt{\left(\frac{2b^2 + 2}{2b^2}\right)} = \frac{4a^2 + 3}{4a^2 + 1}$, a very near approximation. Put $b = 2a$, and by substitution $\sqrt{\left(\frac{b+2}{b}\right)} = \frac{2b+3}{2b+1}$; therefore $$\frac{1}{2} \log_b \frac{b+2}{b} = \log_b \frac{2b+3}{2b+1}.$$ Hence half the alternate differences of the logarithms of the series $b, b+1, b+2, \ldots$ added to the logarithm of $2b+1$, must give the logarithm of $2b+3$. By this simple process then, any table of logarithms is carried to double its actual extent through all the odd numbers, those of the even ones being found by the mere addition of the logarithm of 2. To find the limits of approximation, let three terms of the fractional series be taken, and $\sqrt{\left(\frac{a^2 + 1}{a^2}\right)} = \frac{8a^4 + 8a^2 + 1}{8a^4 + 4a^2}$, or $\sqrt{\left(\frac{b+2}{b}\right)} = \frac{2b^3 + 4b^2 + 6b + 1}{2b^3 + 10b^2 + 10b + 1}$. Whence $$\frac{1}{2} \log_b \frac{b+2}{b} = \frac{2b+3}{2b+1} \left(1 + \frac{1}{(2b+3)(2b+1)b}\right).$$ and, therefore, since this last quantity exceeds unit only by a very minute difference, $\frac{1}{2} \log_b \frac{b+2}{b} = \log_b \frac{2b+3}{2b+1} + \frac{M}{(2b+3)(2b+1)b}$, where $M$ denotes the modulus of the system. If the number $2b+3$ or $2b+1$ be expressed by $N$, this small correction will amount but to $\frac{M}{N^3}$ or $\frac{2M}{N^3}$. Consequently $\log_b \frac{2b+3}{2b+1} = \frac{1}{2} \log_b \frac{b+2}{b} - \frac{2M}{N^3}$. It may hence be computed, that the correction on the first approximation will only reach unit in the last figure for the numbers un- The corrections needed in Briggs's Tables will therefore correspond to these limits, \[ \begin{array}{ccc} 85150 & -2 & 23151 \\ 90706 & -3 & 22143 \\ 27899 & -4 & 21290 \\ 25898 & -5 & 20557 \\ 24372 & -6 & 19913 \end{array} \] Suppose it were required to find the logarithms of the odd numbers above 300, to seven places of decimals. Assuming the logarithms of the series of half those numbers, let their alternate differences be taken, and these again bisected. | Numbers | Logarithms | |---------|------------| | 150 | 2.1760913 | | 151 | 2.1789769 | | 152 | 2.1818436 | | 153 | 2.1846914 | | 154 | 2.1875297 | | 155 | 2.1903317 | | Alternate Differences | Their Halves | |-----------------------|--------------| | 57523 | 28761 | | 57145 | 28572 | | 56771 | 28386 | | 56403 | 28201 | Hence the logarithms of the doubles are formed by the mere addition of these halves. | Numbers | Logarithms | |---------|------------| | 301 | 2.4785665 | | | 28761 | | 303 | 2.4814426 | | | 28572 | | 305 | 2.4842998 | | | 28386 | | 307 | 2.4871384 | | | 28201 | | 309 | 2.4899585 | In this manner, the operation may be continued; but, to prevent any accumulation of errors, the logarithms of the composite numbers should serve as standards, being formed by the addition of the logarithms of their several factors. The logarithms of the intermediate even numbers, 302, 304, 306, 308, and 310, are easily determined by adding .3010300 to the logarithms of 151, 152, 153, 154, and 155. To extend the process a little farther, let Vlacq's logarithms be computed for the numbers above 4000. | Numbers | Logarithms | |---------|------------| | 2000 | 3.3010299957 | | 2001 | 3.3012470886 | | 2002 | 3.3014640731 | | 2003 | 3.3016809493 | | 2004 | 3.3018977172 | | 2005 | 3.3021143770 | | Alternate Differences | Their Halves | |-----------------------|--------------| | 4340774 | 2170387 | | 4338607 | 2169303 | | 4336441 | 2168220 | | 4334277 | 2167139 | Whence are derived, | Numbers | Logarithms | |---------|------------| | 4001 | 3.8021885514 | | | 2170387 | | 4003 | 3.6023855901 | | | 2169303 | | 4005 | 3.6026025204 | | | 2168220 | | 4007 | 3.6028193424 | | | 2167139 | | 4009 | 3.6030360563 | Again, to compute the logarithms in Briggs's Canon. | Numbers | Logarithms | |---------|------------| | 9995 | 3.99978279845419 | | | 4344682707 | | 9996 | 3.99982624745441 | | | 4344248108 | | 9998 | 3.999913241658 | | | 4343813596 | | 10000 | 4.00000000000000 | | | 4343379171 | The additive parts here consist of those differences diminished by 11 and the last one by 10, since the numbers now approach to the limit 20557. The first mode of interpolating, thus derived from the nature of logarithms, and so commodious for their computation, might likewise be deduced from general considerations. Let \(A, B, C, D, E, \ldots\) represent any series of numbers. If they advance regularly and slowly, their first differences, \(B-A, C-B, D-C, E-D, \ldots\) may be viewed as constituting an arithmetical progression. Wherefore the sum of the extremes will be equal to that of the mean terms, or \((E-D) + (B-A) = (D-C) + (C-B)\), that is, \(E-A = 2D-2B\), and therefore \(D-B = \frac{E-A}{2}\), whence \(D = B + \frac{E-A}{2}\). Applying this to the logarithms of eight places of figures, let \(A, B, C, D, E, \ldots\) represent... the logarithms of 500, 501, 502, 503, 504, &c., then \[ \log_5 503 = \log_5 501 + \frac{\log_5 504 - \log_5 500}{2} = \log_5 501 \] \[ + \frac{\log_5 252 - \log_5 250}{2} = 2.69983773 + \frac{1}{2}(2.40140054 \] \[-2.59794001) = 2.79156799; \text{ the halves of the alternate differences of the logarithms of 250, 251, 252, 253, &c. being thus taken, as before, to compose by their additions the logarithms of the odd numbers 503, 505, 507, &c.}\] But since \(E-A=2D-2B\), it follows that \(E=A+2(D-B)\). Therefore, in any series, the fifth term will be found nearly, by adding to the first term the double the difference between the second and fourth terms. In this way the tables of natural sines, tangents, and secants, could easily be framed. Thus, the logarithmic sines of the successive arcs, 50°, 50° 1', 50° 2', and 50° 3' being from Vlacq's Tables, to find the logarithmic sine of 50° 4'. | Arcs | Logarithmic Sines | |------|------------------| | 50° 0' | 9.8842539665 | | 1' | 9.8843599396 | | 2' | 9.8844658502 | | 3' | 9.8845716981 | | 4' | 9.8846774835 | Here, passing over the middle term, the difference between the logarithmic sines of 50° 1' and of 50° 3' is doubled, and added to that of 50°, to form the logarithmic sine of 50° 4'. But a nearer approximation may be obtained, by supposing the second differences of any series to form the arithmetical progression. The sum of the extreme terms \(C-2B+A\) and \(F-2E+D\) would, therefore, be equal to the sum of the mean terms \(D-2C+B\) and \(E-2D+C\); whence \(F-A=3B+3E-2C-2D\), or \(F=A+3(B+E)-2(C+D)\). Thus, the natural sines of the successive arcs 30, 31, 32, 34, and 35 degrees may be easily computed to seven places of figures. | Arcs | Sines | |------|-------| | 30° | .5000000 | | 31° | .5150381 | | 32° | .5299193 | | 33° | .5446390 | | 34° | .5592929 | | 35° | .5735764 | The sines of 31° and of 34° are here added together, and the sum tripled, and from this amount is taken the double of the sum of the sines of 31° and of 33°; the sine of 30° being subtracted from that remainder, leaves finally the sine of 35°. Employing the same number of terms of the series, a still closer approximation may be discovered, by considering the third differences only as uniformly progressive. Wherefore the extreme differences \(D-3C+3B-A\) and \(F-3E+3D-C\) will be together equal to double the middle one, \(E-3D+3C-B\), and consequently \(F-A=5E-10D+10C-5B\), or \(F=A+5(E-B)-10(D-C)\). Hence the logarithms even of low numbers may be computed exact to eight decimal places. Thus, the logarithms of 150, 151, 152, 153, and 154, being given, that of 155 is found by this process: | Numbers | Logarithms | |---------|------------| | 150 | 2.17609126 | | 151 | 2.17897695 | | 152 | 2.18189359 | | 153 | 2.18469143 | | 154 | 2.18752072 | | 155 | 2.19033170 | The difference between the logarithms of 151 and 154 is here multiplied by 5, and the difference of the logarithms of 152 and 153 is multiplied by 10; and the excess of the former product above the latter being added to the logarithm of 150, gives the logarithm of 155. It would obviously be preferable, however, to employ the formula in a modified form for interpolation merely. Hence \(D=C+\frac{1}{2}(E-B)+A-F\). If six terms of the series were given, the seventh could be found to a high degree of accuracy. The sum of the extremes of the progressive third differences being now assumed equal to that of the means, we have \(D-3C+3B-A+G-3F+3E-D=E-3D+3C-B+F-3E+3D-C\), and by reduction \(G-A=4F-5E-5C-4B\), whence \(G=A+4(F-B)-5(E-C)\). It seems unnecessary to subjoin any farther illustrations; but the very simple methods of interpolation now proposed, might be applied with great facility and advantage in various physical researches. In this way, much light may be thrown upon the resistance of ss="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids, and upon the force, the density, and the component heat of steam, at different temperatures. ### POPULATION England. 11,261,437; in Wales it was 717,438; and in Scotland it was 9,009,456; as then enumerated, and as is shown in these Summaries, by the numbers of Males and Females. ### THE METROPOLIS. The rapid increase of the population in the suburbs, since the beginning of the last century, shows how rapidly the metropolis increases in extent, although its population has not increased so fast as that of the nation at large. In 1700, the metropolis contained almost an eighth part of the inhabitants of England and Wales; in 1750 and in 1801, about a tenth part; but in 1811 and at present, only about a twelfth part. Objections might be made to the propriety of the limits of the metropolis as herein assumed, and it may therefore be right to add, that the population of all the parishes, of which the churches are situate within eight miles rectilinear around St Paul's Cathedral (including the before mentioned addition of one twenty-fifth part), would, in 1801, have amounted to 1,031,500—in 1811, to 1,220,200—and in 1821, to no less than 1,481,500; without including the parish of Woolwich, which contains 17,008 additional. N. B. The population ascribed to the city of Paris is comprised within a district of full such an extent. The arrivals of coasting vessels in the port of London may be estimated to have been about 5500, in the year 1700;—6400, in the year 1750;—10,400, in 1801;—13,500, in 1811; and at about 17,000 per annum, since the year 1817. This produces a constant, though fluctuating accession to the population, to a larger amount than elsewhere, and consequently, a twenty-fifth, instead of a fiftieth part, is to be added to form a comparison with the Parish Register Returns in the General Abstract. With this addition, the metropolis, in the year 1801, contained about 900,000;—in 1811, about 1,050,000;—and in 1821, about 1,274,800 inhabitants. FLUID

Pages 743-744

an appellation given to all bodies whose particles cavity yield to the least partial pressure, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> force impressed. For the Laws and Properties of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">Fluids</a>, see <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HYDRODYNAMICS">Hydrodynamics</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; and Fluids, ELEVATION OF, in the Supplement. There are various kinds of animalcules to be discerned in different fluids by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>. Of many remarkable kinds of these, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> is given under the article ANIMALCULE. All of these little creatures are easily destroyed by separating them from their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> element. Naturalists have even fallen upon shorter methods. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> point, dipped in spirit of vitriol, and then immersed into a drop of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, readily kills all the animalcules; which, though before frisking about with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> liveliness and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>, no sooner come within the influence of the acid particles, than they spread themselves, and tumble <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to all appearance dead. The like may be done by a solution of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>; only with this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, that, by the latter application, they seem to grow vertiginous, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> round and round till they <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> down. Tincture of salt of tartar, used in the same manner, kills them still more readily; yet not so, but there <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be apparent marks of their first being sick and convulsed. Inks destroy them as fast as spirit of vitriol, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> blood produces the same effect. Urine, sack, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> all destroy them, though not so fast; besides, that there is some diversity in their figures and appearances, as they receive their deaths from this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a> or that. The point of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PIN">pin</a> dipped in spittle, presently killed all the kinds of animalcules in paddle water, as Mr Harris supposes it will other animalcules of this kind. All who are acquainted with microscopic observations, know very well, that in water, in which the best glasses can discover no particle of animated <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, after a few grains of pepper, or a fragment of a plant of almost any kind, has been some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in it, animals full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> are produced; and those in such numbers, as to equal the fluid itself in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>.—When we see a numerous brood of young fishes in a pond, we make no doubt of their having owed their origin to the spawn, that is, to the eggs of the parents of the same <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. What are we then to think of these? <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> we will consider the progress of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in the insect tribes in general, and especially in such of them as are most analogous to these, we shall find it less difficult to give an account of their origin than might have been imagined. A small quantity of water taken from any ditch in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> months, is found to be full of little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>, seeming in nothing so much as in size to differ from the microscopic animalcules. Nay, water, without these, exposed in open vessels to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, will be always found to abound with multitudes of them, visible to the naked eye, and full of life and motion. These we know, by their future changes, are the fly worms of the different species of gnats, and multitudes of other fly species; and we can easily determine, that they have owed their origin only to the eggs of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> fly there deposited. Nay, a closer observation will at any time give ocular <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of this; as the flies may be seen laying their eggs there, and the eggs may be followed through all their changes to the fly again. Why then are we to doubt but that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> abounds with other flies and animalcules as minute as the worms in those fluids; and that these last are only the fly worms of the former, which, after a proper time spent in that state, will suffer changes like those of the larger kinds, and become flies like those to whose eggs they owed their origin? Vid. Reaumur, Hist. Insect. vol. iv. p. 431. The differently medicated liquors made by infusions of different <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, afford a proper matter for the worms of different species of these small flies: and there is no reason to doubt, but that among these some are viviparous, others oviparous; and to this may be, in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, owing the different time taken up for the production of these insects in different fluids. Those which are a proper matter for the worms of the viviparous fly, may be soonest found full of them; as, probably the liquor is no sooner in a state to afford them proper nourishment, than their parents <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> them there; whereas those produced from the eggs of the little oviparous flies, must, after the liquor is in a proper state, and they are deposited in it in the form of eggs, have a proper time to be hatched, before they can appear alive. It is easy to prove, that the animals we find in these vegetable infusions were brought thither from elsewhere. It is not less easy to prove, that they could not be in the matter infused any more than in the water in which it is infused. Notwithstanding the fabulous accounts of salamanders, it is now well known, that no animal, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> or small, can bear the force of fire for any considerable time; and, by parity of reason, we are not to believe, that any insect, or embryo insect, in any state, can bear the heat of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> water for many minutes. To proceed to inquiries on this foundation: If several tubes be filled with water, with a small quantity of vegetable matter, such as pepper, oak bark, truffles, &c., in which, after a time, insects will be discovered by the microscope; and other like tubes be filled with simple water boiled, with water and pepper boiled together, and with water with the two other ingredients all separately boiled in it; when all these liquors come to a proper time for the observation of the microscope, all, as well those which have been boiled as those which have not, will be found equally to abound with insects, and those of the same kind, in infusions of the same kind, whether boiled or not boiled. Those in the infusions which had sustained a heat capable of destroying animal life, must therefore not have subsisted either in the water or in the matters put into it, but must have been brought thither after the boiling; and it seems by no way so probable, as by means of some little winged inhabitants of the air depositing their eggs or worms in these fluids. On this it is natural to ask, how it comes to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, that while we see myriads of the progeny of these winged insects in water, we never see themselves? The answer is equally easy, viz. because we can always place a drop of this water immediately before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a> of the microscope, and keep it there while we are at leisure to examine its contents; but that is not the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with regard to the air inhabited by the parent flies of these worms, which is an immense <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> in proportion to the water proper for nourishing these worms; and consequently, while the latter are clustered together in heaps, the former may be dispersed and scattered. Nor do we want instances of this, even in insects of a larger kind. In many of our gardens, we frequently find vessels of water filled with worms of the gnat kind, as plentiful, in proportion to their size, as those of other fluids are with animalcules. Every cubic inch of water in these vessels contains many <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a> of animals: yet we see many cubic inches of air in the garden not affording one of the parent flies.
