But neither are we positively to declare that the parent flies of these animalcules are in all states wholly invisible to us; if not singly to be seen, there are some strong reasons to imagine that they may in great clusters. Every one has seen in a clear <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, when looking steadfastly at the sky, that the air is in many places disturbed by motions and convolutions in certain spots. These cannot be the effects of imagination, or of fluid faults in our eyes, because they appear the same to all; Fluidity, and if we consider what would be the case to an eye formed in such a manner as to see nothing smaller than an ox, on viewing the air on a marsh fully peopled with gnats, we must be sensible that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> of these insects, though to us distinctly enough visible, would appear to such an eye merely as the moving parcels of air in the former instance do to us: and surely it is thence no rash conclusion to infer, that the case may be the same, and that myriads of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> insects, too small to be singly the objects of our view, yet are to us what the cloud of gnats would be in the former case. Nervous Fluid. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">Elastic</a> Fluids. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> Index.

FLUIDITY

Pages 744-745

is by Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton defined to be, that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of bodies by which they yield to any force impressed, and which have their parts very easily moved among one another. To this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> some have added, that the parts of a fluid are in a continual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. This <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is supported by the solution of salts, and the formation of tinctures. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a small bit of saffron is thrown into a phial full of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> tincture <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> soon be communicated to the water to a considerable height; though the phial is allowed to remain at rest; which indicates a motion in those parts of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> which touch the saffron, by which its colouring <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> is carried up. With regard to water, this can scarce be denied; the constant exhalations from its surface show, that there must be a perpetual motion in its parts from the ascent of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM">steam</a> through it. In <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>, where insensible <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a> does not take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, it might be doubted; and accordingly the Newtonian philosophers in general have been of opinion, that there are some substances essentially fluid, from the spherical <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of their constituent particles. The congelation of mercury, however, by an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, demonstrates that fluidity is not essentially inherent in mercury more than in other bodies. That fluids have vacuities in their substance is evident, because they may be made to dissolve certain bodies without sensibly increasing their bulk. For example, water will dissolve a certain <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>; after which it will receive a little <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, and after that a little <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, without increasing its first dimensions. Here we can scarce suppose anything else than that the saline particles were interposed between those of the fluid; and as, by the mixture of salt and water, a considerable degree of cold is produced, we may thence easily see why the fluid receives these substances without any increase of bulk. All substances are expanded by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and reduced into less dimensions by cold; therefore, if any substance is added to a fluid, which tends to make it cold, the expansion by the bulk of the substance added will not be so much perceived as if this effect had not happened; and if the quantity added be small, the fluid will <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> as much, perhaps more, from the cold produced by the mixture, than it will be expanded from the bulk of the salt. This also may let us know with what these interstices between the particles of the fluid were filled up; namely, the element of fire <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> heat. The saline particles, up on their solution in the fluid, have occupied these spaces; and now the liquor being deprived of a quantity of this element equal in bulk to the salt added, feels sensibly colder. As, therefore, there is scarce any body to be found, but what may become <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> by a sufficient degree of cold, and none but what a certain degree of heat will render fluid; the opinion naturally arises, that fire is the cause of fluidity in all bodies, and that this element is the only essentially fluid substance in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. Hence we may conclude, that those substances which we call fluids are not essentially so, but only assume that appearance in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of an intimate union with the element of fire; <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUMS">gums</a> assume a fluid appearance on being dissolved in spirit of wine, or salts in water. Upon these principles Dr <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> mentions fluidity as an effect of heat. The different degrees of heat which are required to bring different bodies into a state of fluidity, he supposes to depend on some particulars in the mixture and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of the bodies themselves; which becomes extremely probable, from considering that we change the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> state of bodies in this respect, by certain mixtures; thus, if two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> are compounded, the mixture is usually more fusible than either of them separately. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. It is certain, however, that water becomes warmer by being converted into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a>; which may seem contradictory to this opinion. To this, however, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> replies, that fluidity does not consist in the degree of sensible heat contained in bodies, which will affect the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> or a thermometer; but in a certain quantity which remains in a latent state. This opinion he supports from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> length of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> required to melt ice; and to ascertain the degree of heat requisite to keep water in a fluid state, he put five ounces of water into a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> flask, and converted it into ice by means of a freezing mixture put round the flask. Into another flask of the same kind he put an equal quantity of water cooled <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> nearly to the freezing point, by mixing it with snow, and then pouring it off. In this he placed a very delicate thermometer; and found that it acquired heat from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of the room in which it was placed; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> degrees of heat were gained in the first half <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>. The ice being exposed to the same degree of heat, namely, the air of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> room without fire, it cannot be doubted that it received heat from the air as fast as the water which was not frozen; but, to prevent all possibility of deception, he put his hand under the flask containing the ice, and found a stream of cold air very sensibly descending from it, even at a considerable distance from the flask; which undeniably proved, that the ice was all that time absorbing heat from the air. Nevertheless, it was not till 11 hours that the ice was half melted, though in that time it had absorbed so much heat as ought to have raised the thermometer to 140°; and even after it was melted, the temperature of the water was found scarce above the freezing point; so that as the heat which entered could not be found in the melted ice, he concluded that it remained concealed in the water, as an essential ingredient of its composition.

FLUKE

Pages 745-745
or FLOUNDER. See Pleuronectes, Ichthyology Index. FLUKE WORM. See Fasciola, Helminthology Index. FLUKE of an Anchor, that part of it which fastens in the ground. See Anchor.

FLUMMERY

Pages 745-745

a wholesome sort of jelly made of oatmeal. The manner of preparing it is as follows. Put three <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> handfuls of finely ground oatmeal to steep, for 24 hours, in two quarts of fair <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; then pour off the clear water, and put two quarts of fresh water to it; strain it through a fine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> sieve, putting in two spoonfuls of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> flower water, and a spoonful of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>; boil it till it is as thick as a hasty pudding, stirring it continually while it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a>, that it may be very smooth.

FLUOR

Pages 745-745

in Physics, a fluid; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, more properly, the state of a body that was before hard or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>, but is now reduced by fusion or fire into a state of fluidity. FLUOR ACID. See Fluoric Acid, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FLUOR ALBIZZI

Pages 745-745

a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> incident to women, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> known by the name of whites. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. FLUOR <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAR">SPAR</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Blue John, called also fluxing spars, vitreous or glass spars, are minerals composed of calcareous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> united with fluoric acid. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> Index.

FLUSHING

Pages 745-745

a handsome, strong, and considerable town of the United Provinces, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>, and in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WALCHEREN">Walcheren</a>, with a very good harbour, and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> foreign trade. It was put into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, for a pledge of their fidelity, and as a security for the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> she advanced. It was taken by the British in the memorable and ill conducted expedition of 1809, and kept some months. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 32. N. Lat. 51. 26.

FLUTE

Pages 745-746

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of music, the simplest of all those of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> kind. It is played on by blowing it with the mouth; and the tones <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> notes are changed by stopping and opening the holes disposed for that purpose along its side. This is a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> instrument. It was at first called the flute à bec, from bec an old Gaulish word signifying the beak of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> or fowl, but more especially of a cock; the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> flute à bec must therefore signify the beaked flute; which appears very proper, on comparing it with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRAVERSE">traverse</a> or German flute. The word flute is derived from flusta, the Latin for a <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-LAMPREY">lamprey</a> or small eel taken in the Sicilian seas, having <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> holes immediately below the gills on each side, the precise <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of those in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of the flute. By Merennus this instrument is called the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISTULA">fistula</a> dulcis seu Anglicae; the lowest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, according to him, for the treble flute, is C flat, and the compass of the instrument 15 notes. There is however, a flute known by the name of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> flute, the lowest note of which is F. Indeed, ever since the introduction of the flute into concerts, the lowest note of the instrument, of what size soever it is, has been called F; when in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> its pitch is determinable only by its correspondence in respect of acuteness or gravity with one or other of the chords in the scala maxima or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> system. Besides the true concert flute, others of a less size were soon introduced into concerts of violins; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the method was to write the flute <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">key</a> correspondent... correspondent to its pitch. This practice was introduced in 1710 by one Woodcock, a celebrated performer on this instrument, and William Babell organist of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of All-Hallows, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">Bread</a> Street, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. They failed, however, in procuring for the flute a reception into concerts of various instruments; for which reason one Thomas Stanesby, a very curious maker of flutes and other instruments of the like kind, about the year 1732, adverting to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> of Mersennus, in which the lowest note was C, invented what he called the new system; in which, by making the flute of such a size as to be a fifth above concert pitch, the lowest note became C sol fa ut. By this contrivance the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of transposing the flute part was taken away; for a flute of this size, adjusted to the system above mentioned, became an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OCTAVE">octave</a> to the violin. To further this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of Stanesby's, one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> Merci, an excellent performer on the flute, published about the year 1735, six solos for this instrument, three of which are said to be accommodated to Mr Stanesby's new system; but the German flute was now become a favourite instrument, and Stanesby's ingenuity failed of its effect.—One great objection indeed lies against this instrument, which, however, equally affects all perforated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>; namely, that they are never perfectly in tune, or cannot be made to play all their notes with equal exactness. The utmost that the makers of them can do is to tune them to some one key; as the hautboy to C, the German flute to D, and the English flute to F; and to effect this truly, is a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of no small difficulty. The English flutes made by the younger Stanesby came the nearest of any to perfection; but those of Bressan, though excellent in their tone, are all too flat in the upper octave. For these reasons some are induced to think, that the utmost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of proficiency on any of these instruments is not worth the labour of attaining it. German Flute, is an instrument entirely different from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> flute. It is not, like that, put into the mouth to be played; but the end is stopt with a tompon or plug, and the lower lip is applied to a hole about two inches and a half or three inches distant from the end. This instrument is usually about a foot and a half <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>; rather bigger at the upper end than the lower; and perforated with holes, besides that for the mouth, the lowest of which is stopped and opened by the little finger's pressing on a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> or sometimes a silver key, like those in hautboys, bassoons, &c. Its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> is exceeding sweet and agreeable; and serves as a treble in a concert. Flute, or Fluyt, is a kind of long vessel, with flat ribs or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> timbers, round behind, and swollen in the middle; serving chiefly for the carrying of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> in fleets or squadrons of ships; though it is often used in merchandise. The word flute, taken for a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> or vessel, is derived, according to Borel, from the ancient flotte, a little boat. In the verbal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> of St Catherine of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, in the 12th century, we read Unus equum sum una cum mericibus magni ponderis introdum super instrumentum de lignis fabricatum, vulgariter dictum fluta. Upon which the Bollandists observe, that in some copies it is read flotta, an instrument called by the Latins ratis; and that the word flutta or flotta arose from flotten or flot-ten, "to float." Flutes, or Flutings, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, are perpendicular channels or cavities cut along the shaft of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> or pilaster. They are supposed to have been first introduced in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the plaits of women's robes; and are therefore called by the Latins striges and rugae. The French call them cannelures, as being excavations; and we, flutes or flutings, as <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> some resemblance to the musical instrument so called. They are chiefly affected in the Ionic order, in which they had their first rise; though they are also used in all the richer orders, as the Corinthian and Composite; but rarely in the Doric, and scarce ever in the Tuscan.

FLUX

Pages 746-747

in Medicine, an extraordinary issue <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> evacuation of some humour. Fluxes are various, and variously denominated, according to their seats or the humours thus voided; as a flux of the belly, uterine flux, hepatic flux, salival flux, &c. The flux of the belly is of four kinds, which have each their respective denominations, viz. the lientery, or fluxus lientericus; the catiae, or fluxus chylous; the diarrhoea; and the dysentery, or bloody flux. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Flux, in Hydrography, a regular periodical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, happening twice in 24 hours; wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is raised and driven violently against the shores. The flux or flow is one of the motions of the tide; the other, whereby the water sinks and retires, is called the reflux or ebb. There is also a kind of rest or cessation of about half an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> between the flux and reflux; during which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the water is at its greatest height, called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> water. The flux is made by the motion of the water of the sea from the equator towards the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>; which, in its progress, striking against the coasts in its way, and meeting with opposition from them, swells, and where it can find passage, as in flats, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, &c. rises up and runs into the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>. This motion follows, in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, the course of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>; as it loses or comes later every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> by about three <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of an hour, or more, precisely by 48 minutes; and by so much is the motion of the moon slower than that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. It is always highest and greatest in full moons, particularly those of the equinoxes. In some parts, as at Mount St Michael, it rises 80 or 90 feet, though in the open sea it never rises above a foot or two; and in some places, as about the Morea, there is no flux at all. Its runs up some rivers above 120 miles. Up the river <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a> it only goes 80, viz. near to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KINGSTON">Kingston</a> in Surry. Above <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> the water flows four hours and ebbs eight; and below the bridge, flows five hours and ebbs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>. Flux, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METALLURGY">Metallurgy</a>, is sometimes used synonymously with fusion. For instance, an ore, or other <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, is said to be a liquid flux, when it is completely fused. But the word flux is generally used to signify certain saline matters, which facilitate the fusion of ores and other matters, which are difficultly fusible in essays and reductions of ores; such are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALKALIES">alkalies</a>, nitre, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORAX">borax</a>, tartar, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. But the word flux is more particularly applied to mixtures of different proportions of only nitre and tartar; and these fluxes are called by particular names, according to the proportions of these ingredients, as in the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">White</a> Flux, is made with equal parts of nitre and of tartar detonated together, by which they are alkali-ized. The residuum of this detonation is an alkali composed of the alkalies of the nitre and of the tartar, both which are absolutely of the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. As the proportion of nitre in this mixture is more than is sufficient to consume entirely all the inflammable matter of the tartar, the alkali remaining after the detonation is perfectly white, and is therefore called white flux; and as this alkali is made very quickly, it is also called extemporaneous alkali. When a small <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> only of white flux is made, as a few ounces for instance, some nitre always remains undecomposed, and a little of the inflammable principle of the tartar, which gives a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> or even a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> to some <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the flux; but this does not happen when a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantity of white flux is made; because then the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> is much greater. This small quantity of undecomposed nitre and tartar which remains in white flux is not hurtful in most of the metallic fusions in which this flux is employed; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the flux be required perfectly pure, it might easily be disengaged from those extraneous matters by a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and strong calcination, without fusion. Crude Flux. By crude flux is meant the mixture of nitre and tartar in any proportions, without detonation. Thus the mixture of equal parts of the two salts used in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of the white flux, or the mixture of one part of nitre and two parts of tartar for the preparation of the black flux, are each of them a crude flux before detonation. It has also been called white flux, from its colour; but this might occasion it to be confounded with the white flux above described. The name, therefore, of crude flux is more convenient. Crude flux is detonated and alkalized during the reductions and fusions in which it is employed; and is then changed into white or black flux, according to the proportions of which it is composed. This detonation produces good effects in these fusions and reductions, if the swelling and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRAVASATION">extravasation</a> of the detonating matters be guarded against. Accordingly, crude flux may be employed successfully in many operations; as, for instance, in the ordinary operation for procuring the regulus of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>. Black Flux. Black flux is produced from the mixture of two parts of tartar and one part of nitre detonated together. As the quantity of nitre which enters into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of this flux is not sufficient to consume all the inflammable matter of the tartar, the alkali which remains after the detonation contains much black matter, of the nature of coal, and is therefore called black flux.

FLUXIONS

Pages 803-813

Inverse Method. \( (1-x^2)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \), an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> which when expanded by the binomial theorem, is \[ 1 + \frac{1}{2}x^2 + \frac{1}{2 \cdot 4}x^4 + \frac{1 \cdot 3 \cdot 5}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 6}x^6 + \ldots \] therefore, multiplying each <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> by \( x \) and taking the fluent, we get \[ \int \frac{x}{\sqrt{(1-x^2)}} = x + \frac{1 \cdot x^3}{2 \cdot 3} + \frac{1 \cdot 3 \cdot x^5}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 5} + \frac{1 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot x^7}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 6 \cdot 7} + \text{const}. \] <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> we suppose \( x \) to denote the sine of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>, then \( \sqrt{(1-x^2)} \) is its cosine, and \( \frac{x}{\sqrt{(1-x^2)}} \) is the fluxion of the arch itself (\$ 59); therefore the series which we have <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> found expresses the length of the arch of a circle, radius being unity, and the sine of the arch \( x \). If we suppose the series to express the smallest arch that corresponds to the sine \( x \), then, as when the sine of that arch \( = 0 \), the arch itself \( = 0 \), the series expressing the arch must vanish when \( x = 0 \), therefore we must suppress the constant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> added to complete the fluent; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> suppose it \( = 0 \). The same series has already been found by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> method of fluxions in \$ 72. Let \( x \) denote the same as in \$ 137, then, as the sine of 30 degrees, or of \( \frac{\pi}{6} \), is \( \frac{1}{2} \), we have, by substituting \( \frac{\pi}{6} \) instead of \( x \) in the preceding series, and multiplying both sides by 6, \[ x = 3 \left( 1 + \frac{1}{2 \cdot 3 \cdot 2} + \frac{1 \cdot 3}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 5 \cdot 2} + \frac{1 \cdot 3 \cdot 5}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 6 \cdot 7 \cdot 2} + \ldots \<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>) \] by means of this series, which involves only rational numbers, we may compute (but with more labour), the value of \( x \) as before. Suppose the fluxion to be \( \frac{x}{\sqrt{(ax-x^2)}} \), which may be otherwise expressed thus, \( \frac{x}{a} \cdot \frac{x}{\sqrt{(1-\frac{x^2}{a})}} \). By the binomial theorem \( (1-\frac{x^2}{a})^{-\frac{1}{2}} = \) \[ 1 - \frac{x^2}{2a} - \frac{1 \cdot x^4}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot a^2} - \frac{1 \cdot 3 \cdot x^6}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 6 \cdot a^3} - \ldots \] Let each term of this series be multiplied by \( a^{\frac{1}{2}}x^{\frac{1}{2}} \), and the fluent taken by \$ 101, thus we get \( \int \frac{x}{\sqrt{(ax-x^2)}} = \) \[ a^{\frac{1}{2}} \left( \frac{2x^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3} - \frac{1 \cdot 2x^{\frac{5}{2}}}{2 \cdot 5 \cdot a} - \frac{1 \cdot 1 \cdot 2x^{\frac{7}{2}}}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 7 \cdot a^2} - \ldots \right) + \text{const}. \] 141. By resolving a fluxion into an infinite series, the object in view is to transform it into a series of other fluxions, each of which may have its fluent determined by known methods; but it is not always necessary that the terms of the series should be each simply a power of \( x \) multiplied by \( x \) and constant quantities. If for example we have this fluxion \[ \frac{x}{\sqrt{(1-e^2x^2)}} \] in which \( e \) is supposed to denote a small constant quantity, we may expand \( \sqrt{(1-e^2x^2)} \) or \( (1-e^2x^2)^{\frac{1}{2}} \) into a series, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> thus become \[ 1 - \frac{e^2x^2}{2} - \frac{1 \cdot 1 \cdot e^4x^4}{2 \cdot 4} - \frac{1 \cdot 3 \cdot e^6x^6}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 6} - \ldots \] and the fluxion \( \frac{x}{\sqrt{(1-e^2x^2)}} \) will be transformed to \[ \frac{x}{\sqrt{(1-x^2)}} \left\{ 1 - \frac{e^2x^2}{2} - \frac{1 \cdot 1 \cdot e^4x^4}{2 \cdot 4} - \frac{1 \cdot 3 \cdot e^6x^6}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 6} - \ldots \right\} \] the series will converge very fast when \( e \) is small, for that \( \sqrt{(1-x^2)} \) may be a real quantity, \( x^2 \) must be less than 1. We must now multiply each term of the series by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACTOR">factor</a> \( \frac{x}{\sqrt{(1-x^2)}} \) and take the fluents, which being all contained in the general expression \[ \int \frac{x}{\sqrt{(1-x^2)}} \] will be found by \$ 133. Thus, putting \( A \) to denote an arch of which \( x \) is the sine, we have \[ \int \frac{x}{\sqrt{(1-x^2)}} = \] \[ A + \frac{1}{2}e^2 \left\{ \frac{1}{2}x\sqrt{(1-x^2)} - \frac{1}{2}A \right\} \] \[ + \frac{1 \cdot 1}{2 \cdot 4}e^4 \left\{ \frac{1}{4}x^3 + \frac{1 \cdot 3}{2 \cdot 4}x\sqrt{(1-x^2)} - \frac{1 \cdot 3}{2 \cdot 4}A \right\} \] \[ + \frac{1 \cdot 3}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 6}e^6 \left\{ \frac{1}{6}x^5 + \frac{1 \cdot 3}{4 \cdot 6}x^3 + \frac{1 \cdot 3 \cdot 5}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 6}x\sqrt{(1-x^2)} - \frac{1 \cdot 3 \cdot 5}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 6}A \right\} \] \[ + \ldots + \text{const}. \] Of the Fluents of such Fluxions as involve Logarithmic and Exponential functions. 142. Let it be required to find the fluent of \( x^n \cdot \ln(x) \), where \( \ln(x) \) denotes the Napierian logarithm of \( x \). In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, as well as in some following examples, we shall have recourse to the principle already employed in \$ 130, namely, that if \( v \) and \( z \) denote any functions of a variable quantity \( x \), then \[ \int x^v = v \cdot \int x^v \] Let us therefore assume \( x^n = v \), and \( \ln(x) = z \), then, (\$ 101.), \( \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} = v \), and (\$ 57), \( \frac{z}{x} = z \), therefore, substituting substituting these values of \( v, w, \dot{v}, \dot{w} \) in the formula becomes \[ \int x^n \dot{x} (1, x) = \frac{x^{n+1}}{m+1} - \int \frac{x^m \dot{x}}{m+1}, \] or, since \( \int \frac{x^m \dot{x}}{m+1} = \frac{x^{m+1}}{(m+1)^2} + \text{const.} \), \[ \int x^n \dot{x} (1, x) = \frac{x^{n+1}}{m+1} - \left( \frac{1}{m+1} \right)^2 \int \frac{x^m \dot{x}}{m+1}. \] Let us next suppose that the proposed fluxion is \( x^n \dot{x} (1, x)^n \). Put \( x^n = v \) and \( (1, x)^n = z \), then (\$ 101) \[ \frac{x^{n+1}}{m+1} = v, \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{n x (1, x)^n}{x} = z, \] therefore, substituting as before these values in the formula \[ \int x^n \dot{x} = v \int \dot{v} \dot{x}, \] we get \[ \int x^n \dot{x} (1, x)^n = \frac{x^{n+1}}{m+1} (1, x)^{n-1} - \int \frac{n x^n \dot{x} (1, x)^{n-1}}{m+1}. \] It is evident, that by this formula the determination of the fluent of \( x^n \dot{x} (1, x)^n \) is reduced to that of \( x^n \dot{x} (1, x)^n \) which we have already found, and in like manner that the determination of the fluent of \( x^n \dot{x} (1, x)^n \) is reduced to that of \( x^n \dot{x} (1, x)^n \), and so on, from which it appears that the fluent of \( x^n \dot{x} (1, x)^n \) is expressible in finite terms when \( n \) is a whole positive <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. The formula, however, will not apply when \( m = 1 \), because of the denominator \( m+1 = 1+1=0 \). But in this case we have \[ \int \frac{x^n \dot{x}}{x} = \frac{1}{n+1} (1, x)^{n+1} + \text{const.} \] If \( n \) be <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a> or fractional, the fluent of \( x^n \dot{x} (1, x)^n \) can only be expressed by an infinite series. 143. As an example of an exponential <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a>, let it be required to find the fluent of \( a^n \dot{x} \). Here we may put \( \dot{v} \) for \( x^n \dot{x} \), and \( z \) for \( a^n \), then we have \[ \frac{x^{n+1}}{m+1} = v, \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{n x (1, a)^n}{x} = z, \] therefore, substituting these values of \( v, w, \dot{v}, \dot{w} \) in the formula \[ \int a^n \dot{x} = a^n \int \dot{v} \dot{x}, \] we get \[ \int a^n \dot{x} = \frac{a^n x^{n+1}}{n+1} - \int \frac{(1, a) a^n x^{n+1}}{n+1}; \] hence, bringing \( \int a^n \dot{x} \) to stand alone one side of the equation \[ \int a^n \dot{x} = \frac{a^n x^n}{1, a} - \frac{n}{1, a} \int a^n x^{n-1} \dot{x}. \] If we suppose \( n = 1 \), then observing that \( \int a^n \dot{x} = \frac{a^n}{1, a} \) (\$ 56), \[ \int a^n \dot{x} = \frac{a^n x}{1, a} - \frac{a^n}{(1, a)^2} + \text{const.} \] If \( n = 2 \), then \[ \int a^n \dot{x} = \frac{a^n x^2}{1, a} - \frac{2}{1, a} \int a^n \dot{x}. \] In this expression we substitute the value of \( \int a^n \dot{x} \) just found, thus it becomes \[ \int a^n \dot{x} = \frac{a^n x^2}{1, a} - \frac{2}{(1, a)^2} + \text{const.} \] Proceeding in this way, we may find the fluent when \( n = 3 \), or when \( n = 4 \), or in general, when \( n \) is any integer number whatever, the number of terms in the fluent being in this case always finite; it is not so however when \( n \) is either negative or fractional. Of the Fluents of such Fluxions as contain functions related to a circle. 144. Let suppose that \( x \) is an arch whose sine is \( x \), and that it is required to find the fluent of \( x^n \dot{x} \). Put \( x^n = v \), then \[ \int x^n \dot{x} = \int x \dot{v} = x \dot{v} - \int \dot{v} \dot{x}; \] but since \( \dot{v} = x^n \dot{x} \), we have \( v = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} \), \$ 101, and since \( x = \sin x \), we have \( \dot{x} = \cos x \sqrt{1-x^2} \) (\$ 59), and therefore \( \dot{x} = \frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} \); thus we have \[ \int x^n \dot{x} = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} - \frac{x}{n+1} \int \frac{x^{n+1} \dot{x}}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}; \] hence the determination of the proposed fluent is reduced to \( \int \frac{x^{n+1} \dot{x}}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} \) which we have already considered in \$ 133. By the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of reasoning we may determine the fluent when \( x \) denotes the cosine of the arch \( x \). 145. It appears from \$ 59, that \( n \) being put to denote any arch of a circle to radius unity, the fluxion of the sine of that arch is \( n \cos n x \); therefore, on the contrary, \[ \int x \cos n x = \frac{1}{n} \sin n x + \text{const.} \] In like manner, from the formulas of \$ 59, and \$ 60, we find \[ \int x \sin n x. \] \[ \int x \sin^n x = -\frac{1}{n} \cos^n x + \text{const}. \] \[ \int x \cos^n x = \frac{1}{n} \<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAN">tan</a>^n x + \text{const}. \] \[ \int x \cot^n x = -\frac{1}{n} \cot^n x + \text{const}. \] \[ \int x \sec^n x = \frac{1}{n} \sec^n x + \text{const}. \] \[ \int x \csc^n x = -\frac{1}{n} \csc^n x + \text{const}. \] 146. By the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of these expressions we find the fluent of \[ x(A+B \sin x+C \sin 2x+\&c.) \] to be \[ A x-B \cos x-\frac{1}{2} C \cos 2x+\&c.+ \text{const}. \] and from the first expression we find the fluent of \[ x(A+B \cos x+C \cos 2x+\&c.) \] to be \[ A x+B \sin x+\frac{1}{2} C \sin 2x+\&c.+ \text{const}. \] 147. It has been shewn in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">Arithmetic</a> of Sines, (see <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALGEBRA">ALGEBRA</a>, § 356.) that \[ \sin^2 x = \frac{1}{2} (-\cos 2x+1), \] therefore, by what has been shewn in § 145, \[ \int x \sin^2 x = \frac{1}{2} \int (-\cos 2x+x) + \text{const}. \] It has also been shewn that \[ \sin^3 x = \frac{1}{3} (\sin 3x+3 \sin x), \] therefore, multiplying each term of this expression by \( x \), and taking the fluents, \[ \int x \sin^3 x = \frac{1}{3} (\cos 3x-3 \cos x)+ \text{const}. \] In the same manner may the fluent of \( x \sin^n x \) be found, \( n \) being any positive integer number whatever. Again, it has been shewn (ALGEBRA, § 356.), that \[ \cos^2 x = \frac{1}{2} (\cos 2x+1); \] therefore \[ \int x \cos^2 x = \frac{1}{2} \int (\cos 2x+x) + \text{const}. \] and because \[ \cos^3 x = \frac{1}{3} (\cos 3x+3 \cos x) \] therefore, multiplying by \( x \), and taking the fluents, \[ \int x \cos^3 x = \frac{1}{3} (\cos 3x+3 \sin x)+ \text{const}. \] and proceeding in this way we may find the fluents of \( x \cos^n x \), \( n \) being any positive integer number. 148. The fluents of \( x \sin^n x \) and \( x \cos^n x \) may be expressed under another form, by proceeding as in § 142. Thus, beginning with \( x \sin^n x \), and resolving it into \( x \sin x \times \sin^{n-1} x \), if we put \( x \sin x = v \), and \( \sin^{n-1} x = t \), we have by § 145, \( v = \cos x \), and (by § 26 and § 59) \( t = (n-1) \times \cos x \sin^{n-2} x \); therefore, substituting in the formula \( \int v = v - \int vt \), we have \[ \int x \sin^n x = -\cos x \sin^{n-1} x \] \[ + (n-1) \int x \cos^n x \sin^{n-2} x; \] but \( \cos^n x = 1 - \sin^n x \), therefore \( \int x \sin^n x \) is equal to \[ -\cos x \sin^{n-1} x + (n-1) \int x \sin^{n-2} x \] \[ -(n-1) \int x \sin^n x; \] which expression, by bringing together the terms containing \( \int x \sin^n x \) becomes \[ \int x \sin^n x = -\frac{1}{n} \cos x \sin^{n-1} x \] \[ + \frac{n-1}{n} \int x \sin^{n-2} x. \] By giving particular values to \( n \) we have \[ \int x \sin^2 x = -\frac{1}{2} \cos x \sin x + \frac{1}{2} \int x \] \[ = -\frac{1}{2} \cos x \sin x + \frac{1}{2} x + \text{const}. \] \[ \int x \sin^3 x = -\frac{1}{3} \cos x \sin^2 x + \frac{2}{3} \int x \sin x \] \[ = -\frac{1}{3} \cos x \sin^2 x - \frac{2}{3} \cos x + \text{const}. \] We may proceed in this way as far as we please, deducing the fluent of \( x \sin^n x \) from that of \( x \sin^2 x \), and the fluent of \( x \sin^3 x \) from that of \( x \sin^2 x \), and so on. If in the general formula we substitute every where \( x-n \) instead of \( n \), it becomes \[ \int x \sin^{n-x} x = \frac{1}{n-2} \cos x \sin^{n-x} x \] \[ + \frac{n-1}{n-2} \int x \sin^{n-x} x, \] Inverse an expression which, by bringing \( \int \sin^n x \) or \( \int \frac{\sin^n x}{\sin^n x} \) to stand on one side of the equation, becomes \[ \int \frac{\sin^n x}{\sin^n x} = \frac{1}{(n-1)} \cos x + \frac{n-2}{n-1} \int \frac{\sin^{n-2} x}{\sin^n x}. \] This formula is not applicable to the case of \( n=1 \), because then each of the terms of the fluent is divided by \( n-1=0 \), and therefore becomes infinite. In order to obtain the expression for the fluent in this particular case, we proceed thus. It is evident that \[ \frac{1}{\sin^n x} = \frac{1}{1-\cos^2 x}, \quad \text{but} \quad \frac{1}{1-\cos^2 x} = \frac{1}{2(1-\cos x)} + \frac{1}{2(1+\cos x)} \] as will be found by reducing the fractions to a common denominator, therefore \[ \frac{1}{\sin x} = \frac{1}{2(1-\cos x)} + \frac{\sin x}{2(1+\cos x)}, \] and consequently, \[ \int \frac{\sin x}{\sin x} = \frac{1}{2} \int \frac{\sin x}{1-\cos x} + \frac{1}{2} \int \frac{\sin x}{1+\cos x}; \] but if it be considered that the fluxion of \( \cos x \) is \( -\sin x \) (\$59.), it will appear by §103 that \[ \int \frac{\sin x}{1-\cos x} = l(1-\cos x), \quad \text{and that} \quad \int \frac{\sin x}{1+\cos x} = l(1+\cos x), \] therefore \[ \int \frac{\sin x}{\sin x} = \frac{1}{2} l(1-\cos x) - \frac{1}{2} l(1+\cos x) + \text{const.} \] \[ = \frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{1-\cos x}{1+\cos x} \right) + \text{const.} \] \[ = l \sqrt{\frac{1-\cos x}{1+\cos x}} + \text{const.} \] If in the general formula for \( \int \frac{\sin x}{\sin^n x} \) we suppose \( n=2 \), we have \[ \int \frac{\sin x}{\sin^n x} = -\frac{\cos x}{\sin x} = -\cotan x + \text{const.} \] which agrees with what has been already observed (\$145.), and if we suppose \( n=3 \), then \[ \int \frac{\sin x}{\sin^n x} = -\frac{\cos x}{2 \sin x} + \frac{1}{4} \int \frac{\sin x}{\sin^n x} \] In this way we proceed as far as we please, deducing \( \int \frac{\sin x}{\sin^n x} \) from \( \int \frac{\sin x}{\sin^n x} \), and so on. 149. If in the general formulas for \( \int \sin^n x \) and \( \int \frac{\sin^n x}{\sin^n x} \) we substitute \( \frac{\pi}{2} - x \) instead of \( x \), (where \( \frac{\pi}{2} \) denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRANT">quadrant</a>), and observe that \[ \sin \left( \frac{\pi}{2} - x \right) = \cos x, \quad \cos \left( \frac{\pi}{2} - x \right) = \sin x, \] and that the fluxion of \( \left( \frac{\pi}{2} - x \right) \) is \( -x \), we shall immediately obtain \[ \int \frac{\cos^n x}{\sin^n x} = \frac{1}{n} \sin x \cos^{n-1} x \] \[ + \frac{n-1}{n} \int \frac{\cos^n x}{\sin^n x} \] \[ \int \frac{\sin^n x}{\cos^n x} = \frac{1}{n-1} \cos x \sin^{n-1} x \] \[ + \frac{n-2}{n-1} \int \frac{\sin^n x}{\cos^n x}; \] and in like manner from the formula expressing the fluent of \( \int \frac{\sin x}{\sin^n x} \) we deduce \[ \int \frac{\cos^n x}{\sin^n x} = \frac{1}{l} \left( \frac{1+\sin x}{1-\sin x} \right) + \text{const.} \] \[ = l \sqrt{\frac{1+\sin x}{1-\sin x}} + \text{const.} \] 150. It has been shewn in Algebra, §357, that \[ 16 \cos^n x \sin^n x = \sin 5x + \sin 3x + 2 \sin x, \] therefore \[ \int \frac{\cos^n x \sin^n x}{\sin^n x} = \frac{1}{16} \left( \frac{1}{5} \cos 5x - \frac{1}{3} \cos 3x \right) \] \[ - 2 \cos x + \text{const.} \] The same mode of finding the fluent will apply to any fluxion of this form \( \sin^n x \cos^n x \); or by resolving the fluxion into two parts, the determination of its fluent may be reduced to that of a fluxion in which the exponents \( m \) and \( n \) are less than in the proposed fluxion, by the method of proceeding already employed in §148. 151. Let us now denote \( \sin x \) by \( x \), then \( \cos x = \sqrt{1-x^2} \), and since \( x \cos x = x \) (\$59.) therefore \( x = \frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} \); these values being substituted in any function involving \( x \), \( \sin x \) and \( \cos x \) will immediately reduce it to an algebraic form. Thus, for example, we shall have \( x \sin x \cos x \) transformed to \[ x \cdot x \cdot (1-x^2)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \] an expression which may have its fluent determined by the formulas of §133 and §134. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">Sect</a>. II. Application of the Inverse Method of Fluxions to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">Resolution</a> of Problems. To find the Areas of Curves. 152. It has been shewn in §61, that if the abscissa of a curve be denoted by \( x \), the ordinate by \( y \), and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a>... area by \( s \), then \( s = y \dot{x} \). Therefore the general formula expressing the area of any curve will be \[ s = \int y \dot{x} \] Hence to find the area of any curve, we must either find from the equation of the curve the value of \( y \) in terms of \( x \), or else the value of \( \dot{x} \) in terms of \( y \), and \( y \), and either the one or the other of these being substituted in the above formula, and the fluent found by the methods already explained, we shall have a general expression for the curvilinear area as required. **Ex. 1.** Let it be required to find the area of any curve of the parabolic kind, of which, putting the abscissa \( <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">AB</a>=x \), and the ordinate \( BP=y \), the equation is \[ y = ax^n. \] Then we have \( y = ax^n \), and \[ s = \int y \dot{x} = ax^n \dot{x}. \] \[ = \frac{na^{n+1}}{m+n} x^{\frac{m+n}{n}} + C, \] where \( C \) denotes the constant quantity that may be required to complete the fluent. As in the present case, it is required to find the area of the portion of the curve next its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERTEX">vertex</a>, so that when \( x=0 \), then \( s=0 \), therefore also \( C=0 \), and the area is simply \[ \frac{na^{n+1}}{m+n} x^{\frac{m+n}{n}}. \] If it be required to find the area comprehended between two ordinates \( PB, p_b \), put \( AB=d \), then when \( x=d \), we have \( s=0 \), therefore the general expression \[ s = \int y \dot{x} = ax^n \dot{x}. \] becomes in this case \( s = \frac{na^{n+1}}{m+n} d^{\frac{m+n}{n}} + C, \) hence \( C = -\frac{na^{n+1}}{m+n} d^{\frac{m+n}{n}}, \) and consequently the area \( BP_p b \), or \( s \), is equal to \[ \frac{na^{n+1}}{m+n} \left( x^{\frac{m+n}{n}} - d^{\frac{m+n}{n}} \right). \] When \( n \) is an even number, the expression for the area, viz., \( \frac{na^{n+1}}{m+n} x^{\frac{m+n}{n}} \), may be considered as negative as well as positive, on account of the radical quantity \( x^{\frac{m+n}{n}} \), or \( \sqrt{x^{m+n}} \), which has then a twofold value, it may therefore have the sign \( \pm \) prefixed to it; but in this case the same abscissa \( AB \) belongs to two branches of the curve \( APp \) and \( AP'p' \), as in fig. 19. No. 1, therefore the two values of the expression \( \frac{na^{n+1}}{m+n} x^{\frac{m+n}{n}} \) may be considered as indicating the two areas \( APB, AP'B \), on each side of the axis, corresponding the one to the positive, and the other to the negative ordinates. When the exponents \( m \) and \( n \) are both odd numbers, the quantity \( x^{\frac{m+n}{n}} \) has only one sign, and remains always positive whatever be the sign of \( x \), but in this case one of the two branches of the curve has its abscissas and its ordinates negative at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> (as in fig. 19. No. 2); it follows therefore that the areas corresponding to the negative abscissas and ordinates ought to be regarded as positive. If \( n \) alone is odd, then the quantity \( x^{\frac{m+n}{n}} \) becomes negative at the same time as \( x \), but in this case the two branches of the curve are on the same side of the line in which the abscissas are taken (as in fig. 19. No. 3), and the ordinates remain always positive. Upon the whole it may be concluded, that the area of a curve is positive when the abscissas and the ordinates have the same sign, and negative when they have contrary signs. If we suppose \( m=1 \), and \( n=2 \), then the curve is the common parabola, the area of which from the general formula is found to be \[ \frac{2a^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3} x^{\frac{3}{2}} = \frac{2}{3} xy; \] hence it appears that the parabola is \( \frac{2}{3} \) of its circumscribing parallelogram. **Ex. 2.** Suppose the curve to be a circle. Put \( AB=x, BP=y \), the diameter \( <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AD">AD</a>=a \), the area \( ABP=\pi \). From the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the circle \( y^2=ax-x^2 \), therefore \( y=\sqrt{(a-x^2)} \), and \[ s = \int y \dot{x} = \int \sqrt{(a-x^2)}. \] In this case the fluxion is not of such a form as to admit of an algebraic fluent in finite terms, we must therefore have recourse to the method of series, but we have already found the fluent in this way in § 140, therefore, from the series there brought out we have \[ s = \sqrt{a} \left( \frac{2x}{3} - \frac{1}{5} \frac{2x^3}{a} - \frac{1}{7} \frac{2x^5}{a^2} - \cdots \right) \] \[ = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{3}{4} \cdot \frac{5}{6} \cdot \frac{7}{8} \cdots \] this expression does not require a constant quantity to be added to it, because when \( x=0 \) we must also have \( s=0 \). If we suppose the arch \( AP \) to be \( \frac{\pi}{4} \) of the quadrant \( AE \), then it is known that \( PB=\frac{\pi}{2} \) rad. \( AC=\frac{\pi}{2} \), therefore, if we suppose the radius \( =1 \), we have in this case \( BC=\frac{\pi}{3} \), and \( AB=\frac{\pi}{2} \cdot \frac{\pi}{3} = 0.1339746 \) nearly. If this number be substituted instead of \( x \), and a few terms of the series computed, we shall find the area \( ABP=0.452931 \); to this add the triangle \( CBP=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2}=0.2165663 \), and we have the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECTOR">sector</a> \( ACP=0.2165663 \), which number when multiplied by 3 gives \( 0.7833982 \) for the area of the quadrant. This number also expresses the area of a circle of which the diameter is 1. **Ex. 3.** Suppose the curve to be an ellipse. Inverse the transverse axis \( AD = a \), the conjugate axis \( 2CE = b \), also \( AB = x \), \( BP = y \); then by the nature of the curve \( y = \frac{b}{a} \sqrt{(ax - x^2)} \), and \( s = y \dot{x} = \frac{b}{a} \dot{x} \sqrt{(ax - x^2)} \); but if a circle be described on \( AD \) as a diameter, and \( BP \) the ordinate of the ellipse be produced to meet the circle, it appears from last example that \( x \sqrt{(ax - x^2)} \) is the fluxion of \( AQB \) the segment of the circle corresponding to the elliptic area \( APB \) or \( s \); therefore, putting \( v \) for the segment \( AQB \), we have \[ s = \frac{b}{a} \dot{x} = \frac{b}{a} \dot{x} \sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)} \] here the constant quantity \( c \) must be suppressed, because \( s \) and \( v \) must vanish together. Hence it appears that the area of any segment of an ellipse is to the area of the corresponding segment of its circumscribing circle as the lesser axis of the ellipse is to the greater; therefore the whole ellipse must be to the whole circle in the same ratio. Ex. 5. Let the curve be a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPERBOLA">hyperbola</a>, of which \( C \) is the centre. Put the semi-transverse axis \( CA = a \), the semiconjugate axis \( CB = b \), \( BP = y \), the area \( APB = s \). From the nature of the curve \( y = \frac{b}{a} \sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)} \), therefore \[ s = \int y \dot{x} = \frac{b}{a} \int \dot{x} \sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)} \] But it appears from formula B (\$131.) that \[ \int \dot{x} \sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)} = \frac{b}{a} \int \dot{x} \sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)} - \frac{ab}{2} \int \frac{\dot{x}}{\sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)}} \] and again by \$127, \[ \int \frac{\dot{x}}{\sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)}} = 1 \cdot \left\{ x + \sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)} \right\} + c, \] therefore \[ s = \frac{b}{2a} x \sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)} - \frac{ab}{2} \left\{ x + \sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)} \right\} + c. \] To discover the value of the constant quantity \( c \), we must consider that when \( x = a \), then \( s = 0 \), and in this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> case the general equation just found becomes \[ c = -\frac{ab}{2} l. a + c, \] hence \( c = \frac{ab}{2} l. a \), and consequently, observing that \[ -\frac{ab}{2} l. \left\{ x + \sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)} \right\} + ab l. a \] we get \[ s = \frac{b}{2a} x \sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)} - \frac{ab}{2} l. \left\{ x + \sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)} \right\}. \] It immediately follows from this formula that \[ \frac{b}{2a} x \sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)} - s = \frac{ab}{2} l. \left\{ x + \sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)} \right\} \] but if a straight line be drawn from \( C \) to \( P \) so as to form the triangle \( CBP \), it is manifest that \( \frac{b}{2a} x \sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)} \) is equal to \( \frac{1}{2} CB \times BP \), that is, to the triangle \( CBP \), therefore the excess of the triangle \( CBP \) above the area \( s \), that is the hyperbolic sector \( <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">CAP</a> \), is equal to the logarithmic function \[ \frac{ab}{2} l. \left\{ x + \sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)} \right\}. \] Ex. 5. Suppose the curve to be an equilateral hyperbola, that is a hyperbola whose axes are equal, and that it is required to find the curvilinear area \( DCBP \) comprehended between \( DC \), a perpendicular from \( D \) (a given point in the curve) to one of the asymptotes, and \( PB \), a perpendicular from any other point in the curve to the same asymptote. Let \( A \) be the centre, put \( AC = a \), \( CD = b \), \( AB = x \), \( BP = y \), the area \( DCBP = s \). From the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the asymptotes we have \( xy = ab \), and therefore \( y = \frac{ab}{x} \), hence (\$103.) \[ s = \int y \dot{x} = \int \frac{ab}{x} \dot{x} = ab l. x + c. \] To find the value of \( c \), let us suppose \( x = a \), then \( s = 0 \), and the general formula becomes in this case \[ c = ab l. a + c, \text{ and hence } c = -ab l. a, \] therefore \[ s = ab l. x - ab l. a = ab l. \frac{x}{a}. \] If we suppose \( a = b = 1 \), then \( s = l. x \), from which it appears that in this case the hyperbolic area \( DCBP \) represents the Napierian logarithm of the number \( x \); it was from the consideration of this property that the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOGARITHMS">logarithms</a> originally invented by Napier were called hyperbolical logarithms. But the logarithms of any other system may also be represented by areas of the same hyperbola; for this purpose it is only necessary to determine the magnitudes of \( a \) and \( b \), so that \( \frac{b}{a} = M \), where \( M \) denotes the modulus of the system, thus we shall have \( ab = a^2 M \), and \( s = a^2 M l. \frac{x}{a} \), or, putting \( a = 1 \), \( s = M l. x \), an expression for the logarithm of \( x \) according to any system whatever of which the modulus is \( M \) (\$287.) Ex. Let the curve be the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYCLOID">cycloid</a> of which \( AE \) is the axis and \( A \) the vertex, let a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a> be described on \( AE \) as a diameter, draw \( AG \) perpendicular to the axis, and from any point in the curve draw \( PB \) perpendicular to \( AG \) and \( PD \) perpendicular to \( AE \), meeting the circle in \( Q \), and draw \( QC \) to \( C \) the centre of the circle. Put \( AC = a \), \( AB = x \), \( BP = y \), the area \( ABP = s \), and put \( v \) for the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> \( ACQ \), that is for the arch of a circle which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> \( ACQ \), the radius \( a \). Inverse of that circle being unity, then \( AD = a (1 - \cos v) \), \( DQ = a \sin v \), and arch \( AQ = av \), and since from the nature of the curve, \( PD = \text{arch } BQ + DQ \), therefore \( PD = av + a \sin v = a (v + \sin v) \); hence \[ x = a (v + \sin v), \quad x = a \dot{v} (1 + \cos v), \quad (\S 59) \] \[ y = a (1 - \cos v) \] \[ s = \int x y = \int a^2 \dot{v} (1 - \cos^2 v) \] \[ = a^2 \int v \sin^2 v = \frac{a^2}{2} v - \frac{a^2}{2} \sin v \cos v (\S 148) \] \[ = \frac{1}{2} AC \times \text{arch } AQ - \frac{1}{2} CD \times DQ; \] and here no constant quantity is wanted to complete the fluent; because upon the supposition that \( AQ = 0 \) both sides of the equation vanish as they ought to do; now it is obvious that \( \frac{1}{2} AC \times AQ = \text{area of sector } ACQ \), and \( \frac{1}{2} CD \times DQ = \text{area of triangle } DCQ \), therefore \( s = \text{area of circ. seg. } ADQ. \) Let \( AG \) be the greatest value of \( x \); complete the parallelogram \( AGFE \), then from the general expression for the cycloidal area, it follows that the whole cycloidal space \( APFG \) is equal to the semicircle \( AQE \); but from the nature of the curve, \( EF \) is equal to \( AQE \), half the circumference, therefore the rectangle \( EG \) is equal to four times the semicircle \( AQE \); from these equals take away the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> cycloidal space \( AGF \), and the semicircle \( AQE \), which have been shewn to be equal, and the remainders, viz. the internal cycloidal space \( APFE \), and three times the semicircle \( AQE \), are equal to each other. 153. In some <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> it is more convenient to refer a curve line to a fixed point than to an axis. Thus instead of expressing the nature of the circle by the equation \( y^2 = a x - x^3 \), where \( y \) denotes a perpendicular from any point of the curve upon \( a \) the diameter, and \( x \) the distance of that perpendicular from one end of the diameter, we may otherwise express it by the equation \( x = r v \), where \( v \) denotes a variable arch of the circle reckoned from one end of its diameter, \( r \) its radius, and \( v \) the angle contained by a line drawn from the centre of the circle through the extremity of \( x \), which angle is measured by an arch of a circle having its radius unity. The nature of the different <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONIC_SECTIONS">conic sections</a> may be defined in the same manner. Let \( P \) be any point in a conic <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECTION">section</a>, of which \( F \) is one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a>, and \( FA \) a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the axis; let \( DC \) the directrix of the section meet \( FA \) in \( C \), join \( PF \), and draw \( PB \) perpendicular to the axis, and \( PD \) to the directrix; then from the nature of the curve (Conic Sections) \( PF \) has a given ratio to \( PD \), that is to \( FC - FB \); put \( FC = a \), \( FP = r \), the angle \( PFC = v \), and suppose \( PF : PD :: n : 1 \), then \( PF = n.PD = n.FC - n.FB \), hence observing that \( FB = FP \times \cos v \), we get \( r = a n - nr \cos v \), and \( r = \frac{an}{1 + n \cos v} \), which equation expresses generally the nature of a conic section. 154. The formula which we have found for the fluxion of a curvilinear area, in § 61, is not immediately applicable when the nature of a curve is expressed in this way, we shall therefore investigate another formula suited to this particular manner of considering curves. Let us suppose that \( APR \) is a curve the position of Fig. 16, any point \( P \) of which is determined by \( PF \), its distance from a given point \( F \), and the angle which \( PF \) makes with \( AF \) a line given by position. Let a circle be described on \( F \) as a centre with a rad. \( = 1 \), then \( FP \), as also the area \( FAP \), may be considered as functions of \( BD \) the arch of that circle which measures the angle \( PFA \). From \( F \) draw \( FP' \) to any other point \( P' \) of the curve meeting the circle \( BD \) in \( D' \). Put \( FP = r \), the area \( FAP = s \), the angle \( AFP \), or the arch \( BD = v \), then the area \( FP'P' \), and the arch \( DD' \), will be the corresponding increments of \( s \) and \( v \), therefore, § 21, \[ \frac{\dot{s}}{\dot{v}} = \text{limit of } \frac{\text{area } FPP'}{\text{DD'FD'}} \] Here \( DD' \) the increment of \( v \) is multiplied by \( ED = 1 \), to render the terms of the ratio homogeneous. On \( F \) as a centre, with \( FP \) as a radius, describe an arch of a circle meeting \( FP' \) in \( Q \), then, as the sectors \( FDD' \), \( FPQ \) are similar, we have \[ FE : FP' :: FD \times DD' : FP \times PQ = 2 \text{ sect. } FPQ, \] hence \( DD' \times FD = \frac{2FD^2}{FP^2} \text{ sect. } FPQ = \frac{2}{r^2} \text{ sect. } FPQ \), and \( \frac{\dot{s}}{\dot{v}} = \frac{r^2}{2} \times \lim \frac{\text{area } FPP'}{\text{sect. } FPQ} \), but the point \( P' \) being supposed to approach continually to \( P \), it is manifest that the limit of \( \frac{\text{area } FPP'}{\text{sect. } FPQ} \) is unity, or 1, therefore \[ \frac{\dot{s}}{\dot{v}} = \frac{r^2}{2}, \quad \text{and } \dot{s} = \frac{1}{2} r^2 \dot{v}. \] 154. By means of this formula we may find the areas of that class of curves called spirals. Let us take for example the spiral of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHIMEDES">Archimedes</a>, which may be defined thus. Conceive a straight line \( FR \) to revolve about \( F \) the centre of a given circle, departing from a given position \( FB \); conceive also a point \( P \) to move in the revolving line, so that \( PF \) its distance from the centre may be to \( BD \) the arch of the circle passed over by the revolving line, as \( m \) to \( n \), then the point \( P \) will <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATE">generate</a> the spiral. Put \( BF = a \), the angle \( BFR = v \), the line \( FP = r \), and the area <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> by the line \( FP = s \), then the arch \( BD = av \), and since from the nature of the curve \[ r : av :: m : n, \quad \text{therefore } v = \frac{nr}{am}, \quad \text{and } \dot{v} = \frac{n\dot{r}}{am}, \] the general formula \( \dot{s} = \frac{1}{2} r^2 \dot{v} \) becomes \( \dot{s} = \frac{nr^2 \dot{r}}{2am} \), therefore, \[ s = \int \frac{nr^2 \dot{r}}{2am} = \frac{nr^3}{6am} \] this fluent does not require a constant quantity to be added, added, as both \( s \) and \( r \) evidently vanish at the same time. Fig. 11. 156. As the general expression for a curvilinear area \( BCPD \) is \( \int y \cdot x \), where \( x = AB \) the abscissa reckoned from a given point \( A \) in the axis, and \( y = BC \) the ordinate, it follows that \( X \) being put to denote any function of a variable quantity \( x \), the fluent of \( X \cdot x \) may always be exhibited by means of a curvilinear area. Thus let \( CPp \) be a curve of such a nature that \( AD \) and \( DP \) the co-ordinates being denoted by \( x \) and \( y \), the equation of the curve is \( y = X \), then, assuming any ordinate \( BC \) as given by position, we have evidently \[ \int X \cdot x = \text{area } CBDP. \] As the ordinate \( BC \) (which is assumed as given by position) may be taken anywhere, the fluxion of the area being the same wherever it is taken, it appears, as has been already observed (\$ 101) that the function \( \int X \cdot x \) may be considered as <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDETERMINATE">indeterminate</a>, for it admits of innumerable values corresponding to any particular value of \( x \), and in this respect it differs from an algebraic function, which for a given value of \( x \) has always a determinate number of values. If however \( x \) be supposed to increase from any determinate magnitude \( a \), to any other determinate magnitude \( a' \), then taking the abscissa \( AD = a \), and \( AD = a' \), and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> the ordinates \( DP, dp \), we have when \( x = a, \int X \cdot x = \text{area } CBDP, \) and when \( x = a', \int X \cdot x = \text{area } CB dp, \) therefore, while \( x \) increases from \( a \) to \( a' \), or receives the increment \( a' - a \), the function \( \int X \cdot x \) increases from area \( CBDP \) to area \( CB dp \), and thus receives the increment area \( PD dp \), which is of a determinate magnitude, as the ordinates \( PD, pd \) have both a determinate position. Hence it appears that in assigning the fluent of \( X \cdot x \), we only determine the change that takes <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the value of the function \( \int X \cdot x \) while \( x \) passes from one particular value to another particular value. 157. As there are general and known methods by which an approximate value of any curvilinear area may be found, when a fluent is expressed by such an area, those methods may be applied to find an approximate value of the fluent. Let \( PD dp \) be a curvilinear area, supposed to represent the fluent \( \int X \cdot x \) between the limits of \( x = AD \) and \( x = A d \). Conceive \( Dd \) to be divided into a number of equal parts \( DD', D'D'', D'd \), and the ordinates \( P'D', P''D'' \) drawn, and the two sets of parallelograms \( DE, D'E', D''E'' \) and \( D'e, D''e' \) to be completed, the former constituting a rectilineal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> circumscribed about the curvilinear space \( DPP''pd \), and the latter a rectilineal figure <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> in that space; then as the circumscribed figure must necessarily be greater than the curvilinear space, that is, greater than \( \int X \cdot x \) taken between the limits of \( x = AD \) and \( x = A a \), and the inscribed figure must be less, it follows that if we compute the areas of the circumscribed and inscribed figures we shall obtain two limits, the one greater, and the other less than \( \int X \cdot x \). And as by increasing the number of equal parts into which \( Dd \) is divided we may bring the circumscribed and inscribed rectilineal figures as near to a ratio of equality as we please, it is always possible to find two limits which shall differ from each other, and consequently from \( \int X \cdot x \) (which lies between them), by less than any assignable quantity. 158. If we join \( P, P', P'', p \), the tops of the ordinates, the rectilineal space formed by the trapeziums \( DPP'D', D'P''D''D'', D''pd \) will be more nearly equal to the curvilinear area, than the circumscribed rectilineal figure formed by the parallelograms \( DE, D'E', D''E'' \); therefore, the sum of those trapeziums being found, it will be equal to the fluent \( \int X \cdot x \) nearly. Suppose, for example, that it is required to find the value of \( \int \frac{x}{1+x^2} \) between the limits of \( x = 0 \), and \( x = 1 \). In this case \( X = \frac{1}{1+x^2} \), so that the equation of the curve \( Pp \) is \( y = \frac{1}{1+x^2} \); let us suppose \( Dd \) the distance between the extreme ordinates to be divided into ten equal parts, then putting \( 0, 1, 2, \ldots, 10 \) instead of \( x \) in the formula \( y = \frac{1}{1+x^2} \) we obtain eleven successive values of \( y \), or eleven equidistant ordinates, the numerical values of which will be as follows, | \( x \) | \( y \) | |-------|-------| | 0 | 1 | | 1 | 0.901 | | 2 | 0.615 | | 3 | 0.174 | | 4 | 0.062 | | 5 | 0.000 | By the elements of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> the area of the rectilineal figure formed by the trapeziums is found by adding together all the ordinates except the first and last, and half the sum of the first and last, and multiplying that sum by the breadth of one of the trapeziums; now the sum of the ordinates, with the exception of the first and last, together with half the sum of the first and last, is \( 7.84981 \), and the common breadth of the trapeziums is \( 1 \), therefore \( \int \frac{x}{1+x^2} = 7.84981 \times 1 = 7.84981 \) nearly, as required. It is evident from \$ 137, that \( \int \frac{x}{1+x^2} \) taken between the limits of \( x = 0 \), and \( x = 1 \), is accurately equal to an arch of \( 45^\circ \), radius being unity, which arch being \( \frac{\pi}{4} \) will be found \( = 7854 \) nearly. If we recur to the series which has been found to express the above fluent in \$ 137, and put \( a = 1 \), and \( x = 1 \), we shall have \( \int \frac{x}{1+x^2} \) taken between the prescribed limits equal to It is impossible, however, to compute the fluent simply by the addition of the terms of this series, on account of the slowness of its convergency. 159. As the curvilinear area DPpd is the limit of the sum of the parallelograms DP', DP'', &c., which constitute the rectilineal figure inscribed in that area; as also the limit of the sum of the parallelograms DE, D'E', &c., which constitute the circumscribed figure, the number of parts into which Dd is divided being in either case conceived to be increased indefinitely, so that each may be continually diminished (and this being the case it is of no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> whether those parts be conceived as all equal or as unequal) so from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> we may conclude that if \( x', x'', x''', \ldots x^{(n)} \) be put to denote successive values of a variable quantity \( x \), and \( X' \), \( X'' \), \( X''' \), \ldots \( X^{(n)} \) the corresponding values of \( X \) any function of \( x \), the limit of the sum of the products \( X(x'-x), X'(x''-x'), X''(x'''-x'') \), &c., when the number of successive values of \( x \) and \( X \) is continually increased, so that the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between any two of them immediately following each other may be continually diminished, is equal to \( \int X \dot{x} \), the fluent to be taken between the two extreme values of \( x \). 160. It was in this manner that the first writers on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENTIAL">differential</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CALCULUS">calculus</a> conceived a fluent; as the difference between any two of its succeeding values is the product of the function \( X \) by \( x'-x \) the increment of \( x \), they called that product (when \( x'-x \) was conceived to be infinitely diminished) the Differential of the fluent; and as the fluent is the sum of all the products, or differentials, instead of calling it a fluent they called it an Integral; the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> by which an integral is found from its differential or fluxion they called Integration. The terms Integral and Integration are sometimes employed by writers in applying the method of fluxions to mathematical enquiries. To find the Lengths of Curves. 161. It has been shewn in § 63, that if the abscissa of a curve be denoted by \( x \), the ordinate by \( y \), and the curve line by \( z \), then \( z = \int (\dot{x}^2 + \dot{y}^2) \), hence the general formula for finding the length of a curve is \[ z = \int \sqrt{\dot{x}^2 + \dot{y}^2}. \] Therefore, if from the equation expressing the nature of a curve we find the value of \( \dot{y} \) in terms of \( \dot{x} \) and \( x \), or else the value of \( \dot{x} \) in terms of \( \dot{y} \) and \( y \), and substitute the one or the other in the above general formula, we shall obtain a fluxion the fluent of which will be the length of the curve. Ex. 1. Suppose the curve to be a parabola, and that \( AB=x \), \( BP=y \), the arch \( AP=z \), the parameter \( a \), then the equation of the curve being \( ax=y^2 \), we have \[ \dot{x} = \frac{2yy}{a}, \] and \[ z = \int \sqrt{\dot{x}^2 + \dot{y}^2} = \int \sqrt{\left(\frac{4y^2}{a^2} + \dot{y}^2\right)}. \] By comparing this expression with formula (B) in § 131, we find \[ \int \dot{y} \sqrt{(a^2+4y^2)} = \int \dot{y} \sqrt{(a^2+4y^2)} + \frac{1}{a} \int \frac{\dot{y}}{\sqrt{(a^2+4y^2)}}; \] again by § 127, \[ \int \frac{\dot{y}}{\sqrt{(a^2+4y^2)}} = \frac{1}{a} \left\{ 2y + \sqrt{(a^2+4y^2)} \right\} \] therefore \[ z = \frac{y \sqrt{(a^2+4y^2)}}{2a} + \frac{a}{4} \left\{ 2y + \sqrt{(a^2+4y^2)} \right\} + C. \] To determine the value of \( C \), we must consider that when \( y=0 \), then \( x=0 \), so that then the general formula will become simply \[ C = \frac{a}{4} l. a + C, \text{ and hence } C = -\frac{a}{4} l. a, \] therefore, substituting the value of \( C \), and bringing together the logarithmic quantities, \[ z = \frac{y \sqrt{(a^2+4y^2)}}{2a} + \frac{a}{4} \left\{ 2y + \sqrt{(a^2+4y^2)} \right\}. \] Ex. 2. Suppose the curve to be a circle, and that \( C \) Fig. 19 is its centre, and AE a quadrant of the circle. Put \( CB=x \), \( BP=y \), the arch \( EP=z \), the radius of the circle \( =a \), then \( x^2+y^2=a^2 \), and \( y=\sqrt{(a^2-x^2)} \), and \[ y = \frac{-x \dot{x}}{\sqrt{(a^2-x^2)}}, \text{ hence } \] \[ z = \int \sqrt{\dot{x}^2 + \dot{y}^2} = \int \sqrt{\dot{x}^2 + \frac{x^2 \dot{x}^2}{a^2-x^2}} = \int \frac{a \dot{x}}{\sqrt{(a^2-x^2)}}. \] This fluent can only be expressed by an infinite series, under which form it has been already exhibited in § 140, the radius being there supposed unity. Ex. 3. Let the curve be an ellipse, and let it be required to find the length of the curve between E the vertex of the lesser axis, and P any point in the curve. To simplify the calculation, let us suppose that the semi-transverse axis \( AC=1 \); put the semi-conjugate axis \( CE=b \), the eccentricity (that is \( \sqrt{(1-b^2)}=e \), the abscissa \( CB=x \), the ordinate \( PR=y \), the arch \( EP=z \); then, the equation of the curve being \( y^2=b^2(1-x^2) \), we have have \( y = b \sqrt{1 - x^2} \), and \( \dot{y} = \frac{-b x}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}} \), and therefore \[ z = \int \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = \int \sqrt{x^2 + \frac{b^2 x^2}{1 - x^2}} \] \[ = \int \frac{\sqrt{(1 - e^{2x})}}{\sqrt{(1 - x^2)}} \]

FLY

Pages 828-834

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> order of insects, the distinguishing characteristic of which is that their wings are transparent. By this they are distinguished from beetles, butterflies, grasshoppers, &c. Flies are subdivided into those which have four, and those which have two wings. Of those with four wings there are several genera <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> kinds; as the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANT">ant</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEE">bee</a>, the ichneumon, &c. Of those with two wings, there are likewise several kinds, as the gad-fly, gnat, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>-fly, &c. For their classification and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, see Entomology. House Fly. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSCA">Musca</a>. Pestilential Fly. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>. Fly, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> with leaden weights at its ends; or rather, a heavy wheel at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> to the axis of a windlass, jack, or the like; by means of which, the force of the power, whatever it is, is not only preserved, but equally distributed in all parts of the revolution of the machine. See Mechanics. Flies for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">Fishing</a>. See Fishing Fly. Vegetable Fly, a curious natural production chiefly found in the West Indies. "Excepting that it has no wings, it resembles the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRONE">drone</a> both in size and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> more than any other British insect. In the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of May it buries itself in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and begins to vegetate. By the latter end of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, the tree is arrived at its full growth, and resembles a coral branch; and is about three inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and bears several little pods, which dropping off become <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>, and from thence flies, like the British caterpillar." Such was the account originally given of this extraordinary production. But several boxes of these flies having been sent to Dr Hill for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, his report was this: "There is in Martinique a fungus of the clavaria kind, different in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> from those hitherto known. It produces soboles from its sides; I call it therefore clavaria sobolifera. It grows on putrid animal bodies, as our fungus ex pede equino from the dead <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s hoof. The cicada is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in Martinique; and in its nympha state, in which the old authors call it tettigometra, it buries itself under dead leaves to wait its change; and when the season is unfavourable, many perish.
