The seeds of the clavaria find a proper <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> on this dead insect, and grow. The tettigometra is among the cicadae in the British <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a>; the clavaria is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> now known. This is the fact, and all the fact; though the untaught inhabitants suppose a fly to vegetate, and though there is a Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> of the plant's growing into a trifoliate tree, and it has been figured with the creature <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> with this tree upon its back." See Edwards's Gleanings of Natural History. Fly-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">Boat</a>, or Flight, a large flat-bottomed Dutch vessel, whose burden is generally from 600 to 1200 tons. It is distinguished by a very high stern, resembling a Gothic turret, and by very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> buttocks below. Fly-Catcher, in Zoology. See Muscicapa. Venus's Fly Trap, a kind of sensitive plant. See Dionaea Muscipula, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Fly-Tree, in Natural History, a name given by the common people of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> to a tree, whose leaves, they say, at a certain <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the year produce flies. On examining these leaves about the middle of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, the time at which the flies <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to be produced, there are found on them a sort of bags of a tough <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, of about the size of a filbert, and of a dusky greenish colour. On opening one of these bags with a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, there is usually found a single full-grown fly, of the gnat kind, and a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small worms, which in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> or two more have wings, and fly away in the form of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>. The tree is of the mulberry kind, and its leaves are usually very largely stocked with these insect bags; and the generality of them are found to contain the insects in their worm state; when they become winged, they soon make their way out. The bags begin to appear when the leaves are young, and afterwards grow with them; but they never rumple the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> or injure its shape. They are of the kind of leaf-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALLS">galls</a>, and partake in all respects, except size, of a species we have frequent on the large maple, or, as it is called, the sycamore. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FLYERS">Flyers</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, such stairs as go straight, and do not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> round, or have the steps made tapering; but the fore and back <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of each stair and the ends respectively <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to one another: So that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> one flight do not carry you to your designed height, there is a broad half space; and then you fly again, with steps everywhere of the same breadth and length as before. Flyers, the performers in a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXHIBITION">exhibition</a> among the Mexicans, which was made on certain <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> festivals, and is thus described by Clavigero in his History of that people. "They sought in the woods for an extremely lofty tree, which, after stripping it of its branches and bark, they brought to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and fixed in the centre of some large <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>. They cased the point of the tree in a wooden <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a>, which, on account of some resemblance in its shape, the Spaniards called a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>. From this cylinder hung four strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, which served to support a square frame. In the space between the cylinder and the frame, they fixed four other thick ropes, which they twisted as many times round the tree as there were revolutions to be made by the flyers. These ropes were drawn through four holes, made in the middle of the four planks of which the frame consisted. The four <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> flyers, disguised like <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAGLES">eagles</a>, herons, and other birds, mounted the tree with great agility, by means of a rope which was fixed about it from the ground up to the frame; from the frame they mounted one at a time successively upon the cylinder, and after having danced there a little, they tied themselves round with the ends of the ropes, which were drawn through the holes of the frame, and launching with a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> from it, began their flight with their wings expanded. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of their bodies put the frame and the cylinder in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>; the frame by its revolutions gradually untwisted the cords by which the flyers swung; so that as the ropes lengthened, they made so much the greater circles in their flight. Whilst these four were flying, a fifth danced upon the cylinder, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> a little drum, or waving a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a>, without the smallest <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> of the danger he was in of being precipitated from such a height. The others who were upon the frame (10 or 12 persons generally mounted), as soon as they <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the flyers in their last revolution, precipitated themselves by the same ropes, in order to reach the ground at the same time amidst the acclamations of the populace. Those who precipitated themselves in this manner by the ropes, that they might make a still greater display of their agility, Flyers, agility, frequently passed from one rope to another, at Flying, that part where, on account of the little distance between them, it was possible for them to do so. The most essential point of this performance consisted in proportioning so justly the height of the tree with the length of the ropes, that the flyers should reach the ground with 13 revolutions, to represent by such number their century of 52 years, composed in the manner we have already mentioned. This celebrated diversion is still in use in that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; but no particular <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> is paid to the number of the revolutions of the flyers; as the frame is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> hexagonal or octagonal, and the flyers six or eight in number. In some places they put a rail round the frame, to prevent accidents, which were frequent after the conquest; as the Indians became much given to drinking, and used to mount the tree when intoxicated with wine or brandy, and were unable to keep their station on so great a height, which was usually 60 feet.

FLYING

Pages 834-835

the progressive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other winged animal, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. The parts of birds chiefly concerned in flying are the wings and tail; by the first, the bird sustains and wafts himself along; and by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, he is assisted, in ascending and descending, to keep his body poised and upright, and to obviate the vacillations thereof. It is by the size and strength of the pectoral muscles, that birds are so well disposed for quick, strong, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> flying. These muscles, which in men are scarcely a 70th <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the muscles of the body, in birds exceed and outweigh all the other muscles taken together; upon which Mr Willoughby makes this reflection, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it be possible for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to fly, his wings must be so contrived and adapted, that he may make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his legs, and not his arms, in managing them. The tail, Messrs Willoughby, Ray, and many others, imagine to be principally employed in steering and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the body in the air, as a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDDER">rudder</a>; but Borelli has put it beyond all doubt, that this is the least use of it, which is chiefly to assist the bird in its ascent and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> in the air, and to obviate the vacillations of the body and wings; for as to turning to this or that side, it is performed by the wings and inclination of the body, and but very little by the help of the tail. The flying of a bird, in effect, is quite a different thing from the rowing of a vessel. Birds do not vibrate their wings towards the tail, as oars are struck towards the stern, but waft them downwards; nor does the tail of the bird cut the air at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> as the rudder does the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; but is disposed horizontally, and preserves the same situation what way soever the bird turns. In effect, as a vessel is turned about on a centre of gravity to the right, by a brisk application of the oars to the left; so a bird, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> the air with its right wing alone towards the tail, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> turn its fore part to the left. Thus pigeons changing their course to the left, would labour it with their right wing, keeping the other almost at rest. Birds of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> neck alter their course by the inclination of their head and neck; which altering the course of gravity, the bird will proceed in a new <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. The manner of Flying is thus. The bird first <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDS">bends</a> his legs, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> with a violent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a> from the ground; then opens and expands the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> of his wings, so as to make a right line perpendicular to the sides of his body: thus the wings, with all the feathers therein, constitute one continued lamina. Being now raised a little above the horizon, and vibrating the wings with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> force and velocity perpendicularly against the subject air, that fluid resists those successions, both from its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> inactivity and elasticity, by means of which the whole body of the bird is protruded. The resistance the air makes to the withdrawing of the wings, and consequently the progress of the bird, will be so much the greater, as the waist or stroke of the fan of the wing is longer: but as the force of the wing is continually diminished by this resistance, when the two forces continue to be in equilibrio, the bird will remain suspended in the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; for the bird only ascends so long as the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of air the wing describes makes a resistance equal to the excess of the specific gravity of the bird above the air. If the air, therefore, be so rare as to give way with the same velocity as it is struck withal, there will be no resistance, and consequently the bird can never mount. Birds never fly upwards in a perpendicular line, but always in a parabola. In a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> ascent, the natural and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> tendency would oppose and destroy each other, so that the progress would be very slow. In a direct ascent they would aid one another, so that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> would be too precipitate. Artificial Flying, that attempted by men, by the assistance of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>. The art of flying has been attempted by several persons in all ages. The Leucadians, out of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, are reported to have had a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of precipitating a man from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> cliff into the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, first fixing feathers, variously expanded, round his body, in order to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the fall. Friar <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a>, who lived near 500 years ago, not only affirms the art of flying possible, but assures us that he himself knew how to make an engine wherein a man sitting might be able to convey himself through the air like a bird; and further adds, that there was then one who had tried it with success. The secret consisted in a couple of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> thin hollow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> globes, exhausted of air; which being much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> than air, would sustain a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> whereon a person might sit. Father Francisco Lana, in his Prodromo, proposes the same thing as his own thoughts. He computes, that a round vessel of plate <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, 14 feet in diameter, weighing three ounces the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> foot, will only weigh 1848 ounces; whereas a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of air of the same bulk will weigh 2155½ ounces; so that the globe will not only be sustained in the air, but will carry with it a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of 373½d ounces; and by increasing the bulk of the globe, without increasing the thickness of the metal, he adds, a vessel might be made to carry a much greater weight.—But the fallacy is obvious: a globe of the dimensions he describes, Dr Hook shews, would not sustain the pressure of the air, but be crushed inwards. Besides, in whatever ratio the bulk of the globe were increased, in the same must the thickness of the metal, and consequently the weight be increased: so that there would be no advantage in such augmentation. See AEROSTATION. The same author describes an engine for flying, invented by the Sieur Besnier, a smith of Sable, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a>. Vid. Philosoph. Collect. The philosophers of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> the second's reign were mightily busied about this art. The famous Bishop Wilkins was so confident of success in it, that he says, he does not question but in future ages it will be as usual to hear a man call for his wings, when he is going a journey, as it is now to call for his boots. Flying <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">Bridge</a>. See Bridge. Flying Fish, a name given to several <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of fish, which, by means of long fins, can keep themselves out of the water for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. See Exocoetus, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Flying <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PINION">Pinion</a>, is part of a clock, having a fly or fan whereby to gather air, and so <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDLE">bridle</a> the rapidity of the clock's motion, when the weight descends in the striking part.

FO

Pages 835-835
or Foe; an idol of the Chinese. He was originally worshipped in the Indies, and transported from thence into China, together with the fables with which the Indian books were filled. He is said to have performed most wonderful things, which the Chinese have described in several volumes, and represented by cuts. Sect of Fo. See China, No 104. Fo-Kien. See Forien. Foal, or Colt and Filly; the young of the horse kind. The word colt, among dealers, is understood of the male, as filly is of the female. See Colt. Focus, in Geometry and Conic Sections, is applied to certain points in the parabola, ellipse, and hyperbola, where the rays reflected from all parts of these curves concur and meet. See Conic Sections. Focus, in Optics, a point in which any number of rays, after being reflected or refracted, meet. Fodder, any kind of meat for horses or other cattle. In some places, hay and straw, mingled together, is peculiarly denominated fodder. Fodder, in the civil law, is used for a prerogative that the prince has, to be provided with corn and other meats for his horses, by the subjects, in his warlike expeditions. Fodder, among miners, a measure containing 22 hundred and a half weight; in London the fodder is only 20 hundred weight. Foddering a ship. See Fothering. Foenugreek. See Trigonella, Botany Index. FOENUS NAUTICUM. Where money was lent to a merchant to be employed in a beneficial trade, with condition to be repaid with extraordinary interest, in case such voyage was safely performed, the agreement was sometimes called focus nauticum, sometimes usura maritima. But as this gave an opening for usurious and gaming contracts, 19 Geo. II. c. 37, enacts, that all money lent on bottomry, or at respondentia, on vessels bound to or from the East Indies, shall be expressly lent upon the ship or merchandise; the lender to have the benefit of salvage, &c. Blackst. Com. ii. 459. Mol. de Jour. Mar. 361.

FOETOR

Pages 835-835

in Medicine, fetid effluvia arising from the body <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> thereof.

FOETUS

Pages 835-835

the young of all viviparous animals whilst in the womb, and of oviparous animals before being hatched: the name is transferred by botanists to the embryos of vegetables. Strictly, the name is applied to the young after it is perfectly formed; previous to which it is usually fetus, called Embryo. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> fetus are several peculiarities not to be found in the adult; some of them are as follow: 1. The <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a> of the navel string, which are continuations of the hypogastrics, are, after the birth, shrivelled up, and form the ligamenta umbilici infer. 2. The veins of the navel string are formed by the union of all the venous branches in the placenta, and passing into the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a> become the falciform ligament of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a>. 3. The lungs, before being inflated with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> and heavy, but after one <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a> they become <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and as it were spongy; and it may be noted here, that the notion of the lungs sinking in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> before the child breathes, and of their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a> after the reception of air, are no certain proofs that the child had <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> had not breathed, much less that it was murdered: for the uninflated lungs become specifically <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> than water as soon as any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a> takes <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in them; and this soon happens after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the child; besides, where the utmost care hath been taken to preserve the child, it hath breathed once or twice and then died. 4. The thymus gland is very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> in the fetus, but dwindles away in proportion as years advance. 5. The foramen ovale in the heart of a fetus, is generally closed in an adult.

FOG

Pages 835-835
or Mist, a meteor, consisting of gross vapours, floating near the surface of the earth. Mists, according to Lord Bacon, are imperfect condensations of the air, consisting of a large proportion of the air, and a small one of the aqueous vapour; and these happen in the winter, about the change of the weather from frost to thaw, or from thaw to frost; but in the summer, and in the spring, from the expansion of the dew. If the vapours which are raised plentifully from the earth and waters, either by the solar or subterraneous heat, do at their first entrance into the atmosphere meet with cold enough to condense them to a considerable degree, their specific gravity is by that means increased, and so they will be stopped from ascending; and either return back in form of dew or of drizzling rain, or remain suspended some time in the form of a fog. Vapours may be seen on the high grounds as well as the low, but more especially about marshy places. They are easily dissipated by the wind, as also by the heat of the sun. They continue longest in the lowest grounds, because these places contain most moisture, and are least exposed to the action of the wind. Hence we may easily conceive, that fogs are only low clouds, or clouds in the lowest region of the air; as clouds are no other than fogs raised on high. See Cloud. When fogs stink, then the vapours are mixed with sulphureous exhalations, which smell so. Objects viewed through fogs appear larger and more remote than through the common air. Mr Boyle observes, that upon the coast of Coromandel, and most maritime parts of the East Indies, there are, notwithstanding the heat of the climate, annual fogs so thick, as to occasion people, of other nations who reside there, and even the more tender sort of the natives, to keep their houses close shut up. Fogs are commonly strongly electrified, as appears

FOGAGE

Pages 835-836

in the forest <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> grass not eaten up in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>.

FOIBLE

Pages 836-836

a French <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a>, frequently used also in our <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. It literally signifies weak; and in that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> is applied to the body of animals and the parts thereof, as foible reins, foible sight, &c., being derived from the Italian flevoile, of the Latin flebilis, to be "lamented, pitied." But it is chiefly used with us substantively, to denote a defect <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> flaw in a person or thing. Thus we say, Every person has his foible; and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> secret consists in hiding it artfully: Princes are gained by flattery, that is their foible. The foible of young people is <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; the foible of old men is avarice; the foible of the great and learned is vanity; the foible of women and girls, coquetry, or an affection of having gallants: You should know the forte and the foible of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> before you employ him: We should not let people perceive that we know their foible.

FOIL

Pages 836-836

among jewellers, a thin <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> of metal placed under a precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, in order to make it look transparent, and give it an agreeable different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, either deep <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>: thus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> you want a stone to be of a pale colour, put a foil of that colour under it; or if you would have it deep, lay a dark one under it. These foils are made either of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, or gold and silver together. The copper foils are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> known by the name of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUREMBERG">Nuremberg</a> or German foils; and are prepared as follows: Procure the thinnest copper plates you can get; <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> these plates gently upon a well-polished anvil, with a polished hammer, as thin as possible; and placing them between two <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> plates as thin as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> them in the fire; then boil the foil in a pipkin, with equal quantities of tartar and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, constantly stirring them till by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> they become <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>; after which, taking them out and drying them, give them another hammering, till they are made fit for your purpose: however, care must be taken not to give the foils too much heat, for fear of melting; nor must they be too <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> boiled, for fear of attracting too much salt. The manner of polishing these foils is as follows: Take a plate of the best copper, one foot long and about five or six inches wide, polished to the greatest perfection; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> this to a long convex, fasten it upon a half roll, and fix it to a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">bench</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>; then take some chalk washed as clean as possible, and filtered through a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth, till it be as fine as you can make it; and having laid some thereof on the roll, and wetted the copper all over, lay your foils on it, and with a polishing stone and the chalk polish your foils till they are as bright as a looking-glass; after which they must be dried, and laid up secure from dust.

FOKIEN

Pages 836-836

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, commodiously situated for <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it bordering on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, in which they catch <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities of fish, which they send salted to other parts of the empire. Its shores are very uneven, by reason of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> and variety of its bays; and there are many forts built thereon to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is hot, but pure and wholesome. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> are almost everywhere disposed into a kind of amphitheatres, by the labour of the inhabitants, with terraces placed one above another. The fields are watered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, which issue out of the mountains, and which the husbandmen conduct in such a manner as to overflow the fields of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> when they please, because it thrives best in watery ground. They make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> of bamboo for this purpose. They have all commodities in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with the rest of China; but more particularly <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MUSK">musk</a>, precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, quicksilver, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, hempen cloth, callico, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and all sorts of utensils wrought to the greatest perfection. From other countries they have cloves, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDAL">sandal</a> wood, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMBER">amber</a>, coral, and many other things. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> is Fou-tebeou Fou; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, as others would have it written, Fucherofo. But as for Fokien, which most geographers make the capital, Grosier informs us there is no such <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>.

FOLARD

Pages 836-837
CHARLES, an eminent Frenchman, famous for his skill and knowledge in the military art, was born at Avignon in 1669, of a noble family, but not a rich one. He discovered an early turn for the sciences, and a strong passion for arms; which last was so inflamed by reading Caesar's Commentaries, that he enlisted at 16 years of age. His father got him off, and shut him in a monastery; but he made his escape in about two years after, and entered himself a second time in quality of cadet. His inclination for military affairs, and the great pains he took to accomplish himself in that way, recommended him to notice; and he was admitted into the friendship of the first-rate officers. M. de Vendome, who commanded in Italy in 1722, made him his aide-de-camp, having conceived the highest regard for him; and soon after sent him with part of his forces into Lombardy. He was entirely trusted by the commander of that army; and no measures were concerted, or steps taken, without consulting him. By pursuing his plans, many places were taken, and advantages gained; and such, in short, were his services, that he had a pension of 500 livres settled upon him, and was honoured with the cross of St Louis. He distinguished himself greatly, August 15, 1705, at the battle of Cassano; where he received a wound upon his left hand, which deprived him of the use of it ever after. It was at this battle that he conceived the first idea of the system of columns, which he afterwards prefixed to his Commentaries upon Polybius. The duke of Orleans sending De Vendome again into Italy in 1726, Folard had orders to throw himself into Modena to defend it against Eugene; where, though he acquitted himself with his usual skill, he was very near being assassinated. The description which he has given of the conduct and character of the governor of this town, may be found in his Treatise of the Defence of Places, and deserves to be read. He received a dangerous wound on the thigh at the battle of Malplaquet, and was some time after made prisoner by Prince Eugene. Being exchanged in 1711, he was made FOLC made governor of Bourbourg. In 1714, he went to Malta, to assist in defending that island against the Turks. Upon his return to France, he embarked for Sweden, having a passionate desire to see Charles XII. He acquired the esteem and confidence of that famous general, who sent him to France to negotiate the re-establishment of James II. upon the throne of England; but that project being dropped, he returned to Sweden, followed Charles XII. in his expedition to Norway, and served under him at the siege of Fredericksland, where that prince was killed, Dec. 11, 1718. Folard then returned to France; and made his last campaign in 1719, under the duke of Berwick, in quality of colonel. From that time he applied himself intensely to the study of the military art as far as it could be studied at home; and built his theories upon the foundation of his experience and observations on facts. He contracted an intimacy with Count Saxe, who, as he then declared, would one day prove a very great general. He was chosen a fellow of the Royal Society of London in 1749; and, in 1751, made a journey to Avignon, where he died in 1752, aged 83 years. He was the author of several works, the principal of which are: 1. Commentaries upon Polybius, in six volumes, &c. 2. A Book of New Discoveries in War. 3. A Treatise concerning the Defence of Places, &c., in French. Those who would know more of this eminent soldier, may consult a French piece, entitled, Memoires pour servir à l'Histoire de M. le Chevalier de Folard. Ratisbon, 1753, 12mo.

FOLC-LANDS

Pages 837-837

(Sax.) copyhold lands so called in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Saxons, as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>-lands were called boc-lands, Kitch. 174. Folkland was terra vulgi <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> popularis; the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> of the vulgar people, who had no certain estate therein, but held the same, under the rents and services accustomed or agreed, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> only of their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THANE">thane</a>; and it was therefore not put in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, but accounted pradium rusticum et ignobile. Spelm. of Feuds, c. 5.

FOLCMOTE

Pages 837-837
or FOLKMOTE, (Sax. Folgemote, i.e. convenitus populi), is compounded of folk, populus, and mote, or gemote, convenire; and signified originally, as Sonner in his Saxon Dictionary informs us, a general assembly of the people, to consider of and order matters of the commonwealth. And Sir Henry Spelman says, the folcmote was a sort of annual parliament or convention of the bishops, thanes, aldermen, and freemen, upon every May-day yearly; where the laymen were sworn to defend one another and the king, and to preserve the laws of the kingdom; and then consulted of the common safety. But Dr Brady infers from the laws of the Saxon kings of England, that it was an inferior court, held before the king's reeve or steward, every month, to do folk right, or compose smaller differences, from whence there lay appeal to the superior courts; Gloss. p. 48. Squire seems to think the folcmote not distinct from the shiremote, or common general meeting of the county. See his Angl. Sax. Gov. 155. n. Manwood mentions folcmote as a court holden in London, wherein all the folk and people of the city did complain of the mayor and aldermen, for misgovernment within the said city; and this word is still in use among the Londoners, and denotes celebrem ex tota ci- citate conventum. Stow's Survey. According to Ken- net, the folcmote was a common council of all the inhabitants of a city, town, or borough, convened often by sound of bell, to the Mote Hall or House; or it was applied to a larger congress of all the freemen within a county, called the shiremote, where formerly all knights and military tenants did fealty to the king, and elected the annual sheriff on the 1st of October; till this popular election, to avoid tumults and riots, devolved to the king's nomination, anno 1315, 3 Edw. I. After which the city folkmote was swallowed up in a select committee or common council, and the county folkmote in the sheriff's tourn and assizes. The word folkmote was also used for any kind of popular or public meetings; as of all the tenants at the court leet, or court baron, in which signification it was of a less extent. Paroch. Antig. 120.

FOLENGIO

Pages 837-837

THEOPHILUS, an Italian poet, was a native of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>. He was known also by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Merlin Coraggio, a name which he gave to a poem, and which has been adopted ever since for all trifling performances of the same <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, consisting of buffoonery, puns, anagrams, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WIT">wit</a> without <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, and humour without good <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. His poem was called The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACARONI">Macaroni</a>, from an Italian cake of the same name, which is sweet to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, but has not the least alimentary virtue, on the contrary pall's the appetite and clogs the stomach. These idle poems, however, became the reigning taste in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and in France; they give birth to macaroni <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a>, and reaching England, to macaroni clubs; till, in the end, every thing insipid, contemptible, and ridiculous, in the character, dress, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> behaviour, of both men and women, is now summed up in the despicable appellation of a macaroni. Folengio died in 1544.

FOLIA

Pages 837-837

among botanists, particularly signify the leaves of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; those of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> being expressed by the word petals. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>.

FOLIAGE

Pages 837-837

is particularly used for the representations of such <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, leaves, branches, rinds, &c. whether <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>, as are used for enrichments on capitals, friezes, pediments, &c. FOLIATING of LOOKING-GLASSES, the spreading the plates over, after they are polished, with quicksilver, &c. in order to reflect the image. It is performed thus: A thin blotting <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> is spread on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> and sprinkled with fine chalk; and then a fine lamina or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> of tin, called foil, is laid over the paper; upon this is poured <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>, which is to be distributed equally over the leaf with a hare's foot or cotton; over this is laid a clean paper, and over that the glass plate, which is pressed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and the paper gently drawn out with the left; this being done, the plate is covered with a thicker paper, and loaded with a greater <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, that the superfluous mercury may be driven out and the tin adhere more closely to the glass. When it is dried, the weight is removed, and the looking-glass is complete. Some add an ounce of marcasite, melted by the fire; and, lest the mercury should evaporate in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, they pour it into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; and when cooled, squeeze through a cloth, or through <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>. Some add a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an ounce of tin and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to the marcasite, that the glass may dry the sooner. FOLIATING of Globe looking-glasses, is done as follows:

FOLKES

Pages 837-838

MARTIN, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and antiquarian of considerable eminence, was born in Westminster in the year 1693. A Mr Cappel, once professor of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAUMUR">Saumur</a>, was his private <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a>. When 17 years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, he was sent to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLARE">Clare</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, where he successfully applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>; and when only twenty-three years of age he was chosen a fellow of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>. His ingenious communications acquired him so much applause, that he was frequently chosen into its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>. He was in habits of friendship with the illustrious Newton, at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>, and by his influence was elected one of the vice-presidents in the year 1723. Mr Folkes became a candidate for the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton; but the superior <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of Sir Hans Sloane rendered his application ineffectual. In 1733 and the two subsequent years, his residence was for the most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, with the view of improving himself in the knowledge of classical antiquities. To ascertain the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> and value of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> coins, he carefully consulted the cabinets of the curious; and on his return home he presented to the Antiquarian Society, of which he was a member, a dissertation on this subject. He read before the same learned body, a dissertation on the measurement of Trajan's and Antonine's pillar, together with other remains of antiquity. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of his observations he presented to the Royal Society; and, in particular, "Remarks on the standard <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> preserved in the Capitol of Rome," and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of an ancient globe in the Farnesian <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>. He visited <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1739, where he was received with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> respect, and honoured with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of the most eminent literary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> in that <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>. This respect indeed he was entitled to by his unwearied application to many branches of knowledge which were both curious and useful. His valuable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, entitled "A <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of English silver coins, from the Norman Conquest to the present time, with their weights, intrinsic values, and some remarks upon the several pieces," was printed in the year 1745. Among the many honours conferred upon Mr Folkes, he was created <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of laws by both <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, and chosen president of the Antiquarian Society. He <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to furnish the Philosophical Transactions with many learned papers, till his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CAREER">career</a> was stopped by a paralytic stroke, which terminated his useful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in the year 1654. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of very extensive knowledge and great accuracy; but the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> benefit to science which resulted from his labours, was his treatise on the intricate subject of coins, weights, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>. His cabinet and library were <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and valuable, and exposed to public <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> after his death. His private character was distinguished for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a>, generosity, and friendship.

FOLKESTONE

Pages 838-838

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, between <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-HYTHE">Hythe</a>, 72 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, appears to have been a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, from the Roman coins and British bricks often found in it. Stillington and Tanner take it for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPIS">Lapis</a> Tituli of Nennius. It was burnt by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> Godwin, and by the French in the reign of Edward III. It had five churches, now reduced to one. It is a member of the town and port of Dover; and has a weekly market and an annual fair. It is chiefly noted for the multitude of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> boats that belong to its harbour, which are employed in the season in catching mackerel for London; to which they are carried by the mackerel boats of London and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARKING">Barking</a>. About Michaelmas, the Folkestone barks, with others for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>, go away to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a> coasts to catch herrings for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-YARMOUTH">Yarmouth</a> and Leostoff.—Folkestone gives the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Viscount to William Henry Bouvierie, whose grandfather, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a>, was so created in 1747. It has been observed of some hills in this neighbourhood, that they have visibly sunk and grown lower within <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>.

FOLLICULUS

Pages 838-838

(from follis, "a bag,") a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of seed-vessel first mentioned by Linnæus in his Delicatissima Planter, generally consisting of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALVE">valve</a>, which opens from bottom to top on one side, and has no suture for fastening <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> attaching the seeds within it. FOLLICULI are likewise defined by the same author to be small glandular vessels distended with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, which appear on the surface of some <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; as at the foot of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-milfoil, and on the leaves of aldrovanda. In the former the leaves in question are roundish, and furnished with an appearance like two horns; in the latter, pot-shaped, and semicircular.

FOLLIS

Pages 838-839

according to Mr Locke, consists in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> of false conclusions from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> principles; by which it is distinguished from madness, which draws just conclusions from false principles. But this seems too confined a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a>; folly, in its most general acceptation, denoting a weakness of intellect <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a>, or some partial absurdity in sentiment or conduct.

FOMAHAUT

Pages 839-839

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a> of the first magnitude in the constellation <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AQUARIUS">AQUARIUS</a>.

FOMENTATION

Pages 839-839

in Medicine, is a fluid externally applied, usually as warm as the patient can bear it, and in the following manner. Two <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLANNEL">flannel</a> cloths are dipped into the heated liquor, one of which is wrung as dry as the necessary speed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> admit, then immediately applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> affected; it lies on until the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> begins to go off, and the other is in readiness to apply at the instant in which the first is removed; thus these flannels are alternately applied, so as to keep the affected part constantly supplied with them warm. This is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> 15 minutes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> half an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, and repeated as occasion may require. Every intention of relaxing and soothing by fomentations may be answered as well by warm <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> alone as when the whole tribe of emollients are boiled in it; but when discutients or antiseptics are required, such ingredients must be called in as are adapted to that end. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of heat should never exceed that of producing a pleasant <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> heat produces effects very opposite to that intended by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of fomentation.

FONG-CHOU

Pages 839-839

the name of a ridiculous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> among the Chinese. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">CHINA</a>, No 105.

FONG-YANG

Pages 839-839

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of KHANG-NONG. It is situated on a mountain, which hangs over the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol21.html#article-YELLOW_RIVER"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">Yellow</a> river, and encloses with its walls several fertile little hills. Its jurisdiction is very extensive: for it comprehends 18 cities; five of which are of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, and 13 of the third class. As this was the birth-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Hong-vou, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the preceding dynasty, this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> formed a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of rendering it a famous and magnificent city, in order to make it the seat of empire. After having expelled the Western Tartars, who had taken possession of China, he transferred his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> hither, and named the city Fong-yang; that is to say, "The Place of the Eagle's Splendour." His intention, as we have said, was to beautify and enlarge it; but the inequality of the ground, the scarcity of fresh <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and above all the vicinity of his father's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>, made him change his design. By the unanimous advice of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> officers, this prince established his court at NAN-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">KING</a>, a more beautiful and commodious place. When he had formed this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>, a Fong-Yang stop was put to the intended works; the imperial <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> which was to have been enclosed by a triple wall, the walls of the city to which a circumference of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> leagues were assigned, and the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> that were begun, all were abandoned; and nothing was finished, but three monuments that still remain. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> and magnificence of these sufficiently show what the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of this city would have been, had the emperor pursued his original design. The first is the tomb of the father of Hong-vou, to decorate which no expense was spared; it is called Hoan-lin, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Tomb. The second is a tower built in the middle of the city, which is of an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> form, and 100 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. The third is a magnificent temple erected to the god Fo. At first it was only a pagod, to which Hong-vou retired after having lost his parents, and where he was admitted as an inferior <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a>; but having soon become weary of this kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, he enlisted with the chief of a band of banditti, who had revolted from the Tartars. As he was bold and enterprising, the general made choice of him for his son-in-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>; soon after he was declared his successor by the unanimous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of the troops. The new chief seeing himself at the head of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> party, had the presumption to carry his views to the throne. The Tartars, informed of the progress of his arms, sent a numerous <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> into the field; but he surprised and attacked them with so much impetuosity, that they were obliged to fly; and, though they several times returned to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, they were still defeated, and at length driven entirely out of China. As soon as he mounted the throne, he caused the superb temple which we have mentioned to be raised out of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> to the Bonzes, who had received him in his distress, and assigned them a revenue sufficient for the maintenance of 300 persons, under a chief of their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, whom he constituted a mandarin, with power of governing them, independent of the officers of the city. This pagod was supported as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as the preceding dynasty lasted; but that of the Eastern Tartars, which succeeded, suffered it to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> to ruin.

FONTAINBLEAU

Pages 840-840

a town in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of France, and in the Gatinois, remarkable for its fine <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, which has been the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the kings of France used to lodge when they went a hunting. It was first embellished by Francis I. and every successive <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> has added something to it; so that it may now be called the finest <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in the world. It stands in the midst of a forest, consisting of 26,424 arpents of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, each containing 100 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> perches, and each perch 18 feet. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 23. N. Lat. 49. 22.

FONTAINE

Pages 839-840

JOHN, a celebrated French poet, and one of the first-rate geniuses of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, was born at Chateau-Thierry in Champagne, the 8th of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1621, of a good family. At the age of 19 he entered amongst the Oratorians, but quitted that order 18 months after. He was 22 years of age before he knew his own talents for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>; but hearing an ode of Malherbe read, upon the assassination of Henry IV., he was so taken with admiration of it, that the poetical fire, which had before lain dormant within him, seemed to be enkindled from that of the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> poet. He applied himself to read, to meditate, to repeat, in fine to imitate, the works of Malherbe. The first essays of his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a> he confined to one of his relations who made him read the best Latin authors, Horace, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, Terence, Quintilian, &c. and then the Fontaine's best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> in French and Italian. He applied himself likewise to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the Greek authors, particularly <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> and Plutarch. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> afterwards his parents made him marry a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-general, a relation of the great Racine. This young lady, besides her very great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, was remarkable for the delicacy of her <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, and Fontaine never composed any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> without consulting her. But as her temper was none of the best, to avoid dissension, he separated himself from her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> as often as he well could. The famous duchess of Bouillon, niece to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Mazarine, being exiled to Chateau-Thierry, took particular notice of Fontaine. Upon her recall, he followed her to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; where by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of one of his relations, he got a pension settled upon him. He met with great friends and protectors amongst the most distinguished persons of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, but Madame de la Sablière was the most particular. She took him to live at her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and it was then that Fontaine, divested of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> concerns, led a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> conformable to his disposition, and cultivated an acquaintance with all the great men of the age. It was his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, after he was fixed at Paris, to go every year, during the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of September, to his native <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of Chateau-Thierry, and pay a visit to his wife, carrying with him Racine, Despreaux, Chapelle, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> some other celebrated writers. When he has sometimes gone thither alone by himself, he has come away without remembering even to call upon her; but seldom omitted selling some <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his lands, by which means he squandered away a considerable fortune. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Madame de la Sablière, he was invited into England, particularly by Madame Mazarine, and by St Evremond, who promised him all the sweets and comforts of life; but the difficulty of learning the English <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and the liberality of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, prevented his voyage. About the end of the year 1692 he fell dangerously ill; and, as is customary upon these occasions in the Romish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, he made a general confession of his whole life to P. Poguet, an Oratorian; and, before he received the sacrament, he sent for the gentlemen of the French Academy, and in their presence declared his sincere compunction for having composed his Tales; a work he could not reflect upon without the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a> and detestation; promising that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it should please God to restore his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, he would employ his talents only in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> upon matters of morality or piety. He survived this illness two years, living in the most exemplary and edifying manner, and died the 13th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1695, being 74 years of age. When they stripped his body, they found next his skin a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> shirt; which gave room for the following <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of the younger Racine: *Et l'Auteur de Jaconde est orné d'un Cilice.* Fontaine's character is remarkable for a simplicity, candour, and probity seldom to be met with. He was of an obliging disposition; cultivating a real friendship with his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> poets and authors; and what is very rare, beloved and esteemed by them all. His conversation was neither gay nor brilliant, especially when he was not amongst his intimate friends. One <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> being invited to a dinner at a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> general's, he ate a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a>, but did not speak. Rising up from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> very early, under <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRETEXT">pretext</a> of going to the academy, one of Fontaine's company represented to him that it was not yet a proper time: "Well (says he), if it is not, I <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> stay a little longer." He had one son by his wife in the year 1660. At the age of 14, he put him into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of M. de Harley, the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>, recommending to him his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> and fortune. It is said, that having been a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> time without seeing him, he happened to meet him one day visiting, without recollecting him again, and mentioned to the company that he thought that young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> had a good deal of wit and understanding. When they told him it was his own son, he answered in the most tranquil manner, "Ha! truly I am glad on't." An indifference, or rather an absence of mind, influenced his whole conduct, and rendered him often insensible to the inclemency of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. Madame de Bouillon going one morning to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> him, abstracted in thought, sitting in an arbour; returning at night, she found him in the same place, and in the same attitude, although it was very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, and had rained almost the whole day. He carried this simplicity so far, that he was scarcely sensible of the bad effects some of his writings might occasion, particularly his Tales. In a great sickness, his confessor exhorting him to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> and alms deeds: "As for alms deeds (replied Fontaine), I am not able, having nothing to give; but they are about publishing a new edition of my Tales, and the bookseller owes me a hundred copies; you shall have them to sell, and distribute their amount amongst the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>." Another time P. Poguet exhorting him to repent of his faults, "If he has committed any (cried the nurse), I am sure it is more from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> than malice, for he has as much simplicity as an infant." One time having composed a tale, wherein he made a profane application of those words of the Gospel, "<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>, five talents thou didst deliver to me," he dedicated it, by a most ingenious prologue, to the celebrated Arnauld, telling him, it was to show to posterity the great esteem he had for the learned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>. He was not sensible of the indecency of the dedication, and the profane application of the text, till Boileau and Racine represented it to him. He addressed another, by a dedication in the same manner, to the archbishop of Paris. His Fables are an immortal work, exceeding every thing in that kind, both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the learned. People of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, the offerer they read them, will find continually new beauties and charms, not to be met with elsewhere. The descendants of this great poet were long exempted in France from all taxes and impositions; a privilege which the intendants of Soisson thought it an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to confirm to them.

FONTAINES

Pages 840-841
Peter Francis**, a French critic, was born of a good family at Rouen in 1685. At 15, he entered into the society of the Jesuits; and at 30, quitted Fontaine quitted it, for the sake of returning to the world. He was a priest, and had a cure in Normandy; but left it, Fontarabia, and was, as a man of wit and letters, some time with the cardinal d'Auvergne. Having excited some attention at Paris by certain critical productions, the Abbé Bignon in 1724 committed to him the Journal des Savans. He acquitted himself well in this department, and was peaceably enjoying the applause of the public, when his enemies, whom by critical strictures in his Journal he had made such, formed an accusation against him of a most abominable crime, and procured him to be imprisoned. By the credit of powerful friends, he was set at liberty in 1725; the magistrate of the police took upon himself the trouble of justifying him in a letter to the Abbé Bignon; and this letter having been read amidst his fellow labourers in the Journal, he was unanimously re-established in his former credit. This happened in 1725. But with whatever repute he might acquit himself in this Journal, frequent disgusts made him frequently abandon it. He laboured meanwhile in some new periodical works, from which he derived his greatest fame. In 1731, he began one under the title of Nouvelliste du Parnasse, ou Reflections sur les Ouvrages nouveaux: but only proceeded to two volumes; the work having been suppressed by authority, from the incessant complaints of authors ridiculed therein. About three years after, in 1735, he obtained a new privilege for a periodical production, entitled, Observations sur les Ecrits Modernes; which, after continuing to 33 volumes, was suppressed again in 1743. Yet the year following, 1744, he published another weekly paper, called, Jugemens sur les Ouvrages nouveaux, and proceeded to 11 volumes: the two last being done by other hands. In 1745, he was attacked with a disorder in the breast, which ended in a dropsey that proved fatal in five weeks. "He was (says M. Freron) born a sentimental person; a philosopher in conduct as well as in principle; exempt from ambition; and of a noble firm spirit, which would not submit to sue for preferments or titles. In common conversation he appeared only a common man; but when subjects of literature, or anything out of the ordinary way, were agitated, he discovered great force of imagination and wit." Besides the periodical works mentioned above, he was the author of many others: his biographer gives us no less than 17 articles; many of them critical, some historical, and some translations from English writers, chiefly from Pope, Swift, Fielding, &c. The Abbé de la Porte, published, in 1757, L'Esprit de l'Abbé des Fontaines, in 4 vols.

FONTANELLA

Pages 841-841

in Anatomy, imports the quadrangular aperture found betwixt the os frontis and ossa sincipitis, in children <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> born; which is also called fossa pulsatilis.

FONTARABIA

Pages 841-841

a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> port town of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISCAY">Biscay</a>, and in the territory of Guipuscoa, seated on a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> on the sea shore, and on the river Bidassoa. It is small, but well fortified both by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and art; and has a good harbour, though dry at low <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. It is built in the form of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>, on the declivity of a hill, and surrounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> side by the Fontarabia lofty Pyrenean <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. It is a very important Fontanelle <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, being accounted the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">key</a> of Spain on that side. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 43. N. Lat. 43.

FONTENELLE

Pages 841-842

Bernard le Bovier de, was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of letters, born at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROUEN">Rouen</a> in 1657, the most universal genius of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. in the estimation of Voltaire. He received his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of Jesuits at Rouen, where the quickness of his parts became conspicuous at a very early <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. He was capable of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> Latin verses when only 13, which were deemed worthy of being published. He studied the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> at the desire of his father; but as he lost the very first cause in which he was employed as an advocate, he became disgusted with his profession, and devoted himself entirely to literature and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. He composed a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the operas of Psyche and Bellerophon, which were printed under the name of his uncle Thomas Corneille. He wrote a tragedy called Aspar; but as it did not succeed, he consigned the manuscript to the flames, and never afterwards attempted that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>. His Dialogues of the dead were published in the year 1683, which were well received, as a specimen of elegant composition, combining morality with the charms of literature. His "Lettres du Chevalier d'Her," published in 1685 without his name, discovered much <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and ingenuity, but at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> no small share of affectation. His "Entretiens sur la Pluralité des Mondes," has been regarded as one of his ablest performances, combining science and philosophy with vivacity and humour, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> which may be said to belong almost exclusively to the French. It was perused by all, and translated into several foreign languages. In his "<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORACLES">Oracles</a>," he supported the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that oracles were forgeries, in opposition to those who contended that they were supernatural operations of evil spirits, put to silence by the appearing of Christ, and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> he exposed himself to clerical animadversion. His "Pastoral Poems" appeared in the year 1688, with a discourse on the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the eclogue, which were very much admired for their delicacy of sentiment, as was also his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">opera</a> of "Thetis and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELEUS">Peleus</a>;" but his "Enæas and Lavinia" was not so successful. In the year 1699, Fontenelle was chosen secretary of the Academy of Sciences, which office he held during the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> period of 42 years. He published a volume annually of the history of that learned body, filled with analyses of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a>, and eulogiums on deceased members. As a poet, he did not rise above elegance and ingenuity; as a man of science, he rather excelled in throwing <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> on the inventions of others, than in discovering any new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> himself, and as a general writer, he united <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> with the delicacy and refinement of a man of wit. He studied his own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> as much as most men, but he never sacrificed to the promotion of it, the duties of a man of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and virtue. He had many friends, and towards the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, scarcely a single enemy. He was never married, and for a man of letters he acquired considerable influence. Although of a delicate <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, he reached the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> age of 90 without any complaint but dulness of hearing. He died on the 9th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1757, being almost a hundred years of age. When asked by a certain person FOOD Fontenelle person how he could <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> so easily through the world, he replied, "by virtue of these two axioms; All is possible, and every one is in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>."

FONTENOY

Pages 842-842
