Force, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies any unlawful violence offered to things or persons, and is divided into simple and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a>. Simple force is what is so committed, that it has no other crime attending it; as where a person by force enters on another's possession, without committing any other unlawful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>. Compound force, is where some other violence is committed, with such an act which of itself alone is criminal; as if one enters by force into another's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and there kills a person, or ravishes a woman. There is likewise a force implied in law, as in every trespass, rescue, or disseisin, and an actual force with weapons, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of persons, &c.—Any person may lawfully enter a tavern, inn, or victualling-house; so may a landlord his tenant's house to view repairs, &c. But if, in these <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, the person that enters commits any violence or force the law will intend that he entered for that purpose.

FORCEPS

Pages 851-851

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, &c., a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of scissors for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> dividing, the fleshy membranous parts of the body, as occasion requires. See Surgery.

FORCER

Pages 851-851

in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>, is properly a piston, without a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALVE">valve</a>. For by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> up such a piston, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is drawn up, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> follows; then pushing the piston <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> again, the water, being prevented from descending by the lower valve, is forced up to any height above, by means of a side branch between the two.

FORCIBLE

Pages 851-852

who is wrongfully dispossessed of goods may by force retake them. By statute no person shall make an entry on any lands <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> tenements, except where it is given by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and in a peaceable manner, even though they have <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of entry, on pain of imprisonment; and where a forcible entry is committed, justices of the peace are authorized to view the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and inquire of the force by a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURY">jury</a>, summoned by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>; and they may cause the tenements, &c., to be restored, and imprison the offenders till they pay a fine. Likewise a writ of forcible entry lies, where a person seized of freehold, is by force put out thereof. FORCIBLE <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">Marriage</a>, of a woman of estate, is felony. For by the statute 3 H. VII. c. 2, it is enacted, "That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any persons shall take away any woman having lands or goods, or that is heir-apparent to her ancestor, by force and against her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a>, and marry or defile her; the takers, procurers, abettors, and receivers, of the woman taken away against her will, and knowing the same, shall be deemed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> felons; but as to procurers and accessories before the fact, they are to be excluded the benefit of clergy, by 39 <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, c. 9. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a> on the statute Hen. VII. is expressly to set forth, that the woman taken away had lands or goods, or was heir apparent; and also that she was married or defiled, because no other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> is within the statute; and it ought to allege that the taking was for lucre. It is no excuse that the woman at first was taken away with her consent; for if she afterwards refuse to continue with the offender, and be forced against her will, she may from that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> properly be said to be taken against her will; and it is not material whether a woman so taken away be at last married or defiled with her own consent or not, if she was under force at the time; the offenders being in both <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> equally within the words of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>. Those persons who, after the fact, receive the offender, are but accessories after the offence, according to the rules of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law; and those that are only privy to the damage, but not parties to the forcible taking away, are not within the act H. P. C. 119. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> may be indicted for taking away a woman by force in another <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; for the continuing of the force in any country, amounts to a forcible taking there. Ibid. Taking away any woman child under the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 16 years and unmarried, out of the custody and without the consent of the father or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a>, &c., the offender shall suffer fine and imprisonment; and if the woman agrees to any <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> of matrimony with such person, she shall forfeit her estate during <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, to the next of kin, to whom the inheritance should descend, &c. stat. 4 & 5 P. & M. c. 8. This is a force against the parents; and an information will <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> for seducing a young man or woman from their parents, against their consents, in order to marry them, &c. See MARRIAGE.

FORCIBLE ENTRY

Pages 851-851

is a violent and actual entry into houses <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> lands; and a forcible detainer, is where one by violence withholds the possession of lands, &c., so that the person who has a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of entry is barred, or hindered, therefrom. At <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, any person that had a right to enter into lands, &c., might retain possession of it by force. But this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> being abused, to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of the peace, it was therefore found necessary that the same should be restrained: Though, at this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, he

FORCING

Pages 852-852

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>, a method of producing ripe <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> from trees before their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> season. See Gardening <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Forcing, in the wine trade, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> used by the wine coopers, for the fining <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> wines, and rendering them fit for immediate draught. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> inconvenience of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> way of fining down the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> wines with isinglass, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> with whites of eggs, is the slowness of the operation; these ingredients not performing their office in less than a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sometimes a fortnight, according as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> proves favourable, cloudy or clear, windy or calm: this appears to be <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of constant observation. But the wine merchant frequently requires a method that shall, with certainty, make the wines fit for tasting in a few hours. A method of this kind there is, but it is kept in a few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> a valuable secret. Perhaps it depends upon a prudent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of a tartarised spirit of wine, and the common forcing, as occasion is, along with gypsum, as the principal; all which are to be well stirred about in the wine, for half an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> before it is suffered to rest.

FORDOUN

Pages 852-852

John of, the father of Scottish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, flourished in the reign of Alexander III. towards the end of the 13th century. But of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> there is nothing known with certainty, though there was not a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> that possessed not copies of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. The first five books of the history which bears his name were written by him: the rest were fabricated from materials left by him, and from new collections by different persons. There is a manuscript in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VELLUM">vellum</a> of Fordoun's History, in the library of the university of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>.

FORDWICH

Pages 852-852

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, called in Doomsday Book "the little borough of Fordwich," is a member of the port of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDWICH">Sandwich</a>, and was anciently incorporated by the style of the barons of the town of Fordwich, but more lately by the name of the mayor, jurats, and commonality, who enjoy the same privileges as the cinque ports. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is famous for excellent trouts in its river Stour.

HISTORY OF ENTOMOLOGY

Pages 254-265

THOUGH the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> must have been attracted by the vegetables and animals with which he found himself surrounded, and by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> and minerals on which he trod, even at the very earliest periods of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, yet a very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> must have elapsed before any attempts were made at arrangement <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> classification. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> was the first (as far as we know) who deserved the name of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> historian; his arrangement of animals was the only one followed for many centuries. He divided all animals into viviparous and oviparous; the first contained <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> birds, fishes, and insects. Under insects were comprehended all small animals whose bodies were divided into segments. This <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> of insects was followed by all natural historians <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the time of Linnaeus. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOPHRASTUS">Theophrastus</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Aristotle, the only other person among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greeks who deserves the name of natural historian, bestowed the most of his attention on vegetables and minerals. Pliny has given us an account of all that was known in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">natural <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> down to his own times. Though he has mentioned many insects, owing to his want of method little is to be learnt from him respecting entomology. Dioscorides, who was nearly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with Pliny, has confined himself chiefly to natural history connected with medicine. He has given an enumeration of all the natural bodies which entered into the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">materia medica</a>. On the revival of learning in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, writers on natural history seemed to have confined themselves to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> commentaries on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; and nothing was done in entomology till the times of Gesner, who was the greatest naturalist the world had seen from the time of Aristotle, and who was the first who made a collection of the objects of natural history, and formed a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a>. He was born in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZURICH">Zurich</a> in 1516, and died in 1565. Aldrovandus lived nearly about the same time with Gesner, and, like him, formed a museum which served for the foundation of the public museum at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>, where many specimens may be still seen marked with the venerable <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of the first collector. Gesner formed his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">zoology</a> on the principles of Aristotle: his history of animals is very voluminous. Aldrovandus made a collection of all that had been written on natural history before his own time, without discriminating <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> from fiction. He has given a methodical arrangement of insects in the seventh book of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> published in 1602. He followed nearly the same arrangement with Gesner. Gesner, in conjunction with some other natural historians, wrote a treatise on insects, which was published by Mouffet. Mouset, an English physician. About this time our countryman, the illustrious Harvey, ventured to controvert Aristotle's erroneous <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> with respect to equivocal <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>. Though his aphorism, *omnia ex ovo*, at first met with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> opposition, it was at last established by his own experiments and those of Rhedi and Malpighi. From this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> the writers on entomology have been numerous; we shall content ourselves here with giving little more than an enumeration of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> works on the subject. Agricola, in a work entitled *de Animantibus Subterraneis*, published in 1549, has given a methodical arrangement of insects: he divides them into, 1. Creeping insects; 2. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">Flying</a> insects; and 3. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWIMMING">Swimming</a> insects. After giving this arrangement, he proceeds to give an account of each <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. A work entitled *Theatrum Insectorum Thomae Moufetii <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">opera</a> concinnatum*, Lond. 1634, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> labour of several of the most eminent natural historians who lived about the middle of the sixteenth century, though not published till 1734, about 30 years after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Moufet, by whose care the work had been abridged, and prepared to meet the public eye, is the next worthy of notice. It is divided into two books; the first treats of winged insects; the second of insects without wings: these two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> divisions are subdivided into several families, characterized by the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> and position of the legs. There is but little method displayed in the arrangement of the insects which compose the different families. Aldrovandus divides insects into *terrestria et aquatica* (<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> insects, and aquatic insects). The different orders and subdivisions of these two classes, are for the most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> determined by the number, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and position of their wings and legs. He calls his first order *Favifica*, (those which form combs). As to the rest, according to his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a>, he follows Aristotle. Wolfgang Frenzius, in his *Historia Animalium sacra*, published in 1612, has divided insects into three classes, viz. 1. *Aeria*, (such as fly); 2. *Aquatica*, (such as inhabit the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>); 3. *Terrea et Reptenta*, (such as creep about, or are lodged in the earth). His descriptions are much more accurate than those of any of the authors who preceded him. John Johnston has borrowed freely from his predecessors, in his *Historia Naturalis Insectorum*, published in 1653. He divides insects into *terrestria* and *aquatica*, (into land and aquatic insects); the land insects he divides into three orders: 1. Such as have wings and legs; 2. Such as have legs without wings; and 3. Such as have neither wings nor legs. These three orders occupy his three first books; his fourth contains aquatic insects. Walter Charleton follows the system of Aldrovandus in his *Onomasticum Zoicon*, published in 1668. Jo. Goodart published *Metamorphosis et Historia Naturalis de Insectis*, 8vo. Mediol. 1667. Likewise in 1675, a work of his appeared, *de Insectis in Methodum reductis, opera Mart. Leister*. Ebor. In this work insects are divided into ten families: The 1st includes butterflies with erect wings; 2d, Butterflies with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> wings; 3d, Butterflies with deflected wings; 4th, Libellulae, (dragon-flies); 5th, Apes, (bees); 6th, Coleopterous insects; 7th, Locusts, and grasshoppers; 8th, Flies corresponding to the order diptera of Linnæus; 9th, Millepeds; and 10th, Spiders. This work is full of typographical errors and mistakes in natural history. The discovery of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a> in 1618, tended greatly to the advancement of entomology, as by means of it the most minute parts of insects could be viewed, and their organization examined. Naturalists were much engaged in making microscopic discoveries, particularly Borel, Rhedi, Swammerdam, Bonanni, Bone- mo, Leeuwenhoek and Joblot. John Swammerdam, in his *Biblia Nature*, published in 1669, has divided insects into four classes. John Ray published his *Historia Insectorum*, Lond. 1710. This work was properly the joint production of J. Ray and Francis Willoughby. These illustrious friends laboured together with uncommon ardour in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of nature. Death carried off Willoughby in the prime of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, before he had properly digested what the industry of his early years had collected; and his labours would have been lost to the world, and his name might have sunk in oblivion, but for the friendship of Ray. So <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> was the intercourse between these two naturalists, and so intimately were their labours blended together, that it is not easy to assign each his due share of merit. Indeed Ray has been so partial to the fame of his departed friend, and has cherished his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> with such affectionate care, that we are in danger of attributing too much to Mr Willoughby, and too little to himself. Though what Dr <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DERHAM">Derham</a> asserts be not correct, that Mr Willoughby had taken the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ANIMAL_KINGDOM">animal <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> for his task, and Mr Ray the vegetable one, yet it is generally agreed, that the *Historia Insectorum* is principally to be ascribed to Willoughby. In that work insects are divided into *Transmutabilia* and *Intransmutabilia*, (those which undergo a metamorphosis, and those which undergo none). These two grand divisions are subdivided into several orders, which are ascertained by the number of their legs, or total want of legs; by the places which they inhabit; by their size; by the configuration of the various parts of the body; by the smell which they diffuse, &c. The *transmutabili* are divided into four orders. 1. *Faginipennes*, (those which have their wings covered with a sheath). 2. *Papiliones*, (lepidopterous insects). 3. *Quadripennes*, (those which have four wings); and 4. *Bipennes*, (those which have two). The papiliones, quadripennes, and bipennes are again subdivided into families, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of which are taken, either from the appearance and conformation of their larvae, or from the form, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and different properties of the perfect insect. Eleazar Albin published a natural history of English insects in 1722. He likewise published the Natural History of Spiders in 1736. Antony Valisnieri, in his work entitled *Esperienze e Osservazioni intorno agli Insetti*, published in 1730, has divided insects into four orders, according to the situation in which they <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> their lives. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> Sybelle Merian, published in 1730, *Histoire d'Insectes d'Europe et de Surinam*. She likewise published in 1753, *Metamorphosis Insectorum Surinamensium <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AD">ad</a> vivum picta et descripta*; and in 1717, *Eruca-rum Ortus*. George Bernard Rhump published in 1705, and again in 1741, a work entitled *Amboinsche Ravitut-kammer*. Hans Sloane, in the years 1707 and 1725, published a Voyage to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">Islands</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADEIRA">Madeira</a>, Barbadoes, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEVIS">Nevis</a>, Saint Christophers and Jamaica. Henry Rousch in 1710 and 1718 published Theatrum Universale omnium Animalium. J. Petiver published in 1715 his Icones et Nomina Aquatilium Animalium Ambonae. Richard Bradley published in 1721 his Philosophical Account of the Works of Nature. Linnaeus, the most celebrated natural historian the world ever produced, in his first edition of the Systema Naturae, published in 1735, divided insects into four orders, from the number and different appearances of their wings; 1. Coleoptera; 2. Angioptera; 3. Hemiptera; and 4. APTERA. This was but an imperfect sketch, a first <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a>. In the subsequent editions of the System of Nature which he published, to the number of twelve, he completed the arrangement of insects, of which we need say nothing here, as we have followed it in preference to all others; and most authors who have written on the subject for more than half a century past, have either followed it closely, or with very slight alterations. His extensive genius embraced all the three kingdoms of nature. In <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a> and entomology in particular, he far excels all who went before him, and as yet remains unrivalled. Writers on entomology became so numerous after Linnaeus had published his System of Nature, and established entomology on a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> foundation, that a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> enumeration of their names and titles of their books would occupy more room than we can afford to bestow on the article; we shall therefore only notice a few of the most remarkable. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Degeer, in his Memoires pour servir à l'Histoire des Insectes, in 1752, has arranged insects into fourteen orders, distinguished by the different appearances of the various parts which compose their bodies, particularly the elytra, wings, and most remarkable parts of the head. He published again in 1778. M. de Reaumur published his Memoires pour servir à l'Histoire des Insectes at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1737. No one has paid so much attention to the habits of insects, and to everything that concerns them, as Reaumur. He ought to be read by every student of entomology. John Rotzios has simplified the arrangement of Degeer, in a small work entitled Genera et Species Insectorum. But although in this arrangement he has followed the method of Degeer, the terms he has made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of are principally those of Linnaeus. His 14 orders are, 1. Lepidoptera. 2. Alingua. 3. Neuroptera. 4. Hymenoptera. 5. Siphonata. 6. Dermaptera. 7. Hemiptera. 8. Coleoptera. 9. Hasterata. 10. Proscidea. 11. Suctoria. 12. Accenata. 13. Atracheia. 14. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRUSTACEA">Crustacea</a>. M. Geoffroy, in his Histoire Abrégée des Insectes, published at Paris in 1762, has divided insects into six orders; Coleopteres, Hemipteres, Tetrapteres ailes farineuses, Tetrapteres ailes noes, Dipteres, and Apteres. He determined his families by the number of the articulations of the feet, and his genera by characters drawn from all the parts of the body. He has formed a great number of new genera. John Antony Scopoli, in his Entomologia Carniolica, published in 1762, has followed the arrangement of Linnaeus, and only changes the names of some of the orders; e.g. Proboscidea, instead of Hemiptera; Accela, instead of Hymenoptera; Halterata, instead of Diptera; and Pedestria, instead of Aptera. J. C. Scheffer published in 1766, Elementa Entomologica, 135 tabulae are excusa: he follows in many <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> the method of Linnaeus. He divides insects into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> classes. 1. Coleoptero-macroptera. 2. Coleoptero-microptera. 3. Hemiptera. 4. Hymeno-lepidoptera. 5. Hymeno-gynoptera. 6. Diptera; and 7. Aptera. His first and second classes correspond with the Coleoptera of Linnaeus; the fourth with the Lepidoptera, and the fifth with the Hymenoptera. John C. Fabricius is the founder of a new system of Entomology, which he published in his Systema Naturae 1775. He discriminates his orders and genera, by the parts of the mouth, (instrumenta cibaria). He afterwards published Species Insectorum, Entomologia Systematica, and Mantissa Insectorum. The arrangement of Fabricius has acquired great reputation, especially on the continent. It may not therefore be amiss to give a slight view of it. He divides insects into eight classes. Class I. Eleutherata. Mouth armed with jaws, and four or six feelers. The jaws naked and free. Class II. Ulanata. The jaws covered with an obtuse <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a>. Class III. Synistata. The jaws united with the lip. Class IV. Agonata. The under jaw wanting. Class V. Ungata. Mouth armed with jaws and two feelers; the under jaw generally furnished with a small unguis or nail. Class VI. Glossata. Mouth furnished with feelers, and a spiral tongue. Class VII. Rhyngota. Mouth furnished with a snout, and an articulated sheath. Class VIII. Antliata. Mouth furnished with a hausellum and a sheath not articulated. In a supplement to his Entomologia Systematica, he has divided insects into thirteen orders. 1. Eleutherata. 2. Ulanata. 3. Synistata. 4. Piezata. 5. Odorata. 6. Mitosata. 7. Ungata. 8. Polygonata. 9. Kleistognatha. 10. Exochnata. 11. Glossata. 12. Rhyngota. 13. Anthiata. He has lately published a work entitled Systema Eleutheratorium, no more than two volumes of which have as yet made their appearance. Moses Harris published an Exposition of English Insects, &c. with coloured plates, 1776. Jo. Christ published Philosophia Entomologica sistens scientiae fundamenta, &c. Hamb. 1778, 8vo. Archiv. der Insekten geschichte herausgegeben von Joh. Caps. Fussly. Zurich, 1781. Fr. Pauli, v. Schrank; Enumeratio Insectorum Austriae indigenorum. Aug. Vindel. 1781. P. Sim. Pallas; Icones Insectorum. Hamb. 1781. A. W. Knock; Beyträge zur Insekten geschichte, 1781. James Barbut published the Genera Insectorum of Linnaeus, exemplified by various specimens of English insects drawn from nature. Lond. 1781. John Nepomuk de Laicharting, has divided insects into ten orders, characterised by the configuration of various parts of the body. He adheres pretty closely to the the method of Linnæus. His orders are, 1. Scarabaeoidea. 2. Grylloides. 3. Cimicioides. 4. Papilionoides. 5. Libelluloides. 6. Vespidæ. 7. Muscoides. 8. Cancrioides. 9. Aranoides, and 10. Oniscoïdes. Olivier, in 1780, published Entomologie, ou Histoire Naturelle des Insectes, in 3 vols. 4to. Paris. In 1790, in the Dictionnaire des Insectes, forming a part of the Encyclopédie Methodique, he has given an arrangement of insects little different from that of Linnæus. He has added one order which he calls Orthopteres, distinguished by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of folding the lower wings, and a part on the head, which he terms galea. He has likewise subdivided the order Aptera, into Arachnides and Crus-taces. Latreille in 1795, in a work entitled Precis du Caractère des Genres, divides insects into two grand divisions, viz. insectes ailés, et insectes aptères (winged insects, and insects without wings). These two grand divisions he subdivides into 14 orders, viz. Coleopteres, Orthopteres, Hemipteres, Neuropteres, Lepidopteres, Suceurs, Thysanoures, Parasites, Acephalides, Entomostraces, Crus-taces, Myriapodes. Since that he has published a more detailed account of this method in a work entitled les Genres et les Familles des Insectes. Clairville in 1795, in the introduction to his Entomologie Helvetique, has given an arrangement of insects, in which he differs from Linnæus almost in nothing, except in the names of his orders, viz. Elytropteres, Di-tyopteres, Thlebopteres, Haltipteres, Lepidopteres, Heminopteres, Rophoteires, and Pododuneres. Link, in his Magasin sur Thiergeschichte, has divided insects into eleven orders; he follows de Laicharting almost in every thing, even in the names of his orders; he has indeed added an order which he calls Pediculoides. Cuvier and Duméril, in their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPARATIVE_ANATOMY">Comparative Anatomy</a>, have very nearly followed the method of Linnæus; they have however divided the order Aptera into two, viz. Gnathaptera and Aptera; they have likewise altered the arrangement of the orders, and have placed those first which contain insects furnished with jaws, viz. Gnathaptera, Neuroptera, Hymenoptera, Coleoptera, and Orthoptera; and have thrown those last which are desti-tute of jaws, viz. Hemiptera, Lepidoptera, Diptera, and Aptera. We shall refrain from noticing those authors who have written partial treatises; though there are several works of that kind which the entomologist might peruse with advantage, such as the Fauna Suecica, published in 1761 by Linnæus, at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOCKHOLM">Stockholm</a>. Fauna Germanica, by Panzer. La Faune Parisienne de Walknair. Kirby's Monographia apum Angliae. Latreille's treatise on Ants. See a more detailed historical account of the writers on this science, in the article Entomology, Supplement.

Exchange with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. Money <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">Table</a>. \[ \begin{align*} 5 \text{ Soldi} & \quad \text{make} \quad 1 \text{ gros} \\ 24 \text{ Gros} & \quad \text{make} \quad 1 \text{ ducat}=50\frac{1}{2}\text{d. sterling}. \end{align*} \] The money of Venice is of three sorts, viz. two of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> money and the picoli money. One of the banks deals in banco money, and the other in banco current. The bank money is 20 per cent. better than the banco current, and the banco current 20 per cent. better than the picoli money. Exchanges are always negotiated by the ducat banco, the par being 4s. 2½d. sterling, as in the table. Though the ducat be <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> divided into 24 gros, yet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANKERS">bankers</a> and negotiators, for facility of computation, usually divide it as follows, and keep their books and accounts accordingly: \[ \begin{align*} 12 \text{ Deniers d'or} & \quad \text{make} \quad 1 \text{ sol d'or} \\ 20 \text{ Solis d'or} & \quad \text{make} \quad 1 \text{ ducat}=50\frac{1}{2}\text{d. sterling}. \end{align*} \] The course of exchange is from 45d. to 55d. sterling per ducat. **Examp.** How much sterling money is equal to 1459 ducats 18 sols 1 <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENIER">denier</a>, bank money of Venice, exchange at 52½ sterling per ducat? \[ \begin{align*} \text{Duc. d.} & \quad \text{Duc. sol. den.} & \quad \text{d.} \\ \text{<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> } 1 : 52\frac{1}{2} & \quad \text{:: } 1459 : 18 : 1 & \quad 52\frac{1}{2} \text{ rate.} \\ & \quad \text{Sols.} & \quad \text{d.} \\ & \quad 10 & \quad \frac{1}{2} & \quad 26\frac{1}{2} \\ & \quad 2918 & \quad 5 & \quad \frac{1}{2} & \quad 13\frac{1}{2} \\ & \quad 7295 & \quad 2 & \quad \frac{1}{2} & \quad 5\frac{1}{2} \\ & \quad 1 & \quad \frac{1}{2} & \quad 2\frac{1}{2} \\ & \quad 73868 & \quad \text{den.} & \quad 1 & \quad \frac{1}{2} & \quad 0\frac{1}{2} \\ & \quad \frac{1}{2} = 729\frac{1}{2} & \quad \frac{1}{2} = 364\frac{1}{2} & \quad \frac{1}{2} = 47\frac{1}{2} \\ & \quad 76962\frac{1}{2} & \quad \frac{1}{2} = 47\frac{1}{2} \\ & \quad \text{Rem.} & \quad \frac{1}{2} = 77016(6d.) \\ & \quad 2(0)6417(17s.) & \quad \text{L. 320 17 6 sterling. Ans.} \end{align*} \] Bank money is reduced to current money, by allowing for the agio, as was done in exchange with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>; viz. say, As 100 to 120, or as 10 to 12, or as 5 to 6, so the given bank money to the current sought. And current money is reduced to bank money by reversing the operation. And in like manner may picoli money be reduced to current or to bank money, and the contrary. The pezzo of exchange is equal to 5½ lires; and, consequently exchange money is 5½ times better than the lire money. IX. Exchange with <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> and the West Indies. In <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> America and the West Indies, accounts, as in Britain, are kept in pounds, shillings, and pence. In North America they have few coins circulating among them, and on that account have been obliged to substitute a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> currency for a medium of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>; which having no intrinsic value, is subjected to many disadvantages, and generally suffers a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCOUNT">discount</a>. In the West Indies coins are more frequent, owing to their commercial intercourse with the Spanish settlements. Exchange betwixt Britain and America, or the West Indies, may be computed as in the following examples: 1. The neat proceeds of a cargo from Britain to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOSTON">Boston</a> amount to 845l. 17s. 6d. currency: How much is that in sterling money, exchange at 80 per cent.? XII. Arbitration of Exchanges. The course of exchange betwixt <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> and nation naturally rises or falls according as the circumstances and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> of trade happen to vary. Now, to draw upon and remit to foreign places, in this fluctuating state of exchange, in the way that will turn out most profitable, is the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of arbitration. Which is either simple or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a>. I. Simple Arbitration. In simple arbitration the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RATES">rates</a> or prices of exchange from one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to other two are given; whereby is found the correspondent price between the said two places, called the arbitrated price, or par of arbitration; and hence is derived a method of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> and remitting to the best advantage. In negotiations of this sort, a sum for remittance is afforded out of the sum you receive for the draught; and your credit at the one foreign place pays your debt at the other. II. Compound Arbitration. In compound arbitration the rate or price of exchange between three, four, or more places, is given, in order to find how much a remittance passing through them all will amount to at the last place; or to find the arbitrated price, or par of arbitration, between the first place and the last. And this may be done by the following Rules. I. Distinguish the given rates or prices into antecedents and consequents; place the antecedents in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>, and the consequents in another on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, fronting one another by way of equation. II. The first antecedent, and the last consequent to which an antecedent is required, must always be of the same kind. III. The second antecedent must be of the same kind with the first consequent, and the third antecedent of the same kind with the second consequent, &c. IV. If to any of the numbers a fraction be annexed, both the antecedent and its consequent must be multiplied into the denominator. V. To facilitate the operation, terms that happen to be equal or the same in both columns, may be dropped or rejected, and other terms may be abridged. VI. Multiply the antecedent continually for a divisor, and the consequents continually for a dividend, and the quot will be the answer or antecedent required. Examp. 1. If London remit 1000l. sterling to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, by way of Holland, at 35s. Flemish per pound sterling; thence to France, at 58d. Flemish per crown; thence to Venice, at 100 crowns per 60 ducats; and thence to Spain, at 360 mervadies per ducat: how many piastres, of 272 mervadies, will the 1000l. sterling amount to in Spain? Antecedents. Consequents. Abridged. 1l. Sterling = 35s. or 420d. Fl. 1=210 58d. Flemish = 1 crown France 29=31 100 crowns France = 60 ducats Venice 1=0 1 ducat Venice = 360 mervadies Spain 1=45 272 mervadies = 1 piastre 17=1 How many piastres = 1000 sterling = 10 In order to abridge the terms, divide 58 and 420 by 2, and you have the new antecedent 29, and the new consequent 210; reject two ciphers in 100 and 1000; divide 272 and 360 by 8, and you have 34 and 45; divide 34 and 60 by 2, and you have 17 and 30; and the whole will stand abridged as above. Then, 29 X 17=493 divisor; and 210 X 30 X 45 +10=2835000 dividend; and, 493)2835000(57504 piastres. Ans. Or, the consequents may be connected with the sign of multiplication, and placed over a line by way of numerator; and the antecedent, connected in the same manner, may be placed under the line, by way of denominator; and then abridged as follows: \[ \frac{420 \times 60 \times 360 \times 100}{58 \times 100 \times 272} = \frac{210 \times 60 \times 360 \times 10}{29 \times 1 \times 272} \] \[ \frac{210 \times 60 \times 45 \times 10}{29 \times 34} = \frac{210 \times 30 \times 45 \times 10}{29 \times 17} \] \[ \frac{2835000}{493} \] And, 493)2835000(57504 piastres. Ans. The placing the terms by way of antecedent and consequent, sequent working as the rules direct, saves so many statings of the rule of three, and greatly shortens the operation.
